rabat: Rabat stands on Morocco's northwestern Atlantic coast, at the mouth of the river Bou Regreg, opposite Salé, the city's main commuter town. The name comes from the Arabic ar-Ribat, a ribat being an Islamic base or fortification. It is short for Ribat al-Fath, the ribat of conquest or stronghold of victory, a title given by the Almohads when they established the city as a naval base in 1170. The oldest part of the present city is the Kasbah of the Udayas, built by the Almohads in the 12th century.

In the first millennium BCE the Phoenicians founded trading colonies along the Atlantic coast, although archaeologists have debated whether a Phoenician settlement called Sala existed here. By the first century BCE the region had come under the influence of Rome, which annexed the Mauretanian Kingdom and built a city called Sala Colonia at the site now known as Chellah, just south of the walled city. With Lixus it was one of the two main Roman naval outposts on the Atlantic coast of Mauretania Tingitana. In the 10th century the Umayyads of Córdoba, or their Zenata Berber allies, founded a ribat in the area against the Barghawata Berbers.

In 1609 Philip III decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and Rabat and Salé united in 1627 to form the Republic of Bou Regreg, a base for corsairs known as the Salé Rovers. Al-Rashid, founder of the 'Alawi dynasty, conquered the area in 1666, though the sultans allowed piracy to continue until the early 19th century, and Austria shelled the city in 1829 after losing a ship to a pirate attack.

After the Treaty of Fes established the French protectorate in March 1912, General Hubert Lyautey moved the capital from Fez to Rabat. He argued that its coast was pleasanter and more accessible and that it lay close to Casablanca, which he expected to become the main economic centre. In 1913 he hired Henri Prost to design the Ville Nouvelle as an administrative sector. Rabat became the capital of independent Morocco in 1956.

Rabat is the capital of Morocco and one of the country's four imperial cities, and its medina is a World Heritage Site. The Kasbah of the Udayas is a residential district of white and blue houses and contains the Old Mosque, founded in 1150 and largely restored in the 18th century. The Oudayas Museum, in a pavilion built by Sultan Moulay Isma'il, opened in 1915 and is one of the oldest public museums in Morocco. The city hosts the headquarters of several international and African organisations, and Mohammed V University was founded there in 1957.
rabatak-inscription: The stone lay near the top of an artificial hill, a Kushan site beside the main Kabul-Mazar highway, south-east of the Rabatak pass. Afghan mujahideen came upon it while digging a trench, together with other carved pieces such as the paws of a giant stone lion, which have since disappeared. An English aid worker of the demining organisation HALO Trust photographed it and reported the find, and at the British Museum Joe Cribb recognised it as an official document naming four Kushan kings, similar to an inscription found at Surkh Kotal in the 1950s.

Cribb shared the photograph with Nicholas Sims-Williams of the School of Oriental and African Studies, one of a handful of living people able to read Bactrian, and the two published a first translation in 1996. The civil war delayed further study. In April 2000 Jonathan Lee and Robert Kluijver traced the stone to a storehouse of the Department of Mines and Industry at Pul-i Khumri, and in July it was taken to Kabul, where it became the centrepiece of the Kabul Museum's brief reopening on 17 August 2000 until senior Taliban officials objected to the display of pre-Islamic heritage. It is again on display in the reopened museum.

The text opens by calling Kanishka the great salvation, the righteous and just autocrat, worthy of worship, who obtained the kingship from the goddess Nana and from all the gods and inaugurated the year one. It then says that he set aside the Ionian, or Greek, speech and put the text into the Arya language, the name it gives to Bactrian. His new era replaced the Great Arya Era used before, which may have been the Vikrama era of 58 BCE.

Lines 4 to 7 name cities under his rule, of which four can be identified: Saketa, Kausambi, Pataliputra and Champa, though it is unclear whether Champa was his or lay just beyond his realm. They suggest that Kushan rule reached well beyond the boundaries traditionally held. The king then ordered Shafar the Karalrang to build a sanctuary with images of gods including Nana, Umma, Aurmuzd and Mihr, and of his forebears: Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu and Vima Kadphises. B. N. Mukherjee's translation reads several passages differently.
rabaul: Rabaul is a township in the East New Britain province of Papua New Guinea, on the island of New Britain, about 600 km east of the island of New Guinea. It lies on the edge of the Rabaul caldera, a flooded caldera of a large pyroclastic shield volcano, around the harbour known as Simpsonhafen (Simpson Harbour) in the German period. The harbour is large and nearly enclosed. In 1878, before the town existed, an eruption formed a volcano in the harbour.

Rabaul was planned and built during the German New Guinea administration. It was selected as capital in 1905, and in 1910 the colonial government under Governor Albert Hahl moved offices, the district court, a hospital and customs and postal facilities there from Herbertshöhe, today's Kokopo. The name means mangrove in Kuanua, the local language, since the town was partly built on a reclaimed mangrove swamp. Australian forces defeated the German garrison at the start of World War I, and in 1920 the territory was delegated to Australia as a League of Nations Mandate, with Rabaul as capital of the Territory of New Guinea. In 1929 it was the site of the Rabaul Strike, the first industrial strike in Papua New Guinea.

On 6 June 1937 the volcanoes Tavurvur and Vulcan erupted, destroying the town and killing 507 people. The Australian administration decided to move its headquarters to Lae. Japanese aircraft began bombing Rabaul on 4 January 1942, the battle of Rabaul began on 23 January, and the town was captured soon after. Military personnel and most civilians were placed aboard the Montevideo Maru, which was sunk off the Philippines in June 1942.

Under Japanese occupation Rabaul became a much more powerful base than the Australians had planned, with many kilometres of tunnels dug as shelter and about 110,000 Japanese troops there by 1943. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto took off from Rabaul on 18 April 1943 on the flight on which United States fighters shot him down. Allied forces bypassed Rabaul rather than capture it, and its neutralisation was completed with the Japanese surrender in August 1945.

After the war Rabaul flourished as a port and trading hub for the New Guinea Islands region, and its population was 17,044 by 1990, but the capital role went to Port Moresby. On 19 September 1994 Tavurvur and Vulcan erupted again with only 19 hours of warning; the town was evacuated and five people died. Most buildings in the south-eastern half collapsed under ash, and the provincial capital moved to Kokopo, about 20 km away. Rabaul is slowly rebuilding, and a volcanological observatory on the northern ridge of the caldera watches the volcanoes.
rabban-sauma: Rabban Bar Sauma was born around 1220 in or near modern Beijing, then called Zhongdu and later Khanbaliq. Bar Hebraeus gives his origin as Uyghur, while Chinese accounts give his people as the Öngüd, a Turkic people counted in the Mongol caste under Yuan law. His name is Aramaic for Son of Fasting, although his family was wealthy.

A Christian of the Church of the East, he became an ascetic monk at about the age of 20 and taught for decades. In middle age he set out for Jerusalem with a younger student, Rabban Markos, travelling by way of Khotan, Kashgar, Khorasan, Maragha and Mosul. Warnings of danger on the southern Syria turned them back to the Mongol-controlled Persia, the Ilkhanate, where they remained.

Markos was elected patriarch of the Church of the East as Yahballaha III in 1281, and some years later proposed his former teacher as an envoy to Europe. The Ilkhan Arghun wanted a Franco-Mongol alliance against the Mamluk Sultanate at Cairo. Bar Sauma left in 1287 with gifts, letters, a large retinue and 30 riding animals, and Europeans spoke to him in Persian. He was received by Andronicus II Palaeologus at Constantinople, praised the Hagia Sophia, and from a ship saw the eruption of Mount Etna on 18 June 1287.

He arrived in Rome too late to meet Pope Honorius IV, spent the winter of 1287–1288 in Genoa, and then spent a month with Philip IV of France. In Gascony he met Edward I of England, who was friendly but could not join a military alliance because of conflicts with the Welsh and the Scots. On his return to Rome the newly elected Pope Nicholas IV gave him communion on Palm Sunday 1288.

Bar Sauma returned to Baghdad in 1288 with letters and gifts. Arghun's answers followed in 1289, but the alliance came to nothing and was abandoned, though the contacts encouraged communication and trade between East and West, and the papacy later sent missionaries such as Giovanni da Montecorvino to the Mongol court. He spent his last years in Baghdad and died there in 1294.

His account of his travels, probably written there, survives in the History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma, and is valued as a view of Europe at the end of the Crusades by an observer from the East. It has been translated into English by James A. Montgomery in 1927 and E. A. Wallis Budge in 1928.
rabbi-akiva: Akiva ben Joseph was born about 50 CE to humble parents, and according to some sources he descended from converts to Judaism. The Talmud tells that he was an unlettered shepherd in the service of Ben Kalba Sabuaʿ, a wealthy citizen of Jerusalem, when the man's daughter, named Rachel in a later version, offered to marry him if he would begin to study Torah.

Her father drove her from his house, and the couple lived in great poverty. Another tradition has Akiva, at the age of 40, attend the academy of his native town, Lod, headed by Eliezer ben Hurcanus. He also studied under Joshua ben Hananiah and Nachum Ish Gamzu, and later moved his own school to Beneberak.

Akiva was a member of the Sanhedrin that determined the final canon of the Hebrew Bible, and he played a decisive part in the inclusion of the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes. He is called Rosh la-Hakhamim, Chief of the Sages. He worked on the Halakha, systematising its traditional material and developing a method of exegesis. He held that in the language of the Torah nothing is mere form, so that every peculiarity of diction, every particle and every letter carries meaning. Tradition holds that he arranged the Mishnah, and the Mishnah of Judah ha-Nasi and most of the halakhic Midrashim are regarded as derived from his school.

The leading tannaim of the middle of the second century came from his school, among them Rabbi Meir, Judah bar Ilai and Simeon bar Yochai. The Aggadah gives the number of his disciples variously as 12,000, 24,000 and 48,000. He supported Rabban Gamaliel II's aim of a central authority but held that the patriarch's power was limited by the written and oral law. He was in Rome in 95-96 CE, and before 110 in Nehardea. His disciple Aquila gave Greek-speaking Jews a rabbinical Bible.

Accounts of Akiva's death vary, but all agree that he defied a Roman prohibition on teaching Torah, that the consul Turnus Rufus, as Jewish sources call him, ordered his execution, that he was flayed alive and that his last words were the Shema.

In the Babylonian Talmud he explains to his students that he had long wondered how he could fulfil the command to love God 'with all your soul', and he extended the final word Echad, meaning One, until his life expired. He was executed in the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba revolt, on 28 September 135 CE. Tradition also holds that he alone of four sages who entered the Pardes absorbed its wisdom.
rabdentse: The ruins stand on a ridge about 3 kilometres from upper Pelling in West Sikkim, with views of the Khanchendzonga ranges on one side and mountains and valleys on the other. They are reached from an ornamental yellow gate near the Pelling–Geyshing road, a walk of about 15 minutes past a lake and through forest. Pemayangtse Monastery, one of the oldest in Sikkim, stands close by, and the site lies on a Buddhist pilgrimage circuit that begins at the Dubdi Monastery at Yuksom and includes Tashiding Monastery and Khecheopalri Lake.

The reign of Tensung Namgyal, who moved the court here, was peaceful. After his death in 1700 his young son Chador Namgyal was driven out by his half-sister Pendiongmu with help from Bhutan, and spent ten years in Lhasa, where he became state astrologer to the Sixth Dalai Lama, before returning with Tibetan support. Pendiongmu had him killed in 1716 by a Tibetan doctor's bloodletting at the Ralang hot spring; she and the doctor were then put to death.

His son Gurmed Namgyal, who succeeded in 1717, fortified Rabdentse against the Gurkhas and Bhutanese, and died in 1733 aged 26. Under Phuntsog Namgyal II, Nepal made 17 invasions of Sikkim, and Tenzing Namgyal fled from Rabdentse to Lhasa, where he died in 1780. His son Tshudpud Namgyal, finding Rabdentse too close to the Nepalese border, moved the capital to Tumlong, and the city was later reduced to ruins by the Nepalese army.

An avenue of chestnut trees leads to Namphogang, a throne of three standing stones from which judges gave their judgments, and to the half-ruined Taphap Chorten, where visitors to the palace dismounted and removed their hats. The palace had a northern wing for the royal family, with the ruined Dab Lhagang shrine, and a southern wing where the king received his subjects. Three chortens nearby are fairly well preserved, and the Archaeological Survey of India protects the site as a monument of national importance.
rabi-island: Rabi lies in the Vanua Levu Group, about 5 kilometres from Taveuni, of which it is an outlier. It covers 66.3 square kilometres, rises to 463 metres and has 46.2 kilometres of shoreline; it is the eighth largest island of Fiji, and the antimeridian passes through it. Its four main settlements are named after, and peopled by descendants of, four villages on Banaba: Tabwewa in the north, the administrative centre, Uma, Tabiang, which has the island's school and an airstrip, and Buakonikai.

Rabi was the first place in Fiji where Indian indentured labourers worked: when the first of them arrived in 1879 aboard the Leonidas, most European planters refused to employ them, but Captain J. Hill took 106. The island later became a copra plantation of Lever's Pacific Plantations. The British government bought it from Lever Brothers for £25,000, paid from phosphate royalties of Banaba, then called Ocean Island, whose land the mining was ravaging; the indigenous Fijian community of Rabi was moved to Taveuni.

The first 703 Banabans, 318 of them children, arrived on the Triona on 15 December 1945 with 300 other Gilbertese, collected from Japanese internment camps and not given the option of returning home. Told that houses awaited them, they were given tents and rations that lasted only two months in the cyclone season, and 40 of the oldest died. Further groups came in 1975 to 1977 and in 1981 to 1983, after phosphate mining ended in 1979. On 15 December 2005 more than 500 islanders of the later waves were granted Fijian citizenship.

Rabi belongs to the Province of Cakaudrove but has its own council for local affairs, which also administers Banaba. Its Banaban inhabitants have the right to be citizens of both Fiji and Kiribati, as the Citizenship of Fiji Act 2009 confirmed; they remain the legal landowners of Banaba and send a representative to the Kiribati parliament. Gilbertese is the main language of daily life, and many Banaban customs are kept.
rabih-az-zubayr: Rabih was born in Halfaya al-Muluk, later a suburb of Khartoum; he was of Nilotic, possibly Shanqella, origin and was enslaved as a child. At about twenty he joined the Egyptian army, serving mostly in Cairo, then went to the Bahr el Ghazal for the trade in ivory and slaves and entered the service of Al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur. Under Mansur's son Suleiman he became a leading commander. When Suleiman's rebellion of 1878 against Charles George Gordon failed and the surrendered officers were executed, Rabih escaped westwards with about 400 soldiers.

In 1879 the officers' council, the Zubat al-Kubar, elected him emir. Over the next twelve years he raided in what is now the Central African Republic and southern Chad, beginning with the Azande, built fortified camps called zeribas and grew his force by offering prisoners their lives and freedom if they joined him. By the early 1890s he had about 5,000 men and 44 light field guns. In 1887 he accepted the authority of the Mahdist State, and he defeated the Sultanate of Bagirmi.

In the summer of 1893 he invaded Bornu proper with about 3,000 men, about half of them armed with muskets or rifles; Shehu Ashimi sent against him an army under Momman Tahr that may have numbered 30,000. Once Bornu was conquered, for the first time in over a thousand years the Kanem–Bornu Empire was under foreign rule. Rabih ruled from Dikwa as a military dictator with the Zubat al-Kubar, keeping submissive local rulers under his commanders' supervision. He levied a fixed annual tax of one Maria Theresa thaler on every person, collected brutally; his army, perhaps 35,000 strong, was among the best equipped in sub-Saharan Africa.

Britain recognised him as sultan of Borno, while France declared him illegitimate and presented his state as a slave economy. In July 1899 his forces destroyed a French advance guard at the Battle of Togbao, killing Henri Bretonnet. After his death at Kousséri his head was displayed on a pike, and a photograph of it appeared in L'Illustration in March 1901. His son Fadlallah fought on until he was killed at Gujba on 23 August 1901, and the shehus were restored under colonial rule. Rabih is remembered both for his brutal rule and for his resistance to European colonialism.
rabindranath-tagore: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi. His mother died in his early childhood, and he was raised mostly by servants. The family was at the forefront of the Bengal Renaissance, hosting literary magazines, theatre and recitals of Bengali and Western classical music. Tagore wrote poetry at eight, and at sixteen published poems under the pseudonym Bhanusimha that literary authorities took for long-lost classics.

Tagore wrote novels, essays, short stories, travelogues, dramas and thousands of songs. He is credited with originating the Bengali short story. Gitanjali, Gora and Ghare-Baire are his best-known works, and his compositions became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. In 1912 he took translations of his works to England, where William Butler Yeats, who wrote the preface to the English Gitanjali, and others noticed them.

He opposed imperialism and supported Indian nationalists, yet he rebuked strongly nationalist forms of the independence movement. In 1925 he attacked the Swadeshi movement in an essay, The Cult of the Charkha. He urged the masses to seek self-help and education rather than blind revolution, and his religious and philosophical ideas appear in the 1922 lectures Creative Unity and the 1931 Hibbert Lectures at Oxford, published as The Religion of Man.

Tagore conceived a new kind of university to make Santiniketan a connecting thread between India and the world. He named it Visva-Bharati; its foundation stone was laid on 24 December 1918, and teaching was often done under trees. He died on 7 August 1941 at Jorasanko Thakur Bari, the house in which he was born.
racial-segregation: Racial segregation is the separation of people into racial or other ethnic groups in daily life. It can mean spatial separation and the compulsory use of different institutions, such as schools and hospitals, and it may apply to restaurants, buses, housing, hotels and places of worship. Segregation often allows close contact between members of different groups in hierarchical situations, for example when a person of one race works as a servant for a member of another. Involuntary segregation was often used to secure the advantages of a dominant group, such as the Mongols, the Bantu and the Aztecs.

Before modern concepts of race developed, some states enforced separation on grounds of ethnicity or religion. In late antiquity Roman law restricted some marriages between provincials and barbarian soldiers. Legal distinctions between Goths and Romans in Visigothic Spain lasted until 654, and in 1366 the Statutes of Kilkenny prohibited marriage and other close relations between the English and the Irish. In Tang China an edict of 779 forced Uyghurs to wear their ethnic dress and banned them from marrying Han Chinese women, and in 836 the governor of Canton, Lu Chun, banned intermarriage and made it illegal for foreigners to own property.

In 1204 the papacy required Jews to separate themselves from Christians and to wear distinctive clothing, and forced segregation spread across Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries. In the Russian Empire Jews were confined to the Pale of Settlement. From the early 15th century Jews in Morocco were confined to walled quarters called mellahs.

Racial segregation has generally been outlawed worldwide, and can amount to the international crime of apartheid and a crime against humanity under the 2002 Rome Declaration of Statute of the International Criminal Court. In French Algeria a colonial law of 1865 allowed Arab and Berber Algerians to apply for French citizenship only if they gave up their Muslim identity. In Canada segregation was embedded in society before the constitution of 1982, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 1939. The last school segregated for Black pupils in Ontario closed in 1965, the last in Nova Scotia in 1983, and the last racially segregated Indigenous school, in Saskatchewan, in 1996.
raciborz: Racibórz lies in the southwest of the Silesian Voivodeship on the upper Oder, near the border with the Czech Republic, in the Racibórz Basin, which forms the southeastern extension of the Silesian Lowlands. It is the administrative seat of Racibórz County. The town grew at a hill fort where the old trade route from the Moravian Gate down to Kraków crossed the Oder. Its name is Slavic and probably derives from that of a Duke Racibor, the city's founder. It is one of the historic capitals of Upper Silesia, with Opole.

The first confirmed mention is of 1108, in the chronicle of Gallus Anonymus, when the Polish duke Bolesław III Wrymouth was fending off attacks from Duke Svatopluk of Bohemia. From 1155 it was the seat of a castellany, and in 1172, at the first partition of Silesia, the Piast duke Mieszko I Tanglefoot established the Duchy of Racibórz there. He had the settlement beneath his residence laid out and colonised by Flemish merchants, and the first coin with the Polish inscription MILOST was issued in Racibórz in 1211.

In 1241 the local duke Mieszko II the Fat won the Battle of Racibórz during the first Mongol invasion of Poland. Brewing was an important source of the town's income, and from 1299 it was ruled by an autonomous council under Magdeburg law.

In 1327 Duke Leszek paid homage to King John of Bohemia, and when Leszek died in 1336 the Silesian Piast line was extinct and the duchy fell to Bohemia. It was then ruled by the Opava branch of the Přemyslid dynasty until the last duke, Valentin, died in 1521. Later it fell to the Habsburg king Ferdinand I, and the Thirty Years' War devastated the town's economy. After the First Silesian War in 1742 it was ceded to Prussia under Frederick the Great, and in 1871 became part of the German Empire.

In the plebiscite of 1921, 90.9 per cent of votes in the town were for Germany and 9.1 per cent for Poland, so it remained in Germany as a border town. Nazi Germany persecuted local Polish activists from 1937, and during World War II operated a prison and forced labour camps in the town. The Red Army occupied and devastated it on 30 March 1945, and it returned to Poland.

Racibórz has about 55,000 inhabitants. A flood devastated the town in 1997, and the Racibórz Dolny flood control reservoir nearby, with a capacity of 185 million cubic metres, was built in response and opened in 2020. Its German name is Ratibor.
rada-of-the-belarusian-democratic-republ: The Rada grew out of the council of the First All-Belarusian Congress, whose delegates met in secret after the Bolshevik authorities of the Western Oblast had dispersed the Congress by force. When the Germans invaded in February 1918 and the Bolsheviks withdrew from Minsk, its leaders stayed and set up provisional institutions. In March the council was expanded into the temporary legislature of the new republic, and on 25 March it had 77 members: 36 elected at the Congress, representatives of Vilnius's Belarusians, of the Russian, Polish and Jewish minorities, of local authorities and of the major cities.

On the day of independence the Rada sent an appeal to the German Emperor asking for protection in union with the German Empire. The appeal split the council: Paluta Badunova and Tamaš Hryb left the People's Secretariat in protest and formed the Belarusian Socialist-Revolutionary Party. Germany never recognised the republic, but the Rada began to organise local bodies, an army and schools, and made diplomatic contacts with Finland, the Ukrainian People's Republic, Czechoslovakia, the Baltic States and Turkey. As Bolshevik armies approached, it moved to Vilnius, Hrodna and finally Kaunas.

In exile it rejected Jozef Pilsudski's offer of purely cultural autonomy, signed a partnership treaty with Lithuania on 11 November 1920 and never recognised the Belarusian SSR. Several members returned home in 1925; most, among them the former prime minister Vaclau Lastouski, were killed in the Soviet terror of the 1930s. In June 1941 its president Vasil Zacharka wished Hitler victory, but he later turned against the Germans and the Rada refused to recognise the Belarusian Central Rada. Zacharka and Larysa Hienijuš issued papers that saved the Jewish Wolfsohn family.

After 1945 the Rada worked from western Germany, and later from the USA, Canada and the United Kingdom, lobbying Western governments and helping create the Belarusian service of Radio Free Europe in the 1950s. In 1991 Belarus adopted its symbols, the Pahonia and the white-red-white flag, and in 1993 members joined the official celebrations of the republic's 75th anniversary in Minsk. The Rada declined to hand its mandate to a parliament first elected under Soviet rule. Ivonka Survilla became its president in 1997, and in June 2023 the Belarusian KGB declared it an extremist formation.
radama-i: Radama was the son of Rambolamasoandro and King Andrianampoinimerina of Imerina, a growing kingdom on the central plateau around Antananarivo. He was educated at court and learned to read Malagasy in the Sorabe Arabico-Malagasy script used by the Antemoro court astrologers. His father took him on a campaign against the Betsileo, who had broken an oath, and gave him command of the second column of the army, with which he negotiated the submission of several towns.

On his deathbed Andrianampoinimerina reportedly told his son, "The sea is the border of my rice field", and Radama swore to fulfil the ambition. He became king in 1810, at the age of 17, and had at once to put down revolts in principalities his father had conquered, completing the pacification of the Betsileo kingdom.

In 1816 a Mauritian trader, Chardenoux, was sent to Radama by the British governor of Mauritius, Robert Townsend Farquhar, who wished to increase British influence and prevent the return of French trading posts. On 23 October 1817 Radama signed a treaty negotiated by James Hastie that recognised him as King of Madagascar in exchange for horses, uniforms and a pledge to abandon the export of slaves. Hastie became British resident minister in 1820, but the import of slaves from the African mainland continued throughout the reign.

A campaign to Toamasina in 1820 brought Radama into contact with the Welshmen David Jones and David Griffiths of the London Missionary Society, and he began founding schools. Within a year there were 23 schools with 2,300 pupils, a third of them girls. The missionaries wrote Malagasy in the Latin alphabet, introduced the first printing press, printed Bibles and set up craft industries in carpentry, leather, tin plating and cotton. Many of his innovations were rejected by the wider population as a denial of ancestral tradition.

With British help he modernised his army, reportedly admiring Napoleon Bonaparte, and campaigned from 1817 to 1827 against Toamasina, Menabe, the northeast coast, the southeast, the Antalaotra, the Antanosy and Betsimisaraka, and the Antesaka. Fortified garrisons, called rova, were built in conquered territory and staffed by Merina colonists. In all he brought two thirds of the island under Merina rule.

Radama died on 27 July 1828. Sources conflict on the cause, but he had been drinking heavily and his health had declined rapidly. He was buried in a silver coffin in a stone tomb at the Rova of Antananarivo, with rich grave goods that were mostly lost when a fire destroyed the Rova in 1995.

He had named no successor. Custom favoured Rakotobe, the eldest son of his eldest sister, but the officer Andriamamba and others supported Ramavo, Radama's highest-ranking wife, who became Queen Ranavalona I.
radama-ii: Radama II was born Prince Rakoto on 23 September 1829 in the compound of the Rova of Antananarivo. He was officially the son of King Radama I and his widow Queen Ranavalona I, although the king had died more than nine months before the birth. He was probably fathered by a lover of the queen, Andriamihaja, a progressive young officer. Influenced by the French adviser Joseph-François Lambert, the prince admired European culture and was troubled by his mother's repressive policies. Before her death, conservatives backed Ramboasalama, her sister's son, while the prime minister Rainivoninahitriniony and the army chief Rainilaiarivony, brothers and progressives, supported Rakoto.

Rakoto took the throne on 16 August 1861 on his mother's natural death, as Radama II, and was crowned on 23 September 1862. He quickly reversed her traditionalist policies. He opened the country to foreign powers, made treaties of friendship with Britain and France, declared freedom of religion, ended the persecution of Christians and allowed missionaries and their schools to return. He abolished the trial by ordeal of tangena, let swine be kept in Antananarivo, and freed political prisoners taken in Ranavalona's provincial wars, which improved relations between the coasts and the capital.

The Lambert Charter, which Radama had secretly contracted with Lambert in 1855 while his mother still ruled, gave French investors exclusive rights over public works, coinage and mining. Its clauses that would have let Lambert's company own land permanently alarmed Malagasy, who held the land to be sacred ground of the ancestors. The nobles and free men of the court, already alienated by the speed of his changes, objected.

The legalisation of dueling, announced on 7 May 1863, brought the opposition to a head. The prime minister stopped the law's proclamation, and Rainilaiarivony brought troops into the city. Eleven of the king's favourites, the menamaso, were executed, and the rest were speared to death after Radama handed them over on 10 May. On 12 May 1863 soldiers seized the king and strangled him with a silk sash, so that no royal blood was shed. His widow Rabodo succeeded as Rasoherina on the condition that rulers would henceforth govern with the nobles and the heads of the people. The public was told he had killed himself. Rumours soon spread that he had revived and lived on, which the historian Delval takes seriously.
radar: The idea that radio waves could locate objects is older than the systems built on it. In 1886 the German physicist Heinrich Hertz showed that radio waves could be reflected from solid objects. In 1897 Alexander Popov, a physics instructor at the Imperial Russian Navy school in Kronstadt, was testing radio equipment for communication between two ships in the Baltic Sea when he noticed an interference beat caused by the passage of a third vessel. He wrote in his report that the effect might be used for detecting objects, but he did nothing more with it.

Before the Second World War radar research was carried on in the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Soviet Union and the Netherlands. In France in 1934 the research branch of the Compagnie générale de la télégraphie sans fil, headed by Maurice Ponte, began developing an obstacle-locating radio apparatus, parts of which were installed on the ocean liner Normandie in 1935.

A radar system has a transmitter that produces radio or microwave waves, a transmitting antenna, a receiving antenna, often the same one, and a receiver and processor. The waves reflect off objects and return, giving their position and speed. Metals, seawater and wet ground reflect them especially well, which suits the detection of aircraft and ships. A moving object changes the frequency of the returning waves through the Doppler effect.

Distance is found from the time a short pulse takes to return: it is half the round-trip time multiplied by the speed of the signal, since the signal travels to the object and back. In the early days a user marked positions with a grease pencil on the radar screen and worked out the speed with a slide rule; modern sets do the same by computer.

The first use of radar was military: to locate targets in the air, on land and at sea. The device was developed in secret by several countries before and during the Second World War. A key development was the cavity magnetron in the United Kingdom, which allowed relatively small systems with sub-metre resolution. Britain shared the technology with the United States during the Tizard Mission of 1940, and Alfred Lee Loomis organised the secret MIT Radiation Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which developed microwave radar in the years 1941–45. Its use later spread to the civilian field, with applications for aircraft, ships and automobiles, including air traffic control, marine radars and the monitoring of rainfall.
radcliffe-line: The Indian Independence Act 1947 ended British rule on 15 August 1947 and divided British India into the two dominions of India and Pakistan. Baluchistan, Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province went wholly to Pakistan, but Punjab (55.7 percent Muslim) and Bengal (54.4 percent) had no overwhelming majority and were themselves partitioned. Proposals to divide Punjab dated from 1908, and Bengal had been partitioned by Lord Curzon in 1905 and reunited in 1911.

In Punjab no line could cleanly separate Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, and any division risked cutting roads, railways, irrigation and even individual landholdings. In June 1947 Britain appointed Sir Cyril Radcliffe to chair two boundary commissions, one each for Punjab and Bengal.

Each commission had four members, two nominated by the Indian National Congress and two by the Muslim League. They were told to demarcate contiguous majority areas of Muslims and non-Muslims while taking other factors into account, such as natural boundaries, communications and irrigation. The two sides deadlocked, so the decision was essentially Radcliffe's. The commissioners were all lawyers with no advisers and little time, and Radcliffe, who had not previously visited India, destroyed his papers and left on Independence Day.

The awards were ready on 9 and 12 August but were handed to the Indian and Pakistani representatives only on 16 August, with two hours to study them, and published on 17 August. Evidence suggests Nehru and Patel may have learned the Punjab award's content in advance, and part of Ferozepur district was shifted to India.

A Punjab Boundary Force of 50,000 men, less than one soldier to a square mile, could not prevent thousands of killings or protect the refugee columns. Disputes centred on Lahore, which went to Pakistan, on Gurdaspur, and on the Chittagong Hill Tracts, whose population was 97 percent non-Muslim but which was awarded to Pakistan. The Punjab part of the line is now part of the India–Pakistan border and the Bengal part is the Bangladesh–India border. Border conflicts led to wars in 1947, 1965 and 1971, and the Kargil conflict of 1999. The line also divided a centuries-old Sikh pilgrimage and separated people of Punjab of all faiths from each other.
radegund: Radegund was born about 520 to Bertachar, one of the three kings of Thuringia. Her uncle Hermanfrid killed Bertachar in battle and took her into his household. In 531 the Frankish king Theuderic and his brother Chlothar I defeated Hermanfrid and conquered his kingdom, and Chlothar took Radegund back to Merovingian Gaul. He sent the child to his villa of Athies in Picardy for several years and married her in 540.

She was one of six wives or concubines of Chlothar and had no children with him. She was noted for her almsgiving. By 545 her brother was the last surviving male of the Thuringian royal family, and Chlothar had him murdered.

Radegund fled the court and sought the protection of the Church. She persuaded Medardus, bishop of Noyon, to ordain her a deaconess, and around 560 she founded the monastery of Sainte-Croix in Poitiers, where she cared for the sick. She was widely believed to have the gift of healing. The nuns lived under the Rule for Virgins of Caesarius of Arles, which she had received from her niece Caesaria. They had to read and write, to spend several hours a day reading scripture and copying manuscripts, and to weave and sew. The Rule enclosed them strictly, so that they could not attend Radegund's funeral.

The abbey took its name from a relic of the True Cross that Radegund obtained from the Byzantine Emperor Justin II. Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, refused to install it, and at her request King Sigebert I sent Eufronius of Tours to perform the ceremony. For the occasion Venantius Fortunatus composed hymns, among them Vexilla Regis, still sung on Good Friday and Palm Sunday. Radegund was known as an extreme ascetic, who ate only legumes and green vegetables and refused wine, mead and beer.

Radegund died on 13 August 587. Her friends Venantius Fortunatus and Gregory of Tours both wrote about her and attended her funeral three days later. She was buried in Poitiers, in what became the church of Saint Radegonde, where her tomb remains in the crypt and the centre of devotion to her. The nun Baudonivia wrote another life of her. After her death the nuns of the abbey rebelled for two years against an abbess appointed by the male hierarchy.

She is patron saint of several churches in France and England and of Jesus College, Cambridge, built on the site of a priory dedicated to Saint Mary and Saint Radegund. Many places in France are named Sainte-Radegonde, and two Austrian municipalities are named after her.
raden-wijaya: His ancestry is told in several versions. According to the Pararaton he was the son of Mahisa Campaka, a prince of Singhasari and grandson of Ken Arok, founder of the Rajasa dynasty. A controversial 17th-century source, the Pustaka Rajyarajya i Bhumi Nusantara, makes him the son of Rakeyan Jayadarma of Sunda-Galuh. The Nagarakretagama, written in 1365, makes his father Dyah Lembu Tal a great-grandson of Ken Arok, and popular opinion follows it as the earliest account.

In 1289 King Kertanagara of Singhasari refused Kublai Khan's demand for tribute and had the envoy's ear cut off. When Kertanagara was killed putting down the rebellion of Jayakatwang of Gelang-Gelang in 1292, Wijaya fled to Sumenep on Madura with its governor, Arya Wiraraja, who agreed to help him overthrow Jayakatwang's Kediri kingdom in return for a share of Java.

In November 1292 a Mongol force landed at Tuban to punish Kertanagara. Wijaya allied with it against Kediri, and once Jayakatwang was destroyed in 1293 he turned on the Mongols, who had been weakened by tropical disease and the climate and fled Java. He made Tarik, at Trowulan, his seat; the name Majapahit came from the bitter maja fruit of its forest. He took the title Kertarajasa Jayawardhana, gave Wiraraja Madura with a special status and an autonomous region around Lumajang, and formed a royal guard of seven men.

Nobles unhappy with the posts they had been given rebelled. Wiraraja's son Ranggalawe rose in 1295 and was killed by Mahisa Anabrang at the Tambak Beras river, and Lembu Sora died in his rebellion of 1301.

To secure his claim to the legacy of Singhasari he married all four daughters of Kertanagara, among them Tribhuwana and Gayatri Rajapatni, and also Indreswari, probably the Dharmasraya princess Dara Petak. Gayatri bore him two daughters, Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi and Rajadewi, and Indreswari his son Jayanegara, who succeeded him. According to the Nagarakretagama he died in 1309 and was buried in the Simping Temple, portrayed as Harihara, the combination of Vishnu and Shiva.
radhanite: Several etymologies have been suggested for the name. Many scholars, including Barbier de Meynard and Moshe Gil, connect it with a district in Mesopotamia called the land of Radhan in Arabic and Hebrew texts of the period. Others derive it from the city of Ray in northern Iran, or from the Persian rah, way, and dān, one who knows. Cecil Roth and Claude Cahen suggested a link with the Rhône valley, Rhodanus in Latin, arguing that the centre of Radhanite activity was probably in France, where all their routes began.

Ibn Khordadbeh, postmaster and chief of police for the province of Jibal under the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tamid, is the one source that documents them; Ibn al-Faqih's Book of the Countries of the early 10th century mentions them but draws largely on his work. In his account the merchants carried from the West eunuchs, female slaves, boys, brocade, castor, marten and other furs, and swords, and brought back from China musk, aloes, camphor and cinnamon.

One route went by sea from Firanja, France, to Farama, by camel to al-Kolzum, Suez, and on by the East Sea to al-Jar, Jeddah, Sind, India and China. On the way back some sailed to Constantinople and others went to the palace of the King of the Franks. Another went by Antioch and the Euphrates to Baghdad, down the Tigris to al-Obolla and on to Oman and China. A land route ran by Tangier, Kairouan, Damascus, Baghdad and Fars, and a fourth through the country of the Slavs to Khamlidj, the Khazar capital, across the Jorjan Sea to Balkh and beyond the Oxus.

Muslim and Christian states often banned each other's merchants from their ports, and privateers of both sides raided each other's shipping. The Radhanites acted as neutral go-betweens, and the revenue they brought gave Jewish merchants significant privileges under the early Carolingian dynasty in France and throughout the Muslim world, which sometimes vexed local Church authorities. Some scholars believe they played a role in the conversion of the Khazars to Judaism and helped establish Jewish communities along their routes.

After their disappearance many spices in regular use in the early Middle Ages vanished from European tables in the 10th century, and the Italian maritime republics of Genoa, Venice, Pisa and Amalfi, which had seen them as unwanted competitors, rose. Jewish scrolls of the 11th century found in a cave in Samangan Province, Afghanistan, in 2011 have been suggested as a remnant of Radhanites there.
radio-luxembourg: From 1922 British law gave the BBC a monopoly of broadcasting and barred advertising on the radio. Leonard Plugge's International Broadcasting Company showed that the monopoly could be got round by leasing time on continental transmitters. In 1924 the radio technician François Anen built a 100-watt transmitter at his home in Luxembourg, and on 11 May 1929 he gathered a group of mainly French entrepreneurs to press for a commercial licence. A law of 19 December 1930 created a monopoly franchise, awarded on 29 December.

Before the war its Sunday programmes of light music and variety drew listeners when the BBC kept to serious and religious broadcasting, and around 11% of Britons tuned in during the week. Because it could not use Post Office telephone lines, programmes were recorded in London and flown to Luxembourg. The government closed the station on 21 September 1939 to protect the country's neutrality; the invading German forces then used it for English-language propaganda by William Joyce, and from 9 September 1944 the US Army used it for black propaganda.

After the war the English service moved to the night-time on 208 metres medium wave, its skywave signal covering the British Isles. It kept a monopoly of English-language commercial radio heard in Britain until Radio Caroline began broadcasting from a ship in March 1964, and it answered the offshore stations with live disc jockeys and spot advertising. Legislation of 1973 allowed Independent Local Radio in Britain. The 208 service ended at 3 am GMT on 30 December 1991, and the station continued for a time on satellite and shortwave.

By exposing millions of Britons and British companies to commercial broadcasting, the station contributed to the creation of ITV in the 1950s and was a forerunner of pirate and commercial radio. In the Eastern Bloc it was one of the few ways to hear rock music, received at night as far as Leningrad and Moscow; though not jammed itself, its signal suffered from the jamming of Radio Free Europe. Its parent company, RTL Group, owned the British channel Five from 2006 until selling it to Richard Desmond on 23 July 2010.
radioactivity: Radioactive decay, also called nuclear decay or radioactivity, is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation. The three most common types are alpha, beta and gamma decay. Ernest Rutherford named them in increasing order of their ability to penetrate matter, after early researchers found that an electric or magnetic field could split radioactive emissions into three beams. Beta decay is seen in all elements, while alpha decay is observed only in heavier elements of atomic number 52 and above.

For single atoms the process is random: according to quantum theory it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay. For many identical atoms the overall rate is expressed as a decay constant or a half-life, and half-lives range from nearly instantaneous to far longer than the age of the universe. Except in gamma decay, the process transmutes the nucleus, and when the number of protons changes an atom of a different element is created. Lead, with atomic number 82, is the heaviest element with stable isotopes. Twenty-eight naturally occurring elements are radioactive, among them uranium and thorium.

Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel, who was working with phosphorescent materials. He wrapped a photographic plate in black paper and put various phosphorescent salts on it. Results were negative until he used uranium salts, which blackened the plate despite the paper. In 1897 Marie Curie began studying the radiation from uranium compounds, named it rayons de Becquerel, and showed that the rays were a property of atoms. The SI unit of activity, the becquerel, equals one decay per second.

The dangers were slow to be recognised. Physicians and companies marketed radioactive substances as patent medicines, including radium enemas and radium waters, and Marie Curie warned that radium is dangerous in untrained hands. She later died of aplastic anaemia, likely caused by radiation. By the 1930s, after cases of bone necrosis and death among enthusiasts, such products had largely left the market. The first International Congress of Radiology met in 1925 to consider protection standards, and in 1927 Hermann Joseph Muller published research showing genetic effects, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1946.

An atomic battery uses the energy of decay to generate electric power without a chain reaction. Such batteries are costly but long-lived, and power equipment that must run unattended for long periods, such as spacecraft and pacemakers.
radnorshire: The county was bounded by Montgomeryshire and Shropshire to the north, Herefordshire to the east, Brecknockshire to the south and Cardiganshire to the west. Apart from level tracts such as the Vale of Radnor, much of it is forest, moorland and low mountains, with the Cambrian Mountains in the west. Its highest point, Great Rhos at 660 metres, lies in the Radnor Forest, a dome of hills near New Radnor. Its main rivers were the Wye, the Teme, the Elan and the Ithon, and the Elan Valley holds reservoirs supplying Birmingham.

The area roughly matches the Welsh territory of Rhwng Gwy a Hafren, between Wye and Severn, which the Marcher Lords took at the end of the 11th century. Cwmhir Abbey, a Cistercian house, was founded there in 1176, and the Battle of Bryn Glas was fought at Pilleth on 22 June 1402 during the rebellion of Owain Glyndŵr. Its Marcher status gave rise to the saying neither Wales nor England, just Radnorsheer.

The county was named after New Radnor, its first county town. Assizes alternated at first between New Radnor and Rhayader, but after a judge was murdered at Rhayader the law was changed in 1543 to alternate them with Presteigne, which later held them alone. Welsh remained the first language of most parishes well into the second half of the 18th century, retreated westward by 1850 and was fading west of Rhayader by 1900. Poverty made it a county of net emigration: Quakers from Radnorshire settled Radnor Township in Pennsylvania in 1682–1685.

The county council, formed in 1889, chose by 12 votes to 11 to meet at Llandrindod Wells rather than Presteigne. After 1974 the area was the Radnor district of Powys, renamed Radnorshire in 1989, until Powys became a unitary authority in 1996. Llandrindod Wells is its largest town, alongside Knighton, Presteigne and Rhayader. The Royal Welsh Show is held each July at Llanelwedd.
radziwill-family: The Radziwiłł family descends from the extinct Lithuanian noble Astikai line. Its first notable member, Kristinas Astikas, a close associate of the Lithuanian ruler Vytautas, became Castellan of Vilnius. The name Radvila arose from its use by his son Radvila Astikas and his grandson Mikalojus Radvila the Old. The family adopted a variation of the Trąby coat of arms after the Union of Horodło in 1413.

Three sons of Mikalojus Radvila the Old, Mikołaj, Jan and Jerzy, became the progenitors of three lines: Goniądz-Meteliai, Biržai-Dubingiai and Nesvizh-Kletsk-Olyka. The first died out in the next generation, since Mikołaj III became a priest and Bishop of Samogitia and left no known offspring. The second ended with the death of Ludwika Karolina Radziwiłł in 1695. Only the Nesvizh line survives.

The family joined the state's elite after the Union of Krewo in 1385. Its members held high office in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania: 13 were Voivodes of Vilnius, seven Grand Chancellors and seven Grand Hetmans. They were the first nobles in Lithuania and Poland to receive the title of Reichsfürst from the Holy Roman Emperor, a rank held by only five Polish families.

The family divided on religion. Two branches turned to Calvinism after the Reformation, and Mikołaj the Black financed the Radziwiłł Bible, a Polish Protestant translation published at Brest in 1564. His children converted to Roman Catholicism before the end of the century, while the Biržai line stayed Protestant until it died out.

The family's importance peaked in the Polish Golden Age. During the Deluge of the mid-17th century the actions of Janusz Radziwiłł cost it much of its wealth and power. In 1612 the Principality of Slutsk passed to the family when Janusz Radziwiłł married the heiress Zofia Olelkowicz Słucka. Nesvizh Castle was awarded to Mikołaj the Black and his brother Jan in 1533. It was sacked in 1706 during the Great Northern War, Russian forces seized it in 1770 and the Red Army expelled the family in 1939.

The family is credited with 23 palaces, 426 towns and 2,032 estates over the centuries. Prince Antoni Radziwiłł, a composer, turned his Berlin properties into artistic salons and built the hunting lodge of Antonin between 1822 and 1824 with the architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel. Frédéric Chopin stayed there, taught Antoni's daughter Wanda and dedicated his Piano Trio Op. 8 to him.

The last male Radziwiłł living in Lithuania, Konstantinas Radvila, was arrested by the NKVD after the Soviet occupation of 1940 and deported to the Uzbek SSR in 1941, where he died around 1945. The Nesvizh Castle complex, maintained by the family from the 16th century to 1939, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
raedwald-of-east-anglia: Rædwald, whose name means 'power in counsel', was born around 560 to 580. He was the son of Tytila of East Anglia and a member of the Wuffingas dynasty, named after his grandfather Wuffa, and the elder brother of Eni. East Anglia included the present-day counties of Norfolk and Suffolk. Details of his reign are scarce, largely because the Viking invasions of the 9th century destroyed the East Anglian monasteries where documents would have been kept. During the 590s he married a pagan woman whose name is unknown, and they had at least two sons, Rægenhere and Eorpwald. He also had an older son, Sigeberht, whom he drove into exile in Gaul.

Rædwald reigned from about 599, at first under the overlordship of Æthelberht of Kent. He became a Christian, probably around 604 or later, at Æthelberht's court, but he kept a temple with two altars, one to Christ and one to pagan gods. Bede, who disapproved, regarded him as a renouncer of the faith. For a time the only royal Christian altar in England was his, while Kent and Essex returned to paganism after the deaths of Æthelberht, who died on 24 February 616, and of Saebert of Essex.

Edwin, an exile from Northumbria, sought his protection. Æthelfrith of Northumbria sent messengers three times offering silver for Edwin's death or surrender, and Rædwald wavered, but his queen reproached him for betraying a friend and he resolved on war. He marched north with his son Rægenhere and met Æthelfrith's army on the east bank of the River Idle, on the western boundary of Lindsey. Æthelfrith and Rægenhere were both killed, and Edwin became king of Northumbria. The battle was long remembered in the saying that the river Idle was foul with the blood of Englishmen. From about 616 Rædwald was the most powerful English king south of the Humber, and Bede called him Rex Anglorum.

Rædwald died around 624. He was succeeded by his pagan son Eorpwald, who was later persuaded by Edwin to convert, and the ruling house's conversion became permanent only under Sigeberht. During his supremacy the quayside settlement at Gipeswic (Ipswich) became an important trading centre.

Since the excavation of Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo in 1939, historians have considered Rædwald the most likely person buried or commemorated there, though the identification is disputed. The chamber held gold and garnet equipment and a consular sceptre, which may have symbolised the office of overlord. Other candidates include other East Anglian kings and a foreign visitor. A smaller ship-burial found in 1998 nearby is thought to contain Rægenhere.
raetia: Little is known of the origin of the Raetians, who appear in the records as one of the most powerful and warlike of the Alpine tribes. Livy states that they were of Etruscan origin; a tradition reported by Justin and Pliny the Elder held that they were driven into the mountains from the plain of the Po by invading Gauls, and took their name from a leader called Raetus. Celtic tribes already held much of the land when the Romans learned of it, and the later Raetians may generally be regarded as a Celtic people. They kept their independence until they were subjugated in 15 BCE by Tiberius and Drusus.

At first Raetia was a province of its own, but towards the end of the 1st century CE Vindelicia was added to it. It was governed first by a military prefect and then by a procurator, and had no standing army until the 2nd century, relying on native troops and militia. Under Marcus Aurelius it was governed by the commander of the Legio III Italica, based by 179 at Castra Regina (Regensburg).

The province lay between the Helvetii in the west, Noricum in the east, Vindelicia in the north and Venetia et Histria in the south. It covered eastern and central Switzerland, southern Germany, most of Tyrol in Austria and part of northern Lombardy. Its northern border under Augustus and Tiberius was the Danube; later the Limes Germanicus marked it. The capital was Augusta Vindelicorum, present-day Augsburg.

Two great Roman roads crossed it: the Via Claudia Augusta, from Verona and Tridentum over the Reschen Pass to Augsburg, and another from Brigantium (Bregenz) by Chur and Chiavenna to Como and Milan. The country was very mountainous, and its people lived chiefly by breeding cattle and cutting timber. Some valleys produced wine that was rated equal to any in Italy, and Augustus preferred it to any other.

Under Diocletian Raetia was divided into Raetia prima, with its governor at Curia (Chur), and Raetia secunda, with its governor at Augsburg. In its last years under the Western Roman Empire the land was desolate; occupation by the Ostrogoths under Theodoric the Great revived its prosperity to some extent. Much of Raetia prima remained a separate political unit, Raetia Curiensis, for several centuries, until it was attached to the Duchy of Swabia in 917. The Rätikon mountain range takes its name from Raetia.
rafael-antonio-gutierrez: Rafael Antonio Gutiérrez was born in Ilobasco, Cabañas, on 24 October 1845, the son of Marcela Gutiérrez and of a father who was a Spaniard. He married Carlota Mejía, with whom he had eight children; their daughter Marcela married a son of General Fernando Figueroa, later president himself. In May 1885 Gutiérrez backed General Francisco Menéndez in the revolution that overthrew President Rafael Zaldívar, leading indigenous Salvadoran soldiers in Nahuizalco during the coup.

On 29 April 1894 Gutiérrez and other officers rose against President Carlos Ezeta, who had let a financial crisis develop. With help from Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua the Revolution of the 44 deposed Ezeta on 9 June, and after a contest with General Manuel Rivas, who gave way, Gutiérrez became provisional president the next day. He was the only candidate in the 1895 election, winning 61,080 votes, and took office on 1 March 1895. He repealed several of Ezeta's crisis taxes, and Ezeta's attempt to return in 1895 failed.

His government dealt with disputes over the partition of indigenous communal land in Izalco, under a system set up in 1881 and 1882 that had taken land from the Izalco people; in 1897 he declared one partidor's partition invalid. He revived the University Council of the University of El Salvador, but expelled students who protested against him during the economic crisis of 1897, when he answered with railway building that proved unpopular. On 20 June 1895 he signed the Pact of Amapala with Honduras and Nicaragua, founding the Greater Republic of Central America.

On 13 November 1898 General Tomás Regalado, a liberal who had helped him to power in 1894, overthrew him in a coup d'état. Gutiérrez and some of his supporters fled to Honduras. Indians in Izalco revolted the next day, and the union collapsed on 29 November. He stood for president in 1907 and received one vote. He died in San Salvador on 9 January 1921 and was buried in the Cemetery of Distinguished Citizens; President Jorge Meléndez declared three days of national mourning.
rafael-carrera: José Rafael Carrera y Turcios was born on 24 October 1814 in the Candelaria barrio of Guatemala City, towards the end of the Spanish colonial period. He was of humble origin, a mestizo and illiterate, and first worked as a farmhand. He enlisted in the army during the civil war of 1826 to 1829. In 1835 he left the army and moved to Mataquescuintla, where he married Petrona García and worked as a swineherd.

By 1837 rural grievances against the liberal government had led to an uprising. A cholera epidemic added to the frustration, and Carrera rallied the peasants into an armed resistance strongly supported by Catholic clerics, leading indigenous and mixed-race peasants in the east and south. The movement wished to restore colonial traditions the liberals had abandoned. Francisco Morazán repeatedly drove Carrera's forces out of towns, but they retook them when his army left. In 1840 Morazán invaded Guatemala again with 1,500 soldiers and took the capital, but Carrera's surprise attacks defeated him there.

Carrera was appointed president in 1844, and on 21 March 1847 he declared Guatemala an independent republic. In 1848 the liberals drove him from office and he left for Mexico. In 1852 he signed a concordat with the Holy See, ratified in 1854, which gave regular orders of the Church the education of the people, imposed mandatory tithing and let bishops censor publications. In 1854 he was declared supreme and perpetual leader of the nation for life, with the power to choose his successor. A war with El Salvador in 1863 began with a severe Guatemalan defeat at Coatepeque, but Carrera in the end besieged and occupied San Salvador.

Carrera died in office on 14 April 1865, having named Vicente Cerna y Cerna as his successor. A year after his death coins were issued calling him Founder of the Republic of Guatemala. After the liberals returned to power in 1871 his regime was dismissed and presented as the work of an illiterate manipulated by the anti-liberal faction. Other accounts note that he did not significantly improve the life of rural Indians but delayed the destruction of their culture that liberal capitalist development brought.
rafael-nunez: Rafael Wenceslao Núñez Moledo was the first of three children of the cousins Dolores García Moledo and Colonel Francisco Núñez García. At 15 he joined the rebel troops of General Francisco Carmona in the War of the Supremes of 1840, the first of many Colombian civil wars, and took part in the siege of his own hometown, Cartagena. He then studied law and graduated in 1844.

By 1848 he had founded the newspaper La Democracia in Cartagena to promote General José María Obando for the presidency. Obando, elected governor of the Province of Cartagena, appointed him Chief of Staff, and he held the post until 1853. Little is known of his earlier years, but in 1848 he served as a circuit judge in Chiriquí, Panama.

In 1853 Núñez moved to Bogotá as a member of Congress, where he fought the federalist and socialist ideas of Manuel Murillo Toro. After José María Melo's coup of 1854 he went into hiding, then became governor of the department of Bolívar. President Manuel María Mallarino made him Minister of War in 1855 and then Minister of the Treasury, where his results won wide recognition. He left Colombia in 1863, lived two years in New York City, and later served as consul in Le Havre and Liverpool.

Núñez returned in 1876 after an unsuccessful presidential candidacy and was elected senator for Bolívar. From 1878 to 1888 he wrote hundreds of articles on constitutional reform for Bogotá and Cartagena newspapers. He also wrote the words of the Colombian national anthem. He was elected president for 1880 to 1882 and again in 1884, with Conservative support, under the banner of the Regeneration.

During his first administration Núñez allowed exiled Catholic bishops to return, created the Military Academy and the National Academy of Music, opened the international telegraph service and restored diplomatic relations with Spain. Liberal leaders opposed his centralist programme and fought a civil war in 1884 and 1885. When government forces prevailed he proclaimed that the Constitution of 1863 was no more.

A Constituent Assembly, summoned on 10 September 1885, produced the Constitution of 1886 with the help of Miguel Antonio Caro. It renamed the country the Republic of Colombia, replaced the states with departments ruled by appointed governors, lengthened the presidential term from two years to six and gave Congress the election of the president. It also restored links with the Vatican, made Catholicism the official religion and left education to the Church. Núñez was re-elected in 1886 and 1892 but never took office the last time; ill in Cartagena, he left Caro as de facto president. He died on 18 September 1894.
rafael-trujillo: Rafael Leónidas Trujillo Molina was born on 24 October 1891 in San Cristóbal, into a lower-middle-class family. In 1916 the United States began its occupation of the Dominican Republic, after 28 revolutions in 50 years. Trujillo, then 25, worked as an overseer on a sugar plantation at Boca Chica. In 1918 he joined the National Guard, the constabulary the occupiers had created, was soon promoted to second lieutenant and trained with the US Marines.

Trujillo ruled from August 1930 until his death. He was president from 1930 to 1938 and from 1942 to 1952, and held the post of generalissimo throughout, ruling through figurehead presidents when he did not hold the presidency himself. Two and a half weeks after he took office, Hurricane San Zenón killed 2,000 people in Santo Domingo. He declared martial law, rebuilt the city and renamed it Ciudad Trujillo. In 1931 he made the Dominican Party the sole legal party. Government employees had to give 10 percent of their salaries to the treasury, and statues, slogans and renamed places formed a personality cult.

Opponents were killed from the start, first by a gang known as The 42 and later by the secret police, the SIM. Estimates of deaths in the country under his regime range from 25,000 to over 50,000. In 1937 the Dominican Army killed between 17,000 and 35,000 Haitians in the Parsley Massacre. His agents operated abroad: Jesús Galíndez disappeared in New York in 1956, and in June 1960 an attempt to kill Venezuela's president Rómulo Betancourt with a car bomb failed. The murder of the Mirabal sisters in 1960 added to the international condemnation, and the Organization of American States imposed sanctions.

On 30 May 1961 conspirators led by General Antonio Imbert Barrera ambushed Trujillo's car on a road outside the capital and shot him dead. The plotters failed to take control. His son Ramfis took temporary control and executed most of the conspirators, while Imbert was the only one of the seven assassins to survive. By November 1961 the family was pressured into exile by the titular president Joaquín Balaguer. Civil strife followed, ending in the Dominican Civil War and a US-OAS intervention, and in 1966 the country stabilised under a multi-party system.

Trujillo remains a polarising figure in the Dominican Republic. His supporters credit him with long-term stability and economic growth, while critics denounce the violence of his regime, its xenophobia towards Haitians, and the family's corruption and nepotism.
rafael-urdaneta: Rafael José Urdaneta y Farías was born in Maracaibo on 24 October 1788 to a prominent family of Spanish descent. He began his schooling in Maracaibo and continued in Caracas, studying Latin and philosophy. In 1804 he went to Santa Fe, encouraged by his uncle Martín de Urdaneta y Troconis, an official of the Real Audiencia, and spent several years there gaining experience in military administration. On 31 August 1822 he married Dolores Vargas París, a young heroine of Santa Fe.

Urdaneta joined the junta formed in Santa Fe on 20 July 1810 and entered the patriot army of New Granada as a lieutenant on 1 November 1810. Captured by royalists after the Battle of Santa Fe in 1813, he was held for a few months. He then joined Simón Bolívar's Admirable Campaign, distinguishing himself at the Battle of Niquitao on 2 July 1813 and at the Battle of Taguanes. He later led actions including the Battle of Barbula, the Caracas Exodus of 1814, the Siege of Santa Fe, after which he became a lieutenant-general at 26, the Capture of Maracaibo and the march to San Carlos in 1821. Bolívar called him El Brillante for his strategy.

As Minister of War in 1828 Urdaneta presided over the cabinet that tried the September Conspiracy, an attempt on Bolívar's life. Convinced that Francisco de Paula Santander led it, he and most ministers sentenced him to death, but Bolívar, fearing for the union of New Granada and Venezuela, imposed lifelong exile instead.

In 1830 enmity between New Granadians and Venezuelans reached a head in Bogotá, where the Venezuelan battalion Callao, loyal to Bolívar, defeated a battalion loyal to Santander. President Joaquín Mosquera and Vice President Domingo Caycedo fled, and on 5 September 1830 Urdaneta took power as Provisional Chief of the Government. He and his allies hoped to persuade Bolívar, who had resigned in May, to return. When Bolívar would not, Urdaneta called Congress to meet at Villa de Leyva on 15 June 1831.

Before it met, generals José María Obando and José Hilario López took the southern provinces and José Salvador Córdova Muñoz the northern ones. On 14 April 1831 they proclaimed Caycedo head of the executive. Urdaneta negotiated, and the Treaty of Apulo of 28 April 1831 ended the fighting and ended his rule. He and his wife fled, were persecuted in Maracaibo by José Antonio Páez and went to Curaçao. Back in Venezuela from 1832, he sat as a senator until 1845. He died in Paris on 23 August 1845 on his way to Spain as Venezuela's envoy and is buried in the National Pantheon of Venezuela.
rafael-zaldivar: Rafael Zaldívar Lazo was born in San Alejo, then part of the Federal Republic of Central America, to Apolonio Zaldívar and Antonia Lazo. He was tutored in humanities, Latin and classical literature by José Miguel Alegría, a presbyter and deputy of the Legislative Assembly, graduated from the National College of Asunción, and in 1852 enrolled in the Faculty of Medicine of the University of El Salvador.

After an earthquake destroyed the university in April 1854 he moved to the University of San Carlos in Guatemala City, where he completed his doctorate of medicine on 23 May 1860; he later studied obstetrics at the University of Paris. On 25 August 1858 he married Sara Guerra, a Nicaraguan he had met as a student in Guatemala City, and they had four children.

Back in Central America he served as El Salvador's envoy to Guatemala until December 1865, became vice rector of the Faculty of Medicine in 1866 and Protomedic of the Nation in 1867, went as minister plenipotentiary to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1869, and presided over the Legislative Assembly early in 1870. In 1871 he was Minister of War and Public Instruction under President Francisco Dueñas. When Marshal Santiago González overthrew Dueñas that year, Zaldívar fled to San José, Costa Rica, where he opened a pharmacy and befriended President Tomás Guardia Gutiérrez.

In April 1876 the Guatemalan president Justo Rufino Barrios invaded El Salvador after President Andrés del Valle and González refused to back his invasion of Honduras, and within two weeks both resigned. Barrios set up a Junta of Notables to choose the next president, and Zaldívar, endorsed by Guardia, prevailed over General Indalecio Miranda. He became provisional president on 1 May 1876 and signed a peace treaty with Guatemala on 11 May. Attempted coups in 1877, 1879 and 1883 all failed, and his nine-year presidency was the longest in Salvadoran history until Maximiliano Hernández Martínez held power from 1931 to 1944.
rafic-hariri: Rafic Bahaa El Deen al-Hariri was born on 1 November 1944 to a modest Sunni Muslim family in the port city of Sidon. He went to school there and graduated in business administration from Beirut Arab University. In 1965 he went to Saudi Arabia, where he taught for a short time before moving into the construction industry, and in 1978 he took Saudi citizenship alongside his Lebanese one.

After a small subcontracting firm failed, he went into business with the French construction firm Oger on a hotel at Ta'if, whose timely completion won praise from King Khaled. Hariri took over Oger, formed Saudi Oger, and it became the main builder for the Saudi royal family's major projects. In 1979 he founded the Islamic Association for Culture and Education, later the Hariri Foundation, which built educational facilities in Lebanon. During the civil war he acted as an envoy of the Saudi royal family and laid the groundwork for the Taif Agreement, which Saudi Arabia organised to bring the warring factions together.

In 1992 Hariri became the first prime minister after the civil war, under President Elias Hrawi, and also served as finance minister. He headed the reconstruction plan Horizon 2000, whose centrepiece was Solidere, a company formed to rebuild central Beirut. Solidere was given powers of compulsory purchase and compensated owners in company shares rather than cash; critics said owners were underpaid. Inflation, running at 131 percent in 1992, fell to 12 percent within two years, but public debt rose sharply. His first term ended in 1998, after a power struggle with President Émile Lahoud.

He was appointed again in October 2000. In his second term the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon ended an occupation of eighteen years. In September 2004 he defended UN Security Council Resolution 1559, which called for all remaining foreign forces to withdraw from Lebanon, and on 20 October 2004 he resigned.

On 14 February 2005 explosives equivalent to about 1,800 kilograms of TNT, hidden in a parked van, were detonated as Hariri's motorcade passed the St. George Hotel in Beirut. Twenty-three people died, among them Hariri, several bodyguards and the former economy minister Bassel Fleihan. On 14 March between 1.2 and 1.5 million people assembled in Beirut to demand an end to Syria's occupation. These protests, called the Cedar Revolution, were followed by the withdrawal of Syrian troops.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was created at his instigation. In August 2020 it convicted Salim Ayyash, a Hezbollah member, in absentia and acquitted three others; the judges found no evidence of involvement by Hezbollah's leadership. Beirut International Airport was renamed after Hariri in 2005, and his son Saad Hariri succeeded him as leader of the Future Movement.
ragamuffin-war: Unlike other Brazilian provinces, Rio Grande do Sul produced mainly for the home market, above all charque, dried and salted beef, which suffered from competition with charque from Uruguay and Argentina. Landowners resented high taxes and duties on salt imposed by the imperial government, and many wanted greater autonomy from it. The name farrapos, ragamuffins, and its form farroupilha were insults used for radical liberals who favoured provincial autonomy and federalism; according to Lindolfo Collor, the liberals came to wear the label with pride. In 1835 the new provincial president, Antônio Rodrigues Fernandes Braga, accused many farmers of separatism on his first day in office.

On 20 September 1835 General Bento Gonçalves took Porto Alegre, and the president fled to the city of Rio Grande. After the rebel victory at Seival, Antônio de Sousa Neto proclaimed the Riograndense Republic on 11 September 1836, with Gonçalves as president, though Gonçalves was held by imperial forces until he escaped in 1837. Porto Alegre was retaken in June 1836 and the rebels never won it back, governing instead from shifting inland capitals such as Piratini.

The Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Garibaldi and his wife Anita carried the war north into Santa Catarina, where the rebels took Laguna in 1839 and proclaimed the Juliana Republic, lost again after four months. The Uruguayan government of Fructuoso Rivera gave the rebels money and indirect support. Afro-Brazilians made up an estimated third to half of the republican army, many of them enslaved men promised their freedom; the Black Lancers were destroyed in a surprise attack in 1844, the Porongos Massacre. The republic's constitution kept slavery, and most rebel commanders, Gonçalves among them, owned slaves.

The rebels refused an amnesty in 1840. General Lima e Silva, given the imperial command in 1842, opened talks, and on 1 March 1845 the Treaty of Ponche Verde was signed at Dom Pedrito. It granted full amnesty, entry into the imperial army and the choice of the next provincial president, and the rebels chose Lima e Silva. The Empire paid the republic's debts and placed a 25% tariff on imported charque. The war pushed the Brazilian Army to reorganise as a proper fighting force.
ragenfrid: Ragenfrid, also written Ragenfred, Raganfrid or Ragamfred, had his original centre of power in the Véxin. He came to prominence in 715, when the death of Pepin of Heristal left a vacuum in Neustria. The Neustrian nobles named him mayor of the palace of Neustria and Burgundy in opposition to Theudoald, Pepin's grandson and heir, and to Theudoald's grandmother Plectrude, though neither Plectrude nor Charles Martel recognised him.

Allied with Duke Radbod of Frisia, Ragenfrid defeated Theudoald's forces at the Battle of Compiègne on 26 September 715, sending Theudoald back to Plectrude in Cologne. In 716 he and King Chilperic II campaigned deep into the mid-Meuse and the Ardennes, the heartland of Pepin's family. While the Frisians held off Charles Martel, who withdrew to the Eifel mountains, the Neustrians besieged Plectrude in Cologne and forced her to acknowledge Chilperic as king, surrender a large part of the Austrasian treasury and give up her grandson's claim to the mayoralty.

Charles rallied his supporters and defeated Chilperic and Ragenfrid at the Battle of Amblève, recovering much of his father's treasure. After a further defeat in 717 the king and Ragenfrid fled to Paris. In 718 they allied with Odo the Great, duke of Aquitaine, whom the French historian Pierre Riché suggests may have been offered recognition as king of Aquitaine. The allies were defeated at the Battle of Soissons, and Ragenfrid withdrew to Angers with what remained of the Neustrian army.

Once Paris and the Loire Valley had fallen and Odo had handed over Chilperic, Ragenfrid gave himself up and was deprived of his office, keeping only lands in Anjou. In 724 the Neustrians rebelled under his leadership, and he defended Angers so well that Charles chose to negotiate. Ragenfrid was allowed to keep his county for life on condition that he give his son as a hostage for his conduct.

His defeats at Amblève, Vinchy and Soissons marked a shift in the balance of power from Neustria to Austrasia. From then on the Carolingians, the descendants of Charles Martel, ruled the whole Frankish kingdom from their heartland around the mid-Meuse, first Herstal and later Aachen under Charlemagne.
raghupati-raghava-raja-ram: The bhajan was set to music by Vishnu Digambar Paluskar in Raga Mishra Gara.
