Besides the attributions to Tulsidas and Ramdas, it is also claimed to come from the Nama Ramayana, a Sanskrit devotional song attributed to Lakshmanacharya, which tells the Ramayana in 108 verses chanting the many names of Rama, each line ending with Rama. Only some versions of that work contain the verse Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram; others, such as the rendition by M. S. Subbulakshmi, do not.

The legend Gandhi preferred, as Anthony Parel tells it in Gandhi's Philosophy and the Quest for Harmony, credits the song to Tulsidas: on a pilgrimage to the Vishnu temple of Dakore the poet refused to bow in prayer until Vishnu revealed himself as Rama, and Rama then appeared in his mind with Sita and three devotees. Gandhi sang a version of his own, adding that the Ishwar of the Hindus and the Allah of the Muslims are one, to spread a message of reconciliation between the two communities. After his return from Noakhali he replaced the refrain Bhaj man pyare Sitaram with Bhaj man pyare Rama Rahim, bhaj man pyare Krishna Karim.

Gandhi's changes drew objections from both sides. Some Muslims resented his placing Allah on a par with Ram, and some Hindus objected to Islamic elements in a Hindu bhajan; Srila Prabhupada set the version aside as one made to unite Hindus and Muslims rather than for pure devotion. The disputes continued. In September 2022 Mehbooba Mufti accused the BJP of pushing a Hindutva agenda after a government directive had schoolchildren in Kashmir recite the song for Gandhi's 153rd birth anniversary, and in December 2024 the line Ishwar Allah tero naam set off protests at a BJP event in Patna.

The chant appears in many films, among them Bharat Milap (1942), Jagriti (1954), Purab Aur Paschim (1970), Gandhi (1982) and Lage Raho Munna Bhai (2006), where it is an important motif. Pete Seeger recorded it on his album Strangers and Cousins (1964), and a version by Ananda Shankar was played on a radio station of the game Grand Theft Auto: Liberty City Stories.
ragnachar: Ragnachar, also called Ragnarius, was a petty king, or regulus, one of several Frankish rulers of his time. According to the Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium, the deeds of the bishops of Cambrai, he and Clovis I were related through Clovis's mother, Basina, a Thuringian princess. In 486 he joined Clovis in the attack on Syagrius, the Roman ruler of the Domain of Soissons.

After Clovis was baptised a Christian in 496, about half of the 6,000 or so Frankish warriors who made up the armies of the various reguli refused to follow him and kept to Ragnachar, who remained a traditional pagan. Hincmar of Reims, in his life of Saint Remigius, wrote that many of the Frankish army not yet converted followed the king's relative Ragnachar across the Somme.

The Gesta says that his lust reached even the wives of his close associates. He was said to ignore his counsellors in favour of his courtier Farro, sharing every gift or meal with him and saying that it was enough for himself and his Farro. Those he offended plotted against him.

When Ragnachar refused Clovis entry into Cambrai, Clovis bribed his military followers, the leudes, with armlets and belts that looked like gold but were only gilded bronze. His spies, back from watching Clovis's army, are reported to have told him it was strong enough for him and his Farro. After his defeat the leudes caught Ragnachar and his brother as they fled and brought them to Clovis with their hands tied.

Gregory of Tours reports that Clovis asked why Ragnachar had shamed their family by letting himself be bound, then killed him with an axe, and killed the brother for failing to help him. Another brother, Rignomer, was later killed at Le Mans on Clovis's orders, and the family's riches and Ragnachar's kingdom passed to Clovis. When the leudes complained of the false gold, Clovis told them it was their payment for betraying their lord. Hincmar presents the episode as part of the conversion of the Franks by Remigius.
ragnall-ua-imair: The annals name Ragnall only as ua Ímair, grandson of Ímar, never by his father's name, so it cannot be known which of Ímar's three known sons, Bárid, Sichfrith or Sitriuc, was his father, if any; he may have descended through a daughter. He was most probably among the Vikings expelled from Dublin in 902 by Máel Finnia mac Flannacán, overking of Brega, and Cerball mac Muirecáin, overking of Leinster. He seems then to have settled in southern Scotland or the Isle of Man, and some scholars call him a King of Mann. The Irish annals first mention him in 914, defeating Bárid mac Oitir in a naval battle off the Isle of Man.

In 917 Ragnall and his kinsman Sitric Cáech led fleets to Ireland, Sitric to Cenn Fuait in Leinster and Ragnall to Waterford. Niall Glúndub, overking of the Northern Uí Néill, marched south against them, but the Vikings won at Mag Femen in County Tipperary, helped by Ragnall's timely reinforcement, and again at the Battle of Confey, where Augaire mac Ailella, overking of Leinster, was killed. Sitric took Dublin as king. In 918, the Annals of Ulster record, Ragnall left Ireland with Gofraid and the earls Ottir Iarla and Gragabai to fight Constantín mac Áeda, King of Scotland, at the Battle of Corbridge, after which he made himself king at York.

His rule there was challenged at once by Christian Vikings opposed to his paganism, who offered their submission to Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, until her death in June 918 ended the talks. Three issues of coins were struck while he ruled, perhaps on the orders of Hrotheweard, Archbishop of York. In about 920 he and the other northern kings came to an agreement with Edward the Elder; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says they chose Edward as father and lord, but many scholars doubt that Ragnall accepted him as overlord.

Ragnall died in 921, and the Annals of Ulster call him king of the fair foreigners and the dark foreigners. He may already have been dying in 920, when the Irish annals note that Sitric left Dublin and was replaced there by Gofraid. Sitric succeeded Ragnall as king of the Northumbrians at York. A man the annals call Mac Ragnaill, son of Ragnall, who raided Downpatrick in 942 and was killed within a week by Matudán, Overking of Ulster, may have been his son.
rahmon-nabiyev: Rahmon Nabiyevich Nabiyev was born on 5 October 1930 into a family of ordinary farmers of Tajik ethnicity in the Khojent District of the Leninabad Oblast. At 16 he began work as an accountant on a collective farm and entered the Leninabad Agricultural College, from which he graduated in 1949. He then studied at the Tashkent Institute of Irrigation and Agricultural Mechanization Engineers, and after graduating in 1954 he worked for two years as chief engineer of the machine-tractor station in Isfisor. He joined the Communist Party of the Tajik SSR in 1961 and became the republic's Minister of Agriculture in 1971 and Chairman of its Council of Ministers in 1973.

In 1982 Nabiyev became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Tajikistan, which made him head of the republic. He was dismissed in 1985 "for addiction to revelry and alcohol". From 1986 to 1991 he chaired the Tajik SSR's Nature Conservation Society, and on 23 September 1991 he became chairman of the Supreme Soviet, and so president. He stepped down 13 days later under pressure, then won the presidential election of November 1991 amid accusations of fraud by his opponents and was sworn in on 2 December. On 21 December 1991 he signed the Alma-Ata Protocol founding the Commonwealth of Independent States, and in May 1992 the Collective Security Treaty.

Protests against his government began in March 1992 and demanded democratic reforms. After disputes over the election, street demonstrations grew into civil war from 5 May 1992. On 7 September 1992 opposition forces ambushed Nabiyev on his way to Dushanbe airport and forced him to resign at gunpoint in the terminal. The Supreme Soviet accepted his resignation on 19 November and abolished the presidency.

Nabiyev died on 11 April 1993. The official cause was a heart attack, but other versions say he shot himself or was killed, and his family, including his daughter Munavvara Nabiyeva, doubted the official account. He was buried in Khujand after a state funeral. Streets and schools in Tajikistan bear his name. He is remembered for his part in the early history of independent Tajikistan and criticised for the civil war, which killed up to 150,000 people.
rai-people: The Rai, also called Khambu or Jimee, belong to the Kirat family of peoples. Their oral tradition, the Mundum, tells that the first Kirati ancestors came out of Khuwalung and entered Nepal's eastern hills through the Barahachhetra gorge of the Kosi valley, then travelled up the Arun, Dudh Koshi, Sun Koshi and Tama Koshi rivers. According to the genealogies, between 29 and 32 Kirati kings ruled the Kathmandu valley for many centuries, beginning with their chieftain Yalambar, until the Lichhavi dynasty defeated the last of them. The Kirati then moved east, and the groups that followed different rivers became the Rai, Yakkha, Sunuwar and Limbu.

In the eastern hills the Kirati ruled small territories for centuries, later divided into Wallo Kirat, Majh Kirat and Pallo Kirat. From about 1743 King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha began the campaign that united Nepal. When he invaded the Dhulikhel area in 1768, the Kirat king Chaukhat Mahindra Sing Rai and his brother Namsing Rai resisted for a long time, but Kirati rule in the eastern hills ended with the Gorkha conquest of 1772 to 1773.

The Rai number about 750,000 in eastern Nepal, mainly in districts such as Khotang, Bhojpur, Solukhambu, Sankhuwasabha and Dhankuta. They are the largest single ethnic community in Sikkim, live in Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Assam and Bhutan, and some have recently moved to the United Kingdom, Hong Kong and the United States.

Each subtribe, or thar, has its own language or dialect, and is divided into exogamous clans called pacha. A married woman keeps her own clan while her children take their father's. Most Rai are farmers, growing maize, millet, wheat and mustard on dry terraces and rice in wet fields.

Their religion rests on nature and ancestor worship, led by shamans such as the nakchong and bijuwa, with no religious hierarchy. Sumnima, the earth and ancestral mother, and Paruhang, the sky god, are their ancestral deities. Every house keeps Suptulung, the three hearth stones at the centre of every rite from birth to death. In the 2011 census about 65 per cent followed Kirat Mundhum and 30 per cent Hinduism. Sakela, danced at the full moons of Baisakh and Mangsir, is the best-known festival.
raichur: Raichur is a city and the headquarters of Raichur district in Karnataka, lying between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers on the Deccan Plateau at an average elevation of 407 metres. Summers are hot, often well above 40 degrees, and rain falls mainly between May and August. Raichur Junction is an important station on the Mumbai-Chennai railway line.

The recorded history of the district goes back to the third century BCE. Three minor rock edicts of Ashoka are found there, one at Maski and two near Koppal, which shows the area was part of the Mauryan emperor's dominions, governed by a viceroy. It then seems to have belonged to the Satavahanas, later to the Vakatakas and the Kadamba dominions. Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas of Badami made it a province under his son Adityavarma, and from the eighth century it lay within the dominions of the Rashtrakutas.

Raichur Fort has inscriptions in Persian, Urdu and Arabic that refer to its construction in the late 13th century, under the Kakatiya king Rudra. The fort passed to the Vijayanagara kingdom after the decline of the Kakatiyas, and was then disputed for nearly two centuries. The Bahmanis captured it in 1323. Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya expressed in his testament a wish that Raichur be recaptured, and Krishnadevaraya had it in mind from his coronation in 1509.

In 1520 a dispute arose when Krishnadevaraya sent a Muslim in his service, Saeed Maraikar, to Goa with money to buy horses and Maraikar instead went to Adil Khan and offered his services. Adil Khan refused to return him, and during the ensuing peace Krishnadevaraya made extensive preparations for a grand attack on the Raichur doab. Later the area belonged to the Hyderabad State, until the reorganisation of states on 1 November 1956.

Raichur is rich in inscriptions, with hundreds ranging from the Mauryan period to the end of the Muslim period, in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Kannada, Telugu, Arabic and Persian. The most important sites are Maski, Koppal, Kuknur, the Hatti gold mines, Mudgal, Lingsugur and Raichur itself. The ruins of the fort include many irrigation tanks and old temples. The city has a university of agricultural sciences and a university of its own.
rainier-iii-prince-of-monaco: Rainier Louis Henri Maxence Bertrand Grimaldi was born at the Prince's Palace of Monaco on 31 May 1923, the first native-born prince since Honoré IV in 1758. He was the only son of Hereditary Princess Charlotte, whom her father Louis II had legitimised by adoption, and Count Pierre of Polignac, who took the Grimaldi name on marriage. His parents divorced in 1933. He was educated in England at Summerfields and Stowe School, then at the Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland, the University of Montpellier and Sciences Po in Paris. In 1944 his mother renounced her right to the throne and he became Louis II's direct heir. He joined the Free French Army that September and received the Croix de Guerre.

Rainier became Sovereign Prince at 25, when Louis II died on 9 May 1949. He found a treasury that was practically empty, since Monaco's traditional gambling clientele had less money after the Second World War and rival gambling centres had opened. He chose to promote Monaco as a tax haven, a commercial centre and a tourist attraction. The Greek shipping owner Aristotle Onassis took control of the Société des Bains de Mer and wanted a gambling resort alone, but Rainier regained control in 1964.

He suspended the constitution in 1959 and ratified a new one in 1962. It reduced the sovereign's power, ended autocratic rule and placed power with both the prince and a National Council of eighteen elected members. In 1956 he married the American film actress Grace Kelly, with a civil ceremony on 18 April and a religious wedding at Saint Nicholas Cathedral on 19 April, watched by more than 30 million people. Their children were Caroline, Albert and Stéphanie.

Princess Grace died in 1982 after a car crash caused by a cerebral haemorrhage, and Rainier did not remarry. He founded the Princess Grace Foundation-USA that year to support young American artists, and established a postal museum in 1995. He died of complications of a lung infection on 6 April 2005, aged 81, and was buried beside his wife. His son succeeded him as Albert II. His reign lasted 56 years.
rainilaiarivony: Rainilaiarivony was born on 30 January 1828 in Ilafy, one of the twelve sacred hills of Imerina. His father Rainiharo was a military officer and conservative adviser to Queen Ranavalona I, prime minister from 1833 until his death in 1852 and the queen's consort. The family belonged to the Andafiavaratra clan of Ilafy, which with the Andrefandrova clan of Ambohimanga were the two most influential hova (commoner) families of the kingdom and held most political posts not given to the andriana (nobles).

After his father's death the queen promoted him and made him Royal Secretary and keeper of the Royal Seal. At 24 he led his first military expedition with his elder brother Rainivoninahitriniony against an uprising in the south-east. In May 1857 the brothers were drawn into a plot by Joseph-François Lambert and Prince Radama to overthrow Ranavalona; the plot was abandoned, and the brothers kept the queen's confidence. When she died in 1861 he held the palace guards in check and had Radama crowned before the soldiers, and Radama II made him Commander-in-Chief.

After Radama II was strangled on his brother's orders in May 1863, Rainilaiarivony proposed terms under which the sovereign needed the consent of the nobles to pass a death sentence or a new law. On 14 July 1864 Queen Rasoherina deposed Rainivoninahitriniony, and Rainilaiarivony took his place and married her.

In March 1876 he set up eight cabinet ministries and placed state envoys in the provinces to apply the law, collect taxes and report to Antananarivo. About a third of the island remained outside Merina authority. Abroad he established embassies in Mauritius, France and Britain, favoured an alliance with Britain, and agreed a treaty with the United States in 1867. He allowed foreigners to lease land for 99 years but not to buy it, and deliberately built no roads from the coast to the capital.

During the Second Franco-Hova War a French column bombarded the royal palace in September 1895, and he sought terms. Deposed by the French, he sailed for Algiers on 6 February 1896 and died there on 17 July. In 1900 his remains were brought back to the family tomb in Isotry, where General Gallieni spoke at the funeral.
rainulf-drengot: Rainulf belonged to the Drengot family, whose name probably comes from the Old Norse drengr, a valiant man or a lad. Exiled by Duke Richard II of Normandy for a violent crime, he set out with his brothers Osmond, Gilbert Buatère, Asclettin and Raulf on a pilgrimage to the shrine of the archangel Michael at Monte Sant'Angelo sul Gargano, in the Byzantine Catepanate of Italy, bringing a band of 250 warriors made up of other exiles, landless younger sons and adventurers.

Arriving in 1017, the brothers joined the Lombard Melus of Bari, who had rebelled against his Byzantine overlords, but at the Battle of Cannae the army of the catepan Basil Boioannes defeated them and Gilbert was killed. Rainulf, now leader, withdrew to Campania. There the band protected pilgrims for pay and served Pandulf IV of Capua, though, as the chronicler Amatus of Montecassino records, they sold their services to whoever offered most and took care that no Lombard prince won outright. Norman newcomers and local outlaws swelled their numbers.

Changing sides to Sergius IV of Naples, Rainulf received in 1030 the former Byzantine stronghold of Aversa with the title of count and the duke's sister in marriage. After her death in 1034 he married the daughter of the duke of Amalfi, a niece of Pandulf IV, and enlarged his lands at the expense of the abbey of Montecassino. Emperor Conrad II recognised his title in 1037, and after defeating the Byzantines in 1038 Rainulf declared himself prince and independent of Naples.

He conquered Pandulf's principality, and Conrad approved the union, which made the largest state in southern Italy. Rainulf was one of the leaders of the anti-Byzantine coalition that rebelled in 1040, fought in the victory at the Battle of Olivento in March 1041, and in 1042, after the success of his ally William Iron Arm, gained lordship over Siponto and Monte Gargano. He died in June 1045 and was succeeded by his nephew Asclettin, son of Asclettin of Acerenza. Amatus of Montecassino and William of Apulia are the main contemporary sources for his career.
raipur: Raipur lies near the centre of a large plain in central India, sometimes called the rice bowl of India, where hundreds of varieties of rice are grown. The Mahanadi River flows to the east of the city and dense forests lie to the south. The Maikal Hills rise to the north-west, the land to the north merges with the Chota Nagpur Plateau, and the Deccan Plateau lies to the south. The climate is tropical wet and dry. Temperatures stay moderate through the year except from March to June, when they sometimes rise above 48 °C, and about 1,300 mm of rain falls, mostly between mid-June and early October.

Raipur district, like the rest of the Chhattisgarh plain, was once known as Dakshina Kosala and is considered to have been under the Maurya Empire. A Gupta inscription of the sixth century at Arang, near Raipur, shows Gupta hegemony over the region. In the seventh century a Buddhist kingdom based at Bhandak, in modern Maharashtra, ruled it and was described by Xuanzang. A branch of that family moved to Sirpur and took control of all Dakshina Kosala, reaching its height under Tivaradeva, whose son inscribed almost all the temples at Sirpur. The Sharabpuriyas later ousted them and ruled for several centuries.

By the early ninth century the Kalachuris held the region. The Kalachuris of Ratnapura ruled at Ratnapur until the thirteenth century, and by the fourteenth century the Raipur branch had gained power. One of its kings is said to have conquered eighteen garh, or forts, of the enemy, which gave Chhattisgarh, the thirty-six forts, its name. The British set up the Raipur Municipal Committee on 17 May 1867, and it became a municipal corporation in 1973. Raipur was part of Madhya Pradesh until the state of Chhattisgarh was formed on 1 November 2000.

Raipur is the capital of Chhattisgarh and the administrative headquarters of Raipur district and Raipur division. It is the state's most populous city, and the 2011 census counted 1,010,433 people in the municipal corporation and 1,122,555 in the urban agglomeration. Raipur forms a tri-city metropolitan area with Bhilai and Durg. Steel, iron and rice milling are major industries, and a newer capital district, Naya Raipur, lies close by. Raipur Junction station stands on the Howrah–Nagpur–Mumbai line, and the Swami Vivekananda International Airport, formerly Mana Airport, lies 15 km south of the city. Swami Vivekananda spent two teenage years in Raipur, from 1877 to 1879, and Rajkumar College there was founded in 1882.
raja-ampat-islands: Raja Ampat, or the Four Kings, comprises over 1,500 small islands, cays and shoals around the four main islands of Misool, Salawati, Batanta and Waigeo, and the smaller Kofiau. It lies off the north-west tip of the Bird's Head Peninsula of New Guinea, just south of the equator. The regency covers around 70,000 square kilometres of land and sea, of which 8,034.44 km2 is land, and had 64,141 inhabitants at the 2020 census. The islands have a tropical climate, with temperatures ranging from 20 to 33 °C.

Archaeological evidence indicates that people first visited the islands over 50,000 years ago, when Misool and Salawati were connected to New Guinea. At Mololo Cave, excavations show early people processing tree resins and hunting native animals. Pottery-making communities arrived about 3500 to 3000 years ago and may have brought Austronesian languages. The name comes from local mythology about a woman who found seven eggs: three hatched and became kings who occupied the islands, and a fourth settled at Waigama but later migrated to Kalimuri (Seram). The kingdoms are historically named as Waigeo, Salawati, Sailolof, Misool and Waigama, though Waigama is locally not counted among the four, and Tidore does not count Sailolof.

The Portuguese navigator Jorge de Menezes made the first recorded European landing in 1526, on his way from Biak and the Bird's Head to Halmahera. Islam arrived in the 15th century through contacts with the Bacan Sultanate, and in the 16th and 17th centuries the Sultanate of Tidore had close economic and political ties with the islands, so that Raja Ampat was considered part of Tidore. After the Dutch invaded Maluku, they claimed it. William Dampier gave his name to the strait between Batanta and Waigeo, and in 1759 Captain William Wilson named a strait after his ship, the East Indiaman Pitt.

The islands belong to the Vogelkop-Aru lowland rain forests ecoregion, and two species of bird-of-paradise, the red and Wilson's, are endemic to Waigeo, Gam and Batanta. The surrounding waters lie in the Coral Triangle and hold more than 600 species of hard coral, about 75% of those known, and more than 1,700 species of reef fish. The Raja Ampat Marine Recreation Park was designated in 2009, and since 2024 the archipelago has been part of the province of Southwest Papua.
rajah-of-sarawak: Sarawak was part of the realm of Brunei until 1841, when Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II granted James Brooke a sizeable area in the south-west of his lands, around the town of Sarawak, now Kuching, and the nearby mining district of Bau. Brooke was later confirmed as Rajah of the territory, which became an independent kingdom. Under the first two rajahs the Raj grew, by lease or annexation of further land from Brunei, to cover much of northern Borneo.

Brooke's will settled the sovereignty of Sarawak on the male heirs of his nephew Charles Anthony Johnson Brooke. Charles inherited in 1868 and confirmed the succession in his own will of 1913, and on his accession in 1918 his son Vyner swore to uphold the will as the constitution of the state, an arrangement known as the Sarawak Sovereignty Trust.

James Brooke kept many customs and symbols of Malay monarchy but ruled absolutely: the Rajah made the laws and sat as chief judge in Kuching. He replaced the Bruneian system with one on the British model, with a civil service of mostly British officers in the district outstations. The rajahs set out to keep Western business from exploiting the indigenous peoples, while letting the Borneo Company help manage an economy built on antimony and then gold; after the Chinese uprising of 1857 the company took over the mines and helped recapture Kuching. Charles formed the Sarawak Rangers to police the state and man its forts. In 1941, before the Japanese invasion, Vyner ended the rajah's absolute rule by giving new powers to the Council Negri.

Vyner's attempt to cede Sarawak secretly to Britain in 1946 caused much controversy. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, and most native members of the Council Negri opposed it, and Britain passed a Bill of Annexation as well, being unsure of the cession's legality. When Governor Duncan Stewart was assassinated, Brooke fell under suspicion, though documents released later showed the British government knew he was not involved. Kuching keeps buildings of the Brooke era, among them the Astana, Fort Margherita, the Old Courthouse and the Sarawak State Museum, and Sarawak became a state of Malaysia in 1963.
rajahmundry: Rajahmundry stands at an average elevation of 14 metres, with the River Godavari flowing to its west. The Rajahmundry Traps, part of the Deccan Traps, lie on the river and interest geologists. The climate is hot and humid, with heavy monsoon rain at the end of summer. Paddy, sugarcane and many kinds of flowers are grown in the area. The earlier name Rajamahendravaram comes from the Sanskrit Rajamahendrapuram, meaning the city of King Mahendra. Under the Qutb Shahi, Mughal and Nizam rulers government records called it Rajmandri, which the British adapted as Rajahmundry. The state government restored the older name officially on 10 October 2015.

The city was established by Ammaraja Vishnuvardhana I (919–934 CE) and can be traced as a prominent settlement to the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra, who reigned around 1022 CE. Remains of 11th-century palaces and forts still exist. Later rulers included the Cholas, Kakatiyas, the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the Reddy Kingdom, the Gajapati Empire, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Bahmani and Golconda sultanates, and Nizam rule. The Dutch built a fort in 1602, which the British conquered in 1857 and converted into a jail in 1864.

The district of Rajahmundry was created in the Madras Presidency in 1823 and was reorganised in 1859 into the Godavari and Krishna districts. Rajahmundry was the headquarters of Godavari district until it was split into East and West Godavari in 1925. In the 19th century the city became a centre of reform. Kandukuri Veeresalingam, the author of Rajasekhara Charithram, the first Telugu novel, founded a monthly magazine and a girls' school at Dowleswaram in 1874, and the first widow remarriage took place on 11 December 1881. Julia Maitland founded a multilingual school and reading room in the town in 1837.

Rajahmundry is acclaimed as the birthplace of Telugu literature. The poet Nannayya, called Adi Kavi, the first poet, wrote the first third of the Andhra Mahabharatam, a Telugu retelling of the Mahabharata, with Tikkana and Yerrana completing the work. The city is the district headquarters of East Godavari in Andhra Pradesh. Its floriculture is known, and the Havelock Bridge of 1897 and the Godavari Arch Bridge of 1997 cross the river.
rajaraja-i: Rajaraja was born around 947, and the Government of Tamil Nadu recognises 3 November 947 as his birthdate. His birth name was Arulmozhi Varman. He was the son of the Chola king Parantaka II, also called Sundara Chola, and Vanavan Mahadevi of the Malaiyaman-Pari family, with an elder brother, Aditha II, and an elder sister, Kundavai. Aditha II died in mysterious circumstances, and inscriptions suggest he may have been assassinated. After Sundara Chola's death, Madhurantakan took the throne as Uttama Chola. When he died, Arulmozhi Varman became king in mid-985 and took the name Rajaraja, meaning King among Kings.

Rajaraja inherited a small kingdom around Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli that was recovering from attacks by the Rashtrakuta Empire, and he made it a well-organised empire with a powerful army and navy. Around 988 he destroyed Kandalur Salai in present-day Kerala, and his inscriptions in Kerala and the Pandya country show the conquest of Kollam, Madurai and Kodungallur. He took the title Mummudi Chola, three-crowned, for rule over the Cholas, Pandyas and Cheras. In 993 he conquered Anuradhapura, and the Cholas made northern Sri Lanka a province, with a capital at Polonnaruwa, which they renamed Jananathamangalam. A naval campaign brought the Maldives under Chola control.

In the 990s and 1000s Rajaraja annexed Gangapadi, Nolambapadi and Tadigaipadi and fought the Western Chalukyas under Satyashraya. In the east he defeated the Telugu Chola king Jata Choda Bhima over Vengi and arranged the marriage of his daughter Kundavai to the Eastern Chalukya prince Vimaladitya. In 1000 he began a land survey and assessment that reorganised the country into units called valanadus, and hereditary lords were replaced or made dependent officials. He also sent the first Chola mission to China. A follower of Shiva who also dedicated temples to Vishnu, he called himself Shivapada Shekhara. In 1010 he built the Peruvudaiyar Temple at Thanjavur, part of the UNESCO site Great Living Chola Temples.

Rajaraja is credited with gathering the hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, with the help of Nambiyandar Nambi, into the collection known as the Thirumurai, and was called Thirumurai Kanda Cholar. His coins showed the standing king on one side and a seated goddess on the other, and were copied by Sri Lankan kings. Near the end of his reign he made his son Rajendra Chola I co-regent. Rajaraja died in 1014 and Rajendra succeeded him, and went on to lead the Chola invasion of Srivijaya.
rajaram-i: Rajaram was born on 24 February 1670 to Shivaji and his second wife, Soyarabai, and was thirteen years younger than his half-brother Sambhaji. When Shivaji died in 1680, Soyarabai had the ten-year-old Rajaram installed on the throne, but the Maratha generals wanted Sambhaji, who took it. Rajaram married three times: Jankibai, daughter of the army chief Prataprao Gujar; Tarabai, daughter of the general Hambirrao Mohite; and Rajasbai of the Ghatge family of Kagal. Tarabai bore him Shivaji II and Rajasbai Sambhaji II.

After Sambhaji's execution, Rajaram was informally crowned at Raigad on 12 March 1689. As the Mughal general Itikad Khan, later Zulfikar Khan, besieged Raigad, Santaji Ghorpade raided Aurangzeb's camp at Tulapur, and with Dhanaji Jadhav routed Muqarrab Khan, who had captured Sambhaji. Rajaram slipped out of Panhala and, helped by Queen Chennamma of Keladi, reached Jinji in November 1689 after a month and a half; the poet Keshav Pandit's Rajaramacharita tells of the escape. Raigad fell to the Mughals.

Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung laid siege to Jinji in September 1690. With an empty treasury and no central army, Rajaram's government held its commanders with grants of estates, while Aurangzeb offered lands and titles to win them over. Maratha bands raided from Khandesh to the south coast and into Gujarat and Gondwana. Jinji fell on 8 January 1698, but the Shirke family hid Rajaram and gave him horses, and he set up his court at Satara Fort.

In his last campaign Rajaram plundered Jalna, Paithan and Beed, but Zulfikar Khan ambushed his laden army on its return, and he fought rearguard actions for fifty miles to Sinhagad. A lung weakness contracted at Jinji worsened, and he died of lung disease at Sinhagad on 3 March 1700. His widow Ambikabai committed sati. Tarabai proclaimed their son Shivaji II and ruled as regent, but after Shahu's release and his success in the struggle for the throne she set up a rival seat at Kolhapur, where Rajasbai soon deposed her and installed Sambhaji II; the Kolhapur line has continued since.
rajasthan: Rajasthan covers 342,239 square kilometres, about 10.4 per cent of India's area, and includes most of the wide and inhospitable Thar Desert, also called the Great Indian Desert. The Aravalli Range runs through the state from south-west to north-east for more than 850 kilometres, with Mount Abu, the state's only hill station, at its south-western end. About three fifths of the state lies north-west of the range. It borders the Pakistani provinces of Punjab and Sindh and five Indian states. The name means Land of Kings, from the Sanskrit rājā and sthāna. It first appears in print in the 1829 Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, and Rajputana, the earlier name for the region, appears in George Thomas's memoir of 1800.

Parts of the area belonged to the Vedic and Indus Valley civilisations. Kalibangan, in Hanumangarh district, was a major provincial capital of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and a settlement at Balathal, in Udaipur district, dates from 3000 to 1500 BCE. Stone Age tools between 5,000 and 200,000 years old have been found in Bundi and Bhilwara districts. The Rajputs, according to Topsfield, entered India from the north-west in the first millennium CE and set up kingdoms in what is now Rajasthan. The Pratiharas, with their seat at Kannauj, were acknowledged by almost all of North India up to the 10th century.

In 1178 a confederacy of Rajputs under Mularaja II of the Kingdom of Gujarat defeated the Ghurids at the Battle of Kasahrada. Prithviraj Chauhan led a confederacy of Rajput clans that defeated Muhammad Ghori at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, but Ghori decisively defeated him at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, and part of Rajasthan then came under Muslim rulers, with centres at Nagaur and Ajmer. At the beginning of the 13th century Mewar was the most powerful state of the region. The Rajputs resisted the Muslim incursions from the 13th century onwards and preserved Hindu culture at their courts.

The modern state was formed from the states of the Rajputana Agency of British India, which merged into the Indian Union. It includes most of Rajputana: nineteen princely states, three chiefships and the British district of Ajmer-Merwara. Jaisalmer, Marwar (Jodhpur), Bikaner, Mewar (Chittorgarh), Alwar and Dhundhar (Jaipur) were among the main Rajput states, Bharatpur and Dholpur were Jat states, and Tonk was ruled by Pathans.

Rajasthan is a state of India with its capital and largest city at Jaipur. Its main features include the Indus Valley ruins at Kalibangan, the Jain pilgrimage site of the Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu and Keoladeo National Park at Bharatpur, a World Heritage Site known for its birds.
rajatarangini: The chronicle is divided into eight books. The first covers the Gonanda dynasty, whose kings are given a total reign of 1266 years, and the second a line of other rulers given 192 years, none of whom has been traced in any other historical source. The third book tells of the restored Gonandiya dynasty, the fourth of the Karkota dynasty, the fifth and sixth of the Utpala dynasty, and the seventh and eighth of the first and second Lohara dynasties. Kalhana was an educated Sanskrit scholar connected with the highest political circles, and his writing is full of literary devices and allusions.

Historians value the work, but the earlier books show little evidence of authenticity. Ranaditya is given a reign of 300 years, and Mihirakula is dated 700 years before his father Toramana, the Huna king. Only from the fourth book does the account begin to agree with other evidence, and even there Kalhana greatly exaggerates the conquests of Lalitaditya Muktapida.

Later writers continued it. Jonaraja, writing under Zain-ul-Abidin, carried the history from about 1148 to 1459 in a second Rajatarangini; his disciple Srivara covered 1451 to 1486; the lost work of Prajyabhatta went on to 1513; and Suka's fourth Rajatarangini ended in 1597, just before Emperor Akbar's third visit to Srinagar. Zain-ul-Abidin also commissioned a Persian translation.

Horace Hayman Wilson partly translated the work into English and wrote an essay on it, The Hindu History of Kashmir. Fuller English versions followed by Jogesh Chandra Dutt in 1879, Marc Aurel Stein and Ranjit Sitaram Pandit in 1935, and the chronicle has appeared in Hindi, French, Urdu and Telugu. A Doordarshan television series based on it, Meeras, began in 1986.
rajendra-chola-i: Rajendra I was the son of Rajaraja I and was born in Thanjavur, probably around 971, though the exact date is unknown. He fought in the Chola army against the Western Chalukyas and the rulers of Anuradhapura, and acted as co-regent with his father from 1012. In that year he took Iditurai-nadu and Banavasi, and in 1013 Kollipaakkai. He became emperor on his father's death in 1014 and was succeeded by his son Rajadhiraja I in 1044.

During his reign the Chola Empire reached its zenith in the Indian subcontinent. He completed the conquest of Ruhuna in Sri Lanka, recovered the Pandya royal insignia, and subdued the Laccadives and the Maldives. In 1019 his forces marched through Kalinga to the Ganges and defeated Mahipala of the Pala kingdom of Bengal. Historians disagree on the nature of the expedition: early scholars such as V. Venkayya saw a pilgrimage to bring Ganges water to Chola territory, but K. A. Nilakanta Sastri and later historians argued it was military. To celebrate it Rajendra built a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, with a temple resembling the Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur, and took the title Gangaikonda Chola.

In 1025 his forces crossed the Indian Ocean and invaded Srivijaya. They sacked its capital Kadaram and Pannai in Sumatra and Malaiyur on the Malay Peninsula, and captured its ruler Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman. The war followed a request for help against Tambralinga from the Khmer king Suryavarman I, with whom Rajendra was allied. Srivijaya's maritime power declined, and for the next century Tamil trading companies such as the Manigramam and Ayyavole dominated the region's trade. Rajendra also took the title Kadaram Kondan. He was a follower of Shaivism who welcomed Buddhism, and built stupas in South-East Asia and South India.

Rajendra died in 1044 at Brahmadesam, in the present-day Tiruvannamalai district of Tamil Nadu. An inscription of Rajadhiraja I records that his queen Viramahadevi committed sati on his death. Rajendra had several queens and seven sons. Tradition also holds that he composed hymns to Siva. His expedition is recalled in the medieval Malay chronicle Sejarah Melaya as Raja Chulan, and Malay princes have borne names ending in Cholan or Chulan.
rajendra-prasad: Rajendra Prasad was born on 3 December 1884 into a Kayastha family at Ziradei, in what is now the Siwan district of Bihar. His father, Mahadev Sahai, was a scholar of Sanskrit and Persian, and his mother, Kamleshwari Devi, told him stories from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. He was the youngest child, and an elder sister cared for him after his mother died. He placed first in the entrance examination of the University of Calcutta, joined the Presidency College there in 1902 and took his M.A. in Economics with a first division in December 1907. In 1906 he helped to form the Bihari Students Conference at Patna.

He taught English at the Langat Singh College in Muzaffarpur, where he became principal, and later studied law in Calcutta. He passed the master's examination in law in 1915 with a gold medal, took a doctorate in law at Allahabad University and in 1916 joined the High Court of Bihar and Odisha. He formally joined the Indian National Congress in 1911 and met Mahatma Gandhi at the Lucknow session of 1916. Moved by Gandhi's conviction, he gave up his law practice and university duties when the Non-Cooperation resolution passed in 1920.

He organised relief after the Bihar earthquake of 15 January 1934, and was elected President of the Indian National Congress in October 1934, again in 1939 and a third time in 1947. After the Quit India Resolution of 8 August 1942 he was arrested and held in Bankipur Central Jail until 15 June 1945. In the interim government of 1946 he held the food and agriculture portfolio, and on 11 December 1946 he was elected President of the Constituent Assembly.

After the Constitution was ratified on 24 January 1950 he was elected the first President of India. As a ceremonial head of state he acted independently of any party and left Congress politics. He travelled widely abroad and was re-elected in 1952 and 1957, the only president to serve two terms. He took a more active part in state affairs after the dispute over the Hindu Code Bill. He retired in May 1962 and returned to Patna, was honoured with the Bharat Ratna and died on 28 February 1963, aged 78.
rajgad: Rajgad, whose name means ruling fort, stands in the Sahyadri range about 60 km south-west of Pune and about 15 km west of Nasrapur, 1,376 m above sea level. It was built on a hill called Murumbadevi Dongar, the mountain of the goddess Murumba, and the fort itself was formerly known as Murumbdev. The base of the hill is about 40 km across, which made the fort hard to lay siege to and added to its strategic value.

Treasure found at the neighbouring fort of Torna paid for building and fortifying Rajgad, which then served as the first capital of the Maratha Empire under Shivaji for almost 26 years, until the capital was moved to Raigad Fort. Shivaji is held to have spent more days at Rajgad than at any other fort, and many events of his life took place there, among them the birth of his son Rajaram I, the death of his wife Saibai and his return from Agra.

The head of Afzal Khan was buried in the walls of the Mahadarwaja of the Balle Killa. When Shivaji signed the Treaty of Purandar with the Mughal general Jai Singh I in 1665, handing 23 forts over to the Mughals, Rajgad was one of the 12 forts he kept.

The ruins of the fort include palaces, water cisterns and caves, and the Padmavati temple on the fort can hold around 50 people. In 2025 Rajgad was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as a component site of the Maratha Military Landscapes of India. It is much visited, above all during the monsoon, and is large enough that visitors often stay overnight.
rajgir: Rajgir lies in the Nalanda district of Bihar. Its name, from Rājagṛha, means 'house of the king', and it has also been called Girivraja, which Buddhaghosa explains as 'an enclosure of hills'. The Ramayana attributes its founding to Vasu, fourth son of Brahmā, and the Mahabharata to Bṛhadratha. The date of origin is unknown, though ceramics dating to about 1000 BCE have been found there.

Old Rajgir lies in a valley within low hills and was surrounded by an almost 50 km cyclopean wall that followed the hilltops, with 16 towers. Its walls are dated by excavation to about the 6th century BCE. New Rajgir, next to the modern town, was probably fortified around the 1st century BCE.

The Mahabharata tells of the city's king Jarasandha, whom Bhima killed in a wrestling match by splitting him in two. Rajgir was the first capital of Magadha, under the Haryanka kings Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, who kept his father Bimbisara in captivity there. The sources do not agree which of the two built its fortifications. Udayin, son of Ajatashatru, moved the capital to Pataliputra, modern Patna.

The Buddha spent several months at Rajgir meditating and preaching on Gridhra-kuta, the Hill of the Vultures, and initiated King Bimbisara there. The First Buddhist Council was held in the Saptaparni Cave under Maha Kassapa. Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, spent fourteen years at Rajgir and Nalanda, and Jains hold that Munisuvrata, the 20th Tirthankara, was born there. After the 1st or 2nd century CE the city seems to have declined; Xuanzang, visiting in the 7th century, found two old Buddhist monasteries still active but wrote mainly of its past.

Rajgir is a town in Bihar, known for its natural springs and the hills that dominate it. It remained important to Jains, and the Naulakhā temple of Munisuvrata at the foot of the hills holds an image installed in 1447. The cyclopean wall, about 2,500 years old, survives in places along the hills. Nalanda University, founded in 2010 nearby, is named after the ancient Nalanda university that lay near Rajgir.
rajiv-gandhi: Rajiv Gandhi was born in Bombay on 20 August 1944, the son of Indira and Feroze Gandhi, and belonged to the Nehru-Gandhi family, which was associated with the Indian National Congress; he was not related to Mahatma Gandhi. He attended The Doon School and then the University of Cambridge, returned to India in 1966 and became a pilot for the state-owned Indian Airlines. Although his mother was prime minister for much of the 1960s and 1970s, he remained apolitical.

After his younger brother Sanjay died in a plane crash on 23 June 1980, he entered politics at his mother's urging, addressing a national farmers' rally in Delhi on 16 February 1981. He won Sanjay's seat of Amethi that year.

On 31 October 1984 Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, after Operation Blue Star, the military action against Sikh separatists in the Golden Temple. Pressed by Zail Singh and others, Rajiv Gandhi became prime minister that day, at 40 the youngest in India's history. Mobs rioted against Sikhs in the following days, and sources estimate the Sikh dead at between 8,000 and 17,000. In December Congress won 414 of 541 seats in the Lok Sabha, the largest majority to that date.

His first measure, in January 1985, was an anti-defection law. He signed the Rajiv-Longowal Accord with the Akali leader H. S. Longowal in an effort to settle the Punjab problem. He appointed Sam Pitroda as adviser on public information infrastructure, and the public telecom companies MTNL and VSNL were developed. He also tried to liberalise the economy and trade policy. His government's handling of the Shah Bano case, in which Parliament in 1986 overrode a Supreme Court judgement, drew criticism, and in 1987 he sent peacekeeping troops to Sri Lanka, leading to open conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

The finance minister V. P. Singh, moved to defence, uncovered what became known as the Bofors scandal, concerning alleged payoffs by the Swedish arms company Bofors. Later reporting implicated Gandhi personally, though in 2004 he was posthumously cleared. Congress lost the 1989 election.

Gandhi remained Congress president and was campaigning for the 1991 elections when he was assassinated at Sriperumbudur on 21 May 1991. A woman, identified as Kalaivani Rajaratnam of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, bent to touch his feet and detonated explosives under her dress, killing him and at least 14 others. The Supreme Court judgement held that the LTTE chief Prabhakaran acted from personal animosity arising from the sending of the Indian Peace Keeping Force to Sri Lanka. In 1991 the Indian government posthumously awarded him the Bharat Ratna.
rajmahal: Rajmahal lies on the bank of the Ganges, with the Rajmahal hills on one side and the river on the other, in the Sahebganj district of Jharkhand. The area was earlier ruled by the Raja Mal sub-group of the Mal Paharia tribes, and the place was once known as Agmahal. During Mughal rule the region was also called Daman-i-Koh. Man Singh I chose the site for his capital in 1595–96 because it commanded the Teliagarhi Pass and the Ganges.

In 1576 the Battle of Rajmahal was fought between the Mughal Emperor Akbar and Daud Khan Karrani, Sultan of Bengal, of the Karrani dynasty. Daud Khan was captured and later executed by the Mughals. After the conquest of Odisha in 1592, Man Singh I, Mughal governor of Bengal Subah, came to Rajmahal, where he built a palace, a garden and a mosque and renamed the town Akbarnagar in 1595.

In 1610 Islam Khan moved the capital of Bengal to Dacca, now Dhaka. In 1639 Shah Shuja, governor of Bengal Subah and second son of Emperor Shah Jahan, made Rajmahal the capital again. It remained the seat of the Mughal viceroy until 1660 and a mint town until 1661. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Siraj-ud-Daulah halted at Rajmahal while fleeing from Murshidabad towards Patna. Mir Jafar's son Miran captured and murdered him there. In 1763 Mir Qasim was defeated by the British at the Battle of Udhwa nala at Rajmahal.

Under British rule, Santals were increasingly used for land reclamation after the Permanent Settlement of 1793, and the British built the Neel Kothi to process and store indigo. Daman-i-Koh became the origin of the Santhal Rebellion, in which leaders including Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu mobilized more than 10,000 Santhals against colonial authority and the zamindari system.

Rajmahal has an area of 7.5 square kilometres. It had a population of 22,514 at the 2011 census. Its remains include the Teliagarhi Fort, called the ancient gateway of Bengal, the Akbari Mosque, the palace of Shah Shuja with its marble pavilion Singhi Dalan facing the Ganges, the tombs of Miran and of Maina-Bibi, and the Neel Kothi. The nearby plant-fossil beds of the Rajmahal Formation are a National Geological Monument.
rajputana: Rajputana, meaning Land of the Rajputs, was a historical region of the Indian subcontinent that included mainly the whole of present-day Rajasthan, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, and adjoining areas of Sindh in southern Pakistan. Its area is estimated at 343,328 square kilometres. The Aravalli Range divides it into two parts: a sandy, unproductive area to the north-west, which includes part of the Thar Desert, and a higher area to the south-east that is comparatively fertile. The whole forms the hill and plateau country between the north Indian plains and the main plateau of peninsular India.

The region was long known as Gujratra, an early form of Gujarat, a name that came from the Gurjara-Pratiharas. The main settlements west of the Aravalli Hills came to be called Rajputana early in the medieval period. Rajput Kshatriyas from the region began entering it in the seventh century. It was known for its numerous Rajput kingdoms and principalities, with a strong warrior ethos and a tradition of honour, kinship and martial governance.

George Thomas, in his Military Memories, was in 1800 the first to apply the name Rajputana Agency to the region. The historian John Keay holds that the name was coined by the British but gained a retrospective authenticity: in his 1829 translation of Ferishta, John Briggs replaced the phrase Indian princes of an earlier version by Rajpoot princes. The East India Company adopted the name as the Rajputana Agency for its dependencies there.

Most of the ruling princes were Rajputs. Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Jaipur and Udaipur were the largest states, and the Rajputana Agency also included Jat princely states. The count of states differs in the sources: one gives 23 states, a Sardari, a Jagir and a British district, another 26 Rajput and 2 Jat princely states and two chiefships. In 1947 the states were integrated in stages and the State of Rajasthan came into existence, and the official term Rajputana was replaced by Rajasthan in the constitution of 1949. Some old areas of the south-east are now part of Madhya Pradesh and some in the south-west of Gujarat.
rajputs: Rajput, from the Sanskrit rajaputra, "son of a king", names a large cluster of castes, kin bodies and local groups of the northern Indian subcontinent that share a status and an ideology of descent. The literal sense is misleading, because although many Rajputs belonged to ruling clans, most were farmers. Before the 15th century the word meant a horse soldier, a trooper, a village headman or a subordinate chief. Modern scholars hold that nearly all Rajput clans arose from peasant or pastoral communities, and Satish Chandra describes them as miscellaneous groups that included Shudra and tribal groups and some Brahmans who took to warfare.

Scholars date the rise of Rajput clans to the seventh century, when dynasties such as the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Chahamanas, the Tomaras of Delhi, the Chaulukyas, the Paramaras, the Gahadavalas and the Chandela became lords of various localities. The lineages that faced the Ghaznavid and Ghurid invaders in the 11th and 12th centuries were called Rajput only later. Membership of the class became largely hereditary between the 12th and 16th centuries. A list of 1324 names 72 clans, among them the Chouhana, Pamara, Chandella, Kachchvaha and Guhilot.

From the reign of Akbar, Rajput leaders were drawn into the Mughal ruling elite through court appointments and marriage alliances, and the emperors Jahangir and Shah Jahan were born to Rajput mothers. The Sisodia clan of Mewar refused to send its women to the Mughal harem, which led to a siege and a mass suicide at Chittor. Between 1815 and 1823 the British East India Company took many Rajput states, including Udaipur, Jaipur, Bikaner and Sirohi, under its protection in return for tribute. In 1947 the rulers of the 22 princely states of Rajputana acceded to India, and the states were merged into Rajasthan in 1949 and 1950.

Rajput identity rests on patrilineal descent and marriage within recognised clans. In medieval Rajasthan the word was restricted to certain clans, while communities to the east had a fluid and inclusive usage, and the Rajputs of Rajasthan refused to acknowledge claims such as those of the Bundelas. In 1988 about 79 per cent of roughly 38 million Rajputs were estimated to be Hindu, nearly 20 per cent Muslim and about 0.5 per cent Sikh. Many clans honour Karni Mata as a family goddess, and Shiva and Durga are widely worshipped. The British classed Rajputs as a martial race, and the term Rajput painting is used for the art of Rajput courts in Rajasthan, central India and the Punjab Hills.
rakaposhi: Rakaposhi stands in the Karakoram range in Gilgit-Baltistan, about 100 km north of the city of Gilgit, between the Nagar and Bagrote valleys. Its Burushaski name means 'Shining Wall', and it is also called Dumani, 'Mother of Mist'. The mountain is extremely broad, measuring almost 20 km from east to west, and it descends without interruption for almost 6,000 metres from its summit to its base. On the north it rises 5,900 metres in only 11.2 km of horizontal distance from the Hunza River. The people of the Nagar and Bagrot valleys have dedicated the area as a community park, home to Marco Polo sheep, snow leopard, brown bear and wolves.

Martin Conway explored the south side of the mountain in 1892. In 1938 M. Vyvyan and R. Campbell Secord made the first reconnaissance and climbed a north-western forepeak of about 5,800 metres, and in 1947 Secord returned with H. W. Tilman and two Swiss climbers, who ascended by the Gunti glacier to 5,800 metres on the south-west spur. A Cambridge University team under Alfred Tissieres reached only 6,340 metres in 1954, and a British-American expedition under Mike Banks reached 7,163 metres on the Southwest Ridge in 1956.
The first recorded ascent came on 25 June 1958, when Mike Banks and Tom Patey, members of a British expedition, reached the summit by the Southwest Spur, both suffering minor frostbite.

It was over 20 years before another team succeeded. In 1979 a Polish-Pakistan expedition climbed the Northwest Ridge from the Biro Glacier, and a Japanese expedition from Waseda University led by Eiho Ohtani climbed the North Spur over six weeks with 5,000 metres of fixed rope. In 1984 a Canadian team climbed the North Spur in semi-alpine style with much less fixed rope.

The routes that have reached the summit are the Southwest Spur, long but not exceedingly technical, with some tricky rock pinnacles; the Northwest Ridge, longer and more technically difficult; and the North Spur, shorter but much more technically difficult. Attempts have also been made on the East Ridge, the North Face and from the Hinercha Glacier in the Bagrot Valley.
rakhigarhi: The village lies in the Hansi district of Haryana, about 150 km north-west of Delhi and some 27 km from the seasonal Ghaggar river. Jane McIntosh places it in the valley of the prehistoric Drishadvati River. The mounds are numbered RGR-1 to RGR-11. Five closely integrated mounds, RGR-1 to RGR-5, represent the main extent of the mature-phase town. RGR-6, known as Arda, was probably a separate and older settlement, reoccupied more than two thousand years later in the Kushan Period, and RGR-7 was a cemetery. Nearby sites of the civilisation include Bhirrana, Kunal, Siswal and Kalibangan.

Digging has revealed a planned town with roads 1.92 m wide, a little wider than at Kalibangan, and pottery like that of Kalibangan and Banawali. Walled pits are thought to have served religious ceremonies. Finds include terracotta seals, weights, copper fish hooks, a bronze vessel decorated with gold and silver, and a gold foundry with about 3,000 unpolished semi-precious stones. A mud-brick granary of the mature phase has seven chambers, with traces of lime and decomposed grass on its lower walls, perhaps against insects and damp.

In April 2015 four complete skeletons about 4,600 years old were excavated from mound RGR-7: two men, a woman and a child. A man of 35 to 40 and a woman in her early twenties lay side by side, with pots that probably held food and water as offerings. The bones of secondary burials were not charred, which rules out cremation, and the group burials and burials in a prone position set the cemetery apart from other Harappan sites. By 2016 a total of 61 skeletons had been found.

The Archaeological Survey of India began work in 1963, and a Kurukshetra University team under Suraj Bhan documented the site in 1969. Amarendra Nath led excavations from 1997 to 2000, after which digging stopped for years during an investigation into the misuse of funds. Deccan College under Vasant Shinde excavated from 2011 to 2016, and the Survey resumed in 2021. By 2020 only 5 per cent of the site had been excavated.

In May 2012 the Global Heritage Fund named Rakhigarhi one of the ten most endangered heritage sites in Asia, threatened by development pressures, insufficient management and looting. Villagers have built 152 houses on parts of mounds R4 and R5, and the Survey has planned to remove them and rehouse the families elsewhere.
rakoczis-war-of-independence: At the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottoman Empire renounced almost all its claims to Hungarian territories it had held since 1526. Nobles whose lands were returned had to prove their right to them and pay 10 per cent of their worth to the Habsburgs, or the property went to the empire's creditors. Peasants suffered from the long wars, and some wished for a return to Ottoman rule.

Francis II Rákóczi, one of the richest landlords in the kingdom, was brought up in Vienna under Habsburg supervision. He was arrested on 18 April 1700 for his correspondence with France, escaped from the fortress of Wiener Neustadt with the help of his wife Amelia and the prison commander, and fled to Poland, where he met Count Miklós Bercsényi.

The War of the Spanish Succession drew many Austrian troops out of Hungary, and kuruc forces rose at Munkács and asked Rákóczi to lead them. On 15 June 1703 about 3,000 armed men under Tamás Esze joined him near Lawoczne, and Bercsényi arrived with French funds and 600 Polish mercenaries. Most nobles held back, calling it a peasant rebellion, but the Hajdús joined him, and by late September 1703 his forces held most of Hungary east and north of the Danube, then Transdanubia.

The Diet near Szécsény elected him ruling prince of the Confederated Estates in September 1705. The victory of Austrian and English forces at Blenheim on 13 August 1704 prevented a union with his French-Bavarian allies, and French support dwindled. The copper coinage he issued was poorly accepted, and after 1706 his army retreated.
At Ónod on 13 June 1707 the Diet declared the deposition of the House of Habsburg from the Hungarian throne, but Louis XIV refused a treaty and no ally came.

On 3 August 1708 at Trencsén Rákóczi's horse stumbled and he fell unconscious; the kuruc forces thought him dead and fled, a defeat fatal to the uprising. Many leaders then went over to the emperor in hope of clemency. Serbs, Croats and Transylvanian Saxons mostly fought for the Habsburgs, while Slovaks, Rusyns, Polish volunteers and many Romanians fought for the kurucs. Rákóczi left Hungary for Poland on 21 February 1711.

The war ended with the Treaty of Szatmár, which granted political and religious amnesty to the kurucs. Though the uprising failed, it prevented Hungary's full integration into the Habsburg Empire, preserved its constitution and kept the powers of its parliament.
rakvere: Rakvere is the administrative centre of Lääne-Viru County, about 100 kilometres south-east of Tallinn and 20 kilometres south of the Gulf of Finland. The earliest signs of settlement, from the 3rd to 5th centuries CE, were found on Theatre Hill, and a wooden stronghold was built on the nearby hill of Vallimägi, the town's highest point.

A settlement called Tarvanpea, meaning head of an aurochs, was first mentioned in 1226 in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry. The Danish stronghold was recorded as Wesenbergh, a Middle Low German adaptation, in 1252, and the town was widely known as Wesenberg until the early 20th century.

After Denmark conquered northern Estonia it began building in stone in 1220. King Erik VI Menved granted Rakvere Lübeck rights on 12 June 1302. Denmark sold its Estonian lands to the Livonian Order in 1346, and a large stone castle was then built on Vallimägi, protected by towers and courtyards.

Russian troops captured Rakvere in 1558, the first year of the Livonian War, and Sweden heavily damaged it in the Siege of Wesenberg in 1574. Sweden took the town in 1581 and passed it to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1602; Polish troops destroyed the castle in 1605, after which it was never rebuilt. The town was burned down in 1703 during the Great Northern War. Estonia and Livonia capitulated in 1710, and under the Treaty of Nystad of 1721 the region became part of the Russian Empire for the next 200 years.

The Red Army held Rakvere from 16 December 1918 to 12 January 1919, during the Estonian War of Independence. Hundreds of Rakvere's residents were deported on 14 June 1941, and Germany occupied the city from 7 August 1941 to 19 September 1944. Rakvere again became a self-governing municipality on 24 January 1991.

The ruins of the castle on Vallimägi are open to visitors, with exhibitions on everyday life in the 16th century. Trinity Church, originally dedicated to St Michael, dates from the 15th century and was rebuilt after damage in the Livonian War and later conflicts. Pikk Street is the oldest street in the town. A bronze aurochs by Tauno Kangro, unveiled in 2002 for the town's 700th anniversary, recalls the old name Tarvanpea. The composer Arvo Pärt lived in Rakvere from 1938 until at least 1965. Rakvere is reportedly Europe's smallest town with its own professional theatre.
ralpachen: Ralpachen, born about 802, was the second of five brothers and the 40th king of Tibet. His elder brother Tsangma took Buddhist vows, while the third, U Dumtsen, known as Langdarma, is described in the sources as unfit to reign. Under Ralpachen the Tibetan empire reached its largest extent, taking in parts of China, India and Nepal, Khotan, Balti, Gilgit and Hunza, Zhangzhung, almost all of modern Xinjiang and Gansu, and the area of present-day Sichuan. His power rested on the military leadership of Zhang 'Bro sTag, who raided to within two days' journey of the Uyghur capital in 816 and attacked the Chinese town of Yanzhou in 819.

Fighting with China and the Uyghur Khaganate ended with a Sino-Tibetan treaty completed in 821 or 822, which kept the peace for more than two decades; Buddhists in both countries are said to have sought mediation. Tibet also made peace with the Uyghurs and apparently with Nanzhao in 822. A bilingual account of the treaty and the border, inscribed on a stone pillar erected in 823, stands outside the Jokhang in Lhasa, and similar pillars were set up in China and at the border.

Ralpachen was a generous supporter of Buddhism. He invited craftsmen, scholars and translators from China, Nepal, Kashmir and Khotan, and ordered that translations be made directly from Sanskrit. Translation was aided by the Mahāvyutpatti, a Sanskrit-Tibetan lexicon giving standard Tibetan equivalents for thousands of terms. He built a nine-story temple at 'U shang, assigned revenue from seven families to support each monk, and introduced standard weights and measures based on Chinese ones. His nickname means the man with long braids, from the story that he let monks sit on their ends.

According to the most common Tibetan tradition he was murdered by two pro-Bon ministers, who set his anti-Buddhist brother Langdarma on the throne. Other accounts say he slipped on the steps of the temple of Maldro, or, following the Old Book of Tang, fell ill and died, and a Dunhuang manuscript holds a prayer for the king's health. He died late in 838 and was buried near the Yarlung Valley. Langdarma then nearly destroyed Buddhism in Tibet. Tibetans remember Ralpachen as the third of the three Dharma Kings, with Songtsen Gampo and Trisong Detsen.
ralph-abercromby: Ralph Abercromby was born on 7 October 1734 at Menstrie Castle, Clackmannanshire, the eldest surviving son of the lawyer George Abercromby, and spent much of his childhood at Tullibody House. He attended Rugby School, studied moral and natural philosophy and civil law at the University of Edinburgh, and continued civil law at Leipzig University with a view to becoming an advocate. On his return he chose the army instead and became a cornet in the 3rd Dragoon Guards in March 1756.

He served in the Seven Years' War, where he studied the methods of Frederick the Great, and sat in Parliament for Clackmannanshire from 1774. He sympathised with the Patriot cause in the American War of Independence and served in Ireland rather than in North America. When France declared war in 1793 he commanded a brigade under the Duke of York in the Netherlands and was wounded at Fort St Andries on the Waal in 1794.

Appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Leeward and Windward Islands in 1795, he crushed Julien Fédon's rebellion on Grenada, retook Saint Lucia at the cost of 566 men and put down the rising on Saint Vincent in 1796. After Trinidad he secured Demerara and Essequibo, but an assault on San Juan, Puerto Rico, failed in April 1797. As Commander-in-Chief in Ireland in 1798 he publicly criticised the army's indiscipline under his predecessor, the 2nd Earl of Carhampton, sought to restore civil authority and resigned for lack of support. In 1799 he led the landing at Callantsoog in the Anglo-Russian expedition to North Holland.

In 1801 he landed his army at Aboukir against strong opposition. At Alexandria on 21 March the French under Jacques-François Menou attacked before dawn; Abercromby was briefly captured by French dragoons and rescued by a highlander of the 42nd, and a musket-ball struck his thigh. He stayed in command until the battle was won, was carried aboard HMS Foudroyant and died on 28 March 1801. He was buried in Fort Saint Elmo in Valletta, where St John's Bastion was renamed Abercrombie's Bastion. Parliament voted him a monument in St Paul's Cathedral, and his widow was created Baroness Abercromby.
ram-khamhaeng: Ramkhamhaeng was a son of Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao, who ruled as Pho Khun Si Inthrathit, and his queen Sueang, though folk legend gives his parents as an ogress named Kangli and a fisherman. He had two brothers and two sisters. At 19 he took part in his father's successful campaign to capture the city of Sukhothai, formerly a vassal of the Khmer Empire, which established the kingdom's independence. For his courage in battle he was reportedly granted the title Phra Ram Khamhaeng, Rama the Bold.

His elder brother Ban Mueang became king after their father's death and appointed him ruler of Si Satchanalai. Ramkhamhaeng succeeded Ban Mueang. The historian Tri Amattayakun suggests he acceded in 1279, the year he planted a sugar palm in Sukhothai.

The most significant event at the start of his reign was the elopement of one of his daughters with the captain of the palace guards, a commoner. The commoner went on to found the Burmese Hanthawaddy kingdom and to commission the Code of Wareru, which became a basis for the law of Thailand used in Siam until 1908.

Ramkhamhaeng sent embassies to Yuan China from 1282 to 1323 and imported the techniques of making the ceramics known as Sangkhalok ware, long a major export of Sukhothai. He had close relations with the rulers of nearby cities, especially Ngammueang of Phayao and King Mangrai of Chiang Mai. His campaign against Cambodia left the Khmer country utterly devastated. Tradition credits him with creating the Thai alphabet from Khmer, Sanskrit, Pali and Grantha scripts, and with firmly establishing Theravada Buddhism as the state religion.

It is speculated that his kingdom reached Lampang, Phrae and Nan in the north, Phitsanulok and Vientiane in the east, Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south and Mon kingdoms in the west. Yet in the mandala model of politics, kingdoms such as Sukhothai had no distinct borders and were centred on the strength of the capital, so claims of a large kingdom served to assert Siamese dominance over mainland Southeast Asia.
According to the Chinese History of Yuan, Ramkhamhaeng died in 1298 and was succeeded by his son Loe Thai. Legend holds that he perished in the rapids of the rivers of Sawankhalok.

Much of the traditional information about him comes from the Ramkhamhaeng stele, composed in 1292, which holds vague facts about the king. It is kept in the Bangkok National Museum and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2003. Ramkhamhaeng University, the first Thai university with an open-door policy, is named after him.
ram-mohan-roy: Ram Mohan Roy was born on 22 May 1772 at Radhanagar in Hooghly District, in the Bengal Presidency. His great-grandfather was a Rarhi Kulin Brahmin; in the 19th century Kulinism was a synonym for polygamy and the dowry system, both of which he later campaigned against. He became a scholar of Sanskrit, Persian and English, and also knew Arabic, Latin and Greek. In his childhood he witnessed the death of his sister-in-law by sati; he tried to protest, but she was burned alive.

From 1803 to 1815 he worked in the East India Company's Writing Service, first as private clerk at Murshidabad and then with the collector John Digby. In 1804 he wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin, A Gift to Monotheists, in Persian.

In 1814 he started the Atmiya Sabha, a discussion circle in Calcutta that propagated the monotheism of the Vedanta and campaigned against idolatry, caste rigidity and meaningless ritual. He wrote against Trinitarian Christianity and published The Precepts of Jesus in 1820. He founded the Anglo-Hindu School in 1822 and the Vedanta College in 1826. His Bengali weekly Sambad Kaumudi, begun in 1821, covered freedom of the press and the admission of Indians to high office. His Gaudiya Vyakaran, published in 1826, was the first complete Bengali grammar.

In 1828 he founded the Brahmo Sabha with Debendranath Tagore, a forerunner of the Brahmo Samaj, whose beliefs rested on the worship of one God and the equality of all people. He attacked sati, polygamy, child marriage and caste, and he petitioned against sati in 1829. In 1830 he went to England as an envoy of the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who had given him the title of Raja, to make sure that Lord William Bentinck's Bengal Sati Regulation of 1829 was not overturned and to seek a larger stipend for the emperor.

In early September 1833 Roy came to Bristol to visit his Unitarian friend Lant Carpenter. He fell ill in mid-September and died at Stapleton on 27 September 1833 of meningitis or a chronic respiratory ailment. He was first buried at Stapleton Grove and in 1843 reburied at Arnos Vale Cemetery, where a chhatri designed by William Prinsep stands over the tomb.

Roy tried to join Western culture with the best of India's own traditions. His commitment to English education later prompted a debate between Mahatma Gandhi, who objected to it, and Rabindranath Tagore, who answered that Roy had the full inheritance of Indian wisdom and was never a schoolboy of the West.
ram-prasad-bismil: Ram Prasad Bismil was born on 11 June 1897 to Muralidhar and Moolmati Devi in a Tomar Rajput family. He learned Hindi from his father and Urdu from a moulvi, entered an English-language school against his father's wishes and joined the Arya Samaj in Shahjahanpur, where Swami Dayananda Saraswati's Satyarth Prakash inspired him.

Bismil was his pen name, meaning wounded, and Pandit an honorific for his learning. As a student of eighteen he wrote the Hindi poem Mera Janm after the death sentence on Bhai Parmanand and showed it to Swami Somdev. In Lucknow he and friends published a book on American independence under a fictitious author's name, and the government of the province banned it.

Bismil formed the group Matrivedi with the teacher Genda Lal Dixit, whose own youth organisation was called Shivaji Samiti. On 28 January 1918 he distributed the pamphlet Deshvasiyon Ke Nam Sandesh with his poem Mainpuri Ki Pratigya, and the group raised money through three robberies in 1918. When police closed in he escaped by swimming the Yamuna underwater, and the Mainpuri Conspiracy case ended on 1 November 1919 with Bismil and Dixit declared absconders.

He lived in hiding, publishing books including the poems Man Ki Lahar and translations from Bengali. After the Gaya session of 1922 he and other young men broke with Gandhi over the end of non-co-operation, and in 1923 he drafted the party's constitution, which a meeting at Cawnpore on 3 October 1924 named the Hindustan Republican Association.

Over 40 revolutionaries were arrested after the Kakori train robbery, although only ten had taken part, and one passenger, Ahmed Ali, was accidentally shot dead. Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Nath Lahiri were sentenced to death after 18 months of legal process, and an appeal to the Privy Council on 16 September 1927 failed. Lahiri was hanged two days earlier and Bismil at Gorakhpur Jail. He wrote his autobiography as a condemned prisoner, and it was published in 1928 as Kakori ke shaheed. His memorials include a statue at Shahjahanpur, a railway station named for him and a postage stamp issued on 19 December 1997.
rama: The word Rama is Vedic Sanskrit with two contextual meanings. In the Atharva Veda it means dark or black, and in other Vedic texts pleasing, delightful or beautiful. The primary source of his life is the Sanskrit epic Ramayana, composed by the sage Valmiki, which exists in many versions across the regions of India.

Some Hindu texts place Rama in the Treta Yuga, which their authors estimate to have existed before about 5000 BCE. The archaeologist H. D. Sankalia calls this estimate pure speculation and suggests that the incidents of the story could have taken place between 1,500 and 700 BCE. Jain and Buddhist texts also tell the story, calling him Pauma or Padma in Jain accounts, with details that differ from the Hindu versions.

According to Valmiki, Rama was born in Ayodhya, capital of Kosala, to Dasaratha and his first wife Kausalya, and had the half-brothers Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna. He married Sita and spent fourteen years in forest exile, during which Sita was kidnapped by the demon-king Ravana. After the war he returned to Ayodhya and was crowned, and his rule, Rama rajya, is described as just and fair. Many believe that people lit lamps for his return, which links the festival of Diwali with him.

Hindus hold Rama to be a complete avatar of Vishnu, and some regard him as the ultimate Brahman. He is also viewed as the ideal man. By Hindu belief this avatar does not display Vishnu's divine powers and lives as a human. Scholars such as Paula Richman note that there are hundreds of versions of his story, none the single original, each valid in its local tradition.

The Ramayana has been retold in most major Indian languages, among them Kambar's Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century, Krittibas Ojha's Bengali version in the 15th and Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramacharitamanasa in the 16th. Kalidasa's Raghuvamsa suggests that the legend was well established by the 4th or 5th century CE. The Ramanandi Sampradaya, founded by the 14th-century poet-saint Ramananda, became the largest Hindu monastic community in modern times.

The story arrived in Southeast Asia in the 1st millennium CE, and its influence grew in Java, Bali, Malaya, Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. It inspired Madhubani and Rajput paintings and the Ramlila performances held each autumn.
rama-i: Rama I was born Thongduang in 1737, during the reign of King Boromakot of Ayutthaya. His father, Thongdi, was a nobleman of Mon ancestry at the royal court, a descendant of Kosa Pan, who had led King Narai's embassy to the French court. His mother, Daoreung, was the eldest daughter of a wealthy Hokkien Chinese magnate. As a young man he entered the court as a royal page to King Uthumphon, spent a time as a monk in 1757, married Nak in 1760 and became deputy governor of Ratchaburi, a frontier town on the western approaches of the kingdom.

When Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, he joined Phraya Wachiraprakan, later King Taksin, who founded the Kingdom of Thonburi in 1768. Together with his brother Bunma he became Taksin's most successful general. He rose to Chaophraya Chakri, chief minister for the northern provinces, and commanded armies against the Burmese, Khmer and Lao. In 1774 he went to Lan Na to free it from Burmese rule with the help of Phraya Kawila of Lampang, and in 1778 the three Lao kingdoms of Vientiane, Luang Prabang and Champasak fell to Siam. He became the first Somdet Chao Phraya, a rank equal to that of royalty.

In 1781 he was campaigning in Cambodia when the rebellion of Phraya Sun deposed Taksin. Returning in 1782, he defeated the rebels, took power and crowned himself on 6 April 1782, founding the Chakri dynasty. Later sources widely report that Taksin was executed, contradicting some earlier ones.
