Rama I moved the capital to the east bank of the Chao Phraya River, for its better position and to start with a clean slate, and named it Rattanakosin, keeping place of the Emerald Buddha, which he installed at Wat Phra Kaew within the new Grand Palace.

The Burmese–Siamese War of 1785 to 1786, called the Nine Armies War, was the last major Burmese assault on Siam; King Bodawpaya's attack was defeated, and a second attempt the next year was quickly beaten at Tha Din Daeng. He convened a council on the Buddhist canon in 1788, and in 1805 the court compiled the Three Seals Law, which served as a reference for Siam's traditional legal system into the modern reform era.

Rama I died in Bangkok on 7 September 1809, aged 72, after a short acute illness, and was succeeded by his son Prince Isarasundhorn as Rama II. His reign marked a revival of Siamese culture and state organisation after the collapse of the kingdom in 1767, and Siam reasserted itself as a mainland Southeast Asian power with suzerainty over Laos, Cambodia and the northern Malay states.
rama-ii: Rama II was born Chim in Amphawa District, during the Ayutthaya Kingdom, a son of Luang Yokkrabat of Ratchaburi, who later became King Rama I, and of Nak, later Queen Amarindra. When Ayutthaya fell to Burmese invaders in 1767, his father joined Taksin's forces to recapture it and rose to high military rank under Taksin. In 1782 his father crowned himself King of Siam, and Chim became Prince Itsarasunthon. In 1807 he was appointed to the Front Palace as Uparaja, succeeding his uncle Maha Sura Singhanat, who had died in 1803. His children included Prince Thap, the future Rama III, and Mongkut, the future Rama IV.

As the eldest surviving legitimate son of Rama I, he succeeded to the throne in 1809. No royal naming system existed at his coronation: his son Nangklao later called him Loetlasulalai, and his other son Mongkut changed this to Loetlanaphalai. Soon after his accession Prince Kshatranichit, a surviving son of Taksin, rebelled as a pretender, and Prince Thap crushed the revolt. In the same year the Konbaung king Bodawpaya marched into Chumphon and razed Thalang. The Thalang campaign that recaptured it was the last Burmese invasion of Thai territory.

The reign was largely peaceful and is known as the golden age of Rattanakosin literature. Rama II was himself a noted poet and artist, and poets employed at his court included Sunthorn Phu, author of Phra Aphai Mani, and Narin Dhibet. In 1811 the grand royal funeral of Rama I was held, and a cholera epidemic broke out in Bangkok. He established an education and examination system for Buddhism in nine levels and restored the Vesak festival in 1817. The first mission to China, to the Jiaqing Emperor, was sent in 1810, and the Portuguese governor of Macau sent the first formal Western mission since Ayutthaya in 1818.

Rama II died very suddenly in July 1824. Contemporary accounts gave strangury as the cause, but there were persistent rumours of poison. Under the succession rule in theory in force the throne would have passed to Mongkut, son of the queen, but Prince Chetsadabodin, his elder half-brother, succeeded on the same day, since his experience in putting down the revolt and in the ministry of trade counted for more. The king is believed to have had over 240 grandchildren, and he had 83 children.
rama-iii: Nangklao was born Prince Thap on 31 March 1788 to Prince Itsarasunthon, the future Rama II, and Chao Chom Manda Riam, who came from a Muslim noble family of the south. When Itsarasunthon became king in 1809, Prince Kshatriyanuchit, a surviving son of Taksin, revolted as a pretender, and Thap was sent to suppress the rebellion. His father praised his competence, gave him the title Chetsadabodin and made him Kromma Tha, minister of trade and foreign affairs. He gained the sobriquet Chao Sua for his commercial acumen and developed an affection for Chinese goods and culture. John Crawfurd, who met him in 1822, called him the most intelligent of the princes and chiefs of the Siamese court.

When Rama II died suddenly in 1824 without naming a successor, the assembled senior officials considered Chetsadabodin the more competent choice than his half-brother Prince Mongkut, who had become a monk that year. Foreign observers, who expected the queen's son to inherit, wrongly saw a usurpation. Chetsadabodin was crowned in 1824, strengthened the tax-farming system and, through the Burney Treaty, further liberalised foreign trade and reduced the royal warehouse monopoly. He is remembered as the father of Thai commerce.

The Laotian king Anouvong advanced on Korat and towards Saraburi in 1825 but withdrew when the Korat captives rebelled. Siamese forces defeated him and took Vientiane, and in 1827 Nangklao ordered the city's total destruction; Anouvong was captured and died in 1829. In Cambodia, Siam and Vietnam fought over influence for years, and the war ended when Ang Duong was installed as Cambodian king under the patronage of both. In 1833 Edmund Roberts concluded a treaty of amity and commerce, signed on 20 March.

A devout Buddhist, Nangklao built or repaired more than fifty temples, among them Wat Pho, the site of the first university in Thailand. He also had the Tipitaka, the Buddhist canon, revised for distribution throughout the kingdom.

Nangklao died on 2 April 1851 without naming a successor. He had 51 children but had raised none of his consorts to queen, and the throne passed to his younger half-brother Mongkut. His reign saw Siam's territory reach its largest extent. In Thailand 31 March is observed as King Nangklao Memorial Day.
ramadan: Muslims hold that the Quran was revealed during Ramadan, and that Muhammad received his first revelation on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, generally believed to be an odd-numbered night in the last ten days of the month. They also hold that all earlier scriptures were revealed in this month. They were first commanded to fast in the second year of the Hijra, 624 CE, but believe that fasting has always been necessary for believers to attain fear of God. Philip Jenkins argues that the fast grew out of the strict Lenten discipline of the Syrian Churches, a view other scholars share and some Muslim academics dispute.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and each month begins when the first crescent of the new moon is sighted. Since the calendar has no intercalation, Ramadan migrates through the seasons. It lasts 29 or 30 days. Many Muslims insist on a local sighting of the moon to mark the start, while others use the calculated time of the new moon or the declaration of Saudi Arabia, so dates differ between countries, usually by a day.

Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty and are not ill, travelling, elderly, breastfeeding, pregnant or menstruating. The predawn meal is the suhur and the meal that breaks the fast at sunset is the iftar, traditionally opened with dates in memory of Muhammad's practice. Muslims also abstain from sinful speech, devote more time to prayer and charity, and are encouraged to read the whole Quran over the month. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, declared after the crescent of the next month is sighted or after 30 days of fasting.

Customs of the month vary widely. In some Islamic countries lanterns are strung up in public squares, a tradition believed to have originated under the Fatimid Caliphate, when the rule of Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah was acclaimed by people holding lanterns. In the Middle East a mesaharati beats a drum through the neighbourhood to wake people for suhur. In Shia Islam the 19th to 21st days of the month are marked in mourning for Ali, the fourth Rashidun caliph, who was struck during morning prayer on the 19th day in 40 AH and died on the 21st. In the USSR the practice of Ramadan was suppressed by officials, and in Albania Ramadan festivities were banned during the communist period, though many Albanians fasted in secret.
ramakien: The Ramayana reached Southeast Asia with Buddhist missionaries, Indian traders and scholars who dealt with Khmer kingdoms such as Funan and Angkor and with Srivijaya. Maritime trade with the Chola and Pallava empires of South India may also have helped to carry the Ramakatha tradition, and Kamban's Ramayan, popular at the Pallava court, may have led to a more many-sided Tosakanth, the Ramakien's Ravana, than Valmiki's. The Thai took the epic from the Khmer, and it was told in the shadow theatre, nang. Its first written form was made in the 18th century under Ayutthaya, and most editions were lost when armies from Burma destroyed the city in 1767.

King Rama VI traced the sources of the Ramakien and found three: Valmiki's Ramayana, the Vishnu Purana and the Hanuman Nataka. The version known today was compiled under the supervision of Rama I, founder of the Chakri dynasty, who wrote parts of it. His son Rama II rewrote parts for khon drama, giving Hanuman a larger role and adding a happy ending.

The story is set in the landscape and culture of Ayutthaya, where Phra Narai, the Thai form of Vishnu, is reborn as Phra Ram. The first part tells the origins of the main characters, including Thotsakan (Ravana), who is Nonthok reborn, and Hanuman. In the second, Phra Ram and Nang Sida fall in love before an archery contest, he is banished to the forest, and Thotsakan abducts Sida to Lanka. With Hanuman and the ape king Sukhrip, Phra Ram builds a causeway to Lanka and kills Thotsakan and his son Intharachit, and Sida passes a fire ordeal.

In the third part Phra Ram sends Sida away after she draws a picture of Thotsakan. She finds refuge with the hermit Valmiki and bears two sons, Phra Monkut and Phra Loph. When Phra Ram asks her to return she refuses and disappears into the Underworld, and Phra Isuan finally brings the two together again.

The clothes, weapons, topography and nature of the epic are described in Thai style, and its Buddhist outlook gives Thai legend a creation myth and spirits that sit with Thai animist belief. Both the khon and the nang dramas derive from it. A painted version covers the walls of the Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok, and many statues there show its characters. The Ramakien of Rama I is regarded as a masterpiece of Thai literature and is still read and taught in schools. In 1989 Satyavrat Shastri translated it into a Sanskrit epic poem, the Ramakirtimahakavyam, which won eleven awards.
ramakrishna-mission: Ramakrishna (1836 to 1886) was a priest at the Dakshineswar Kali Temple who attracted monastic and household disciples. In 1886, shortly before his death, he gave ochre cloths of renunciation to young disciples planning to become renunciants and entrusted them to Vivekananda. After his death they formed the first monastery, or Math, at Baranagore and took informal monastic vows on the night of 24 December 1886.

Vivekananda became a wandering monk and in 1893 was a delegate at the Parliament of the World's Religions, where his speech opening with the words Sisters and Brothers of America brought him wide recognition. He founded the first Vedanta Society in the United States, in New York. Returning to India, he founded the Ramakrishna Mission on 1 May 1897. The same year Swami Akhandananda began famine relief at Sargachi, and Swami Brahmananda became the first president of the Order. After Vivekananda's death in 1902, Sarada Devi, the spiritual counterpart of Ramakrishna, acted as advisory head of the young organisation.

The Math and the Mission are the two organisations directing the Ramakrishna movement. The Math, also called the Ramakrishna Order, is the monastic body concerned with spiritual development; the Mission is the humanitarian body that carries out medical, relief and educational work. The Mission was registered in 1909 under Act XXI of 1860, and the elected trustees of the Math also serve as its Governing Body. The Baranagar monastery moved to Alambazar in 1892, then to a garden house near the present site in 1898, and in January 1899 to the plot at Belur acquired by Vivekananda.

The movement teaches a modern Vedanta rooted in Advaita, with elements of Shakta and Vaishnava traditions, structured around the four paths of jnana, bhakti, karma and raja yoga, and holds that all religions lead to the same goal. Its work covers hospitals, dispensaries, schools, a university, colleges, vocational centres, rural and tribal welfare and relief after famines, floods, earthquakes and cyclones. Its monks are its principal workers. It is non-sectarian and ignores caste distinctions, and its ashramas hold satsang and arati and observe Hindu festivals along with Christmas Eve and the birthday of the Buddha. By March 2025 it had 263 centres, 200 of them in India.

The Mission states that its aims are spiritual and humanitarian and have no connection with politics, though it supported the movement for Indian independence and some political revolutionaries later joined the Order. In 1980 it petitioned the courts to be declared a non-Hindu minority religion under Article 30 of the Indian constitution. The Calcutta High Court accepted the plea, but the Supreme Court of India ruled against it in 1995, finding that the Mission had all the characteristics of a Hindu organisation. Its awards include the Gandhi Peace Prize in 1998.
ramanathaswamy-temple: In the Yuddha Kanda of the Ramayana, Rama tells Sita on the way back to Ayodhya of the worship of Shiva as a lingam on Rameswaram before he built his bridge to Lanka, and calls the spot able to expiate great sins. In the Shiva Purana, Shiva appears to Rama there, grants him victory over Ravana and agrees to remain on the island. Believers hold that two lingams stand in the sanctum: the Ramalingam, made by Rama from sand, and the Vishvalingam, brought by Hanuman from Kailash, which by Rama's instruction is worshipped first. The temple is also one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams praised in the songs of the Nayanar poet-saints Appar, Sundarar and Sambandar.

The temple was expanded in the 12th century under the Pandya dynasty, and the Sri Lankan kings Parakrama Bahu (1153–1186) and Nissanka Malla contributed to its sanctum and its building. King Jeyaveera Cinkaiariyan of Jaffna (1380–1410) shipped stone blocks from the Koneswaram temple at Trincomalee to renovate the sanctum. According to the historian Firishta, Malik Kafur, general of Alauddin Khalji of the Delhi Sultanate, reached Rameswaram in the early 14th century, and the Sultanate's court historians record that he raided its temples. In the 17th century Dalavai Setupati built part of the main eastern gopuram, and between 1745 and 1837 the Maratha kings of Thanjavur gave rest houses to the temple.

A high wall encloses the precinct, with towers to the east and west; the main gopuram is 53 m tall. The third corridor, called the Chokkatan Mandapam, was built by Muthuramalinga Setupati, who ruled from 1763 to 1795, and his statue and those of his two ministers stand at its western entrance. The corridors measure about 3,850 feet in all, and the outer corridor has about 1,212 pillars, most carved with individual compositions. Twenty-two holy water bodies lie within the temple, said to stand for the arrows of Rama's quiver, and bathing in them is central to the pilgrimage. The temple is one of the Char Dham sites and the southernmost of the twelve jyotirlingas.
ramanuja: Ramanuja was born into a Tamil Brahmin family at Sriperumbudur, in present-day Tamil Nadu, under the Chola Empire. The traditional hagiographies, some written centuries after his death, name his parents as Kanthimathi and Asuri Keshava Somayaji and give his life as 1017 to 1137. Modern scholars, using temple records and regional literature from outside the Sri Vaishnava tradition, suggest 1077 to 1157, but one of them notes that reconstructing his historical life is nearly impossible.

He studied at Kanchipuram under Yadava Prakasa, a scholar traditionally placed in the Advaita Vedanta school but probably a Bhedabheda teacher. The two disagreed over the interpretation of the Upanishads and parted. According to tradition, Ramanuja was the great-grandson of Yamunacharya, the head of the Sri Vaishnava community at Srirangam, but Yamunacharya died before they could meet. One hagiography states that Periya Nambi, also called Mahapurna, initiated him into Sri Vaishnavism.

Ramanuja served at the Varadharaja Perumal temple at Kanchipuram and later led the community at Srirangam. According to hagiographies composed centuries after his death, a Chola king called Krimikanta Chola persecuted Sri Vaishnavas, and Ramanuja's disciple Koorathazhwan persuaded him to leave. He spent 14 years in the Hoysala kingdom, where King Vishnuvardhana helped him build the Thirunarayanaswamy temple at Melukote. Some historians hold that the king's hostility to Ramanuja was personal and not a persecution of Vaishnavas. He is also said to have drawn people regarded as untouchables into the movement, calling them Tirukulattar, of noble descent, and admitted them to the temple at Melukote.

The tradition attributes nine Sanskrit works to him, among them the Vedarthasamgraha, the Sri Bhashya, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya and the Gadya Trayam. Some scholars question the authenticity of all but the three largest works and the Gadya Trayam.

Ramanuja is the chief proponent of Vishishtadvaita, qualified non-dualism, one of the three most influential Vedantic philosophies of the second millennium, with Shankara's Advaita and Madhva's Dvaita. He holds that Brahman is identical with Vishnu-Narayana and has infinite auspicious attributes. Passages describing Brahman as without attributes, he argued, deny only worldly, defiling attributes. He affirms three equally real things: matter, conscious souls and God. The universe, both souls and matter, forms the body of God. Against Shankara he opposed the idea of maya, or illusion.

For Ramanuja liberation is the joy of contemplating Brahman, reached by devotion, bhakti, in which the soul keeps its own existence and does not become identical with Brahman. He also taught sharanagati, complete surrender to Vishnu, as a path open to all regardless of caste, status or gender. After Ramanuja's time the Sri Vaishnava community split into the Vadakalai and Tenkalai groups.
ramappa-temple: The Ramappa Temple is a Hindu temple at Palampet in eastern Telangana, also called the Rudreshwara Temple after Shiva, to whom it is dedicated. An inscription on a basalt pillar in a nearby courtyard records that it was commissioned in 1213 by Recherla Rudra, a Kakatiya general, and built over about 40 years in the reign of Ganapati.

Rudra had served as commander-in-chief when Ganapati was installed as ruler after the death of Mahadeva in 1199, and Ganapati granted him the town of Palampet in gratitude. There he dug an artificial reservoir, Ramappa Lake, and began the temple. Its remote site in forested foothills integrated it into a natural setting, and its design followed earlier Kakatiya temples such as the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda.

The temple stands on a star-shaped base on a platform about 6 feet high and faces east. It has a sanctum, an antechamber and a large pillared assembly hall, and a five-storied vimana rises over the sanctum. Its superstructure is mainly sandstone, with granite for the ceiling slabs, columns and beams, and its sculptures were carved in dolerite and polished to a mirror finish. The vimana was built of lightweight porous bricks made from clay mixed with gum, jute fibre and rice husks, which burned away to leave air pockets, so the bricks are lighter than water. The foundation is a sandbox of sand that cushions earthquake loads.

The bracket figures of Gaja-Vyala and of female dancers and musicians called Madanikas are the temple's best-known sculpture, and in all it holds about 600 dance-related sculptures. A hollow-carved stone branch near the antechamber produces the seven notes of the musical scale when struck. The temple is named after the sculptor Ramappa, who built it, making it the only temple in India named after its craftsman.

The temple suffered minor damage when Malik Kafur besieged Warangal in 1310, and after the Kakatiya dynasty fell in the 14th century it was largely abandoned and overgrown. It survived a strong earthquake in the 17th century. In December 1916 the archaeologist Ghulam Yazdani described the temples at Palampet as perhaps the brightest stars in the galaxy of medieval Deccan temples and began conservation, propping a collapsing section of roof. The Archaeological Survey of India took over its care in 1948. UNESCO declared the temple a World Heritage Site on 25 July 2021. The dancer Nataraja Ramakrishna revived the Perini dance after seeing the sculptures.
ramathibodi-i: Ramathibodi I, known as King U-thong, was born in 1314 and is regarded as the founder and first king of the Ayutthaya Kingdom. He is described as the son of a monarch of mixed Siamese Mon and Chinese descent, Baramaraja, who had been a prince of Si Satchanalai before taking the throne of Ayodhya, and of Sunandhadevi, a princess of the court of Suvarnaraja. Before his accession he was known as Prince Uthong, meaning Golden Cradle.

The name Uthong was first attached to him by Prince Damrong Rajanubhab, who equated him with a figure in several chronicles, but later scholarship has shown the assumption to be inaccurate. A seventeenth-century account by the Dutchman Jeremias van Vliet tells of a Chinese trader who rose to rule Phetchaburi, a figure now identified with Uthong II.

In 1351 Ramathibodi moved the capital about 80 kilometres east to an island in the Chao Phraya River, where he founded Ayutthaya. On 4 March 1351 he was formally established as sovereign of a centralised state in the Chao Phraya valley, supported by the centres of Ayutthaya, Lop Buri and Suphan Buri. The city remained the capital for over 400 years. He kept relations with the Sukhothai Kingdom, fought the Khmer Empire, and promoted maritime trade with Persian and Chinese merchants. Royal chronicles say his authority reached Korat, Chanthaburi, Tavoy, Tenasserim and parts of Malaya. In 1352 he besieged Yasodharapura (Angkor), took it the next year and placed one of his sons on the throne, but the Khmers regained it in 1357.

He set up four Great Officers of State, for the Interior, the Treasury, the King's Household and Agriculture, and allied himself with the Ming dynasty. Between 1350 and 1359 he is credited with codifying laws drawn from Tai custom, which served as the kingdom's legal base until the reforms of Chulalongkorn in the late 19th century. He patronised Buddhism and commissioned temples including Wat Phutthaisawan, Wat Pa Kaeo and Wat Phra Ram.

After his death in 1369 his son Ramesuan took the throne but yielded it to Ramathibodi's brother-in-law Borommarachathirat I of the Suphannaphum dynasty. Ramesuan regained it in 1388 by deposing Borommarachathirat's young son Thong Lan. In 1409 Borommarachathirat's nephew Intharacha took Ayutthaya back, securing long-term control for Suphannaphum. The Uthong line then declined into a noble family within the Ayutthayan administration until the 16th century.
ramathibodi-ii: Prince Chettathirat was the youngest of King Trailokanat's three sons. His eldest brother, Prince Borommaracha, governed Ayutthaya as regent while their father campaigned against the Lanna Kingdom, and another brother, Prince Indraracha, died in the Lanna wars. In 1485 Chettathirat was named uparaja, or crown prince, and installed at the same time as King of Sukhothai, a title traditionally held by the heir to Ayutthaya. When Trailokanat died in 1488, however, the throne passed to Borommaracha, and Chettathirat succeeded only on his brother's death in 1491.

The Siamese campaign of 1500 against Malacca brought tribute from Pattani, Pahang and Kelantan as well as from Malacca itself. In 1511 the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Malacca, seven years before their first embassy reached Ayutthaya. In 1513 King Kaew of Lanna invaded Sukhothai. Ramathibodi II led the Siamese forces himself, drove the Lanna army back and advanced into Lanna territory, sacking Lampang in 1515 in a punitive raid without lasting occupation. He then appointed his son, Prince Athittayawong, King of Sukhothai.

In mainland Southeast Asia political and military strength rested on the control of manpower, and the corvée system he set up in 1518 organised it. All men aged eighteen were registered, either for military service as phrai thaan or for public works as phrai luang, and the system comprised several distinct categories and obligations. A department of the royal bureaucracy, the Krom Phra Suratsawadi, oversaw the registration and mobilisation of this labour.

Ramathibodi II died in 1529, in July or on 10 October, when Halley's Comet appeared. The Siamese Chronicles record a white aerial sign like an arrow of the god Indra seen from the south-west to the north-west in Chula Sakarat 891, the Year of the Ox, and the king's death on a Sunday, the 8th day of the waxing moon in the 12th month. His son Prince Athittayawong succeeded him as Borommaracha IV.
ramayana: The Ramayana is a Hindu smriti epic poem, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, and one of the two Itihasas, narratives of past events interspersed with teachings on the goals of human life; the other is the Mahabharata. Its name means Rama's journey. Scholars place the oral composition of its core before the rise of Buddhism, since the narrative does not mention Buddhism and names Ayodhya as the capital of Kosala rather than by the later name Saketa. Later stages of the text extend over centuries. Two major regional recensions, the northern and the southern, descend from a common oral source; the southern is more archaic and is the backbone of modern critical editions.

In its extant form the poem has over 24,000 couplet verses, called shlokas, in seven kāṇḍas, or books. Rāma, prince of Ayodhya and son of King Daśaratha, is to be crowned, but Kaikeyī, provoked by the maidservant Mantharā, demands that Rāma be exiled for fourteen years while her son Bharata succeeds. Sītā and his brother Lakṣmaṇa follow him into the forest.

Rāvaṇa, the king of Lanka, carries off Sītā. Rāma allies himself with the vānaras, among them Hanumān, who becomes his biggest devotee. Hanumān leaps across the sea to Lanka to find Sītā, and the army crosses over a bridge built by the vānaras Nala and Nīla. In the war that follows Rāma defeats Rāvaṇa, and he returns to Ayodhya with Sītā to be crowned.

The Ramayana strongly influenced later Sanskrit poetry and Hindu life and culture, and its moral influence includes the ideal of Rāmarājya, a state in which Rama is king. Diwali marks Rama's return to Ayodhya. There are many other versions, including Buddhist and Jain adaptations. Kamban wrote the Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century. In Cambodia the Reamker is a national epic; the earliest mention of its manuscript is a 7th-century inscription, and the surviving text dates from the 16th century.
rambagh-palace: The first building in the Rambagh Gardens, south of the old city and about 5 miles (8.0 km) outside its walls, was a garden house for the wet nurse of Prince Ram Singh II. Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II later enlarged it for Kesar Badaran, his maid and an attendant of his queen. At first it was a simple pavilion on the forested outskirts of Jaipur, and by the late 19th century it served as a royal hunting lodge and guesthouse for relatives and visitors hunting in the surrounding country.

In the early 20th century the lodge was rebuilt as a palace in the Indo-Saracenic style to designs by Sir Samuel Swinton Jacob, blending Rajput and Mughal forms. Built mainly of pale pink sandstone with marble detail, it has chhatris, carved stone balconies, jali screens, bracketed eaves and arched verandahs with scalloped openings around its courtyards. Inside are hand-painted ceilings, stucco cornices and Venetian glass chandeliers. Its 47 acres of gardens follow Mughal formal patterns, with geometric flowerbeds, promenades, reflecting pools, fountains and lotus ponds, and peacocks still roam the lawns.

Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II, who ruled from 1922 to 1970, added royal suites and lived there with Maharani Gayatri Devi. His coronation was held there in 1931, and the palace was the setting for royal weddings, polo matches, balls and the stays of dignitaries; by some accounts India's first president, Rajendra Prasad, was entertained there in 1950.

After independence in 1947 and the integration of the princely states, the maharaja refitted the royal chambers for guests and opened the palace as a hotel. On 2 May 1972 its management passed to Taj Hotels, which reduced the number of rooms and modernised its plumbing and air-conditioning while keeping its historic character. Guests have included Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India, and the palace has served as a film location, for Lamhe (1991) and Bajirao Mastani (2015).
ramesses-ii: Ramesses II was not born a prince. His grandfather Ramesses I was a vizier and military officer under the pharaoh Horemheb, who named him as his successor when Ramesses II was about eleven. His father Seti I made him prince regent at about the age of fourteen. His date of accession is recorded as the 27th day of the eleventh month, which most Egyptologists take to be 31 May 1279 BCE, when he was about 25. A papyrus calendar and the historian Josephus agree that his reign lasted 66 years and about two months, the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh.

In his second year he defeated the Sherden sea pirates, who raided cargo ships on the Mediterranean routes to Egypt, by ambushing them in a sea battle near the mouth of the Nile. He founded Pi-Ramesses in the Nile Delta as a new capital, close to his territories in Canaan and Syria, with huge temples and a vast palace. His campaign in Syria in his fourth year took the Hittite vassal state of Amurru, and in his fifth year came the Battle of Kadesh against the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II, generally considered a stalemate.

In his twenty-first year, 1259 BCE, he concluded a treaty with the Hittites at Kadesh, after a crisis over the fugitive Hittite king Muršili III brought the two empires close to war. He also campaigned in Nubia and Libya.

Ramesses began in his third year the most ambitious building project since the pyramids, building from the Delta to Nubia. He had his carvings cut deep into the stone so that later rulers could not easily alter them, and he used reliefs as propaganda for his victories. His mortuary temple at Thebes is known as the Ramesseum, and in 1255 BCE he and his queen Nefertari went into Nubia to inaugurate the temple at Abu Simbel. He held thirteen or fourteen Sed festivals, more than any other pharaoh.

Ramesses died in about July 1213 BCE, probably at Pi-Ramesses, at the age of about 90 or 91 by the most likely estimate. He was buried in tomb KV7 in the Valley of the Kings, but because of looting priests moved the body several times, and it was found in 1881 in the tomb TT320. It now lies in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo. Later pharaohs called him the Great God, and he was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a deity in his lifetime. Greek sources knew him as Ozymandias.
ramesses-iii: Ramesses III was the son of Setnakhte and Tiy-Merenese, and was not closely related to Ramesses I or Ramesses II. Setnakhte's origin is unknown. He seized the throne during a time of crisis and unrest, probably from Twosret, and was presumably a minor descendant of Ramesses II through a different family line from that of Seti II, Siptah and Twosret. Scholars differ on the dates of Ramesses III's reign, and one calculation gives about 31 years.

His reign fell in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Egypt faced invaders including the Sea Peoples and Libyans, along with economic difficulties. In Year 5 and Year 11 he fought Libyan tribesmen in the Western Delta. In Year 8 the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, Denyen, Shardana and Tjekker, invaded by land and sea. He defeated them at the Battle of Djahy on the eastern frontier and at the Battle of the Delta, where he ambushed their ships at the mouth of the Nile with a fleet and archers on the shore. He settled the defeated Sea Peoples in southern Canaan, and their presence there may have contributed to the rise of states such as Philistia.

The cost of these wars drained the treasury. In Year 29 the first known labour strike in recorded history took place at Deir el-Medina, when rations could not be supplied to the royal tomb-builders. His monuments ignore such troubles. He added to the temples at Luxor and Karnak and built Medinet Habu, one of the largest and best-preserved funerary temples in Egypt, enclosed by massive fortifications.

Trial papyri record a harem conspiracy against his life, made at a celebration at Medinet Habu. It was instigated by his wife Tiye, who hoped her son Pentaweret would inherit; Ramesses III had not clearly settled the succession among his sons. Many officials were implicated, three trials were held, and 38 people were sentenced to death. A CT scan of his mummy showed a deep knife wound across the throat, which would have been rapidly fatal.

The conspirators failed in one respect: the crown passed to his designated successor, Ramesses IV. The succession crisis accelerated Egypt's decline, and Ramesses III is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power.
ramesses-xi: Menmaatre Ramesses XI is generally counted the tenth and final pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty. He was once thought to be the son of Ramesses X and Queen Tyti, but research on the Harris papyrus showed that Tyti was a queen of Ramesses III, so his mother is unknown. He is believed to have married Tentamun, daughter of Nebseny, and to have fathered Duathathor-Henuttawy, later wife of the high priest Pinedjem I, though these connections remain tentative.

He ruled for at least 29 years, and some Egyptologists think a little over 30. His highest certain date is Year 11 of the wḥm-mswt, the era called the Renaissance, which equals Year 29 of his reign. The era began in his Year 19, probably to stress a return to normal conditions after a coup. Pinehesy, the Viceroy of Kush, had ousted the High Priest of Amun, Amenhotep, and for some time controlled the region around Thebes.

How this period of suppression ended, and who forced Pinehesy out of Thebes, is unknown. He seems to have kept a power base in Nubia, and in Year 10 of the Renaissance the general and High Priest Piankh went on an expedition to Nubia, though the sources do not make clear whether it was a campaign against him.

His reign has left many papyri, among them the Adoption Papyrus, accounts of tomb-robbery trials and the Late Ramesside Letters written by scribes of the Necropolis and by Piankh. In one of these letters Piankh speaks disparagingly of the pharaoh and orders secret arrests, which suggests that the political situation was complex and that Piankh may have acted on a hidden agenda. Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb workmen, was abandoned either in his reign or shortly afterwards, apparently because the Royal Necropolis was shifted north to Tanis.

Ramesses XI died under unknown circumstances. He prepared a tomb in the Valley of the Kings (KV4) but left it unfinished, and he seems to have arranged to be buried away from Thebes, possibly near Memphis or at Pi-Ramesses. In the 21st Dynasty, under Pinedjem I, the tomb served as a workshop for processing materials from the burials of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III and perhaps Thutmose I.

Most Egyptologists hold that Smendes succeeded him as the first Lower Egyptian king of the Twenty-first Dynasty, though the problem of a possible king between them remains. Herihor and Smendes founded that dynasty with a new royal capital at Tanis, while Middle and Upper Egypt passed in effect to the High Priests of Amun at Thebes.
ramesseum: The Ramesseum lies in the Theban Necropolis on the west bank of the Nile, across from the modern city of Luxor, and is the second largest temple in Egypt, covering about 10 hectares. It was originally called the House of millions of years of Usermaatra-setepenra, the prenomen of Ramesses II. Work began shortly after the start of his reign and continued for 20 years. The temple followed the standard canons of New Kingdom architecture: two stone pylons, each leading into a courtyard, then a hypostyle hall of 48 columns around the inner sanctuary.

Its pylons and outer walls carried scenes of the pharaoh's victories, above all the Battle of Kadesh, c. 1274 BCE, with the Hittites fleeing before him. One block atop the first pylon records the pillaging of a city called Shalem in his eighth year, which may or may not have been Jerusalem.

In the first courtyard stood colossal statues of Ramesses, called Sun of the princes, and of his mother Tuya. The syenite statue of the enthroned king is estimated to have weighed 1,000 tonnes and stood 16 to 19 metres high; it was moved 220 kilometres from its quarry. Thirty-nine of the 48 columns of the hypostyle hall still stand. A smaller temple beside it was dedicated to Tuya and to his chief wife Nefertari.

The complex held storerooms, granaries, workshops and a royal palace. Its mud-brick granaries include the oldest true arch still standing in Egypt, from about 1300 BCE. Papyri and ostraca of the Third Intermediate Period show that it was also the site of an important scribal school. On the second pylon a king list names 14 ancestors of Ramesses; Hatshepsut and the Amarna pharaohs are omitted. In the early Christian era the temple was used as a church.

The annual flood on the edge of the floodplain gradually undermined the temple's foundations. French engineers with Napoleon's expedition of 1798 identified it with the Tomb of Ozymandias described by Diodorus of Sicily. In 1815 Giovanni Belzoni was hired to remove the torso of the Younger Memnon, a granite statue of Ramesses; the head reached London in 1818, and is in the British Museum. The excitement that followed led Percy Bysshe Shelley to write his sonnet Ozymandias, in which a fallen statue at the Ramesseum is now seen, since its cartouche gives the throne name that Diodorus rendered as Ozymandias. Jean-François Champollion, who visited in 1829, coined its name.

A joint French-Egyptian team has explored and restored the site since 1991, finding kitchens, bakeries and supply rooms, and a school where boys were taught to be scribes. Preservation has been made harder by modern farmers using the area for farming and encroaching on the ruins.
rameswaram: Rameswaram lies in the Ramanathapuram district of Tamil Nadu, on Pamban Island, which is separated from mainland India by the Pamban channel. The island is shaped like a conch, with the Palk Strait to the north-west and the Gulf of Mannar to the south-east, and it lies about 40 kilometres from Mannar Island in Sri Lanka.

Its average elevation is 10 metres, and about 74 per cent of its area has sandy soil. The Pamban Bridge, a cantilever railway bridge of 2,065 metres with a double-leaf bascule section that can be raised for ships, opened to traffic in 1914. Dhanushkodi, at the southern tip of the island, was washed away in the cyclone of 1964, though its temple of Rama alone remained intact.

The history of Rameswaram centres on its role as a transit point to Sri Lanka and on the Ramanathaswamy Temple. Tamil hymns of the 7th and 8th centuries on Shiva by the Nayanars Appar, Sundarar and Sambandar glorify the temple. The Chola king Rajendra Chola I, who reigned from 1012 to 1040 CE, held the town for a short time.

The Jaffna kingdom, which lasted from 1215 to 1624 CE, had close ties with the island, made generous contributions to the temple and took the title Setukavalan, meaning custodians of Rameswaram; Setu appeared on its coins and inscriptions. The temple in its present form was built in the 12th century by the Pandya dynasty.

The name means Lord of Rama in Sanskrit, an epithet of Shiva. According to the Ramayana and the Puranas, Rama prayed to Shiva after his war against the demon-king Ravana. Hanuman was sent to bring a lingam from the Himalayas, and because he took too long, Sita made one of sand from the shore, which is believed to be the one in the sanctum. Tradition also places the bridge Rama built to Lanka near here.

Rameswaram has been run by a municipal body since 1994, and its population was 44,856 at the 2011 census. It is the end of the railway line from Chennai and Madurai. Tourism and fishing are the main sources of employment. The Ramanathaswamy Temple is one of the 12 Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva and is described as having the longest corridors of any Hindu temple in India, columned passages 5.2 to 6.4 metres wide and 7.6 metres high.

Rameswaram is one of the four Char Dham sites, with Badrinath, Puri and Dwarka, and many Hindus hold that a pilgrimage to Varanasi is incomplete without one to Rameswaram. Pilgrims bathe in its holy water bodies, of which there are sixty-four in and around the town.
ramiro-i-of-aragon: Ramiro was born before 1007, the illegitimate son of Sancho III of Pamplona and his mistress Sancha of Aybar. A story holds that his father's wife Muniadona adopted him because he alone of Sancho's children came to her aid, but no record of these events survives and the story is probably apocryphal. He appears as a witness of royal charters from 1011 and was given numerous properties in the county of Aragon.

When Sancho's realm was divided on his death in 1035, Navarre and the Basque country went to the eldest half-brother García, Castile to Ferdinand, and Sobrarbe and Ribagorza to Gonzalo. Ramiro received the county of Aragon with the title of baiulus, or steward, to hold under García.

Ramiro's status was vague. His vassals, neighbours, the church and even his sons called him king, yet he styled himself only Ramiro, son of King Sancho, and in his two wills spoke of his lands as held in stewardship, first from García and then from God. Charters from Navarre call him regulus, not rex, and quasi pro rege, acting as if king. Because of his growing independence and the small size of his Pyrenean holdings he is sometimes called a petty king and Aragon a pocket kingdom.

He sought to enlarge his lands at the expense of both the Moors and García. After his father's death he supported the emir of Tudela in an invasion of Navarre; he was defeated at the Battle of Tafalla but gained territory, including Sangüesa, and established a state of semi-autonomy. With García's apparent approval he annexed Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, creating a pseudo-independent state with its capital at Jaca. He then began to advance towards Huesca and Zaragoza. The first charter for the royal town of Jaca is attributed to him; it gave protection even to non-residents and set an example for urban rights late into the Middle Ages.

Ramiro died in 1063 at the Battle of Graus while trying to take the city, and was buried at the monastery of San Juan de la Peña. His son Sancho Ramírez succeeded him as king of Aragon. By his first marriage, in 1036 to Gisberga, daughter of Bernard Roger of Bigorre, he had five children, among them García, Bishop of Jaca.
ramiro-i-of-asturias: Ramiro was the son of King Bermudo I. According to the Chronicle of Alfonso III, the childless Alfonso II chose him as successor, but while Ramiro was in Castile for his own marriage ceremonies, Nepocian, the late king's kinsman and comes palatii, claimed the throne with the support of Astures and Vascones. Ramiro raised an army in Galicia and defeated Nepocian at the Battle of the Bridge of Cornellana on the river Narcea. Nepocian was captured by Counts Scipion and Sonna, blinded and confined to a monastery.

In 844 a Viking fleet landed at Corunna and began to raid the countryside. Ramiro marched against it, routed the invaders, took prisoners and burned much of their fleet, and the Vikings no longer raided the Asturian coast. When Emir Abd ar-Rahman II of Córdoba was occupied with Vikings and with a rebellion of Musa ibn Musa of the Banu Qasi, Ramiro tried to repopulate León. In 846 an army led by the emir's son forced the settlers out and burned the city, which was not reoccupied until 856, under Ordoño I.

The later part of the reign brought conflict with nobles. Ramiro condemned the rebel grandee Piniolo to death with his seven sons and had the comes palatii Aldroito blinded. He also acted against thieves and against magos, presumably pagans in isolated settlements, and the Chronica Albeldense called him the Rod of Justice.

Ramiro died on 1 February 850 at his palace of Santa María del Naranco near Oviedo and was buried in the Pantheon of Asturian Kings in the Cathedral of San Salvador, beside his second wife, Paterna. His son Ordoño succeeded him. A legend placed a victory over the Moors at Clavijo in his reign, with the apparition of Saint James, but neither Asturian nor Arab chronicles of the period mention it, and it rests on a charter forged in the early 12th century.

His court is remembered for the Ramirense style of pre-Romanesque architecture. Santa María del Naranco, San Miguel de Lillo and Santa Cristina de Lena are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and their barrel vaults of tufa were new in the Europe of their time.
ramiro-ii-of-aragon: Ramiro was born on 24 April 1086, the youngest son of Sancho Ramírez, king of Aragon and Navarre, and Felicia of Roucy. His father placed him as a child in the Benedictine monastery of Saint Pons de Thomières. A respected monk, he was elected abbot of the Castilian royal monastery of Santos Fecundo y Primitivo in Sahagún and later abbot of San Pedro el Viejo at Huesca. His brother Alfonso the Battler, wishing to limit his power within Navarre-Aragon, blocked his elections as bishop of Burgos and of Pamplona.

In 1134 Ramiro was elected bishop of Barbastro-Roda, and the death of his childless brother made him one of the candidates for the crown. Others were Alfonso VII of Castile, who as a foreign king found little support, and Pedro de Atarés, the choice of the Navarrese nobility. At an assembly at Borja a misunderstanding alienated Pedro from his supporters, yet they would not accept Ramiro, and in the end the kingdoms were divided: Navarre chose García Ramírez, a protégé of Alfonso VII, while Aragon chose Ramiro, who suspended his monastic vows to take the crown.

His reign was tumultuous. His nobles had expected a docile king and found him inflexible, and he had to put down a rebellion. To produce an heir he married Agnes, daughter of Duke William IX of Aquitaine, and their daughter Petronilla was betrothed at the age of one to Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona. The contract, signed at Barbastro on 11 August 1137, made Petronilla heir to Aragon, which would pass to Ramon Berenguer and any children by other wives if she died childless. Ramon accepted Ramiro as King, Lord and Father, and Barcelona and Aragon were united into the Crown of Aragon.

Knowing himself not to be a war king, Ramiro handed royal authority to his son-in-law on 13 November 1137. Ramon Berenguer became Princeps Aragonensis, effective chief of the kingdom's armies, and Ramiro returned to San Pedro in Huesca. He became linked with the passionate legend of the Bell of Huesca. He died there on 16 August 1157 and was buried at the abbey.

The union gave the formerly landlocked Aragonese state, which had lost Navarre, a window on the western Mediterranean that it would come to dominate. His daughter Petronilla used the title queen in her will of 1152, before his death.
ramiro-ii-of-leon: Ramiro was the son of Ordoño II and Elvira Menéndez. After Alfonso III of Asturias was forced by his sons to abdicate, shortly before his death in 910, the kingdom fell into successional crises, was partitioned among his sons, and was reunited and divided again.

When Fruela II died in 925, Alfonso Fróilaz was crowned but could not extend his power and was marginalised by his cousins, the three sons of Ordoño II, who had the backing of the Kingdom of Pamplona. They partitioned their share: Sancho Ordóñez ruled in Galicia, Alfonso IV in León, and Ramiro in the newly conquered lands to the south, where the chronicler Ibn Hayyan located his court at Coimbra.

When Sancho died in 929 Alfonso IV absorbed his kingdom, but in 931 Ramiro forced Alfonso IV to abdicate and had him and the three sons of Fruela II blinded so that they could not rule. He became king of León, and with it Galicia, the scant Anales castellanos primeros being a primary source for his reign. He stood out as a military commander, expanded his lands south into Salamanca and Ledesma, and founded or repopulated frontier strongholds such as Osma and Clunia. The Moors called him the Devil for his ferocity in battle.

Ramiro masterminded a coalition of Pamplona and León that defeated a joint Andalusian counter-offensive at the Battle of Simancas in 939, which let the Leonese border advance from the Duero to the Tormes. In his last years he lost the support of his brother-in-law and son-in-law García Sánchez I of Pamplona, who then helped Count Fernán González of Castile gain brief de facto independence. In 950 Ramiro still led an expedition to the valley of the Edge and defeated the Umayyads of Córdoba at Talavera.

Ramiro died on 1 January 951. His first wife was Adosinda Gutiérrez, by whom he had Ordoño III, his successor, and his second was Urraca Sánchez of Pamplona, whose marriage brought an alliance and a son, Sancho I of León.

These marriages set the stage for further succession conflict, with Ordoño and his son Vermudo II backed by the Galician nobility and Sancho and his son Ramiro III by Urraca's relatives in Pamplona and Córdoba. Legend gave him a place in the poem Miragaia, which tells of a son by an Arab lord's daughter, ancestor of the Maia family, but modern scholars dismiss the Lara connections later attached to this tale.
ramiz-alia: Ramiz Alia was born on 18 October 1925 in Shkodër to Gheg Albanian parents who were Muslim and had fled persecution in Yugoslavia. He grew up in Tirana, joined the underground Albanian Communist Youth Organisation in 1941 and became a member of the Albanian Communist Party in 1943.

He rose rapidly under the patronage of Enver Hoxha. He was elected to the Central Committee in November 1948, became a candidate member of the Politburo in 1956 and a full member by 1961, and was the party's chief ideologist in social and cultural fields. Hoxha named no official successor, but there were clear signs that he favoured Alia.
Alia was the second and last leader of the People's Socialist Republic of Albania, serving as First Secretary of the Party of Labour from 1985 to 1991. He was also head of state from 1982 to 1992.

Alia tried to change the system on a limited, cautious basis, but reform from above threatened to become reform from below, largely because of the demands of Albania's youth. On 9 December 1990 students marched in Tirana demanding reforms, and Alia met them and agreed to further steps towards democratisation. On 12 December 1990 he signed a law allowing political pluralism, which he later called a failure.

In the 1991 elections, the first democratic ones in the country, he ran for parliament in a Tirana constituency and was defeated by the mining engineer Franko Kroqi, a candidate of the new Democratic Party of Albania. After that loss and the Democratic Party's landslide in the spring 1992 general election, he resigned as president on 3 April 1992. On 9 April the People's Assembly elected the party's leader, Sali Berisha, as head of state.

Alia was placed under house arrest in August 1992 and imprisoned in August 1993. In May 1994 he went on trial with other senior officials for abuse of power and misappropriation of state funds and received a nine-year sentence, later cut on appeal. He was freed on 7 July 1995 and charged again in 1996 with crimes against humanity. He died in Tirana on 7 October 2011.

His legacy remains polarising. Some dissidents accuse him of continuing Hoxha's repressive practices, while others praise him for dissolving the Party of Labour's monopoly peacefully and avoiding the bloodshed seen in Romania.
ramla: Ramla lies in the Central District of Israel. Its strategic and economic value came from its position at the crossing of the Via Maris, the road linking Egypt with Syria, and the road from the Mediterranean port of Jaffa to Jerusalem. It takes its name from raml, the Arabic word for sand, from the sandy ground on which it stands. Its limited water was gathered in cisterns.

Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik founded Ramla as the seat of his administration of Jund Filasṭīn, replacing Lydda, the first Muslim provincial capital, before he became caliph in 715. He built it close to Lydda but not inside it, probably for lack of space and because agreements from the Muslim conquest of the 630s limited the seizure of property there. His first buildings were a palace that also housed the administration, the House of the Dyers and a congregational mosque, later called the White Mosque, completed under Umar II. An aqueduct brought water from Gezer. Many of Lydda's Christian, Samaritan and Jewish inhabitants were moved to the new city, which became the commercial centre of Palestine, a market for dyeing, weaving, pottery and olive oil.

The Abbasids confiscated the Umayyad properties in 750. The Fatimids took Ramla in 969, and about ten years later the Jarrahids, a branch of the Tayy tribe, destroyed it. The geographer al-Muqaddasi still called it a fine city. The city lost its role as capital shortly before the First Crusade, and the crusaders took it without a fight in 1099. It became the seat of a lordship in the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a station for pilgrims.

By the 19th century Ramla was a decaying town of about 3,000 people. Napoleon Bonaparte used the Franciscan hospice as his headquarters on 2 March 1799. Ramla had an almost exclusively Arab population until it was captured by Israeli forces on 12 July 1948, shortly after Lydda, and most remaining inhabitants were expelled; some scholars, including Ilan Pappé, call this ethnic cleansing, a claim that is disputed.

Ramla is one of Israel's mixed cities, with both Jewish and Arab citizens. The White Tower, six storeys high, was built in the 13th century as the minaret of the White Mosque, of which only remnants survive. The Pool of Arches, an underground cistern built in 789, and the Great Mosque, a Crusader cathedral converted by the Mamluks, also stand. The city is the centre of Karaite Judaism in Israel.
ramlila: The word combines Rama with lila, meaning play or sport. James Lochtefeld describes it as a playful drama about Rama that is also a deeply serious religious act. When the first performances took place is unclear. According to tradition, Megha Bhagat, a student of Tulsidas, began the Ramcharitmanas-based Ramlila in 1625, but Norvin Hein holds that Ramlila was in vogue in North India between 1200 and 1500, based then on Valmiki's Ramayana, and that a dance-drama of Ramayana enactment flourished in the Mathura region much earlier, possibly in the early centuries CE.

John Brockington argues that the tradition is probably ancient, since epics as long as the Ramayana, with 20,000 verses, must have been recited and acted out to be preserved. James Prinsep gave an eyewitness account of the Varanasi festivities in 1825.

Ramlila is staged in villages, towns and urban neighbourhoods during the autumn Navaratri season, usually in September or October. It tells the story of Rama from his childhood and the marriage of Sita to his exile, the abduction of Sita by Ravana, the war on Lanka and his return to Ayodhya as king. It ends on the night of Vijayadashami (Dussehra), when effigies of Ravana are burnt. Most performances are open-air productions by amateur companies, run by local committees called samitis and paid for by the community, and their dialogue draws on the verses of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.

The audience takes part: it chants with the actors, walks with them from site to site, and cheers when good prevails. UNESCO says the festival brings people together without distinction of caste, religion or age.

Elsewhere a Ramlila is usually an abridged event of ten days, but at Ramnagar, across the Ganges from Varanasi, it runs for 31 days and recites the whole Ramcharitmanas. It was begun around 1830 by Maharaja Udit Narayan Singh, and the royal house of Benares has patronised it since. The whole town becomes a set, with stages named after sites of the epic such as Lanka, and the audience moves with the players. Roles such as Ravana were held by the same family from 1835 to 1990. UNESCO's 2008 report named Ayodhya, Ramnagar, Varanasi, Vrindavan, Almora, Satna and Madhubani as the most notable traditions.

The epic and its drama reached Southeast Asia in the first millennium CE, and Ramlila forms part of the performing culture of Bali, Myanmar, Cambodia and Thailand. Indian indentured labourers carried it in the 19th and 20th centuries to Fiji, Guyana, Mauritius, South Africa, Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago. UNESCO declared Ramlila part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
ramnagar-varanasi: Ramnagar lies just beside the city of Varanasi and is a municipal board in Varanasi district. Ramnagar Fort, set near the Ganges, dominates the town, and many houses and structures around the fort are a century old or more. The scenic position of the fort has made the town a frequent setting for films and series, among them Chokher Bali, Raanjhanaa, Gangs of Wasseypur and Mirzapur.

Raja Balwant Singh, the Kashi Naresh or king of Kashi, the ancient name of Benares, built Ramnagar Fort in the eighteenth century of creamy Chunar sandstone. It is in a typically Mughal style, with carved balconies, open courtyards and pavilions. The fort and its museum hold the history of the kings of Benares, whose home it has been since the 18th century. The people of Benares long revered the Kashi Naresh as their religious head and chief cultural patron, and considered him an incarnation of Shiva; he took an essential part in all the city's religious celebrations.

Ramnagar is known above all for its Ramlila, held once a year under the patronage of the king of Varanasi, which draws over a million pilgrims to its processions and performances. It is run by the Maharaja of Banaras with the help of Pt. Laxmi Narayan Pandey and his family, and its venues are scattered across Ramnagar, Lanka, Janakpuri, PAC, Kodopur and several smaller places.

The 2011 Census of India counted 49,132 people in Ramnagar. On 31 March 2023 the Ramnagar Bhanta, a brinjal grown in the area, was given a Geographical Indication tag, the first brinjal variety from Uttar Pradesh to receive one.
ramnulfids: The family took its name from its founder, Ramnulf I. His son Ramnulf II claimed the title of King of Aquitaine in 888, but the title did not survive him. The house's power base shifted from Toulouse to Poitou, and in the early 10th century it contested the dominance of northern Aquitaine, and the ducal title to the whole, with the House of Auvergne. Through Ramnulf II's illegitimate son Ebalus came the line of dukes who ruled Aquitaine continuously from the succession of William III in 927.

In 1032 the Ramnulfids inherited the Duchy of Gascony and united it with Aquitaine, and by the end of the 11th century they were the dominant power in the south-western third of France. The dukes were officially titled counts of Poitiers. Daughters of the house married into the leading dynasties: Adelaide married Hugh Capet and became the first queen of France of the Direct Capetians, and Agnes married Henry III, Holy Roman Emperor, and ruled as regent for the young Henry IV.

The male line of the dukes ended in 1137. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought the inheritance first to Louis VII of France and then to Henry II of England, and her second marriage created the Angevin Empire, a cause of much discord between France and England.

The family encouraged art, literature and piety. Under William V, William IX and William X, Aquitaine became the centre of poetry and song in the vernacular, where the troubadour tradition was born and the ideal of courtly love was invented, and the Peace and Truce of God were fostered there.

A younger branch founded by Raymond of Poitiers, a son of William IX, gave the last princes of Antioch and counts of Tripoli; Antioch was lost in 1268, and Lucia, the last princess, died in 1299. Henry of Antioch's marriage to Isabella of Lusignan, heiress of Cyprus, founded the second House of Lusignan, the kings of Cyprus, and this lineage died out with the death of Queen Charlotte of Cyprus in 1487.
ramon-berenguer-i-count-of-barcelona: Ramon Berenguer succeeded his father, Berenguer Ramon I the Crooked, in 1035, and during his reign the dominant position of Barcelona among the Catalan counties became clear. He campaigned against the Moors, extending his lands as far west as Barbastro and imposing heavy tributes, the parias, on other Moorish cities; historians hold that these tributes brought the first wave of prosperity in Catalan history. Catalan sea power also began to be felt in the western Mediterranean in his time, and he was the first count of Catalonia to gain lands and influence north of the Pyrenees, in the counties of Carcassonne and Razès.

He began the written codification of Catalan law in the Usatges of Barcelona, which became the first full compilation of feudal law in Western Europe. The codification was part of his effort to advance and in some way control the process of feudalisation that had begun under his weak father. The Church contributed as well through the Peace and Truce of God, which imposed a general truce among warring lords in a region for a set time; the earliest known date for the Truce of God in Western Europe is 1027, in Catalonia, under his father.

While still married to his second wife, Blanca of Narbonne, he became involved with Almodis de La Marche, countess of Limoges and wife of the Count of Toulouse. The two quickly married and were excommunicated by Pope Victor II. With Almodis he founded the Romanesque cathedral of Barcelona, replacing an older basilica presumably destroyed by Almanzor, and their wooden coffins, bound in velvet and brass, are still displayed in the Gothic cathedral that later replaced it. His son Peter Raymundi, by his first wife, murdered Almodis and was exiled. Ramon Berenguer died on 26 May 1076 and was succeeded by his twin sons with Almodis, Ramon Berenguer II and Berenguer Ramon II.
ramon-berenguer-iii-of-barcelona: Ramon Berenguer III was born on 11 November 1082 in Rodez, the son of Ramon Berenguer II. He succeeded his father as count of Barcelona, Girona and Ausona in 1086, ruling jointly with his uncle Berenguer Ramon II, and became sole ruler in 1097 when his uncle was forced into exile. His first wife was María Rodríguez de Vivar, second daughter of El Cid, who died around 1105 and left three daughters. His second wife, Almodis, had no children. His third wife was Douce, heiress of Provence, with whom he had seven children.

In 1102 he answered increased Almoravid raids on his lands with a counter-attack, helped by Ermengol V, Count of Urgell, but was defeated at Mollerussa, where Ermengol was killed. By marriage, vassalage and inheritance he brought almost all the Catalan counties, except Urgell and Peralada, into his realm. He inherited Besalú in 1111 and Cerdanya in 1117, and through his marriage to Douce in 1112 took Provence, so that his lands stretched as far east as Nice. With the Count of Urgell he conquered Balaguer.

He established relations with the maritime republics of Pisa and Genoa. In 1114 and 1115 he attacked the then-Muslim islands of Mallorca and Ibiza with Pisa, and they became his tributaries, with many Christian slaves recovered and freed. With Pisa's help he also raided Valencia, Lleida and Tortosa. In 1116 he travelled to Rome to ask Pope Paschal II for a crusade to liberate Tarragona, which by 1118 he had captured and rebuilt as the metropolitan seat of the church in Catalonia, which had before depended on Narbonne. In 1127 he signed a commercial treaty with Genoa.

On 14 July 1130 he became an associate member of the Templars. He gave his five Catalan counties to his eldest son Ramon Berenguer IV, who married Petronilla of Aragon, and Provence to his younger son Berenguer Ramon. He died in Barcelona in 1131, the sources giving 23 January or 19 July, and was buried at the monastery of Santa Maria de Ripoll.
ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-barcelona: Ramon Berenguer IV, sometimes called the Saint, was born in 1114, the son of Count Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona and Countess Douce I of Provence. He inherited the county of Barcelona from his father on 19 August 1131. On 11 August 1137, aged about 24, he was betrothed to Petronilla of Aragon, who was then one year old. Her father, King Ramiro II of Aragon, had sought Barcelona's aid against Alfonso VII of León, and on 13 November 1137 he withdrew from public life, leaving his kingdom to Petronilla and Ramon Berenguer.

Ramon Berenguer never took the title of king, though he used it at least once, in 1139. He commonly styled himself Count of the Barcelonans and Prince of the Aragonians, and occasionally Marquis of Lleida and Tortosa. Historians differ on his position: one holds that he ruled Aragon for Petronilla as prince consort, another that he ruled as sovereign prince, and a third that his authority was subordinate to hers and to Ramiro's. His treaty with Ramiro stipulated that their descendants would rule both realms jointly, each keeping its own laws and institutions. Historians consider this arrangement the political masterstroke of the Hispanic Middle Ages, because it gave Aragon an outlet to the sea.

In October 1147, as part of the Second Crusade, he helped Castile conquer Almería. In December 1148 he captured Tortosa after a six-month siege, with the help of southern French, Anglo-Norman and Genoese crusaders, and the next year Fraga, Lleida and Mequinenza fell to him after a seven-month siege. He also acted as regent of Provence between 1144 and 1157 for his nephew Ramon Berenguer II. In 1151 he signed the Treaty of Tudilén with Alfonso VII, which defined the two rulers' zones of conquest in Andalusia, and he founded the royal monastery of Poblet. In 1154 he accepted the regency of Gaston V of Béarn.

Ramon Berenguer IV died on 6 August 1162 at Borgo San Dalmazzo in Piedmont. Petronilla succeeded him, and when she abdicated in 1164 their eldest surviving son, Ramon Berenguer, inherited Aragon and took the name Alfonso II of Aragon. His younger son Pere inherited Cerdanya and the lands north of the Pyrenees, and took the name Ramon Berenguer. The Chronicle of San Juan de la Peña described him as a man of great nobility, prudence and probity, and large and well proportioned.
ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-provence: Ramon Berenguer was the son of Alfonso II, Count of Provence, and Garsenda, Countess of Forcalquier. After his father's death in 1209 his mother sent him to the Templar castle of Monzón in Aragon, in the company of his cousin James, whose life was also under threat. He left Monzón in 1216 to claim his inheritance, which included Forcalquier from his mother. He was the first count of Provence in over a hundred years to live in the county. On 5 June 1219 he married Beatrice of Savoy, a daughter of Thomas, Count of Savoy, who gave the 21-year-old count a powerful father-in-law to protect his interests.

Ramon Berenguer and his wife supported troubadours, and he composed Provençal verse himself. He wrote laws forbidding nobles from doing menial work such as farming. He fought border disputes with the counts of Toulouse, and in 1226 began to reassert his rights in Marseille, whose citizens turned first to Thomas of Savoy and then to Raymond VII of Toulouse. In 1228 he supported Thomas in a war against Turin and Guigues VI of Viennois, over control of the trade routes from Italy into France.

In 1233 Blanche of Castile sent a knight to Provence, and she then arranged the marriage of her son Louis to his eldest daughter Margaret, with a dowry of ten thousand silver marks, for which the count had to pledge castles. Henry III of England then sought Eleanor's hand, and the count negotiated that no dowry be paid, promising her ten thousand marks in his will.

In 1238 Ramon Berenguer joined his brother-in-law Amadeus IV at the court of Emperor Frederick II in Turin. In January 1244 Pope Innocent IV decreed that only the pope could excommunicate him, and in 1245 he sent representatives to the First Council of Lyon. He died at Aix-en-Provence in August 1245 and left the county to his youngest daughter Beatrice. At least two planhs, Occitan funeral laments, were written in his honour. The chronicler Giovanni Villani called him a wise and courteous lord whose court drew gentle persons from Provence, France and Catalonia.
ramon-caceres: Ramón Arturo Cáceres Vasquez, nicknamed Mon Cáceres, was born on 15 December 1866 in Moca, in the Cibao region. His father, Manuel Altagracia Cáceres, had been president of the Dominican Republic, and his mother was Remigia Vásquez; his cousin Horacio Vásquez later held the presidency too. He studied law, took part in politics as a young man and was known for his physical strength, his horsemanship and his marksmanship. On 26 July 1899, in Moca, he took part in the killing of President Ulises Heureaux, known as Lilís.

Cáceres served as vice president under Carlos Felipe Morales before taking the presidency, and he led the right-wing Red Party. During his government the Dominican American Convention of 1907 was signed, and a new constitution promulgated that year allowed his re-election in 1908. He faced repeated attempts to overthrow him, among them the guerrilla rising of the Northwest Line led by Desiderio Arias. Moving to Monte Cristi with his troops, he concentrated the food supply in certain places and ordered livestock moved to the interior of the Cibao within 20 days, which devastated the area but brought the insurgents under control.

He used the same methods in the south, and he lured regional leaders to peace meetings in neutral places, where the army surrounded and eliminated them. He created a professional army to replace the private armies of regional leaders and turned the Rural Guard of the Morales government into a national police force, the Republican Guard, popularly called the Mon Guard, known for its loyalty to the president.

On 19 November 1911 a group led by Luis Tejera intercepted the car in which Cáceres was riding, and he was shot several times and killed. Tejera was taken to the Ozama Fortress and executed. The president's death was followed by a civil war and, in 1916, by the U.S. occupation of the Dominican Republic. A metro station in Santo Domingo is named after him.
ramon-castilla: Ramón Castilla was born in Tarapacá, then part of the Viceroyalty of Peru, the second son of Pedro Castilla, of Spanish-Argentine origin, and Juana Marquezado de Romero, who was of part Aymara descent. He began his military career in the royalist army and was captured at the Battle of Chacabuco on 12 February 1817. He escaped, returned to Peru in 1821 and joined José de San Martín's patriot army.

He helped recruit and train the cavalry of the Peruvian Legion, fought under Simón Bolívar at the Battle of Ayacucho, and was named governor of Tarapacá in 1825. At the Battle of Yungay in 1839 he fought beside the Chilean general Manuel Bulnes against the Peru–Bolivian Confederation, and as minister of finance under Agustín Gamarra he was responsible for Peru's first lucrative guano exports.

After years of struggle among caudillos Castilla took the presidency in 1844 as the head of a junta and was elected in 1845. His government repaid the internal and external debts from guano revenue, produced Peru's first official budget in 1847, reopened the Bellavista Military Academy, and in 1851 oversaw the building of South America's first railway, from Lima to Callao. On 14 June 1850 it issued the first Regulations for Public Instruction.

In 1854 he led a liberal rebellion from Arequipa against his successor José Rufino Echenique; a law abolishing slavery was passed at Huancayo on 3 December 1854, and Castilla defeated Echenique at La Palma on 5 January 1855. The elections for a National Convention that year were the first in Peru held with direct and universal suffrage. A new constitution was enacted in December 1860 and remained in force until 1920.

Castilla was succeeded in 1862 by Miguel de San Román. In 1864 he became senator for Tarapacá and was sent into exile after rebuking President Juan Antonio Pezet over the Spanish naval aggression. Back in Peru in 1866, he opposed President Mariano Ignacio Prado, who deported him to Chile.

He landed at Pisagua to defend the 1860 constitution and died in the Tiliviche Valley on 30 May 1867. He is remembered in Peru as taita, father, and as the liberator of the enslaved, and two monuments to him stand in Lima, one unveiled in 1915 and an equestrian statue in 1969. His second government also left the border dispute with Ecuador unresolved, until the 1997 Itamaraty treaty.
ramon-grau-san-martin: Ramón Grau San Martín was born on 13 September 1881, the son of Francisco Grau Vinals, a rich tobacco grower who wanted his son to follow him, and Pilar San Martin y del Collado. Ramón wanted to be a doctor. He graduated with a Doctor of Medicine degree from the University of Havana in 1908 and then went to Europe to expand his medical knowledge. He returned to Cuba in 1921 and became a professor of physiology at the University of Havana. In the 1920s he took part in student protests against President Gerardo Machado, and he was jailed in 1931. After his release he was exiled and lived for a time in the United States.

After the Cuban Revolution of 1933, Grau was one of the five members of the Pentarchy, which governed from 5 to 10 September. On 9 September the Directorio Estudiantil Universitario agreed on Grau as the next president. His government, known as the One Hundred Days Government, ended on 15 January 1934. It mixed moderate reformers such as Grau with radicals such as Antonio Guiteras. It decreed an eight-hour working day, a higher minimum wage, a Department of Labor and the nationalization of the Cuban Electric Company, granted the University of Havana autonomy, and required employers to engage at least 50 per cent native-born Cuban workers.

The United States did not recognize the government, and the traditional parties and the ABC either opposed it or wanted a more inclusive administration. Army chief of staff Fulgencio Batista nominally surrendered the army's power to it but held talks with Sumner Welles and U.S. Ambassador Jefferson Caffery. Army officers camped at the Hotel Nacional until the Battle of the Hotel Nacional on 2 October 1933, and Batista forced Grau's resignation on 15 January 1934.

In 1934 Grau founded the Partido Auténtico. He presided over much of the convention that passed the Constitution of 1940, but lost the presidential election of that year to Batista. In 1944 he won the popular vote against Carlos Saladrigas Zayas, Batista's chosen successor, and served until 1948, though accusations of corruption tainted his administration.

Grau turned the presidency over to his protégé Carlos Prío in 1948 and withdrew almost entirely from public life. He emerged in 1952 to oppose Batista's coup, and ran in the elections of 1954 and 1958 but withdrew before each, claiming government fraud. After Fidel Castro came to power in 1959, Grau retired to his home in Havana and kept a low profile. He died there on 28 July 1969.
ramon-llull: Llull was born in Palma in 1232 or 1233 into a wealthy family of Barcelona patricians who had come to the Kingdom of Majorca in 1229 with the armies of James I of Aragon. Muslims still made up a large part of the island's population, and Jews were present in its cultural and economic life. In 1257 he married Blanca Picany, with whom he had two children.

In 1263, by his own account, he saw Christ on the Cross five times while writing a love song. The visions gave him three aims, among them to convert Muslims to Christianity. He sold his possessions, went on pilgrimages, and on returning to Majorca bought a Muslim slave to teach him Arabic. In 1270 he founded the hermitage of Miramar.

In 1274, at Puig de Randa, Llull says the form of his great book was given to him by divine revelation. This was the Art, a system of universal logic made of general principles and combinatorial operations, meant to prove Christian doctrine to people of every faith. It is distinctive for its use of letters and diagrams, which give it an algebraic character.

To make the Art accessible he wrote in Catalan as well as Latin. The Book of the Gentile and the Three Wise Men, written in the 1270s, imagines a Muslim, a Jew and a Christian showing a Gentile their faiths with the help of trees whose leaves carry the principles of the Art. Blanquerna, written about 1276 to 1283, is the best known of his novels. His first work was a compendium of the logic of Al-Ghazali.

Llull urged the teaching of Arabic and other languages in Europe, and a language school for Franciscan missionaries was founded at Miramar in 1276. He travelled to Tunis about 1291 and again about 1304. In 1315 he was stoned by a mob in Bougie or Tunis; tradition held that he died of this and was a martyr, but there is evidence that he was rescued and died early the next year, at sea or shortly after reaching Majorca. His tomb, made in 1448, is in the Franciscan church in Palma.

His Art was never adopted by mainstream academia, and the inquisitor Nicholas Eymerich condemned Lullism in Aragon in the 1360s. Nicholas of Cusa and Gottfried Leibniz drew on his ideas, and in the early modern period alchemical treatises were falsely attributed to him. He was beatified by Pope Pius IX on 11 September 1847, and some regard his ideas as prefiguring computation theory.
ramon-magsaysay: Ramon del Fierro Magsaysay was born at Iba on 31 August 1907, of mixed Tagalog, Visayan, Spanish and Chinese descent. His father was a blacksmith and his mother a schoolteacher. He studied at the University of the Philippines and then took a degree in commerce at José Rizal College, and worked as a bus company mechanic and shop superintendent.

When the Bataan garrison surrendered in 1942 he escaped to the hills and organised the Western Luzon Guerrilla Forces. He was commissioned captain on 5 April 1942, and later commanded a force of 10,000. He helped clear the Zambales coast of the Japanese before the American landing in January 1945. In April 1946 he was elected to the House of Representatives for the Liberal Party, and was re-elected in 1949.

In September 1950 President Elpidio Quirino appointed him Secretary of National Defense after Magsaysay offered a plan to fight the Hukbalahap guerrillas, drawing on his wartime experience. With Colonel Edward Lansdale, a former advertising man and CIA agent, he sent soldiers to distribute relief goods and aid in outlying communities, and the army's image improved among rural people who had regarded it with apathy and distrust.
