In 1951 he went to Negros Occidental after the torture and killing of his ally Moises Padilla, and carried the body himself to the morgue. He resigned on 28 February 1953 and ran for president for the Nacionalista Party. He won the election of 10 November 1953 over Quirino and was the youngest president elected to that date.

Magsaysay was sworn in on 30 December 1953 wearing the barong tagalog, a first for a president, and he opened the gates of Malacañang Palace to the public. His Presidential Complaints and Action Committee heard nearly 60,000 complaints in a year. His agrarian laws included the Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1954 and the Land Reform Act of 1955, and he created the National Resettlement and Rehabilitation Administration, which gave land to landless families, and the Agricultural Credit and Cooperative Financing Administration for rural credit.

In 1954 the Hukbalahap leader Luis Taruc surrendered on 17 May, and the number of Huks fell below 2,000. He brought the Philippines into the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, founded at Manila on 8 September 1954, and worked towards the Reparation Agreement, in which Japan obliged itself to pay 550 million dollars for war damages. Magsaysay died in a plane crash at Cebu on 17 March 1957.
ramon-matias-mella: Mella was born in Santo Domingo on 25 February 1816, during the period known as the España Boba, to Antonio and Francisca, of Spanish descent; his father was a merchant. Little is recorded of his schooling, which was probably private. As a young man he was said to be skilled with sword and sabre, and at 19 he began working as a cutter of precious woods in San Cristóbal. His name is debated: most documents of his lifetime, including his baptism and marriage records, call him Ramón Mella Castillo.

In 1838 he joined La Trinitaria, the secret society Juan Pablo Duarte founded to win independence from Haitian rule, and became one of Duarte's closest collaborators. On the night of 27 February 1844, when fewer conspirators gathered than expected and some proposed delay, he refused to turn back and fired his blunderbuss into the air at the Puerta de la Misericordia. He then sat on the Central Government Board and went to the Cibao to organise the defence of Santiago.

After Pedro Santana's coup of July 1844 his position weakened and he went into exile, returning under the amnesty of President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. He held a command at the Battle of Las Carreras in 1849, and from December 1853 led a diplomatic mission to Spain seeking a protectorate or at least recognition. In the revolution against Buenaventura Báez that began in 1857 he directed the seizure of Samaná in May 1858.

When the country was annexed by Spain on 20 March 1861, Mella refused allegiance, was held in the Ozama Fortress and deported to Saint Thomas, where he lived in poverty. He returned in secret, joined the provisional government in Santiago as Minister of War and in January 1864 issued a manual of guerrilla warfare suited to the country's terrain. Ill, he died in Santiago on 4 June 1864, having asked to be buried in the national flag. In 1894 President Ulises Heureaux recognised Duarte, Mella and Francisco del Rosario Sánchez as the Founding Fathers, and since 1944 their ashes have lain at the Altar of the Homeland at the Puerta del Conde.
ramon-villeda-morales: José Ramón Adolfo Villeda Morales was born on 26 November 1909 and trained as a physician, specialising in paediatrics. A liberal who favoured the democratisation of Honduras after a long period of military rule, he was the Liberal Party candidate in the presidential election of 1954, the first free election in over two decades. He won a plurality over a divided National Party but fell short of a majority, and the deadlock led to a coup by Vice-President Julio Lozano Díaz. He and his wife, Alejandrina Bermúdez Milla, had six sons.

After the military junta of 1955, the country's constituent assembly chose Villeda Morales in 1957 to serve as president and oversee the transition to democracy. He at once began a campaign to help the poorer parts of society, introducing welfare benefits and a new labour code that favoured the large working class. These measures were popular with the masses but angered the traditional holders of power in Honduras, the military and the upper classes.

When it seemed likely that the Liberal candidate, Modesto Rodas Alvarado, would win the 1963 election with an even stronger mandate for social reform, the military answered with a coup ten days before the vote. Villeda Morales was a leading supporter of the Alliance for Progress.

Villeda Morales died of a heart attack on 8 October 1971 in New York City, where he was serving as the Honduran ambassador to the UN. He is credited with helping to modernise Honduras and to build its public health, public education and social security systems. San Pedro Sula International Airport is named after him, and his son Mauricio Villeda Bermúdez became a leader of the Liberal Party and was its candidate for the presidency in 2013.
rampjaar: After the death of William II of Orange in 1650 the republican party governed without a stadtholder in most provinces, and from 1653 Grand Pensionary Johan de Witt led the government of the regents. Louis XIV, who felt betrayed by his former Dutch allies after the Triple Alliance with England and Sweden, won Charles II of England with subsidies, and the two kings signed the secret Treaty of Dover in June 1670. By early 1672 Sweden had agreed to stay neutral, while de Witt secured promises of help from Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg and a treaty with Spain in December 1671.

The army of the States General had been weakened by two wars with England and by financial cuts. Under public pressure de Witt accepted that the young William III would become Captain-General for life on his 23rd birthday.

The war began on 12 March 1672 with an English attack on the Dutch Smyrna fleet. A French army of some 53,000 men gathered at Liège, besieged the Rhine fortresses, crossed the Lower Rhine on 12 June and took Arnhem and Zutphen, while Bernhard von Galen, Prince-Bishop of Münster, took the surrender of Overijssel. William withdrew behind the Holland Water Line, and releasing the floods on 22 June halted the French. At sea Admiral De Ruyter attacked the Anglo-French fleet at Solebay on 7 June and kept control of the coastal waters.

Orangist pamphlets accused the de Witt brothers of handing the country to France. After an attempt on Johan de Witt's life on 22 June, riots began in Dordrecht and spread through Holland and Zeeland, and on 3 July the States of Holland repealed the Perpetual Edict and appointed William stadtholder. Johan resigned on 3 August. On 20 August he was lured to the prison in The Hague where his brother Cornelis was held, and a mob killed them both. William's attacks on Naarden and Woerden and his siege of Charleroi in December failed, and late in December French troops crossing the frozen floods destroyed Bodegraven and killed many of its inhabitants.

The war went on until 1678, but by the following year most of the lost territory had been retaken. The crisis convinced William III that France aimed at a universal monarchy, and he followed an anti-French policy for the rest of his life, committing the republic to war until 1713. The Dutch economy never fully recovered, and the art market collapsed: the painter Johannes Vermeer went bankrupt for lack of buyers.
ran-min: His father, Ran Zhan, came from an aristocratic family of Wei Commandery and was captured at the age of 11 by Shi Le, founder of the Later Zhao, who had his nephew Shi Hu adopt him. Ran Min therefore grew up as Shi Min, and Shi Hu treated him as a grandson. The Book of Jin describes him as over 1.9 metres tall, fighting with a halberd in one hand and a double-edged spear in the other. In 338, when the Later Zhao army fled after the long siege of Jicheng, his was the only force that stayed intact, and in 339 he helped defeat the plans of the Jin general Yu Liang and was created Duke of Wuxing.

After Shi Hu's death in May 349 Ran Min led the vanguard when Shi Zun, Prince of Pengcheng, seized the capital Yecheng and deposed the young emperor Shi Shi. Shi Zun broke his promise to make Ran Min crown prince and later planned to execute him; warned by Shi Jian, Ran Min surrounded the palace, killed Shi Zun and his family and made Shi Jian a puppet emperor. When the Jie general Sun Fudu attacked him, Ran Min concluded that he could not rely on the Jie and other Hu. He promised promotion to every Han who brought him a Hu head and himself led the killing; over 200,000 people died, many of them Han whose features were taken for those of non-Han.

Ran Min killed Shi Jian and 38 of Shi Hu's grandsons, wiping out the Shi clan in Yecheng, and declared himself emperor of Wei. His siege of Xiangguo, held by Shi Zhi, ended in a rout by Former Yan, Shi Kun and the Qiang under Yao Xiang, with more than 100,000 dead. In 352 he marched against Former Yan; Murong Ke drew his infantry onto open ground and surrounded it with Xianbei cavalry, and when his horse Zhu Long died he was captured. Murong Jun had him whipped and executed, then, fearing his spirit was causing a drought, gave him the title Heavenly King.

The historian Lü Simian compared his courage with that of Xiang Yu and Sun Ce. Fan Wenlan wrote that despite his brutality he won sympathy among the Han, who saw the massacre as retribution, while Cai Dongfan condemned him as an opportunist who usurped the Shi clan.
rana-kumbha: Kumbhakaran Singh was born at Madariya in 1417, a son of Rana Mokal Singh of Mewar and his wife Sobhagya Devi, daughter of Jaitmal Sankhla, the Paramara fief-holder of Runkot in Marwar. His father was murdered by kinsmen named Chacha and Maira. During Kumbha's minority his grandmother, the dowager queen Hansa, and his great-uncle Ridmal acted as regents; Hansa was his main teacher and kept much influence over him.

With the help of Rao Ranmal Rathore of Marwar he defeated his father's murderers, but as Rathore power grew at the Mewar court he had Ranmal assassinated and took Marwar. Ranmal's son Jodha won it back over several years, capturing Mandore in 1453, after which a treaty restored peace and Jodha's daughter married Kumbha's son Raimal.

When Mahmud Khilji of Malwa sheltered one of Mokal's assassins, Kumbha defeated him at Sarangpur and besieged Mandu, taking Gagron, Ranthambore and other districts. He placed Shams Khan on the throne of Nagaur and later drove him out, and in 1456 he turned back the Sultan of Gujarat near Mount Abu and Kumbhalgarh. Mewari accounts credit him with 56 battles and no defeats.

Of the 84 fortresses that defended Mewar, 32 are credited to Kumbha, the chief among them Kumbhalgarh, the highest fort in Rajasthan. His Vijay Stambha at Chittor is a nine-storey tower 37 metres high, covered with sculptures of Hindu gods and scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and completed probably between 1458 and 1468; its inscriptions praise his wars against Malwa and Nagaur. The Jain temple at Ranakpur and the Kumbhashyam temple at Chittor were also built in his reign.

Kumbha played the veena and kept musicians and artists at court. He wrote a commentary on the Gita Govinda of Jaidev, treatises on music including the Sangeet raj, and four dramas in Sanskrit, Prakrit and local Rajasthani dialects. He was killed while praying near the temple of Kumbhaswami at Kumbhalgarh.
rana-sanga: Sangram Singh was born to King Raimal and Queen Ratan Kunwar, a Jhala princess from Halvad. Contemporary texts give no year of birth, only the planetary positions at the time, from which the historian Gaurishankar Hirachand Ojha calculated 1482. Sanga was Raimal's third son, and he came to the throne of Mewar after a struggle with his brothers Prithviraj and Jagmal in which he lost an eye. He ruled from Chittorgarh.

Sanga reunited the warring Rajput clans through diplomacy and marriage. Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi marched against him in 1517 and was defeated at Khatoli, where Sanga lost an arm and was lamed for life, and again at Dholpur in 1518–1519. Supporting Medini Rai, a rebel minister of the Malwa sultan, Sanga beat the combined forces of Gujarat and Malwa at Gagron in 1519 and took eastern and northern Malwa and Chanderi, ordering the jizya tax on Hindus there removed.

In Gujarat he restored Rai Mal to the throne of Idar, and in 1520 he invaded with 40,000 Rajputs, plundered the royal treasuries, destroyed several mosques and annexed Idar. At its height in 1521 his realm reached from Mandu in the south to the Indus in the west.

After Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, Sanga united several Rajput clans and advanced towards Agra. He beat Babur's forces at the Battle of Bayana in February 1527, but on 16 March, at Khanwa, the Mughals prevailed with cannon and matchlocks. Struck by an arrow, Sanga was carried unconscious from the field, and Babur raised a tower of enemy skulls.

Sanga vowed not to return to Chittor until he had defeated Babur, but while preparing a new war he was poisoned by nobles who wanted no more fighting. He died at Kalpi in January or May 1528 and was succeeded by his son Ratan Singh II. Babur admired his reign, and the Mughal historian Abd al-Qadir Badayuni ranked him with Prithviraj Chauhan as the bravest of the Rajputs. Legend credits him with a hundred battles and only one defeat.
ranavalona-i: Ranavalona was born Ramavo in 1778 at the royal residence of Ambatomanoina, about 16 kilometres east of Antananarivo. When her father warned King Andrianampoinimerina of a plot against him, the king betrothed her to his son Radama in return. She was not Radama's preferred wife and bore him no children. After Radama became king in 1810, she and other court ladies spent their days with the missionary David Griffiths, a friendship that lasted three decades.

Radama died without descendants on 27 July 1828. By custom the heir was Rakotobe, the eldest son of Radama's eldest sister, but the officer Andriamamba and others rallied the army behind Ramavo. On 11 August 1828 she declared herself successor, taking the throne name Ranavalona, and put her rivals to death, including Rakotobe. Her coronation took place on 12 June 1829.

Her reign of 33 years aimed to strengthen the authority of Imerina over subjugated provinces and preserve Madagascar's sovereignty amid European rivalry. She ended the friendship treaty with Britain, restricted the London Missionary Society and in 1835 forbade the practice of Christianity among the Malagasy. In 1829 she repelled an attack by six French ships on Foulpointe. The Frenchman Jean Laborde, shipwrecked in 1832, built factories for cannon, muskets and gunpowder, ending the dependence on Europe for arms.

She continued the wars of expansion with a standing army of 20,000 to 30,000, raised through fanompoana, forced labour in place of taxes. The army exacted harsh penalties from resisting communities; mass executions were common and survivors were taken as slaves. The historian Gwyn Campbell estimated 60,000 non-Merina deaths in violent conflict between 1816 and 1853 and 160,000 Merina soldiers' deaths from 1820 to 1853, many from malaria. Justice used the tangena ordeal, in which accused people took a poison from a tree nut. By some estimates the population of Madagascar declined by as much as half during her reign.

Ranavalona died in her sleep on 16 August 1861 at Manjakamiadana palace in Antananarivo. Her son Radama II succeeded her and quickly reversed her traditionalist policies. European contemporaries generally condemned her as a tyrant or a madwoman, a view that lasted in Western writing until the 1970s.

Later historians often see her as a traditionalist who refused foreign occupation of her kingdom, and Campbell argues that her economic and military policies were rational ways of guarding Madagascar from imperial domination. Malagasy views are varied: most condemn her reign, a view common among Christians, while others admire her defence of tradition and independence.
ranavalona-ii: Ranavalona II was born Princess Ramoma in 1829 at Ambatomanoina, near Antananarivo in the central highlands, to Prince Razakaratrimo and Princess Rafarasoa Ramasindrazana. Like her cousin Rasoherina she was married to King Radama II, in 1845 or 1846, and was widowed when he was assassinated in the nobles' coup of 1863.

The prime minister Rainivoninahitriniony played a major part in the plot and was forced from his post. His younger brother Rainilaiarivony took his place, married Queen Rasoherina and, when she died, helped designate Ranavalona II the next monarch and married her to keep his position. At court she was tutored by Protestant missionaries, who greatly influenced her religious and political views.

Ranavalona II succeeded to the throne on the death of Rasoherina on 1 April 1868. On 21 February 1869 she entered a political marriage with Rainilaiarivony in a public ceremony at Andohalo, at which the court officially converted to Christianity. The conversion brought the increasingly powerful Protestant faction under the influence of the court. Declaring Madagascar a Christian nation, she had the traditional royal talismans, the sampy, burned in a bonfire in September 1869 and replaced their authority with that of the Bible.

Under her rule deforestation was considered. She authorised construction in brick and other durable materials within the walls of Antananarivo, which King Andrianampoinimerina had forbidden, and banned the slash-and-burn farming called tavy, charcoal making and house building in forests.

Ranavalona II died in 1883 and was buried at Ambohimanga. In 1897, to desacralise the holy city, the French colonial authority disinterred her remains and those of other monarchs buried there and moved them to the tombs in the compound of the Rova of Antananarivo, where her bones were placed in the tomb of Rasoherina. She was succeeded by Ranavalona III, the last monarch of the kingdom.
ranavalona-iii: Ranavalona III was born Princess Razafindrahety on 22 November 1861 at Amparibe, outside Antananarivo, the niece of Queen Ranavalona II and a great-granddaughter of King Andrianampoinimerina. She was educated by teachers of the London Missionary Society and at several mission schools, and was baptised as a Protestant on 5 April 1874. She married a nobleman named Ratrimo, who died on 8 May 1883 aged 22. Rumour held that Prime Minister Rainilaiarivony had him poisoned so that she could marry the prime minister and succeed to the throne, as the constitutional monarchy of 1863 required a political marriage between queen and prime minister.

She was proclaimed queen on the death of Ranavalona II and crowned on 22 November 1883, her 22nd birthday, with 500 boys and 400 girls from the capital's schools beside the customary soldiers. Her role was largely ceremonial, and Rainilaiarivony made nearly all political decisions. She delivered speeches on his behalf and opened buildings such as a hospital and a girls' school.

France had bombarded the north-western coast and occupied Mahajanga and Toamasina in 1883. Rainilaiarivony engaged the Briton Digby Willoughby to train the army. A peace treaty was ratified in 1886, and France then declared a protectorate despite the opposition of the Malagasy government. Britain accepted it in the Anglo-French agreement of 1890. Diplomatic relations were broken off in November 1894, and French troops took Toamasina and Mahajanga, losing more than 6,000 of 15,000 soldiers to disease. After French artillery bombarded the Rova compound in September 1895, the queen surrendered her kingdom. France annexed Madagascar on 1 January 1896, and the menalamba rebellion, a peasant guerrilla war, began in December 1895 and was put down by the end of 1897.

Joseph Gallieni placed the queen under arrest, exiled her on 27 February 1897 and abolished the monarchy the next day. She lived in Réunion, then from 1899 in a villa in Algiers, with an allowance that rose from 25,000 to 75,000 francs after public pressure in France. From 1901 she visited France several times and became popular with the public. She was never allowed to return to Madagascar, and she died of an embolism at her villa on 23 May 1917.

She was buried in Algiers, and in November 1938 her remains were moved to the tomb of Queen Rasoherina at the Rova of Antananarivo. After a fire in 1995 they were re-interred in the royal tombs at Ambohimanga.
ranbir-singh-of-jammu-and-kashmir: Ranbir Singh was born at Ramgarh in August 1830, the third son of Gulab Singh by his first wife, Rakwal Maharani. He was adopted by his childless uncle, Raja Suchet Singh, and inherited all his jagirs on his death in 1844. His father, suffering from edema, abdicated in his favour and became governor of Kashmir.

During the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 the state sided with the British, sending money to their troops in Punjab, refusing asylum to the mutineers and sheltering British women and children in the Kashmir Valley; after Gulab Singh's death Ranbir sent a battalion to the siege of Delhi. In reward the Treaty of Amritsar was amended in 1860 to let a Dogra ruler adopt an heir from a collateral branch, and in 1862 he received the Order of the Star of India.

In 1860 his army under Colonel Devi Singh Narania, Colonel Bijai Singh and General Hoshiara Singh retook Gilgit, and by the end of 1870 Hunza and Nagar paid tribute in return for an annual subsidy. He created departments for foreign, home and civil affairs and the army, held two durbars a day to hear petitions, founded a silk factory and saw the shawl industry flourish.

In 1873 he rejected Lord Northbrook's proposal to place a British Resident in Kashmir. In 1882 he asked that his younger son Amar Singh succeed him, but on his death on 12 September 1885 Lord Ripon named Pratap Singh, who then accepted a Resident.

Following the example of Zain-ul-Abidin and Avantivarman, former rulers of Kashmir, he employed pandits and maulvis to translate religious and medical texts into Urdu, Dogri and Hindi; Sir Aurel Stein later catalogued 5,000 such works. He knew Sanskrit and Persian and spoke Pashto with his Afghan bodyguards. He founded a Sanskrit school in the Raghunath Temple complex and the Ranveer Sanskrit Vidyalaya in Varanasi, and in 1882 gave 100,000 rupees to the new University of the Punjab, which made him its first fellow.
rangaku: Rangaku, or Dutch learning, and by extension Yōgaku, Western learning, grew out of contact with the Dutch enclave of Dejima in Nagasaki, where the Dutch traders were the only Europeans tolerated in Japan. Their movements were watched and strictly controlled. In the first phase Western books were prohibited except those on nautical and medical matters, and a small group of hereditary Japanese-Dutch translators worked in Nagasaki.

The Dutch gave the shōgun news of world events and novelties each year on their trip to Edo. The surgeon Caspar Schamberger, one of the most important physicians at Dejima, induced a continuing interest in medical books, instruments and treatment methods. In 1720 the shōgun Tokugawa Yoshimune relaxed the rules, which started an influx of Dutch books and their translation into Japanese.

Medicine was the first field. Debates between proponents of traditional Chinese medicine and the new Western learning led to experiments and dissections, and the New Text on Anatomy of 1774, compiled by scholars led by Sugita Genpaku from a Dutch translation of a German work, became a reference. In 1804 Hanaoka Seishū performed a mastectomy under general anaesthesia, combining Chinese herbal medicine with Western surgery.

In 1838 Ogata Kōan founded the school Tekijuku, whose alumni included Fukuzawa Yukichi. Shizuki Tadao translated a work on Newton's theories in 1798 and coined terms still in use, such as the words for gravity and centrifugal force. Udagawa Yōan's Opening Principles of Chemistry of 1840 introduced Lavoisier's findings and terms such as oxidation and reduction.

Other fields followed. Hiraga Gennai obtained an electrostatic generator from the Dutch around 1770, which the Japanese called the elekiteru and sold as a curiosity. Kunitomo Ikkansai built Japan's first reflecting telescope in 1831. Inō Tadataka made maps between 1800 and 1818 that served as the definitive maps of Japan for nearly a century. In 1824 the German physician Philipp Franz von Siebold began a medical school at Narutaki near Nagasaki that grew into a meeting place for about fifty students.

In 1839 scholars of Western studies briefly suffered repression in the Bansha no goku, after they opposed a measure enacted by the shogunate to introduce the death penalty against foreigners other than the Dutch who came ashore. Rangaku became obsolete when Japan opened up during the last decades of the Tokugawa regime, as students went abroad and foreign employees came to teach.

The Nagasaki Naval Training Center, established in 1855 beside Dejima, was directed by Dutch naval officers until 1859. Rangaku scholars such as Fukuzawa Yukichi, Katsu Kaishū and Sakamoto Ryōma then shifted the main language of learning from Dutch to English, and because they took a pro-Western stance several were assassinated, among them Sakuma Shōzan in 1864 and Sakamoto Ryōma in 1867.
ranganathaswamy-temple-srirangam: The temple is dedicated to Ranganathar, a form of Vishnu, and his consort Ranganayaki, a form of Lakshmi. It stands on an island between the Kaveri and Kollidam rivers, about 12 kilometres north of Tiruchirappalli. According to the Sriranga Mahatmyam, the shrine's Vimanam emerged when Brahma performed austerities during the churning of the cosmic ocean. Rama gave it to King Vibhishana, who on his way to Sri Lanka left it at the island, where it would not move; he gave it to a local king, Dharmavarma, on condition that the deity face south, as it does, in a reclining posture.

Its first builder is said to have been the Chola ruler Dharmavarma; after a Kaveri flood destroyed the vimanam, the early Chola king Killivalavan is said to have rebuilt the complex. Inscriptions from the Cholas, Pandyas, Hoysalas, Marathas and Vijayanagara range from the 7th to the 17th centuries. The temple took a central place in Sri Vaishnavism in the centuries after Ramanuja (1017 to 1137) and his predecessors Nathamuni and Yamunacharya.

Its island site left it open to floods and to invading armies, which repeatedly used it as a camp. Delhi Sultanate armies looted and destroyed it in a raid on the Pandyan kingdom in the early 14th century, and it was rebuilt in the late 14th century. In the 16th and 17th centuries it was fortified and gained more gopurams. The Rajagopuram, begun under Achyuta Deva Raya of Vijayanagara, was left unfinished after the empire fell in the late 16th century and reached its present 73 metres only in 1987, when the Ahobila Matha raised the funds; it was consecrated on 25 March 1987.

More than 800 inscriptions, about 640 of them on temple walls, run from the late 9th century to the 16th and are in Tamil, Sanskrit, Kannada, Telugu, Marathi and Odia. They show that the temple also ran a free kitchen, granaries and a hospital, and financed local projects.

The complex occupies 63 hectares and is laid out as a temple town in seven concentric enclosures, the inner five holding the shrines and the outer two homes and markets. It has 21 gopurams, 39 pavilions and many water tanks. Among its halls is the thousand-pillar mandapam of the Vijayanagara period.

Ranganathaswamy is the only one of the 108 Divya Desams praised by all the Alvars, with 247 hymns. An annual 21-day festival in the month of Margazhi attracts one million visitors. In 2017 the temple received UNESCO's Asia-Pacific Award of Merit for conservation, and it is on UNESCO's tentative list for World Heritage status.
rani-karnavati: Karnavati, also called Karmavati, was born a Hada Chauhan princess of Bundi, the daughter of Rao Nirbudh and granddaughter of Rao Banduji, the sixth Rao of Bundi. She and her sister Lakhu Devi were both married to Rana Sanga of Mewar, and she bore his younger sons Vikramaditya and Udai Singh. Through Udai Singh she was the grandmother of Maharana Pratap.

After Rana Sanga's death in 1528 her stepson Ratan took the throne, and Karnavati lived with her sons at Ranthambore Fort, with her cousin Rao Suraj Mal of Bundi as her representative. Ratan ordered her back to Chittor to give up the treasure Sanga had taken from the kings of Malwa, but she evaded the demand, and she is said to have negotiated with Babur for the land of Bayana, without result.

In 1531 Ratan and Suraj Mal killed each other on a hunt, and the throne passed to Vikramaditya, who was thought a weak ruler and had already been defeated by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat. When Bahadur Shah attacked Mewar again, the nobles would not fight for Vikramaditya. Karnavati wrote to them to come forward for the honour of the Sisodias, and they agreed on condition that Vikramaditya and Udai Singh go to Bundi for safety. She sent the boys there in the care of her trusted maid Panna Dai.

The outnumbered defenders lost, and Bahadur Shah entered and sacked Chittorgarh for the second time. As defeat came, Karnavati and the other noble women of the court burned themselves in jauhar, while the men put on saffron clothes and rode out to fight to the death in saka. It was the second of the three jauhars performed at Chittor. The later legend that she sent a rakhi to Humayun tied her name to the festival of Raksha Bandhan, but no contemporary writer records it, and historians such as Satish Chandra regard it as a fable.
rani-mangammal: Mangammal, also called Mangamma, was the daughter of Tupakula Lingama Nayaka. When her husband died in 1682 he was succeeded by her son, Rangakrishna Muthu Virappa Nayak, who ruled until his death in 1689. Her son's widow was then pregnant, and the throne passed to Mangammal's grandson. The young king's mother committed sati, and Mangammal became regent during his minority. The capital of the kingdom in her time was Tiruchy.

Her regency is remembered for its public works, many of them still in use. Irrigation channels were repaired, new roads built and avenue trees planted, and temples and municipal buildings were completed, among them her Spring Palace at TumKum, which now houses the Gandhi Memorial Museum in Madurai. The highway from Cape Comorin, first built in her time, was known as Rani Mangammal Salai. She also first held the Unjal festival in the Meenakshi temple in the Tamil month of Ani, when the royal families visit the temple and pay tribute to Meenakshi Amman.

She aided the Mughal army at the Siege of Jinji. Seeing that Rajaram, entrenched in Jinji, meant to attack Thanjavur and Madurai if the Mughal army withdrew, she recognised Aurangzeb as her suzerain and helped Zulfiqar Khan against the fort. When it was taken after eight years, she and her family held it under Mughal leadership.

When her grandson came of age in 1704, Mangammal and her prime minister, Achayya, refused to give up power. They were seized by the army commander and executed. She is still widely remembered as a maker of roads and avenues and a builder of temples, tanks and choultries, and for her diplomatic and political skill. A portrait of her made in her own time can still be seen in the Unjal Mandapam of the Meenakshi temple.
ranjit-singh: Ranjit Singh was born to Maha Singh and Raj Kaur in Gujranwala, in a Sandhawalia Jat Sikh family. He was named Buddh Singh at birth, and his father renamed him Ranjit, 'victor in battle', to commemorate his army's victory over the Chattha chief Pir Muhammad. Smallpox in infancy cost him the sight of his left eye. His father died in 1792, when he was about twelve, and he became the minor head of the Sukerchakia Misl, raised by his mother. He never learned to read or write beyond the Gurmukhi alphabet, but was trained at home in riding, musketry and other martial arts.

Ranjit Singh was prominent among the Sikh leaders who opposed the Durrani ruler Zaman Shah's third invasion of the Punjab. After Zaman Shah's retreat in 1799 he attacked the Bhangi Sikhs who held Lahore with an army of 25,000, joined by another 25,000 led by his mother-in-law Rani Sada Kaur. The Bhangis escaped, and the people of Lahore welcomed his rule. In 1802 he took Amritsar and promised to rebuild the Harmandir Sahib in marble and gold. On 1 January 1806 he signed a treaty with the East India Company by which neither side would cross the Sutlej River in arms.

By 1813 he had annexed the Sikh misls; later decades brought Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. At his death the empire reached from Ladakh to the borders of Sindh, and from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej. Muslims made up about 70 per cent of its population, Hindus about 24 per cent and Sikhs 6 to 7 per cent. His army and government included Sikhs, Muslims, Hindus and Europeans such as the Frenchman Jean-François Allard, though he avoided recruiting Britons. Nineteenth-century Muslim writers such as Shahamat Ali judged his government despotic.

In the 1830s Ranjit Singh suffered several health complications and a stroke, which some records attribute to alcohol. He died in his sleep on 27 June 1839. Among his possessions was the Koh-i-Noor diamond, taken from Shuja Shah Durrani, which he left to the Jagannath Temple in Puri.

After his death the empire failed to create a stable succession or lasting structure of government. Clive Dewey argues that its decline owed much to the jagir tax system inherited from the Mughals, over whose spoils nobles and his family fought. Palace coups and assassinations followed, and the British and the Sikh Empire fought two Anglo-Sikh wars, the second ending the empire. His lasting legacy is the restoration of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, much of whose gilding and marblework dates from his time.
ranjitsinhji: Ranjitsinhji was born on 10 September 1872 at Sadodar, a village of Nawanagar in Kathiawar, into a Hindu Jadeja Rajput family. In October 1878 the ruler Vibhaji, who had disinherited his violent son Kalubha, chose him as heir, but never completed the adoption, and in August 1882 a woman of his court bore him a son, Jaswantsinhji. Ranjitsinhji was educated at the Rajkumar College, run like an English public school, and in 1888 its principal Chester Macnaghten took him to England. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge, but concentrated on sport and never graduated.

Joining Sussex, he became in 1896 the first amateur to reach 1,000 runs in a season. In 1899 he scored 3,159 runs at an average of 63.18, the first batsman to pass 3,000 first-class runs in a season. He played more on the back foot than earlier batsmen and popularised, and may have invented, the leg glance. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1897, and Neville Cardus wrote that when he batted a strange light from the East flickered in the English sunshine.

He was often in debt and faced bankruptcy in 1901. Early in his career he met racism, and once used the pseudonym Smith. He has been called the Father of Indian Cricket, and the Ranji Trophy was named after him in 1935, but critics such as Mihir Bose note that he did nothing to develop the game in India, telling its board that he and his nephew Duleepsinhji were English cricketers.

Jaswantsinhji, known as Jassaji, took over Nawanagar in March 1903 and died of a fever on 14 August 1906; there is circumstantial evidence that he may have been poisoned. After six months the British chose Ranjitsinhji. Early in his rule he imposed a land rent that, with drought, provoked rebellion, and he had his army destroy the villages in retribution. In August 1915 he lost his right eye in a shooting accident. His administrator Berthon carried out slum clearance, irrigation and the extension of the railway. Ranjitsinhji worked to unite the princes against democracy and the independence movement, helped found the Chamber of Princes, and died on 2 April 1933.
rann-of-kutch: The Rann of Kutch covers over 26,000 square kilometres, mostly in the Kutch district of Gujarat, with a smaller part in Sindh in Pakistan. The word Rann means desert in Hindi. The Great Rann has the Thar Desert to the north, the low hills of Kutch to the south and the Indus River Delta to the west, while the Little Rann lies to its south-east and reaches the Gulf of Kutch.

Once a shallow part of the Arabian Sea, the area became an inland lake when tectonic uplift cut it off, and it is the seasonal salt marsh left as the waters recede. The surface is flat and close to sea level, with sandy islands called bets two to three metres above the flood level, and most of it floods in the monsoon, to about 50 centimetres, and dries again before the next.

The region's history begins with early Neolithic settlements, and people of the Indus Civilization seem to have settled there around 3500 BCE. Dholavira, the largest Indus site in India, lies in the Rann, as does the industrial site of Khirasara, where a warehouse was found. Some Indologists hold that in Indus times the Rann was a navigable archipelago rather than a salt marsh, so that it may have had ports serving the civilization's maritime trade. It was later part of both the Maurya and Gupta empires. In the early twentieth century, during the British Raj, a ban on salt harvesting led to a protest march by Mahatma Gandhi.

The Rann of Kutch is the only large flooded grassland in the Indomalayan realm, with grassland, thorn scrub, mangroves and desert vegetation. It has about 50 species of mammals, including the Indian wild ass, which is limited to the Rann, and over 200 bird species such as the lesser flamingo. The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary was established in 1973 in the Little Rann and the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary in 1986, and Pakistan has the Rann of Kutch Wildlife Sanctuary. The Rann Utsav, a three-month festival, celebrates local art forms.
rano-raraku: Rano Raraku is a volcanic crater of consolidated volcanic ash, or tuff, on the lower slopes of Terevaka on Easter Island, which belongs to Chile. It lies within Rapa Nui National Park, a World Heritage Site, and gives its name to one of the park's seven sections. Its sides are high and steep except on the north and north-west, where they are lower and gently sloping. The interior holds one of the island's three freshwater crater lakes, bordered by nga'atu or totora reeds. These plants were once thought to show contact with the South American mainland, but are now known to have grown on the island for at least 30,001 years; the Rapa Nui used them for thatched shelter and swimming aids.

The crater served as a quarry for about 500 years, until the early eighteenth century, and supplied the stone for about 95 per cent of the island's known monolithic sculptures, the moai. It is a visual record of moai design and carving technique, and 887 moai remain there.

The unfinished statues in the quarry are notable for their number, for the inaccessibility of some high on the outer crater wall, and for the size of the largest, at 21.6 metres almost twice that of any moai ever completed, with an estimated weight of 270 tonnes, far more than any moved. Some seem to have been abandoned after the carvers met inclusions of very hard rock. Others may never have been meant to be separated from the rock in which they are carved.

Outside the quarry stand moai, some partly buried to their shoulders in the spoil. Their eyes were not hollowed out, they have no pukao, and they were not cast down in the island's civil wars, so they have supplied some of its best-known images. Tukuturi is an unusual figure with a beard and a kneeling posture, called tuku turi, which was used by the men and women who formed the chorus at the festivals called riu. It may be related to the Tangata manu cult, in which case it would be one of the last moai made.
ranoji-scindia: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court. He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.
ranthambore-fort: Ranthambore Fort stands within Ranthambore National Park near Sawai Madhopur in eastern Rajasthan. The park was the hunting ground of the Maharajas of Jaipur until Indian independence. The fortress commands a strategic position 700 feet above the surrounding plain, and was considered impregnable owing to its site and design, which is one reason why so many rulers wanted it. It gives a panoramic view of the park and is now a popular tourist attraction. In 2013 the World Heritage Committee, meeting at Phnom Penh, declared it, with five other forts of Rajasthan, a World Heritage Site under the group Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

Its earlier name was Ranastambhapura, Sanskrit for City of the Battle Post. It was associated with Jainism under Prithviraja I of the Chauhan dynasty in the 12th century, when Siddhasenasuri listed it among the holy Jain tirthas. After the defeat of Prithviraja III in 1192 the fort came under the Ghurid ruler Muhammad of Ghor. The Delhi Sultan Iltutmish captured it in 1226, and the Chauhans retook it after his death in 1236. Forces of Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud, led by the future Sultan Balban, besieged it unsuccessfully in 1248 and 1253 and took it from Jaitrasingh Chauhan in 1259. Shakti Dev succeeded Jaitrasingh in 1283, recaptured the fort and enlarged the kingdom.

Sultan Jalal ud din Firuz Khalji besieged it without success in 1290-91. In 1299 Hammiradeva sheltered Muhammad Shah, a rebel general of Sultan Ala ud din Khalji, and refused to hand him over, and the Sultan besieged and took the fort in 1301.

Later the fortress was held by various kings of Mewar, directly under Rana Hamir Singh, Rana Kumbha and Rana Sanga. In the reign of Rana Udai Singh I it passed to the Hada Rajputs of Bundi, and Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat held it briefly from 1532 to 1535. The Mughal emperor Akbar took it from the Hadas in the Siege of Ranthambore. In the 17th century it passed to the Kachwaha Maharajas of Jaipur and remained part of Jaipur state until independence; Jaipur acceded to India in 1949 and joined Rajasthan in 1950.

Within the fort are three Hindu temples, to Ganesha as Trinetra Ganesha, Shiva and Ramlalaji, built in the 12th and 13th centuries from red Karauli stone, and a Jain temple of Sumatinath and Sambhavanath. The Ganesha temple draws thousands of visitors every Wednesday.
ranuccio-i-farnese-duke-of-parma: Ranuccio I Farnese was born on 28 March 1569, the son of Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, and Infanta Maria of Portugal. Through his mother he stood first in line for the Portuguese throne by feudal custom when his great-uncle King Henry died, when he was eleven.

His father was an ally of Philip II of Spain, another claimant, so Ranuccio's rights were not pressed, and Philip's troops occupied the country. He was engaged in 1599 to Archduchess Catherine Renata of Austria, who died soon after, and on 7 May 1600 he married Margherita Aldobrandini, niece of Pope Clement VIII. They had nine children, of whom only Odoardo and several daughters survived infancy.

Ranuccio reigned as Duke of Parma, Piacenza and Castro from 1592. A firm believer in absolute monarchy, he centralised the administration of Parma and Piacenza in 1594 and so removed the nobles' vast prerogatives. He is best remembered for the Great Justice of 1612, in which many Piacentine nobles suspected of plotting against him were executed.

His mistress Claudia Colla and her mother were accused of using witchcraft to keep him from having children and were sentenced to burning. A condemned conspirator, Gianfrancesco Sanvitale, falsely named Vincenzo Gonzaga of Mantua and Cesare d'Este of Modena, and Ranuccio's acceptance of this confession damaged his reputation among Italian rulers, so that in the early 1620s no Italian family offered a bride for his heir.

The duchy annexed Colorno, Sala Baganza and Montechiarugolo under Ranuccio. He guided a cultural renewal of Parma, revitalised its university, completed the expansion of the city walls and built the Farnese Theater, which held 4,500 people. The Palazzo della Pilotta, the Farnese court palace, was completed in 1620. He died on 5 March 1622 and was succeeded by his son Odoardo, at first under the regency of Ranuccio's brother, Odoardo Farnese. His eldest surviving son Alessandro, deaf and mentally disabled from birth, had been excluded from the succession.
raoul-wallenberg: Raoul Wallenberg was born on 4 August 1912 in Lidingö, near Stockholm. His father, a naval officer, died of cancer three months before his birth, and his mother and grandmother raised him together. His paternal grandfather, Gustaf Wallenberg, had been a diplomat and envoy to Tokyo, Istanbul and Sofia. He worked as an architect and businessman. From 1941 he made frequent trips to Budapest as the representative of his business associate Kálmán Lauer, and he learned Hungarian. Within a year he was a joint owner and international director of the company.

The War Refugee Board recruited Wallenberg in 1944. He reached the Swedish legation in Budapest on 9 July 1944. Miklós Horthy had halted the transports from Hungary two days earlier, after warnings from Roosevelt, Churchill, the King of Sweden and the Pope, but between May and early July Eichmann and his associates had deported more than 400,000 Jews, all but 15,000 of them to Auschwitz-Birkenau. About 230,000 Jews remained.

With the Swedish diplomat Per Anger and Miklós Krausz, he issued protective passports identifying the bearers as Swedish subjects awaiting repatriation. The documents were not legal, but they looked official and were generally accepted by German and Hungarian authorities, who were sometimes bribed. He also sheltered Jews in buildings declared Swedish territory. Some have claimed that he rescued 100,000 Jews, but historians regard that figure as an exaggeration; Yad Vashem estimates that about 4,500 people received protective paperwork.

On 17 January 1945, during the Siege of Budapest, Wallenberg went to Marshal Malinovsky's headquarters in Debrecen to answer allegations of espionage and was detained by Soviet agents. On 6 February 1957 the Soviet government released a document dated 17 July 1947 which said that he had died in his cell, probably of heart failure. Vyacheslav Nikonov, investigating in 1991, concluded that he was executed in 1947, but there is no conclusive proof, and some former prisoners claimed to have seen him later. The Swedish Tax Agency declared him dead in absentia in 2016.
Yad Vashem named him one of the Righteous Among the Nations in 1963. In 1981 he became an honorary citizen of the United States, the second person after Winston Churchill.
raphael: Raphael was born in Urbino, a small city of the Papal States whose court had been established by Federico da Montefeltro, created Duke of Urbino by Pope Sixtus IV. His father, Giovanni Santi, was court painter to the Duke and also a poet who wrote a rhymed chronicle of Federico's life. Raphael's mother Màgia died in 1491, and his father on 1 August 1494, so that he was an orphan at eleven. His guardian became his uncle Bartolomeo, a priest, who engaged in litigation with his stepmother. Raphael probably took part in managing his father's workshop from a very early age.

He probably trained in the workshop of Pietro Perugino and was described as a fully trained master by 1500. From about 1504 he spent a good deal of time in Florence, though possibly never as a continuous resident. A letter of recommendation of October 1504 describes him as a young painter who had decided to study there.

In 1508 Raphael moved to Rome, where he lived for the rest of his life. Pope Julius II invited him, perhaps at the suggestion of the architect Donato Bramante, who came from just outside Urbino and was distantly related to him. Julius at once commissioned him to fresco what was meant to become the Pope's private library in the Vatican Palace, a far larger commission than any he had had before. The Raphael Rooms, with The School of Athens in the Stanza della Segnatura, became the largest work of his career.

According to Vasari, Raphael eventually had a workshop of fifty pupils and assistants, arguably the largest team under any single old master painter. The most important were Giulio Romano and Gianfrancesco Penni, who were left many of his drawings and continued the workshop after his death. In 1514 he became engaged to Maria Bibbiena, Cardinal Bibbiena's niece, but the marriage had not taken place when she died in 1520.

Raphael was one of the finest draftsmen in the history of Western art and used drawings extensively to plan his compositions; over four hundred sheets survive. He made no prints himself but collaborated with Marcantonio Raimondi on about fifty engravings, which were the main way his art was experienced outside Italy until the twentieth century. His influence in his own century was less than that of Michelangelo, but those who disliked the excesses of Mannerism soon held him up as the ideal balanced painter. In the 18th and 19th centuries his serene and harmonious qualities were again regarded as the highest models.
rapperswil: Rapperswil lies on the northern shore of Lake Zurich, at the point where the Seedamm isthmus, an ice age moraine, cuts the lake in two. The upper, eastern part is called the Obersee. Part of the old town, the castle and a monastery stand on a peninsula. The town is often called the town of roses because of its rose gardens, where about 15,000 plants of 600 kinds can be seen between June and October.

Settlement in the area goes back at least 5,000 years. Remains of a first wooden bridge to Hurden, dated to 1523 BCE, and neighbouring prehistoric pile dwellings are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. At Kempraten the Roman vicus Centum Prata became an important trading centre in the 1st century CE.

Rapperswil Castle was built around 1200 by the Counts of Rapperswil, Rudolf II and his son Rudolf III, and the town was founded when the family moved across the lake from Altendorf. The last countess of the house, Elisabeth von Rapperswil, died in 1309. Her grandson Johann II of Habsburg-Laufenburg led the opposition to Rudolf Brun, the mayor of Zurich, and in 1350 Brun destroyed the town walls and the castle, which Albrecht II, Duke of Austria, rebuilt in 1352/54.

Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria, built a wooden bridge across the lake between 1358 and 1360, about 1,450 metres long, which was used until 1878. The town bought its freedom in 1415, and in 1458 it came under the Swiss Confederation as a common lordship of Glarus and Schwyz. After the Act of Mediation of 1803 it joined the canton of St. Gallen.

On 1 January 2007 Rapperswil and Jona merged into the municipality of Rapperswil-Jona. Since 1870 the castle has housed the Polish National Museum, founded by Polish exiles including Count Wladyslaw Broel-Plater. The castle, the medieval town hall and the Seedamm area with the Heilig Hüsli chapel are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance.
raqqa: Raqqa lies on the north bank of the Euphrates in Syria, about 160 kilometres east of Aleppo. The mounds of Tall Zaydan and Tall al-Bi'a, the second identified with the Babylonian city of Tuttul, show that the area was inhabited from remote antiquity. The modern city traces its history to the Hellenistic foundation of Nikephorion, which Pliny attributes to Alexander the Great and Appian to Seleucus I Nicator. Seleucus II Callinicus enlarged it and renamed it Kallinikos after himself. In Roman times it belonged to the province of Osrhoene.

The Byzantine emperor Leo I rebuilt the city in 466, but the name Kallinikos prevailed. By treaty it was one of the few official cross-border trading posts between the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. It fell to the Muslim commander Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639 or 640 and took the Arabic name al-Raqqah, 'the morass', after its marshy surroundings. Its Christians were allowed to keep their existing churches but not to build new ones. In 770-1 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur began a new garrison city, al-Rafiqah, about 200 metres west of Raqqa, to strengthen the frontier with the Byzantine Empire; about 2,660 metres of its walls survive, with its congregational mosque.

The caliph Harun al-Rashid made the city his capital from 796. Raqqa declined in the late 9th century through warfare between the Abbasids and the Tulunids and the rise of the Qarmatians, and declined rapidly under the Hamdanids in the 940s. From the late 10th century to the early 12th it was controlled by Bedouin dynasties such as the Banu Numayr. Under the Zangid and Ayyubid dynasties it flourished again on agriculture and industry, and the blue-glazed Raqqa ware dates from then. The Mongol invasions of the 1260s destroyed it. The Ottomans established a garrison there in 1864, which began the revival of the modern city.

Raqqa is a city of Syria on the Euphrates. Its growth in the 1950s was stimulated by a worldwide cotton boom, and cotton is still the main agricultural product of the region. The Baghdad Gate, the Qasr al-Banat and the Abbasid walls and mosque are among the surviving monuments. From 2014 to 2017 the city was the capital of the Islamic State. The Raqqa Museum held many cuneiform tablets, some excavated at Tell Sabi Abyad, which survive today as casts and 3D reconstructions.
raqqada: Ibrahim II ibn Ahmad, the ninth Aghlabid emir, moved his residence from al-Abbasiyya to find a quiet place away from the noise of the city, and Raqqada became the dynasty's second capital, about ten kilometres south-west of Kairouan. It was furnished with several palaces and a mosque, and the Aghlabids set up a textile and paper factory there to supply the House of Wisdom, the Bayt al-Hikma. For a time the city grew even larger than Kairouan.

Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, founder of the Fatimid dynasty, settled at Raqqada after first moving to Kairouan, but he later chose another capital and founded Mahdia. After the troops of the fourth Fatimid caliph, al-Muizz, entered Fustat on 7 July 969 and Cairo was founded as the new capital, Raqqada was demolished. After 1960 a presidential palace was built on part of the site.

The palaces have been only partly excavated, but remains spread over about 9 square kilometres show that the city grew large. Carved stucco similar to that of Abbasid Samarra and glazed pottery with a metallic sheen have been found. The one palace studied, probably the Qasr as-Sahn or Courtyard Palace, was a mudbrick enclosure of 55 by 55 metres with round buttresses, a central courtyard over a cistern, a bent entrance and a columned reception hall with an apse that probably marked the emir's seat; it was later enlarged to 105 by 105 metres.

North-east of it lay a water basin between 90 and 130 metres wide, perhaps part of the Qasr al-Bahr or Water Palace named in the sources, the earliest such palace in the Mediterranean region. Ibrahim II's own residence, the Qasr al-Fath or Palace of Victory, has not been located.

Since 1986 the site has housed the National Museum of Islamic Art. Its collections include ceramics from the 9th and 10th centuries, when Raqqada was occupied, finds from Kairouan and al-Mansuriyya, coins spanning more than six centuries of the history of Ifriqiya, and manuscripts from the library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, among them leaves of the 10th-century Blue Koran.
raramuri: The Rarámuri are believed to be descended from a people of the Mogollon culture. They once lived across much of Chihuahua and withdrew to the high sierras and canyons, such as Copper Canyon in the Sierra Madre Occidental, as the Spanish colonisers arrived. The Spanish called them Tarahumara. In their own language the term rarámuri refers specifically to men; women are called mukí individually and omugí or igómale collectively. The early ethnographer Carl Lumholtz took the name to mean runners on foot, though that reading is not fully agreed.

By the early 17th century the Spanish had established mines in Rarámuri territory and made some slave raids to find workers for them. The Jesuit Juan Fonte founded the mission of San Pablo Balleza at the southern end of their lands, but the Tepehuan revolt of 1616 killed him and seven other Jesuits and closed the mission for over a decade. The discovery of the Parral mines in 1631 brought more slave raids and missionaries, with missions at Las Bocas, Huejotitán, San Felipe and Satevó.

In 1648 the Rarámuri gathered at Fariagic and destroyed the mission of San Francisco de Borja; two of the leaders were captured and executed. They then divided. Those in the lower missions moved into the general Catholic population and largely lost their tribal identity, while those of the upper country went to war under Tepóraca and others and drove out the Jesuits and settlers. The Jesuits returned in the 1670s and baptised thousands, who kept a separate identity. Tepóraca was executed in 1690, and a war of 1696 to 1698 ended in defeat. The Jesuits were expelled from Spanish territories in 1767, and the missions declined.

The Rarámuri speak a Uto-Aztecan language, which is still widely used though pressed by Spanish. Their staple crops are maize and beans, and many raise cattle, sheep and goats and move between places over the year. Their religion combines Indigenous customs with Catholicism: Riosi, God, is identified with the deity Onoruame, the Great Father, and God's wife with the Virgin Mary. Maize beer, batári, is shared at communal gatherings called tesgüinadas, which accompany footraces, work parties and ceremonies.

With widely dispersed settlements, they developed a tradition of long-distance running, up to 200 miles over two days, for communication, transport and hunting. In rarajipari relay races men kick a wooden ball, and women race with a stick and hoop; races can last from a few hours to a couple of days. They also hunt deer and wild turkeys by persistence, following them for a day or two until the animals tire. Their huaraches, the sandals they run in, became known in minimalist running circles after Christopher McDougall's book Born to Run.
raron: Raron is a municipality in the Westlich Raron district of the canton of Valais, Switzerland, and its district capital. It lies on the right side of the Rhône valley at the entrance to the Bietsch valley, west of Visp, and covers 30.3 square kilometres. The municipality includes the villages of Raron and Sankt German and the hamlets of Turtig and Rarnerchumma. Raron is first mentioned in the 12th century as Rarogni.

Finds near Raron show settlement from the Neolithic to the La Tène period, after which the site seems to have been abandoned in Roman times. In the Middle Ages the hill was fortified. The Viztum of Raron was established in the 12th century and the Viztume tower house added, and the Raron, Asperlin and de Chevron-Villette families held the office of Vizedominat as a fief of the Bishop of Sion. The Meier tower was built in the 13th century. The Viztume tower was partly destroyed in the Raron affair of 1417 and bought by the municipality in 1538, when it became town hall and jail.

A flood of the Bietschbach destroyed the church of St Romanus in 1494, except for its tower. Ulrich Ruffiner converted the Meier tower into a Gothic church in 1508 to 1514, dedicated to St Romanus. It was abandoned in the 1970s and replaced in 1974 by a modern rock church at the foot of the hill. The large stone houses of Raron record the prosperity of the 17th and 18th centuries, which owed much to traffic over the St German pass to Visp. The draining of the swamps from 1865 to 1885 and the Lonza canal of 1920 opened the valley to agriculture.

Raron had a population of 1,949 in December 2020, and in 2000 most people spoke German as their first language. A military airfield built in the 1940s was abandoned in 1994, and the south portal of the Lötschberg Base Tunnel opened east of the village in 2007. The prehistoric site of Heidnischbühl, the Church of St Roman and the Viztume tower house are Swiss heritage sites of national significance. Raron is known for periodic Passion plays, and the poet Rainer Maria Rilke is buried in the cemetery of the old church.
ras-al-khaimah: The name Ras Al Khaimah means 'Headland of the Tent'. The Arabic word khaimah means tent, but it also refers to the palm frond or areesh houses that were common in the area. A creek divides the city into two parts, the old town in the west and Al Nakheel in the east.

The site has been continuously inhabited for 7,000 years, with finds dating back to the Neolithic. The city succeeded the port and trading hub of Julfar, which was a separate settlement with its own history and was abandoned in the early 17th century as Ras Al Khaimah rose. Julfar itself had a predecessor, Kush, in the suburbs to the north.

The navigator and cartographer Ibn Majid came from the town, and his writing suggests that it was already called Ras Al Khaimah, having eclipsed Julfar as the principal port of the Shimal coast. From 1507 the city came under Portuguese control. In the early 18th century the Qawasim, the Al Qasimi, established themselves at Ras Al Khaimah and Sharjah and became a significant maritime force with holdings on both the Persian and Arabian coasts, often in conflict with British shipping.

After attacks on shipping the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1809, which largely destroyed the Al Qasimi fleet; the expedition ended on 14 November with British casualties of five killed and 34 wounded. An arrangement of 1815 broke down, and in November 1819 a second expedition under Major-General William Keir Grant bombarded the town and stormed it on 9 December, finding it nearly deserted.

At Dhayah Fort, 398 men and some 400 women and children held out for three days before they surrendered on 22 December. The General Maritime Treaty of 1820, which called for the end of piracy and slavery, laid the foundation of the British protectorate over the Trucial States, which lasted until 1 December 1971.

Ras Al Khaimah became fully independent of Sharjah in 1869. It was part of Sharjah again from September 1900 until 7 July 1921. Under Sheikh Saqr bin Mohammad Al Qasimi it was the last of the Trucial States to join the United Arab Emirates, on 10 February 1972, following the Iranian seizure of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs.

Ras Al Khaimah is an industrial port city and the capital of the Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates. Arabic is the language of the government-funded schools, and the city also has Indian schools and several colleges, among them the American University of Ras Al Khaimah and the Ras Al Khaimah Medical and Health Sciences University.
rasa-river: The Raša, Arsa in Italian, is a river of Croatia's Istria County, 23 kilometres long, with a basin of 279 square kilometres. It rises in springs near Pićan and flows south through a steep-sided valley. Its mouth lies in the long ria of Raša Bay, once called Porto d'Arsia in Italian: a river valley scoured out when world sea levels fell and drowned again by the rising waters after the last glacial period.

By Roman times the Arsia divided the Histri, west of it, from the Liburni on the coast to the east, with the Iapydes in the valleys behind them. After the Romans conquered the Histri in 177 BCE, the river marked the limit of Roman territory in coastal Istria for a generation, until the gap to the northernmost Roman posts in Illyria was closed in 129 BCE. It then long divided Italia from Illyricum. The Via Flavia from Tergeste, present-day Trieste, ended at its crossing, and the 8th-century Irish geographer Dicuil still gave the north-eastern boundary of Italia as the flumen Arsia.

The river kept its role as a frontier. In the early 10th century the state of Tomislav of Croatia reached from the Raša to the Drina. In the 13th century the counts of Gorizia held the east bank and the patriarchs of Aquileia the west. After centuries of Venetian rule over Istria up to the river, it became the border between Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and the Austrian Empire, and after Napoleon's fall the border between two Austrian provinces.

In 1936 and 1937 the planned town of Raša, then named Arsia, was built on drained wetlands near the river's inner inlet, to gain farmland and serve the expanding coal mines, as part of Mussolini's urban colonization and Italianization of Istria. Barban is the other main settlement near the river.
rashi: Rashi was an only child, born at Troyes in Champagne, in northern France. His mother's brother, Simeon bar Isaac, was rabbi of Mainz. According to tradition his father, Yitzhak, brought him to learn Torah at the age of five and remained his main teacher until his death. At seventeen Rashi married and went to study in Worms at the yeshiva of Yaakov ben Yakar. When Yaakov died in 1064 he studied for another year under his relative Isaac ben Eliezer Halevi, then moved to Mainz to study under Isaac ben Judah.

His teachers were students of Gershom ben Judah, and he was also influenced by the exegetical principles of Menahem Kara. Jewish oral tradition holds that he was a vintner; there is no evidence for it, though his writings show extensive knowledge of winemaking.

Rashi returned to Troyes at the age of 25 and joined the beth din, the rabbinical court. He began answering halakhic questions, and on the death of its head, Zerach ben Abraham, led the court. Around 1070 he founded a yeshiva that attracted many disciples. In 1096 the People's Crusade swept through Lorraine, murdering 12 Jews and uprooting whole communities, and among those killed at Worms were three sons of his teacher Isaac ben Eliezer Halevi. Rashi wrote penitential poems mourning the slaughter, seven of which survive.

He had no sons. His three daughters married his disciples, and most present-day Ashkenazi rabbinical dynasties trace their descent to Miriam or Yocheved. Yocheved's sons Rashbam, Rivam and Rabbeinu Tam were among the most prolific Tosafists. Rashi died on 13 July 1105 and was buried in Troyes.

Rashi wrote the first comprehensive commentary on the Talmud, covering 30 of the 39 tractates of the Babylonian Talmud. It explains each passage phrase by phrase and translates difficult words into the spoken Old French of his day. It has been included in every edition since the first printing. His commentary on the Tanakh, which covers all books except Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah, concentrates on grammar and word choice and seeks the plain meaning, or peshat, together with such rabbinic interpretations as fit the words. It was accepted as authoritative by Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities alike.

About 300 of his responsa survive. His commentary on the Chumash is the basis of more than 300 supercommentaries. The French monk Nicholas de Lyra, called the ape of Rashi, relied on it in a work that was among the sources for Luther's Bible.
rashid-al-din-hamadani: Rashid al-Din was born in 1247 into a Persian Jewish family from the province of Hamadan. His grandfather had been a courtier to Hulagu Khan, founder of the Ilkhanate, and his father was an apothecary at the court. He converted to Islam around the age of thirty. He trained as a physician and entered service under Hulagu's son Abaqa Khan, rose to be grand vizier, and served as vizier and physician under the Ilkhans Ghazan and Öljaitü. He kept the office of vizier until 1316.

Ghazan commissioned the Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh, the Compendium of Chronicles. It began as a history of the Mongols and their dynasty and grew into a history of the world from Adam to Rashid al-Din's own time. He was helped by Bolad, a Mongol nobleman and the Great Khan's emissary at the Ilkhanid court, and the work was completed between 1307 and 1316. Its first volume covers the Turkish and Mongol tribes and the Mongol conquests from Genghis Khan to the end of Ghazan's reign; the second describes the peoples with whom the Mongols fought or exchanged embassies. A third volume, on historical geography, is lost or was never finished.

The work includes a history of the Franks and, in twenty chapters, the most extensive and well-informed presentation of Buddhism in any Muslim source. Abu al-Qasim Kashani claimed that he was the true author, and the work is generally considered a collective effort, partly carried out by research assistants.

In 1314 Öljaitü died and power passed to his son Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, who sided with Rashid al-Din's rival Taj-al-Din Ali-Shah Jilani. In 1318 Rashid al-Din was charged with having poisoned Öljaitü and was executed on 13 July. His Jewish ancestry was referred to repeatedly at court. His property was confiscated and the Rab'-e Rashidi, his scriptorium with its precious copies, passed to the Mongol soldiery. His son Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad briefly served as vizier after him. A century later, in the reign of Timur's son Miran Shah, his bones were dug up from the Muslim cemetery and reburied in the Jewish one.
rashid-al-din-sinan: Rashid al-Din Sinan was born between 1131 and 1135 in Basra, in southern Iraq, to a prosperous family. According to his autobiography, of which only fragments survive, he went as a youth to Alamut, the fortress headquarters of the Nizari Ismailis, after a quarrel with his brothers, and there received the order's usual training. In 1162 the Nizari leader Hassan II sent him to Syria, where he proclaimed the Qiyama, which in Nizari terms meant the time of the Qa'im and the lifting of Islamic law.

Based first at al-Kahf and later at Masyaf, Sinan controlled the northern Syrian districts of Jabal as-Summaq, Maarrat Misrin and Sarmin. Some writings gave him a semi-divine standing usually reserved for the Nizari Imam. His chief enemy was Sultan Saladin, who ruled Egypt and Syria from 1174 and who, while marching against Aleppo, devastated the Nizari lands.

In 1176 Saladin besieged Masyaf. According to the account of the siege, he had chalk and cinders strewn round his tent to show the footsteps of intruders, yet woke one night to find hot scones of the shape peculiar to the Assassins beside his bed and a note pinned by a poisoned dagger, threatening his death if he did not withdraw. Saladin lifted the siege and came to an agreement with Sinan, which kept the crusaders from allying with the Nizari Ismailis against him.

Sinan's last notable act came in 1191, when he ordered the killing of Conrad of Montferrat, the newly elected King of Jerusalem. Whether this was done in concert with King Richard I of England, with Saladin or with neither remains unknown. A letter in which Sinan supposedly took the blame, addressed to Leopold V, Duke of Austria, is believed by modern historians to be a forgery written after his death.

Sinan died in 1193 at al-Kahf Castle and was buried in Salamiyah. His successor, the Persian da'i Abu Mansur ibn Muhammad, also called Nasr al-'Ajami, was appointed from Alamut, which then brought the Syrian branch under closer supervision. A fictional version of Sinan appears as the mentor Al Mualim in the Assassin's Creed video games.
rashid-ali-al-gaylani: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.
rashid-bin-saeed-al-maktoum: Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum succeeded as ruler of Dubai on the death of his father, Saeed bin Maktoum Al Maktoum, on 10 September 1958. He had effectively managed the emirate's affairs since the late 1930s, having refused under considerable British pressure to force his father to abdicate. By the 1950s Dubai's port was the most important in the Gulf, and its merchants grew rich supplying gold to India, shipped by air from London and carried by dhow to the edge of Indian waters.

Dubai's creek was silting up. A plan drawn up by the British consultancy Halcrow in 1954 led to dredging between 1958 and 1959, paid for partly by creek bonds and a loan of £500,000 from Kuwait, so that larger ships could enter. Rashid also commissioned a town plan, founded a municipal council in 1957, started water and electricity companies and had Maktoum Bridge, the first crossing of the creek, built in 1963 with a loan from his son-in-law, the emir of Qatar.

Dubai found oil in 1966 at the Fateh field, 60 miles offshore. Raising credit against the expected revenue, Rashid ordered a deep-sea container terminal, Port Rashid, which he enlarged from the planned four berths to 21 and which opened in 1972. Dubai's population grew from 59,000 in 1968 to over 278,000 in 1980. In 1960 he had pressed the British for an airstrip, and an asphalt runway for jetliners followed in May 1965. Jebel Ali Port, with 66 berths, opened in 1983.

When Britain announced in January 1968 that it would end its protection of the Trucial States, Rashid and Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi first urged London to reconsider. On 18 February 1968 the two men met in a tent in the desert near Semeih and agreed the principle of a union with a handshake. The United Arab Emirates was declared on 18 July 1971, with Rashid as vice president. He negotiated parity with Abu Dhabi in the Federal National Council and, with Abu Dhabi, a veto in the Supreme Council, and he became prime minister on 30 April 1979.

Rashid died on 7 October 1990 after almost a decade of illness. His son Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum, prime minister of the Emirates from 1971 to 1979, succeeded him as ruler of Dubai, and another son, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, later followed Maktoum. Mohammed had been given charge of Dubai's airport and civil defence in the late 1960s and developed its aviation and tourism with his father's approval.
rashid-rida: Rashid Rida was born in 1865 in al-Qalamoun, in the Beirut Vilayet, into a distinguished Sunni Shafi'i clerical family. The family lived on a limited holding of olive trees and the fees of its scholars, and for several generations had charge of the al-Qalamoun mosque, where his father was imam. They were Sayyids who claimed descent from Husayn ibn Ali. Rida met Muhammad Abduh as an exile in Lebanon in the mid-1880s and came to regard him as his mentor. In 1897 he went to Istanbul to study under Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, but after al-Afghani's death that year, which Rida suspected the Hamidian administration of causing, he left to rejoin Abduh in Egypt.

In Egypt the two began the monthly al-Manar, of which Rida was chief editor and owner until his death in 1935. His study of Ibn Taymiyya led him to revulsion against folk Sufism, criticism of taqlid and the wish to revive hadith studies. In 1897 he helped found the Ottoman Consultative Society in Cairo, which called for Islamic unity under Ottomanism and condemned Hamidian rule; it disbanded after the Young Turk Revolution of 1908, and Rida became a vocal critic of the Young Turks. During the First World War he negotiated with the British and Sharif Hussein of Mecca for a united Islamic state, but he distrusted Britain, and more so after the Sykes–Picot Agreement.

After the war he turned to Ibn Saud of Najd, whom he saw as the best candidate to free the Hejaz from Hashemite rule, and he welcomed his campaigns of 1924 and 1925. He took part in preparations for the 1926 Islamic Congress for Caliphate in Cairo and was a prominent delegate at the Pan-Islamic Congress that Ibn Saud convened in Mecca the same year, drafting protocols and the king's opening address. No significant resolutions were passed there.
