In The Caliphate or the Supreme Imamate (1922–23) Rida proposed a comprehensive pan-Islamism and urged Muslims to shun nationalism. After the 1900s he abandoned his early rationalism for a stricter scripturalism, supported the Wahhabis and revived the works of Ibn Taymiyyah, and he gave naql, textual sources, precedence over aql. He condemned tawassul and the veneration of graves as polytheism, and by the 1920s regarded Western-educated secularists as his chief opponents, attacking Ali Abdel Raziq among others. He grew sharply critical of Shi'ism. His commentary on the Qur'an, begun by Abduh, reached sura Yusuf.

Rida died on the way back from Suez to Cairo after seeing off King Ibn Saud, and he died in debt, having put most of his money into publishing. Historians regard him as one of the ideological forefathers of later Islamist movements and as a link between classical theories of the caliphate and the twentieth-century idea of the Islamic state.
rashidi-dynasty: The Rashidi dynasty took its name from Abdullah bin Ali Al Rashid, the first emir, who began the establishment of the Emirate of Ha'il. It was based at Ha'il, a city in northern Najd that drew its wealth from lying on the Hajj route to Mecca and from trade. Abdullah came to power after leading a revolt with his brother Ubayd against the ruler of Ha'il, Muhammad bin Ali, and received the support of Imam Faisal bin Turki Al Saud. He was praised for bringing peace and stability, and asked Ubayd for a covenant that the emirate would stay in his own line.

His son Talal, emir from 1848 to 1868, is remembered for relative liberalism and building projects, including the Barzan Palace. He established regular trade with Iraq and widened the Rashidi sphere of influence, and was considered tolerant towards foreign traders. In the 1860s disputes inside the House of Saud allowed a Rashidi and Ottoman alliance to oust it, and the Rashidi occupied Riyadh in 1865. Talal died in a shooting incident called mysterious; Charles Doughty wrote that he killed himself.

The dynasty had no accepted rule of succession, and disputes over whether the emirate should pass to a brother or a son were often settled violently. Mutaib bin Abdullah was shot in the Barzan Palace in 1869 by his nephew Bandar, who was killed within the year by another uncle, Muhammed. Muhammed ordered the execution of Bandar's brothers and cousins, and only Naif, one of Talal's sons, survived. His rule, from 1869 to 1897, was the longest of the dynasty and a period of stability, expansion and prosperity, reaching al-Jawf and Palmyra to the north and Tayma and Khaybar to the west. Six Rashidi leaders died violently in the last years of the 19th century.

Muhammed's adopted heir Abdulaziz bin Mutaib ruled from 1897 and found Rashidi power insecure, since the Ottoman allies were unpopular and weakening. Ibn Saud, the future founder of Saudi Arabia, returned from exile with a small force and retook Riyadh. Abdulaziz died fighting him at Rawdat Muhanna in 1906. Four emirs followed in quick succession, several killed by relatives, and Saud bin Abdulaziz, made emir as a boy of ten, was ruled by regents of the Al Sabhan family until he was assassinated by a cousin in 1920. His successor surrendered to Ibn Saud, and Ha'il was captured by Abdulaziz Al Saud in 1921.

Some Rashidi left the country in exile, mostly to Iraq, Pakistan, Oman, Kuwait and the UAE. By the 1990s only a handful were still in Saudi Arabia. Widows of the last rulers married into the Saudi house, among them the mother of King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia.
rashidi-kawawa: Rashidi Mfaume Kawawa was born on 27 February 1926 in Matepwende village, in what is now Namtumbo District of the Ruvuma Region. He enrolled at the Tunduru Urban School in 1935, attended Dar es Salaam Central School from 1942 to 1947 and later Tabora Boys School. In 1951 he married Sofia Kawawa. Before entering party politics he was Secretary General of the Government Employees Federation, and in 1955 he was one of the founders of the Federation of Workers, becoming its first General Secretary and mobilising workers for independence.

Because government employees were barred from politics, Kawawa left his union post in February 1956 and joined TANU, the movement for independence. He sat on its Central Committee from 1957 and became its vice-president in 1960, the year he was named Minister of Local Government and Housing. On 22 January 1962 he became prime minister, without a ministry of his own, when Julius Nyerere stepped down to strengthen the party.

When Tanganyika became a republic in December 1962 he was made vice-president, and after the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar in 1964 second vice-president. In those years he helped lay the foundations of the Tanzania People's Defence Force and founded the Nation Building Army, and in 1964 he attended the second summit of the Non-Aligned Movement in Cairo. He was prime minister of Tanzania from 1972 until 13 February 1977, when Edward Moringe Sokoine succeeded him, and then Minister of Defence and National Service until 1981.

Kawawa represented Nachingwea and then Liwale in parliament from 1965 to 1985, became General Secretary of the ruling Revolutionary Party in 1980 and Vice Chairman of the CCM in 1982, and remained a permanent member of its Central Committee. He died aged 83 at Muhimbili National Hospital on 31 December 2009. After a public farewell at the Karimjee Gardens in Dar es Salaam, he was buried at his home in Wazo Ward, Kinondoni District, on 3 January 2010. Makerere University and the University of Dodoma awarded him posthumous honorary degrees.
rashidun-caliphate: According to the traditional account, Muhammad began receiving what Muslims consider divine revelations in 610 CE and migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. By his death in 632 CE almost all the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam, but Muslim leaders disagreed over who should lead the community. The Rashidun caliphs were not hereditary rulers: they were chosen by a small group of prominent members of the Quraysh tribe in shūrā, or consultation, or nominated by their predecessor, as Umar was by Abu Bakr.

Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close companion and father-in-law, was chosen first caliph in Medina and reigned from 632 to 634. Umar ruled from 634 to 644, Uthman from 644 to 656, and Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, from 656 to 661. The term Rashidun, meaning rightly guided, comes from Sunni doctrine. Shi'a Muslims accept only Ali as a legitimate caliph.

After suppressing rebellions in Arabia, Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid into Sasanian-controlled Iraq in 633 with an army of 18,000, and Khalid won four battles in succession before the city of Hira fell. Under Umar the caliphate expanded at an unprecedented rate and took more than two-thirds of the Byzantine Empire and nearly the whole of the Sasanian Empire; Uthman's reign completed the conquest of Persia in 651. The conquests are explained partly by the exhaustion of both empires in the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602 to 628.

Umar allowed local administrations of conquered lands to continue much as before, appointing a governor with full powers over each province. Dhimmis, meaning Jews, Zoroastrians and Christians, kept their religion and a measure of autonomy in return for paying the jizya. Uthman was assassinated in June 656 and Ali's accession led to the First Fitna, in which the governor of Syria, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, refused to recognise him until Uthman's killers were punished.

The Battle of Siffin between Ali's Iraqi army and Mu'awiya's Syrian forces ended in stalemate and an inconclusive arbitration, after which the Kharijites seceded. A Kharijite assassinated Ali in 661. Mu'awiya then invaded Iraq, obliged Ali's son Hasan to abdicate and founded the Umayyad Caliphate. Three of the four caliphs died by assassination.

Later historians wrote of this period as a golden age, and Sunni tradition holds it second in sanctity only to Muhammad's lifetime. Some scholars, among them Donner and Chamieh, write that the community came to regard the four as rightly guided only after memories of the fighting had faded.
rasht: Rasht is the capital of Gilan province, of Rasht County and of its district, and the largest city on Iran's Caspian Sea coast. It lies between the coast and the mountains, and the climate is humid subtropical and among the wettest in Iran, with average humidity above 80 percent. A temperate rainforest lies to its south, in contrast to the mostly arid rest of the country. Its nickname is the City of Silver Rain. The name has several explanations: the word resh, meaning very light rain; the verb reshtan, to spin, from the silk thread trade; or a low, sunken place, from an early market called rasht bazar. The people are mostly Gilaks, who speak the Rashti variety of Western Gilaki.

Rasht was first mentioned in Umayyad historical documents in 682 CE. The Hudud al-'Alam, a tenth-century geography, names it as a district. Its modern history dates to the Safavid era, when it was a major centre of the silk trade with many textile workshops. Cossacks under Stenka Razin plundered it in 1669, an earthquake destroyed it in 1714, and Russia occupied it from 1722 to 1732. In the Qajar period it became the gateway to Europe for Iran, trading with Russia through the port of Bandar-e Anzali; Russian, British, French and Ottoman consulates opened there. A Russian visitor at the end of 1860 counted 5,463 houses, 22 mosques and 27,314 people. The plague devastated the city in 1901.

People of Rasht played a prominent part in the Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1907, and Mīrzā Kūchak Khān, a leader of its Jangali movement, was born there. In 1920, after the defeat of the constitutional forces, he and Iranian communists established a short-lived socialist republic in Gilan, supported at first by the Russian Red Army, with its capital at Rasht. The Soviet government withdrew its support, internal conflicts divided the republic, and the Iranian army under Reza Shah defeated it. Iran's first public library, first girls' school and first fire station are said to have been built in Rasht, and the Nasim-e-Shomal newspaper was first published there. Its first university was established in 1974.

The 2016 census counted 679,995 people in the city, the most populous in northern Iran. Rasht is a major trade centre between Caucasia, Russia and Iran, using the port of Bandar-e Anzali, and the surrounding plain is the most important rice-growing region of Iran. The resort village of Masouleh lies in the nearby mountains. In 2015 UNESCO admitted Rasht to its network of creative cities for gastronomy. Its cuisine includes Mirza Ghassemi, and Rasht embroidery is a local handicraft. The Rosa 'de Rescht', a rose reported in England at the end of the nineteenth century, was rediscovered near the city by Nancy Lindsay in 1945.
rashtriya-swayamsevak-sangh: K. B. Hedgewar, a doctor in Nagpur, founded the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh in 1925, to propagate the ideology of Hindutva and give what it called new physical strength to the majority community. Its initial aim was character training and 'Hindu discipline' in order to unite the Hindu community and establish a Hindu Rashtra, a Hindu nation. After Tilak died in 1920, Hedgewar and other followers of Tilak in Nagpur parted ways with Gandhi, whose stance on the Khilafat Movement concerned them and whose Congress did not take up cow protection. Hedgewar was jailed for a year in 1921 on a charge of sedition.

The 1920s saw Hindu-Muslim relations deteriorate, with the Moplah rebellion of August 1921 and riots in Nagpur in 1923. Christophe Jaffrelot describes a theme of stigmatisation and emulation: Muslims, Christians and the British were treated as foreign bodies, and Hindu nationalists copied what they saw as the source of their strength, such as paramilitary organisation and unity. The Hindu Mahasabha was an important influence.

The organisation kept apart from political organisations then fighting British rule, and it did not take part in the independence movement against British rule. During the Partition it helped Hindu refugees fleeing West Punjab, and its activists also took part in communal violence in North India. It was banned briefly in Punjab Province in January 1947, and after independence three times: in 1948, after Nathuram Godse, a member, assassinated Mahatma Gandhi; during the Emergency of 1975 to 1977; and after the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992.

In a letter of December 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru called it a private army proceeding on the strictest Nazi lines. It at first did not recognise the national flag or the Constitution of India, and its magazine Organiser criticised the Constitution on 30 November 1949 for not mentioning the Manusmriti. In 1954 its volunteers took part in the removal of Portuguese rule from Dadra and Nagar Haveli.

The RSS has no formal membership. Men and boys join by attending the nearest shakha, or branch, which is the basic unit, and women are not allowed to join. It is the progenitor and leader of a large body of Hindutva organisations, the Sangh Parivar, which includes the Bharatiya Janata Party. Its affiliated organisations have set up numerous schools, charities and clubs. Its supporters describe an aim of upholding Indian culture and its civilisational values, while critics accuse it of intolerance of minorities, particularly Muslims.
rasoherina: Rasoherina was born in 1814 as Princess Rabodozanakandriana, a niece of Queen Ranavalona I, and the daughter of Prince Andriantsalamanandriana of Ambohitraina and Princess Rafaramanjaka. As a young woman she married Raharolahy, a statesman who held fifteen state honours and had served as secretary to the embassy to the United Kingdom in 1836–37. They divorced in 1847, and that year she married Ranavalona's son and heir Rakoto. When he became King Radama II in 1861 she was crowned with him as queen consort.

After two years Radama's decisions had displeased his ministers so much that a coup was organised, in which he was believed assassinated. A study of the 1960s offers evidence that he in fact survived and lived to old age as an ordinary citizen. The Hova council, headed by the brothers Rainivoninahitriniony and Rainilaiarivony, invited her to the throne on condition that she sign a contract in effect creating a constitutional monarchy with real power in the hands of the prime minister.

It suppressed the tangena trial by ordeal and committed the monarchy to freedom of religion. She was crowned on 13 May 1863. A year later she deposed Rainivoninahitriniony, who had grown despotic and violent, and appointed his younger brother Rainilaiarivony prime minister, marrying him in turn.

Her reign sent ambassadors to London and Paris and banned Sunday markets. The Lambert Charter was declared void and 240,000 ariary was paid to France in reparation. She signed a treaty with the United Kingdom on 27 June 1865 and one with the United States on 14 February 1867.

In March 1868 a conspiracy to put a prince named Rasata on the throne was crushed, and on 27 March a crowd tried to storm the Rova of Antananarivo while she lay gravely ill with dysentery. She died on 1 April 1868 after being received into the Roman Catholic Church, and her first cousin Ramoma, another of Radama II's wives, succeeded her as Ranavalona II. A treaty with France was signed only after her death.
rassemblement-democratique-africain: After the Second World War, the French Union of 1946 gave the colonies of French Africa wider citizenship and the right to elect members of the French National Assembly. Félix Houphouët-Boigny of the Ivory Coast persuaded Lamine Guèye of Senegal, the leading African socialist, to work for a wider movement seeking autonomy, and African deputies signed a manifesto calling a meeting at Bamako. The French Socialist leadership, seeing a threat to its own ties, made its African members withdraw, so the new party was backed only by the French Communist Party, with which it sat in coalition in the Assembly.

In the elections of November 1946 the RDA won 10 seats from French West and Equatorial Africa. The communist alliance drove some deputies to form the rival Indépendants d'Outre-Mer. In the Ivory Coast in 1949 the French authorities used local rivalries to justify mass arrests and violent repression; in Dimbokro French troops shot 13 Ivorian civilians, and on 1 February 1950 all RDA meetings in French West Africa were banned. The year left over 50 dead and 3,000 RDA supporters imprisoned.

Houphouët-Boigny then broke with the communists, made a secret accord with the Indépendants d'Outre-Mer on 9 August 1950, and in December voted for the government of René Pleven, beginning a long partnership with the Democratic and Socialist Union of the Resistance and François Mitterrand. In the 1956 elections the RDA became the largest party of the African colonies, and Houphouët-Boigny became the first representative from French West or Equatorial Africa to sit in the French cabinet.

As minister, Houphouët-Boigny shaped the 1958 vote that let each colony choose immediate independence or a community with France. The question of independence and federalism split the RDA, and the regional party largely dissolved that year, though many national parties kept its name. The RDA parties of Guinea and Mali joined Ghana in the Union of African States, while the Ivory Coast, Niger and Dahomey formed the Conseil de l'Entente. The party opposed colonial rule and held pan-Africanist views without seeking outright secession from France.
rastafari: Rastafari developed out of the legacy of the Atlantic slave trade and of British rule in Jamaica, where slavery was abolished in 1834 but racial prejudice remained. It drew on Christian Revivalism, Ethiopianism and the Back-to-Africa movement promoted by black nationalists such as Marcus Garvey. Haile Selassie was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, and several Jamaican clergymen said that his coronation fulfilled prophecies in the Book of Revelation, the Book of Daniel and the Psalms. Street preachers including Leonard Howell, Archibald Dunkley, Robert Hinds and Joseph Hibbert began to teach that he was the returned Jesus, first in Kingston and then across a Jamaica hit hard by the Great Depression. The movement grew among poor and disenfranchised Afro-Jamaicans.

Rastafari is an Abrahamic religion with no central authority and much diversity among its followers. Its beliefs rest on a reading of the Christian Bible. Rastas worship one God, Jah, a shortened form of Jehovah, who is held to dwell within each person, and they speak of knowing Jah rather than believing in him. They give Haile Selassie central importance: many see him as the Second Coming of Jesus and Jah incarnate, while others regard him as a human prophet. Rastas call the Western world Babylon, where the African diaspora lives in exile, and they see Zion, meaning Ethiopia or Africa more broadly, as the ideal to which they aspire.

Their way of life is called livity. It includes ital food, often grown organically and avoiding pork and crustaceans, and dreadlocks, which Rastas link to the Book of Numbers and to the hair of Samson. Communal meetings, called groundings, feature drumming, chanting, hymns and poetry, and the smoking of cannabis, the movement's principal ritual. Rastas also use their own speech, called Iyaric or dread talk, which developed in Jamaica in the 1940s.

For its first thirty years Rastafari had a conflictual relationship with the Jamaican authorities. Police arrested Rastas for cannabis possession, and in 1958 militants tried unsuccessfully to capture Kingston and Spanish Town in the name of Haile Selassie. The Coral Gardens incident of 1963 caused several deaths, and in 1964 the government passed tougher cannabis laws. In the 1960s and 1970s the movement won greater respectability in Jamaica, and the worldwide popularity of reggae, above all Bob Marley, introduced Rastafari themes to audiences abroad. Many Rastas resented the commercialising of their faith by those who listened to reggae without sharing its beliefs.

The movement has no single leader. Its main branches, called mansions, are the House of Nyabinghi, the Bobo Ashanti and the Twelve Tribes of Israel. An estimated 700,000 to 1 million Rastas live worldwide, with the largest population in Jamaica, and communities exist in Britain, North America, Ghana, Ethiopia, Australia and New Zealand.
rastatt: Rastatt is a town in the district of Rastatt in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It lies in the Upper Rhine Plain, on the Murg River, 6 kilometres above the river's junction with the Rhine. Close to the Black Forest and the French border, it has a Baroque core.

Until the end of the 17th century Rastatt held little influence. After the French destroyed it in 1689 it was rebuilt on a larger scale by Louis William, Margrave of Baden, the Imperial general in the Great Turkish War, who was popularly known as Türkenlouis. The town remained the residence of the Margraves of Baden-Baden until 1771. It was the location of the First and Second Congress of Rastatt. The first gave rise to the Treaty of Rastatt, which belongs to the War of the Spanish Succession, while the second ended in failure in 1799.

In the 1840s fortifications were built around the town to form the Fortress of Rastatt, and for about 20 years before 1866 it was occupied by troops of the German Confederation. The Baden Revolution of 1849 began with a mutiny of soldiers at Rastatt in May of that year, under Ludwik Mieroslawski and Gustav Struve, and ended there a few weeks later with the capture of the town by Prussia. For some years Rastatt was one of the strongest fortresses of the German Empire, until its fortifications were dismantled in 1890. In the same year the railway station was moved closer to the centre of the town.

Between 1946 and 1954 about 20 major criminal proceedings, known as the Rastatt Trials, took place before the Tribunal Général of the French Military Administration. They concerned crimes against foreign workers and prisoners in the smaller camps of the National Socialist camp system in south-western Germany, and involved more than 2,000 defendants.

Rastatt has a population of around 51,000. Its historical buildings include the palaces of Schloss Rastatt and Schloss Favorite. A Mercedes-Benz car factory began production in the town in 1992. Rastatt also appears in literature: the historical novel The Lenz Papers by Stefan Heym, published in London in 1964, is set there in 1849, during the failed revolutions in Germany.
rastislav-of-moravia: According to the Annals of Fulda, Rastislav was a nephew of Mojmir I, the first known ruler of Moravia. His career before 846 is unknown, though he may have served as a hostage for his uncle at the court of Louis the German. Louis invaded Moravia in 846, removed Mojmir I and installed Rastislav as duke. He was probably already Christian, but was baptised by 846 at the latest, as a condition of the king's support.

For his first eight years Rastislav seems to have stayed loyal to Louis, while acquiring territory in the east and setting a border with the First Bulgarian Empire. By 855 he felt strong enough to challenge Frankish overlordship. In 855 Louis invaded with a large army but failed before one of Rastislav's strongholds, perhaps Mikulčice, and withdrew, while Moravian forces pillaged Frankish estates on the Danube. Louis's son Carloman led a failed expedition in 858 and later allied with Rastislav against his father. In August 864 Louis besieged the fortress of Dowina, perhaps Devín Castle, took Rastislav by surprise and forced him to give hostages and swear a new oath, though this did not subdue him.

Around 862 Rastislav, hoping to limit the Frankish missionaries in his realm, turned first to Rome and then to Constantinople for teachers able to work in the Slavic language. The Byzantine emperor Michael III sent the brothers Cyril and Methodius, who arrived in 863, taught and said mass in Slavonic, and Cyril created a script for the Slavs. Frankish clergy saw a threat in their work, but they enjoyed Rastislav's protection. In late 866 they left for Venice and Rome, where Pope Hadrian II approved their Slavic translations of the Scriptures. In 868 Charles the Fat burned Rastislav's fortifications.

Rastislav's nephew Svatopluk negotiated with Carloman and accepted his lordship without Rastislav's knowledge. Rastislav is said to have been enraged and to have plotted to have him strangled at a banquet, but Svatopluk was warned, captured his uncle and sent him in bonds to Carloman. At Regensburg in 870 the Franks, Bavarians and Slavs condemned Rastislav to death for treason, but Louis the German commuted the sentence to blinding and imprisonment. He died in prison. The Czech and Slovak Orthodox Church canonised him in 1994.
ratchis: Ratchis was the son of Duke Pemmo of Friuli and the nephew of the Lombard king Liutprand, who had a history of strife with Pemmo but nonetheless appointed Ratchis to succeed his father. Ratchis married a Roman woman named Tassia. While ruling Friuli he led an expedition against the Slavs in Carniola, across the Eastern Alps, and fought in the battles in person. Paulus Diaconus records that he entered Carniola with his men, killed a great number of Slavs and devastated their land.

Ratchis became king of the Lombards in 744, after the deposition of Hildeprand, most likely with the support of the more autonomous Lombard dukes. He ruled at first in peace, in particular with the neighbouring Byzantine exarchate of Ravenna. In 749, perhaps pushed by the more traditional parties among his followers, he invaded the Duchy of the Pentapolis and besieged Perugia. Pope Zachary persuaded him to lift the siege, which further reduced his prestige among the dukes, and later that year an assembly of the dukes at Milan ended his reign.

His brother Aistulf succeeded him. Ratchis first tried to raise opposition to the assembly's decision, but he was soon forced to take refuge in Rome, and he later entered the abbey of Montecassino with his family. After Aistulf died in 756, Ratchis fought to reclaim the throne and, with the support of several Lombard nobles, gained control of the royal palace at Pavia. Desiderius, the duke of Tuscany, defeated him with the support of Pope Stephen II and the Frankish king Pepin the Short. In 757 Ratchis retired again to a monastery, either Montecassino or Cervaro.
rathcroghan: The complex lies near Tulsk and spreads over some 6 square kilometres, with over 240 archaeological sites, 60 of them protected national monuments. Its focal point is Rathcroghan Mound, a broad, flat-topped circular mound about 89 metres across at the base and 5.5 metres high, reached by gently sloping ramps from the east and west. Surveying has shown that it was built over an earlier monument of two concentric stone ring banks, and that an enclosure 360 metres in diameter surrounds it, as at Tara, Emain Macha and Dún Ailinne.

Rathnadarve, a large ringfort to the west, is traditionally where the bulls Donn Cuailnge and Finnbennach fought at the end of the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Charcoal from Dathí's Mound, said to be the grave of Dathí, the last pagan High King of Ireland, gives a building date between 200 BCE and 200 CE, centuries before his supposed death around 429. A lintel in the souterrain at the mouth of Oweynagat bears an ogham inscription read as 'of Fraech, son of Medb'.

In medieval Irish literature Cruachan is the home of Medb and her husband Ailill mac Máta, and Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats, is an entrance to the Otherworld from which destructive creatures emerged at Samhain. Yet no historical record or archaeological evidence proves that the site was a royal residence or fortress as the tales describe. It was an important cemetery, named by the scribes with Tailtiu and Tara as one of three great burial sites, and a gathering place or oenach.

Many believe that Medb was a local earth goddess and that a king was inaugurated on Rathcroghan Mound by marrying the land. The site's religious importance declined after the arrival of Christianity, and the Martyrology of Oengus contrasts the end of Cruachan's power with the rise of Clonmacnoise. The promulgation of St. Patrick's law there in 783 and St. Ciaran's law in 814 may be the earliest genuinely historical references to the site.

Surveying began in the mid-eighteenth century, when Gabriel Beranger made a colour drawing of the mound, and the Ordnance Survey of the 1830s, with local help, gave the monuments the names still in use. Little has been excavated: Macalister investigated Dathí's Mound in 1913, and a limited excavation there followed in 1981. Radar and magnetic surveys have revealed features closely resembling those of Tara and Emain Macha, and the Cruachan Ai visitor centre in Tulsk opened in 1999.
ratnagiri: Ratnagiri is a port city on the Arabian Sea in south-western Maharashtra, in the Konkan division, and the seat of the district of the same name. It stands at an average elevation of 11 metres, with the Sahyadri mountains to the east. The climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rain from June to October and the rest of the year warm and dry. The Ratnagiri Municipality was established in 1876.

Archaeological evidence suggests that the area has been settled for at least 12,000 years. Ratnagiri served as an administrative capital under the Sultanate of Bijapur, and its strategic location made it an important military and trade centre. The Bijapur Sultanate built Ratnadurg Fort, which the Maratha king Shivaji rebuilt in 1670 as a key coastal defence post. In 1731 the area came under the Kingdom of Satara, the beginning of its integration into the Maratha Empire, and the British annexed it in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War.

The independence leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak, called Lokmanya, was born in Ratnagiri on 23 July 1856 and moved to Pune with his family at the age of 10. After the British annexed his country, the last king of Burma, Thibaw, was exiled to Ratnagiri with his consort Supayalat and two infant daughters. He lived the rest of his life there under British surveillance, in a two-storey brick mansion now called Thibaw Palace. Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was confined in Ratnagiri from 1921 to 1935, first in prison and then under local confinement.

Ratnagiri is known for Hapus, or Alphonso, mangoes, and is sometimes called the Mango City. It is a major railhead on the Konkan Railway, one of whose two divisions is based there, and National Highways 66 and 166 pass through it. Thibaw Palace still stands as a reminder of the king's exile.
ratu-sir-kamisese-mara: Kamisese Mara was born on 6 May 1920 at Sawana, Lomaloma, on Vanuabalavu in the Lau archipelago. His father, Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba III, was Tui Nayau and head of the chiefly Vuanirewa clan, and Mara succeeded him as Tui Nayau in 1969. He studied medicine at the University of Otago from 1942 to 1945, but his great-uncle and mentor Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna, wishing to groom him for national leadership, arranged for him to study history at Wadham College, Oxford, where he took an MA in 1949. On 11 September 1949 he married Ro Lala, a paramount chief of Rewa in her own right; the marriage lasted more than 53 years.

Mara served as Chief Minister from 1967 to 1970. With independence the office became Prime Minister, and he held it from 1970 to 1992 apart from one brief interruption in 1987. His Alliance Party lost narrowly to the National Federation Party in March 1977, but the party splintered and the Governor-General called on Mara to form a government, and the Alliance won 36 of 52 seats in a second election that September. In 1987 a multiracial coalition led by Timoci Bavadra defeated him. After two military coups led by Sitiveni Rabuka he was recalled to head an interim administration, and in 1992 he handed power to an elected government.

Mara was elected Vice-President in June 1992 and became President when Ratu Sir Penaia Ganilau died on 16 December 1993. On 19 May 2000 gunmen led by George Speight seized Parliament and took the Prime Minister, Mahendra Chaudhry, hostage. Mara was taken aboard a naval ship on 28 May and left office, with a resignation retroactive to 29 May 2000. Commodore Frank Bainimarama said the resignation was voluntary, while Mahendra Chaudhry supported Mara's own account that he refused to suspend the Constitution.

Under him the sugarcane crop more than doubled between 1970 and 1987. Many Indo-Fijians criticised him for not doing more to stop the 1987 coups and for consenting to the 1990 constitution, which guaranteed indigenous Fijian supremacy, and in 1996 he apologised to the Indo-Fijian community for his part in drafting it.

After his resignation Mara retired to Lakeba and remained a member of the Great Council of Chiefs. He suffered a stroke in 2001 and died in Suva on 18 April 2004. About 200,000 people, almost a quarter of Fiji's population, lined the streets during his three-day state funeral, and he was regarded as the father of the nation. He wrote an autobiography, The Pacific Way: A Memoir.
ratzeburg: Ratzeburg is surrounded by four lakes, and the isthmuses between them form the access lanes to the town. It is the capital of the district of Herzogtum Lauenburg in Schleswig-Holstein. The town was founded in the 11th century as Racisburg, a name traditionally derived from the local Wendish ruler, Prince Ratibor of the Polabians, who was nicknamed Ratse.

In 1044 Christian missionaries led by the monk Ansverus came to the region and built a monastery, which a pagan rebellion destroyed in 1066; the monks were stoned to death. Ansverus was canonised in the 12th century and his relics were entombed in the cathedral. Henry the Lion became ruler of the town in 1143 and founded a bishopric in 1154. He also had the late Romanesque cathedral built in the north German red-brick style. From 1180 part of the diocese formed a prince-bishopric, the last state in northern Germany to remain Catholic, which turned Lutheran in 1554.

The town itself lay outside the prince-bishopric, in the old Duchy of Saxony, and became part of Saxe-Lauenburg around 1296, staying with that duchy until 1876. In 1619 the capital of Saxe-Lauenburg moved to Ratzeburg from Lauenburg on the Elbe. In 1693 Christian V of Denmark bombarded the town into rubble in an unsuccessful attempt to win the dukedom from the House of Hanover; it was rebuilt in the baroque style, but the castle was never rebuilt. After the Second Schleswig War of 1864 the estates offered the dukedom to the Prussian Hohenzollern dynasty, and on 1 July 1876 the duchy merged into the Kingdom of Prussia's Province of Schleswig-Holstein.

The Romanesque cathedral survives, and monuments in two of the town's churches commemorate the missionaries of 1066. From 1945 to 1989 the Iron Curtain ran just east of the town, which stood on the border with the German Democratic Republic. The sculptor Ernst Barlach made his home in Ratzeburg and is buried in one of its cemeteries.
raul-alfonsin: Raúl Ricardo Alfonsín was born on 12 March 1927 in Chascomús, 123 kilometres south of Buenos Aires. His parents were shopkeepers. He attended the General San Martín Military Lyceum, because his father thought a military school would match a private school in quality at less cost. Alfonsín disliked the military, but the schooling helped him understand its outlook. He did not pursue a military career and studied law at the National University of La Plata and the University of Buenos Aires.

He joined the Radical Civic Union, in the faction of Ricardo Balbín, and was elected to the legislature of Buenos Aires Province in 1958. During the National Reorganization Process he opposed both sides of the Dirty War and filed writs of habeas corpus on behalf of victims of forced disappearance. After Balbín's death he became leader of the party and won the 1983 election.

Alfonsín governed from 10 December 1983 as the first democratically elected president after the military regime. Three days after taking office he sent Congress a bill to revoke the military's self-amnesty law and ordered cases against guerrilla leaders and the heads of the juntas. He set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, whose Nunca más report documented the scope of the crimes, and the Trial of the Juntas followed. Discontent in the army led to the Carapintada mutinies, which he answered with the full stop law and the law of Due Obedience.

His government settled the Beagle dispute, increased trade with Brazil and legalised divorce in 1987, over the opposition of the Church. It clashed with the trade unions, which Peronism still controlled. The UCR lost its legislative majority in 1987, and the Austral plan and the Spring plan failed to bring inflation under control. After the Peronist Carlos Menem won the 1989 election, Alfonsín handed over power on 8 July, five months earlier than scheduled.

Alfonsín led the UCR again in later years and negotiated the Pact of Olivos with Menem, which set the terms for the constitutional amendment of 1994. Historians disagree about it: Félix Luna thought it a necessary evil, while Miguel Angel de Marco and Fernando Rocchi saw it as the biggest mistake of his career. He died of lung cancer on 31 March 2009, aged 82, and was buried in La Recoleta Cemetery.
The same historians praise his role in the aftermath of the Dirty War and the restoration of democracy. He received the Princess of Asturias Award for international cooperation in 1985.
ravanica: The monastery stands on the Kučaj mountains near the village of Senje, in the municipality of Ćuprija. Built between 1375 and 1377 as Prince Lazar's endowment, it received his body after his death at the Battle of Kosovo and became a place of pilgrimage and a centre of cultural life and assemblies for the Serbian people. Ottoman forces attacked and damaged it in 1386, 1398 and 1436.

In the great war that followed the second siege of Vienna in 1683, Ottoman soldiers killed a number of its monks, and in 1690 the survivors fled with the relics of the canonised prince. Only in 1717 did a teacher named Stefan, the last survivor, come back to find the monastery looted and empty; with the help of local people he restored it and added a new narthex. Repeated assaults during the Serbian Revolution of the early 19th century led to further restoration in the mid-19th century. During the Second World War the occupying German forces detained, tortured and killed its archimandrite Makarije on 24 February 1943. Ravanica was declared a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance in 1979.

The church, dedicated to the Ascension of Jesus, blends the Mount Athos plan with the cross-in-square five-domed model that had become standard under King Milutin. Its ground plan is an enlarged trefoil, with a nine-sided central dome and smaller octagonal domes over the corner bays, and 62 window lights. It is built in alternating courses of one line of stone and three of brick, with ceramic decoration of geometric, floral, animal and human shapes. A strong wall with seven towers, only partly preserved, once surrounded it.

The frescoes, dated between 1385 and 1387, were not all painted at once or by the same hands. The finest, in the middle register, are the work of two artists, one of whom, Constantine, signed a fresco of a warrior saint. Among the main compositions are the Communion of the Apostles and the Adoration of the Lamb in the altar apse. The founders' composition shows Princess Milica and her sons Vuk and Stefan; it was later repainted, and a fresco of Lazar's death was added.
ravensburger: Otto Robert Maier began publishing in Ravensburg, a town in Upper Swabia in southern Germany, in 1883, when he signed his first author contract. Instruction folders for craftsmen and architects gave the firm a solid financial basis, and its first board game, Journey Around the World, appeared in 1884. By the turn of the 20th century the range had widened to picture books, children's activity books, art manuals, non-fiction and reference books, children's games such as Happy Families, and activity kits. The blue triangle trademark was registered with the Imperial patent office in 1900.

By 1912 many games had export versions sold in Western Europe, the lands of the Danube Monarchy and Russia, and before the First World War the firm offered about 800 products. The publishing house was damaged in the Second World War but went on producing games during reconstruction, concentrating on children's games and books and on books for art, architecture and hobbies. It grew strongly from 1962. In 1964 it began making jigsaw puzzles and opened subsidiaries in Austria, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, and in 1977 it split into book and game publishing arms.

In September 2010 it set a world record for the largest jigsaw puzzle with Keith Haring: Double Retrospect, 32,256 pieces measuring 5.18 by 1.82 metres; a 51,300-piece puzzle released by Kodak later took the record. The group bought the Swedish toy train maker BRIO on 8 January 2015, the American game company Wonder Forge in 2017 and a majority stake in the toy company Steiff in June 2026.

The group includes the labels Alea, for experienced players, and F.X. Schmid, for games, playing cards and children's books; under the latter it makes a 54-card Tarock pack used for the game of Cego in the Black Forest. Its North American division is based in Seattle and sold about 3 million games in 2018, its most successful title being Villainous, based on Disney properties. Ravensburger Interactive was sold to JoWooD Productions in May 2002, and the film and television arm, renamed RTV Family Entertainment in 1998, was sold in 2005.
ravi-shankar: Ravi Shankar was born Robindro Shaunkor Chowdhury on 7 April 1920 in Benares, now Varanasi, into a Bengali Hindu family, the youngest of seven brothers. His father, Shyam Shankar Chowdhury, a barrister, served as dewan of Jhalawar State and later worked in London. At the age of 10 Shankar went to Paris with the dance group of his brother, the choreographer Uday Shankar, and toured Europe and the United States in the early and mid-1930s. On tour he was sporadically taught by Allauddin Khan, the court musician of Maihar, who offered serious training on condition that he give up touring.

In 1938 Shankar left dancing and went to Maihar, where he lived with Khan's family and learned the sitar and surbahar, studying with Khan's children Ali Akbar Khan and Annapurna Devi. He made his sitar debut in December 1939. After finishing his studies in 1944 he moved to Mumbai, and from 1949 to 1956 was music director of All India Radio in New Delhi, where he founded the Indian National Orchestra. He also composed the music for Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy.

He resigned in 1956 to tour the United Kingdom, Germany and the United States, and recorded the album Three Ragas in London that year. The Beatles' guitarist George Harrison took lessons from him in India in 1966 and 1968, and the friendship helped bring Indian instruments into Western pop music. Shankar played at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 and at the Concert for Bangladesh in August 1971, whose live album won him a Grammy Award. He sat in the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of India's Parliament, from 1986 to 1992.

Shankar gave his last concert with his daughter, the sitarist Anoushka Shankar, on 4 November 2012 in Long Beach, California, and died on 11 December 2012 in San Diego at the age of 92. His other daughter is the singer Norah Jones.

His concerts opened with a slow alap, jor and jhala shaped by the dhrupad tradition, followed by a tabla section in the khyal style. He introduced at least 31 ragas and popularised the jugalbandi duet format. Among his honours were the Bharat Ratna in 1999, the Polar Music Prize in 1998 and four Grammy Awards.
ravidas: Ravidas was born in the village of Sir Gobardhanpur, near Varanasi, a place now known as Shri Guru Ravidass Janam Asthan. Tradition names his mother as Mata Kalsi and his father as Santokh Dass. He first worked with leather but came to spend most of his time in spiritual pursuits on the banks of the Ganges, in the company of Sufi saints, sadhus and ascetics. He was married at 12 to Lona Devi, and they had a son, Vijay Dass. His exact dates are disputed; his tie to the princess Mira Bai (1498–1547) helps scholars place him in the late 15th and early 16th centuries.

Medieval texts such as the Bhaktamal make him a disciple of the Brahmin poet Ramananda, and he is traditionally treated as a younger contemporary of Kabir; most scholars believe he met Guru Nanak. He travelled to pilgrimage sites in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and the Himalayas. The main sources for his life are late: the Parcais of Anantadas, of which about 30 manuscripts survive, the earliest complete ones dated to 1662, and the Sikh Premambodha of 1693. Historians such as Peter Friedlander and David Lorenzen read the legends of his struggles with Brahmins and with Sultan Sikander Lodi as reflections of the social conflicts of the centuries in which they were written.

Besides the Sikh scripture, the Panchvani of the Hindu Dadupanthi tradition is the other oldest source of his poems. They speak of a just state with no second or third class citizens, of dispassion and of the true yogi, and often of Sahaj, a mystical union of the many and the one; scholars place his thought in the Nirguna current of the Bhakti movement. Many later poems were attributed to him out of reverence.

Mainstream Sikhs honour him as a bhagat, while the Ravidassia movement, which declared itself a religion separate from Sikhism after a 2009 attack on its temple in Vienna, holds him as its guru and compiled the Amritbani Guru Ravidass Ji of 240 hymns. His birthplace shrine draws devotees on Ravidas Jayanti, and his word Begumpura, a land without sorrow, named a political party founded in 2012.
rawa-voivodeship: In the 15th century the Duchy of Masovia, ruled by a branch of the Piast dynasty, was divided into three parts, one of them the Duchy of Rawa. Siemowit VI, Duke of Płock and Rawa, died on 1 January 1462 at the age of eighteen, and his teenage brother Wladyslaw II died a few weeks later. King Kazimierz Jagiellonczyk then incorporated the lands of Rawa and Gostynin into the Crown, the first part of Masovia to return to Poland; the Land of Sochaczew followed in 1476. Together with the Płock and Masovian Voivodeships, Rawa made up the former duchy.

Its borders stayed unchanged for more than 300 years. According to Zygmunt Gloger's Historical Geography of the Lands of Old Poland, it covered 92 square miles and was divided into three lands of roughly equal size, each of two counties: Rawa and Biała, Gostynin and Gąbin, Sochaczew and Mszczonów. In the mid-16th century it had 100 Roman Catholic parishes and 15 towns, among them Łowicz, Skierniewice, Kutno and Grodzisk. It shared its coat of arms with the Płock Voivodeship.

The voivodeship sent four senators to the Senate of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth: the Voivode of Rawa, the Castellan of Rawa and the castellans of Sochaczew and Gostynin. Starostas resided in Rawa, Sochaczew and Gostynin. Its sejmiks met at Rawa, Sochaczew and Gąbin and elected two deputies to the Sejm and two to the Greater Poland Tribunal.

The voivodes, from Mikołaj z Kutna in 1465 to Bazyli Walicki, who held the office until 1789, came from families such as the Gostomski, Grudziński and Załuski; Łukasz Opaliński held it in 1653 and 1654. The province ended when the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 gave it to the Kingdom of Prussia.
rawanduz: Rawandiz lies in the Soran district of the Erbil Governorate, close to the borders with Iran and Turkey, 7 km from the centre of Soran city, 10 km east of the Bekhal Waterfall and 123 km from Erbil. The Zagros mountains surround it, with Korek Mountain to the south, Hindren Mountain to the north, Zozik Mountain to the west and Bradasot Mountain to the east. The name means fortress of the Rawand and comes from the Kurdish noble family of the Rawwadi or Rawandi, a leading family of the Hadhbāni Kurdish tribe.

From the 10th to the 7th centuries BCE, in the time of the Assyrian kings, the area lay on the trading route to Nineveh. The town was founded by the Rawadid dynasty in the 10th century CE. After the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 it came under the Emirate of Bradost, and later under the Soran Emirate until 1836. A Yazidi manuscript of the kind called Mişûr, dedicated to the saint Pīr Khatīb Pisī and copied in 1862, names the town as Randūz among the places owing dues.

In 1915, during the First World War, Russians and Assyrians occupied the town, and in the Rawandiz massacre the Russian army and allied Assyrian militants killed much of its Kurdish Muslim population: after Nikolai Baratov's Cossacks recaptured it, only 20 per cent of the Kurds had survived. Turkish troops held it in 1922 until they were driven out at the end of the year, and the British army occupied it on 22 April 1923. Between 1928 and 1932 the British built a strategic road from Erbil through Rawandiz to the Iranian border, directed by the New Zealand engineer A. M. Hamilton.

Hamilton wrote in 1930 that the town had always been a place of grim deeds and bloody retributions, whose rulers had nearly all met violent deaths. The anthropologist Edmund Leach came in 1938 to study the Rawandiz Kurds; the Munich crisis cut his field trip short, but he published Social and Economic Organization of the Rowanduz Kurds two years later. In 1940 the town had 1,970 inhabitants.

Rawandiz has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate, with very hot dry summers and cool wet winters. Its population is Kurdish. Hamilton reported that its gorge was said to be the finest in Asia, and a cable car 4 km long runs from the Bekhal station to Mount Korek, which has been developed as a resort.
raymond-iii-of-tripoli: Raymond III was born in 1140, the only son of Count Raymond II of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem. The family came from the County of Toulouse, though by the middle of the 12th century its links with its homeland had weakened. In the early 1150s Nizari Assassins murdered Raymond II at the southern gate of Tripoli. King Baldwin III of Jerusalem, who was staying in the town, recalled Hodierna and made her regent. Raymond spent several years at the royal court in Jerusalem and came of age in 1155.

Raymond fought Nur ad-Din, the Zengid ruler of Aleppo and Damascus. On 10 August 1164 he was captured at the Battle of Harim and held at Aleppo for almost ten years, while King Amalric of Jerusalem administered Tripoli. William of Tyre says he spent his captivity "in beggary and iron" but also learnt to read. A large ransom, borrowed from the Knights Hospitaller, freed him, and in 1174 Amalric gave him as wife Eschiva of Bures, widow of the prince of Galilee, which made him prince of Galilee and one of the richest men of the kingdom.

After Amalric died in July 1174, Raymond claimed the regency for the boy king Baldwin IV as his closest male relative and most powerful vassal, and held it until 1176. In April 1180 he and Bohemond III of Antioch marched to Jerusalem, and Baldwin hastily married his sister Sibylla to Guy of Lusignan. Bernard Hamilton sees an attempted coup against the influence of the king's mother, Agnes of Courtenay, while Steven Runciman and Baldwin point to Sibylla's love for Guy. Raymond became regent again in 1185, for Baldwin V, who died in the summer of 1186. He then refused to do homage to Sibylla and Guy and allied himself with Saladin, who placed a garrison in Tiberias.

In the summer of 1187 Raymond was reconciled with Guy. When Saladin besieged Tiberias, Raymond advised against a pitched battle, but Ridefort and Raynald of Châtillon accused him of cowardice and the king marched. Raymond commanded the vanguard at Hattin and was one of the few commanders neither killed nor captured. He fled to Tyre and then Tripoli, where he died, probably of pleurisy, leaving the county to his godson Raymond of Antioch.

William of Tyre held him in high regard, as did contemporary Muslim historians, but after Hattin Western historians tended to blame him for the defeat. Modern opinion is divided: Baldwin accepts William's assessment, while Kevin J. Lewis calls his career a litany of inconsequential, misguided or disastrous endeavours and Barber stresses his personal ambitions.
raymond-iv-of-toulouse: Raymond of Saint-Gilles was a son of Pons of Toulouse and Almodis de La Marche. He received Saint-Gilles with the title of count from his father. In 1094 he displaced his niece Philippa, Duchess of Aquitaine, daughter of his brother William IV, from inheriting Toulouse, and the same year the margravial title of Provence passed to him on the death of William Bertrand. He married three times: first the daughter of Godfrey I, Count of Arles, then Matilda, daughter of Roger I of Sicily, and in 1094 Elvira, an illegitimate daughter of Alfonso VI of León. He was twice excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII, in 1076 and 1078, for marrying within forbidden degrees of kinship.

Described as deeply religious, Raymond was one of the first to take the cross for the First Crusade. The oldest and richest of the leaders, he left Toulouse at the end of October 1096 with a large army and the papal legate Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy. He alone of the leaders refused to swear an oath of fealty to the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, offering an oath of friendship instead, because he thought fealty conflicted with his vow to serve God. His army reached Antioch in October 1097, and the city fell in June 1098 after a long siege. Raymond took the palace of the emir Yaghi-Siyan, and a struggle with Bohemond of Taranto over possession of Antioch followed.

After Adhemar died Raymond became the leading figure of the crusade and led it towards Jerusalem, besieging Arqa in 1099 in an attempt to carve out a territory around Tripoli. Jerusalem was captured on 15 July 1099. Raymond refused the crown of the new Kingdom of Jerusalem, saying that he shuddered to think of being called its king, but he held the Tower of David and gave it up only with difficulty to Godfrey of Bouillon. He was defeated at the Battle of Mersivan in Anatolia in the crusade of 1101.

In 1102 Raymond sailed from Constantinople to Antioch, where Tancred imprisoned him until he promised not to conquer land between Antioch and Acre. He broke the promise at once by capturing Tartus and began building a castle on Mons Peregrinus, Pilgrim's Mountain, to support his siege of Tripoli. In September 1104 the qadi of Tripoli, Fakhr al-Mulk ibn Ammar, attacked the castle and set a wing on fire. Raymond escaped across a rooftop but was badly burned, and he died on 28 February 1105 before Tripoli was taken.

Tripoli was captured in 1109 and the County of Tripoli was founded, and it stayed with the counts of Toulouse through the 12th century. Raymond seems to have been driven by both religious and material motives.
raymond-of-poitiers: Raymond was a younger son of Duke William IX of Aquitaine and Philippa of Toulouse. When his brother William X inherited their father's titles in 1126, Raymond was left landless, and by 1130 he had joined the court of King Henry I of England, where he was knighted. William of Tyre considered him impulsive and too fond of gambling, but respected his chivalry.

In 1130 Prince Bohemond II of Antioch died, leaving an infant daughter, Constance. King Fulk of Jerusalem and the Antiochene nobles opposed to her mother, Alice, chose Raymond as her husband. After Henry's death in December 1135 he travelled in disguise to avoid arrest by Roger II of Sicily. At Antioch in 1136 the Latin patriarch Ralph of Domfront married him to the eight-year-old Constance, in return for liege homage.

Raymond's first aim was to recover Cilicia from the Armenian prince Leo I, but fighting ended in early 1137. In mid-1137 Emperor John II Komnenos besieged Antioch and demanded that the Latins honour the oath given to Alexios I Komnenos. Raymond swore fealty, and John promised him Aleppo, Shaizar, Hama and Homs if they were conquered, whereupon Antioch would revert to the emperor. Raymond quarrelled with Ralph, had him imprisoned, and in 1140 coerced a synod to condemn him; the patriarch was replaced by a fellow Poitevin, Aimery of Limoges. John returned in 1142 and demanded Antioch, but died in March 1143.

Raymond then invaded Cilicia from John's successor Manuel I Komnenos and was driven back to Antioch. His relations with Count Joscelin II of Edessa broke down, and Raymond refused help when Imad al-Din Zengi took Edessa on 24 December 1144. In 1145 he travelled to Constantinople and paid homage to Manuel.

The fall of Edessa led to the Second Crusade. King Louis VII of France and Queen Eleanor, Raymond's niece, reached Port Saint Symeon on 19 March 1148. John of Salisbury reports that Raymond's constant conversation with Eleanor aroused the king's suspicions. Eleanor wished to stay and seek an annulment, but Louis took her away by force, and Raymond took no part in the crusade that ended in defeat at Damascus.

In 1149 Nur al-Din, Zengi's son, defeated Raymond at Baghras and besieged Inab. On 29 June Raymond and his ally Ali ibn Wafa were surrounded; his army was annihilated and he was killed by the general Shirkuh. Constance, left with four young children, remarried in 1153 to Reynald of Châtillon. Their son Bohemond III later succeeded her, and their daughter Maria became empress by marrying Manuel I.
raymond-roger-of-foix: Raymond-Roger was the son and successor of Roger Bernard I, Count of Foix, and his wife Cécilia Trencavel, and he became the sixth count from the House of Foix when he succeeded his father in 1188. When he and Arnaud, viscount of Castelbon, sought to join their possessions, Count Ermengol VIII of Urgell and Bernard de Villemur, bishop of Urgell, saw a threat in it and declared war. The two were defeated, captured and imprisoned from February to September 1203.

King Peter II of Aragón intervened for them, wishing to keep them for his own struggle to conquer Languedoc, and granted Raymond-Roger various Catalan seigniories in 1208 and the castles of Trenton and Quérigut as a fief in 1209. He was a close relative and staunch ally of Raymond VI of Toulouse, a patron of troubadours and an author of verse himself. He was not a Cathar, but several of his relatives were: his wife, Philippa of Montcada, became a parfaite, and his sister Esclarmonde de Foix received the consolamentum at Fanjeaux in 1204.

In the Albigensian Crusade he defeated a contingent of German and Frisian crusaders at the Battle of Montgey in 1211, but was defeated at the Battle of Saint-Martin-Lalande the same year and at the Battle of Muret in 1213. At the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 he defended Raymond of Toulouse before Pope Innocent III; accused of having murdered priests, he did not deny it and told the pope he regretted not having murdered more. He fought in the second siege of Toulouse in 1218 and defeated a crusader army at the Battle of Baziège in 1219.

He went on resisting the crusaders after Baziège and died of an ulcer on 27 March 1223 while besieging the castle of Mirepoix. With Philippa of Montcada he had two children: Roger-Bernard, who succeeded him as count, and Cécile de Foix, who married Count Bernard V of Comminges around 1224. He also had two illegitimate children.
raymond-vi-count-of-toulouse: Raymond VI was born on 27 October 1156 at Saint-Gilles, the son of Raymond V and Constance of France, whose father was Louis VI of France. He was count of Melgueil from 1173 to 1190, and succeeded his father as count of Toulouse and marquis of Provence in 1194, immediately making peace with Alfonso II of Aragon and the Trencavel family. He was the most powerful patron of troubadours in the south of France and a friend of Raimon de Miraval. He married five times, and in 1196 married Joan of England, daughter of Henry II, a marriage in which Richard I gave up his claim to Toulouse.

Raymond held vast territories, owing allegiance in theory to the king of France and holding Provence from the Holy Roman Emperor. In Toulouse he upheld the freedoms of the commune and extended exemptions from taxation. Pope Innocent III first tried to deal with the Cathars by peaceful conversion, but Raymond declined to help, and the historian Kenneth Setton doubts that he could have dealt with heresy even if he had wished. The assassination of the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau on 15 January 1208 led to Raymond's excommunication.

He lifted it briefly in June 1209 by being flogged at Saint-Gilles, and the crusaders turned to the lands of his rival Raymond Roger Trencavel, taking Béziers and Carcassonne. In 1211 his excommunication was repeated and an interdict placed on Toulouse. Simon de Montfort captured Toulouse, and after the Battle of Muret Raymond was exiled to England.

In 1215 Raymond and his son, later Raymond VII, went to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council to dispute the loss of their lands. His son retook Beaucaire in 1216, and Raymond re-entered Toulouse on 12 September 1217. Simon de Montfort besieged the city and was killed on 25 June 1218. The failure of Louis VIII's campaigns, from 1219 to 1226, let Raymond and his son recover most of their territories.

After a sudden illness that left him mostly speechless, Raymond died in August 1222, kissing a pall bearing a cross thrown over him by the Knights Hospitaller. His body was taken to their house in Toulouse but never buried. In 1998 a medieval sarcophagus found at the former Grand Priory there was briefly thought to hold his bones, and the mayor, Dominique Baudis, asked Pope John Paul II to lift the excommunication, without success.
raymond-vii-count-of-toulouse: Raymond was born in July 1197 at the Château de Beaucaire, the son of Raymond VI of Toulouse and Joan of England. Through his mother he was a grandson of Henry II of England and a nephew of the kings Richard I and John. In March 1211, at the age of 13, he married Sancha of Aragon; they had one daughter, Joan, and were divorced in 1241.

During the Albigensian Crusade, in May 1216, Raymond set out from Marseille and besieged Beaucaire, which he captured on 24 August. He fought to reconquer the county of Toulouse from Simon de Montfort and later from Simon's son Amaury VI of Montfort. He succeeded his father in 1222 as count of Toulouse, duke of Narbonne and marquis of Provence, and at his accession he and Roger Bernard II the Great, the new count of Foix, besieged Carcassonne.

In 1225 the council of Bourges excommunicated him and launched a crusade against him. King Louis VIII wished to renew the conflict in order to enforce his royal rights in Languedoc, and rejected an embassy from Roger Bernard, so the counts of Foix and Toulouse took up arms again. The war was largely a discontinuous series of skirmishes, and in January 1229 Raymond, defeated, was forced to sign the Treaty of Paris, also known as the Treaty of Meaux. By it his daughter Joan was made to marry Alphonse, the brother of the king.

In 1242 Raymond allied with Count Hugh of La Marche and King Henry III of England against Louis IX in the Saintonge War. Louis sent an army under the constable Imbert de Beaujeu and Bishop Hugh of Clermont, and Raymond was forced to surrender the castles of Saverdun and Bram. In 1243 he married Margaret of Lusignan, who bore no children, and the Council of Lyons granted him a divorce in 1245. He then sought to marry Beatrice of Provence, but she married Charles, a son of Blanche, the mother of Louis IX.
Raymond died on 27 September 1249 and was buried beside his mother Joan in Fontevrault Abbey. Alphonse became count of Toulouse, and after Alphonse's death the county was annexed by France.
raynald-of-chatillon: Raynald was the younger son of Hervé II, Lord of Donzy, a family of influential noblemen in the Duchy of Burgundy. He inherited the lordship of Châtillon-sur-Loire, and later complained to Louis VII of France that part of his patrimony had been violently and unjustly confiscated. He came to the Kingdom of Jerusalem in Louis's army during the Second Crusade in 1147 and stayed behind, and in early 1153 he fought at the siege of Ascalon under Baldwin III of Jerusalem.

Before that siege ended he became engaged to Princess Constance of Antioch, a widow. William of Tyre, his political opponent, called him a kind of mercenary knight, and her subjects were astonished at the match. Short of money, Raynald arrested and tortured Aimery of Limoges, the Latin Patriarch of Antioch, in 1154 after Aimery refused him a subsidy. In 1160 or 1161 the governor of Aleppo captured him at Marash, and he spent fifteen years in prison.

He was released in 1176 for a ransom of 120,000 gold dinars, most probably paid by Emperor Manuel I Komnenos. Constance had died, so he had no claim to Antioch. He married Stephanie of Milly, heiress of Transjordan, and Baldwin IV also granted him Hebron. From Kerak and Montréal he controlled the routes between Syria and Egypt, and he was the only Christian leader to fight Saladin in the 1180s, raiding caravans as far as Tabuk. Historians debate whether he sought booty or meant to stop Saladin annexing new territory.

In late 1186 or early 1187 Raynald attacked a caravan despite a truce and refused compensation. Saladin pillaged his lands for a month and crushed the crusaders at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187. Raynald was captured, and Saladin personally beheaded him after he refused to convert to Islam. Most of what is known of him was recorded by hostile Muslim authors such as Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, and Christian writers followed William of Tyre. Many modern historians see an irresponsible adventurer, while Bernard Hamilton holds that he alone tried to stop Saladin unifying the neighbouring Muslim states.
raza-library: Nawab Faizullah Khan founded the library in 1774 from his personal collection of old manuscripts and specimens of Islamic calligraphy. The nawabs who followed him were patrons of scholars, poets, painters, calligraphers and musicians, and the collection grew quickly. After the rebellion of 1857 many Mughal book collections were destroyed, taken to Britain or dispersed, and on the subcontinent their place was taken by the libraries of the Nawabs and Nizams of Rampur, Avadh, Arcot, Bhopal, Hyderabad and Tonk.

Nawab Kalb Ali Khan, who ruled from 1865 to 1887 and was himself a scholar and poet, collected rare manuscripts, paintings and calligraphy. Nawab Hamid Ali Khan (1889–1930) had his chief engineer, W. C. Wright, build the palace of Hamid Manzil early in the 20th century, and the library moved into it in 1957. Raza Ali Khan, after whom the library is named, came to the throne on 21 June 1930; a lover of Indian music, he bought many rare manuscripts and books on the subject.

After Rampur State joined the Union of India in 1949, the library passed to a trust that Raza Ali Khan created on 6 August 1951. The trust ran it until July 1975, when Parliament passed the Raza Library Act. Nawab Syed Murtaza Ali Khan was then named vice-chairman of the new board for life, and the post lapsed with his death on 8 February 1982.

Besides its manuscripts, historical documents, calligraphy and miniature paintings, the library holds astronomical instruments and illustrated works in Arabic and Persian, and about 30,000 printed books and periodicals, with works in Sanskrit, Hindi, Urdu, Pashto, Tamil and Turkish. It is an autonomous institution of national importance under the Department of Culture, fully funded by the central government, and a Manuscript Conservation Centre of the National Mission for Manuscripts. The Indian government issued commemorative stamps for it in 2009.
razakars-hyderabad: The Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen was founded in 1926 by Mahmud Nawaz Khan, a retired Hyderabad official. It insisted that Hyderabad be declared a Muslim state and worked to marginalise the political aims of Hindus and progressive Muslims. The Razakars were its armed wing, and they grew considerably under Qasim Razvi, a leader educated at Aligarh University who claimed that Muslim supremacy in Hyderabad rested on the right of conquest.

Under the Indian Independence Act 1947 the princely states could join India or Pakistan or seek independence. Mir Osman Ali Khan, the Nizam, a Muslim ruler over a largely Hindu population, chose independence, hoping to keep it with the help of the Razakars, and on 29 November 1947 signed a standstill agreement with India. Most of his Hindu subjects wanted accession to India.

The Razakars demanded and misused special powers, and the Nizam had to follow their dictates. They crushed armed revolts by communist sympathisers and peasants in the Telangana Rebellion, and killed Muslim advocates of union with India such as the journalist Shoebullah Khan. Their abuses against the Hindu majority included mass killings, rapes and the looting of villages, and many people fled to the jungles, abandoned mud forts or neighbouring Indian provinces. The Hyderabad State Congress was banned and its leaders escaped to Bezawada or Bombay, while the Nizam sent a delegation to refer his case to the United Nations Security Council.

The Indian home minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, then decided on police action. In Operation Polo the Indian Army under Major General J. N. Chaudhuri entered the state from five directions, and the Razakars, the main resistance, fought briefly before surrendering on 18 September 1948.

The Nizam's prime minister, Mir Laik Ali, and Qasim Razvi were arrested, and on 22 September 1948 the Nizam withdrew his complaint to the Security Council. The Pandit Sunderlal Committee Report estimated that between 27,000 and 40,000 people died in the violence that followed the operation. Razvi spent almost a decade in Indian prisons and then went to Pakistan. The Majlis was banned, but in 1957 it was rechartered under new leadership as the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen.
razia-sultan: Razia was the eldest daughter of Shamsuddin Iltutmish, an Ilbari Turkic slave (mamluk) of his predecessor Qutb ud-Din Aibak, and probably his first-born child. Her mother, Turkan Khatun, was a daughter of Aibak. Iltutmish had groomed his eldest son, Nasiruddin Mahmud, as his successor, but the son died unexpectedly in 1229.

Minhaj-i-Siraj is the only near-contemporary source for the story that Iltutmish ordered a decree naming Razia his heir and told doubting nobles that she was more capable than his sons. He did not witness it: he was in Gwalior and did not return to Delhi until 1238. After Iltutmish died the nobles appointed his son Ruknuddin Firuz, and the story may have been circulated by Razia's supporters after her accession.

Ruknuddin left the administration to his mother, Shah Turkan. Their blinding and execution of Iltutmish's popular son Qutubuddin led several nobles to rebel. While Ruknuddin marched against them, Shah Turkan planned to execute Razia. At a congregational prayer Razia roused the people of Delhi, a mob attacked the palace and detained Shah Turkan, and nobles and the army pledged allegiance to Razia. Ruknuddin was imprisoned and probably executed on 19 November 1236.

Turkic nobles opposed her from the start, since she had come to power through the support of Delhi's people rather than that of the provincial governors. The wazir Nizamul Mulk Muhammad Junaidi and four Turkic nobles marched against her. Razia led an army out of Delhi and camped on the Yamuna; two of the rebels joined her, and the others were captured, killed or fled. She appointed Malik Jamaluddin Yaqut as Amir-i Akhur. On 5 March 1237 the Qarmatian leader Nuruddin Turk and his followers entered the Jama masjid in Delhi and began killing Sunnis at the Friday prayers, before being killed themselves.

The nobles who backed Razia had meant her to be a figurehead, but she asserted herself. Her first coins carried her father's name, and by 1237–1238 she issued them in her own. According to Isami she at first observed purdah, but later appeared in public in male dress and rode elephants through Delhi. Her appointment of non-Turkic officers, above all the Abyssinian Yaqut, angered Turkic officers, and several chroniclers blame her closeness to Yaqut for her fall. In April 1240 her army at Tabarhinda rebelled, killed Yaqut and imprisoned her.

Delhi's nobles set Muizuddin Bahram, a son of Iltutmish, on the throne. Razia married the rebel Ikhtiyaruddin Altunia in September 1240 and tried to win the throne back, but they were defeated by Bahram in October and killed soon after. Her grave lies near Turkman Gate in Old Delhi, and Ibn Batuta records that her tomb had become a pilgrimage centre.
real-audiencia-of-quito: Philip II of Spain created the audiencia by a royal decree issued in Guadalajara on 29 August 1563. The decree set it in the city of San Francisco de Quito with a president, four judges who heard both civil and criminal cases, a crown attorney, a chief bailiff and other officials. Its district ran along the coast from the port of Paita to Buenaventura and inland to Pasto, Popayán and Cali, bordering the audiencias of New Granada and Panama to the north and of Lima to the south. To the east it was left open, taking in provinces not yet conquered or discovered.

The audiencia was in practice autonomous, since the viceroy to whom it answered in political matters was too far away to govern its lands. Power was devolved to its president and the political, military and religious officials under him. It belonged to the Viceroyalty of Peru, except between 1717 and 1723 when it formed part of the first Viceroyalty of New Granada; after New Granada was suppressed it returned to Peru until the viceroyalty was re-established in 1739. Its first president was Hernando de Santillán, from 1563 to 1571.

After the Quito revolution of 1809 the territory governed itself through two autonomous juntas, the first under Juan Pío Montúfar and the second under José Cuero y Caicedo, until Spanish rule was restored in 1812 under Toribio Montes. The last royal presidents were Melchor Aymerich and Juan de la Cruz Mourgeón. In 1822 the territory was liberated and joined the Republic of Gran Colombia.

Within Gran Colombia the lands of the audiencia were divided on 25 June 1824 into the departments of Ecuador, Guayaquil, Azuay and Cauca. The first three formed the Southern District and on 13 May 1830 separated to found the new state of Ecuador, whose first president, Juan José Flores, tried without success to add the Department of Cauca. The audiencia's territory also reached into parts of what is now northern Brazil.
reamker: The name means Glory of Rama. The Ramayana reached Southeast Asia from South India with Hinduism, and the earliest Cambodian evidence for it is a 7th-century inscription at Veal Kantel in Stueng Treng (K.359), which records the gift of Ramayana manuscripts to a temple and their daily recitation. Carvings at Angkor Wat and Banteay Srei show scenes of the story, and statues of its heroes were worshipped in temple sanctuaries. No literary text earlier than the 15th century survives, but from then on the Rama story became a mainspring of Khmer epic poetry, composed as recitatives for the masked drama called Khol.

The surviving text is the work of at least three unknown authors over centuries. Its first part runs from the main events of the Bālakāṇḍa and Ayodhyakāṇḍa to the moment when Ravana gathers his army for the last battle; the death of Ravana, Sita's rescue and trial by fire, and the return to Ayodhya are missing. A second part, composed in the 18th century, tells the later story of Rama and Sita: her second rejection and exile, the birth of their two sons, their meeting again and her descent into the earth.

Though Preah Ream is understood as an incarnation of Vishnu, he and the other characters are read in Cambodia as mortals rather than gods. The Khmer story adds episodes not found in Valmiki's Ramayana, such as fishes destroying Rama's causeway to Lanka, shown on a lintel at Phimai, and Hanuman's love for the mermaid princess Sovanna Maccha, who bears his son Macchanu. That episode is absent from the standard written Reamker but appears in the Cambodian Royal Ballet and the Thai Ramakien.

The Reamker is the national epic of Cambodia, alongside the Trai Bhet, and a mainstay of the royal ballet's repertoire and of Lakhon dance theatre at festivals. L'berk Angkor Wat, written in 1620 by Pang Tat, describes the Rama reliefs of Angkor Wat. In the 1900s two old men, Ta Krud and Ta Chak, were known for reciting the whole story from memory; Ta Chak's narration was recorded in 1969 over 10 days, five hours a day, though he died before finishing it.
reapers-war: The war came out of Catalan resentment at the royal army, made up mostly of mercenaries of different nations, which was quartered on Catalan peasants during the Franco-Spanish War of 1635–1659. Peasants reported sacrilege, destruction of property and rape by the soldiers and answered with local rebellions. At the same time the Count-Duke of Olivares, chief minister of Philip IV, pursued his Union of Arms to spread the burden of the empire more evenly. Catalan institutions resisted, and the Courts of 1626 and 1632 were never concluded because the measures violated the Constitutions of Catalonia. In 1638 the canon Pau Claris was elected president of the Generalitat.

The revolt came to a head on Corpus Christi in 1640 with the uprising called Bloody Corpus in Barcelona. It began with the death of a reaper and ended with the killing of the viceroy, the second Count of Santa Coloma. Claris summoned the Junta de Braços, which set up councils of justice, defence and treasury and sought French help. Under a pact at Ceret in September 1640 France promised support.

On 17 January 1641 the Catalan Republic was proclaimed under French protection, but after the defeat at Martorell on 23 January the Catalans recognised Louis XIII as Count of Barcelona. A Franco-Catalan victory at Montjuïc on 26 January 1641 followed, and Claris died a month later, probably poisoned by Spanish agents. A personal union with France was ratified at Peronne on 19 September 1641.

French control of Catalan affairs gradually undermined enthusiasm for the alliance. The Franco-Catalan attacks on Tarragona, Lleida and Tortosa failed, though Perpignan fell after a ten-month siege and all of Roussillon came under French control. Famine, plague, Philip IV's 1644 promise to respect Catalan institutions and the Fronde in France allowed Spain to take Barcelona in 1652 after a year's siege. The Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 ceded Roussillon and the northern half of Cerdanya to France. The war also helped Portugal win its Restoration War, since Spanish troops were busy in Catalonia.
rebellion-of-the-alpujarras-1499-1501: Muhammad XI of Granada, known as Boabdil, surrendered the emirate to Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile in January 1492 under the Treaty of Granada, which guaranteed the Muslims religious tolerance and fair treatment. Their number in the former emirate was estimated at 250,000 to 300,000, about half the Muslims of Spain.
