Archbishop Hernando de Talavera at first left them alone in the hope of gradual conversion, but Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, archbishop of Toledo, who arrived in the summer of 1499, imprisoned those who resisted, especially noblemen, until they converted. He also summoned elches, former Christians who had become Muslims, and jailed those who refused to return to Christianity.

On 18 December 1499 the constable Velasco de Barrionuevo was killed in the Albaicín while taking a female elche for questioning. The quarter barricaded its streets and chose its own leaders; after ten days, following negotiations by Talavera and the Marquis of Tendilla, it gave up its weapons and the killers, who were executed. Cisneros persuaded the monarchs to pardon the rebels on condition that they convert, and the leaders fled to the Alpujarra mountains, where the villages rose.

By February 1500 some 80,000 Christian troops had been mobilised, and in March Ferdinand arrived to direct operations, leading the assault on Lanjarón himself. The rebels fought a guerrilla war but had no central leadership. Places taken by storm were treated harshly: at Laujar de Andarax troops under Louis de Beaumont killed 3,000 prisoners, at Velefique all the men were killed and the women enslaved. On 16 March 1501 rebels in the Sierra Bermeja routed the army of Alonso de Aguilar, who was killed.

Ferdinand then offered the rebels exile or baptism, but passage to North Africa from Estepona cost ten gold doblas, so most stayed and were baptised, and by the end of 1501 the rising was over. A proclamation of 1502 extended forced conversion to the rest of Castile, though not to Valencia or Aragon. The Moriscos kept their language, names, food and dress, and many practised Islam in secret; Philip II's Pragmatica of 1 January 1567 ordered them to give up their customs and provoked the Morisco revolt of 1568-1571.
rebellion-of-the-seven-states: At the start of the Han dynasty, Liu Bang, Emperor Gaozu of Han, gave princely titles to many relatives over territories covering roughly a third to a half of the empire, to hold for the Liu family the lands not ruled directly through the commandery system. Under Emperor Wen the princes set their own laws, minted coins with his approval and collected their own taxes, and many ignored the imperial government. When Emperor Jing came to the throne in 157 BCE, the rich principality of Wu, with its copper and salt, was especially domineering.

Jing also had a personal quarrel with Liu Pi, Prince of Wu. Around 179-175 BCE, as Crown Prince Qi, he had beaten Liu Pi's heir, Liu Xian, to death with a liubo board in an argument over the game. His key advisor Chao Cuo, proposing to cut down the principalities for offences Emperor Wen had ignored, argued that if the princes were going to rebel, it was better they did so early rather than later, when they might be better prepared.

Liu Pi was joined by the princes of Chu, Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan, Jinan and Zhao. Qi and Jibei agreed to join but did not, and the southern kingdoms of Donghai and Minyue sent troops, while the Xiongnu promised help and sent none. Liu Pi massed the Wu and Chu armies against Liang, ruled by the emperor's brother Liu Wu, and besieged its capital.

Zhou Yafu, warned of assassins on his road from Chang'an, let Liang take the brunt, refused even the emperor's order to relieve it, and sent cavalry to cut the rebels' supply lines. Held off by Liang's generals Han Anguo and Zhang Yu, the Wu and Chu forces turned on Zhou's camp, failed to break it, starved and collapsed. Liu Pi fled to Donghai, which killed him. Elsewhere Luan Bu relieved the Qi capital Linzi, and Handan, the capital of Zhao, fell when a levee was broken to flood its walls.

The princes of Chu and Zhao killed themselves, the four princes who had besieged Linzi were executed or allowed to commit suicide, and their lands were seized by the central government. Had the princes prevailed, the Han would in all likelihood have broken up into a loose confederation of states. Instead the principality system survived, but under Emperor Jing and his son Emperor Wu the princes' powers and lands were gradually reduced, and the idea that a unified empire was normal began to settle in.
reccared-i: Reccared was born about 559, the younger son of King Leovigild by his first wife. Like his father, he had his capital at Toledo. The Visigothic kings and nobles were traditionally Arian Christians, while the Hispano-Roman population was Catholic. Bishop Leander of Seville had been instrumental in converting Reccared's elder brother and heir Hermenegild to Chalcedonianism, and was exiled for supporting his rebellion. Reccared himself had been associated with his father in ruling the kingdom.

Leovigild died within a few weeks of 21 April 586, and Leander quickly returned to Toledo. Reccared was acclaimed king by the Visigothic nobles without opposition. In January 587 he renounced Arianism for Chalcedonian Christianity, the single great event of his reign. Most Arian nobles and clergy followed, but there were Arian uprisings, notably in Septimania under the Arian bishop Athaloc, where Reccared's army defeated the insurgents and slew Desiderius, the duke sent by Guntram of Burgundy. A conspiracy in Lusitania under Sunna, the Arian bishop of Merida, was put down, and a third plot in 588, headed by Bishop Uldila and the queen dowager Goiswintha, was detected.

The Third Council of Toledo, organised by Leander but convened in the king's name in May 589, set the tone of the new Catholic kingdom. The king's public confession was read aloud by a notary and had been written for him. Leander and the Roman bishops then began a programme of forced conversion of Jews and the removal of the remains of Arianism. Modern historians have revised the view that Reccared persecuted the Jews: his laws removed the death penalty for Jews convicted of proselytising among Christians, and E. A. Thompson found no canon of the five synods of his reign that disadvantaged them.

Information about the later years of the reign is scanty. Isidore of Seville praised his peaceful government, clemency and generosity, and says he returned properties confiscated by his father and founded many churches and monasteries. Pope Gregory I wrote to him in August 599 and sent gifts including a piece of the True Cross. Reccared was married to Baddo and possibly to Chlodoswintha. He died a natural death at Toledo in December 601 and was succeeded by his young son Liuva II. At a synod at Toledo in 633 the bishops took upon themselves the nobles' right to select a king.
recceswinth: Recceswinth ruled the Visigothic Kingdom of Hispania and Septimania jointly with his father Chindaswinth until his father's death in 653. His Gothic name is believed to have been Raikaswinþs, from roots meaning king and strong. Under him the kingdom enjoyed an unbroken peace for nineteen years, except for a brief rebellion of the Vascons led by a noble named Froya, an exiled Goth who had settled in Basque territory like many others fleeing the king's persecutions. Froya and the Vascons ravaged the Ebro Valley, looted churches, murdered clerics and besieged Zaragoza. Recceswinth broke the siege and killed Froya.

From 654 Recceswinth was responsible for promulgating the Liber Iudiciorum, a law code meant to replace the Breviary of Alaric. It set a single Visigothic common law over both Goths and Hispano-Romans, and it showed little Germanic influence, keeping closer to the old Roman laws. The code of 654 also outlawed a set of essential Jewish practices, among them male circumcision, dietary laws, marriage laws and ceremonies, and the celebration of Passover.

The church councils at Toledo, the Visigothic capital, had become the most powerful force in government, and the bishops were the monarchy's chief support. Will Durant wrote that the bishops dominated the nobles who sat with them in the councils, and that although the king's authority was in theory absolute and he chose the bishops, the councils elected him and exacted pledges of policy in advance.

Recceswinth died on 1 September 672, just before the first Arab raid on Hispania Baetica. His votive crown is among the Treasure of Guarrazar, a goldsmith's treasure of crowns and crosses that several kings of Toledo offered as a sign of their orthodox faith and their submission to the church. Found between 1858 and 1861 at Guadamur near Toledo, it is now in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid. Gemstones hang beneath filigree Latin letters at its base, which read RECCESVINTHVS REX OFFERET, King Receswinth offered it.
rechiar: Rechiar, or Flavius Rechiarius, was the son of the pagan king Flavius Rechila, whom he succeeded, and of a daughter of the Visigothic king Wallia. He was the first Suevic king born in Gallaecia and had a Roman education. The only contemporary source for his life is Hydatius, the bishop and chronicler from Galicia, who portrayed him as a barbarian with little sense of Roman law or custom, a view historians no longer accept.

He was almost certainly not raised a Christian, but Isidore's Historia Suevorum records that he had become a Catholic before taking the throne, half a century before Clovis of the Franks. When and how he converted is unknown; Roman missionaries may have played a part, since he did not adopt the Arianism preached by Visigothic missionaries. His people stayed pagan, and his marriage to an Arian princess from Toulouse helped bring the Suevi later to Arianism rather than Catholicism.

Rechiar kept his capital at Braga and minted silver siliquae with the legend IVSSV RECHIARI REGES, by order of King Rechiar, claiming the right to strike coin. He seems to have carried the royal treasure with him on campaign. Hydatius records opposition to his succession without giving its grounds. In 448 the Roman count Censorius was executed at Seville by the Suevic noble Agiulf. Rechiar attacked the Basques in February 449, and after visiting his father-in-law in Gaul he joined Basilius, a leader of the Bagaudae, in raiding the Ebro valley, attacking Caesaraugusta and entering Ilerda by a trick.

He did not fight at the Catalaunian Plains in 451. After the murders of Flavius Aëtius, Valentinian III and Petronius Maximus in 455 he attacked Carthaginiensis and then Tarraconensis, the last Roman province in Hispania. Acting for the emperor Avitus, Theodoric II invaded in 456 with Goths, Franks and Burgundians and defeated him on 5 October at the Campus Paramus, twelve miles from Astorga. Wounded, Rechiar fled to Porto, where he was captured and executed in December. The Visigoths sacked Braga, and the Suevic monarchy broke into rival factions.
rechila: Rechila was the son of the Suevic king Hermeric, who fell ill in 438, withdrew from political life and handed his son the government and the royal title; Hermeric lived on until 441. The primary sources for Rechila's life are few, but the chronicler Hydatius, a non-Arian Christian, lived at the same time in Galicia and recorded his reign. Rechila may have been the father, or perhaps the uncle, of the magister militum Ricimer.

Rechila set out to expand the Suevic kingdom into the vacuum left by the departing Vandals and Alans. On the river Genil, the Singillio, he defeated Andevotus, the comes Hispaniarum, and the Roman position in Iberia became so weak that three magistri utriusque militiae, masters of both services, were sent to the peninsula between 441 and 446. Nothing is known of the sequence of events that led to his capture of the provincial capitals of Mérida in 439 and Seville in 441, though these were conquests of great significance. Lusitania, Baetica and Carthaginiensis were brought under the Suevi, except for the Levante and the Mediterranean seaboard.

He was at war with the Romans almost without pause. In 440 the Roman legate Censorius, returning from his third embassy to the Suevi, was captured by Rechila near Mértola, the ancient Myrtilis, and kept in prison for the rest of the reign.

Rechila died a pagan at Mérida. Hydatius says plainly that he died a gentile, while Isidore of Seville, writing more than a century and a half later and relying on Hydatius, adds the words so they say. Historians see no reason to accept Isidore's doubt, which was probably prompted by the fact that Rechila's son and successor, Rechiar, was a Catholic. Some scholars have argued that Rechila had his son raised in that faith to keep good relations with the Church and ease the conversion of the Suevi.
recife: Recife stands on the northeastern Atlantic coast of Brazil, at the confluence of the Beberibe and Capibaribe rivers before they drain into the South Atlantic. The city is formed by three islands, Recife, Santo Antônio and Boa Vista, with other rivers including the Jiquiá, Tejipió, Jordão and Pina. More than 50 bridges link them, and the city is often called the Venice of Brazil. Its name alludes to the stone reefs that lie offshore. The climate is tropical monsoon, warm to hot with high humidity throughout the year, relieved by trade winds from the ocean.

Recife began as a collection of fishing shacks, inns and warehouses on the delta between the two rivers, in the captaincy of Pernambuco, sometime between 1535 and 1537, in the earliest days of Portuguese colonisation of the land later called Brazil. It was a settlement of fishermen and a way station for Portuguese sailors and passing ships. It became the main harbour of the Captaincy of Pernambuco, known for its large-scale production of sugar cane.

Portuguese rule lasted from the founding to 1630. The Dutch West India Company then held the city from 1630 to 1654, when it was known as Mauritsstad and served as the capital of the colony of New Holland in Dutch Brazil. Portuguese rule resumed in 1654 and continued through the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves (1815 to 1822), the Empire of Brazil (1822 to 1889) and the Republic of Brazil from 1889. Many places of significance in the city date to both the Portuguese and Dutch periods. Football in Pernambuco began in 1902, when English and Dutch sailors landed at Recife and played a game on the beach.

Recife is the capital of the state of Pernambuco and its largest city, with 1,488,920 residents at the 2022 census and a metropolitan population of 3,726,974. It is a major seaport and the most important commercial hub of the north and northeast of Brazil. The Federal University of Pernambuco is the largest university in the state. The Historic Centre of Olinda, 7 kilometres to the north, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, and the carnivals of Recife and Olinda are nationally known. Frevo and maracatu are characteristic music and dance of the region.
recklinghausen: Recklinghausen is the northernmost city of the Ruhr area and the capital of the Recklinghausen district. It borders the rural Münsterland, and its landscape is characterised by large fields and farms in the north and industry in the south. Its Westphalian name is Riäkelhusen. The city is linked to the larger waterways by the Rhein-Herne-Kanal, and the motorways A2 and A43 cross its area.

The settlement was first mentioned in 1017 as Ricoldinchuson. In 1236 it received town privileges, and Jews are recorded there as early as 1305. As part of the County of Vest, its ownership changed several times in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and in 1576 the whole county was pawned to the Elector of Cologne. In 1582–83, and again in 1586 and 1587, partisan armies plundered the city during the Cologne War, a feud over religious parity in the Electorate of Cologne and electoral influence in the Holy Roman Empire.

More than 100 witchcraft trials were held in Recklinghausen between 1514 and 1710, with peaks in 1580–81 and 1588–89. The last person convicted was Anna Spickermann, who spent 16 months in prison and was sentenced to death by the sword and then burned. Around 1600 the administration of the Vest was divided in two, and Recklinghausen administered the eastern part. From 1803 to 1811 it was the capital of a sovereign principality of the Dukes of Arenberg, and around 1815 the Vest became a Bürgermeisterei with the town as its seat. Herten joined it in 1819 and Erkenschwick in 1821.

During World War II a prisoner-of-war camp, Stalag XX-B, was founded there in December 1939 but moved after a few days, and a forced labour camp operated from 1941 to 1943. The RAF bombed oil production at Recklinghausen on 15 January 1945, and the US 137th Infantry captured the south of the city on 1 April 1945.

Recklinghausen has a museum of icons, founded in 1956, which holds more than 1,000 Orthodox works from Russia, Greece and the Balkan countries as well as early Coptic Christian art from Egypt; it is the largest such museum outside the Orthodox world. The Ruhrfestspiele, a cultural festival with an international reputation, takes place every year from 1 May, with its main stage at the Ruhrfestspielhaus. A sculpture by Henry Moore stands there, and a large brick sculpture by Per Kirkeby stands at the Lohtor before a memorial to the dead of the First World War. The central station is served by Intercity and EuroCity trains.
reconquista: In 711 a predominantly Berber army under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and defeated the Visigothic King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete, at a time of severe division in the Visigothic kingdom. In the north, a Visigothic nobleman named Pelagius was chosen leader of the Asturians and led an uprising. Traditional historiography dates the start of the Reconquista to his victory at Covadonga, about a decade after the conquest began, where the army of the Kingdom of Asturias won its first victory over the forces of the Umayyad Caliphate. Medieval writers did not use the word Reconquista; it developed in modern historiography.

The northern realms grew from mountain strongholds into the kingdoms of León, Castile, Navarre and Aragon, with Portugal proclaimed in 1139. The Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba fell apart in civil wars by 1031 into up to 34 small taifa kingdoms, which often paid tribute called parias to the Christian kings. Alfonso VI of León and Castile took Toledo in 1085. The Almoravids, called in by the taifa rulers, defeated him at Sagrajas in 1086 and halted the Christian advance, and the Almohads later took over most of al-Andalus.

A Christian coalition defeated the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248, and by 1252 only the Emirate of Granada remained. Christian rulers often fought each other or allied with Muslim kings. Ferdinand and Isabella waged the Granada War from 1482, and Granada surrendered on 2 January 1492.

After Granada's surrender the whole peninsula was under Christian rulers. On 30 July 1492 some 200,000 Jews of Castile and Aragon were forcibly expelled. Muslims in Castile, Navarre and Aragon were forced to convert by edicts between 1499 and 1526, and from 1609 decrees expelled them from Habsburg Spain; about three million Muslims emigrated or were driven out between 1492 and 1610.

In the nineteenth century Spanish historiography consolidated the idea of a single continuous Reconquista, tied to Spanish nationalism. Recent scholarship describes it as a process of several episodes that varied by region and questions the national myth. The festivals called moros y cristianos, held especially in towns of the Valencian Community, still recreate the fighting as parades.
reconstruction-era: Eleven Southern states, all permitting slavery, seceded after the election of Abraham Lincoln and formed the Confederate States of America. The Confederacy dissolved in 1865. The war had devastated the Southern economy, and emancipation altered the legal status of millions of people. Congress passed Confiscation Acts, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation and the Freedmen's Bureau was set up on 3 March 1865 to give food, clothing and fuel to freedpeople. Lincoln favoured a ten percent plan for readmitting states, while Radical Republicans wanted harsher terms.

After Lincoln's assassination in April 1865, Andrew Johnson pardoned Confederate leaders and let Southern states enact Black Codes limiting freedpeople's rights. He vetoed the Civil Rights Act on 27 March 1866, and Congress overrode him. Radical Republicans won large majorities in the 1866 midterm elections, and in 1867 Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts over his vetoes, placing ten Southern states under military districts until they accepted the Fourteenth Amendment and Black men's right to vote. The Thirteenth Amendment of 1865 abolished slavery, the Fourteenth of 1868 granted citizenship and equal protection, and the Fifteenth, passed in 1870, forbade denying the vote because of race.

State conventions held in 1867 to 1869 gave Black men the vote. Republican governments of freedmen, white Southerners who supported them and Northern newcomers set up the South's first state-funded public school systems. Groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, White League and Red Shirts used terrorism against them. Under President Ulysses S. Grant, Congress passed the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871, including the Ku Klux Klan Act, and the Justice Department prosecuted the Klan, while the Civil Rights Act of 1875 outlawed discrimination in public accommodations.

Resistance in the South, the cost of enforcement and a waning Northern will weakened support. The disputed presidential election of 1876 was settled by the Compromise of 1877, which gave the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes on the understanding that federal troops would stop playing an active role in Southern politics. He withdrew the last of them, and historians generally date the end of Reconstruction there. Efforts to enforce federal civil rights in the South ended in 1890 with the failure of the Lodge Bill. The Supreme Court overturned the Civil Rights Act of 1875 in 1883.

Historians disagree about its legacy. The Dunning School, early in the 20th century, saw it as a failure of corrupt carpetbaggers and unqualified Black voters. W. E. B. Du Bois in 1935 and the neo-abolitionists of the 1960s, among them Eric Foner, stressed its achievements, including public schools, and the constitutional framework of birthright citizenship, due process and equal protection.
records-of-the-grand-historian: The work was begun by Sima Tan, Grand Historian (Taishi) of the Han court in the late 2nd century BCE, who drafted plans for it and left fragments and notes that may have been incorporated into the final text. After his death in 110 BCE it was continued and completed by his son and successor Sima Qian, who is generally credited as its author. Its original title was Taishigongshu; the name Shiji, 'Historical Records', was originally used for any historical text and came to mean this work only after the Three Kingdoms period.

Sima Qian had access to the early Han archives and to ancient books on bamboo and wooden slips, many now lost. He also interviewed people and travelled across China to check what he was told, and he often names his sources. He noted that records were fragmentary and contradictory, and in one chapter wrote that he had set down only what was certain and left doubtful cases blank.

The Shiji runs to about 526,500 Chinese characters in 130 chapters, in five sections. The twelve Basic Annals cover periods and dynasties, then rulers from the First Emperor of Qin to the early Han, and include de facto rulers such as Xiang Yu and Empress Dowager Lü. Ten chapters of Tables give reigns and lineages in chronological form, and eight Treatises deal with ritual, music, the calendar, astronomy, sacrifices, rivers and canals, and finance.

The Hereditary Houses hold accounts of the leading states of the Zhou period, such as Qin and Lu, and biographies from the Han. The Ranked Biographies make up 42 per cent of the work and profile about 130 men, from Boyi and Laozi to Sima Qian's near contemporaries, some in groups such as assassins or Confucian scholars. They use anecdotes to show character and have supplied many set phrases (chengyu) still used in Chinese.

The Shiji is the first of the Twenty-Four Histories and set the model for later dynastic histories. Sima Qian has been observed to place favourable material in the annals of rulers and less favourable matter in other chapters, so the work must be read as a whole. Scholars doubt the historicity of its earliest rulers, the Five Emperors. Joseph Needham noted, however, that twenty-three of the thirty Shang rulers' names appear on the Anyang oracle bones.

After about 91 BCE the manuscript was hidden in the house of Sima Qian's daughter, and it was made public under Emperor Xuan by his grandson Yang Yun. Other writers added to it, such as Chu Shaosun, and ten chapters were lost in the Eastern Han and later reconstructed. The earliest printed editions are of the Song dynasty.
records-of-the-three-kingdoms: The Records of the Three Kingdoms was compiled by Chen Shou, who was born in what is now Nanchong, Sichuan, then in the state of Shu Han. After the Conquest of Shu by Wei in 263 he became an official historian under the Jin dynasty. His work received the praise of the senior minister Zhang Hua after the Conquest of Wu by Jin in 280.

Cao Wei and Wu had already produced official histories: the Book of Wei by Wang Chen, Xun Yi and Ruan Ji, and the Book of Wu by Wei Zhao, Hua He and others. Yu Huan had privately compiled the Weilüe. Chen Shou used these as his foundation. Shu had no official history bureau, so he wrote its book himself from his own notes and other sources, among them his earlier collection of the writings of Zhuge Liang.

The work has 65 fascicles, about 360,000 Chinese characters, in three books: the Book of Wei with 30 fascicles, the Book of Shu with 15 and the Book of Wu with 20. Each fascicle consists of one or more biographies. It stands with the Book of Han as one of the first entries in the Twenty-Four Histories, after Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian.

Because it is arranged by biography rather than by year, dating its contents is imprecise. Some biographies reach back centuries to a subject's ancestors. The first event described in detail is the Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184. The books end at different dates: the Book of Wei with the abdication of Cao Huan in February 266, the Book of Shu with the death of Liu Shan in 271 and the Book of Wu with the death of Sun Hao in 284. It takes 220 CE, when the last Han emperor abdicated to Cao Pi, as the founding of Wei, and calls Wei's rulers emperors but those of Shu and Wu lords.

In the fifth century Pei Songzhi (372-451) of the Liu Song dynasty annotated the work, completing his commentary in 429 and doubling its length. He quoted other records, explained places, gave several accounts of the same event, even where they contradicted each other, and cited his sources almost every time.

The Records is the main source for Luo Guanzhong's fourteenth-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which adds fictional characters and stories. It also gives the first detailed account of Goguryeo, the Yemaek and the Wa; its passages on Japan, including Yamatai-koku and Queen Himiko, are called the Wajinden. No complete English translation exists, only selections of its fascicles.
red-army: The Workers' and Peasants' Red Army was the army and air force of the Russian Soviet Republic and, from 1922, of the Soviet Union. It was established in January 1918 by a decree of the Council of People's Commissars to oppose the forces of the new state's adversaries in the Russian Civil War, above all the groups known together as the White Army. In September 1917 Vladimir Lenin had written that the standing army should be replaced by the arming of the entire people. The Imperial Russian Army was by then collapsing: the Tsarist general Nikolay Dukhonin estimated 2 million deserters, 1.8 million dead, 5 million wounded and 2 million prisoners.

At first the Red Army was a voluntary formation, without ranks or insignia, and its officers were chosen by democratic election. A decree of 29 May 1918 imposed compulsory military service for men aged 18 to 40.

In 1919 the White armies advanced from the south under General Anton Denikin, from the east under Admiral Aleksandr Kolchak and from the northwest under General Nikolai Yudenich, and at first beat the Red Army back on each front. Leon Trotsky reformed it and counterattacked: Kolchak's army was repelled in June and those of Denikin and Yudenich in October. The Red Army also invaded Poland in the Polish-Soviet War, reaching the centre of the country in 1920 before a decisive defeat at Warsaw ended the war.

In the 1930s the army fought border conflicts with Japan, culminating in the victory at Khalkhin Gol in September 1939. In the Winter War against Finland, which began on 30 November 1939, it had three times as many soldiers as the Finns and a hundred times as many tanks, but its performance was hindered by the Great Purge of 1937, in which more than 30,000 of its officers were executed or imprisoned. Finland held out much longer than the Soviets expected.

In the Second World War, which the Soviets called the Great Patriotic War, the Red Army provided the largest ground force in the Allied victory in Europe and fought the largest and deadliest land war in history. Up to 34 million soldiers served in it. Its performance in the opening stages of Operation Barbarossa was mixed and often poor, but it ultimately broke the Axis front and took Berlin. Its personnel were also involved in Soviet war crimes against civilians and prisoners of war, particularly in Eastern and Central Europe. Officially it lost 8,668,300 killed, missing or dead of disease or in captivity, though other estimates run to almost 11 million.
In February 1946 the Red Army was renamed the Soviet Army. After the dissolution of the Soviet Union it was split between the post-Soviet states, and its bulk became the Russian Ground Forces.
red-cloud: Red Cloud was born near the forks of the Platte River, close to the present North Platte, Nebraska. His mother, Walks as She Thinks, was an Oglala Lakota, and his father, Lone Man, a Brulé Lakota leader. When his parents died around 1825 he was taken into the household of his maternal uncle, Old Chief Smoke, leader of the Bad Faces, in keeping with Lakota matrilineal custom. As a young man he fought neighbouring Pawnee and Crow bands.

Red Cloud's War, as the army called the conflicts of 1866 to 1868 in the Wyoming and Montana Territories, was fought by the Northern Cheyenne with Lakota and Arapaho allies. In December 1866 Captain William J. Fetterman left Fort Phil Kearny with 79 soldiers and two civilians and pursued a decoy band led by Crazy Horse into an ambush by more than 2,000 Sioux, Cheyenne and Arapaho. All 81 of his men were killed, against 14 casualties among the Native Americans.

Charles Eastman wrote that Red Cloud signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868 last, once the forts in Lakota territory were to be vacated. It created the Great Sioux Reservation, but gold was soon found in the Black Hills. In 1870 he met President Ulysses S. Grant in Washington, and in 1875 he returned to ask Grant to honour the treaties, but the delegates refused an offer of $25,000 for the land. He did not take part in the Great Sioux War of 1876, believing the Oglala had to seek peace.

In 1884 Red Cloud and his family were baptised as Catholics. He opposed the Dawes Act in 1887, which broke up communal holdings into plots of 160 acres, and in 1889 a treaty to sell more Lakota land, which agents obtained only by subterfuge such as using children's signatures. He died on the Pine Ridge Reservation in 1909, aged 87.

The army and newspapers mistakenly took him for leader of all the Sioux, and early historians called him the Red Napoleon of the Plains, though the Lakota never had one overall leader. He was the most photographed American Indian of the nineteenth century, with 128 known photographs. The Red Cloud Indian School, founded at his request in 1888, took his Lakota name, Maȟpíya Lúta, in 2023.
red-clouds-war: The Bozeman Trail, opened in 1863, ran through the traditional territory of the Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota as the shortest route from Fort Laramie and the Oregon Trail to the Montana gold fields; about 3,500 miners and settlers used it between 1864 and 1866. The country west of the Powder River had been Crow land under the Fort Laramie treaty of 1851, but by 1860 the Lakota and their allies had driven the Crow from it. The Crow sided with the US Army, judging that cooperation best served their interests.

Talks at Fort Laramie began in June 1866. When Colonel Henry B. Carrington arrived on 13 June with troops of the 18th Infantry and orders to build forts on the trail, Red Cloud accused the United States of bad faith and walked out.

Carrington left with about 700 soldiers, many of them new recruits armed with muzzle-loading rifles, reinforced Fort Reno, founded Fort Phil Kearny on Piney Creek on 14 July and Fort C. F. Smith on the Bighorn River on 13 August. The war was mostly constant small raids that wore the garrisons down. On 21 December 1866 Captain William J. Fetterman led a relief party of 81 officers and men out of Fort Phil Kearny, and all were killed. It was the army's worst defeat on the Great Plains until the Little Bighorn. Carrington was relieved of command.

In the summer of 1867 reinforcements brought breech-loading Springfield rifles, and on 1 August soldiers and civilians cutting hay near Fort Smith held off several hundred warriors in the Hayfield Fight.

With the transcontinental railroad taking priority and the forts costly, the government sought peace. Red Cloud would not meet the commissioners until the forts were abandoned in August 1868; the warriors burned them the next day. He signed in November. The treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills, and declared the Powder River country unceded Indian territory. The Crow lost their hunting grounds there. The Lakota hold lasted eight years, until the Great Sioux War of 1876, and in 1980 the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians that the treaty lands had been taken illegally.
red-eyebrows: The Red Eyebrows were one of the two major peasant rebel movements against Wang Mang's Xin dynasty, the other being the Lülin. Wang's land reform and a major Yellow River flood in modern Shandong and northern Jiangsu left many people unable to live by farming, and about 17 CE they rebelled in numerous, scattered risings. Fan Chong began his own in 18 CE in Ju and Langya counties, using Mount Tai as a base and gathering about 10,000 men.

Mother Lü, a landowner whose son an official had executed, sold her property to recruit poor young men and stormed a county seat in 17 CE. After her death most of her followers joined Fan Chong. The rebels' only laws were that a murderer would die and a person who wounded another must care for the victim, and their leaders took modest titles such as county educator and sheriff.

In 22 CE the rebels, who had killed the Xin general Jing Shang, painted their eyebrows red so as to tell friend from foe when facing over 100,000 regular troops under Wang Kuang and Lian Dan. They defeated them at Chengchang, where Lian died. After the Lülin took Chang'an in 23 CE and killed Wang Mang, the Red Eyebrows leaders briefly submitted to the Gengshi Emperor, but received no real lands and went home.

In late 24 CE they marched on Chang'an with two armies that joined at Hongnong in spring 25 and numbered about 300,000. They chose by lot a 15-year-old Han descendant, Liu Penzi, as emperor and took Chang'an in the autumn, and Xie Lu strangled the captive Gengshi Emperor. Their soldiers robbed the people of Guanzhong, who turned against them.

In 26 CE the Red Eyebrows burned Chang'an's palaces and pillaged the city, then suffered famine and a cold spell that froze many soldiers to death. In spring 27 they won a victory at Hu against Deng Yu and Feng Yi by a feigned retreat that left a decoy of food, but a month later Feng defeated them, colouring his own troops' eyebrows red to confuse them.

At Yiyang they met Liu Xiu's overwhelming force and surrendered after he agreed to spare Liu Penzi. Their generals were settled at Luoyang with stipends but no posts. Fan Chong and Pang An were executed when a plot to rebel again was found out, and Liu Xiu gave the blinded Liu Penzi farmland to live from.
red-fort: Shah Jahan commissioned the fort after deciding to move the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi. Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the architect of the Taj Mahal. Supervised by the emperor, it was completed on 6 April 1648. It was originally known as the Blessed Fort, Qila-i-Mubarak, and was adorned in red and white. The later name Lal Qila comes from its red sandstone walls.

The boundary walls are asymmetrical, unlike those of other Mughal forts, so as to contain the older Salimgarh Fort. The fort straddles the Yamuna River, which once fed the moats around most of the walls, and it formed the centrepiece of Shahjahanabad, the city now called Old Delhi. Aurangzeb later added the Moti Masjid, the Pearl Mosque.

The fort is octagonal, with its north to south axis the longer, and is enclosed by 2.41 kilometres of walls that rise from 18 metres on the river side to 33 metres on the city side. The Lahori Gate, named for its orientation towards Lahore, is the main entrance and leads to the Chhatta Chowk, a covered bazaar where silk and jewellery were sold to the imperial household.

The Diwan-i-Aam, the Public Audience Hall, was where the emperor heard matters brought by commoners, such as taxation and inheritance. The Diwan-i-Khas, the Hall of Private Audience, was built of white marble inlaid with precious stones; François Bernier described seeing the Peacock Throne there in the 17th century. The World Heritage Convention calls the fort the zenith of Mughal creativity, combining Persian and Indian traditions.

Nadir Shah of the Afsharid Empire plundered the fort in 1739, seizing its treasures, including the Peacock Throne. After the British defeated the Marathas at the Battle of Delhi, the East India Company installed a resident at the fort. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor to occupy it, became a symbol of the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and was tried in 1858 and exiled to Rangoon.

After the rebellion the British demolished about 80 per cent of the fort's structures, replacing the harem apartments and gardens with stone barracks, though the defensive walls largely survived. Lord Curzon began restoration after 1899. The trials of Indian National Army officers took place there from November 1945, and on 15 August 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru raised the Indian flag above the Lahori Gate. The Red Fort Complex was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
red-guards-china: The first students to call themselves Red Guards came from the Tsinghua University High School, who used the name to sign two big-character posters issued between 25 May and 2 June 1966. Led by Zhang Chengzhi at Tsinghua Middle School and by Nie Yuanzi at Peking University, they criticised the administrations of their schools for intellectual elitism and bourgeois tendencies. Most early Red Guards came from the Five Red Categories. School administrators and fellow students denounced them as counter-revolutionaries, and they met in secret among the ruins of the Old Summer Palace.

Mao Zedong then ordered their manifesto broadcast on national radio and printed in the People's Daily, which gave them political legitimacy. By the end of August 1966 almost every Chinese city had Red Guard activity, and by October 1966 so did eighty-five per cent of counties.

On 1 August 1966 Mao wrote to the Tsinghua Red Guards approving their action, and on 18 August he appeared at a rally in Tiananmen Square wearing an olive green military uniform and waved to 800,000 Red Guards and onlookers. It was the first of eight receptions that autumn, and in all he greeted eleven to twelve million Red Guards. After the rally the Cultural Revolution Group directed them to attack the Four Olds: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Old books and art were destroyed, museums were ransacked, and many temples, shrines and heritage sites in Beijing were attacked. In Red August many people in the Five Black Categories were persecuted and killed, and the army had been told not to interfere.

Red Guards also fought among themselves. In Beijing they split into the conservative Heaven faction and the radical Earth faction, though both were loyal to Mao and the Chinese Communist Party. By the end of 1966 most of the Cultural Revolution Group thought the Red Guards had become a political liability. In February 1967 the People's Liberation Army suppressed the more radical groups in several provinces, and Mao outlawed the May Sixteenth Army Corps in late 1967.

By the end of 1968 the Red Guards had dissolved as a formal movement. On 22 December 1968 Mao directed the People's Daily to publish a piece saying that intellectual youth must go to the countryside, and in 1969 many youths were sent to rural areas. Between 1962 and 1979, 16 to 18 million youths were sent to the countryside to be re-educated. Scholars have debated whether Red Guard factions arose from students' family backgrounds or from political processes during the Cultural Revolution.
red-guards-finland: After the February Revolution of 1917 the Russian-controlled police lost its standing in Finland, and law enforcement passed to local labour organisations and then to a People's Militia, which the Senate disbanded after the Social Democrats lost their majority in the October 1917 election. Following a violent clash between striking farm workers and their employers at Huittinen on 13 July, right-wing farmers formed Protection Guards, and the labour movement answered with Workers' Order Guards. By the end of the general strike on 20 November they had 40,000–50,000 members under their first commander-in-chief, the newspaperman Ali Aaltonen.

On 6 January 1918 the Helsinki guard broke from the Social Democratic Party and took the name Helsinki Red Guard. After the Senate declared the Protection Corps to be government troops on 25 January, the guards merged into the Red Guard of Finland, and revolution was proclaimed on the evening of 26 January with a red lantern on the tower of the Helsinki Workers' Hall.

The guards were made up of industrial workers, landless rural workers and crofters, mostly trade union members, aged on average between 20 and 30. A company was usually formed from one trade union local, such as the Helsinki shoemakers or tailors. Fighters were paid, sometimes more than in their usual work, which drew recruits at a time of high unemployment. Their strength rose from about 40,000 at the start of the war to 80,000–100,000 men and women, including 2,600 female fighters. Few had military training, officers were elected and discipline was lax, and most arms came from Russian troops.

The Reds held a front from the Gulf of Bothnia to the Karelian Isthmus, but three offensives in February and March failed. After the Whites broke the front in northern Häme, the Battle of Tampere, fought from 23 March to 6 April, ended with mass executions of surrendering Reds. German troops landed in the south and took Helsinki on 13 April, and more than 100,000 Red refugees headed east, of whom about 12,000 reached Soviet Russia. The Whites took Viipuri on 29 April, and the last Reds surrendered to the Germans on 6 May.

About 80,000 Red Guards were taken prisoner, and 12,000 to 14,000 of them died in the prison camps of disease, malnutrition and execution. Most were pardoned in late 1918. Some of those who had fled fought in the Russian Civil War and the Estonian War of Independence, and the Red Guards ceased to exist as an organised force by 1920.
red-guards-russia: The Red Guards were paramilitary volunteer formations for the protection of Soviet power, part of the Bolshevik Military Organizations. They consisted mainly of urban workers and cossacks, with some peasants, soldiers and sailors. Units were created from March 1917 at manufacturing companies by Factory and Plant Committees and by party cells of the Bolsheviks and the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. They were modelled on the workers' strike forces of the Russian Revolution of 1905. Other militias formed after the February Revolution, such as the people's militia, self-defence squads and workers' squads, were gradually merged into them.

On 26 March 1917 the Bureau of the Central Committee of the RSDRP(b) published a resolution on the Provisional Government, and from then the term Red Guards came into wide use. The Moscow Committee of the Bolsheviks resolved to create its own guard on 14 April, and in Petrograd a commission for workers' guards was formed on 17 April. Before April 1917 seventeen Russian cities had Red Guard squads, and by June there were 24.

Enlistment was voluntary but required a recommendation from a soviet, a Bolshevik party unit or another public organisation. Workers often trained without leaving their plants, and there were both infantry and mounted regiments. Units were not centralised and were usually formed by decision of a local party and local soviet members, so subordination, numbers and training varied. This state was often called half-partisan. In Petrograd the Red Guards, 30,000 strong, were headed by Konstantin Yurenev. At the time of the October Revolution the Red Guards across Russia had 200,000 personnel.

After the revolution the Red Guards performed some functions of a regular army, between the demobilisation of the old Russian military and the creation of the Red Army in January 1918. They fought successfully in local conflicts, for example against Ataman Alexander Dutov in Orenburg guberniya, but their loose organisation was inefficient against the larger, organised forces of the White Army.

When the Red Army was decreed, the Red Guards became its reserve and the base for forming regular detachments, and some units were reorganised into it during 1918. The term is therefore often used as another English name for the Red Army in the period of the revolution and the Civil War.
red-jacket: In his youth Red Jacket was called Otetiani, Always Ready; the name Sagoyewatha, roughly he keeps them awake, was given about 1780 for his oratory. His birthplace is disputed: Kanadaseaga near present-day Geneva, New York, Cayuga Lake and Keuka Lake have all been named, but he grew up at Basswood Creek, where his mother was buried. Under the Haudenosaunee matrilineal system he belonged to her Wolf Clan. He was a bitter rival of the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant, who called him cow killer, alleging that at the Battle of Newtown in 1779 he had passed off a cow's blood as a rebel's.

In 1792 he led a delegation of 50 Native leaders to Philadelphia, where George Washington gave him a silver peace medal that he wore in every portrait; it was returned to the Seneca Nation in May 2021. In 1794 he signed the Treaty of Canandaigua with Cornplanter, Handsome Lake and fifty other leaders, ceding much Seneca land. He opposed the sale of lands west of the Genesee River to Robert Morris under the Treaty of Big Tree in 1797, but gave way when the other chiefs would not follow him. In the War of 1812 he supported the American side, telling the agent Erastus Granger in July 1812 that his people cared more for peace than war.
In 1805 he answered the missionary Jacob Cram at Buffalo Creek, arguing that the Great Spirit had given each people a religion suited to it and that the Seneca wished only to keep their own.

He struggled with alcohol, lost most of his children to illness, and spent his last years in Buffalo, giving his last public speech in 1829. He died on 20 January 1830 and was buried in an Indian cemetery in what is now Seneca Indian Park; on 9 October 1884 his remains were reinterred in Forest Lawn Cemetery. George Catlin painted him twice, and buildings, a clipper ship and places in western New York carry his name.
red-river-asia: The Red River, or Hong River, is 1,149 km long. It is also called the Sông Cái, "Main River", in Vietnamese and the Yuan River in Chinese. It begins in the mountains of Yunnan south of Dali and flows south-east through areas of the Yi and Dai peoples, entering Vietnam at Lào Cai province, where it forms part of the border with China. Its main tributaries, the Black River and the Lô River, join it near Việt Trì. Below Việt Trì the river and its distributaries spread out into the Red River Delta, pass Hanoi and empty into the Gulf of Tonkin.

It takes its name from the reddish-brown silt it carries. It is known for violent floods and wide seasonal changes in volume, and the delta, a major agricultural area with much land under rice, is protected by an elaborate network of dikes and levees.

In the 19th century the Red River was thought to be a lucrative trade route to China. Late in the century French explorers travelled up it as far as Manhao in southern Yunnan and then overland towards Kunming. It remained the main commercial route between French Indochina and Yunnan until the Kunming–Haiphong Railway opened in 1910. French steamers could go as far upstream as Lao Cai in the rainy season, but from November to April steamships could not pass Yên Bái, and goods went in small vessels such as junks.

Because of the river, Haiphong was in the early twentieth century the sea port most easily reached from Kunming. Western authorities reckoned the journey at 28 days: 16 by steamer and small boat up the river to Manhao and 12 overland. Yunnan products such as tin came down to Manhao by pack mule. Going upstream from Manhao to Lao Cai was much harder than going down; one report gives 10 hours downstream and 10 days, sometimes a month, in the other direction.
red-river-colony: Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk, troubled by the Highland Clearances, came to see emigration as the way to improve the lives of Scottish farmers, and became interested in the Red River after reading Alexander MacKenzie's Voyages in 1801. In 1811 the Hudson's Bay Company granted him about 300,000 square kilometres, five times the size of Scotland, on condition that he supply it 200 men a year and keep the colony out of the fur trade. Selkirk called it the District of Assiniboia. The concession took in parts of present-day Manitoba, Minnesota and North Dakota; its lands south of the 49th parallel passed to the United States under the Treaty of 1818.

Miles Macdonell led the first settlers, mainly Irish and Scottish; after wintering at York Factory only 18 reached Red River the following August, too late to plant. They built Fort Douglas and hunted bison. Poor harvests led Macdonell, as governor, to issue the Pemmican Proclamation in January 1814 forbidding the export of pemmican, which drew the colony into the rivalry between the Hudson's Bay Company and the North West Company. The Battle of Seven Oaks forced the settlement's temporary abandonment, but Selkirk's arrival soon after revived it.

In 1821 the British government forced the two companies to merge, and until 1870 the Council of Assiniboia, appointed from the colony's French and English, Catholic and Protestant, Métis and Scottish communities, governed it. Farming grew: by 1827 there were over 1,000 farmers, and flour output passed 23,000 kilograms a year by the mid-1830s. In 1841 James Sinclair led 200 settlers west across the Rockies in an attempt to hold the Columbia District for Britain. The Church Missionary Society worked in the colony from the 1820s.

During the Red River Rebellion, Senator Alexander Ramsey of Minnesota and others in the United States pressed for annexation. The Canadian government answered with the Manitoba Act, which received royal assent on 12 May 1870; Manitoba became a province on 15 July 1870, and the Métis provisional government was disbanded. The former colony is now part of that province.
red-river-resistance: The Red River Colony had grown up under the Hudson's Bay Company. Most of its people were francophone, Catholic Métis, descended from First Nations and French fur traders; there were also English-speaking descendants of Scottish and English traders, a few Presbyterian Scottish settlers and newer Protestant arrivals from Ontario, many of them hostile to Catholicism. Canada agreed to buy the territory, and in 1869 Public Works Minister William McDougall sent a survey party under Colonel John Stoughton Dennis. The Métis, who held only a tenuous right of occupancy on long river lots, feared the square-township survey would bring Canadian settlers and the loss of their farms.

On 11 October 1869 Louis Riel and other Métis stopped the survey, and on 2 November they turned McDougall back to Pembina, in Dakota Territory, while Riel led about 400 men to seize Fort Garry without bloodshed. A Métis National Committee declared a provisional government on 8 December, after the arrest of John Christian Schultz and the pro-Canadian party. Riel became its president on 27 December. Special commissioner Donald Alexander Smith addressed large public meetings in January 1870, and a convention of 40, divided evenly between French- and English-speaking settlers, drew up a list of rights and a constitution.

Another pro-Canadian rising failed in February, and its leader, Major Charles Boulton, was sentenced to death and then pardoned. The prisoner Thomas Scott, an Orangeman, was tried for insubordination and shot by a firing squad on 4 March 1870, an act historians have called Riel's one great political blunder. Delegates led by Abbé Joseph-Noël Ritchot then negotiated in Ottawa with John A. Macdonald and George-Étienne Cartier.

Manitoba entered Confederation on 15 July 1870, but no amnesty was secured, and anger at Scott's death grew in Ontario. When Colonel Garnet Wolseley's troops reached Fort Garry on 24 August, soldiers of the 1st (Ontario) Battalion of Rifles assaulted many Métis around the fort. Riel was formally exiled in 1875, was elected to Parliament three times without taking his seat, and was hanged after the North-West Rebellion of 1885. Some scholars prefer the word resistance, since the Métis opposed an expanding authority rather than an established government.
red-ruthenia: Red Ruthenia, also called Red Rus or Red Russia, is a term used since the Middle Ages for the south-western principalities of Kievan Rus', namely the Principality of Peremyshl and the Principality of Belz. A Polish chronicle of 1321 is the first to use the name. The term is closely related to the Cherven Cities, thought to mean Red Cities. Its limits vary between sources. Centred on Przemyśl and Belz, the region has included Lviv, Chełm, Zamość, Rzeszów, Krosno, Sanok and Ternopil, and sometimes parts of Lesser Poland, Podolia and Volhynia. The Polish historian Janeczek has advised against using the term, because the region's inhabitants did not call it red but simply Rus, and its geographical meaning is ambiguous.

Early inhabitants included the Lendians, a Lechitic tribe that founded many of the Cherven Cities, the White Croats and the Vistulans. The region belonged to Great Moravia in the 9th century, was invaded by the Magyars at its end, and was captured by Vladimir the Great in the late 10th century. Part of it joined the new Polish kingdom in 1018 and fell back to Rus in 1031. It then changed hands often between Poland and Rus and its successor states, and from 1199 it was part of the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia. The Mongol invasion of the 13th century brought a period of Mongol overlordship.

When the Romanovichi princes of Galicia and Volhynia died out in 1340, the Galicia-Volhynia Wars began and lasted until 1392. Casimir the Great of Poland took Galicia in 1340, while the Grand Duchy of Lithuania obtained Volhynia. Most of Red Ruthenia then belonged to Poland for about 400 years as the Ruthenian Voivodeship, centred on Lwów, with Bełz as a separate voivodeship. Casimir founded several cities, and 325 towns were founded under Polish rule between the 14th century and the later 17th century. Germans, Poles, Armenians, Jews and Vlachs settled in the region. The 16th and 17th centuries brought Tatar and Ottoman raids, the Khmelnytsky Uprising of 1648 to 1654 and the Swedish invasions of the Deluge.

In 1772, at the First Partition of Poland, the Austrian Empire took Red Ruthenia, except for Podolia, and kept it until 1918. Between the world wars it belonged to the Second Polish Republic. The region is now divided between south-eastern Poland, around Rzeszów, Przemyśl, Zamość and Chełm, and western Ukraine, around Lviv.
red-sea: The Red Sea is a mediterranean sea lying between the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, an inlet of the Indian Ocean. It connects to the ocean in the south through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden. To the north lie the Sinai Peninsula, the Gulf of Aqaba and the Gulf of Suez, which leads to the Suez Canal. It is about 2,250 km long and 355 km across at its widest point, with an average depth of 490 m and a maximum of 2,730 m in the central Suakin Trough.

The sea lies over the Red Sea Rift, part of the Great Rift Valley. It formed as the Arabian Peninsula split from the Horn of Africa, a movement that began in the Eocene and accelerated in the Oligocene. The sea is still widening and is considered likely to become an ocean in time. With high evaporation, little rain and no significant rivers draining into it, it is one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world.

The earliest known exploration was by the ancient Egyptians, who sought commercial routes to Punt. One such expedition took place around 2500 BCE and another around 1500 BCE, under Hatshepsut. The Book of Exodus tells of the Israelites crossing a sea that the Hebrew text calls Yam Suph, traditionally identified as the Red Sea; Rabbi Saadia Gaon (882 to 942 CE) placed the crossing at the Gulf of Suez.

In the Middle Ages the sea formed an important part of the spice trade route. In 1183 Raynald of Châtillon launched a raid down the sea against Muslim pilgrim convoys, causing fury across the Muslim world, although his target appears to have been the lightly armed convoys rather than the cities of Mecca and Medina. The opening of the Suez Canal in November 1869 let more than a thousand marine species of the Red Sea migrate northward into the Mediterranean.

Six countries border the Red Sea proper: Saudi Arabia and Yemen on the eastern shore, and Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Djibouti on the western. The Gulf of Suez lies wholly within Egypt, while the Gulf of Aqaba borders Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Ships passing between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean shorten the route between Asia and Europe by almost half compared with sailing round Africa. Its shallow shelves hold coral reefs, and more than 1,200 fish species have been recorded, about 10 per cent of them found nowhere else.
red-square: Red Square is one of the oldest and largest squares in Moscow, lying in the historic centre along the eastern wall of the Kremlin and north of the Moskva River. It is almost rectangular, 70 metres wide and 330 metres long, and covers almost 73,000 square metres. It is bounded on the northeast by the GUM department store and the old district of Kitay-gorod, on the northwest by the State Historical Museum and the Resurrection Gate, and on the southeast by Saint Basil's Cathedral. A moat that separated it from the Kremlin was paved over in 1812.

The eastern side of the Kremlin was the most vulnerable to attack, since no river protected it, so the wall was built highest there. Italian architects convinced Ivan the Great to clear the area outside it, and decrees of 1493 and 1495 called for the demolition of all buildings within 110 sazhens of the wall. The square was meant to serve as Moscow's main marketplace and was the site of public ceremonies and proclamations, and occasionally a coronation.

It was once called Pozhar, the burnt-out place, because earlier buildings on the site had burned down. Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich extended the name Red Square, which originally described only the area between Saint Basil's Cathedral, the Spasskaya Tower and the Lobnoye Mesto, to the whole square. In old Russian the word krasnaya meant beautiful.

Under Catherine the Great the upper floor of the market lines was made of stone in 1786. The square was paved in stone in 1804, and after the Napoleonic invasion and the fire of 1812 the moat was filled in 1813 and rows of trees planted. The Monument to Minin and Pozharsky was erected in 1818. The State Historical Museum was built in the years 1875 to 1883.

In the Soviet era Red Square became the official address of the Soviet government and a showcase for military parades from 1919 onward, and Lenin's Mausoleum was part of the square from 1924, serving as a grandstand for dignitaries. In the 1930s the Kazan Cathedral and the Iverskaya Chapel with the Resurrection Gates were demolished to make room for heavy military vehicles; both were rebuilt after the fall of the Soviet Union. A legend holds that Lazar Kaganovich showed Stalin a model of the square without Saint Basil's, and Stalin answered: Lazar, put it back.

Red Square has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990. Apart from the road leading through it to the Savior Gate of the Kremlin, it is a pedestrian zone. It has been the scene of executions, demonstrations, riots, parades and speeches, and its history is reflected in paintings by Vasily Surikov and Konstantin Yuon.
red-terror-hungary: In March 1919 the Party of Communists in Hungary, allied with the Social Democratic Party of Hungary, took over the government after President Mihály Károlyi stepped aside, and proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic. Its campaigns to recover parts of present-day Slovakia and Transylvania failed and cost it support, and on 24 June the Social Democrats attempted a coup, which was followed by reprisal arrests and looting. According to the historian Robin Okey the communists had considerable support among the workers of the industrial centres, above all Budapest, while in the countryside, as John Lukacs writes, the government's authority was often absent.

The terror took its name and methods from the Red Terror of Soviet Russia. Tibor Szamuely wrote in the newspaper Vörös Újság that counter-revolutionaries should be suffocated in their own blood, and with his support József Cserny organised some 200 men as the Lenin Boys to hunt out counter-revolution in the countryside; similar groups worked in Budapest. At checkpoints in the capital civilians were arrested and tortured with burning cigars, water and nails.

In April Szamuely had hostages taken in Makó, among them the former Speaker of the House Lajos Návay, his nephew Iván Návay and the town's mayor, who were made to dig their own graves and shot on the way to Budapest. Travelling by armoured train, the communists took hostages in villages they believed hostile or that lay ahead of advancing Romanian or Czech troops, and used the terror to seize grain from peasants. The revolutionary tribunals executed between 370 and 587 people, and others give a figure of 590.

The republic ended in the first week of August 1919 when Romanian forces reached Budapest. The party's leaders fled, and Szamuely killed himself after his capture in Austria. Cserny was tried in November 1919 and executed in December with 13 other Lenin Boys. The White Terror that followed struck leftists, revolutionaries and Jews; the historian Andrew C. Janos judged it more savage than the violence of the Red Guard. A monument to the victims, a reconstruction of one of 1934, was put up in Budapest in November 2019.
red-turban-rebellion: The Yuan court was split in the early 1300s between a Mongol-centric faction and one inclined to a Han-based Confucian style of government, and the last emperor, Toghon Temür, came to the throne as a child in 1332. The Yuan garrisons, mostly Han soldiers, were in steep decline, and by 1340 repeatedly failed to put down local rebellions. From the 1340s the Yellow River flooded constantly, and epidemics and cold weather struck China. One epidemic that began in Hebei in 1331 is said to have killed 13 million people by 1333.

The Red Turbans appeared in Jiangxi and Hunan in the 1330s, and their sects worshipped Mile Pusa, the Maitreya. The movement is traced to the monk Peng Yingyu, who led an uprising in Yuanzhou in 1338.

In 1351 about 150,000 farm workers were mobilised to rechannel the Yellow River and open the Grand Canal in western Shandong, on the orders of the chancellor Toqto'a. Han Shantong and Liu Futong recruited from the discontented workers. Han was captured and executed, but his son Han Lin'er was proclaimed the Young Prince of Radiance, claiming descent from the Song, and Liu set up a Red Turban government. In the south Peng Yingyu and Zou Pusheng enthroned the cloth peddler Xu Shouhui as emperor of Tianwan in 1351. Chen Youliang later murdered Xu, took the throne in 1360 and renamed the dynasty Han.

Yuan armies suppressed most of the Red Turbans by 1353, but Toqto'a was dismissed in January 1355 while campaigning against the rebel Zhang Shicheng, after which the court lost control of its own forces.

Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphan and former monk born in 1328, joined the rebels in 1352 under Guo Zixing and took Nanjing in 1356. He accepted Han Lin'er as emperor but presented himself as a Yuan subject restoring order against rebels.

In 1363 he defeated Chen Youliang at the Battle of Lake Poyang, then eliminated Zhang Shicheng, who died in 1367, and Fang Guozhen. Han Lin'er drowned crossing the Changjiang in January 1367. Zhu proclaimed himself the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty at Yingtian on 12 January 1368, calling for the overthrow of the barbarians and the restoration of the Chinese.

The remnants of the Yuan court retreated north and are known as the Northern Yuan. Zhu ordered mass relocations afterwards: people from Shanxi were moved into devastated provinces in the north, and about 500,000 were settled in his hometown of Fengyang in 1367.
red-vienna: After the First World War the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye forbade any union of the new Austrian republic with Germany and left it with little territory and limited access to the Hungarian breadbasket that had fed Vienna for decades. The middle classes, many holding worthless war bonds, were plunged into poverty by hyperinflation, apartments were overcrowded, and tuberculosis, the Spanish flu and syphilis raged. People elsewhere in Austria called the capital Wasserkopf, big head, a city too big for so small a country.

In the municipal elections of 4 May 1919, the first in Austrian history in which all adult citizens of both sexes could vote, the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Austria, the SDAP, won a majority and Jakob Reumann became mayor. Nationally it won only 40.8 per cent of the vote, and after its coalition with the Christian Social Party broke down in 1920 it never again led the federal government. The two parties agreed to separate Red Vienna from Black Lower Austria, and on 1 January 1922 Vienna became the ninth federal state.

From 1925 to 1934 more than 60,000 apartments were built in municipal blocks round green courts, as at the Karl-Marx-Hof, housing as many as 200,000 people, a tenth of the population. Tenants were chosen by a ranking that gave priority to people with disabilities and other vulnerable groups. The Housing Tax paid forty per cent of the costs and the rest came from the Luxury Tax and federal funds. The finance councillor Hugo Breitner refused to borrow and taxed luxuries such as riding horses, large private cars, servants and hotel rooms.

The health councillor Julius Tandler built up welfare services. By 1931 the city had handed out 53,000 clothing packages to parents in need; kindergartens grew fivefold, schools gave subsidised lunches and free medical and dental examinations, and public baths were built. Infant mortality fell below half its pre-war level. The Feuerhalle Simmering crematorium, opened in 1923, set the city against Ignaz Seipel's national government, and in 1924 the Constitutional Court sided with Vienna.

Much of the city's welfare relied on federal money, and in the early thirties the federal government began to starve Vienna of funds, forcing cuts. The First Republic collapsed in 1934, a year after Bundeskanzler Engelbert Dollfuß had suspended the Nationalrat, and the banning of the SDAP ended the project. Karl Polanyi wrote in 1944 that Vienna had achieved one of the most spectacular cultural triumphs of Western history. Many of the housing complexes survive.
redemption-song: Some of the song's key lines come from a speech by the Pan-Africanist orator Marcus Garvey, given at Menelik Hall in Sydney, Nova Scotia, in October 1937 and published in his Black Man magazine. Garvey told his audience that they would emancipate themselves from mental slavery, because while others might free the body, none but themselves could free the mind. Marley recited the speech in public as early as July 1979, during his appearance at the Amandla Festival.

By then Marley had been diagnosed with the cancer in his toe that killed him in 1981. According to Rita Marley, he was already secretly in a lot of pain and dealing with his own mortality, which she found clearly apparent in the album and above all in this song.

Unlike most of Marley's recordings, the album version is a solo acoustic performance in G major, his voice and an acoustic guitar with no accompaniment and no reggae rhythm. Its best-known lines urge listeners to "Emancipate yourself from mental slavery", because "None but ourselves can free our minds". Biographer Timothy White called it an acoustic spiritual, and Stephen Davis a total departure.

Marley first played it in public at the opening show of the Uprising Tour in Zürich on 30 May 1980, and it was in every known setlist of that tour, performed with the full band. A full band version was also issued on the single released in the UK and France in October 1980, later added to the 2001 reissue of Uprising, but the solo take remains the one most listeners know.

In 2009 the Jamaican poet and broadcaster Mutabaruka chose it as the most influential recording in Jamaican music history. It has been recorded by Manfred Mann's Earth Band in 1983 and by Stevie Wonder in 1996, and Joe Strummer's version with the Mescaleros appeared on Streetcore in 2003, after his death; Strummer also sang it as a duet with Johnny Cash. On 5 February 2020, the eve of what would have been his 75th birthday, Marley's estate released an animated video for the song.
redonda: Redonda is the remnant of an ancient extinct volcano in the Leeward Islands. The island is about 1.6 kilometres long and 0.5 kilometres wide, and 296 metres high at its highest point. It lies 56.2 kilometres south-west of Antigua, 22.5 kilometres north-west of Montserrat and 32 kilometres south-east of Nevis. The land rises mostly as sheer cliffs, especially on the western side, to a tilted area of grassland at the top that slopes to the east. Its land area is hard to estimate because of the steep slopes. There is no fresh water except rain and no safe place to land a boat, which makes the island inhospitable to people.

In 1493, on his second voyage, Christopher Columbus and his crew became the first known Europeans to see the island. He claimed it for the Crown of Castile without landing, and named it Santa María la Redonda, meaning Saint Mary the Round, after its apparent profile seen from the side. Because it offered little to the powers colonising the Americas, it was for centuries a refuge for pirates.

Deposits of phosphate derived from seabird guano were found in the 1860s, and commercial mining began, with labourers from Montserrat. The island was annexed to the British colony of Antigua to regulate extraction, and the Redonda Annexation Act of 1872 formalised the step. The annual yield was up to 7,000 tons, and 120 people lived there in 1901. Aluminium phosphate for gunpowder was mined later, and a cableway carried the material down to the pier.

Mining stopped in 1914 during the First World War. Maintenance workers stayed until 1929, when a hurricane destroyed almost all the remaining facilities, and the island has been uninhabited since. Two stone huts of the mining period still stand. In 1967 Redonda became a dependency of Antigua, now part of Antigua and Barbuda, though Montserrat and Nevis are closer.

Redonda is uninhabited and is a dependency of Saint John, Antigua and Barbuda. It is a breeding colony of seabirds, including red-footed, brown and masked boobies and frigatebirds, and BirdLife International has designated it an Important Bird Area. The Redonda ground dragon and the Redonda anole live only here. Goats and rats introduced to the island harmed its ecology for almost a century, and a restoration programme began in 2016 with the removal of about 60 goats and 6,000 rats. A literary legend, begun by the author M. P. Shiel, claims a Kingdom of Redonda whose title has been passed down since.
reflections-on-the-revolution-in-france: Edmund Burke sat in the House of Commons for the Whigs, in close alliance with Lord Rockingham. He had defended constitutional limits on the Crown, denounced the persecution of Catholics in Ireland, supported American independence and pursued the impeachment of Warren Hastings, so allies and opponents alike were surprised by the force of his hostility to the French Revolution. Soon after the fall of the Bastille in 1789, Depont asked him for his impressions, and Burke replied with two letters; the longer, second one became the Reflections. By the following September it had gone through eleven editions.

Burke held that liberty was a construct of law rather than licence to do as one liked, and that there were no rights without corresponding duties. He treated society as a living organism too complicated to be reduced to a deductive system, and he defended private property, tradition and prejudice, which in his phrase renders a man's virtue his habit. As a Whig he rejected divinely appointed monarchy, but he argued for gradual, constitutional reform and saw the inherited rights of England, from Magna Carta to the Declaration of Right, as firmer than abstract rights. He predicted that disorder would make the army mutinous and that a popular general would become master of the republic.

Most of the House of Commons disagreed with Burke, and the Whigs split into New and Old Whigs, Burke leading the latter. The book found favour with George III and the philosopher Joseph de Maistre, and Hippolyte Taine repeated its arguments in the 19th century. It became the founding work of conservatism once the Reign of Terror of 1793 to 1794 and the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte seemed to bear out its predictions, and Friedrich Hayek acknowledged a debt to Burke. Historians have been more critical: Alfred Cobban judged its account of the Revolution's causes misleading, built on weak sources, though he praised it as literature and as political theory.
reform-act-1832: Before 1832 the House of Commons had 658 members, 513 of them for England and Wales, elected by counties and boroughs. The number of electors in a borough ranged from a dozen or so to 12,000, and many small constituencies were controlled by rich landowners: the Duke of Norfolk controlled eleven, the Earl of Lonsdale nine. Support for reform fell away after the French Revolution, and in the 1820s reformers such as Lord John Russell won only the disfranchisement of the corrupt borough of Grampound.

After the death of George IV in 1830, reform became a major election issue, political unions such as Thomas Attwood's Birmingham Political Union campaigned for it, and Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, became prime minister pledged to carry it.

Russell introduced the bill on 1 March 1831. It narrowly failed in the Commons, and after the Whigs won the 1831 election a second bill passed the Commons by more than 100 votes in September but was rejected by the Lords. A third bill passed the Commons by larger majorities in March 1832. When it was weakened by procedural manoeuvres, Grey resigned, unrest spread in the Days of May, and the Whigs gained the King's support for a threat to fill the House of Lords with Whigs, which made the opposition give way.

The act abolished the 56 smallest English boroughs and took one member from 30 more, 143 borough seats in all, and created 130 new seats in England and Wales, among them two members each for 22 large towns. It gave the vote to small landowners, tenant farmers, shopkeepers and householders paying a yearly rent of £10 or more, and it defined a voter as a male person.

By one estimate the English electorate rose from about 400,000 to 650,000. The property qualifications still barred most of the working class, which divided it from the middle class and fed the growth of the Chartist Movement, and a few rotten boroughs and much bribery remained. Historians have long debated whether the act was a radical step towards democracy or a conservative concession made to preserve aristocratic rule. It was repealed by the Representation of the People Act 1948.
reggio-calabria: The history of the area before the Greeks arrived in the eighth century BCE is not reliably known. Mythical accounts name a series of peoples there, among them the Osci, Trojans, Oenotrians, Ligures, Ausones and Sicels, and say the land was first called Saturnia or Neptunia.

The name Italia first referred to the area around Reggio before it spread to southern Calabria and, around the third century BCE, to the whole peninsula. By tradition it comes from Italus, an Oenotrian king. The city has borne many names: Rhegion in Greek times, briefly Phoibeia under Dionysius II of Syracuse, Regium or Rhegium in Latin, Rhegium Julii under the empire, Riyyu under the Emirate of Sicily and Rìsa under the Normans.

In the 5th and 6th centuries the Vandals, Lombards and Goths invaded. Under Byzantine rule Reggio became a metropolis of the Byzantine possessions in Italy and several times the capital of the Duchy of Calabria between 536 and 1060. Spanish Habsburg viceroys governed it from 1504 to 1713.

The 16th and 17th centuries brought decay through taxes, plague, the earthquake of 1562 and Ottoman raids: in 1534 the townspeople fled a fleet under Hayreddin Barbarossa, who captured eight hundred who remained and burned the town, and Barbary pirates took most of the inhabitants as slaves to Tripoli after an attack in 1558. On 21 August 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi took the city from the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

Reggio lies near the fault line where the Eurasian and African plates meet along the Strait of Messina, and earthquakes have destroyed it several times: in 91 BCE, after which Augustus ordered its reconstruction, then in 17 CE, 305, 374, 1562, 1783 and 1908. The quake of 1562 destroyed the medieval port and submerged the promontory of Calamizzi, where the first Greek settlers had landed. The 1783 and 1908 disasters, the second the worst natural calamity in Europe in human memory, produced the present layout of straight, intersecting streets, planned by Giovanbattista Mori in 1784 and Pietro de Nava in 1911.

Reggio Calabria is the largest city of Calabria, on the toe of the Italian peninsula opposite Sicily, with a population of 167,925.
