Its National Archaeological Museum of Magna Graecia houses the Bronzes of Riace, which have given it the nickname City of Bronzes. It is also called the City of bergamot, which is cultivated only in the region. Travellers who visited it include Pieter Bruegel around 1550, Stendhal in 1817, Edward Lear in 1847 and D. H. Lawrence around 1920.
reggio-emilia: Reggio Emilia lies on a plain crossed by the Crostolo stream, in the region of Emilia-Romagna. Its old town has a hexagonal form that derives from its ancient walls, and its main buildings date from the 16th and 17th centuries. The city began with the construction of the Via Aemilia from Piacenza to Rimini by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in 187 BCE. It became a judicial centre with a forum first called Regium Lepidi, then simply Regium, which gave the city its name. Its people are called Reggiani, and until 1861 the city was known as Reggio di Lombardia.

In the Roman age Regium was a flourishing municipium with its own statutes, magistrates and art colleges, though by the end of the 4th century Saint Ambrose counted it among the dilapidated cities. It passed through the realm of Odoacer, then came under Ostrogothic control and later to the Lombards, who made it the seat of a duchy, until the Franks took it in 773. In 899 the Magyars heavily damaged it and killed Bishop Azzo II.

Reggio became a free commune about the end of the 11th or the start of the 12th century, belonged to the Lombard League in 1167, and signed the Treaty of Konstanz in 1183. Violent struggles between noble and plebeian parties and between Guelphs and Ghibellines marked the 12th and 13th centuries.

The city then passed between several lords, among them the Gonzaga and the Visconti. In the early 15th century Nicolò III d'Este became its lord, and in 1452 Frederick III made Borso d'Este Duke of Modena and Reggio. The poets Matteo Maria Boiardo and Francesco Guicciardini served as its governors, and Ludovico Ariosto, author of Orlando Furioso, was born there in 1474. Este rule continued until 1796, apart from short interruptions.

French republican troops drove off the ducal garrison on 21 August 1796. Napoleon formed the Cispadane Republic, which was proclaimed in Reggio on 7 January 1797; the Italian tricolour was sewn on that occasion by Reggio women. In the same period the Polish lieutenant Jozef Wybicki composed there the Mazurek Dąbrowskiego, which became the Polish national anthem in 1927. After the Este returned in 1815 and the revolts of 1831 and 1848, Reggio joined united Italy in 1859, confirmed by the plebiscite of 10 March 1860.

Reggio Emilia, with a population of 172,921, is the fourth-largest city in Emilia-Romagna. Jews began to settle there in the early 15th century, and its rabbinic scholars were numerous; an unused synagogue and burial ground remain. The Basilica della Ghiara, begun at the end of the 16th century on a site where a miracle was believed to have occurred, is among its buildings.
reginald-dyer: Reginald Edward Harry Dyer was born on 9 October 1864 in Murree, in the Punjab, the son of Edward Dyer, a brewer who managed the Murree Brewery, and Mary Passmore. He was educated in Murree and Shimla and from the age of eleven at Midleton College in County Cork, briefly studied medicine in Ireland, and graduated from the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in August 1885. He was fluent in several Indian languages and in Persian.

He was commissioned into the Queen's Royal Regiment (West Surrey), served in the Third Burmese War of 1886 to 1887, and then transferred to the Bengal Army. He fought on the Black Mountain in 1888, in the Chitral Relief of 1895 and in the Mahsud blockade of 1901–02. In the First World War he commanded the Seistan Force and became a temporary brigadier-general in 1916.

In April 1919 Punjab was tense. A strike called by Mahatma Gandhi had turned violent in places, and the lieutenant-governor, Michael O'Dwyer, ordered the arrest of two local leaders. Mobs then burned buildings in Amritsar, beat three bank employees to death and assaulted the missionary teacher Marcella Sherwood. Dyer, commanding a brigade at Jalandhar, took command in the city on 11 April. On 13 April he proclaimed a curfew and a ban on meetings, and learned that a gathering was to be held in the Jallianwala Bagh.

He entered the walled garden with 50 riflemen and ordered them to fire directly into the crowd, without warning. The firing lasted about ten minutes, with 1,650 rounds spent. The Hunter Commission quoted 379 identified dead and about 1,100 wounded, while other estimates ran above a thousand dead. Afterwards Dyer ordered Indians to crawl on their bellies along the street where Sherwood had been attacked, and had youths flogged there. In May 1919 he relieved the garrison at Thal in the Third Anglo-Afghan War.

The Hunter Commission said Dyer had committed a grave error by firing as long as he did. The Commander-in-Chief, General Charles Monro, told him to resign, and he retired on 17 July 1920. Winston Churchill, then Secretary of State for War, called the massacre a monstrous event. The Morning Post named Dyer the man who saved India and raised over £26,000 for him, while Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. Dyer suffered strokes in his last years and died on 23 July 1927 near Bristol.
reginald-ii-duke-of-guelders: Reginald was the son of Reginald I of Guelders and Marguerite of Flanders. From 1316 he acted as regent of the county, and in 1318 he imprisoned his father and governed in his own right as son of the count. When his father died in 1326 he took the titles of Count of Guelders and Count of Zutphen. In 1311, at Roermond, he married Sophia Berthout, Lady of Mechelen, who died in 1329; their four daughters included Mathilde and Marie, both of whom later held the duchy.

Reginald made laws on customary law in 1321 and on dykes and canals in 1335. Widowed, he married Eleanor of Woodstock, daughter of King Edward II, at Nijmegen in May 1332. The marriage made him brother-in-law of Edward III, whom he joined against the French: in 1338 he warned the English of a French fleet gathering in the mouth of the Zwin, and in the first phase of the Hundred Years War he was Edward's closest ally among the German princes.

In the same year, 1338, he excluded Eleanor from his court, claiming that she had leprosy; after his death she became a nun. Their two sons both ruled Guelders after him, Reinald III from 1343 to 1361 and Edward from 1361 to 1371.

Reginald died at Arnhem on 12 October 1343 after a fall from his horse. His son Reinald III succeeded him as duke, and the duchy later passed to his daughters' line: Mathilde held it from 1371 to 1379 and Marie, wife of William II, Duke of Jülich, from 1371 to 1405.
reginald-johnston: Reginald Fleming Johnston was born in Edinburgh on 13 October 1874. He studied at the University of Edinburgh and then read modern history at Magdalen College, Oxford, where he began a lifelong friendship with Cecil Clementi, who shared his interest in sinology. He joined the Colonial Service in 1898 and was posted to Hong Kong, and in 1904 he moved to Weihaiwei on the Shandong Peninsula as a District Officer under Sir James Stewart Lockhart, earning a name as a capable magistrate.

Johnston travelled widely, through Tonkin, Laos and Siam in 1902 and from Peking to Mandalay in 1906, and published From Peking to Mandalay (1908), Lion and Dragon in Northern China (1910) and Buddhist China (1913). Fascinated by Chinese Buddhism, he had a private audience with the 13th Dalai Lama in 1908, while his outspoken criticism of Christian missionaries may have held back his promotion.

Chosen in 1919 to teach the thirteen-year-old Puyi, he and Isabel Ingram, the empress's tutor, were the only foreigners admitted to the inner court of the Qing. He held imperial titles, befriended the isolated boy, recorded the corruption of eunuchs who sold off the dynasty's treasures, and obtained for Puyi a bicycle, a telephone and, against the retainers' wishes, spectacles. After Puyi's expulsion in 1924 Johnston arranged a refuge at the British legation, but Puyi went instead to the Japanese legation on the advice of Zheng Xiaoxu. Appointed Commissioner at Weihaiwei in 1927, Johnston was its last British Commissioner.

In 1931 he became Professor of Chinese at the University of London, based at the School of Oriental and African Studies, to which he left a library of over 16,000 volumes. He visited Puyi in Manchukuo in July 1935, and on his island of Eilean Rìgh in Loch Craignish he was allowed to fly the flag of Manchukuo. He died in Edinburgh on 6 March 1938, and his ashes were scattered on the island. His fiancée Elizabeth Sparshott burned many of his papers, including letters from Puyi's childhood. Twilight in the Forbidden City (1934) became a source for Bernardo Bertolucci's film The Last Emperor, in which Peter O'Toole played him.
reginar-duke-of-lorraine: Reginar was probably the son of Giselbertus, count of the Maasgau, and a daughter of Emperor Lothair I whose name is not known. He may already appear as Rainerus in a charter of 877 in the Capitulary of Quierzy, beside his probable father as one of the regents of the kingdom while Charles the Bald was campaigning in Italy. Modern scholars call his dynasty the Reginarids, after the name its members often used.

He was lay abbot of Saint-Servais in Maastricht, Echternach, Stavelot-Malmedy and Saint-Maximin in Trier, abbeys that lay on or near the boundary drawn between the eastern and western Frankish kingdoms by the Treaty of Meerssen in 870. His secular titles are known mostly from later sources of uncertain reliability: Dudo of Saint-Quentin calls him duke of Hainaut and Hesbaye and an opponent of Rollo, founder of Normandy. A charter at Stavelot of 21 July 905 shows that he called himself duke.

He supported Zwentibold, king of Lotharingia, in 895 but broke with him in 898 and, with other magnates, invited Charles the Simple to become king. When his lands were confiscated he refused to give them up and entrenched himself at Durfost, downstream from Maastricht. He killed Zwentibold in battle in August 900. In 908 he recovered Hainaut after the death of Sigard, and after Duke Gebhard fell fighting the Magyars in 910 he led the magnates who rejected Conrad I of Germany and chose Charles the Simple.

He probably commanded the region militarily under Charles, though he never appears as duke of Lorraine. By his wife Alberada, probably a second wife, who died before him, he left Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine, who succeeded him, Reginar II, Count of Hainaut, and a daughter who married Berengar, Count of Namur. Unlike the Liudolfings in Saxony or the Liutpoldings in Bavaria, the Reginarids did not establish their supremacy in Lotharingia.
reginarids: The family were magnates of Lower Lotharingia in the Carolingian and Ottonian periods, and their modern name comes from Reginar, the name many of them bore. The first probable ancestor known with any confidence is Gilbert, Count of the Maasgau, mentioned in 841, who served King Lothair I but went over to Lothair's half-brother Charles the Bald in the civil war of 840 to 843. In 846 Gilbert abducted and married a daughter of Lothair to force the king to reinstate him. Reginar, Duke of Lorraine, is believed to have been Gilbert's son.

After the death of Charles the Fat the Reginarids fought a long struggle with the Conradines for supremacy in Lotharingia, and when they won, in 910, they elected Charles the Simple as king. Reginar and his son Gilbert were dukes of Lorraine, and the family also held the county of Hainaut. Their power was finally broken by the combined forces of Bruno I of Lorraine and the Carolingians of West Francia: in 958 Reginar III's lands were confiscated and given to Gerard, Count of Metz, of the Matfridings, the family's enemies since the reign of Zwentibold.

The Reginarids backed Lothair of France against Otto II, but came to terms with Otto in 978. By the end of the 10th century they were no longer a single family. Two brothers who returned to power founded the first dynasties of the counties of Hainaut and Louvain; Lambert I, son of Reginar III, became the first Count of Louvain in 1003. Their descendants at Mons and Louvain kept up the family's opposition to the king.

The counts of Louvain became landgraves and then dukes of Brabant, Lothier and Limburg, and Adeliza of Leuven became queen of England as the wife of Henry I. The Brabant line ended in 1355, when its duchies passed to the House of Luxembourg, and from it to the House of Valois-Burgundy in 1383. Henry I, Landgrave of Hesse, a younger half-brother of Duke Henry III of Brabant, founded the House of Hesse, which ruled Hesse from 1264 to 1918; the medieval Percy earls of Northumberland were another junior branch.
regino-of-prum: According to statements of a later era, Regino was the son of noble parents and was born at the stronghold of Altrip on the Rhine near Speyer, at an unknown date. He entered the Benedictine Order, probably at Prüm itself, and was a diligent student. The Imperial Abbey of Prüm suffered greatly from Norse raids in the 9th century and was twice seized and ravaged, in 882 and 892. After the second devastation the abbot Farabert resigned and Regino was elected in 892. His work of restoration was hampered by the struggle between contending parties in Lorraine.

In 899 Richarius, later Bishop of Liège, drove Regino from office and became abbot himself. Regino went to Trier, where Archbishop Ratbod received him honourably and made him abbot of St Martin's, which he reformed and rebuilt after Norse devastation. He supported the archbishop's church reforms and accompanied him on visitations. He died at Trier in 915 and was buried in St Maximin's Abbey, where his tomb was found in 1581.

His earliest work was a treatise on music, the Epistola de harmonica institutione, written as a letter to Ratbod to improve liturgical singing in the diocese. He also compiled the Tonarius, a collection of chants. At Ratbod's request he drew up a collection of canons for use in visitations, divided into 434 sections and dedicated to Hatto I, Archbishop of Mainz. Large parts of it were later included in the Decretum of Burchard of 1012. Its section 364 is the Canon Episcopi, which deals with popular superstition.

His most influential work is the Chronicon, a universal history from the Incarnation to 906 that centres on the Carolingian empire and links the rise and fall of the dynasty with his own affairs. Its first book runs to the death of Charles Martel in 741 and draws on Bede, Paulus Diaconus and the Annals of Saint-Amand. The second book begins with a long excerpt of the Royal Frankish Annals down to 813, and later sections criticise Zwentibald, son of Arnulf, in the contest for Lotharingia.

Regino changed Bede's Anno Mundi dating to one counted from the Incarnation, and modern scholars consider the Chronicon the first chronicle to apply that system conventionally, although its chronological accuracy has been questioned. It is the only contemporary text that hints at the organisation of the Council of Preslav. The Chronicon was continued to 967 and was used by later writers such as Cosmas of Prague. It was first printed at Mainz in 1521, and Simon MacLean published an English edition in 2009. Around 900 Regino also named four marks of a people: descent, custom, language and law.
regni: The Regni, also called the Regini, were a Celtic tribe or group of tribes living before the Roman conquest in what is now Sussex and small parts of Hampshire, Surrey and Kent. Their neighbours were the Belgae to the west, the Atrebates to the north and the Cantiaci to the east. Ptolemy calls them Regni, with a single city, Noiomagus, and some scholars prefer that name or the Brythonic Regini to Regnenses. A comparison with other civitas capitals suggests another reading of Noviomagus Reginorum, New Market, Land of the Regini.

By the end of the Middle Iron Age, about 100 BCE, the downland hillforts had been abandoned and settlements on the coastal plain had multiplied. The Regni were probably native tribes influenced by the Belgae, perhaps under a Belgic elite, though increased trade may have mattered more than migration. They were closely tied to the Atrebates, and Noviomagus served as an early capital of the Atrebates.

After the conquest the Romans seem to have kept a nominally independent client kingdom, perhaps as a buffer, and the Regni are the only people its king certainly ruled; Tacitus records that certain civitates were given to him and remarks on his loyalty. The Romans made heavy use of Chichester Harbour right after 43 to supply their legions in the south-west. After the king's death around 80 the region became a civitas of the province, governed from Noviomagus, with ports, villas and roads such as the route to Londinium later called Stane Street.

In the late 3rd century the fort of Anderitum, modern Pevensey, was built in the civitas against raids across the Channel. After Roman rule ended, the Kingdom of Sussex formed in the former civitas, traditionally with the arrival of King Aelle in 477, though his existence is debated.

The Regni farmed the coastal plain, worked iron in the Weald, made textiles and salt and traded with the continent; they were probably among the British peoples most assimilated to Roman culture even before the conquest. Cremation was established in their territory by the 70s BCE, and shrines stood at Hayling Island, Lancing Down and Westhampnett. Their coins blended Roman imagery, such as the goddess Roma, with goddesses of their own, and the Weald later held the third-largest iron works of the Roman Empire, at Beauport Park near Hastings.
regolini-galassi-tomb: The tomb is one of the wealthiest Etruscan family tombs of Caere, an ancient city about 50 to 60 kilometres north-northwest of Rome. Its architecture and contents show that it was built by a wealthy family of the city. Two burial chambers lie on either side of a corridor 37 metres long and 1.8 metres wide. The lower part is cut into the tufa rock, while the upper part is built of square stone blocks, each course projecting over the one below to form an overhang. The whole structure lies under a tumulus 46 metres across, which gives it the face of a monument.

The excavators found a royal woman buried in the end cell and a cremated man in the right-hand cell. The body of a third person lay on a bronze bed in an annex chamber, and who this was has never been explained. The grave goods included gold jewels, silverware, gilded and bronze ware, bronze cauldrons and a chariot. Several pieces carry seventh-century BCE Villanovan decorative motifs, among them a great fibula with five small lions striding across its surface and a plaque 25 centimetres long decorated with animals of Eastern origin.

The fibula has been praised for the mastery of its technique, as have the Phoenician metal bowls. The Orientalizing influences in the tomb fuse Etruscan customs with those of Greece and the Eastern Mediterranean. The many materials used, iron, tin, copper, silver and gold among them, show the importance of mineral wealth to a region where Villanovan settlements grew from poor farming villages into thriving cities.

General Vincenzo Galassi, a senior official of the papal army, and Alessandro Regolini, archpriest of Cerveteri, had both opened and excavated tombs around Caere before they found this one undisturbed in 1836. After the excavation the antiquities were kept under guard in a room of Galassi's residence, and they were later sold to the Vatican. Luigi Grifi published the contents in detail in 1841.
regulamentul-organic: Moldavia and Wallachia had long paid tribute to the Ottoman Empire, which ruled them through Phanariote princes appointed by the Porte, while Russia claimed a right to intervene on behalf of Orthodox subjects under the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774. The Akkerman Convention of 7 October 1826 ended Phanariote rule, provided for princes elected for seven years by each Divan, granted free foreign trade and first mentioned new statutes to govern the two countries. These were drafted only after the Russo-Turkish War of 1828–1829, under Russian occupation.

The occupation was widely felt as abusive: Russia seized both treasuries, and the governor Zheltukhin packed the drafting commission and expelled anti-Russian boyars such as Iancu Văcărescu. His successor Pavel Kiselyov, governor from 19 October 1829 to 1 April 1834, fought plague, cholera and famine and oversaw the enforcement of the new law.

The Regulament partly confirmed the traditional government, including rule by the hospodars, set up a common Russian protectorate that lasted until 1854, and gave the two principalities their first common system of government. Towns received a local administration. In the countryside it favoured the great estates: peasants could keep about 70% of the harvest of a leased plot, the corvée was fixed at up to 12 days a year, boyars could use a third of an estate as they pleased, and peasants were divided by wealth into fruntași, mijlocași and codași, the last with no right to pasture.

Russia also made each assembly pass an Additional Article forbidding any change without the consent of both Istanbul and Saint Petersburg. In Wallachia this caused a four-year standstill, during which a nationalist group drafted its own constitution declaring the Russian protectorate and Ottoman suzerainty at an end. The Additional Article passed through the interference of Prince Alexandru II Ghica, and the group's radical leader, Ion Câmpineanu, had to take refuge in Central Europe.

Though conservative, the statute opened a period of reform and the Westernization of local society. Trade grew, the urban population had doubled by 1850, and Brăila, Giurgiu and Galați prospered on grain. Romanian Romantic nationalism flourished, with its interest in the Latin origin of Romanians. Under its last reforms Moldavia freed its Roma slaves on 22 December 1855 and Wallachia banned slave ownership on 20 February 1856. The Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 placed the principalities under the protection of all the European powers.
regulating-act-of-1773: By 1773 the East India Company was in deep financial trouble. It paid the government £400,000 a year to keep its monopoly but had been unable to meet the payment since 1768, after losing its tea sales in America, where about 85% of the tea was smuggled Dutch tea. It owed money to the Bank of England and the government and had 15 million lbs of tea rotting in British warehouses. Lord North's government, holding that company men were not trained to govern lands of national importance, moved towards state supervision. The shareholders opposed the act, and the company remained a powerful lobby in Parliament.

The act limited the company's dividends to 6% until it repaid a £1.5m loan granted by an accompanying act, and replaced the yearly election of all 24 directors with four-year terms, a quarter of the court retiring each year. It forbade company servants to engage in private trade or accept presents or bribes. Four men, John Clavering, George Manson, Richard Barwell and Philip Francis, were named for five years to sit with the Governor-General on the Supreme Council of Bengal, which decided by majority; the Governor-General voted only to break a tie. The Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William was set up in 1774 with Sir Elijah Impey as its first chief justice. The company kept its territorial possessions.

The act marked the beginning of parliamentary oversight of the company's administration and ended the dual government that had existed in Bengal since 1765. It had clear weaknesses: the Governor-General had no veto and could be outvoted, which led to conflict in Warren Hastings's time; the Supreme Court's jurisdiction was poorly defined; and Bombay and Madras were left largely outside central control. These gaps led to Pitt's India Act of 1784. Most of the act was repealed by the Government of India Act 1915, and the rest by an amending act of 1916.
rehoboam: According to the Hebrew Bible, Rehoboam was the son and successor of Solomon and a grandson of David, and the last king of the united kingdom of Israel. His mother, Naamah, was an Ammonite, one of the foreign wives whom Solomon married. The biblical account says that Solomon had angered God by marrying foreign women and building shrines to the gods of Moab and Ammon, and that God declared he would tear the kingdom away from Solomon's son. Even before Solomon's death Damascus under Rezon had won independence, and Jeroboam, a superintendent of works, had fled to Egypt.

Rehoboam's reign is told in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, and the Bible gives it as 17 years. The ten northern tribes met at Shechem to proclaim him king and asked for relief from Solomon's burdens. The older men advised him to speak to them civilly, but the young men he had grown up with told him to show no weakness and to tax them more, and he did. Jeroboam and the northern tribes then rebelled and formed a separate kingdom, leaving Rehoboam the Kingdom of Judah with Jerusalem as capital. He raised an army of 180,000 against Israel but was advised not to fight his brethren.

In the fifth year of his reign Shishak, king of Egypt, invaded and took the fortified towns on the approach to Jerusalem. Rehoboam gave him the treasures of the temple, and Judah became a vassal of Egypt. Shishak is generally identified with Shoshenq I, whose record at the Bubastite Portal in Karnak confirms an invasion, though its surviving list does not include Jerusalem.

Rehoboam had 18 wives and 60 concubines, who bore him 28 sons and 60 daughters. His son Abijah succeeded him, and he was buried beside his ancestors in Jerusalem. Outside the Bible there is little evidence of a stable monarchy in Judah in his time, and Christian Frevel suggests that the accounts of Rehoboam and Jeroboam may be a later construction projected back onto the past. In the Gospel of Matthew he appears in the genealogy of Jesus.
reich-chamber-of-culture: The chamber was created by a law of 22 September 1933 in the course of the Gleichschaltung process, at the instigation of Joseph Goebbels as the professional organisation of all German creative artists. It prevailed over the rival ambitions of the German Labour Front under Robert Ley and was meant to control the whole of German cultural life and promote Aryan art in keeping with Nazi ideals. Every artist had to apply for membership with an Aryan certificate, and a refusal meant in practice a ban on working.

The chamber was attached to the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda on Wilhelmplatz in Berlin. Goebbels headed it, and a state secretary of his ministry served as vice-president: Walther Funk, Karl Hanke, Leopold Gutterer and finally Werner Naumann. The SS officer Hans Hinkel, one of its officials, was Goebbels' special commissioner for removing Jews from German cultural life. Its seven chambers covered film, music, fine arts, theatre, literature, the press and radio; the music chamber was first led by Richard Strauss and from 1935 by Peter Raabe, and the literature chamber by Hans-Friedrich Blunck and from 1935 by Hanns Johst.

Jews were at first admitted, but were purged from the chamber in mid-1935, and after the annexation of Austria in March 1938 its control extended there. The fine arts division under Adolf Ziegler organised the Entartete Kunst exhibition of works condemned as degenerate, which opened at the Hofgarten in Munich in July 1937 and toured cities such as Berlin, Leipzig, Düsseldorf, Salzburg and Hamburg until 1941, drawing millions of visitors. Some dealers were allowed to emigrate to New York to sell such works and raise money for the war effort. The Allied Control Council dissolved the chamber by Law no. 2 of 10 October 1945, and its records are kept by the German Federal Archives and the Berlin Document Center.
reich-ministry-for-the-occupied-eastern-: Adolf Hitler first spoke of an Eastern Ministry on 3 March 1941, in a conversation with Wilhelm Keitel about the planned invasion of the Soviet Union, holding that the political tasks there were too difficult to leave to the Wehrmacht. On 26 March Reinhard Heydrich noted Hermann Göring's suggestion that it be given to Alfred Rosenberg, the Nazi Party's chief racial theorist and a Baltic German. After the invasion of 22 June 1941, Hitler set up the ministry on 17 July, though it was not announced to the public until November. Its deputy minister, Alfred Meyer, later represented Rosenberg at the Wannsee Conference.

Rosenberg planned four Reichskommissariats. Ostland, covering the Baltic countries and Belarus, was set up at once under Hinrich Lohse, and Ukraine on 20 August 1941 under Erich Koch; Moskowien and Kaukasien were never established, as the Wehrmacht failed to hold those regions firmly. The ministry shared in drawing up and carrying out Generalplan Ost and was one of the main agencies that oversaw the Holocaust in the Soviet Union.

Rosenberg hoped to win over the non-Jewish population by presenting the Germans as liberators, and a land reform of February 1942 promised to abolish the collective farms. Göring insisted they be kept under another name, and Hitler called the redistribution stupid. The SS and its auxiliary police acted as they wished, Hitler ordered Koch to rule Ukraine harshly, and the ministry had no authority over the army or the security forces. By late 1944 the Red Army had retaken the territories, and the Flensburg Government abolished the ministry on 5 May 1945.

Its staff wore brown uniforms like those of Nazi Party and SA officials but with a dark brown collar. The colour of the collar tabs showed the level of office, from the district commissariats to the Reich Commissariat and the ministry itself, and rank was shown by four-pointed stars of a special pattern and by borders of oak leaves, embroidered in gold for the senior leadership. The minister's tabs carried a large eagle with lowered wings.
reich-ministry-of-public-enlightenment-a: Shortly after the Reichstag elections of March 1933 Adolf Hitler presented his cabinet with a draft resolution to establish the ministry, and he pushed it through despite the scepticism of some non-National Socialist ministers. On 13 March 1933 President Paul von Hindenburg issued the decree. The ministry moved into the 18th-century Ordenspalais across from the Reich Chancellery in Berlin. On 25 March Goebbels told broadcasting directors that it had the task of carrying out an intellectual mobilization, comparable in the field of the spirit to the Ministry of Defense in the field of security. A decree of 30 June 1933 transferred numerous functions of other ministries to it, to centralise Nazi control of German cultural, media and intellectual life.

The ministry began in 1933 with five departments and 350 employees; by 1939 it had 2,000 employees in 17 departments, and its budget rose from 14 million Reichsmarks in 1933 to 187 million in 1941. Departments covered administration and law, propaganda, broadcasting, press, film, theatre, music and art, and security. Goebbels headed it with three state secretaries, including Otto Dietrich for the press from 1937.

Its work overlapped with that of other bodies. The Reich Chamber of Culture supervised creative artists, and three Nazi Party leaders with media duties, Goebbels, Max Amann and Dietrich, sometimes issued contradictory directives. The Foreign Office claimed foreign propaganda, and Hitler's directive of 8 September 1939 confirmed its leading role, though Goebbels's ministry kept interfering until the end of the war.

The main instrument of press control was the Reich press conference, held daily from 1 July 1933. Between 80,000 and 100,000 instructions were issued by 1945, and participants had to destroy them after use. Control combined indirect pre-censorship with direct censorship after publication. Some journalists resisted: staff of the Frankfurter Zeitung hid their notes, and Walter Schwerdtfeger was imprisoned for treason for passing instructions to the foreign press.

The film department approved every project before shooting, and after the Reich Film Law was revised in 1934 a film could be banned for violating National Socialist, moral or artistic sensibilities. It also ran the newsreel Deutsche Wochenschau, which in 1942 reached 20 million moviegoers a week. Regional radio corporations were brought under the Reich Broadcasting Corporation in 1933, and a unified programme was broadcast from June 1940. The Flensburg Government abolished the ministry on 5 May 1945.
reich-security-main-office: In 1934 the Nazi regime abolished the sovereignty of Germany's federal states, and the Gestapo under Heinrich Himmler had already asserted nationwide authority before the Reich Security Main Office existed. Himmler established the office on 27 September 1939, in his dual capacity as Chief of German Police and Reichsführer-SS. It placed under one roof the Nazi Party's Sicherheitsdienst, the SS intelligence service, and the Sicherheitspolizei, which was nominally under the Interior Ministry and comprised the Gestapo and the Kriminalpolizei. Reinhard Heydrich headed it until his assassination in 1942, and from January 1943 Ernst Kaltenbrunner led it until the end of the war in Europe.

The office was divided at its simplest into seven offices. Amt IV was the Gestapo under Heinrich Müller, and Amt V the Criminal Police; Amt III and Amt VI were the intelligence services at home and abroad. Adolf Eichmann headed the subdepartment IV B4, responsible for the deportation of Jews. Its leaders were socially uniform: about three-quarters were born after 1900, and nearly a third held doctorates. Historian Michael Wildt describes their shared outlook as uncompromising and aimed at turning ideology into radical practice.

The office controlled the Einsatzgruppen, the death squads that followed the German army into Eastern Europe. Raul Hilberg estimates that between 1941 and 1945 they, related agencies and foreign auxiliaries killed more than two million people, including 1.3 million Jews. On 20 January 1942 Heydrich convened the Wannsee Conference to settle the administrative details of the Final Solution, and mass deportations to Auschwitz, supervised by Eichmann, began in late March 1942.

The office was not tried as an entity at Nuremberg, but the Gestapo, the SD and the SS were declared criminal organisations. Kaltenbrunner was convicted and hanged on 16 October 1946. The Einsatzgruppen Trial prosecuted 24 commanders, and fourteen received death sentences, of which four were carried out. Many members of the office escaped prosecution.
reichenau-island: Reichenau lies in Lake Constance almost due west of the city of Konstanz, between the Gnadensee and the Untersee, the two parts of the lake. The island has a land area of 4.3 square kilometres and a circumference of 11 kilometres. It is 4.5 kilometres long and 1.5 kilometres wide at its widest, and its highest point, the Hochwart, stands about 43 metres above the lake. A causeway completed in 1838 connects it to the mainland, crossed by a waterway, the Bruckgraben, which a low road bridge spans.

People lived on Reichenau in the Bronze Age and Iron Age, but archaeological evidence suggests that it was abandoned in the Roman era and stayed empty until 724. In that year the monk Pirmin received the support of the Carolingian ruler Charles Martel to build a monastery. The first monastery, at Mittelzel, was of wood and had been replaced in stone by 746.

In the early 9th century the community flourished under the patronage of the Carolingian and later the Ottonian dynasty. In 816 the monastery church was rebuilt as a cruciform basilica. Two further churches were built, for Saints Peter and Paul, consecrated in 799, and for Saint George, in 896. Relics of Saint Mark arrived at the abbey in the middle of the 9th century.

The abbey produced poets and authors such as Walafrid Strabo, who served as abbot, and scholars such as Hermann of Reichenau and Abbot Reginbert, as well as artists. The Ottonian murals of the miracles of Christ in the church of Saint George are unique survivals from the 10th century, and the Plan of St. Gall, the only surviving architectural drawing from the Middle Ages, may also have been made on the island.

In the 16th century the territory of the Prince-Bishopric of Constance was extended to include Reichenau, and the abbey's influence waned. When the Prince-Bishopric was secularised in 1803, many smaller chapels were demolished, the manuscripts and archives went to Karlsruhe and the University of Heidelberg library, and the surrounding farms were divided up and sold.

The three churches and the abbey were declared a World Heritage Site in 2000. The abbey's bailiff lived in a two-storey stone house to which two more storeys of timber framing were added in the 14th century, one of the oldest timber-frame buildings in southern Germany, now a museum of local history. The island is also known for its vegetable farms, and the Wollmatinger Ried beside it is a large reed wetland and nature reserve where many birds stop on their annual migration.
reichsdeputationshauptschluss: The full name of the measure was the Hauptschluss der außerordentlichen Reichsdeputation, the Principal Conclusion of the Extraordinary Imperial Delegation, and it is sometimes called the Final Recess in English. During the French Revolutionary Wars France had annexed the lands of the Holy Roman Empire west of the Rhine, and the Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 set out the broad principle that the German princes who lost territory there should be compensated inside the Empire. The detailed plan was agreed between France and Russia in June 1802 and then laid before an Imperial Delegation, which passed its resolution to the Reichstag.

The law secularised nearly 70 ecclesiastical states, among them prince-bishoprics, prince-priories, prince-abbeys and imperial abbeys. Most were annexed to neighbouring secular principalities, while several abbeys were given as secular fiefs to small princes who had lost their estates beyond the Rhine. Only three kept their ecclesiastical character: the Archbishopric of Regensburg, raised from a bishopric by taking in part of the Archbishopric of Mainz, and the lands of the Teutonic Knights and of the Knights of Saint John.

The former Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg became an enlarged secular duchy and an electorate. Of the 51 imperial cities, 45 were abolished and annexed to neighbouring states. The Reichstag accepted the measure unanimously and Emperor Francis II approved it, though he made a formal reservation about the new allocation of votes in the Reichstag, which had shifted the balance heavily from the Catholic to the Protestant states.

In all, 112 imperial estates covering 10,000 square kilometres and more than three million people changed hands. Baden, Württemberg, Bavaria, Saxony and Prussia made the largest gains, and Baden, Hesse-Kassel and Württemberg became electorates in place of three that had disappeared. Only Augsburg, Bremen, Frankfurt am Main, Hamburg, Lübeck and Nuremberg survived as free cities.

A commission set up by the Diet to compensate the dispossessed princes worked until at least 1820, and its archives are now in the German Federal Archives. The settlement also established that Napoleon's allies could expect gains in land and rank, a principle repeated in 1806, when over 80 small and mid-sized states were mediatised on the founding of the Confederation of the Rhine and the Empire was dissolved the same year.
reichskommissar: The title, rendered as Commissioner of the Empire, Reich Commissioner or Imperial Commissioner, was first used in the unified German Empire after 1871 for officials given special tasks, such as the Reichskommissar for emigration in Hamburg. Adolf Wermuth held it on Heligoland, handed over by the UK on 9 August 1890 under the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty.

It was also the title of the governors of most of the early colonial protectorates. Gustav Nachtigal held it in Kamerun and Togo in July 1884 and in German South West Africa from 7 October 1884, Hermann von Wissmann in East Africa from 1888 to 1891, and Wilhelm Knappe and Franz Leopold Sonnenschein on Nauru. In each case regular governors or other officials later took over.

Adolf Hitler revived the title before the war for regions taken back or annexed: Josef Bürckel became Reichskommissar for the return of the Saar on 1 March 1935 after the plebiscite of 13 January, and Konrad Henlein for the Sudetenland on 21 October 1938. Bürckel held a similar post in Vienna from 1 May 1939. In each case the office later gave way to that of a Reichsstatthalter.

In the war the Reichskommissars governed occupied countries as civil administrators with wide authority, and depending on circumstances they could be severely dictatorial and repressive, most notably Erich Koch in Ukraine. In Norway Terboven proclaimed the deposition of King Haakon VII on 25 September 1940 and outlawed every party but Nasjonal Samling. Belgium and Northern France received a Reichskommissar, Joseph Grohé, only on 18 July 1944, after four years of military government.

Alfred Rosenberg had proposed five Reichskommissariats for conquered Soviet lands; only Ostland, set up on 17 July 1941, and Ukraine, on 20 August 1941, came into being, while Siegfried Kasche and Arno Schickedanz were named for Moskowien and Kaukasien, which the Germans never controlled. The eastern administrations lasted until the Germans were driven out in 1943–44.
reichstag-fire-decree: By the early 1930s successive presidential cabinets of the Weimar Republic governed through emergency decrees under Article 48 of the constitution rather than through stable parliamentary majorities. Article 48 allowed the president, where public order and security were seriously disturbed or endangered, to take emergency measures and suspend specific rights, and it let the Reichstag revoke them. Adolf Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 at the head of a coalition with the German National People's Party, and new elections were called for 5 March.

On the evening of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building in Berlin was set on fire. The circumstances of the fire remain controversial among historians, but there is broad agreement that the Nazi leadership exploited it at once. Hitler and his supporters blamed the Communist Party of Germany and presented the fire as the signal for a Communist uprising. Dozens of Communists were arrested within hours.

Hindenburg signed the decree on 28 February 1933, and Hitler, Interior Minister Wilhelm Frick and Justice Minister Franz Gürtner countersigned it. Its official title was the Decree of the Reich President for the Protection of People and State. Section 1 suspended articles of the Weimar Constitution protecting personal liberty, the home, the privacy of mail and telecommunications, freedom of expression and of the press, freedom of assembly and association, and property rights, 'until further notice'. Sections 2 and 3 empowered the Reich government to intervene in state governments that failed to restore public safety and order. Sections 4 and 5 set severe penalties for resisting the decree and extended the death penalty to several offences, including arson and sabotage.

The decree was applied at once. Thousands of Communists and Social Democrats were arrested, and opposition meetings and newspapers were banned. The heaviest early repression came in Prussia, where Hermann Göring controlled the largest police force in Germany, and on 3 March he instructed the police to use the decree first against Communists. Ernst Thälmann was detained, while Wilhelm Pieck and Walter Ulbricht escaped arrest.

The decree prepared the way for the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933, which passed with many Communist and Social Democratic deputies arrested, expelled or in hiding. Evans argued that the decree left the states no longer properly constituted, making the Act's passage irregular. The decree remained in force throughout the Third Reich and was never formally revoked by the regime. Its use later led the framers of the postwar Basic Law to curtail sharply the powers of the federal president.
reichswehr: After Germany's defeat in World War I the Imperial German Army was dissolved to be reshaped into a peacetime army. On 10 November 1918 Chancellor Friedrich Ebert and General Wilhelm Groener concluded the Ebert–Groener Pact. Groener assured Ebert of the armed forces' loyalty; Ebert promised action against leftist uprisings and that the military would keep its command within the professional officer corps and its traditional status as a state within a state, largely independent of civilian government.

A provisional Reichswehr was formed in March 1919. Under Part V of the Treaty of Versailles the army was limited to 100,000 professional soldiers and the navy to 15,000, with no general staff, no air force, no submarines or large warships, and no armoured vehicles or heavy weapons above set calibres. Officers had to serve 25 years and others 12, to prevent a pool of trained reservists. The official formation took place on 1 January 1921, once the limits had been met.

The Republic used the Reichswehr mainly against left-wing insurgents, such as the Spartacist uprising of 1919. In March 1920 its generals, among them Hans von Seeckt, advised against using troops against the Kapp Putsch, Seeckt reportedly saying that Reichswehr would not fire on Reichswehr. Seeckt took over army command and had the Communist and Nazi parties banned in 1923.

The leadership evaded the Versailles limits in secret. It sponsored the Black Reichswehr, civilian work groups of about 20,000 men, and from 1923 cooperated with the Soviet Union, training pilots at Lipetsk and tank specialists at Kazan. Philipp Scheidemann disclosed the cooperation to the Reichstag in December 1926. Seeckt resigned in October 1926 after inviting Crown Prince Wilhelm to manoeuvres in imperial uniform, and Kurt von Schleicher then gained power.

After Adolf Hitler became chancellor in January 1933 he promised the generals that the Reichswehr would remain the sole armed force. The Reichswehr supported him against the SA in 1934; in the Night of the Long Knives the SA's leadership and the generals Schleicher and Ferdinand von Bredow were murdered, and the officer corps acknowledged this without objection. The name ended with Hitler's 1935 proclamation of the restoration of military sovereignty, when it became part of the Wehrmacht.

The Reichswehr consisted of the Reichsheer, with seven infantry and three cavalry divisions in seven military districts, and the Reichsmarine, in two naval stations. The treaty allowed 4,000 army officers; the actual corps numbered 3,718, down from 227,081 in 1918. An average of 23.8 per cent of its officers were of noble origin, and most held a conservative, monarchist outlook. Recruits were preferred from rural areas, and its members could not vote.
reign-of-terror: Historians disagree about when the Terror began. Some give 10 March 1793, when the Revolutionary Tribunal was created, or 5 September 1793; others point to the September Massacres of 1792. France had declared war on 20 April 1792, and after the execution of Louis XVI the First Coalition, made up of Russia, Austria, Prussia, Spain, Holland and Sardinia, attacked from all sides. Albert Soboul wrote that terror, at first an improvised response to defeat, became an instrument of victory once it was organised.

Within France, the Federalist revolts and the rising in the Vendée, which began in March 1793 in response to mass conscription, added to the sense of emergency. The urban workers known as sans-culottes pressed the National Convention for harsh measures against opponents. Robespierre held that a republic needed virtue and that those who resisted it had to be removed.

On 6 April 1793 the Convention established the Committee of Public Safety, which gradually became the wartime government. On 2 June the sans-culottes surrounded the Convention, which arrested 29 Girondist leaders. Robespierre joined the Committee on 27 July. On 5 September Bertrand Barère proposed that terror be made the order of the day. The Law of Suspects of 17 September authorised the imprisonment of vaguely defined suspects and overfilled the prisons. Marie Antoinette was executed on 16 October and the Girondins on 31 October.

In the provinces, representatives on mission put down revolts: Joseph Fouché and Jean-Marie Collot d'Herbois at Lyon, Jean-Baptiste Carrier at Nantes, where he ordered drownings. In March 1794 the Hébertists were executed, and on 5 April the Dantonists, led by Georges Danton, who had called for clemency. The Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June, simplified procedure; the period that followed is called the Great Terror, and 1,366 people were executed between 10 June and 27 July.

The French victory at Fleurus on 26 June 1794 undermined the case for wartime measures. Robespierre was overthrown by men who wanted a more radical policy together with moderates who opposed the revolutionary government; the Law of 22 Prairial was one of the charges against him. He was arrested, wounded in the jaw in circumstances that remain unclear, and guillotined the next day with Saint-Just and Georges Couthon.

At least 300,000 suspects were arrested; some 17,000 were officially executed, and perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial. Jean-Clément Martin argues that the Convention never instituted a system of terror as such, while Albert Mathiez held that terror was a necessary reaction to circumstances.
reims: Before the Roman conquest of northern Gaul, Reims was the capital of the Remi tribe, founded about 80 BCE. In Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul the Remi allied themselves with the Romans and secured the special favour of the imperial power. Christianity was established there by 260, when Saint Sixtus of Reims founded the diocese. The Vandals captured the city in 406 and killed Bishop Nicasius, and in 451 Attila the Hun put it to fire and sword.

Remigius, bishop of Reims, baptised Clovis, King of the Salian Franks, with oil from a sacred phial said to have been brought from heaven by a dove. For centuries the monarchy used the event as a symbol of the divine right to rule. Archbishop Adalberon, with the monk Gerbert, later Pope Silvester II, founded schools in the 10th century that taught the liberal arts. The archbishops held the right to consecrate the kings of France, which they exercised, with few exceptions, from Philippe II Augustus, anointed in 1179, to Charles X, anointed in 1825.

In 1429 Joan of Arc had Charles VII consecrated in the cathedral. In the First World War German bombardment and fire in 1914 severely damaged the cathedral. On 7 May 1945 General Eisenhower and the Allies received the unconditional surrender of the German Wehrmacht at Reims, signed by General Alfred Jodl.

Reims is the most populous city of the department of Marne, 129 kilometres north-east of Paris on the Vesle river. Reims Cathedral, the adjacent Palace of Tau and the Abbey of Saint-Remi were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 1991. The Basilica of Saint-Remi is the largest Romanesque church in northern France. The city lies on the northern edge of the Champagne wine region, and many of the major champagne houses have their headquarters there.
reinforced-concrete: The early development of reinforced concrete took place in parallel in England and France in the mid-19th century. The French builder François Coignet was the first to use iron-reinforced concrete as a building technique. From 1853 he built for himself a four-storey house in the suburbs of Paris. His descriptions suggest that he reinforced the concrete not to add strength but to keep walls in monolithic construction from overturning.

In 1854 the English builder William B. Wilkinson reinforced the concrete roof and floors of a two-storey house he was building. The placing of his reinforcement showed that, unlike his predecessors, he understood tensile stresses. Between 1869 and 1870 Henry Eton designed, and Messrs W and T Phillips of London built, the wrought iron reinforced Homersfield Bridge, which has a span of 15.25 metres over the River Waveney between Norfolk and Suffolk.

Reinforced concrete is a composite material in which concrete's low tensile strength and ductility are compensated for by reinforcement of higher tensile strength, usually steel bars known as rebar. Concrete is a mixture of coarse and fine aggregates with a paste of binder, usually Portland cement, and water. Typical mixes resist compression well, at about 28 megapascals, but any appreciable tension, for instance from bending, breaks the rigid lattice and causes cracking.

Steel placed in the concrete takes the tension, so the composite resists compression, bending and other tensile actions and can be made into almost any shape. The two materials work together for three reasons: the steel bonds well to the hardened cement paste, their coefficients of thermal expansion are close, which avoids large internal stresses, and the concrete protects the embedded steel from corrosion and from softening at high temperature.

In prestressed concrete, the steel in the part of a beam that will be in tension in service is stretched before the concrete is poured around it. When the concrete has hardened and the tension is released, a built-in compressive force remains, and since the concrete is then always under compression it is less liable to crack.

Reinforced concrete can fail through inadequate strength or through loss of durability. Rust expands and flakes, cracking the concrete and unbonding the bar, and de-icing salts are probably one of the main causes of early failure of bridge decks and roadways. High alumina cement was banned in the UK in 1976 after three roofs of prestressed beams collapsed, though inquiries found the beams improperly made.
reinhard-heydrich: Reinhard Tristan Eugen Heydrich was born on 7 March 1904 in Halle an der Saale. His father, Richard Bruno Heydrich, was a composer and opera singer who founded the Halle Conservatory of Music, Theatre and Teaching, and his mother taught piano there. Heydrich was trained in music from an early age and kept up the violin into adulthood. In 1922 he joined the German Navy as a cadet at Kiel and became a first lieutenant in July 1928. His discharge from the navy took legal effect on 30 May 1931. He joined the Nazi Party in Hamburg that year, and the SS on 14 July 1931.

In 1931 Heinrich Himmler hired him to set up an intelligence service for the SS, and in mid-1932 Heydrich became chief of the Sicherheitsdienst (SD). On 22 April 1934 Himmler named him head of the Gestapo. With Himmler, Göring and others he drew up the lists of those to be killed in the purge of the SA on 30 June 1934, the Night of the Long Knives. In 1938 he coordinated the pogrom of Kristallnacht on 9–10 November by telegram to SD and Gestapo offices, authorising arson and the arrest of as many Jews as the detention facilities could hold. From September 1939 he led the Reich Security Main Office.

On 27 September 1941 he was appointed Deputy Reich Protector of Bohemia and Moravia, replacing the policies of Konstantin von Neurath. Heydrich proclaimed martial law, and 142 people were executed within five days of his arrival in Prague. In January 1942 he chaired the Wannsee Conference, which formalised plans for the deportation and murder of all Jews in German-occupied Europe.

The Czechoslovak government-in-exile in London resolved to kill him, and Jan Kubiš and Jozef Gabčík, trained by the British Special Operations Executive, parachuted into the Protectorate on 28 December 1941. Heydrich was ambushed in Prague and mortally wounded on 27 May 1942 in Operation Anthropoid, and died of sepsis on 4 June. German intelligence falsely linked the assassins to the villages of Lidice and Ležáky. Both villages were razed, the men and boys aged 14 and over were shot, and most of the women and children were deported and murdered in concentration camps. Hitler called Heydrich the man with the iron heart, and many historians regard him as one of the most sinister figures of the Nazi regime.
reinhard-keiser: Reinhard Keiser was born on 9 January 1674 in Teuchern, in present-day Saxony-Anhalt, the son of the organist and teacher Gottfried Keiser. He was taught by other organists in the town and from the age of eleven at the Thomasschule in Leipzig, where his teachers included Johann Schelle and Johann Kuhnau. In 1694 he became court composer to the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, whose court he had probably joined as early as 1692 to study its operas.

About 1697 Keiser settled in Hamburg and became chief composer of the Oper am Gänsemarkt, which he directed at times from 1702, his tenure often broken by political unrest. From 1703 to 1709 he turned the house from a public institution into a commercial venture with two or three performances a week. He introduced more varied arias and helped carry opera from the middle to the late Baroque. Early in 1704 the Hamburg season ended unexpectedly, and he went to Brunswick and Weissenfels, where his Almira was performed; he then answered Handel's Hamburg operas Nero and, later, Florindo and Daphne with works of his own, and in 1712 wrote his own passion music.

With the Hamburg Opera defunct in 1718, he left to seek work in Thuringia and Stuttgart. Between 1721 and 1727 he travelled back and forth between Hamburg and Copenhagen, receiving the title of Master of the Danish Royal Chapel, perhaps because Georg Philipp Telemann had been engaged in Hamburg in his absence. Relations between the two stayed good, and Telemann staged several of Keiser's operas.

In 1728 Keiser succeeded Johann Mattheson as precentor of St. Mary's Cathedral in Hamburg, and he wrote mostly church music there until his death on 12 September 1739. In an obituary Mattheson praised him above every other opera composer, and in 1745 Johann Adolf Scheibe ranked him with Kuhnau, Handel and Telemann, but his work was then largely forgotten for many decades. Besides his operas he wrote oratorios, among them a Brockes Passion of 1712.
reinheitsgebot: The Reinheitsgebot is a series of regulations limiting the ingredients of beer in Germany and the states of the former Holy Roman Empire, of which the Bavarian order of 1516 is the best known. Beer rules existed earlier, in Nuremberg in 1293, Erfurt in 1351 and Weißensee in 1434. The most influential predecessor was a law adopted in the Duchy of Bavaria-Munich in 1487, and after Bavaria was reunited the Munich law was adopted across the whole duchy on 23 April 1516.

The order was introduced partly to stop brewers competing with bakers for wheat and rye, so that bread stayed affordable. It may also have protected Bavarian brewers from northern beers that used additives, and it excluded plants allegedly used in pagan rituals, such as gruit, henbane and wormwood.

The 1516 law allowed only water, barley and hops in beer. It does not name yeast, although yeast was in use in brewing. It set the price of beer, which varied with the season, from Michaelmas to Georgi and from Georgi to Michaelmas, limited the profits of innkeepers, and made confiscation of the barrels the penalty for impure beer. Bavaria itself began to allow coriander, bay leaf and wheat in the mid-1500s, and the Degenberger family held an exclusive right from Duke William IV to brew wheat beer, so wheat beers became common in Bavaria.

For a long time the law applied only in Bavaria. Bavaria insisted on it as a condition of German unification in 1871, brewers elsewhere resisted, and an imperial law of 1873 taxed other ingredients in the north instead of banning them. It applied consistently across Germany only from 1906, and it was not formally called the Reinheitsgebot until the Weimar Republic. In 1952 its basic rules entered the West German Biersteuergesetz. In 1987 the European Court of Justice found in Commission v Germany that the law was protectionist as applied to imported beer. The Provisional Beer Law of 1993 replaced the earlier regulations, and a court ruling in 2005 turned the law into a labelling standard.

Some sources call the 1516 law the first food safety law, but such rules go back to ancient Rome. Others say it has stayed unchanged, though yeast was added to later versions. German brewers have used the Reinheitsgebot to market their beer abroad, and Norway adopted a similar law in 1912.
reinsurance-treaty: The Dreikaiserbund, the League of the Three Emperors of Germany, Austria and Russia, lapsed in 1887 because Austria-Hungary and Russia competed for spheres of influence in the Balkans. In early 1887 a Russian diplomat went to Berlin and proposed a treaty in which Russia would be a friendly neutral in a war between Germany and France, and Germany would recognise Russian dominance in Bulgaria. Bismarck strongly supported the idea. Alexander III rejected it until Foreign Minister Nikolay Girs convinced him it was best for Russia in the absence of French friendship. Bismarck's long-term policy was to preserve peace in Europe and keep France isolated, to avoid a two-front war against France and Russia.

The treaty, signed by Bismarck and Girs, was secret and known to only a handful of officials in Berlin and St Petersburg. It held that both parties would observe benevolent neutrality if either became involved in a war with a third great power, except if Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria-Hungary. Germany also agreed that Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia lay in the Russian sphere of influence, and would declare neutrality if Russia intervened over Ottoman control of the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. Bismarck refused Russia's request for German neutrality if Russia went to war against Austria, because Germany was in the Triple Alliance with Vienna.

After Wilhelm II removed Bismarck in 1890, Russia asked for a renewal, but Germany refused. The chancellor Leo von Caprivi saw no need to mollify Russia, and Count von Berchem of the Foreign Office wrote a memorandum against renewal, arguing that the treaty contradicted other German positions, including the Austro-Romanian Treaty of 1883. Russia, which had not wished to end the arrangement, then opened negotiations with France, and the Franco-Russian Alliance took shape. In 1896 the retired Bismarck revealed the treaty to a German newspaper and blamed Caprivi for the lapse.

Norman Rich writes that most historians hold the treaty itself to have been of little importance while in force, but its non-renewal a decisive turning point in Russia's movement toward France, and so one of the causes of the First World War. Sidney Fay agrees it was a turning point but argues that it was one of several factors pushing Russia and Germany apart, among them the German treaty with Britain in July 1890 and Russian Pan-Slavism.
relic-of-the-tooth-of-the-buddha: The Mahāparinibbāna Sutta records that four teeth of the Buddha remained after his death and cremation. Two of them it places in mythological realms, the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa and the realm of the Nagaraja, and two in earthly places, Gandhāra and Kaliṅga; of these, the Nagaraja tooth and the Kaliṅga tooth are held to survive. According to the Mahāvaṃsa and the Dāṭhavaṃsa, the left canine was taken from the cremation by the disciple Khema, who gave it to King Brahmadatte of Kaliṅga, and it was kept for veneration at Dantapura, the modern Dantapuram.

In time the relic gained the reputation of giving whoever held it the divine right to rule the land, and the Dāṭhavaṃsa tells of a war over its possession between Guhasiva of Kaliṅga and a king named Pandu. Legend says that after a conflict in Kaliṅga the tooth was brought to the Abhayagiri Vihāra in Anuradhapura. From then on it moved whenever the seat of government on the island moved, until it reached Kandy.

The Portuguese chroniclers João de Barros and Diogo do Couto give a different account of its later history. They write that a tooth relic, kept in the Jaffna Kingdom after Veediye Bandara, commander of the Kingdom of Kotte, was defeated at Nallur, was seized in 1560 during the Portuguese expedition against Jaffna and taken to Goa, where it was destroyed on the orders of the Viceroy, Constantino de Bragança. The historian Paulus Edward Pieris records that it was burnt and its remains thrown into the sea.

Tooth relics of the Buddha are claimed in many places besides Sri Lanka: a survey of 2024 found 32 museums and temples that said they held one or more. Among them are the Lingguang Temple in Beijing, the Buddha Memorial Center of the Fo Guang Shan Monastery in Kaohsiung, Engaku Temple in Kamakura, the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum in Singapore and the Lawkananda Pagoda in Bagan.
religious-pluralism: Religious pluralism is an attitude or policy regarding the diversity of religious belief systems that coexist in a society. It can mean recognising and tolerating that diversity, promoting freedom of religion, and treating the state as neutral on religion. It can also mean a form of inclusivism, in which one's own religion is not the sole source of truth, or the view that religions with mutually exclusive claims are equally valid. Perennialism holds that the exclusive claims of different religions are variations of universal truths. The term is sometimes used as a synonym for ecumenism, or for the harmonious coexistence of adherents of different religions.

Chris Beneke distinguishes pluralism from toleration. By the 1730s most American colonies had granted religious toleration, which relieved minorities of some penalties and burdens but did not make them equal, since they could still be barred from civil offices and university posts. Between the 1760s and the 1780s the colonial governments replaced it with what is usually called religious liberty.

The German philosophers Ludwig Feuerbach and Ernst Troeltsch concluded that Hinduism and Buddhism were the earliest proponents of religious pluralism. Jainism and Daoism have also long favoured it. In ancient Rome religion was part of daily life, with household shrines, neighbourhood shrines and a calendar of as many as 135 days of festivals and games in the imperial era. According to Chad Meister, pluralist trends in Western thought since the 18th century brought mainstream Christianity and Judaism closer to the Asian traditions of philosophical pluralism and tolerance.

In early Islamic history, Muhammad declared religious freedom for Muslims, Jews and pagans in the Constitution of Medina. The Islamic caliphate later guaranteed religious freedom to non-Muslim communities that accepted dhimmi status, with adult males paying the jizya tax in place of the zakat. Dhimmis did not have the same political rights as Muslims, but they enjoyed equality under the laws of property, contract and obligation.

Religious traditions answer pluralism in different ways. The Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches each claim to be the one true church, and most Christians consider the maximal form, that all religions are equally true, logically impossible, though the philosopher John Hick argues for a version of pluralism. Jainism's principle of anekantavada holds that reality is perceived differently from different points of view, so that no single view is the complete truth. The Sikh gurus taught many paths to one God.

The Bahá'í Faith teaches that religion has been revealed progressively through founders such as Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad. Voltaire's Candide of 1759 is among the places where the argument from inconsistent revelations appears: that revelations contradict one another, so that one cannot choose among them.
remaclus: Remaclus grew up at the Aquitanian ducal court and studied under Sulpitius the Pious, bishop of Bourges. In 625 he became a Benedictine monk at Luxeuil Abbey and was later ordained a priest. Around 631 Eligius founded Solignac Abbey and sent to Luxeuil for monks, among them Remaclus, who became its first abbot. Solignac followed the rule of Luxeuil, quickly gained importance according to Audoin, and became known for its silversmith's workshop.

Remaclus was later also given charge of the abbey of Cougnon in the duchy of Luxemburg. As an adviser to Sigebert III of Austrasia he persuaded the king to found the double monastery of Malmedy and Stavelot, which he governed as abbot. When Amandus, Bishop of Maastricht, resigned his see in 650 to return to missionary work, Remaclus was appointed in his place and brought with him Hadelin, the abbot of Visé.

Some of his predecessors in the troubled diocese had been murdered by its inhabitants, but Remaclus spread monasticism in the region and was the spiritual teacher of Trudo, Babolen, Theodard and Lambert. After twelve years as bishop he resigned in favour of Theodard, who also succeeded him as abbot, and retired to Stavelot around 662.

Remaclus died at Stavelot, where his relics lie in St. Sebastian Church; his feast day is 3 September. Popular legends tell of a wolf that accompanied him and of springs he found with his staff that were held to be healing waters. Churches dedicated to him stand mainly in the Eifel and Moselle regions of Germany and in the Belgian, Luxembourg and French Ardennes. The abbeys of Stavelot-Malmedy ceased to exist at the time of the French Revolution, and in 1950 St. Remaclus' Priory was founded at Wavreumont, between Stavelot and Malmedy.
rembrandt: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was born on 15 July 1606 in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic, the ninth child of Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn and Neeltgen Willemsdochter van Zuijtbrouck. The family was quite well-to-do: his father was a miller and his mother a baker's daughter. His mother was Catholic and his father belonged to the Dutch Reformed Church. As a boy he attended a Latin school and in 1620 enrolled at Leiden University, but he leaned towards painting and was soon apprenticed to Jacob van Swanenburg, with whom he spent three years. He then spent six months with the history painter Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam, and a few months with Jacob Pynas in 1625.

In 1625 Rembrandt opened a studio in Leiden, which he shared with his friend and colleague Jan Lievens. He began to accept students in 1627, among them Gerrit Dou and Isaac de Jouderville. In 1629 the statesman Constantijn Huygens discovered him and procured important commissions from the court at The Hague, and Prince Frederik Hendrik went on buying his paintings.

At the end of 1631 he moved to Amsterdam, a city rapidly expanding as a centre of business and trade, and practised as a professional portraitist for the first time, with great success. He first stayed with the art dealer Hendrick van Uylenburgh and in 1634 married Hendrick's cousin Saskia van Uylenburgh. That year he became a citizen of Amsterdam and a member of the local painters' guild. He ran a large workshop, and his pupils included Ferdinand Bol and Govert Flinck. His influence on painters around him was so great that it is hard to tell who worked in his studio and who only copied his style.

Unlike most Dutch painters of the 17th century, Rembrandt worked in a wide range of styles and subjects: portraits and self-portraits, landscapes, genre scenes, allegorical and historical scenes, biblical and mythological subjects and animal studies. He never went abroad, but was influenced by the Italian Old Masters and by Dutch and Flemish artists who had studied in Italy. His roughly 100 self-portraits, over 40 of them paintings, form an intimate autobiography. Among his best-known works are The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp (1632) and The Night Watch (1642). In 1633 he began signing with the spelling Rembrandt, adding a d to the Rembrant he had used before.

The size of his surviving output has been revised. Early in the 20th century connoisseurs credited him with well over 600 paintings, nearly 400 etchings and 2,000 drawings. The Rembrandt Research Project, begun in 1968, reassessed the attributions with technical methods, and recent scholarship puts his paintings nearer 300. His prints number slightly under 300.
remi: Their name comes from a Proto-Celtic form reconstructed as *reimos, first, prince or chief, related to Latin primus. Caesar, Pliny and Tacitus name them in Latin, and Strabo, Ptolemy and Cassius Dio in Greek. According to the archaeologist Jean-Louis Brunaux, large migrations in northern Gaul in the late 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE may mark the coming of the Belgae, but cremation reached the Aisne valley only around 200–150 BCE, so the Remi were probably not seen as fully part of the Belgae when Caesar arrived.

Their villages, such as Nizy-le-Comte, Thugny-Trugny and Acy-Romance, lay along natural routes, and in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE they built oppida at Bibrax, Nandin, Moulin à Vent, La Cheppe and Vieux Reims. Until 57 BCE they shared one law, one set of magistrates and one commander with the Suessiones, a union that probably favoured the Suessiones. In that year they defended Bibrax against the other Belgae at the Battle of the Axona, and Caesar sent Numidian, Cretan and Balearic troops to save it.

Under Rome they left sites badly placed in the new economy: Bibrax was abandoned in the mid-1st century BCE, while Moulin à Vent, on the road from Reims to Trier, grew into the town of Voncq. Durocortorum, whose name comes from the Gaulish duron, an enclosed or market town, became their capital at the end of the 1st century BCE. Flodoard of Reims, who died in 966, made Remus, brother of Romulus, their founder.

The densely settled Aisne valley was organised around trade with Mediterranean merchants, with large farms held by aristocrats and surrounded by hamlets, and a landed nobility grew rich from farming and mining. Their elite imported wine in large quantities and was influenced by Latin culture. Sanctuaries at La Soragne, Flavier and Nepellier held offerings of miniature or destroyed weapons, coins and Celtic sun crosses. In the Roman period Mars Camulus was probably their principal god.
remonstrants: Jacobus Arminius disagreed with Calvin above all on predestination and defended free examination over the doctrines of established churches. In 1610 his followers presented the Five Articles of Remonstrance to the States of Holland and Friesland, setting out their disagreements with the Calvinism of the Dutch Reformed Church. Their opponents, led by Franciscus Gomarus, became known as Gomarists or Counter-Remonstrants. Although the States General issued an edict tolerating both sides and forbidding further dispute, the quarrel merged with the political conflicts of the Dutch Republic.

Maurice of Orange turned his political power against the Remonstrants. Their chief ally, Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, was executed, other leaders were imprisoned, and city governments such as Amsterdam's were purged. The Synod of Dordrecht expelled thirteen Arminian pastors led by Simon Episcopius, confirmed the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, and had Remonstrant ministers deposed and some banished. An exile community formed in Antwerp in 1619, and from 1621 exiles settled in Schleswig, where they built the town of Friedrichstadt.

Episcopius wrote their Confession in 1621, and Jan Uytenbogaert gave them a catechism and a church order. After Maurice's death in 1625 some exiles returned, and from 1630 they could live anywhere in the Republic, though until the Batavian Republic of 1795 they could not build churches and met in house churches. Their seminary in Amsterdam trained Curcellaeus, Limborch, Wetstein and Le Clerc, and its theology grew more liberal and even rationalist.

In the mid-19th century the Remonstrant Brotherhood was shaped by Dutch liberal theology. Its chief congregation is in Rotterdam, and in 2016 it had about 5,000 members and friends in more than 40 congregations in the Netherlands, besides one in Friedrichstadt. In 1986 it became the first Christian denomination in Europe to allow the blessing of same-sex partnerships on an equal footing with marriage. Being non-creedal, it treats its confessions of 1621, 1940 and 2006 as without binding authority, and the wider Arminian current reached the Church of England and Methodism.
renaissance: Many scholars place the origin of the Renaissance in Florence at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries, with the writings of Dante Alighieri and Petrarch and the paintings of Giotto di Bondone. One proposed starting point is 1401, when Lorenzo Ghiberti and Filippo Brunelleschi competed for the contract for the bronze doors of the Baptistery of Florence Cathedral. Italy was divided into city-states and was one of the most urbanised areas of Europe, with many cities standing among Roman ruins.

Scholars have pointed to the Black Death of 1348 to 1350 and to the patronage of the Medici banking family, but no single factor fully explains why it began in Florence. Historians disagree on whether the Renaissance broke with the Middle Ages or extended them.

Renaissance humanism was less a philosophy than a method of learning. Humanists studied ancient texts in their original languages and appraised them with reasoning and empirical evidence, rather than resolving contradictions between authors as medieval scholastics did. Their education rested on the Studia Humanitatis: poetry, grammar, history, moral philosophy and rhetoric. In the 14th century scholars such as Petrarch and Poggio Bracciolini searched European libraries for Latin works by authors such as Cicero, Lucretius, Livy and Seneca. By the early 15th century a Greek phase was under way, recovering Greek literary, historical and theological texts.

In art, the Renaissance developed linear perspective. Giotto is credited with first treating a painting as a window into space, and Brunelleschi and Leon Battista Alberti formalised the technique. Printing with movable type, from a single shop in Mainz around 1440, had spread to around 270 cities and produced more than 20 million volumes by the end of the 15th century. Navigation also advanced: Columbus sailed in 1492 and the Magellan–Elcano expedition made the first circumnavigation between 1519 and 1522.

From Florence the Renaissance spread across Italy and by the 16th century through Europe, changing as it met local cultures. Albrecht Dürer and the printing press marked its arrival in Germany, Erasmus was the best-known humanist of the Netherlands, and the Elizabethan era is usually seen as the height of the English Renaissance. Many leading theologians, including Erasmus, Huldrych Zwingli, Thomas More, Martin Luther and John Calvin, followed the humanist method.

The artist and writer Giorgio Vasari first used the term rinascita in The Lives of the Artists (1550). The word Renaissance comes from French and was popularised by the historian Jules Michelet in 1855. The term has also been applied to earlier revivals, such as the Carolingian and Ottonian Renaissances and the Renaissance of the 12th century.
renaud-de-dammartin: Renaud, or Reginald, was the eldest son of Alberic III of Dammartin and Matilda of Clermont. Brought up at the French court, he was a childhood friend of Philip Augustus, but at his father's insistence he fought for the Plantagenets.
