Received back into Philip's favour, he married Marie of Châtillon, daughter of Guy II of Châtillon and Adèle of Dreux, a royal cousin.

In 1191 his father kidnapped Ida, Countess of Boulogne, and had Renaud marry her, so that the county became a vassal of the French king rather than of the count of Flanders. The marriage made him a power but also made him enemies in the Dreux family and in that of the count of Guînes, who had been betrothed to Ida. In 1203 he and Ida gave Boulogne a merchants' charter, probably for payment. Philip made him count of Aumale in 1204 and, after taking Normandy, granted him Mortain and the honour of Warenne, centred on Mortemer and Bellencombre.

Renaud nonetheless drew away from the king. In 1211 he refused to appear before Philip in a suit with Philippe de Dreux, bishop of Beauvais, and Philip seized his lands. On 4 May 1212 at Lambeth he made an agreement with King John of England, who gave him fiefs in England and an annuity, and he drew other nobles, among them the count of Flanders, into the coalition against Philip; each promised not to make a separate peace with France.

In 1214 he joined Emperor Otto IV and Count Ferdinand of Flanders in the attack on France that ended at the Battle of Bouvines, where he commanded the Brabançons. He was one of the last to surrender and refused to submit to Philip. His lands went to the king's illegitimate son Philip Hurepel, who married Renaud's daughter Matilda II. Held at Péronne for the rest of his life, he was chained to a heavy log, as the historian Jim Bradbury describes, and lost hope when Ferdinand was released. His life ended in suicide.
renault: The company was founded on 25 February 1899 as Société Renault Frères by Louis Renault and his brothers Marcel and Fernand. Louis, a young engineer, had already designed and built several prototypes. He handled design and production, while Marcel and Fernand, who had gained their business skills in their father's textile firm, managed the business. The first Renault car, the Voiturette 1CV, was sold to a friend of Louis' father after a test ride on 24 December 1898. Louis also invented a direct drive gear with no drive belt, which gave much better performance uphill. Marcel Renault's racing interests took the firm into motor sport early: he won the 1902 Paris-Vienna rally but lost his life in the Paris-Madrid rally of 1903.

After 1918 Louis Renault widened the firm's scope to agricultural and industrial machinery. The war of 1914 to 1918 had led to many new products, and the first Renault tractor, the Type GP, built from 1919 to 1930, was based on the FT tank. The company struggled to compete with increasingly popular small, affordable cars, and in 1920 Louis signed one of its first distribution contracts with Gustave Gueudet of Amiens.

After the French capitulation in 1940 German forces took control of the Renault factories. On 3 March 1942 the Royal Air Force sent 235 low-level bombers against the plant on the Île Seguin at Billancourt, the largest number aimed at a single target during the war; 460 metric tons of bombs fell on the plant and its surroundings, with heavy civilian casualties. American bombing followed on 4 April 1943, and the plant was hit again in September of that year. Under Pierre Lefaucheux after the war the company recovered commercially but met labour unrest that continued into the 1980s.

The Renault 5 of January 1972 anticipated the energy crisis of 1973, and the Espace of 1984 was Europe's first multi-purpose vehicle. In 1984 the company was losing a billion francs a month, and the government installed Georges Besse as chairman; he sold non-core assets and cut staff, but was murdered by the group Action Directe in November 1986. His successor Raymond Lévy sold American Motors to Chrysler in 1987. The state-owned company was privatised in 1996.

Renault has been prominent in motor sport. It won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1978 with the Alpine A442 and introduced the turbo engine to Formula One with the RS01 at Silverstone in 1977. Its early work on mathematical curve modelling for car bodies is significant in the history of computer graphics. It is headquartered at Boulogne-Billancourt, near Paris, and has belonged to an alliance with Nissan since 1999.
rendlesham: Rendlesham is a village and civil parish near Woodbridge in Suffolk. Its name is recorded in Old English about 730 as Rendlæsham, which may mean the homestead of a man named Rendel, or may come from a supposed Old English word rendel, little shore. The archaeological project there has identified a settlement covering more than 124 acres (50 hectares).

Rendlesham was a royal centre of authority for the kings of the East Angles, and the nearness of the Sutton Hoo ship burial may point to a link between that cemetery and the East Anglian royal house, the Wuffingas. Some scholars have suggested Rendlesham as the place where the Old English epic Beowulf was first composed and performed.

King Swithhelm of Essex, son of Seaxbald, who reigned from 660 to around 664, was baptised at Rendlesham by Bishop Cedd, with King Æthelwold of East Anglia, who reigned from about 654 to 664, as his godfather. Swithhelm died around the time of the great plague of 664 and may have been buried at the palace there.

The Church of St Gregory the Great is a Grade I listed medieval church, while Rendlesham Hall, a large manor house, was demolished in 1949. Rendlesham Forest, owned by Forestry England, is a mixed woodland of 1,500 hectares and part of the Sandlings Forest Site of Special Scientific Interest. The Rendlesham Forest incident of December 1980 was a series of reported sightings of unexplained pulsing lights off the coast of Orford Ness. The village lies in the East Suffolk electoral ward of Rendlesham and Orford; the former Rendlesham ward, which included Campsea Ashe, had 3,388 people at the census of 2011.
rene-barrientos: René Emilio Barrientos Ortuño was born on 30 May 1919 in Tarata, in the department of Cochabamba, to a father of Spanish ancestry and a Quechua mother. After his father died he was sent to a Franciscan orphanage, which he left at 12 to attend a private high school while working odd jobs. He graduated from the military academy in La Paz in 1943 and earned his pilot's licence in 1945. He drew towards the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement of Víctor Paz Estenssoro, took part in the Bolivian National Revolution of 1952, and was named commander of the Bolivian Air Force in 1957.

Paz Estenssoro had the constitution amended so that he could be re-elected, and chose Barrientos as his running mate. They were sworn in on 6 August 1964. Three months later Barrientos and the army commander Alfredo Ovando overthrew Paz in a coup and ruled as co-presidents of a junta. Barrientos resigned in early 1966, stood in the July election with the main civilian leaders in exile, and was sworn in as president in August 1966. He spoke Quechua fluently, courted the church, was anti-communist and pro-free market, and accepted US military aid and the training of special forces under the Alliance for Progress.

In 1967 a guerrilla force under Ernesto "Che" Guevara was found in the south-east. When the miners of Siglo XX declared support for the insurgents, Barrientos sent troops, and soldiers fired on the miners on 24 June 1967, killing around 30 men and women in what is called the San Juan massacre. Bolivian Army Rangers captured Guevara and executed him in October 1967 on Barrientos's direct order. In 1968 his interior minister, Antonio Arguedas, disappeared with Guevara's captured diary, which surfaced in Havana, and he denounced Barrientos and aides as paid by the CIA.

Some saw Barrientos as a brutal dictator serving foreign interests, and he travelled the country to repair his relations with the campesinos. On 27 April 1969 the Air Force helicopter carrying him struck telephone cables near Arque and killed him, his aide-de-camp and the pilot. An assassination has been considered possible but has never been proven.
rene-descartes: René Descartes was born in La Haye en Touraine, in the Province of Touraine, on 31 March 1596. His mother, Jeanne Brochard, died in May 1597, a few days after giving birth to a stillborn child, and he lived with his grandmother and great-uncle. His father, Joachim, was a member of the Parlement of Rennes. In 1607, late because of his fragile health, he entered the Jesuit College of La Flèche, where he was introduced to mathematics and physics. He then studied at the University of Poitiers and took a degree in canon and civil law in 1616, as his father wished.

His Discourse on the Method of 1637 introduced essays on optics, meteorology and geometry. The Meditations on First Philosophy followed in 1641, and the Principles of Philosophy, a Latin textbook meant to replace the Aristotelian ones used in universities, in 1644. The Discourse appeared in a single edition of 500 copies, and the French edition of the Meditations had not sold out by his death, but a Latin edition of the Meditations was a commercial success. He died on 11 February 1650.

Descartes used hyperbolic doubt: he rejected any idea that could be doubted, then tried to rebuild knowledge on a firm foundation. The first principle he reached was that he thinks, expressed as cogito, ergo sum, or I think, therefore I am. Since doubting needs a doubter, the fact of doubt proved his existence. He concluded that perceiving his body through the senses was unreliable evidence, and that the only indubitable knowledge was that he is a thinking thing.

In mathematics he and Pierre de Fermat developed analytic geometry, which uses algebra to describe geometry; the Cartesian coordinate system is named after him. He is credited with representing unknowns by x, y and z and with using superscripts for powers. In his Principles he stated three laws of motion and claimed that the total quantity of motion in the universe is conserved, and Isaac Newton's laws were later modelled on his exposition. By shifting the question from what is true to what he could be certain of, he is often called the father of modern Western philosophy.
rene-ii-duke-of-lorraine: René II was born at Angers on 2 May 1451, the son of Yolande of Lorraine and Frederick, Count of Vaudémont. He spent his youth at the court of his grandfather René I of Anjou, between Angers and Provence. He succeeded his father as count of Vaudémont in 1470, and in 1473 he succeeded his cousin Nicholas as duke of Lorraine, being both heir-general and heir-male of the duchy. Lorraine was then under pressure from Louis XI of France and Charles the Bold of Burgundy, with whom René first allied. When Charles began to garrison Lorraine, René secretly allied with Louis in 1474.

Charles invaded and forced René to leave Nancy on 30 November 1475. René regained the city on 5 October 1476, went to Switzerland to hire an army of Swiss mercenaries and killed Charles at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477, ending the Burgundian Wars. His alliance with Louis XI did not last, as Louis moved to acquire René's lands.

In 1478 Louis transferred to him his rights to Luxembourg and the County of Burgundy as compensation for the seizure of Anjou and Provence, but these came to little. René conquered the prévôté of Virton in 1482 and annexed it to Bar. In 1482 he also went to Italy and defeated the Duke of Ferrara at the Battle of Adria as an ally of Venice.

After his mother Yolande died in 1483, René inherited her claims to the kingdoms of Naples and Jerusalem. The Neapolitans offered him the crown in 1488, but Charles VIII of France halted his expedition, intending to claim Naples himself. In 1495 he settled a dispute with Jean IV de Rieux by ceding him Harcourt and receiving Aumale. He married Philippa of Guelders at Orléans on 1 September 1485, and their sons included Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, and Claude, first Duke of Guise. René fell ill during a hunt at Fains and died on 10 December 1508, aged 57.
rene-magritte: René François Ghislain Magritte was born on 21 November 1898 in Lessines, in the province of Hainaut, the oldest son of Léopold Magritte, a tailor and textile merchant, and Régina, a milliner before her marriage. Little is known of his early life. He began drawing lessons in 1910. On 24 February 1912 his mother drowned herself in the River Sambre at Châtelet, after an earlier attempt. Some writers have linked the image of her dress covering her face to paintings of 1927–28 showing people with cloth over their faces, such as Les Amants.

His earliest paintings, from about 1915, were Impressionistic. He studied at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels in 1916–18 but found the teaching uninspiring. In 1922 he married Georgette Berger and saw a reproduction of Giorgio de Chirico's The Song of Love, which moved him to tears. He worked as a poster designer until a contract with Galerie Le Centaure in Brussels let him paint full-time in 1926, the year of his first surreal painting, The Lost Jockey.

His first solo exhibition, in Brussels in 1927, was poorly reviewed, and he moved to Paris, where he befriended André Breton and joined the Surrealist group. In 1930 he returned to Brussels and went back to advertising with his brother Paul. He stayed in Brussels during the German occupation, which led to a break with Breton. In 1946 he signed the manifesto Surrealism in Full Sunlight. During the lean postwar years he produced fake works by Picasso, Braque and de Chirico, and at the end of 1948 returned to his prewar style.

Magritte showed ordinary objects in unfamiliar settings, giving new meanings to familiar things. The Treachery of Images shows a pipe above the words Ceci n'est pas une pipe; asked about it, he replied that it was not a pipe, since one could not fill it with tobacco. He often painted rocks floating in the sky. His surrealism was more representational than the automatic style of Joan Miró, and he said that his paintings were visible images that conceal nothing.

Popular interest rose in the 1960s, and he influenced pop, minimalist and conceptual art, although he rejected the connection with pop art. He died of pancreatic cancer on 15 August 1967, aged 68. The Magritte Museum opened in Brussels on 30 May 2009.
rene-of-anjou: René was born on 16 January 1409 in the castle of Angers, the second son of Duke Louis II of Anjou and Yolanda of Aragon. His sister Marie married the future Charles VII of France. In 1419, when he was ten, he was legally married to Isabella, elder daughter of Charles II, Duke of Lorraine, and he was brought up in Lorraine.

He joined the French army at Reims in 1429 and was present at the consecration of Charles VII. He inherited the duchy of Bar in 1430 and that of Lorraine in 1431, but the heir-male Antoine de Vaudemont, with Burgundian help, defeated him at Bulgneville in July 1431, and he was a prisoner of the Burgundians until 1432. On the death of his brother Louis III in 1435 he became Duke of Anjou.

Joanna II, queen of Naples, offered René her kingdom, and he sailed for Naples in 1438. Alfonso V of Aragon also claimed it and laid a six-month siege to the city in 1441. René returned to France in 1442, keeping the title of king of Naples but never recovering effective rule. In 1444 he took part in the negotiations with the English at Tours, and his younger daughter Margaret married Henry VI of England at Nancy. After his second marriage, to Jeanne de Laval, he took a less active part in public affairs and turned to poetry, miniature painting, gardening and raising animals.

He patronised the painter Barthélemy d'Eyck and wrote two allegorical works, Le Mortifiement de vaine plaisance and Le Livre du Cuer d'amours espris, and a tournament book describing the rules of a tournament. He founded the Ordre du Croissant, which did not survive him. His house declined in his old age. His son John died at Barcelona in 1470, and his daughter Margaret was defeated in the Wars of the Roses in 1471 and ransomed by Louis XI in 1476.

René retired to Aix-en-Provence and made a will in 1474 leaving Bar to his grandson René II of Lorraine and Anjou and Provence to his nephew Charles, count of Le Maine. Louis XI seized Anjou and Bar, and the duchy of Anjou lapsed to the crown, while the annexation of Provence was postponed until the death of Charles of Le Maine. René died on 10 July 1480 at Aix and was buried in Angers Cathedral. Nineteenth-century historians gave him the epithet the Good.
rene-of-chalon: René, also known as Renatus of Chalon, was born in Breda, the only son of Count Henry III of Nassau-Breda and Claudia of Chalon. Claudia's brother Philibert of Chalon was the last Prince of Orange from the House of Chalon, and when Philibert died in 1530, René inherited the principality on condition that he used the name and coat of arms of the Chalon-Orange family. For this reason he is known as René of Chalon rather than René of Nassau-Breda.

Besides ruling Orange, he was stadtholder of Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and Gelre. On 20 August 1540 he married Anna of Lorraine at Bar-le-Duc, and in the same year he was made a knight of the Golden Fleece. The couple's only child, a daughter named Maria, lived only three weeks and was buried in the Grote Kerk in Breda.

In 1544 René took part in the siege of St. Dizier in the service of Emperor Charles V. He was mortally wounded in the fighting and died on 15 July 1544 with the emperor at his bedside. He was buried in the Grote Kerk at Breda near his daughter, and a commemorative monument, the Cadaver Tomb of René of Chalon, stands in the church of St. Etienne in Bar-le-Duc.

Having no surviving children, he left all his lands, the principality included, to his paternal cousin William of Nassau-Dillenburg, on the single condition that William receive a Catholic education. William's father agreed on behalf of his son, who was still a minor, and the emperor, overlord of most of René's possessions, endorsed the succession. William the Silent added the name of Orange to his own and so became in 1544 the founder of the House of Orange-Nassau, although he was not descended from any of the families that had held Orange before.
rene-robert-cavelier-sieur-de-la-salle: Robert Cavelier was born on 22 November 1643 into a comfortably well-off family in Rouen. He studied with the Jesuits and took initial vows in 1660, which required him to give up his father's legacy, so he was nearly destitute when he sailed for New France in the spring of 1666. On 27 March 1667 he was released from the Society of Jesus, citing moral weaknesses. He then received a seigneurie at the western end of the Island of Montreal, which became known as Lachine. The title Sieur de La Salle came from a family estate near Rouen, and he took it with his purchase of Lachine from the Sulpician order around 1667.

His first expedition, which left Lachine on 6 July 1669, was meant to find a river the Seneca had described, the Ohio, as a western passage to China. The factual record of it ends in obscurity, and La Salle himself never claimed to have discovered the Ohio. In 1673 he was left in command of the fort at Cataraqui, later Fort Frontenac, built to control the fur trade of the Great Lakes, and he secured the fort's grant and letters of nobility during a voyage to France in 1674–75.

In December 1678 he and Henri de Tonti were the first Europeans documented to have seen Niagara Falls. The ship Le Griffon, launched on 7 August 1679, vanished on its return from Green Bay with a load of furs.

In January 1680 La Salle and Tonti built Fort Crèvecoeur on the Illinois River, and soldiers there mutinied and destroyed it while he was away. He reached the Mississippi in February 1682, and on 9 April 1682 he claimed the river's basin for France, naming it La Louisiane in honour of Louis XIV.

On 24 July 1684 La Salle left France with four ships and 300 colonists to found a colony at the mouth of the Mississippi. Pirates took one ship, another sank, and the flagship La Belle ran aground, stranding the colony on the Texas coast on Garcitas Creek. After several attempts on foot to find the river, he was killed on 19 March 1687 by Pierre Duhaut in an ambush, after some of his men had mutinied.

The colony lasted until 1688, when Karankawa-speaking people killed the 20 remaining adults and took five children captive. Only 15 of the original 180 colonists at the fort are known to have survived. La Salle's alliances with the Illinois and other peoples cemented the French policy of containing both Iroquois influence and Anglo-American colonisation. La Belle was found in Matagorda Bay in 1995.
rennes: Rennes lies in the east of Brittany, in northwestern France, at the confluence of the rivers Ille and Vilaine. The ancient centre is built on a hill, with the north side higher than the south. The city is about 50 km from the English Channel, near Saint-Malo, Dinard and Mont Saint-Michel, and has an oceanic climate with much less rain than western Brittany. A protected green belt lies between the dense city and the rural parts of its urban area.

Rennes goes back more than 2,000 years, to a small Gallic village named Condate. Together with Vannes and Nantes it was one of the major cities of the old Duchy of Brittany. From the early 16th century until the French Revolution it was the parliamentary, administrative and garrison city of the province of Brittany within the Kingdom of France, as its 17th-century Parlement de Bretagne shows. The city played an important role in the Stamped Paper Revolt of 1675.

Its ramparts were built between the 3rd and the 12th centuries and were largely destroyed between the early 16th century and the 1860s. In 1720 a great fire destroyed most of the timber-framed houses in the northern part of the city. The north was rebuilt in stone on a grid plan, while the poorer southern part was not. Because the Parlement sat there, many hôtels particuliers were built in the richer northern half in the 18th century.

Rennes remained mostly rural until the Second World War. From the 1950s it grew through migration from the countryside and modern industry, partly in the automotive sector, and in the 1980s it became a centre of telecommunications and high-tech industry.

Rennes is the prefecture of the Brittany region and of the Ille-et-Vilaine department, with 230,890 inhabitants in 2023. It is labelled a city of art and history, with over 90 buildings protected as historic monuments. The Parlement de Bretagne, its main 17th-century building, was rebuilt after a fire in 1994 and houses the Rennes Court of Appeal. Colourful half-timbered houses survive along streets such as Saint-Georges and Saint-Michel, and the weekly Marché des Lices is one of the largest markets in France.
rennes-cathedral: A cathedral has stood on the site more or less since the see was founded in the 6th century. The first building was replaced in the 12th century by a Gothic cathedral, whose tower and entire west front collapsed in 1490. The present façade, with its neoclassical granite towers in four stages, took about two centuries to build, with long pauses: the lowest level dates from 1541 to 1543, the second from 1640 to 1654 under Tugal Caris, and the fourth from 1654 to 1678 under Pierre Corbineau. François Hoguet completed the towers between 1679 and 1704 at their present height of 48 metres.

It was in this cathedral, on 25 December 1483, that Henry Tudor, the future Henry VII of England, then in exile in Brittany, promised to marry Elizabeth of York in order to rally the army that had stayed loyal to the late Edward IV. Their marriage in 1486 sealed the end of the Wars of the Roses.

The nave and choir had never been restored. During vespers on 11 February 1754 a great stone fell from the choir roof, and it was decided to demolish both before the whole body of the church fell. The demolition, carried out between 1756 and 1768, left only the towers and west front. Rebuilding began in 1787 but was suspended during the French Revolution and resumed only in 1816 under Mathurin Crucy; after his death in 1826 the local architect Louis Richelot carried it on. While the cathedral was unusable, from 1803 the abbey church of Notre-Dame-en-Saint-Melaine, named after Saint Melaine, traditionally the first bishop of Rennes, served as a pro-cathedral.

The interior was first decorated in a plain neoclassical style, but during the 19th century it was refurbished with gilding, stucco and paintings inspired by those of the Parliament of Rennes. The rich decoration, which includes slabs of rare marble from the Roman Forum before the altar, a gift of Pope Pius IX, contrasts with the sombre granite of the structure. The cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Rennes, Dol and Saint-Malo, and has been a monument historique since 1906.
rennyo: Rennyo, a descendant of Shinran, was born as Hoteimaru and later named Kenju. He was the son of Zonnyō, who became the seventh head of the Hongan-ji, and was born out of wedlock when his father was 18. His mother, a servant whose name is not known, was sent away when he was six, and he tried several times in later life to find her. As the eldest son he assisted his father in temple duties. After Zonnyō died in 1457, his stepmother Nyoen tried to have her own son Ogen made successor, but Rennyo's uncle Nyojō set the idea aside.

Rennyo first preached in Ōmi Province, where the wealthy Katada congregation and artisan followers gave funds and protection. In 1465 warrior monks of the Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei destroyed most of the Hongan-ji on charges of heresy, probably moved as much by their economic interests in Ōmi. The congregations raised money and men, the attackers were bribed away, and the Hongan-ji had to become a branch temple of Mount Hiei and pay yearly dues.

In 1471 he set up a new centre at Yoshizaki in Echizen Province, where a town grew up around the temple and hundreds of lodges housed the pilgrims. There he moved from preaching tours to pastoral letters, and he sat with the lowborn at gatherings rather than on raised platforms. Village congregations called kō, meeting once or twice a month, formed the base of the organisation. When the situation in Hokuriku became too unsettled he returned to the Kyoto area in 1475. He married five times and had twenty-seven children.

Rennyo held that he was restoring Shinran's original teaching. The historian James C. Dobbins judged that his chief accomplishment was to turn Shinran's abstractions into simple formulas for the humblest believer. His short creed, the Ryōgemon, is still recited, and his letters, called Gobunshō or Ofumi, are used in daily liturgy; the Letter on White Ashes is often read at funerals. Scholars of the sect debate his legacy: some credit him with giving the movement structure, others hold that institutionalisation departed from its original egalitarianism.
republic-of-new-granada: The Republic of New Granada was a centralist unitary republic that existed from 1831 to 1858. It consisted mainly of present-day Colombia and Panama, with smaller portions of today's Costa Rica, Ecuador, Venezuela, Peru and Brazil. It was created after Gran Colombia dissolved in 1830 through the secession of Ecuador and Venezuela. Its national flag, in the Gran Colombian colours, was adopted on 9 May 1834 and used until 26 November 1861, while the merchant ensign carried an eight-pointed white star. The territory was divided into provinces, each made up of cantons and districts, and from 1855 to 1857 seven states were created out of the provinces.

The republic's history was marked by competing economic and political interests and by civil wars, chiefly over the position of the Roman Catholic Church and the autonomy of the regions. In 1839 the Congress dissolved some monasteries, a dispute that grew into the War of the Supremes, which lasted two years and became a conflict over regional autonomy and a border conflict with Ecuador. Panama tried unsuccessfully to break away in 1840 and 1850.

In 1851 a civil war followed the Liberal reforms of President José Hilario López: the emancipation of slaves, the expulsion of the Jesuits, freedom of the press and the abolition of the death penalty. Conservative and pro-slavery groups from Cauca and Antioquia, led by Julio Arboleda, Manuel Ibánez and Eusebio Borrero, rose against him. A Liberal constitutional reform came in 1853 under José María Obando. In April 1854 General José María Melo overthrew Obando and proclaimed himself dictator, and another civil war ended with Melo's ouster.

A federal constitution was introduced in 1858, and the state was renamed the Granadine Confederation. In 1860 General Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera rose and began a civil war that lasted until 1862. After he captured Bogotá in 1861 and proclaimed himself president, the country received a new constitution, in answer to demands for decentralised administration.
republic-of-serbian-krajina: The name Krajina, meaning frontier, came from the Military Frontier that the Habsburg monarchy carved out of Croatia and Slavonia between 1553 and 1578 against the Ottoman Empire. In the 1991 census Serbs made up about 12.2 per cent of the population of Croatia. After Franjo Tuđman was elected president of Croatia in April 1990, the Serb Democratic Party of Jovan Rašković broke with the Croatian parliament. In August 1990 Serbs blocked roads with logs in what became known as the Log Revolution, cutting Dalmatia off from the rest of the country, and a referendum confined to Serbs backed Serb sovereignty and autonomy by 99.7 per cent.

The Croatian constitution of December 1990 reduced the Serbs from a constituent people to a national minority. On 21 December 1990 the administration of Milan Babić announced a Serbian Autonomous Oblast of Krajina, which on 1 April 1991 declared that it would secede from Croatia.

Wider war began in August 1991. Between August and December approximately 80,000 Croats were expelled and some were killed; estimates of all exiled Croats and other non-Serbs range from 170,000, the figure of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, to a quarter of a million, that of Human Rights Watch. On 19 December 1991 the autonomous oblasts of Krajina and Western Slavonia proclaimed the republic, and that of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia was added on 26 February 1992.

The Vance plan and the Sarajevo Agreement of January 1992 established four United Nations Protected Areas and froze the front lines for three years. Refugees were not allowed to return. Babić, who opposed the plan, was replaced as president on 26 February 1992 by Goran Hadžić; Milan Martić won the presidency in January 1994. The economy depended wholly on the rump Yugoslavia: by 1994 only 36,000 of 430,000 citizens were employed. Croatian forces took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995.

In Operation Storm between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled, and only 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, remained; some who refused to leave were murdered, tortured or expelled by the Croatian army and police. The remaining territory in eastern Slavonia was placed under a United Nations transitional authority by the Erdut Agreement and returned to Croatia in 1998.

The tribunal sentenced Babić, who pleaded guilty, to 13 years in 2004 and Milan Martić to 35 years in 2007. The Croatian generals Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač were convicted in April 2011 of crimes during Operation Storm and acquitted on appeal in November 2012.
republic-of-the-congo: The Republic of the Congo lies on the western coast of Central Africa, west of the Congo River, along the Equator. It is bounded by Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda, and has 170 kilometres of beaches on the Atlantic. The southwest is a coastal plain drained by the Kouilou-Niari River, and the interior is a central plateau between two basins. The climate is consistent year-round, with a dry season from June to August.

The country is named after the Congo River, whose name derives from Kongo, a Bantu kingdom at its mouth around the time the Portuguese first arrived in 1483 or 1484. It is a distinct country from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its capital, Brazzaville, is named for the colony's founder, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazzà. Under France it was known as the French Congo or Middle Congo.

Bantu-speaking peoples mostly displaced and absorbed the earlier inhabitants, the Pygmy peoples, about 1500 BCE. By the 13th century there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin: the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza in the east, Mpemba to its south, and a confederation of Vungu, Kakongo and Ngoyo to the west across the Congo River. The Tio Kingdom formed in the 14th century. The association of kingship with smithing is believed to have originated among the Tio before spreading to Loango and Kongo.

The Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo in 1484, and trade grew between the inland kingdoms and European merchants, who dealt in commodities, manufactured goods and enslaved people. The area north of the river came under French sovereignty in 1880 through Pierre de Brazza's treaty with the Tio king Iloo I, and Iloo's widow, Queen Ngalifourou, upheld its terms. In 1908 France organised French Equatorial Africa, with Brazzaville as federal capital. The Congo–Ocean Railway, built after the First World War, has been estimated to have cost at least 14,000 lives.

The Republic of the Congo became independent from France in 1960 and was a Marxist–Leninist state under the name People's Republic of the Congo from 1969 into the early 1990s. Its capital is Brazzaville. French is the official language, with Kituba and Lingala as national languages, and the Kongo are the largest ethnic group, roughly half of the population. Most of the population lives in the southwest, in Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and the towns along the railway that joins them.
republican-party-united-states: The Republican Party began in 1854 as an anti-slavery party, formed to oppose the expansion of slavery into the western territories after the Democrats under Stephan Douglas passed the Kansas-Nebraska Act. It was formed in the Northern and Border states but not in the South, and it rapidly gained support in the North, drawing in former Whigs, Free Soil Democrats and former Know Nothings. It emerged as the main rival of the Democratic Party, and the two have dominated American politics since.

The founders chose the name in homage to the republican values of the Democratic-Republican Party that Thomas Jefferson had called the Republican Party. The idea came from an editorial by the party's leading publicist, Horace Greeley, who asked for a simple name like Republican to designate those who had united to restore the Union to its true mission as champion of liberty.

Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860 led to the secession of Southern states and the outbreak of the American Civil War. Under Lincoln and a Republican-controlled Congress the party led the effort to preserve the Union, defeat the Confederacy and abolish slavery. By 1865 it encompassed northern Protestants, factory workers, professionals, businessmen, prosperous farmers and black former slaves. Radical Republicans, hard-line abolitionists, pressed for abolition as a war aim and clashed with Lincoln's moderate Reconstruction plans. During Reconstruction the party sought to extend civil rights protections to freedmen, and by the late 1870s it turned its attention to business interests and industrial expansion.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it dominated national politics, promoting protective tariffs and infrastructure development. In the 20th century it split between an Old Right and a moderate faction in the Northeast, and opposition to Roosevelt's New Deal produced the conservative coalition. After the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Southern states became more reliably Republican in presidential elections. The party won five of the six presidential elections from 1968 to 1988, and Ronald Reagan, in office from 1981 to 1989, was a transformative leader.

The nickname Grand Old Party originated in 1875 in the Congressional Record, which referred to the party of the Union's military defence as this gallant old party. The following year the Cincinnati Commercial used the phrase grand old party, and the abbreviation GOP is first recorded in 1884. Nineteen Republicans have served as president, the most from any single party.
republican-peoples-party: The party has its origins in the Defence of Rights Associations, the resistance organisations created in the Turkish War of Independence after the First World War. At the Sivas Congress, Mustafa Kemal Pasha and his colleagues united them into the Association for the Defence of National Rights of Anatolia and Rumelia. Most of its members had earlier been Young Turks associated with the Committee of Union and Progress. The party counts the Sivas Congress as its first party congress. It was founded as the People's Party in 1923 and took the prefix Republican shortly after the proclamation of the Republic.

In 1924 a right-wing opposition led by Kâzım Karabekir, reacting against the abolition of the Caliphate, formed the Progressive Republican Party. It was accused of involvement in the Sheikh Said rebellion and of conspiring to assassinate Atatürk. Martial law was declared, every party but the CHP was banned and Karabekir's supporters were purged from government. Republican Turkey became the third one-party state of interwar Europe, after the Soviet Union and Fascist Italy. After the Second World War İsmet İnönü allowed multi-party elections. The CHP lost in 1950 and stayed in opposition for ten years, during which it began a long shift towards social democracy.

Under Bülent Ecevit, chairman from 1972, the party took a left-wing course, and in 1977 it won 41 per cent of the vote, its best result in a free multi-party election, but not a majority. Political violence and partisan deadlock ended in the military coup of 1980, which banned every party. The name CHP was banned until 1987. Successor parties formed, among them the Social Democratic Populist Party under Erdal İnönü, and on 9 September 1992 Deniz Baykal re-established the CHP under its original name.

The party's logo is the Six Arrows, which stand for the principles of Kemalism: republicanism, reformism, laicism, populism, nationalism and etatism. It is cited as the founding party of modern Turkey, and under its one-party rule it was the main instrument for carrying out far-reaching political, cultural, social and economic reforms. It is the oldest political party in Turkey. In the 2002 election it won 20 per cent of the vote and 32 per cent of the seats, because only it and the new AK Party passed the 10 per cent threshold.
reric: Reric was one of the multi-ethnic Slavic and Scandinavian emporia of the southern Baltic coast in the Viking Age. It was probably founded in 735, shortly after Slavs of the Obodrite tribe had begun to settle the region. At the turn of the 9th century its people allied with Charlemagne, who used the port on a trade route that avoided the lands under Saxon and Danish control. This placed it in the war between Denmark and the Frankish Empire, in which the Franks were allied with the Obodrites.

According to the Royal Frankish Annals, Gudfred had taken plenty of tribute from Reric before he destroyed it in 808. The destruction may not have been total: the Obodrites rebuilt the place, and the Obodrite duke Drasco was murdered there soon afterwards at Gudfred's instigation. The medieval chroniclers Adam of Bremen and Helmold of Bosau called the Obodrites Reregi, probably a rendering of the town's name.

Where Reric lay was long disputed. Older theories placed it at Oldenburg, Lübeck, Mecklenburg Castle or Alt-Gaarz, which was renamed Rerik in 1938. Since the 1990s it has been identified with the site near Groß Strömkendorf on the eastern shore of the Bay of Wismar, of which Kiel University and the state archaeology department of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern excavated part of about 20 hectares between 1995 and 1999. The founding and destruction dates of the two match. Remains of open Slavic settlements lie within 10 kilometres, and the strongholds of Mecklenburg and Ilow nearby were founded about the same time.

Groß Strömkendorf was a deep-water port with a planned layout, stretching 500 metres along the coast. The first settlement lay to the north and was moved south in the 760s, its old area becoming a cemetery. Its sunken-floor buildings resemble those of West Stow in England. Most pottery is of the West Slavic Sukow type, with less of the later Feldberg type and few western imports. Hoards of Norwegian schist whetstones and traces of work in textiles, iron, bronze, glass, amber and horn point to production for local use. The latest datable wood comes from 811, and the settlement ended a little later.
resid-mehmed-pasha: Reşid Mehmed, also known as Kütahı, was born in Circassia and was of Georgian origin. Captured as a child and enslaved by the Ottomans, he entered the service of the Kapudan Pasha Koca Hüsrev Mehmed Pasha, whom his intelligence and ability impressed, and he rose quickly. After a short posting in Karađorđe's Serbia he became governor of Kütahya at 29, the origin of his sobriquet. In 1820 Sultan Mahmud II sent him with other pashas against the rebel Ali Pasha of Yannina, and after Ali's death in 1822 he turned against the Greeks, who had risen in March 1821.

As commander in Epirus he crushed the force of Alexandros Mavrokordatos at the Battle of Peta on 4 July 1822, but his first siege of Missolonghi with Omer Vrioni failed: the Greeks drew out negotiations until reinforced by sea, the planned Christmas assault was leaked to them, and the siege was lifted. After subduing Pelion he became commander-in-chief in Rumelia. In April 1825 he invested Missolonghi again with more than 35,000 men and, after quarrelling and then cooperating with Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt, took it when the starving defenders' breakout on 10 April 1826 ended in a massacre.

Turning to Athens, he besieged the Greek garrison on the Acropolis for ten months, until his victory over a relief force at the Battle of Phaleron on 24 April 1827 forced it to surrender. In the Russo-Turkish War he was defeated by General Diebitsch at the Battle of Kulevicha.

Reşid Mehmed was grand vizier from January 1829 to 17 February 1833. He orchestrated the Monastir massacre of 1830, in which hundreds of Albanian beys were killed, and marched against the Bosnian leader Husein Gradaščević, who opposed the grant of autonomy and six Bosnian districts to Serbia. Gradaščević defeated him at Shtime, but the vizier, aided by Ali-paša Rizvanbegović, later defeated the Bosnian army outside Stup. In the Egyptian-Ottoman War he was captured by Ibrahim Pasha at the Battle of Konya in 1832.

Appointed governor of the Diyarbakir and Raqqa eyalets in 1834, he campaigned against the Kurdish tribes and the Yazidi of Sinjar, subdued the Milli tribe in Mardin in 1835 and defeated the Soran Emirate in 1836. He died the same year.
respendial: Respendial, also written Respindal, ruled one of two groups of Alans in western Europe early in the 5th century. He is named in the Frigeridus fragment, a passage that Gregory of Tours embedded in his own work, which describes the war between the Vandals and the Franks that came before the Crossing of the Rhine.

Over what were probably several battles, the Roman-allied Franks had killed 20,000 Vandal warriors and the Vandal king Godigisel, and the Vandals were on the verge of being wiped out when Respendial came to their aid and defeated the Franks. The historian MacDowall (2016) places this rescue probably in the summer or autumn of 406. Prosper of Aquitaine dated the crossing that followed to 31 December 406, though it is sometimes put in 405.

Frigeridus leaves unclear what became of Goar's Alans, but other sources show that the Romans eventually settled them in Gaul near Orléans. Respendial's Alans went on with the Vandals and the Suebi into Spain. According to the chronicle of Bishop Hydatius, the Vandals, both Silings and Asdings, arrived first, in September or October 409, while Gregory notes that the Suebi and Alans, presumably those led by Respendial, followed later.

Respendial's fate is unknown. By 418 he was no longer king and had been succeeded by Attaces, who was killed when the Visigoths invaded Hispania. This group of Alans then united with the Asding Vandals, with whom they crossed into Africa and established an independent kingdom.
rethel: Rethel is a commune in the Ardennes department of northern France, a sub-prefecture and the third most important city of the department. It stands on the river Aisne near the northern border of Champagne, 37 km from Reims. Its inhabitants are called Rethelois. The name possibly derives from Registestensis, the Roman name of the settlement, and the coat of arms shows three rakes, which suggests a popular derivation from the Old French rastel, "rake". According to legend Julius Caesar founded the city by making a camp on the site during his campaigns.

The parents of Saint Arnulf of Metz were said to have given all they owned in villa Reistete, in Rethel, to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, so that their prayers for a child would be answered. The city belonged to the Abbey of Saint-Remi and was administered by its advocates, one of whom, Manasses I, became the first Count of Rethel. In 1481 the county, with Rethel as its seat, was raised to the Peerage of France, in 1581 it became a duchy, and in 1663 it became the Duchy of Mazarin. Baldwin II, later King of Jerusalem, was born there in 1075.

During the Franco-Spanish War, Spanish forces under Louis de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, captured the town on 30 October 1652 after a four-year siege, and the French retook it in July 1653. In 1814 Spanish prisoners of war from the Napoleonic Wars brought typhus to the city, and Jean-Baptiste Reberotte-Labesse cared for the sick soldiers. Cholera epidemics struck in 1832 and 1849, and typhoid fever ravaged the town in 1839, killing an average of thirty people a day. In the Battle of France, from May to June 1940, French troops under Jean de Lattre de Tassigny held off German assaults on Rethel for a month before it fell. In 1974 the town absorbed the former commune of Pargny-Resson.
reting-rinpoche: Reting Rinpoche is the title of the abbots of Reting Monastery, a Buddhist monastery in central Tibet, and holders of the title have at times acted as the selector of a new Dalai Lama. The first, Ngawang Chokden, lived from 1677 to 1751. Thubten Jamphel Yeshe Gyaltsen was the fifth in the line, which had passed before him through Lobsang Yeshe Tenpa Rabgye, Ngawang Yeshe Tsultrim Gyaltsen and Ngawang Lobsang Yeshe Tenpai Gyaltsen. He held the office of regent, or desi, for the Dalai Lama whose search he had led.

He was replaced as regent in 1941, and was later alleged to have organised an uprising against his successor. He died in 1947 in the prisons of the Potala in Lhasa, apparently poisoned. A jailor allegedly reported that he had been tortured to death. The historian Melvyn C. Goldstein records the words of Tsepon W. D. Shakabpa, who said that many people believed this, but an investigation of the body was made for the Tibetan Assembly by a committee of Shakabpa, Tsarong, Khenchen Lobsang Tashi, Gyetakba and representatives of Reting and Sera Monasteries, and Tsarong told the Assembly there was no evidence that Reting had been strangled and no wound.

The affair exposed the politics of the religious hierarchy in Lhasa. His critics accused him of widespread corruption and, though a monk, of involvement with married women. His defenders held that his imprisonment owed something to his attraction to the teachings of the Nyingma lineage, a politically sensitive leaning, and that the case against him had been fabricated by the cabinet minister Kapshopa. His regency, imprisonment and death are told in Martin Scorsese's film Kundun (1997). His reincarnation, Tenzin Jigme Thutob Wangchuk, was born in Lhasa in 1948 and enthroned in 1955.
reuss-river: The Reuss is one of the four major rivers that rise in the Gotthard region, with the Rhine, Ticino and Rhône, and its drainage basin of 3,426 square kilometres roughly covers Central Switzerland. The Gotthardreuss emerges from Lago di Lucendro, a reservoir built in 1947, and the Furkareuss rises east of the Furka Pass, only about 5 kilometres from the source of the Rhône, though it flows to the other side of the continent. They join at Hospental, and below Andermatt the river turns north through the Schöllenen Gorge, which is 3 kilometres long and narrow and deep, beneath the Devil's Bridge.

From Göschenen it forms the main valley of the canton of Uri and enters Lake Lucerne. It leaves the lake at Lucerne, where the Kapellbrücke, first built in 1333, and the Spreuerbrücke of 1408 cross it. It joins the Aare just downstream of Brugg, and that river flows into the Rhine at Koblenz.

Ptolemy records the river's pre-Germanic name as Silana, from which the name of Silenen derives. The Germanic name appears as Rusa or Rusia from the 9th century. Until the 13th century the Schöllenen Gorge was impassable and separated Urseren from Uri. It was made passable in the 1230s, opening the Gotthard Pass, and the Reuss valley gained immense strategic value, which is reflected in the grant of imperial immediacy to Uri and in the founding of the Old Swiss Confederacy.

The lower valley lay under Habsburg rule in the 14th century. In the 15th century the river became a border between territories of the Swiss Confederacy, first in 1429 between Lucerne and Zürich, and downstream of Ottenbach it came to lie within Aargau when that canton was created in 1803. In the late medieval period the Reuss was an imperial road and served as a waterway for traffic between Lucerne and Zurzach and, by way of the Aare and the Rhine, Basel, until transit roads were built in the 18th century. In 1528 the Catholic cantons blocked the trade routes across the river for the Protestant cantons.

Because ferries and bridges brought in income, new crossings were opposed in the early modern period, and only one new bridge was built, at Sins in 1640. More than a dozen crossings exist now, including railway and motorway bridges. The river was canalised between Attinghausen and Altdorf in 1850–1863 and to its mouth in 1900–1912, which greatly increased arable land. A large river-engineering project was completed during 1971–1985. Hydroelectric plants have been built at Amsteg (1922), Wassen (1949) and Göschenen (1962).
revolt-of-the-comuneros: After the death of Queen Isabella I in 1504 the Crown of Castile passed to her daughter Joanna, who was confined because of her mental instability. Ferdinand II of Aragon ruled as regent until his death in 1516, when Joanna's sixteen-year-old son Charles became co-monarch. Raised in the Netherlands with little Castilian, he arrived in Spain in October 1517 with a large retinue of Flemish nobles and clerics, which bred mistrust among Castile's social elites.

Charles was elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1519, after more than a million florins had been spent on bribes. To cover the debt he convened the Cortes at Santiago de Compostela in late March 1520 and tried to fill it with representatives he could bribe. When he left for Germany in 1520 he put the Dutch cardinal Adrian of Utrecht in charge of Castile.

In April 1520 Toledo rose. A crowd drove out the royal administrators and elected a committee under Juan López de Padilla and Pedro Laso de la Vega, calling itself a Comunidad. Segovia, led by the noble Juan Bravo, held out against the royal investigator Rodrigo Ronquillo in June. A revolutionary Cortes, the Santa Junta, met at Ávila, and Padilla became its Captain-General. When royal troops under Antonio de Fonseca tried on 21 August to seize artillery at Medina del Campo, a fire destroyed much of the town. Valladolid and other cities then declared for the rebels, and Adrian fled.

The comuneros moved to Tordesillas on 29 August to proclaim Joanna sole sovereign, and thirteen cities sent representatives. Joanna, however, refused to sign their edicts. Risings against the landed nobility alarmed the aristocrats, who turned against the rebels, and Burgos left the Junta in October. The royalists took Tordesillas. On 23 April 1521 their army defeated the comuneros at the Battle of Villalar, and Padilla, Bravo and Francisco Maldonado were beheaded the next day. Toledo held out under María Pacheco until October 1521.

María Pacheco escaped to Portugal and lived there in exile for her remaining ten years. Bishop Antonio de Acuña of Zamora was executed after killing a guard while trying to escape. Charles V returned to Spain on 16 July 1522 and, because many important people had supported the rebels or been slow to declare for him, pressed repression only sporadically. Historians disagree about the revolt. Some see one of the first modern revolutions, others a rebellion against high taxes and foreign control. From the 19th century Spanish liberals mythologised it, and 23 April is now observed as Castile and León Day.
revolt-of-the-three-feudatories: After the Qing conquest of China proper the central government could not yet rule the south directly, and under a policy of letting the Han Chinese govern the Han Chinese it gave former Ming generals who had defected the provinces there. In 1655 Wu Sangui became the Pingxi Prince with Yunnan and Guizhou, while Shang Kexi and Geng Zhongming held Guangdong and Fujian. The three lords had their own armies and could alter taxes, and their costs came to empty almost half of the imperial treasury. In 1673 Shang Kexi, then Wu Sangui and Geng Jingzhong, asked to retire; against the majority of his council the Kangxi Emperor accepted and ordered them to resettle in Manchuria.

In December 1673 Wu Sangui broke with the Qing under the banner of opposing the Qing and restoring the Ming, and his forces took Hunan and Sichuan. Geng Jingzhong in Fujian, Shang Zhixin in Guangdong, Sun Yanling in Guangxi and Wang Fuchen in Shaanxi rose in turn, and Zheng Jing of the Kingdom of Tungning landed troops from Taiwan. Wu proposed through the 5th Dalai Lama to divide China along the Yangtze, but the emperor refused.

The Qing relied chiefly on the Han Chinese Green Standard Army rather than the Bannermen, and after 1676 the tide turned: Wang Fuchen, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin surrendered. In 1678 Wu proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Zhou at Hengzhou but died of illness that year, and his grandson Wu Shifan retreated to Yunnan. By 1680 Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi and Sichuan were retaken, and in 1681 a three-pronged attack proposed by the general Zhao Liangdong captured Kunming; Wu Shifan killed himself in December.

Shang Zhixin was forced to commit suicide in 1680 and Geng Jingzhong was executed, and the princely titles were abolished. Having helped topple the Southern Ming, the feudatories never won broad Han support. The last act was the conquest of Tungning: the admiral Shi Lang defeated its navy at the Battle of Penghu, and Zheng Keshuang surrendered in October 1683, bringing Taiwan into the Qing Empire. Former Zheng soldiers armed with rattan shields later fought for the Qing against the Russians at Albazin.
revolucion-libertadora: Juan Domingo Perón, elected in 1946, was re-elected in 1951 under a constitutional amendment of 1949 that allowed unrestricted re-election. A military rebellion led by Benjamín Menéndez on 28 September 1951 collapsed within half a day. Economic downturns, Perón's personality cult, the suppression of the press, the harassment and exile of dissidents and a growing conflict with the Catholic Church and the armed forces' leadership eroded his support. On 14 June 1955 a Corpus Christi procession turned into an anti-government demonstration.

Two days later, on 16 June 1955, 30 Navy and Air Force aircraft bombed the Plaza de Mayo while a crowd gathered there in support of Perón, killing over 300 civilians in the largest aerial bombing ever carried out on the Argentine mainland. That night extremist Peronist groups burned several churches.

On 16 September 1955 a new rising led by General Eduardo Lonardi, General Pedro E. Aramburu and Admiral Isaac Rojas began, with Lonardi's command at Córdoba, where he declared himself provisional president. Fighting broke out at Córdoba, the naval bases of Puerto Belgrano and Río Santiago and at Curuzú Cuatiá, where Aramburu's rising was at first defeated. Rebel warships blockaded the Río de la Plata and on 19 September bombarded Mar del Plata.

That day Perón wrote an ambiguous letter to the Army minister, General Franklin Lucero, hinting at resignation. A junta of loyal generals under José Domingo Molina treated it as one and negotiated with the rebels aboard a cruiser, agreeing on 21 September that Lonardi would take charge. Seeing the country on the brink of civil war, Perón took shelter aboard the ARP Paraguay and sought asylum in Paraguay. Lonardi was sworn in on 23 September.

Lonardi promised neither victors nor vanquished, echoing Urquiza after the Battle of Caseros, but in November hard-liners deposed him in favour of Aramburu. The regime closed Congress, purged the Supreme Court and the universities, accused Perón of treason and forbade any public mention of him or his late wife; Eva Perón's remains were taken secretly to Italy and buried in Milan under a false name. Uruguay and the Eisenhower administration aided the new government. Peronism remained proscribed until Perón's return in 1973.
revolution-nationale: The programme adapted ideas of the French far right, including monarchism and the thought of Charles Maurras, whose notion of an Anti-France of internal foreigners shaped the regime's persecutions. The Constitutional Acts of 11 July 1940 merged legislative and executive power in Pétain, who rejected parliament and the multi-party system. A Labour Charter replaced trade unions with corporations organised by profession and abolished the right to strike. The programme opposed almost every change the French Revolution had brought, and Pétain blamed France's decadence on political and economic liberalism and its outgrowths, socialism and communism.

The regime was never precise about it: Pétain was rumoured to dislike the term and used it only four times in his wartime speeches, so its supporters, from counter-revolutionary reactionaries to advocates of a French fascism and reforming technocrats, each read it in their own way.

Pétain's portrait appeared on money, stamps and walls, and the song Maréchal, nous voilà! served as an unofficial anthem. Joan of Arc replaced Marianne as the national symbol, and Vercingetorix was presented as the founder of the nation. The first law on the status of Jews was issued on 3 October 1940; the Crémieux Decree was abrogated on 7 October, stripping Algerian Jews of citizenship, and Jews were detained in camps in France and deported through Drancy. Propaganda attacked Britain above all, citing Dunkirk, Mers-el-Kébir and Dakar. A sports commissariat founded on 7 August 1940 banned professionalism in some sports and closed several federations.
None of these measures was forced on France by Germany. The Riom Trial of 1942-43, meant to blame the Third Republic's leaders for the defeat, was suspended after the defendants rebutted the charges.

Historians disagree on whether Vichy was fascist. Stanley G. Payne called it rightist and authoritarian but never fascist, and Olivier Wieviorka also rejects the label; Robert Paxton and Zeev Sternhell argued that it qualified, and Roger Griffin called it para-fascist. By late autumn 1940 most of the French hoped for a British victory. After the war the label neo-Pétainism was applied to parts of the French far right.
revolutionary-armed-forces-of-colombia: The group grew out of peasant self-defence groups formed from 1948, during the period of La Violencia, and promoted agrarianism and anti-imperialism. The Colombian Communist Party, accredited by the Comintern in 1930, organised peasant leagues and communist-controlled self-defence communities in the south that could resist state forces. In the 1960s the government's Accelerated Economic Development policy favoured large export farms; thousands of peasants were evicted, and the number of landless families rose from 40,000 in 1961 to 400,000 by 1969.

In the early 1960s the government began attacking the communist-held territories. After a military assault on the community of Marquetalia, in which about 16,000 troops faced 48 armed fighters, Manuel Marulanda Vélez and 47 others escaped into the mountains. These 48 men, two of them women, formed the core of the FARC.

At its Seventh Guerrilla Conference in 1982 the group decided to become an irregular army able to stage large attacks, helped by income from the coca boom, and added the letters EP, for Ejército del Pueblo or People's Army, to its name. In November 1998 President Andrés Pastrana granted it a safe haven of 42,000 square kilometres around San Vicente del Caguán in peace talks. Under President Álvaro Uribe, from 2002, military pressure forced it into a strategic withdrawal, and many fighters and commanders were captured or deserted. By 2014 it was avoiding open combat with the army and concentrating on small ambushes.

Its strength varied: 18,000 members by its own claim in 2007, and fewer than 10,000 according to President Juan Manuel Santos in 2011. It was financed by kidnapping for ransom, extortion, taxation of economic activity including the drug trade, and mining. The state, right-wing paramilitaries and other guerrilla groups also committed atrocities in the conflict.

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the United Nations accused the group of violations including murders of civilians, hostage-taking, the use of landmines and gas cylinder mortars, and the recruitment of children. Women made up perhaps a third of its members, and the group formally banned rape, though former members have reported forced abortions.

In June 2016 the FARC signed a ceasefire with Santos in Havana. A referendum on the first accord failed on 2 October, with 50.24 percent against, and a revised deal was signed in November and approved by Congress. On 27 June 2017 the FARC handed its weapons to the United Nations, and soon afterwards reformed as a legal political party, later renamed the Commons. Dissident groups of about 2,000 to 2,500 people continued to use its doctrine.
revolutions-of-1848: The revolutions grew out of the changes of industrialisation and the political legacy of the French Revolution: rapid population growth, urbanisation, a repressive political order set up in reaction to that revolution, and the spread of liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In the countryside peasants lost customary rights to common land and forests through enclosure and privatisation.

The most immediate cause, according to the economic historians Helge Berger and Mark Spoerer, was the crisis of 1845-1847. Potato blight devastated harvests in northern Europe from 1845. The Great Famine killed over an eighth of Ireland's population, and the blight caused 60,000 deaths in the Netherlands. Drought in 1846 damaged the grain harvests and food prices rose sharply, and there were more than 400 food riots in France in 1846-1847.

The first revolution came in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in January 1848, but it was France that mattered most to contemporaries. Protests in Paris began on 22 February, and the army's killing of 65 demonstrators on 23 February made them a revolution. On 24 February King Louis Philippe I abdicated and fled. News spread across the continent within a week; on hearing it Klemens von Metternich is reported to have said, in French, that it was all over.

Demonstrations began in Baden on 27 February, and the revolution succeeded in Vienna on 13-15 March and in Berlin on 18-19 March. In Denmark a march to Christiansborg on 21 March led the new king, Frederick VII, to meet the liberals' demands. In Paris the closing of the national workshops on 21 June led to the June Days, an insurrection that General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac suppressed with great bloodshed. In 1849 the revolutions gained new strength in central Italy and Hungary.

Many revolutions were quickly suppressed, tens of thousands of people were killed and more went into exile, since the temporary coalitions of workers and middle-class reformers did not hold together for long. Some lasting changes followed. The Netherlands introduced representative democracy, and Switzerland, after a short civil conflict in November 1847 in which around 100 people died, adopted a new constitution in 1848 that made it a federal state.
revolutions-of-1989: The earliest protests that led to the revolutions began in Poland on 14 August 1980, with a general strike that produced the August Agreements and the independent trade union Solidarity, led by Lech Wałęsa, whose membership peaked at 10 million. On 13 December 1981 the prime minister, Wojciech Jaruzelski, declared martial law, suspended the union and temporarily imprisoned its leaders. Through the mid-1980s Solidarity survived as an underground organisation supported by the Catholic Church.

The rise of Mikhail Gorbachev in 1985 signalled greater liberalisation. The Soviet Union faced severe economic decline and needed Western technology and credit. Gorbachev's abrogation of the Brezhnev Doctrine was perhaps the key factor: once it was clear that the Soviet Army would not intervene, the regimes were exposed to popular uprisings against one-party rule.

In 1988 strikes in Poland forced the government into talks with Solidarity, and in the elections that began on 4 June 1989 Solidarity won an overwhelming victory, so that communism fell peacefully in Poland. Hungary, influenced by Poland, held round-table talks and began dismantling its section of the Iron Curtain. In August 1989 over a quarter of the population of the Baltic states formed a human chain of 675 kilometres in the Baltic Way, and the opening of a border gate between Austria and Hungary set off a chain reaction in which the Eastern Bloc disintegrated.

Mass demonstrations followed in East Germany, and the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, which opened the way to German reunification in 1990. Revolts spread to Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia, and even to Albania. Civil resistance was the common feature, and Romania was the only country where citizens and opposition forces used violence to overthrow the regime. The Tiananmen Square protests in China ended in a military crackdown on 4 June that kept the Communist Party in power.

Between June 1989 and April 1991 every communist or former communist country in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia held competitive parliamentary elections for the first time in many decades. The Warsaw Pact was dissolved on 1 July 1991. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, and many historians treat 26 December 1991 as the true end of the Cold War. Yugoslavia split into five countries, and Czechoslovakia split peacefully on 1 January 1993.

Communist parties lost their monopoly of power in all but five countries: China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam. The breakdown of economic ties brought severe economic crisis and a fall in living standards in the post-Soviet states during the 1990s. In many countries the communist party simply changed its name.
reynald-of-sidon: Reynald, also called Reginald or Renaud Grenier, was the son of Gerard Grenier and Agnes of Bures and a grandson of Eustace Grenier. He rose to prominence in 1170 by marrying Agnes of Courtenay, the former wife of Amalric of Jerusalem and mother of Baldwin IV and Sibylla. When Baldwin IV succeeded his father in 1174 as a leprous minor, Reynald became the king's stepfather and backed Raymond III of Tripoli as regent. The Lignages d'Outremer describe him as extremely ugly and very wise.

He fought at the Battle of Montgisard in 1177 but reached the Battle of Jacob's Ford in 1179 too late; William of Tyre blamed him for refugees killed in ambushes after he turned back. He supported the crowning of the child Baldwin V in 1183 and tried in vain to keep Sibylla and Guy of Lusignan from the throne in 1186. At Hattin he was in the rearguard with Balian of Ibelin and escaped. Later western chronicles called them cowards, though they were more likely trying to break the encirclement. A later account says he was negotiating the surrender of Tyre until Conrad of Montferrat expelled him, but Arab chroniclers are silent and the two were afterwards close allies.

In 1189, bargaining over Beaufort, he offered to retire to Damascus and convert to Islam, a ruse to gain time; he told the guards in Arabic to stand down and in French to keep fighting. He was imprisoned in Damascus until the castle's surrender bought his release.

After his release he married Helvis, eldest daughter of Balian of Ibelin and Maria Comnena, more than 40 years his junior. He backed the annulment of Isabella of Jerusalem's marriage to Humphrey IV of Toron so that she could marry Conrad, and was on good terms with Saladin's brother Al-Adil, which led partisans of Richard I to accuse him falsely of secret conversion. Sidon was recovered in 1197, and on his death in 1202 his son Balian succeeded him as Count of Sidon.
reynosa: Reynosa lies on the south bank of the Rio Grande, directly across the Mexican border from Hidalgo, Texas, and about 18 kilometres south of McAllen. It is the municipal seat of Reynosa Municipality and the largest city of the state of Tamaulipas. The municipality covers 3,156.34 square kilometres, 3.7 per cent of the state's territory. The climate is semi-arid, with short, mild winters and hot summers in which temperatures can exceed 40 degrees from May to August. Annual rainfall averages 452 millimetres.

On 6 July 1686 Agustín Echeverz y Zuvízar, governor of the Nuevo Reino de León, camped on the site during an exploratory expedition. In December 1748 an expedition led by José de Escandón y Helguera left Querétaro to found 14 villages, with 1,500 colonists and 755 soldiers. On 14 March 1749 Captain Carlos Cantú founded the Villa de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe de Reynosa on Escandón's behalf, with 279 pioneer residents in the care of Friar Agustín Fragoso. It was named after Reinosa, the birthplace of the viceroy Juan Francisco de Güemes y Horcasitas.

The first flood was recorded in August 1750. In 1757 inspectors counted 280 inhabitants and obtained royal permission to move the village to Santa María de las Lajas, but Escandón no longer considered the river a risk and it stayed. A great flood in September 1800 forced the villagers to escape to the hills of El Morrillo by canoe and raft, and in 1802 the village moved to its present site, where a census counted 1,631 inhabitants.

The old church of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe was begun in 1810 and finished in 1815. The American army invaded Reynosa during the Mexican-American War in 1846, and General Lucio Blanco took it for the constitutional army on 10 May 1910, in the Mexican Revolution. Reynosa became a city on 24 November 1926.

Reynosa is the largest and most populous city in Tamaulipas, and part of the international Reynosa-McAllen metropolitan area. Several satellite U.S. companies operate there, drawn by lower labour costs and industry incentives. The General Lucio Blanco International Airport serves the city, and the McAllen Miller International Airport in Texas is close by.
reza-abbasi: Reza Abbasi, also known as Agha Reza, was possibly born in Kashan, since Āghā Reżā Kāshānī is one version of his name. His father, the miniature artist Ali Asghar, worked in the atelier of Prince Ibrahim Mirza and then in the workshop of Shah Ismail II in the capital Qasvin. Reza probably trained under his father and joined the workshop of Shah Abbas I at a young age. By then royal commissions for illustrated books had diminished, and album miniatures had replaced them as the main employment of the royal workshop's artists.

Unlike most earlier Persian artists Reza typically signed his work, often with dates and other details, though scholars now reject many signed pieces. His first dated drawing is from 1601. In 1603, at about 38, he received from the shah the honorific Abbasi. He followed the shah to Khurasan in 1598 and to the new capital at Isfahan. Soon afterwards he left the shah's employ, apparently seeking greater independence and the company of athletes, wrestlers and other unrespectable types in Isfahan. In 1610 he returned to court, probably because he was short of money, and stayed in the shah's service until his death.

His earlier works are signed Aqa Riza, which is also the name of a contemporary artist who worked for the Mughal emperor Jahangir in India. Scholars debated in the early 20th century whether this artist and Reza Abbasi were the same person, and it is now accepted that they were. He is generally credited with the 19 miniatures of a Khusraw and Shirin of 1631–32, though critics have questioned their quality.

His speciality was the single miniature for the albums, or muraqqas, of private collectors. These typically show one or two figures against a lightly drawn garden background, ranging from pure pen drawings to fully painted subjects. The favourite subjects were idealized, stylishly dressed young men. Barbara Brend wrote that the line of his ink drawings has an absolute mastery, conveying texture, form, movement and even personality.

His style changed about the time he returned to court. The bright colours and virtuoso technique of his early portraits gave way in the 1620s to darker, earthier colours and a heavier line. He painted many older men, perhaps scholars, Sufi divines or shepherds, as well as birds and Europeans, and in his last years sometimes satirized his subjects. The style he pioneered influenced later Persian painters, and his pupils included Mo'en Mosavver and his own son, Muhammed Shafi Abbasi.
reza-shah: Reza Khan was born on 15 March 1878 at Alasht in Savadkuh County, Mazandaran, the son of Major Abbas-Ali Khan, a Mazanderani who served in the Second Herat War of 1856, and Noush-Afarin, whose family had come to Qajar Iran from the Caucasus. He joined the Persian Cossack Brigade at the age of 14 and rose through the ranks. By 1920 the Qajar government had lost virtually all power outside its capital, and British and Soviet forces controlled most of the country. In February 1921, as leader of the whole Cossack Brigade in Qazvin province, Reza Khan marched on Tehran and seized the capital. He installed Zia ol Din Tabatabaee as prime minister, while he became commander-in-chief and minister of war.

Tabatabaee's government soon met resistance from provincial governors and the aristocracy, and Reza Khan became prime minister in 1923. In 1925 a constituent assembly deposed Ahmad Shah, the last Qajar monarch, and amended the constitution of 1906 so that Reza Pahlavi could be elected shah. During his sixteen years of rule the Trans-Iranian Railway was built, highways grew from 2,000 to 14,000 miles and the University of Tehran was founded. He created a 100,000-man army and a 90,000-man civil service and introduced free, compulsory education for boys and girls. In 1935 he asked foreign delegations to use the name Iran instead of Persia.

He clashed with the Shia clergy over a law of 1928 requiring Western dress, over the discouragement of the veil and over the confiscation of land from shrine endowments. Elections to parliament were managed by the interior ministry. In 1932 he cancelled the oil concession of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, and a new concession was signed on 26 April 1933 after the British took the dispute to the League of Nations.

In August 1941 the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union invaded neutral Iran, and its army collapsed within days. Reza Shah was forced to abdicate in favour of his eldest son, Mohammad Reza Shah. He was taken to the British colony of Mauritius and then to Johannesburg, where he died of a heart ailment on 26 July 1944, aged sixty-six. His defenders say that he reunified and modernised Iran; his critics say that his rule was often despotic and that his policy of cultural unity suppressed several ethnic groups. In 1950 the National Consultative Assembly named him Reza Shah the Great.
rezin: Rezin was an Aramean king ruling from Damascus, known in Assyrian texts as Raḫiānu. For part of his reign he paid tribute to King Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria. He then conspired with a number of Levantine kings, among them Hiram II of Tyre, to rebel against Assyria. According to 2 Kings 16, he and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, turned on Ahaz of Judah after Ahaz refused to join their coalition against Assyria.

Assyrian inscriptions describe a three-year campaign in the Levant from 734 to 732 BCE. In its first year Tiglath-Pileser sacked Tyre and Sidon; in the second he devastated Aram and beat the Arameans in the field but failed to take Damascus; in the third he took the city. His own account says that Rezin fled into his city like a mongoose and was shut in like a bird in a cage for forty-five days, while his leading men were impaled before his people and his orchards cut down. The king claims to have taken Rezin's birthplace and destroyed 591 cities in 16 districts of the land of Damascus.

In the same campaign Tiglath-Pileser destroyed villages in northern Israel, boasted of slaying Pekah and placed Hoshea on the throne, leaving only the fortified capital of Samaria. Archaeology confirms that many cities destroyed in this period were never rebuilt.

In the biblical account of the Syro-Ephraimite War, the prophet Isaiah urged Ahaz to trust in God rather than foreign help and foretold the birth of a child named Immanuel, God is with us, as a sign that the lands of the two kings would be deserted. Ahaz nevertheless turned to Tiglath-Pileser, and according to 2 Kings 16:7–9 this prompted the sack of Damascus.
rhadamistus: Rhadamistus was the eldest son of King Pharasmanes I of Iberia and a member of the Pharnavazid dynasty. His mother, whose name is not preserved, was an Armenian princess of the Artaxiad dynasty, daughter of Tigranes IV and his sister-wife Erato. He was known for his ambition, strength, size and good looks, and he was openly impatient to inherit Iberia from his aging father. Pharasmanes, fearing a usurpation, diverted him by persuading him to conquer Armenia, then ruled by Pharasmanes' brother Mithridates. Rhadamistus pretended to be at feud with his father and visited Mithridates' court to reconnoitre, and Mithridates received him like a son.

Rhadamistus returned with a large Iberian army and forced Mithridates to take shelter in the fortress of Gorneas, which had a Roman garrison under Caelius Pollio. He opened negotiations, citing his marriage to Mithridates' daughter Zenobia, while Pollio was swayed by bribes and threatened to abandon the fortress. Mithridates surrendered. Rhadamistus had promised that he would not harm him by sword or poison, and then had him smothered. He also killed Mithridates' sons, for weeping over their father, and Mithridates' wife, who was his own sister.
