He became king of Armenia in 51. The Romans officially chose not to aid their Armenian allies, though the governor of Cappadocia, Paelignus, invaded and ravaged the country. The Parthian king Vologases I then sent a large army into Armenia, driving out the Iberians in 53, and Rhadamistus regained control after a plague forced the Parthians to withdraw. He treated the Armenians' loyalty as permanently suspect and punished cities that had surrendered to the Parthians, which provoked a revolt that replaced him with the Parthian prince Tiridates I in 55.

He fled back to Iberia. His pregnant wife Zenobia, who could not endure the ride, asked him to kill her. He stabbed her and dropped her in the Araxes, but she survived and was rescued by peasants, who sent her to Artaxata.

On his return to his father's lands in 58, Rhadamistus was executed for treason. His death ended Pharasmanes' fears of usurpation and demonstrated Iberian loyalty to Rome, and in particular to Emperor Nero. Pharasmanes died later that year and was succeeded by his second son Mihrdat. Rhadamistus and Zenobia became subjects of opera and painting, including Handel's Radamisto of 1720 and Paul Baudry's Shepherds Find Zenobia on the Banks of the Araxes of 1850.
rhayader: The town lies 20 miles from the source of the Wye on Plynlimon, the highest point of the Cambrian Mountains, at the junction of the A470 and A44 roads, 13 miles north of Builth Wells and 30 miles east of Aberystwyth. Its Welsh name, Rhaeadr Gwy, means the waterfall on the Wye, but little remains of the fall, which was destroyed in 1780 to make way for the bridge to Cwmdauddwr and the Elan Valley. Cairns and standing stones around the town date from several thousand years BCE.

The route was long a stopping place for travellers: the Romans had a camp in the Elan Valley, monks passed between the abbeys of Strata Florida and Abbeycwmhir, and drovers took their livestock to market. Documented history begins with Rhayader Castle in 1177, of which only a dry moat survives. A hoard of gold jewellery of the 1st and 2nd centuries, found nearby in 1899 and known as the Rhayader Hoard, is now in the British Museum. The Old Swan, one of the town's oldest buildings, is recorded in 1676 as one of its two inns.

During the Rebecca Riots against costly turnpike tolls, local farmers dressed as women demolished six of Rhayader's tollgates, and a Commission of Inquiry followed. In the 1890s Birmingham, 80 miles to the east, chose the Elan Valley as a source of clean water; thousands of workers came to build its dams and reservoirs, a railway and a village for them were built, and King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra opened the scheme in 1904.

Rhayader is a market town and community within the historic county of Radnorshire, with a population of 2,088 at the 2011 census. By area it is the largest community in Wales and includes the Elan Valley. Its railway station closed on 31 December 1962, and tourism and agriculture are its main industries.
rhazuns: Rhäzüns is a municipality in the Imboden Region of the Swiss canton of Grisons, on the Hinterrhein, shortly before it joins the Vorderrhein. It has an area of 13.3 square kilometres, of which 69.1 per cent is forest. The linear village lies in the valley between Bonaduz and the narrow entrance to the Domleschg valley. Before 2017 it belonged to the Rhäzüns sub-district of the Imboden district. It had a population of 1,611 at the end of 2020. In 2000 most people spoke German, with Romansh the second most common language and Italian the third. About 61.7 per cent of residents were Roman Catholic and 23.3 per cent belonged to the Swiss Reformed Church.

Rhäzüns is first mentioned about 840 as Raezunne, and until the Reformation it formed a single parish with Bonaduz. It was part of the Grey League from 1424. The House of Habsburg acquired the lordship in 1497, but it remained part of the Three Leagues for the purposes of jurisdiction.

In the Treaty of Schönbrunn of 1809 the Habsburg monarchy ceded the lordship of Rhäzüns to France. It reverted to the Habsburg monarchy after Napoleon's defeat in 1814, and the Congress of Vienna in 1815 assigned it to Grisons. Grisons was by then a canton of the restored Swiss Confederacy, and the transfer of administrative power took effect only on 19 January 1819.

The frescoes of the Church of St George and the Church of St Paul are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance. The village is known for the mineral water Rhäzünser and the beer Rhäzünser Pils, and the Rhaetian Railway serves it with a station of its own.
rheinfels-castle: The ruin stands above the left, west bank of the Rhine at Sankt Goar in Rhineland-Palatinate. It is the largest castle overlooking the Rhine and once covered five times its present area. The main entrance is a tall square clock or gate tower of about 1300, from which a path along the former moat leads to the remains of the Darmstadt Building, the living quarters of the landgraves of Hesse-Darmstadt, built in Tudor style with pointed gables.

Beneath the path lies a great cellar, arched over in two phases in 1587–1589. It is 24 metres long and about 16 metres wide and high, with walls up to 4 metres thick, the largest self-supporting vaulted cellar in Europe, and it can hold 400 people. It once housed a wine barrel of 200,000 litres and, restored in 1997, now serves for concerts and theatre. Beside the Darmstadt Building stood a tower 54 metres tall, to which a narrow round top was added in the 14th century.

The former chapel, the only finished room of the original castle, houses a museum with a model of the castle before its destruction. Beyond it lay the medieval courtyard, with a bakery, pharmacy, garden, brewery, well and livestock that allowed the castle to withstand a long siege. In peacetime 300 to 600 people lived in the complex; during a siege the number could swell to 4,500. Traces of the original white-painted 13th-century plaster survive on some walls.

After its expansions the castle was the largest fortress in the Middle Rhine Valley between Koblenz and Mainz. In 1924 the state gave the ruin to the town of St Goar on condition that it was not sold, and in 1998 the town leased it to a nearby hotel; some of the outer buildings now house a hotel, wellness centre and restaurant.

Georg Friedrich, Prince of Prussia, claimed that the lease breached the terms of the gift and that the castle should be returned to the Hohenzollern family. A court dismissed the claim in June 2019, and in January 2020 he reached an out-of-court settlement with the town, under which St. Goar works with the Princess Kira of Prussia Foundation, a charity for socially disadvantaged young people.
rhenish-hesse: Rhenish Hesse, Rheinhessen, is a region and former government district in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate. It lies on the west bank of the Upper Rhine and stretches west to the Nahe and Alsenz rivers and south to the mouth of the Isenach. It borders the Rhineland to the north-west, the Palatinate to the south-west and South Hesse across the Rhine. Its hilly landscape includes the Rhenish-Hessian Hills along the Selz river, known as the land of the thousand hills, which rise to 358 m at the Kappelberg.

The Mainz Basin, a marine basin, covered the area about 38 to 12 million years ago, and the land is marked by loess and marl. The Hunsrück and Taunus protect it from cold winds, so that wine and fruit are grown on a large scale. The region holds the cities of Mainz, capital of Rhineland-Palatinate, and Worms, and the districts of Mainz-Bingen and Alzey-Worms.

The lands gained importance when the Treaty of Verdun of 843 allotted them to King Louis the German. They formed part of the core of Rhenish Franconia and held the Imperial Cathedrals of Worms and Mainz, built in the High Middle Ages. The Worms Synagogue and the Jewish Cemetery are among the oldest in Europe. After the Thirty Years' War the area became a patchwork of the Catholic Electorate of Mainz, the Prince-Bishopric of Worms and the Protestant Electoral Palatinate.

The First French Republic occupied Rhenish Hesse in 1792, during the War of the First Coalition. At the Congress of Vienna Grand Duke Louis I of Hesse had to give up his Westphalian territories and received this district on the left bank of the Rhine in compensation. He changed his title to Grand Duke of Hesse and by Rhine, from which the name of the region comes. The region was later part of the People's State of Hesse, and in Allied-occupied Germany it was made a district of the new state of Rhineland-Palatinate in 1946.

Rhenish Hesse is the largest of the 13 regions producing German wine, and is best known abroad as the home of Liebfraumilch. Most of the wine is white, from varieties such as Riesling, Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau, and the best-known area is the Rhine Terrace near Oppenheim and Nierstein. Red varieties are grown around Ingelheim and Gundersheim. The snack Weck, Worscht un Woi is known beyond the region, partly through the Mainz carnival. Many inhabitants commute to Mainz, Wiesbaden or Frankfurt.
rhind-mathematical-papyrus: The papyrus, also designated papyrus British Museum 10057 and 10058 and Brooklyn Museum 37.1784Ea-b, is one of two well-known mathematical papyri, the other being the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus. It is the larger but the younger of the two. In its opening lines the scribe Ahmose, whom historians of mathematics call Ahmes, presents the work as giving accurate reckoning for inquiring into things and the knowledge of all things. He writes that it was copied in regnal year 33 under the king Awserre, the prenomen of the Hyksos king Apepi, from an ancient copy made in the time of Nimaatre, the prenomen of Amenemhat III of the Twelfth Dynasty.

A separate historical note on the back, probably from year 11 of Apepi's successor Khamudi, records that the Theban ruler broke into Tjaru; Thomas Schneider infers that the Hyksos capital Avaris fell to Ahmose I not much later.

The text opens with a title page, a table of 2/n for odd n from 3 to 101 written as sums of unit fractions, and a smaller table for the numbers 1 to 9 divided by 10. Ninety-one numbered items follow. Problems 1 to 40 treat arithmetic and elementary algebra, among them the division of loaves among ten men, linear equations called aha problems and measures of grain. Problems 41 to 60 are geometry: the volumes of cylindrical and rectangular granaries and the areas of rectangles, triangles, trapezoids and the circle. Problem 48 treats a circle's area as 64/81 of its circumscribing square, which implies a value of pi of 256/81, about 3.16.

The third part is a miscellany: tables, problems on the strength of bread and beer, and the feed of fowl and oxen. Problem 79 lists seven houses, 49 cats, 343 mice, 2401 ears of spelt and 16807 hekats, a geometric progression whose wording resembles the later riddle As I was going to St Ives.

Alexander Henry Rhind, a Scottish antiquarian, bought two parts of the papyrus at Luxor in 1858, and it was said to have been found in one of the small buildings near the Ramesseum. The British Museum, where most of the papyrus is kept, acquired it in 1865 together with the Egyptian Mathematical Leather Roll. The American Egyptologist Edwin Smith independently bought fragments in the mid-1860s; his daughter gave them in 1906 to the New York Historical Society, and they are now in the Brooklyn Museum. An 18 cm central section is missing. T. Eric Peet published the text in 1923, and Arnold Buffum Chace's compendium of 1927 to 1929 included photographs.
rhine: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometres long and drains an area of 185,000 square kilometres. It begins in the Swiss canton of Graubünden, where the Anterior Rhine, traditionally traced to Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass, joins the Posterior Rhine near Reichenau. As the Alpine Rhine it turns north near Chur and forms the Swiss border with Liechtenstein and Austria before entering Lake Constance.

The High Rhine runs west from Stein am Rhein over the Rhine Falls and is joined by the Aare, which more than doubles its discharge. At Basel the river bends north through the Upper Rhine Plain, takes in the Neckar, the Main and the Moselle, and from Bonn runs through the North German Plain as the Lower Rhine. In the Netherlands it forms, with the Meuse and the Scheldt, the largest river delta in Europe, splitting into the Waal, the Nederrijn and the IJssel.

About 11,000 years ago the Rhine's estuary lay in the Strait of Dover, and dry land called Doggerland still joined Britain to the continent until the sea overtopped it about 9,000 years ago. The river enters recorded history in the 1st century BCE, when Roman geographers made it the boundary between Gaul and Germania. By then La Tène culture covered almost its whole length, and the Upper Rhine formed a contact zone between Celtic and Germanic peoples. The Rhine and the Danube made up much of the Roman Empire's northern inland boundary.

By the 6th century the Rhine lay within Francia. In the 9th century it formed part of the border between Middle and Eastern Francia, and in the 10th century it lay wholly within the Holy Roman Empire. The mouths of the Rhine, in the county of Holland, passed to the Burgundian Netherlands in the 15th century. Archduke Sigismund of Austria sold Alsace to Burgundy in 1469, and it fell to France in the Thirty Years' War. When the Holy Roman Empire collapsed, the length of the river fell to the First French Empire and its client states. The many castles along the river show its importance as a trade route.

Among the largest cities on the Rhine are Cologne, Rotterdam, Düsseldorf, Duisburg, Strasbourg, Mannheim, Ludwigshafen, Arnhem and Basel. It passes through four countries and forms six different country borders. The German states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate and the French departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin take their names from it, and its name derives from the Gaulish Rēnos.
rhine-province: The Rhine Province, also called Rhenish Prussia, was the westernmost province of the Kingdom of Prussia and later of the Free State of Prussia, from 1822 to 1946. Its capital was Koblenz, and the provincial assembly met in Düsseldorf. Cologne was the largest and most important city. The province was divided into five districts, Koblenz, Düsseldorf, Cologne, Aachen and Trier, and about 200 km of the Rhine lay inside it. In 1905 it had 6,435,778 inhabitants, mostly Catholics on the left bank, and it was the most densely populated part of Prussia. Its coal, iron and other minerals made it the most important manufacturing district of Germany, with Aachen and Düsseldorf as its two chief industrial centres.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Prussia gained the duchies of Cleves, Berg, Gelderland and Jülich, the ecclesiastical principalities of Trier and Cologne, the free cities of Aachen and Cologne and nearly a hundred small lordships and abbeys. In 1822 these were joined to form the Rhine Province, which had 8.0 million inhabitants by 1939. After the Armistice of 1918 Allied forces occupied the Rhineland, and the Treaty of Versailles continued the occupation and demilitarised the area. The treaty separated the Saar from the province and gave the cantons of Eupen, Malmedy and Sankt Vith to Belgium. The last Allied troops left in 1930.

On 7 March 1936 Nazi Germany remilitarised the Rhineland with very little force, in violation of the Treaty of Versailles. France did not intervene, and the British government did not oppose the step in principle, though it disliked the manner of it. In the fighting of 1944 and 1945 the U.S. Army lost 24,000 troops in the Hürtgen Forest. In February and March 1945 Operation Veritable cleared German forces from the west bank of the Rhine, and on 7 March 1945 U.S. troops captured the last intact Rhine bridge at Remagen.

After Germany's unconditional surrender in 1945 the province was split between the French and British occupation zones, and it was abolished in August 1946. Its northern part, under British administration, merged with the former province of Westphalia to form North Rhine-Westphalia, and most of the southern part, under French administration, joined the Palatinate and other territories to form Rhineland-Palatinate. The Saarland became a separate protectorate in February 1946 and joined the Federal Republic in 1957. The Landschaftsverband Rheinland, set up in 1953 within North Rhine-Westphalia, can be regarded as the direct successor of the province's administration.
rhineland: The Rhineland has no fixed boundary. It reaches west to the borders with Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands, east to the Bergisches Land and south to the North Palatine Uplands. Its southern and eastern parts are hill country, the Westerwald, Hunsrück, Siebengebirge, Taunus and Eifel, cut by river valleys, chiefly the Middle Rhine and its tributaries the Ahr, Moselle and Nahe. It also takes in the western part of the Ruhr industrial region and the Cologne Lowland. The lands on the western shore show strong Roman influence, including viticulture, and in the core territories much of the population is Catholic.

At the earliest historical period the territories between the Ardennes and the Rhine were held by the Treveri, the Eburones and other Celtic tribes. Julius Caesar conquered those on the west bank and Augustus set up fortified posts on the Rhine, but the Romans never gained a firm footing on the east bank. As Roman power declined the Franks pushed forward on both banks. In the Holy Roman Empire the Rhineland broke up into many small principalities, among them the ecclesiastical electorates of Cologne and Trier, the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg and the Free Imperial Cities of Aachen and Cologne. Aachen was the place of coronation of the German emperors.

At the Peace of Basel in 1795 France took the whole left bank, then home to about 1.6 million people. French rule until 1814 swept away feudal privileges and historic taxes and introduced the Napoleonic Code, which stayed in effect for a century. The Congress of Vienna gave the lower Rhenish districts to Prussia, and in 1822 they became the Rhine Province.

Allied forces occupied the Rhineland after the Armistice of 11 November 1918, and the Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the area west of the Rhine and within 50 kilometres east of it. The last occupation ended on 30 June 1930. On 7 March 1936 German troops marched in, in breach of the treaty, and met no opposition from France or the United Kingdom. In 1946 the region was divided among the new states of Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate. North Rhine-Westphalia is a major industrial area, while in Rhineland-Palatinate agriculture matters more, including the vineyards of the Ahr, Middle Rhine and Moselle.
rhineland-palatinate: Rhineland-Palatinate is a landlocked state in western Germany, bordering France, Luxembourg and Belgium. Its major rivers are the Rhine, including the Middle Rhine, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Moselle. The northern half is formed by the Rhenish Massif, which includes the Eifel, the Moselle Valley, the Hunsrück and the Westerwald, while the Palatinate and Rhenish Hesse form most of the southern half. The mild climate of the deep Rhine and Moselle valleys allows fig, olive and almond trees to grow there. Forests cover 42 percent of the area.

The region has a long history, from the control of the Franks to the Holy Roman Empire, and saw fighting in both world wars. The league of ShUM cities, the Jewish communities of Mainz, Speyer and Worms, became the centre of Jewish life in medieval times. The state itself is young. The French military administration formed it on 30 August 1946, mainly from the southern part of the Prussian Rhine Province, Rhenish Hesse, the western part of Nassau and the Bavarian Rhenish Palatinate, and it was the last state in the Western Zone of Occupation to be established. The name Rhineland-Palatinate was first confirmed in the constitution adopted by referendum on 18 May 1947.

War damage meant that Mainz could not house the new administration, and the government and parliament sat provisionally in Koblenz until the Landtag decided on 16 May 1950 to move to Mainz. A sense of community developed only gradually in a state drawn up largely without regard to its inhabitants' historical affiliations. Referendums held on 19 January 1975 on transferring regions to other states produced no majority anywhere.

The state has about 4.05 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Mainz. It became part of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949. Six of Germany's thirteen quality wine regions lie within it, Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Mosel, Nahe, Mittelrhein and Ahr, and between 65 and 70 percent of the country's wine grapes originate there. The chemical industry, represented by BASF at Ludwigshafen, is the principal employer.
rhins-of-galloway: The peninsula ends in the north at Corsewall and Milleur Points, measures 28 miles (45 kilometres) from end to end and takes its name from the Gaelic rinn, point. Its west coast, on the North Channel, has steep cliffs, while the calmer east coast has sandy beaches. Exposed to Atlantic westerlies, it receives around 1,000 millimetres of rain a year and is mainly dairy and beef farmland, and the North Atlantic drift keeps frosts rare enough for palms to grow at the Logan Botanic Garden. In ancient times boats were dragged across the isthmus between the East and West Tarbets to avoid the currents off the Mull.

The Britons are recalled in the farm name Drumbreddan, the ridge of the Britons; their chieftains lived in hill-forts such as Dunman and in brochs such as Doon Castle at Ardwell Point. The Novantae, a Celtic tribe, were based in the area. When Agricola was in Britain in 81, a road was built west from Dalswinton to Stranraer, leading some to argue that any attack he made on Ireland would have started here. Crofting, salt pans and kelp harvesting long sustained a sparse population.

Sea links to Ireland, Glasgow and Liverpool later carried farm produce out, and a railway was laid to Portpatrick for the mail boat to Donaghadee. As ships grew, the route moved in 1849 to Stranraer Harbour in Loch Ryan, from where ferries still sail to Belfast and Larne. In the Second World War the area was an important station for anti-U-boat work, with flying boats at RAF Station Wig Bay and RAF Station Stranraer, and Luce Bay was a bombing range.

The Rhins are a patchwork of farms, increasingly turning to tourism. The Mull of Galloway is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and an RSPB nature reserve where razorbills, guillemots and puffins nest. The Southern Upland Way begins at Portpatrick, and Lochnaw Castle near Leswalt is the ancestral seat of Clan Agnew.
rhodes: Rhodes is the largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands and their historical capital, and the ninth largest island in the Mediterranean. It lies northeast of Crete and southeast of Athens. The island is shaped like a spearhead, 79.7 kilometres long and 38 across at its widest, with an area of about 1,400 square kilometres. The city of Rhodes stands at the northern tip, at the site of the ancient and modern harbours. The interior is mountainous and forested with pine and cypress. Its Greek name, Ródos, resembles the word for rose, and it is called the Island of the Sun after its patron god Helios.

Humans lived on Rhodes from at least the late Neolithic. Urban settlements such as Asomatos arose at the end of the third millennium BCE, the Minoan Civilisation established a settlement at Tiranda in the sixteenth century BCE, and Mycenaean Greeks settled in the fifteenth. The Dorians who came in the eighth century BCE built the three cities of Lindus, Ialysus and Camirus. Athens defeated the Persians, who had overrun the island, in 478 BCE, and the Rhodian cities joined the Athenian League.

In the third century BCE the Rhodo-Egyptian alliance with the Ptolemies of Alexandria controlled trade through the Aegean. The Colossus of Rhodes, completed in 280 BCE, fell in an earthquake in 226 BCE. In 164 BCE Rhodes concluded a formal alliance with Rome, which confirmed Rome's predominance in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Byzantine period began in 395, and Rhodes became capital of the Roman province of the Islands. The Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem ruled the island from 1310 to 1522, and an earthquake on 3 May 1481 destroyed much of the city. Under the Ottomans the Kahal Shalom Synagogue was established in 1557. Italy seized Rhodes in 1912, and Turkey ceded it by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. German forces occupied it after the Italian Armistice of 8 September 1943, and most of the Jewish community was deported and killed. The island was ceded to Greece in 1947.

Rhodes forms a municipality of the South Aegean region, with 125,113 inhabitants in 2022. The medieval Old Town of the City of Rhodes is a World Heritage Site. The predominant religion is Greek Orthodox, with Latin Catholic, Muslim and Jewish communities as well. The Kahal Shalom Synagogue, in the Jewish quarter of the old town, is the oldest synagogue in Greece.
rhodesian-bush-war: The war's origins lie in the conquest of the region by the British South Africa Company in the late 19th century and the dissent of African leaders who opposed foreign rule. Britons began settling in Southern Rhodesia in the 1890s, and from 1923 the settlers effectively governed it. Property requirements kept many Black Africans from voting. After Harold Macmillan's Wind of Change speech Britain would grant independence to its African colonies only under majority rule, and many white Rhodesians feared chaos, as in the former Belgian Congo. Rhodesia's unilateral declaration of independence on 11 November 1965 won no diplomatic recognition, though South Africa and Portugal gave private support.

Nationalists and the British government of the time saw a war of national and racial liberation, and considered the country occupied and dominated by Britain since 1890. The Rhodesian government saw a fight by one part of the population on behalf of the whole against externally financed radicals and communists.

On 4 July 1964 ZANU insurgents murdered a white foreman, Pieter Oberholzer, and the Smith government detained ZANU and ZAPU leaders in August. Operating from bases in Zambia and later Mozambique, guerrillas began attacks. The Soviet Union supported ZIPRA, the armed wing of ZAPU, and China supported ZANLA, the armed wing of ZANU. The two sometimes fought each other. Rhodesia met sanctions by obtaining oil and arms through South Africa and Portugal.

After 1972 guerrilla activity grew, especially in the northeast. According to Rhodesian figures, from December 1972 to December 1979, 1,120 members of the security forces, 10,050 guerrillas killed in Rhodesia, 7,790 black civilians and 468 white civilians died. An internal settlement led to the election of 24 April 1979, in which Bishop Abel Muzorewa became the first black prime minister of Zimbabwe-Rhodesia. Nkomo's and Mugabe's forces rejected it as a puppet government, and it won no international recognition.

Talks at Lancaster House in London in December 1979 between the Zimbabwe-Rhodesian government, the United Kingdom and Mugabe and Nkomo's Patriotic Front produced the Lancaster House Agreement. The country returned temporarily to British control, and elections in March 1980 under British and Commonwealth supervision were won by ZANU. Robert Mugabe became the first Prime Minister of Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980. The Rhodesian army was merged with the guerrilla forces. Norma Kriger has questioned the nationalist account of peasant support, and Luise White the claim that the Rhodesian army won every battle but lost at Lancaster House.
rhodesian-front: The party was founded on 13 March 1962 by a merger of the Dominion Party, defectors from the anti-Whitehead wing of the United Federal Party and former members of the Southern Rhodesia Liberal Party. Its members, from advocates of gradual change to open segregationists, were united mainly against Prime Minister Edgar Whitehead's plans for a transition to majority rule and against the UK's demands for majority rule before independence. First led by Winston Field, it was led through most of its life by its co-founder Ian Smith. It campaigned in 1962 on white fears of events in the Congo and Kenya, pledging to keep power in responsible hands.

Its fifteen founding principles included keeping the Land Apportionment Act, opposing compulsory racial integration, protecting white workers' jobs and the practice of Christianity. Its membership was all white, and it kept separate schools and public services under a policy it called separate economic advancement, which Smith claimed would lead to an equal partnership between black and white. Unlike South Africa's National Party it passed no laws on marriage between races, but it upheld the white minority's hold on land and the economy.

The constitution of 1969 divided the electoral rolls by race, giving about 270,000 whites 50 seats in the Assembly and about 6 million Africans 16. The Land Tenure Act of the same year reserved equal areas of 45 million acres for each, while the most fertile farmland stayed in white hands. In 1977 hardliners opposed to Smith's talks with black nationalist leaders broke away to form the Rhodesian Action Party.

In the elections of 1980 the party won all 20 seats reserved for whites under the power-sharing agreement it had negotiated. It became the Republican Front on 6 June 1981 and, on 23 July 1984, the Conservative Alliance of Zimbabwe, open to members of every colour. Eleven of its 20 members of parliament defected over the next four years, yet it won 15 of the white seats in 1985. In October 1987 the government of Robert Mugabe abolished the reserved seats, and many white members became independents or joined ZANU–PF.
rhodope-mountains: The Rhodopes are the largest mountain range by area in Bulgaria, with over 83 percent of their area in the south of that country and the rest in Greece. They are part of the Rila-Rhodope massif, the oldest landmass on the Balkan Peninsula, about 240 kilometres long and 100 to 120 kilometres wide. The highest peak is Golyam Perelik, at 2,191 metres. The range is a complex system of ridges and deep river valleys, with karst areas, gorges and large caves.

The name is of Thracian origin and is interpreted as a river name meaning rusty or reddish river. In Greek mythology, Queen Rhodope of Thrace, wife of King Haemus, offended the gods and was changed into a mountain by Zeus and Hera as a punishment.

The mountains have been inhabited since prehistoric times. The first known inhabitants were the Thracians, who built temples, cities and fortresses, among them the sacred city of Perperikon, 15 kilometres north-east of Kardzhali. Frequent mention of the Rhodope in Greek and Latin sources suggests that the mountain played an important part in the political and religious life of the Thracian tribes. An oracle on its summits was consulted by Alexander the Great and later by the father of Octavian Augustus. The Rhodope was the Thracians' last refuge of resistance against the Romans.

In the Middle Ages the range belonged to the Bulgarian and Byzantine empires, which often exchanged it, and a dense network of castles guarded the trade routes. It fell under Ottoman rule between 1371 and 1375, and in the 16th and 17th centuries the Ottoman authorities began a process of Islamisation. After the April Uprising of 1876 the Ottomans killed about 5,000 people in Batak alone. The northern Rhodopes passed in 1878 to Eastern Rumelia, and the rest of the range was annexed by Bulgaria after the First Balkan War. After the Second Balkan War and the First World War, Greece occupied the southern slopes and the Bulgarian population there fled to Bulgaria.

The range has long been a place of ethnic and religious diversity. Eastern Orthodox Bulgarians and Greeks live there alongside Muslim communities, including the Pomaks in the west and Bulgarian and Greek Turks, especially in the east, as well as Sarakatsani and Aromanians. The Western Rhodopes hold the Eastern Orthodox Bachkovo Monastery and the winter resort of Pamporovo. The Greek part includes the Rodopi Mountain Range National Park and the Dadia Forest reserve, a habitat for birds of prey.
rhodri-the-great: Rhodri ap Merfyn was the son of Merfyn Frych, king of Gwynedd, and Nest, daughter of Cadell ap Brochfael of Powys. Merfyn set out from his native Isle of Man, probably with Norse help, and made his bid for the throne of Gwynedd in 826 as a representative of the line of Cynan Dindaethwy, whose only child Esyllt was Merfyn's mother. Merfyn died in 844 and Rhodri succeeded him. He appears to have kept his father's rule in both Gwynedd and the Isle of Man, since a contemporary poem on his death in the margin of the Annals of Ulster calls him Ruaidri of Man.

Few events of the reign are known. In 853 Burgred of Mercia and Æthelwulf of Wessex invaded Wales and received its submission, and Rhodri may have been among those who submitted. In 856 he killed Orm, a leader of the viking faction that Irish sources call the Dubgenti, and this may be the victory marked by a Latin poem by Sedulius Scottus. In 877 the Dubgenti attacked him in the Sunday Battle in Anglesey and forced him to take refuge in Ireland.

Rhodri returned to Wales in 878 and was killed, together with his son Gwriad, by Ceolwulf II of Mercia. Three years later the Annales Cambriæ record a Battle of the Conwy, as revenge for Rhodri, fought by his sons against Ceolwulf's successor Æthelred of Mercia. After Mercian overlordship was broken, his sons Anarawd and Cadell overran all of Wales except the south-east, with Anarawd keeping Gwynedd and Cadell holding Ceredigion and later Dyfed. His reign probably saw the codification of the earliest surviving Welsh genealogies, those of the First Dynasty of Gwynedd, the oldest such collection in medieval Welsh literature.
rhon: The Rhön Mountains are a group of low mountains in central Germany, around the border area where Hesse, Bavaria and Thuringia meet. They lie at the extreme southeast end of the East Hesse Highlands and are partly the result of ancient volcanic activity. The Fulda and its valley separate them from the Vogelsberg to the west. The range is bounded by the Knüll to the northwest, the Thuringian Forest to the northeast, the Grabfeld to the southeast, Lower Franconia to the south and the Spessart to the southwest.

Geographers divide the Rhön by the effects of volcanic activity into the Anterior Rhön, the Kuppen Rhön and the High Rhön. The High Rhön covers 344 square kilometres, and its plateaux, starting at 600 to 700 metres, are covered by solid basalt. Its highest peak is the Wasserkuppe, about 950 metres, in Hesse. The kuppen of the surrounding Kuppen Rhön are the stumps of weathered former volcanoes. The Fulda rises on the Wasserkuppe and is the left headstream of the Weser, and the Franconian Saale, the Sinn and the Ulster also rise in or near the range.

The name Rhön is often thought to derive from a Celtic word, raino, meaning hilly, though other explanations are possible. A Celtic presence is well established, with an important Celtic town at the Milseburg. Up to the 10th century parts of the Rhön belonged to the Altgau Buchonia, a term coined by the Romans in Late Antiquity for an ancient beech forest. Monks of Fulda Abbey used the name for the area around Fulda and more distant parts of the Rhön. In the Middle Ages beech was an important raw material, and large-scale clearing produced the land of open spaces, of which about 30 per cent is forested today.

The far view from the heights made them sites for hilltop castles. Hauneck Castle on the Stoppelsberg oversaw the ancient road Antsanvia and protected the villages of the Haune valley, and its ruins can still be seen. The Würzburg Defences, a landwehr, were built on the High Rhön to protect its farmers. A Christian community, the Bruderhof, lived in the Rhön from 1926 until Nazi persecution dissolved it in 1937.

In 1991 UNESCO declared parts of the Rhön a Biosphere Reserve on account of its high-altitude ecosystem. The area is rich in habitats and species, among them raised bogs such as the Red Moor and the Black Moor and the silver thistle, the symbol of the region. The mountains attract hikers, with nearly 6,000 km of trails, and gliding enthusiasts have come since the early 20th century. Observation Post Alpha, a Cold War lookout, is now a memorial.
rhone: The Rhône begins as meltwater of the Rhône Glacier in the Swiss canton of Valais, at an altitude of about 2,208 metres. It flows southwest through Gletsch and the Goms, becomes a great mountain river in a glacial valley, and at Martigny turns sharply north. The narrowing of its valley near Saint-Maurice has long given it strategic importance for the control of the Alpine passes. It enters Lake Geneva near Le Bouveret and leaves it at the city of Geneva, after 290 kilometres in Switzerland.

In France it passes through the southern Jura and receives its largest tributary, the Saône, at Lyon, the most populous city on its course. It then follows a southward course in the valley between the Alps and the Massif Central, joined by the Isère, the Durance, the Ardèche and others. At Arles it divides into the Grand Rhône and the Petit Rhône, which form the delta of the Camargue before reaching the Mediterranean. Its name continues the Latin Rhodanus, and the Gaulish name was probably *Rodonos or *Rotonos.

The Rhône has been an important highway since the times of the Greeks and Romans. It was the main trade route from the Mediterranean to east-central Gaul, and helped convey Greek cultural influences to the western Hallstatt and the later La Tène cultures. Celtic tribes living near it included the Seduni, Sequani, Allobroges, Helvetii, Vocontii and Volcae Arecomici.

Navigation was difficult, because of fierce currents, shallows, spring floods and late-summer droughts. Until the 19th century passengers travelled in water coaches drawn by men or horses, or under sail, often carrying a painted cross as protection. Sailing barges of 75 tonnes were hauled upstream by 50 to 80 horses. The first experimental steamboat was built at Lyon by Jouffroy d'Abbans in 1783, and regular steam services ran from 1829 to 1952.

The Compagnie Nationale du Rhône was founded in 1933 to improve navigation, generate electricity, irrigate land and protect riverside towns from flooding. From 1948 the French government built a series of dams and diversion canals, each with a lock beside a hydroelectric plant, and twelve plants were built between 1964 and 1980.

Before railways and highways the river joined Arles, Avignon, Valence, Vienne and Lyon to the Mediterranean ports of Fos-sur-Mer, Marseille and Sète, and a barge trip down it took three weeks. Today a motorised vessel takes three days. The Saône links the Rhône to a canal network reaching the Seine, Marne, Moselle and Rhine. The river is, with the Po and the Nile, one of the three Mediterranean rivers with the largest discharge, and the Rhône valley's dams produce about 16 per cent of French hydroelectric power.
rhuddlan: The name joins the Welsh words rhudd, red, and glan, riverbank. The town lies mainly on the right bank of the Clwyd, directly south of the seaside town of Rhyl, and was historically in Flintshire. People camped by the river here more than 9,000 years ago: in February 2021 Aeon Archaeology announced the find of more than 300 Stone Age tools and pieces, among them scrapers, microliths and flakes of chert and flint.

In 921 the Anglo-Saxon king Edward the Elder founded a burh named Cledematha, the mouth of the Clwyd, at the site. In the following century Rhuddlan was the seat of a Welsh cantref and served as the capital of Gwynedd for Gruffydd ap Llywelyn, who ruled from 1055 to 1063. About 1072 the Norman Robert of Rhuddlan built a castle at Twthill, and in 1086 the Domesday Book recorded a small settlement in the hundred of Ati's Cross in Cheshire.

In the 1180s Dafydd ab Owain set up a mint at Rhuddlan, later kept by Llywelyn the Great, which struck the first native Welsh coins since the reign of Hywel Dda. Edward I had the new castle built between 1277 and 1282, soon after his conquest of Wales; its great round tower and many walls survive. Here he signed the Statute of Rhuddlan, laying down how the Principality of Wales created by the princes of Gwynedd was to be governed. The poet Hugh of Rhuddlan wrote in Old French at the end of the 12th century.

Rhuddlan is a town and community in Denbighshire, with 3,709 people at the 2011 census, and gave its name to a district from 1974 to 1996. Its first Welsh chapel, at 17 Cross Street, dates from 1771. The hymn tune Rhuddlan, spread by Ralph Vaughan Williams in The English Hymnal of 1906, is named after the town.
rhydderch-hael: Rhydderch, also called Riderch I of Alt Clut, ruled a Brittonic kingdom of the Hen Ogledd, the Old North of Britain, and is recorded as flourishing from 580 to about 614. Adomnán's Life of Columba, written around 700, tells that he sent a secret message to the saint asking how he would die, and that Columba foretold he would die at home in his bed. Historians take this as accurate, since Adomnán wrote when the king's life was probably still well remembered.

The 9th-century Historia Brittonum names Rhydderch with Urien, Gwallog and Morcant as kings who fought Hussa of Bernicia. This is often read as an alliance, though the text does not say they fought together; if they did, he may have been at the siege of Ynys Metcaut, Lindisfarne, where Urien was assassinated by Morcant. He was possibly the leader of the victorious army at the Battle of Arfderydd, which the Annals Cambriae date to 573 without naming the combatants.

Rhydderch appears often in later medieval works in Welsh and Latin. The 13th-century Black Book of Chirk tells of an expedition by Clydno Eidyn and the Tri Hael, Rhydderch, Nudd Hael and Mordaf Hael, to Gwynedd to avenge Elidir Mwynfawr, a story whose historical value is doubted. In the Life of Saint Kentigern he is the saint's royal patron, and so linked to the founding of Glasgow; Kentigern saves his queen, Languoreth, by finding her lost ring, and the salmon with a ring in its mouth on the city's arms recalls the story.

Several Welsh Triads name him, pointing to a once well-known story now lost. He owns the sword Dyrnwyn, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, which burst into flame when a well-born man drew it; everyone who asked for it received it, and this, the list says, is why he was called the Generous.
rhys-ap-gruffydd: Rhys was the fourth son of Gruffydd ap Rhys and Gwenllian ferch Gruffudd, daughter of Gruffudd ap Cynan of Gwynedd. When he was born his father held only the commote of Caeo in Cantref Mawr. In the revolt of 1136 his mother was defeated and killed leading an army against Kidwelly, and his father died in 1137. Rhys first appears in 1146, fighting beside his brothers Cadell and Maredudd at the capture of Llansteffan Castle, and he became ruler of Deheubarth when Maredudd died in 1155.

Henry II forced him to submit in 1158 and left him little more than Cantref Mawr. In 1163 Rhys was seized and taken to England, then freed after a few weeks to rule that cantref. He joined the Welsh princes under Owain Gwynedd against Henry's invasion of 1165, which torrential rain turned back; Henry had Rhys's hostage son Maredudd blinded. Rhys then took Cardigan and Cilgerran and, after Owain's death in 1170, was the acknowledged leader of the Welsh princes.

From 1171 he kept peace with Henry, sending troops to help him against his rebellious sons in 1173 and 1174. He built Cardigan Castle, the earliest recorded native-built stone castle in Wales, and Carreg Cennen, founded Talley Abbey, the first Premonstratensian house in Wales, and the nunnery of Llanllyr. After Henry died in 1189 he attacked the surrounding Norman lordships, and in 1196 he took Carmarthen, Colwyn, Radnor and Painscastle and defeated Roger de Mortimer and Hugh de Say near Radnor.

His last years were troubled by his sons Maelgwn and Gruffudd, and in 1194 Maelgwn and Hywel defeated him and held him in Nevern castle. He died on 28 April 1197, excommunicate after a quarrel with Bishop Peter de Leia, who had his corpse scourged before burial in St Davids Cathedral. His chosen heir Gruffudd was soon captured by Maelgwn. The historian R. R. Davies credits him with making Deheubarth the premier Welsh kingdom but notes that his accord with Henry was personal and that he could not control his sons. Through his daughter Gwenllian he was an ancestor of the Tudors.
rhys-ap-tewdwr: Rhys ap Tewdwr was born in what is now Carmarthenshire, a member of the House of Dinefwr, a branch descended from Rhodri the Great, and a great-grandson of Einion ab Owain and so a descendant of Hywel Dda. He claimed the throne of Deheubarth after his second cousin Rhys ab Owain was beheaded following the battle of Gwdig, at modern Goodwick, against Caradog ap Gruffydd in 1078. He married more than once; his last wife was Gwladys ferch Rhiwallon, daughter of Rhiwallon ap Cynfyn of the Mathrafal dynasty of Powys.

In 1081 Caradog ap Gruffydd invaded Deheubarth and Rhys took sanctuary in the Monastery of St David. Allied with Gruffudd ap Cynan, who was seeking to regain Gwynedd, he defeated and killed Caradog and his allies Trahaearn ap Caradog and Meilyr ap Rhiwallon at the Battle of Mynydd Carn the same year. After William the Conqueror's visit, Rhys paid him £40 a year for his kingdom, which kept relations good for the rest of William's life.

In 1088 Cadwgan ap Bleddyn of Powys drove him to Ireland, but Rhys returned the same year with a fleet from Ireland and defeated the men of Powys, killing two of Cadwgan's brothers, Madog and Rhiryd. When Cedifor ap Gollwyn, who traced his descent from the old kings of Dyfed, died in 1091, his sons demanded that Rhys give up the throne to Gruffudd ap Maredudd; Rhys defeated the rebels at St. Dogmaels and killed Gruffudd.

The Welsh chronicles record that Rhys was slain by the Frenchmen settled in Brycheiniog, and the Brut y Tywysogion adds that with him fell the kingdom of the Britons. The Normans then seized much of south Wales and fought the chieftains of Powys and Gwynedd over it. His eldest son Gruffydd was later allowed a small part of the kingdom, and through him Rhys was an ancestor of the Tudor dynasty. His daughter Nest bore a son to Henry I and then married Gerald de Windsor, Constable of Pembroke; their sons and grandsons, the FitzGerald conquerors of Ireland, were known as the sons of Nest.
riad-al-solh: Riad Al Solh was born in Sidon on 17 August 1894 to Sunni Muslim parents. His father, Reda Al Solh, was vice-governor in Nabatiyyah and in Sidon and a leading Arab nationalist. In 1915 Ottoman forces tried him, and he went into exile in Smyrna. He later served as Minister of the Interior in Emir Faisal's government in Damascus. Riad spent most of his youth in Istanbul, where his father was a deputy in the Ottoman Parliament, and he studied law and political science at the University of Paris.

Solh served as prime minister of Lebanon twice. His first term ran from 25 September 1943 to 10 January 1945, and President Bishara Al Khouri chose him as the first prime minister. In November 1943 the two made the National Pact, al Mithaq al Watani, an unwritten gentleman's agreement that gave the offices of president, prime minister and speaker of parliament to the Maronite Christians, the Sunni Muslims and the Shiite Muslims, on the basis of the 1932 census. During this term he was also Minister of Finance from September 1943 to July 1944 and minister of supplies and reserves from 3 July 1944 to 9 January 1945.

He held the premiership again from 14 December 1946 to 14 February 1951, again under Khouri. He was critical of King Abdullah, and in his second term he played a significant part in winning the blessing of the political committee of the Arab League for the All-Palestine Government. He is regarded as one of the founders of Lebanon, for he was able to unite the religious groups in the struggle for independence.

Solh escaped unhurt from an assassination attempt in March 1950 by a member of the Syrian Social Nationalist Party. Several months after he left office he was shot dead on 17 July 1951 at Marka Airport in Amman by three gunmen of the same party, who acted in revenge for the execution of Anton Saadeh, one of its founders.

He was married to Fayza al-Jabiri, a Syrian and sister of the former Syrian prime minister Saadallah al-Jabiri. They had several daughters and a son, Reda, who died in infancy. Their eldest daughter, Alia, followed his path, and Leila became one of the first two women ministers in Lebanon. Patrick Seale's book The Struggle for Arab Independence (2011) focuses on Solh's career, and a square in downtown Beirut, Riad al-Solh Square, bears his name.
rialto: The Rialto lies in the sestiere of San Polo, on the left bank of the Grand Canal. By the ninth century a small area in the middle of the Realtine Islands, on either side of a channel called the Rio Businiacus, was known as the Rivoaltus, meaning high bank. In time the Businiacus came to be called the Grand Canal, and the name Rialto came to refer only to the district on its left bank.

The district gained in importance in 1097, when the city's market moved there. In the following century a bridge of boats was laid across the Grand Canal to reach it, and this was soon replaced by the Rialto Bridge. The market grew into both a retail and a wholesale centre. Warehouses were built, among them the Fondaco dei Tedeschi on the far side of the bridge, and shops selling luxury goods, banks on Rialto Square and insurance agencies opened. The city's tax offices and its abattoir were also in the Rialto.

A fire in 1514 destroyed most of the district's buildings, and the church of San Giacomo di Rialto was the only one to survive. The area was rebuilt gradually. The Fabriche Vechie date from this period and the Fabbriche Nuove from 1553, and the statue known as Il Gobbo di Rialto was carved in the same century.

The Rialto became a byword for trade in literature. In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, Salanio opens Act III, Scene I by asking: "What news on the Rialto?" Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote in Sonnet 19 of her Sonnets from the Portuguese that "The soul's Rialto hath its merchandise". The poet and satirist Pietro Aretino, who lived opposite the market in the Palazzo Bollani, wrote in 1550 of his view across the Grand Canal: "So I can truly say that I enjoy the most beautiful street and the liveliest view in the world."

The Rialto remains a busy retail quarter and the commercial heart of the city. The Erberia greengrocers' market is held there daily, and the fish market on the Campo della Pescheria sells shellfish, squid, cuttlefish, eels, crabs, octopus and lobsters.
riau: Riau extends from the eastern slopes of the Barisan Mountains to the Strait of Malacca, and includes several large islands in the strait. It borders North Sumatra, West Sumatra and Jambi on land, and has a maritime border with Malaysia. Its climate is wet and tropical, with a rainy and a dry season. Stone tools found in the Sengingi River area suggest the region was inhabited in prehistory.

The name has three suggested origins. One derives it from the Portuguese rio, river, recalling a Portuguese expedition of 1514 up the Siak River in search of a kingdom and of followers of Sultan Mahmud Shah, who had fled after the fall of the Malacca Sultanate.

Muara Takus is a Buddhist temple complex believed to be a remnant of the Srivijaya empire, and many parts of Riau are thought to have been under Srivijaya between the 7th and 14th centuries. Islam reached the archipelago through the Samudera Pasai Sultanate in Aceh, spreading by trade, marriage and the work of clerics. Later the region came under the Malay sultanates of Siak Sri Indrapura, Indragiri and Johor, which became Dutch protectorates and then puppet states of the Dutch East Indies.

Japan occupied Rengat on 31 March 1942 and soon all of Riau. Prisoners of war and more than 100,000 romusha, mostly Javanese, were made to build a 220-kilometre railway from Pekanbaru to Muaro Sijunjung; almost a third of the European prisoners and more than half of the Indonesian workers died. After independence Riau belonged to the provinces of Sumatra and then Central Sumatra, and on 10 August 1957 Central Sumatra was divided into Riau, Jambi and West Sumatra.

Riau is a province of Indonesia with Pekanbaru as its capital and largest city. It is divided into ten regencies and two cities. Indonesian is the official language, while a local dialect of Malay is the lingua franca; Minangkabau, Hokkien and Batak languages are also spoken. Malays are the largest ethnic group, with Javanese, Minangkabau, Batak and Chinese also represented.

The economy rests on petroleum, natural gas, rubber, palm oil and fibre plantations. Forest cover fell from 78 per cent in 1982 to 33 per cent in 2005, and fires linked to clearing have caused haze across the region. Riau is regarded as the homeland of the Malays, and its customs are largely Malay.
riau-archipelago: The Riau Archipelago is a geographic term rather than an administrative one: it names the core group of islands of the Riau Islands Province, lying south of Singapore and east of the province of Riau on Sumatra. In Indonesian both the archipelago and the province are called Kepulauan Riau, and the initials BBK, for Batam, Bintan and Karimun, are also used for the islands. The main islands are Batam, Rempang, Galang, Bintan, Combol, Kundur and Karimun. Historically the name did not cover the Natuna Islands, while Singapore was counted among the islands, at least in the Islamic era.

Between about 650 and 1377 the area seems to have lain well within the bounds of the Srivijaya empire. The Jambi Kingdom sacked the Srivijaya capital in 1088 and spread Malay as a lingua franca, and the Pamalayu expedition of the Singhasari empire attacked the Jambi and Srivijaya forces in 1275. In the Malay Annals Bintan is the staging ground for the founding of a state at Temasek, the later Singapore. How far the Kingdom of Singapura, which lasted from 1299 to 1398, reached into the islands is not known.

When control passed to the Malacca Sultanate is unknown; that sultanate lasted until the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511. The Johor Sultanate held the islands until the death of Sultan Mahmud III in 1811, and after the succession dispute that followed they became part of the Riau-Lingga Sultanate, whose first sultan, Abdul Rahman, was crowned in 1812. Under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 Singapore ceased to be administered with them, and the rest of the archipelago became part of the Dutch Residency of Riau and Dependencies.

Tanjung Pinang, in the south of Bintan, is the capital of the Riau Islands Province, which was carved out of Riau Province in 2002. The Sijori Growth Triangle was formed in 1989 to speed up development, above all on Batam, and the area was formally included in a free-trade zone in 2009. The Malay population, once the dominant group, now makes up about a third of the population, mainly because of migration from elsewhere in Indonesia.
ribat: The word ribat is Arabic and means a hospice, hostel, base or retreat. It first named a small fortification built along a frontier in the early years of the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb to house volunteer soldiers, called murabitun. Ribats soon appeared along the frontier with the Byzantine Empire as well, where they attracted converts from Khorasan, in an area that became known as al-Awasim in the ninth century. In the abstract the word refers to the voluntary defence of Islam, and the one who performs ribat, classically a guard duty at a frontier outpost, is a murabit.

Over time the ribat took on other roles. Some became hostels for travellers on the main trade routes and so served as caravanserais, and others became centres for isolated Muslim communities. As soldiers no longer needed to be housed and supplied, many ribats turned into refuges for mystics and into Sufi lodges, known in Persian as khanqah and in former Ottoman lands as tekkes. The tradition was perhaps one of the early sources of the tariqas, the Sufi brotherhoods, and of the later zawiya, which spread across North Africa and the Sahara to West Africa, where such places are the homes of marabouts, religious teachers who are usually Sufis.

A ribat was usually inhabited by a shaykh, whose family and visitors could come to learn from him, and often held the tomb of its founder. Donations from wealthy merchants, landowners and influential leaders helped to establish these centres, and some received regular stipends. Most had a similar plan: a surrounding wall with an entrance, living rooms, storehouses, a watch tower for signalling an invasion, four to eight towers, and a mosque in the larger ones. Rabati Malik in Uzbekistan, built c. 1068–80, is partly intact. Some ribats were convents or retreat houses for Sufi women, where female shaykhas, scholars of law and many widows or divorcees lived in abstinence and worship.
ribchester: Ribchester is a village and civil parish in the Ribble Valley district, six miles north-west of Blackburn and twelve miles east of Preston. It stands at the foot of Longridge Fell on boulder clay laid by the River Ribble, whose meanders have left terraces around the village; the river is prone to spates and often floods it in winter. Stonygate Lane, running north, partly follows the old Roman road.

Excavations at Parsonage Avenue found a circular ditch of about 1300 BCE with urns holding cremated remains. The first Roman fort was built in timber in 72 or 73 CE by the 20th legion, renovated late in the 1st century and rebuilt in stone early in the 2nd, and a fort remained until the 4th century. Covering about 6 acres and garrisoned by cavalry, it was a large fort; work by the Manchester Classical Association in 1913 traced its headquarters building, which unusually fronted the main street with a colonnade. The Ribchester Hoard, found in 1796 about 10 feet below the surface, held the helmet with paterae, two basins and a bust of Minerva.

St Wilfrid's Church, first recorded in 1193 and believed to have been founded in the 8th century, stands almost over the fort's headquarters. John Leland in the 1540s described great squared stones, vaults and ancient coins, and William Camden recorded the saying that Ribchester was as rich as any town in Christendom. In the 17th and 18th centuries the village became a centre of cotton weaving, first in the weavers' homes and later in Bee Mill and Corporation Mill; the last weaving business closed in the 1980s.

The village had 1,598 people at the 2011 census and is chiefly a home for commuters to Blackburn, Preston and Manchester. The excavated granaries beside the churchyard and the Roman baths can be seen, and the Ribchester Roman Museum, founded by Margaret Greenall in 1915, holds many finds from the fort, with a replica of the helmet.
ribe: Ribe was a centre of commercial activity in the early 8th century, and the riches of Denmark may have originated there, with royal influence. Coins may have been struck there in 720, and whichever king dug the Kanhave Canal may have been involved in founding the town. Its trade contacts were mostly with Frisia and England.

Of over 300 sceatas found in Denmark, 216 come from in or around Ribe, most of them of the Frisian Wodan type and probably minted there in the early 8th century. In the early 9th century a ditch two metres wide, a demarcation rather than a fortification, was dug round a 12-hectare area, and later in the century it was replaced by a moat six to seven metres wide.

Archaeology shows an active and impressive market place in the 8th and 9th centuries and again at the end of the 11th, with little evidence between, so the town may have dwindled or even disappeared. About 860 Archbishop Ansgar asked King Horik II for the first Scandinavian church to be built in Ribe, then one of the most important trading cities in Scandinavia. Excavations have found between 2,000 and 3,000 Christian graves of the 9th century, which show a large Christian community living peacefully with the Vikings. A bishop and a cathedral are confirmed only from 948, when Leofdag was consecrated the first bishop.

Construction of Ribe Cathedral began in 1150 on top of an earlier church, most probably Ansgar's. The Treaty of Ribe was proclaimed in 1460. The town lies in a large region of low-lying marshland and has been repeatedly hit by storm floods, the most devastating being the Burchardi flood of 1634, whose marks can still be seen on the cathedral walls.

The Catholic diocese was dissolved in 1536 in the Reformation and succeeded by a Diocese of Ribe within the Protestant Church of Denmark. Hans Tausen, the leader of the Reformation in Denmark, was its bishop from 1542 to 1562. Before 1864 Ribe and its surroundings were an exclave of the Kingdom of Denmark, surrounded on three sides by the Duchy of Schleswig, until the Second Schleswig War and the Treaty of Vienna drew a new boundary south of the town.

Ribe is a town in south-western Jutland and is regarded as the oldest town in Denmark. It is the seat of the Diocese of Ribe and, since 2007, part of Esbjerg Municipality. The cathedral school, Ribe Katedralskole, has its roots in the Latin School of Ribe, which dates back to at least 1145. Among the sights are the cathedral, an art museum, the ruins and moat of Riberhus castle, probably built by Eric V of Denmark in the 1200s, and the Wadden Sea Centre.
ricardo-palma: Manuel Ricardo Palma was born on 7 February 1833, by the official account in Lima, though Monsignor Salvador Herrera Pinto, drawing on oral tradition and testimonies, concluded that he was born in Talavera in the province of Andahuaylas. His mother was a mestiza with African roots, and his parents separated when he was young. He studied at a Jesuit school, attended the University of San Carlos irregularly, and served for six years as a volunteer in the Peruvian navy. At 15 he published his first verses and edited a satirical political sheet, El Diablo.

A liberal, Palma was believed to have taken part in a failed plot against President Ramón Castilla in 1860 and went into exile in Chile, returning in October 1862. After a journey to Europe in 1864–1865 he served as Peru's consul in Pará, Brazil, as senator for Loreto and as an official of the Ministry of War and Navy. He wrote for the satirical papers El Burro and La Campana and founded La Broma, and in 1863 he published a study of the Inquisition in Lima.

The War of the Pacific destroyed his own library as well as the National Library, which Chilean troops ransacked in 1881. As its director until his retirement in 1912 he restored it to its former standing, recovering about 10,000 books from Chile through his friendship with President Domingo Santa María.

His tradiciones mix history and fiction, written by his own account both to amuse and to instruct, and draw on hearsay and oral narrators as well as documents; one of the best known is La camisa de Margarita. Some critics count them among the works of 19th-century Romanticism. The bawdier Tradiciones en salsa verde appeared only after his death. A scholar of language, he wrote Neologismos y americanismos and pressed the Real Academia Española to recognise Latin American contributions to Spanish. His son Clemente Palma and his daughter Angélica Palma also became writers. He died on 6 October 1919.
richard-arkwright: Richard Arkwright was born in Preston, Lancashire, on 23 December 1732, the youngest of seven surviving children of Thomas, a tailor, and Sarah. His parents could not afford to send him to school, and a cousin, Ellen, taught him to read and write. He was apprenticed to a barber at Kirkham and began his working life as a barber and wig-maker, setting up a shop at Churchgate in Bolton in the early 1760s. There he invented a waterproof dye for periwigs, and its income later funded his prototype cotton machinery. He married Patience Holt in 1755; she died the next year, and in 1761 he married Margaret Biggins.

In 1768 Arkwright and the clockmaker John Kay returned to Preston and worked on a spinning machine, patented in 1769, that twisted thread with wooden and metal cylinders instead of human fingers. In 1775 he patented a carding engine, an improvement on a machine Lewis Paul had invented in 1748. For capital he formed a partnership with the hosiery manufacturers Jedediah Strutt and Samuel Need, and in 1771 the partners built a mill at Cromford that handled both carding and spinning and employed 200 people. A second, larger mill followed there in 1776, with others at Bakewell, Wirksworth and elsewhere.

Because Cromford's own population could not supply the labour, Arkwright brought in workers and housed them in cottages beside the mill. Work ran in two 13-hour shifts, the gates were shut at 6 am and 6 pm, and towards the end of his tenure nearly two thirds of the 1,150 employees were children. His grand patent of 1775 met hostility, and in 1785 a court case he had begun in 1781 was settled against him because his specifications were deficient; the court had also heard claims that the frame was the work of John Kay or of Thomas Highs. His mill at Birkacre in Lancashire was destroyed in the anti-machinery riots of 1779.

Arkwright served as High Sheriff of Derbyshire and was knighted in 1786. He built Willersley Castle at Cromford, but a fire in 1792 delayed its completion and he never lived in it. He died at Rock House, Cromford, on 3 August 1792, aged 59, leaving a fortune of £500,000. The Cromford mill complex is now part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site and is owned by the Arkwright Society. The Arkwright Scholarships Trust, founded in 1991, awards scholarships to students of engineering and technical design.
richard-chancellor: Chancellor, a native of Bristol, was brought up in the household of Sir William Sidney. In 1550 he sailed as an apprentice pilot to the eastern Mediterranean in the bark Aucher under Roger Bodenham, and he learned more geography and seamanship from the explorer Sebastian Cabot and the geographer John Dee. Cabot had long wanted to reach Asia through the Arctic, and in 1552-1553 London merchants chartered the Company of Merchant Adventurers for the purpose, with the Duke of Northumberland as principal patron, hoping also to find a market for English woollen cloth.

Chancellor went as chief navigator and second-in-command to Sir Hugh Willoughby, under orders from Cabot to behave peaceably and keep a journal. A violent storm off the North Cape separated the ships. Willoughby sailed east, reached Novaya Zemlya and died with all his men during the winter on the Kola Peninsula. Chancellor, in the Edward Bonaventure, called at Vardø, where Scottish fishermen warned him of the dangers ahead, then found the White Sea and anchored at the mouth of the Dvina River, where Archangel now stands.

Invited by Tsar Ivan the Terrible, he travelled over 600 miles to Moscow by sleigh. He found the city much larger than London and built mostly of wood, the tsar's palace and dinners luxurious. Russia then had no access to the Baltic Sea, and the Hanseatic League held a monopoly of its trade with the West, so the tsar welcomed a sea route and gave Chancellor letters inviting English traders and promising them privileges.

Chancellor returned in the summer of 1554 to find King Edward dead and Northumberland executed by Mary. No stigma attached to him, and the Muscovy Company, as the association was now called, sent him back to the White Sea in 1555. He learned what had become of Willoughby, recovered his papers and spent the season organising trade and asking how China might be reached by the northern route.

In July 1556 he sailed for home with Osip Nepeya, the first Russian ambassador to England, in a fleet of four ships. Off Norway the weather turned: the Bona Esperanza sank, the Bona Confidentia was never heard of again, and only the Philip and Mary reached London, in April 1557. The Edward Bonaventure was driven ashore at Pitsligo near Aberdeen on 10 November 1556, and Chancellor died with most of the crew. Nepeya and a few others survived.
richard-de-clare-2nd-earl-of-pembroke: Richard de Clare was the son of Gilbert de Clare, the first Earl of Pembroke, and Isabel de Beaumont, a daughter of Robert de Beaumont, Earl of Leicester, and mistress of King Henry I. Gilbert died in about 1148, and Richard inherited his possessions at roughly eighteen. In 1154 Henry II took the title from him because he had sided against the king's mother, Empress Matilda, during the Anarchy, and his contemporaries called him Earl of Striguil, after his marcher lordship with its castle.

The nickname Strongbow, Arc-Fort in Anglo-Norman, was also his father's. An annal written between 1300 and 1304 calls him Richard, known as Stranghose, earl of Striguil, the name being probably a different spelling of Striguil, and the form Strongbow appears in the 14th century.

In 1167 Rory O'Connor, the High King of Ireland, deposed Dermot MacMurrough as King of Leinster. Dermot asked Henry II in Aquitaine for help, but Henry only permitted him to recruit English mercenaries. He failed to recruit in Wales but met Richard and other lords of the Welsh Marches, and agreed that Richard would have his eldest daughter Aoife and the succession to the crown if he helped regain Leinster. Richard received the king's consent in 1168.

A large army under Raymond FitzGerald, with Welsh archers, took the Ostman towns of Wexford, Waterford and Dublin between 1169 and 1170. On 23 August 1170 a royal messenger forbade Richard to sail from Milford Haven, but he sailed anyway. He married Aoife in Reginald's Tower in Waterford. When Dermot died in May 1171 his son Donal claimed Leinster under the Brehon laws, and Richard claimed it through his wife.

Henry, worried at his growing power, offered to return Richard's confiscated lands in France, England and Wales in exchange for the conquests in Ireland. Richard surrendered Dublin, Waterford and other fortresses and kept only Kildare. Richard helped him against the revolt in France in 1173 and was given Leinster back. In 1174 he tried to advance into Munster but was defeated at the battle of Thurles.

Richard died in 1176 of an infection in a leg or foot and was buried in Christ Church Cathedral in Dublin, within sight of the cross according to the eyewitness Giraldus Cambrensis. Henry took his possessions and placed a royal official over them. His son Gilbert, born in 1173, succeeded as a minor and died by about 1185 to 1189, and the inheritance went to his daughter Isabel de Clare, whom Henry II and Richard the Lionheart gave in marriage to William Marshal. A purported tomb effigy stands in the cathedral, and the original effigy was destroyed when the roof collapsed in 1562.
richard-francis-burton: Richard Burton was born in Torquay, Devon, on 19 March 1821, although his autobiography incorrectly places his birth at Barham House in Elstree, Hertfordshire. His father was an Anglo-Irish army officer, and his mother, Martha Baker, was the daughter of a wealthy Hertfordshire squire, Richard Baker, after whom he was named. He grew up between Elstree and Tours in France, where his father sought a better climate for his asthma. He abandoned his university studies and in 1842 was commissioned into the Bombay Army, beginning an eighteen-year military career.

In India he served in the 18th Regiment of Native Infantry under General Charles James Napier and earned the nickname Ruffian Dick. He passed six formal language examinations and became proficient in Persian, Arabic, Hindustani, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi, Saraiki and Marathi. In 1853 he made the Hajj to Mecca in disguise, as a Persian mirza and then a Sunni sheikh, doctor and dervish, having prepared by studying Muslim culture.

In 1854-1855 he led a Royal Geographical Society expedition to Somaliland with John Hanning Speke. Disguised as an Arab merchant, he reached Harar on 3 January 1855 and spent ten days there, officially a guest of the Emir but in reality his prisoner. In 1857 he and Speke left Zanzibar for the African Great Lakes with a caravan of 132 people, hindered by malaria and other fevers, and became the first Europeans known to have seen Lake Tanganyika. Burton married Isabel Arundel on 22 January 1861 and then entered the Diplomatic Service as consul at Fernando Po. He later served at Santos in Brazil, at Damascus and at Trieste, and was knighted in 1886.

Burton wrote over forty books, including Abeokuta and the Cameroons Mountains (1863), The Highlands of Brazil (1869) and Letters from the Battlefields of Paraguay (1870). With Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot he created the Kama Shastra Society to circulate privately books that would have been illegal to publish after the Obscene Publications Act 1857. It printed his translation of The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night in ten volumes in 1885, in a subscribers-only edition of one thousand. Burton died at Trieste on 20 October 1890 of a heart attack. Isabel afterwards burned many of his papers, including a planned translation of The Perfumed Garden, an act that remains controversial, though much of his writing survives at the Huntington Library.
richard-i-of-capua: Richard came from near Dieppe in the Pays de Caux, in eastern Normandy, and was a son of Asclettin I, count of Acerenza, and a nephew of Rainulf Drengot. He reached southern Italy shortly after Rainulf's death in 1045 with forty Norman knights. According to Amatus of Montecassino, the people of Aversa followed him as if he were a count, which disturbed his cousin, Count Rainulf Trincanocte, who asked him to leave. He then served Humphrey of Hauteville and became lord of Genzano, which his brother Asclettin had ruled.

Drogo of Hauteville later captured and imprisoned him. When Trincanocte died leaving an infant son, Herman, Prince Guaimar IV of Salerno had Richard released and made him the boy's guardian in 1048; Herman soon disappeared from the records, and Richard titled himself count.

At the Battle of Civitate in 1053 Richard commanded the Norman right wing and routed the Lombards of the papal army. Pressing his Lombard neighbours, he reduced the principality of Gisulf II of Salerno almost to the city itself, and when Pandulf VI of Capua died in 1057 he besieged Capua and took the princely title in 1058 from Landulf VIII, though the keys of the city stayed in Lombard hands until 12 May 1062.

In 1059 he aided Pope Nicholas II against the antipope Benedict X at the request of Hildebrand, the future Pope Gregory VII, and at the synod of Melfi the pope confirmed him as count of Aversa and prince of Capua. In 1061 he installed Alexander II against the antipope Honorius II, but in 1066 he marched on Rome and was beaten back by the pope's Tuscan allies. From 1064 he and his son Jordan held the ducal titles of Gaeta.

He backed the rebellion of Robert Guiscard's barons in 1071, but in 1076 the two Norman leaders allied and took Salerno from Gisulf. Richard was besieging Naples when Gregory VII excommunicated both on 3 March 1078. Dying in Capua soon after, he was reconciled with the church, and Jordan renewed his fealty in Rome and was confirmed in his father's titles. Richard's wife was Fredescende, a sister of Robert Guiscard.
richard-i-of-england: Richard was born on 8 September 1157, probably at Beaumont Palace in Oxford, the third of five sons of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. As a younger son he was not expected to become king, but his two elder brothers died before their father. By the age of 16 he had taken command of his own army to put down rebellions in Poitou against his father. When Henry the Young King led a revolt against Henry II, Richard joined him at the French court, where Louis VII supported them and knighted Richard.

Richard was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 3 September 1189. A rumour that he had ordered all Jews killed set off an attack on the Jews of London, with homes burnt and some forcibly converted. Richard had taken the cross in 1187, and he and Philip II of France agreed to go on the Third Crusade together, each fearing that the other might usurp his lands in his absence.

In Sicily he captured Messina on 4 October 1190, and a treaty with Tancred was signed on 4 March 1191. He took Lemesos on Cyprus on 1 May 1191 after its ruler Isaac Komnenos refused to release prisoners and treasure, and married Berengaria of Navarre there on 12 May. He landed at Acre on 8 June 1191, supporting Guy of Lusignan against Conrad of Montferrat for the kingship of Jerusalem.

On the way home he was captured shortly before Christmas 1192 near Vienna by Leopold of Austria, who accused him of arranging the murder of Conrad of Montferrat. During his captivity his brother John revolted with Philip's help, and Philip took part of Normandy. Richard forgave John and named him his heir. He was crowned a second time at Winchester on 11 March 1194. He spent perhaps as little as six months of his reign in England.

In March 1199 Richard was in Limousin putting down a revolt and besieging the castle of Châlus-Chabrol. On 26 March he was struck in the shoulder by a crossbow bolt, and the wound turned gangrenous. He died on 6 April 1199. According to some accounts he forgave the crossbowman and had him freed with 100 shillings.

Contemporaries admired him as a king and knight famed for martial prowess, though some also called him cruel. Later historians sometimes judged that he treated England only as a source of revenue, a view that modern scholars regard as anachronistic given his continental responsibilities. His second Great Seal of 1198 is the first to show three lions passant-guardant, a design that later became the Royal Arms of England.
richard-ii-duke-of-normandy: Richard II was the eldest surviving son and heir of Richard the Fearless and his wife Gunnor de Crêpon. He succeeded his father as ruler of Normandy in 996. During his minority, the first five years of his reign, his uncle Count Rodulf of Ivry acted as regent, held the power and put down a peasant insurrection at the start of the reign.

Richard had deep religious interests and found much in common with King Robert II of France, whom he helped militarily against the Duchy of Burgundy. He also forged a marriage alliance with Duke Geoffrey I of Brittany, marrying Geoffrey's sister Judith while his own sister Hawise married Geoffrey.

By 1000 Vikings had begun raiding England again and sold their plunder in Normandy. Richard gave them sanctuary and welcomed them, which broke a treaty between his father and King Æthelred II of England. Æthelred ordered that Richard be captured, bound and brought to England, and sent an attack on the Cotentin Peninsula. The English were not prepared for the rapid response of the Norman cavalry and were defeated.

Richard then tried to improve relations by marrying his sister Emma to Æthelred. The marriage later gave his grandson William the Conqueror the basis of his claim to the English throne.
