Emma fled to Normandy with her sons Edward and Alfred, and Æthelred followed. After Æthelred died in 1016, Cnut the Great married Emma, and Richard had to recognise the new regime.

He kept contact with Scandinavian Vikings throughout his reign and employed Viking mercenaries. After the St Brice's Day Massacre ordered by Æthelred in 1013, King Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark sailed for England, stopped at Rouen and was well received. Richard concluded an alliance with him.

Richard continued his father's commission to his clerk and confessor Dudo of Saint-Quentin to write a history of the dukes of Normandy. Dudo had written records and eyewitnesses to draw on, but his history is more panegyric than chronicle, telling of the pagan conversion to Christianity and the legitimacy of the dukes' rule, and should not be read uncritically.

In 1025 and 1026 Richard confirmed gifts of his great-grandfather Rollo to the abbey of Saint-Ouen at Rouen. His grants to monasteries indicate where he held ducal control: Caen, the Éverecin, the Cotentin, the Pays de Caux and Rouen. He died in 1026 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Richard III.
richard-ii-of-england: Richard was born on 6 January 1367 at the Archbishop's Palace of Bordeaux, in the duchy of Aquitaine, the younger son of Edward the Black Prince and Joan of Kent. When the Black Prince died in June 1376, the Commons in the Good Parliament feared that Richard's uncle, John of Gaunt, would usurp the throne, and Richard was quickly invested with his father's titles and publicly recognised as heir. His early years as king were governed by regency councils influenced by Gaunt and by Thomas of Woodstock, another uncle.

The poll tax of 1381 sparked the Peasants' Revolt, whose roots lay in tensions between peasants and landowners after the Black Death. Bands under Wat Tyler, John Ball and Jack Straw gathered at Blackheath on 12 June and killed Archbishop Simon Sudbury and Robert Hales. On 20 January 1382 Richard married Anne of Bohemia, daughter of Emperor Charles IV, a match meant to win allies against France; it was unpopular in England and childless. Anne died of plague in 1394.

In 1387 control of government passed to the Lords Appellant. Richard took full control on 3 May 1389 and then ruled peacefully for eight years. In July 1397 he had Gloucester, Arundel and Warwick arrested. Arundel was executed, Gloucester died in custody at Calais, probably on the king's order, and Warwick was condemned but sentenced to life imprisonment. Historians call the following period his tyranny.

Bolingbroke landed at Ravenspurn in Yorkshire at the end of June 1399, and met little resistance because Richard had taken many loyal nobles to Ireland. On 19 August Richard surrendered at Flint Castle, promising to abdicate if his life was spared, and he was imprisoned in the Tower of London on 1 September. After the Epiphany Rising, a plot to restore him, he is thought to have died of starvation at Pontefract Castle on or around 14 February 1400, though the date and manner of his death are questioned. He was buried at Kings Langley Priory on 6 March.

Shakespeare's play shaped his reputation by presenting his misrule and deposition as the cause of the Wars of the Roses, which modern historians do not accept. Most authorities hold that his policies were not unrealistic but that the way he carried them out was unacceptable to the political establishment.
richard-iii-of-england: Richard was born on 2 October 1452 at Fotheringhay Castle in Northamptonshire, the eleventh of the twelve children of Richard, 3rd Duke of York, and Cecily Neville. His childhood fell in the opening phase of the Wars of the Roses, in which the Yorkists, who supported his father, opposed the Lancastrians loyal to the crown. His brother Edward IV gained the throne in 1461 and made him Duke of Gloucester that year. Richard became the richest and most powerful noble in England and showed loyalty to Edward during Warwick's rebellion of 1470. He married Anne Neville on 12 July 1472 and governed the north for Edward as the dominant magnate.

Edward IV died on 9 April 1483 and Richard was named Lord Protector for the 12-year-old Edward V. Robert Stillington, bishop of Bath and Wells, is said to have told Richard that Edward IV's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville was invalid because of an earlier union with Eleanor Butler, which made Edward V and his siblings illegitimate. Richard accepted the throne on 26 June after a petition from London's nobles and commons, and was crowned on 6 July 1483. Edward V and his brother Richard of Shrewsbury, called the Princes in the Tower, disappeared from the Tower of London around August 1483.

In October 1483 a rebellion nominally led by his former ally Henry Stafford, 2nd Duke of Buckingham, failed. Richard set up the Council of the North, with his nephew John de la Pole as president, to keep the peace and settle land disputes; it lasted until 1641. His only son, Edward of Middleham, died on 9 April 1484.

In August 1485 Henry Tudor and his uncle Jasper Tudor landed in Wales with French troops. At the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August Richard's army, believed to be substantially larger, met Henry's. Richard was killed, the last English king to die in battle, and Henry became Henry VII. His body was buried without ceremony in Greyfriars Church in Leicester.

Sources for his reign are largely partisan and none was written by someone who knew him closely, so the debate over his character continues. William Shakespeare made him the protagonist of Richard III. In 2012 a search for the lost Greyfriars site found a skeleton, which the University of Leicester identified through radiocarbon dating, trauma sustained at Bosworth and mitochondrial DNA. He was reburied in Leicester Cathedral on 26 March 2015.
richard-nixon: Richard Milhous Nixon was born on 9 January 1913 in Yorba Linda, California, in a house his father built on the family's lemon ranch. His mother, Hannah Milhous Nixon, was a Quaker, and his father, Francis A. Nixon, converted from Methodism to the Quaker faith. Offered a tuition grant to attend Harvard University, he stayed at home because his brother Harold's illness needed his mother's care, and enrolled at Whittier College in September 1930.

He graduated from Whittier in 1934 and from Duke University School of Law in 1937, was admitted to the California bar that year and practised law in Whittier. In January 1942 he and his wife Pat moved to Washington, D.C., where he worked at the Office of Price Administration. Although he could have claimed an exemption as a birthright Quaker, he sought a commission and was appointed a lieutenant junior grade in the Naval Reserve on 15 June 1942.

Nixon won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1946, defeating Jerry Voorhis, and entered the Senate in 1950 after a bitter campaign against Helen Gahagan Douglas, in which opponents first called him Tricky Dick. As running mate of Dwight D. Eisenhower he served as vice president from 1953 to 1961. He lost the 1960 presidential election narrowly to John F. Kennedy and the 1962 race for governor of California to Pat Brown, then moved to New York. In 1968 he defeated Hubert Humphrey and was inaugurated on 20 January 1969.

His visit to China in 1972 led to diplomatic relations between the two nations, and his first term also saw the end of American combat involvement in Vietnam in 1973, the Apollo 11 Moon landing, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency and the end of the dollar's direct convertibility to gold in 1971. He was re-elected in 1972, defeating George McGovern.

From 1973 revelations about the administration's part in Watergate, which began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee office ordered by administration officials, eroded his support in Congress and the country. On 9 August 1974, facing almost certain impeachment and removal, Nixon resigned, the only president to do so. On 8 September 1974 his successor, Gerald Ford, granted him a pardon. In nearly twenty years of retirement he wrote nine books and made many foreign trips, rehabilitating his image into that of an elder statesman. He suffered a stroke on 18 April 1994 and died four days later.
richard-pipes: Richard Pipes was born in Cieszyn, Poland, to an assimilated Jewish family whose name had originally been spelled Piepes in the German manner. His father Marek was a businessman and a Polish legionnaire in the First World War, and co-owned the Dea chocolate factory before moving to Warsaw in 1929. By Pipes's own account he never thought about the Soviet Union in his youth, and the main cultural influences on him were Polish and German.

At sixteen he saw Adolf Hitler in Warsaw on his tour after the invasion of Poland. The family fled in October 1939 and reached the United States in July 1940 after seven months in Italy. Pipes became a naturalized citizen in 1943 while serving in the United States Army Air Corps, and he studied at Muskingum College, Cornell University and Harvard University.

Pipes directed Harvard's Russian Research Center from 1968 to 1973 and guided over 80 graduate students to their doctorates. He was an adviser to Senator Henry M. Jackson in the 1970s and a critic of détente. In 1976 he headed Team B, a group of civilian experts and retired officers agreed to by the CIA director George H. W. Bush as a competitive analysis exercise, set against CIA officials known as Team A. It argued that the CIA's yearly estimate underestimated Soviet strategy and ambition.

Critics disagreed: Fred Kaplan wrote that it was wrong on nearly every point, and one CIA employee called it a kangaroo court. Pipes himself called its evidence soft, and in 1986 maintained that it had helped produce more realistic defence estimates.

In 1981 and 1982 he was Director of East European and Soviet Affairs on the National Security Council under Ronald Reagan. A March 1981 interview with Reuters, meant to be off the record, led the White House and State Department to repudiate his remarks. In 1992 he was an expert witness at the Russian Constitutional Court's trial of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

His books include Russia under the Old Regime (1974), The Russian Revolution (1990) and Russia Under the Bolshevik Regime (1994). He argued that the Soviet Union's origins lay in the separate path of 15th-century Muscovy, where everything was regarded as the Tsar's property, a patrimonial order possibly shaped by Mongol influence. He saw the October Revolution as a coup carried out by a tiny group of radical intellectuals. Lynne Viola and Sheila Fitzpatrick wrote that he focused too narrowly on intellectuals, and Peter Kenez, once his student, said he approached Soviet history as a prosecutor. Pipes died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 17 May 2018.
richard-seddon: Richard John Seddon was born on 22 June 1845 at Eccleston, near St Helens in Lancashire, the third of eight children of a headmaster and a teacher. He did poorly at school, left at 12, and trained as an engineer at foundries in Sutton and Liverpool. In 1862 he worked his passage to Melbourne on the SS Great Britain and tried the railway workshops at Williamstown and the goldfields at Bendigo. In 1866 he moved to the West Coast of New Zealand's South Island, worked the goldfields, kept a store and became a publican, and in 1869 he married Louisa Jane Spotswood.

He entered local politics in 1870, sat on the Westland Provincial Council as an advocate for the miners, and in 1877 became the first Mayor of Kumara. Elected to Parliament in 1879, he was mocked for his accent and lack of education but became an authority on mining and a skilled obstructor of legislation. When John Ballance's Liberals took office in January 1891 he became minister of public works, mines, defence and marine, and after Ballance's death in April 1893 he was asked to form a ministry, avoiding a leadership vote against Robert Stout by arguing it would split the party.

Women's suffrage passed in 1893 against his opposition, after his attempt to have the Legislative Council reject it failed. His Old-age Pensions Act of 1898 laid a basis for the later welfare state. His government bought large areas of land from Māori, and it raised the poll tax on Chinese immigrants to £100 a head in 1896; Seddon spoke of the Chinese in racist terms. After the Colonial Conference of 1897 he became known as a pillar of British imperialism; his hopes for Fiji and Samoa were checked by London, but the Cook Islands came under New Zealand in 1901.

He took many portfolios himself and was accused of cronyism and of an autocratic style, which earned him the name King Dick. He led the Liberals to five consecutive election victories. He died of a heart attack at sea, returning from Australia on the Oswestry Grange, on 10 June 1906, and was buried in Wellington.
richard-the-justiciar: Richard was a Bosonid, the son of Bivin of Gorze and Richildis. His elder brother was Boso of Provence, and his younger sister Richildis became the second wife of Charles the Bald. In 875, after the death of the Emperor Louis II, Richard and Boso accompanied Charles to Italy for his imperial coronation. In February 876, at Pavia, Charles named Boso Duke and Viceroy of Italy and Duke of Provence. When Charles died in 877, Boso returned to France and left the government of Italy and Provence to Richard and Hugh the Abbot as missi dominici.

In 879 Boso declared himself King of Provence after the death of Louis the Stammerer, but Richard broke with him and took his county of Autun, which Carloman II confirmed to him in 880. The two brothers fought on the Saône, and Richard captured Mâcon and garrisoned it in the name of Carloman and Louis III under Bernard Plantapilosa. After taking Lyon he besieged Vienne, Boso's capital, where Louis, Carloman and the Emperor Charles the Fat joined him. In 882 he drove Boso out and sent Boso's wife Ermengard and their children Engelberga and Louis to Autun as prisoners.

After the death of Charles the Fat in 888, Richard supported the claim of Duke Rudolph to be King of Upper Burgundy and married Rudolph's sister Adelaide, daughter of Conrad II of Auxerre. In 890 he also supported the coronation of his nephew Louis as King of Provence. He gained suzerainty over all the counties of Burgundy except Mâcon. He was called dux by 890 and marchio by 900, and by 918 dux Burgundionem or dux Burgundiae, a title that probably meant feudal suzerainty over many counties of one region rather than a unified duchy.

Richard died in 921 and was buried at Sens. At his deathbed a bishop urged him to ask pardon for the blood he had shed. He answered that when he killed a brigand he had saved the lives of honest men, since the death of one prevented his accomplices from doing more evil. By Adelaide he had several sons and daughters, among them Rudolph, his successor and later King of Francia, and Hugh the Black, later Duke of Burgundy. His daughters married Gilbert, Duke of Burgundy, Reginar II, Count of Hainaut, and Litaud I, Count of Mâcon.
richard-wagner: Wilhelm Richard Wagner was born on 22 May 1813 in Leipzig into a family of musicians, the ninth and youngest child of Carl Friedrich Wagner, a clerk in the Leipzig police service, and Johanna Rosine Wagner, a baker's daughter. His father died of typhoid fever six months after his birth. His mother then lived with Carl's friend, the actor and playwright Ludwig Geyer, whom she probably married in August 1814, and the family moved to Dresden. Until he was fourteen Wagner was known as Wilhelm Richard Geyer, and he almost certainly believed Geyer to be his biological father.

Geyer's love of the theatre was shared by his stepson. At nine Wagner was greatly impressed by Carl Maria von Weber's opera Der Freischütz, which he saw Weber conduct. His first creative effort was a tragedy called Leubald, begun in 1826, and he persuaded his family to let him take music lessons. Back in Leipzig he studied harmony from 1828 to 1831. Hearing Beethoven's 7th and 9th symphonies in 1828 inspired him, and he wrote a piano transcription of the 9th.

Wagner wrote both the libretti, which he called poems, and the music of all his stage works. His earliest attempts at opera were often left unfinished. Rienzi (1842) was his first opera to be staged successfully, and he later said he did not consider his early works part of his oeuvre.

From 1849 he urged a new concept of opera, often called music drama, in which musical, poetic and dramatic elements were fused in a Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. He set out these ideas in essays published between 1849 and 1852 and realised them most fully in the first half of The Ring of the Nibelung. The orchestra became as important as the singers, and leitmotifs, musical phrases tied to characters, places and plot elements, are interwoven through the drama. To stage his works he had the Bayreuth Festspielhaus built, which hosted the premieres of The Ring and Parsifal.

Wagner died on 13 February 1883. After his death his wife Cosima took over the leadership of the Bayreuth Festival, which has since remained under the management of their descendants. From Tristan und Isolde onwards he explored the limits of the traditional tonal system, and some music historians date the beginning of modern classical music to its first notes. Anton Bruckner, Hugo Wolf, Richard Strauss and Gustav Mahler were among the composers indebted to him.

He remained controversial in his lifetime and afterwards. His hostile writings on Jews, including Jewishness in Music, correspond to trends of thought in 19th-century Germany, though he also had Jewish friends and supporters. The extent to which antisemitic stereotypes appear in his operas is debated.
richard-wellesley-1st-marquess-wellesley: Richard Colley Wellesley was born in 1760 at Dangan Castle in County Meath, the eldest son of Garret Wesley, 1st Earl of Mornington, and a member of the Anglo-Irish Ascendancy. His younger brother was Arthur Wellesley, later the Duke of Wellington. He was educated at the Royal School, Armagh, Harrow, Eton, where he distinguished himself as a classical scholar, and Christ Church, Oxford.

He entered the Irish House of Commons in 1780 and succeeded his father the next year as 2nd Earl of Mornington. Heavily indebted through the extravagance of his father and grandfather, he sold all the Irish estates. In 1784 he joined the British House of Commons and was soon appointed a Lord of the Treasury by William Pitt the Younger.

In 1793 Wellesley joined the Board of Control over Indian affairs, and he went to India as Governor-General. On the voyage out he formed the design of curbing French influence in the Deccan. In April 1798 he learned that Tipu Sultan was negotiating an alliance with France, and he ordered preparations for war, beginning with the disbandment of the French troops employed by the Nizam of Hyderabad.

Seringapatam was captured on 4 May 1799 and Tipu was killed in action. In 1803 the restoration of the Peshwa Baji Rao II led to war with Daulat Rao Sindhia of Gwalior and Raghoji II Bhonsle, raja of Berar, in which his brother Arthur took a leading role. French influence in India was reduced to Pondicherry.

He founded Fort William College to train those who would govern India, and Government House in Calcutta was built during his tenure. His commercial policy and educational projects brought him into hostility with the East India Company's court of directors, and a motion to impeach him over the expulsion of British traders from Oudh was defeated in 1808 by 182 votes to 31.

In 1809 he was ambassador to Spain, and from late that year Foreign Secretary under Spencer Perceval until February 1812, when he resigned partly from dissatisfaction at the support given to Wellington. He supported Catholic emancipation, and was Lord Lieutenant of Ireland from 1821 and again from 1833.

Wellesley died on 26 September 1842 and was buried in Eton College Chapel. His brother Arthur, after a long estrangement, wept at the funeral and said he knew of no greater honour than being Lord Wellesley's brother. Places named after him include Province Wellesley in Penang, now Seberang Perai, the Wellesley Islands off Queensland, named by Matthew Flinders, and Mornington Island, the largest of them. The Mornington Peninsula south of Melbourne bears his title.
richborough: Richborough lies north of Sandwich on the east coast of Kent, close to the Isle of Thanet, and is now some distance from the sea. From prehistory to the early medieval period it stood at the southern end of the Wantsum Channel, which separated Thanet from the mainland and gave ships a safe route from the continent to the Thames estuary. Before the channel silted up, Richborough was an important natural harbour.

Until October 2008 it was uncertain whether the Claudian invasion had landed here, and some archaeologists favoured the area of modern Chichester. That year two ditches dated to the Roman period were shown to belong to a defended beachhead protecting 700 metres of coast. After the Romans withdrew, a Saxon religious settlement occupied the site, following St Augustine's landing at nearby Ebbsfleet in 597. By the time of the Venerable Bede the name Rutupiae had become, in his words, Reptacaestir.

In the First World War, when Dover and the other nearby ports proved too small, a large secret harbour was built at Richborough to supply the British Expeditionary Force with tanks, guns, locomotives, ammunition, horses and fuel. From 10 February 1918 three train ferries carried railway wagons and vehicles from there to Calais and Dunkirk, the first sea-going roll-on/roll-off ferries used from Britain. By mid-1918 the site covered 2000 acres and handled 20,000 tons a week, and after the Armistice even more material came back through it in 1919 than had gone out in 1918.

The Roman site is managed by English Heritage. Richborough Power Station, opened within the port in 1962 and burning coal, then oil and finally Orimulsion, closed in 1996, and its three cooling towers were demolished on 11 March 2012. The settlement forms part of the civil parish of Ash.
richilde-countess-of-hainaut: Richilde may have been a daughter of Reinier of Hasnon and Adelheid of Egisheim. Reinier had been installed in 1047 as margrave of Valenciennes in place of Baldwin V of Flanders, who had rebelled against the empire and lost his fiefs, and around 1049 Richilde succeeded him there as his only heir. Her rights and position were long poorly understood, and sources count her as ruling countess of Hainaut for different periods: she was countess of Valenciennes in her own right and of Hainaut through her first husband, Herman of Mons, who died around 1050 or 1051.

Her claim made her an attractive match, and under threat of invasion Baldwin V forced her to marry his eldest son Baldwin. Because Hainaut and Valenciennes were imperial fiefs and Emperor Henry III had not been consulted, the marriage led to a war between the emperor and the Baldwins that ended in their total defeat in 1054. Even so, her husband ruled Hainaut by right of his wife, and her children by Herman were disinherited: her son Roger, probably lame, became a cleric and later Bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne, and her daughter a nun. When Baldwin VI succeeded in Flanders in 1067, Flanders, Hainaut and Valenciennes were joined under one ruler.

On Baldwin VI's death on 17 July 1070, Flanders went to Arnulf III and Hainaut to his younger brother Baldwin II, and Richilde became regent for Arnulf. Baldwin VI's brother Robert broke his oath to protect his nephew and claimed Flanders. Richilde won the support of King Philip I of France and married William FitzOsbern, 1st Earl of Hereford, who helped her with a small force, but at the Battle of Cassel both William and Arnulf were killed and she was captured, then released.

Philip I later married Robert's stepdaughter Bertha and recognised him as count. Richilde and Baldwin II kept Hainaut, placed it in fief to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège and formed a coalition with Godfrey of Bouillon, Albert I of Namur and other nobles, but failed to recover Flanders. She built the Château de Beaumont with a chapel of St Venantius and, with Baldwin, founded the monastery of Saint-Denis-en-Broqueroie. Apparently deposed by her son in 1076, she retired to the Abbey of Messines and died on 15 March 1086.
richmond-virginia: Richmond stands at the fall line of the James River, the rocky point that separates Virginia's Piedmont from the Tidewater and the highest point the river can be navigated. The Piedmont is a region of low, rolling hills lying between the flat Tidewater and the Blue Ridge Mountains. The site was an important village in the Powhatan Confederacy; the name of the Powhatan people is traced to Pawat-hanne, meaning falls in a stream, a reference to the falls of the James. After Jamestown was founded in April 1607, Captain Christopher Newport led explorers up the river to this inhabited area.

English colonists from Jamestown briefly settled the place from 1609 to 1611. Richmond was founded in 1737, with a street grid laid out between what are now Broad, 17th and 25th Streets and the river, and was incorporated in 1742.

In 1775 Patrick Henry delivered his speech ending 'Give me liberty or give me death!' at St. John's Church. The state capital moved there from Williamsburg on 18 April 1780, partly to give a more central position for Virginia's growing western population. In 1781 Loyalist troops led by Benedict Arnold raided and burned the city, and Governor Thomas Jefferson fled. Richmond recovered quickly. The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson, was enacted in 1786, and the State Capitol, designed by Jefferson and Charles-Louis Clérisseau in the Greek Revival style, was completed in 1788.

The Virginia Convention voted to secede from the United States on 17 April 1861, five days after the attack on Fort Sumter, pending a popular vote. On 20 May the Confederate States Congress voted to move its capital from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond, and on 23 May Virginia voters ratified the Ordinance of Secession. After the war the city again became a major centre of production, with iron-front buildings and large brick factories, a railway crossroads with what is described as the world's first triple railway crossing, and a centre of tobacco processing.

Richmond is the capital of Virginia and has been an independent city since 1871; its population was 226,610 at the 2020 census. In the early twentieth century its Jackson Ward, a business district built by freed people and their descendants, was known as the Wall Street of Black America, and in 1903 Maggie L. Walker chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank and became the first Black woman to serve as a bank president in the United States. The city contains many buildings in Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival styles, among others, and has designated 45 historic districts.
richomer: Richomer, also written Richomeres or Ricomer and known by the Roman name Flavius Richomeres, was a Frank who took service in the Roman army in the late 4th century and made his career as comes, magister militum and consul. He was the uncle of the general Arbogastes, whose fortunes later crossed his own. He is possibly to be identified with the Richomeres who married Ascyla, whose son Theodemer later became king of the Franks.

Around 377 or 378 Richomer was comes domesticorum of Emperor Gratian, and he was transferred from Gaul to Thracia, where he was involved in the Gothic wars of Emperor Valens. At Adrianople he tried to persuade Valens to wait for Gratian's support. When the Gothic leader Fritigern demanded hostages to secure peace, Richomer volunteered and left the Roman camp, but before he reached Fritigern some units of the two armies got out of control and the battle began. Caught in the chaos, he withdrew and survived, while Valens fell with many of his officers.

Around 383 Richomer was magister militum per orientem, general in the East, and in 384 he was consul. In 388 Theodosius I sent him, with his nephew Arbogastes and the generals Promotus and Timasius, against the usurper Magnus Maximus, who was defeated. From that year until his death he was supreme commander in the eastern part of the empire, with the title comes et magister utriusque militiae.

Richomer took an interest in literature and knew rhetoricians such as Libanius and Augustinus. He introduced the rhetorician Eugenius to Arbogastes. A few years later Arbogastes seized power in the western part of the empire, and after the death of Valentinian II he made Eugenius emperor while keeping the real power himself. In 393 Theodosius I organised a campaign against Arbogastes and asked Richomer to lead the cavalry against his nephew. Richomer died on the way from the East before the battle was fought. Arbogastes lost it and killed himself with his own sword.
ridda-wars: In May 632 Muhammad ordered an expedition against the Byzantine Empire to avenge those killed at the Battle of Mu'tah, and named Usama ibn Zayd to command it. Muhammad died in June 632 and Abu Bakr was chosen as caliph at Saqifah. Rebellions were rising, and many regions of Arabia were withholding zakat and leaving Islam. Usama's army was still to march, and Usama sent Umar to Abu Bakr to ask that it stay at Medina, since none would be left to defend the city. A detailed reconstruction of the events is made difficult by contradictory and partisan accounts in the primary sources.

In July 632 Abu Bakr sent envoys to the rebel tribes calling on them to stay loyal and pay zakat, and they refused. Tulayha, whom many tribes also acknowledged as a prophet, gathered an army at Zhu Qissa, about thirty miles east of Medina. Abu Bakr formed guard units under Ali ibn Abi Talib, Talha ibn Ubayd Allah and Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, which intercepted the rebel force at night until it retreated.

After Usama's army returned on 4 August, Abu Bakr moved to Zhu Qissa and fought at Abraq. He then divided the available men into eleven corps, each with its own commander and standard. The strongest, under Khalid ibn al-Walid, moved against Tulayha at Buzakha, while others were sent later according to Khalid's progress.

Abu Bakr planned to clear west-central Arabia first, then deal with Malik bin Nuwaira, and then with Musaylima, leader of the Banu Hanifa and a rival claimant to prophethood at Yamamah. Hudaifa bin Mihsan and Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl defeated Laqit bin Malik, called Dhu'l-Taj, at Dibba in Oman in November 632, and Laqit was killed. Musaylima was killed at the Battle of Yamamah, where he had an army of allegedly 40,000.

Ala bin Al Hadhrami took Hajr in Bahrain by a night attack, finishing at about the end of January 633. The last great revolt, by the Kinda of Hadhramaut under al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, began in January 633 and ended with the siege of the fortress of al-Nujayr, where the besieged fighters were executed and al-Ash'ath was spared.

The campaigns ended in June 633 with all the tribes of Arabia under Abu Bakr. The wars established Khalid ibn al-Walid's reputation as a tactician and cavalry commander. It is unclear whether Abu Bakr then intended a full expansion or pre-emptive raids to make a buffer against the Sasanian and Byzantine empires. Khalid was sent to Iraq with 18,000 volunteers, and Abu Bakr then sent armies against Roman Syria.
riesling: Riesling was long said to descend from wild vines of the Rhine region, without much support for the claim. DNA fingerprinting by Ferdinand Regner showed that one parent is Gouais blanc, known in Germany as Weißer Heunisch, a variety widely grown by French and German peasants in the Middle Ages. The other parent is a cross between a wild vine and Traminer. Because both parents have a long history in Germany, the cross is presumed to have happened in the Rhine valley, though it could have occurred anywhere between the parents' homelands.

The modern spelling Riesling was first documented in 1552, in Hieronymus Bock's Latin herbal. A local claim that the name comes from a stream and vineyard called Ritzling in the Wachau has no documentary evidence behind it. A red-skinned version, Roter Riesling, is very rare; whether it is a mutation of the white grape or its forerunner is unsettled.

Riesling is an aromatic white grape with flowery aromas and high acidity. It is made into dry, semi-sweet, sweet and sparkling wines, usually from the one variety and seldom aged in oak. Its character depends strongly on where it is grown: wines from cool regions such as the Mosel often show apple and tree-fruit notes, while warmer sites bring citrus and peach. Its acidity suits long ageing, and old wines may take on a petrol note caused by the compound TDN.

In Germany the prädikat system classifies wines by must weight and sweetness, from dry to the beerenauslese and trockenbeerenauslese dessert wines. The use of noble rot in Riesling is traced to the late 18th century at Schloss Johannisberg, where permission from the Abbey of Fulda to start picking arrived too late and the rotted grapes still made excellent wine.

Riesling is the leading grape of Germany and is also the basis of its sparkling Sekt. In Alsace over a fifth of the vineyards carry it. In 1838 William Macarthur planted vines near Penrith in New South Wales, and it was Australia's most planted white grape until the early 1990s. German immigrants took it to the United States in the late nineteenth century, with plantings in California by 1857 and Washington in 1871.

German breeders also used it for crosses. Müller-Thurgau, developed at the Geisenheim institute in 1882, is a cross of Riesling and Madeleine Royale, and Kerner crosses it with Trollinger. Several grapes with Riesling in their names, such as Welschriesling, are unrelated.
rieti: Rieti is a town and comune in Lazio, central Italy, the administrative seat of the province of Rieti and the see of a diocese. Its centre stands on a small hilltop at the southern edge of the wide Rieti valley, at the foot of the Sabine hills and the Monti Reatini, which include Mount Terminillo. The Latin name was Reate. The plain is now the fertile basin of the Velino River, and only the small Ripasottile and Lungo lakes remain of the waters that once covered more of it.

According to legend, Reate was founded by a divinity named Rea, and it was founded at the beginning of the Iron Age. It was a major site of the Sabines well before the foundation of Rome. After the final Roman conquest by Manius Curius Dentatus in 290 BCE, it became a strategic point on the Via Salaria, the salt road linking Rome to the Adriatic. The Sabines gained full citizenship in 268 BCE. Curius Dentatus diverted the Velino into the Nera, which created the Marmore Falls and left the fertile Rieti Valley. The town was laid out on Roman lines and fortified, with a stone bridge over the Velino.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Rieti suffered destruction but remained an important centre during the Lombard domination, and was a county capital under the Franks. Saracens sacked it in the ninth and tenth centuries and King Roger II of Sicily in 1149. From 1198 it was a free commune. As a favourite papal seat it saw Pope Gregory IX canonize Saint Dominic in 1234 and Pope Nicholas IV crown Charles I of Anjou in 1289. It was a provincial capital of the Papal States from 1816 to 1860, and became capital of its own province on 2 January 1927.

Rieti has about 47,700 inhabitants. Piazza San Rufo is traditionally considered the exact centre of Italy. The cathedral was begun in 1109, consecrated in 1225 and almost entirely rebuilt in 1639, with a Romanesque bell tower of 1252. The most striking Roman remains are the stone bridge across the Velino and the viaduct. The Rieti Meeting, an international athletics event, has been held every year since 1971.
riez: Riez is a hilly commune in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department, in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region of south-eastern France. It lies northwest of the Lac de Sainte-Croix, on the road to Valensole, at the confluence of the Auvestre and Colostre, two small rivers that join in a glacially widened valley. The surrounding district has fields of commercially grown lavender, which support a honey-making industry, and truffles are found there.

The domed hill was the hillfort headquarters of the Reii, a Celto-Ligurian tribe, who gave their name to the Roman community in the valley below. It was called Alebaece Reiorum, then Alebaece Reiorum Apollinares, after the Roman temple of Apollo, of which four Corinthian columns still stand. The name evolved to Regium, used until the 8th century, and then Regina, used until the 11th.

A bishop of Riez is known from an early date, though the first bishop is purely traditional. The first definitely known bishop was Saint Maximus (433–460), who had succeeded Saint Honoratus as Abbot of Lérins and in 439 held a council at Riez to reform the churches of southern Gaul. His successor Saint Faustus of Riez, from about 461 to about 493, wrote against the Predestinationists. Later bishops include Robert Ceneau (1530–1532) and Gui Bentivoglio (1622–1625). The diocese was suppressed on 29 November 1801 and its territory included in the diocese of Digne.

The 5th-century free-standing baptistery, with a small dome rebuilt in the 12th century, is one of only a few surviving from Christian Gaul. It stands about 100 metres from healing waters once sacred to Asclepius, and Riez kept its reputation for healing waters into the 19th century. The former cathedral on the baptistery's axis was built over a much larger Roman public building of the 1st and 2nd centuries and was destroyed at the end of the 15th century.

The baptistery now holds a small archaeological museum of altars, funerary steles and Roman inscriptions, including an inscribed taurobolium altar and a milestone from the Aurelian Way. In the Middle Ages the town was rebuilt on higher ground because rising river beds had extended the floodplain, and deep alluvium still covers much of the Roman site.
rif: The Rif is bounded by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Ouergha River to the south and the Moulouya River to the east. It is the homeland of the Riffians, the Senhaja de Srair, the Jebala and the Ghomara. The mountains belong geologically to the Gibraltar Arc and are an extension of the Baetic System of the southern Iberian Peninsula, so they are not part of the Atlas system. The western Rif, often called the Jebala, is largely Arabized and speaks Moroccan Arabic, though the Ghomara keep their own Berber language. The eastern Rif, the Rif proper, speaks Tarifit.

The region has more rainfall than any other part of Morocco, in places over 2,000 millimetres a year. Its western and central parts are forested with Atlas cedar, cork oak and holm oak, and hold the only remaining forests of Moroccan fir. Its mountains shelter subpopulations of the endangered Barbary macaque.

Berbers have lived in the Rif since prehistoric times. From the 11th century BCE the Phoenicians founded trading posts and cities on its coast, such as Rusadir, now Melilla, and in the 5th century BCE Tingi, now Tangier. After the Third Punic War the coast came under Rome and the Rif became part of the Kingdom of Mauretania; when Mauretania was divided under Claudius, Tangier became the capital of Mauretania Tingitana. Roman rule ended in the 5th century CE, and the Byzantine Empire later held part of the region. In 710 Salih I ibn Mansur founded the Emirate of Nekor in the Rif, and the Berbers began converting to Islam.

In the 15th century many Muslims expelled from Spain settled in the western Rif, bringing Andalusian music and founding Chefchaouen. Portugal invaded Ceuta in 1415 and Spain conquered Melilla in 1490. The Hispano-Moroccan War began in 1859 at Tetouan and ended in Moroccan defeat. The Berber guerrilla leader Abd el-Krim proclaimed the Republic of the Rif in 1921, and the Riffians won several victories over Spain in the Rif War before they were defeated; Spanish forces used chemical weapons extensively. Spain restored its zone to Morocco in April 1956, a month after the French zone became independent. The 1958 Rif riots followed, and the Moroccan government suppressed the uprising.

The Rif is divided into an eastern part around Nador, Driouch and Al Hoceima and a western part around Tangier, Tétouan, Chefchaouen and Taounate. Farmers there grow most of Morocco's cannabis. Since the 1950s overgrazing, forest fires and clearing for agriculture have caused heavy deforestation and soil loss.
rif-war: Spain claimed influence over Morocco at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, and the Rif was assigned to it, but Spanish sovereignty there was strictly de jure: the Berber tribes of the Rif had long fought off outsiders. The region was rich in iron ore, and Horacio Echevarrieta received the concession to mine it. The mining displaced local people, who received no share of the profits and began to oppose it. After losing Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines in 1898, Spain saw an Africanist faction press for a new empire in Africa, and it began pushing into the Rif in 1909.

General Manuel Fernández Silvestre spread his troops over 144 forts and outposts deep in the mountains with little logistical support, and in July 1921 the Spanish army collapsed in the disaster of Annual. The death toll reported to the Cortes was 13,192. On 9 August some 2,000 soldiers were killed after surrendering Monte Arruit, and in September Abd el-Krim proclaimed the Republic of the Rif.

A stalemate followed, and from 1924 Spain used chemical weapons, also against civilians. Mutinies and protests against the war broke out in Spain, and General Miguel Primo de Rivera seized power on 13 September 1923. On 12 April 1925 about 8,000 Riffians attacked a French line of posts north of the Oureghla River, and France intervened with an expeditionary force under Marshal Philippe Pétain.

In September 1925 the Spanish fleet and army landed at Alhucemas Bay, the first amphibious landing to use tanks and seaborne air support. Against 12,000 Rifians the allies ranged 123,000 men and 150 aircraft. Abd el-Krim surrendered to the French on 27 May 1926, and the last pocket of resistance, at Akhmas, fell on 9 July 1927. French deaths totalled 8,628. Historians disagree about the war: some see a harbinger of decolonisation in North Africa, others one of the last colonial wars. It left a deep memory in both Spain and Morocco.
rifaa-al-tahtawi: Tahtawi was born in 1801 in the village of Tahta in Sohag, the year French troops evacuated Egypt. He studied at al-Azhar, and his teacher and mentor Hasan al-Attar recommended him as chaplain to a group of students whom Muhammad Ali sent to Paris in 1826. He was meant to serve as imam, but was allowed to associate with the other members of the mission. Such missions went to Europe in the early 19th century to study arts and sciences and to acquire technical skills such as printing, shipbuilding and modern military techniques.

In France Tahtawi studied ethics, social and political philosophy, mathematics and geometry, and read Condillac, Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and Bézout. He returned to Egypt in 1831 to join the effort to modernise infrastructure and education. In 1835 he founded the School of Languages, also called the School of Translators, which became part of Ain Shams University in 1973. It graduated the earliest modern Egyptian intellectual milieu. Tahtawi translated and supervised translations of military manuals, geography and European history, over 2,000 foreign works in all. In the late 1860s he sat on the Educational Council of the new Ministry of Education, and from 1870 to 1873 he edited its magazine Rawdat al-Madaris. He died in Cairo in 1873.

His account of his stay in France, Takhlis al-ibriz fi talkhis Bariz, appeared in 1834 and made him one of the first Egyptian scholars to write about Western culture, seeking understanding between Islamic and Christian civilisations. His writings on political and moral philosophy introduced Egyptian readers to Enlightenment ideas of secular authority, political rights and liberty, and to ideas of the public good and of what made a civilised or good Egyptian. He also wrote a history of ancient Egypt and translated French civil law in 1866 and trade law in 1868. The Honest Guide for the Education of Girls and Boys, published in 1873, answered a request from the Ministry of Education for a book on pedagogy for both sexes.

He is counted among the early Islamic modernists, arguing that Islam's principles were compatible with European modernity, and his work influenced later scholars such as Muhammad Abduh. Shaden Tageldin has argued that his admiration for French culture fostered an intellectual colonisation.
rifling: Muskets are smoothbore weapons that fire ball-shaped ammunition at relatively low velocity. Because of the cost and difficulty of precision manufacture and the need to load quickly from the muzzle, the balls were generally a loose fit, so they bounced off the sides of the barrel and their destination was unpredictable. Where accuracy mattered, as in hunting, a tighter combination of a ball nearer the bore size and a patch was used. The main inspiration for rifling came from archers and crossbowmen, who found that projectiles flew faster and more accurately when twisted fletchings made them rotate.

The inventor of rifling is not definitively known. Straight grooving was applied to small arms from at least 1480, originally as soot grooves to collect gunpowder residue. Among the earliest recorded European attempts at spiral-grooved barrels are those of the Vienna gunsmith Gaspard Kollner in 1498 and of Augustus Kotter of Nuremberg in 1520. Some scholars allege that Kollner's works used only straight grooves until he received help from Kotter.

Rifling is the helical grooving machined into the inside of a firearm's barrel to spin the projectile and improve its stability and accuracy. The ridges left between the grooves are called lands. Its strength is measured by the twist rate, the distance the rifling takes to complete one revolution, and the longer and narrower a projectile is, the faster the twist it needs. In 1879 George Greenhill, a professor of mathematics at the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich, devised a rule of thumb for the best twist, still known as the Greenhill formula.

True rifling dates from the 16th century, but it had to be engraved by hand and did not become commonplace until the mid-19th century. Early rifled firearms were used mainly by wealthy recreational hunters, who did not need rapid fire and valued accuracy. Military users disliked them because they were hard to clean and hard to load: a bullet that fitted the rifling had to be forced down the bore with a mallet, and a smaller one did not engage the grooves. The first practical military weapons to use rifling with black powder were breech-loaders such as the Queen Anne pistol.

Patches helped transfer spin to the ball until the hollow-based Minié ball, which expands to seal the bore and engage the rifling. Gain-twist rifling, in which the twist increases towards the muzzle, was used before and during the American Civil War, including in Colt revolvers.
rigs-ula: Ríg first comes to a farm-hut owned by Ái (great-grandfather) and Edda (great-grandmother), who give him poor, rough food; he sleeps between them, and nine months later Edda bears a dark son, Þræll. He marries Thír, and their 12 sons and nine daughters, with names suggesting ugliness, become the race of serfs. At a pleasant house Ríg is fed well by Afi and Amma, and their son Karl, ruddy of complexion, marries Snör; his children become the free farmers, craftsmen and herdsmen.

In a mansion Faðir and Móðir serve Ríg excellent food, and Móðir bears the fair-haired Jarl. When Jarl grows up and handles weapons, hawks, hounds and horses, Ríg returns, claims him, gives him his name, teaches him runes and urges him to seek lordship. Through warfare Jarl becomes lord of 18 homesteads and marries Erna, daughter of Hersir. Their youngest son, Konr, understands the speech of birds, quenches fire, heals minds and has the strength of eight men.

The poem survives on the last surviving sheet of the Codex Wormianus (AM 242 fol), after Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda. The name Rígr appears to come from Old Irish rí, ríg, king, cognate with Latin rex. Finnur Jónsson and Rudolf Simek suggested the tradition transferred the name from Óðinn to Heimdall, and the prose introduction may have been added by the compiler to match the opening of Völuspá. The modern consensus ascribes the poem to an Icelandic author, though Jean Young and Ursula Dronke, among others, have argued for a Celtic origin.

Historians read the poem allegorically: slaves, freemen and aristocrats did not necessarily look different. Its picture of Þræll follows slave tropes of Old Norse literature, while Karl is taken to stand for the free-born peasant proprietor, the bondi. Thomas Hill held that the poem reflects an aristocratic rather than royalist view, since the king is simply the youngest son of Jarl. Georges Dumézil read Konr's magic as a Germanic adaptation of the Indo-European priestly function. Arngrímur Jónsson's epitome of the lost Skjöldungasaga and the Ynglinga saga in Snorri's Heimskringla both tie a Ríg to Danp and to Dan, from whom the Danes were named.
rigveda: The Rigveda is the oldest known Vedic Sanskrit text, and its early layers are among the oldest extant texts in any Indo-European language. Philological evidence indicates that the bulk of the Rigveda Samhita was composed in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent, most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE, although a wider estimate of c. 1900 to 1200 BCE has also been given. All proposals are inferred from the style and content of the hymns, and the scholars Jamison and Brereton wrote in 2014 that the dating is likely to remain a matter of contention.

According to Witzel, the hymns were first collected after the Bharata victory under King Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and the codification took place about 1200 BCE among the early Kuru tribe.

The Rigveda Samhita is a collection of ten books, called maṇḍalas, with 1,028 hymns in about 10,600 verses. Books 2 to 7, the family books, are the oldest and shortest, each associated with a clan, and they mention prominent Bharata and Pūru kings. The ninth book is entirely dedicated to Soma and the Soma ritual. Books 1 and 10 in part deal with philosophical questions such as the origin of the universe.

The hymns are addressed to many deities. Chief among them are Indra, a heroic god praised for slaying his enemy Vrtra, Agni, the sacrificial fire, and Soma, the sacred potion or the plant it is made from. Mitra and Varuna and Ushas, the dawn, are equally prominent. Tradition associates a rishi, or composer, with each verse, and ten families of rishis account for more than 95 per cent of the verses.

The hymns were composed and preserved orally, and memorised and handed on with what is called unparalleled fidelity through structured methods of enunciation. According to Barbara West the text was probably first written down about the 3rd century BCE. Thirty manuscripts, collected in the 19th century and now in Pune, were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007.

The Rigveda's archaic syntax and morphology are of vital importance for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European, and some verses are still recited at Hindu weddings and other rites of passage, which makes it probably the world's oldest religious text in continued use.
riigikogu: The opening session of the Estonian Constituent Assembly on 23 April 1919 is regarded as the founding date of the Estonian parliament. Under the constitution of 1920 the Riigikogu had 100 members, elected for three years by proportional representation. The first elections took place in 1920, and four more followed between 1923 and 1932. Elections were held on a regional basis, with no threshold in the first two, and a moderate threshold of 2 per cent from 1926. The sessions meet in Toompea Castle, where a new building in an unusual Expressionist style was put up in the former courtyard of the medieval castle in 1920–1922.

In 1933 amendments to the first constitution were approved by referendum, giving more power to an executive president. The following year the president used these powers to adjourn parliament and declared martial law to avert an alleged coup. A second constitution, approved by referendum in 1937, introduced a legislature of two chambers, the Chamber of Deputies (Riigivolikogu) and the State Council (Riiginõukogu). Elections in 1938 allowed only individual candidates to run.

During the Soviet occupation of 1940–41, the German occupation of 1941–44 and the second Soviet occupation of 1944–1991 the parliament was disbanded, and its premises were used by the Supreme Soviet of the Estonian SSR. In September 1992, a year after Estonia regained its independence from the Soviet Union, elections were held under the third constitution, adopted by referendum that summer. It draws on the constitutions of 1920 and 1938 and asserts continuity with the Estonian state as it existed between 1918 and 1940.

Under the 1992 constitution the Riigikogu is again a single chamber of 101 members and holds legislative power. Besides approving laws it appoints high officials, including the prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court, and elects the president, alone or, if necessary, with representatives of local government in a broader electoral college. It also ratifies significant foreign treaties, approves the state budget as law and monitors the executive. Members are elected for four years, and every citizen over 18 may vote, while candidates must be at least 21. The Chancellery of the Riigikogu, established on 5 October 1992, supports its constitutional work.
rijeka: Rijeka lies on the Kvarner Gulf in the northern Adriatic, in western Croatia, 131 kilometres southwest of Zagreb. Its bay is about fifty metres deep, deep enough for large commercial ships, and its position and deep-water port made it fiercely contested over the centuries, between the Holy Roman Empire, the Republic of Venice, the Kingdom of Italy and Yugoslavia. In Croatian the name means river; it is Fiume in Italian, and Latin sources called it Tarsatica, Flumen and Vitopolis. Pliny the Elder mentions it as Tarsatica in the 1st century CE, and Ptolemy about 150 CE.

The earliest settlements on the site were the Celtic Tharsatica, on the hill of Trsat, and the Liburni, a tribe of mariners, in the harbour below, and the city long kept this dual character. Croats settled it from the 7th century, when it was a walled feudal stronghold. It stayed under Habsburg rule for over 450 years, except for brief French rule from 1809, until 1918. Before the First World War its shipyards produced warships for the Austro-Hungarian navy, and it was the main centre for torpedo production. Italy's declaration of war in May 1915 opened a front only 90 kilometres away, and several hundred Italians considered disloyal were deported to camps in Hungary, where many died.

The disintegration of Austria-Hungary in October 1918 produced rival Croatian-Serbian and Italian administrations, and both Italy and the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes claimed the city. On 12 September 1919 Italian nationalist irregulars led by the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio captured it, and they set up the Italian Regency of Carnaro. A free state of Fiume was approved in an election on 24 April 1921, with Riccardo Zanella as its first president, but strife continued, including a Fascist putsch in March 1922. By the Treaty of Rome of 27 January 1924 Italy and Yugoslavia partitioned the territory, and Italy annexed the city on 16 March 1924, beginning about twenty years of Italian government in which the Croatian minority met discrimination.

After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941 an insurgency began in the surroundings and lasted until the war's end. After the war the city was ceded to Yugoslavia, and 58,000 of its 66,000 inhabitants gradually chose to emigrate.

Rijeka is the principal seaport and the third-largest city of Croatia, and the seat of Primorje-Gorski Kotar County. Its economy rests on shipbuilding and maritime transport. The 2021 census counted 107,964 inhabitants. Apart from Croatian and Italian, the city has its own dialect of Venetian, Fiuman, which long served as the common language of its peoples. The Rijeka Carnival, held since 1982, is the largest in Croatia.
riksdag: The Swedish word riksdag derives from the genitive of rike, referring to royal power, and dag, meaning diet or conference; the German Reichstag and the Danish Rigsdag are cognate. The roots of the institution lie in a meeting at Arboga in 1435, traditionally thought to be the first assembly, at which probably only three estates were present: the nobility, the clergy and the burghers. In 1527 the first modern Swedish king, Gustav I Vasa, reshaped this informal body to include representatives of all four social estates: the nobility, the clergy, the burghers and the yeomanry, the freehold farmers.

Representation by estate lasted until 1866. On 22 June of that year the Riksdag decided to reconstitute itself as a bicameral legislature. The First Chamber, with 155 members, was elected indirectly by county and city councillors, and the Second Chamber, with 233 members, was elected directly. The reform came out of discontent with the old Estates, which after the beginnings of the Industrial Revolution could no longer represent large parts of the population. The Riksdag did not become a parliament in the modern sense until parliamentary principles were established in the Swedish political system in 1917.

By an amendment to the Instrument of Government of 1809, the general election of 1970 was the first to a single chamber of 350 seats. The election of 1973 gave the government 175 members and the opposition 175, so that tied votes had to be settled by lot. To avoid a repeat, the number of seats was reduced to 349 from 1976.

Today the Riksdag is a unicameral parliament of 349 members, elected proportionally, and since 1994 for fixed four-year terms. It meets in Parliament House on the island of Helgeandsholmen in central Stockholm. It enacts laws, amends the constitution and appoints a government. Constitutional amendments must be approved twice, in two successive electoral periods with a general election between them. Under the Instrument of Government enacted in 1974, the task of commissioning a politician to form a government was taken from the monarch and given to the speaker of the Riksdag, who nominates a prime minister.

A party needs at least 4 percent of the national vote to enter the Riksdag, or 12 percent in a constituency. Of the 349 seats, 310 are fixed constituency seats and 39 are adjustment seats that correct deviations from proportional representation. No party has won a majority on its own since 1968, so parties form coalitions or other alliances.
riksdag-of-the-estates: The four estates followed the historic lines of division in Swedish society, and until its dissolution the assembly was the highest authority in Sweden after the king. Its peasant estate, Bondeståndet, did not include the whole peasantry. Crofters, lodgers, seasonal labourers and other unlanded or semi-landed groups had no seat, and of the three kinds of bönder only two were represented: the skattebönder, tax-paying yeomen who owned their land, and the kronobönder, who farmed Crown land. The frälsebönder, who farmed land owned by the nobility, were held to be represented by their landlords.

The meeting at Arboga in 1435 is usually counted as the first Riksdag, though there is no sign that the farmers attended it. The first true meeting was probably the one at Uppsala in 1436, after the death of the rebel leader Engelbrekt.

The assemblies settled many turning points. In 1517 the regent Sten Sture the Younger and the Privy Council deposed Archbishop Gustav Trolle at the Riksdag; at Västerås in 1527 Lutheranism replaced Catholicism as the state religion, and in 1544 an order of royal succession ended elective monarchy. The name Riksdag was first used at Arboga in 1561. At Söderköping in 1595 Duke Charles was chosen regent in place of King Sigismund, a Catholic who was also king of Poland, and in 1612, after lobbying by the Lord High Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna, the nobility gained the right to hold all higher offices.

The first open conflict among the estates came in 1650, when the three lower estates attacked the nobility's privileges and Queen Christina used the quarrel to secure her cousin Charles Gustav as her heir. In 1680 the Riksdag enacted a large reduction, the return to the Crown of lands granted to the nobility, and Sweden became an absolute monarchy, confirmed in 1693. The constitution of 1719 restored the Riksdag's powers. The Union and Security Act of 1789 abolished most noble privileges, and in 1809 the Riksdag elected Charles XIII king after Gustav IV Adolf had been deposed.

In 1866 all the estates voted to dissolve themselves and form a new assembly, Sveriges Riksdag. The House of Nobility remained a quasi-official body until 2003. In Finland, ceded to the Russian Empire in 1809, the estates met at Porvoo that year to confirm their new allegiance, and the Diet of Finland kept the Swedish forms. It was not assembled again until Alexander II summoned it in 1863, and in 1905 it passed an act forming a new unicameral parliament.
rila-monastery: The Monastery of Saint John of Rila stands in the deep valley of the Rilska River in the south-western Rila Mountains, 117 km south of Sofia. It is named after its founder, the hermit Saint Ivan of Rila, who lived from 876 to 946. Tradition holds that it was founded during the rule of Tsar Peter I. The hermit himself lived in a cave not far away, and the complex was built by his students.

Almost every tsar of the Second Bulgarian Empire made large donations before the Ottoman conquest, and the monastery became a centre of Bulgarian national consciousness. In the first half of the 14th century the feudal lord Hrelja re-erected it on its present site, and the Tower of Hrelja of 1334 to 1335 and a small church of 1343 survive from that time.

The monastery was destroyed in the middle of the 15th century after Ottoman raids. With donations from Sultana Mara Branković, the Russian Orthodox Church and the Rossikon monastery of Mount Athos, it was rebuilt at the end of the 15th century, and the relics of Ivan of Rila were moved there from Tarnovo in 1469. A fire in 1833 destroyed much of it, and it was reconstructed between 1834 and 1862 under the architect Alexi Rilets.

The rectangular complex centres on an inner yard, and its high stone walls and small windows resemble a fortress. The residential part has 300 chambers, four chapels and a library of 250 manuscripts. The main church has five domes and a gold-plated iconostasis, with frescoes finished in 1846 by masters including the brothers Zahari Zograf and Dimitar Zograf. The museum holds Rafail's Cross, a wooden cross carved by the monk Rafail with 104 religious scenes and 650 miniature figures, completed in 1802.

The monastery acted as a depository of Bulgarian language and culture during foreign rule, and revolutionaries such as Vassil Levski and Gotse Delchev found shelter there. It was declared a national historical monument in 1976 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. Since 1991 it has been wholly subordinate to the Holy Synod of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. About sixty monks live there, and it is a pilgrimage site for many Orthodox Christians.
rim-sin-i: Rim-Sîn I ruled the city-state of Larsa, and succeeded his brother Warad-Sin. His father Kudur-Mabuk, his grandfather Šimti-šilhak and his daughter Manzi-wartaš all had Elamite names. His sister En-ane-du was high priestess of the moon god in Ur. He was a contemporary of Hammurabi of Babylon and of Irdanene of Uruk.

Dating by the middle chronology, Rim-Sîn immediately began to expand Larsa by attacking the neighbouring city-states of Uruk, Isin and Babylon. Around 1808 BCE the city had grown so large that other cities were worried, and the king of Isin, the ruler of Uruk and the chief of Babylon campaigned against him. He defeated them. He then occupied Pi-Naratim, the mouths of the Tigris and Euphrates, around 1807 BCE, Zibnatum around 1805, Bit-Susin and Uzarbara around 1804 and Kisarra around 1802, and in the last of those years he also destroyed Der.

Around 1801 BCE he sacked Uruk, sparing its inhabitants. Around 1797 BCE he invaded the territory of Isin, and he finally seized its capital around 1792 BCE. The conquest was so important to him that every year name of his rule after it was named for the sack of Isin. Around 1787 BCE Hammurabi attacked Isin and reported that he had conquered it, though this is more likely an exaggeration of a successful raid.

Around 1764 BCE Hammurabi turned against Rim-Sîn, who had refused to support him in his war against Elam despite pledging his troops. Hammurabi, with troops from Mari, first attacked Mashkan-shapir on the northern edge of Rim-Sîn's realm. His forces quickly reached Larsa, and after a six-month siege the city fell. Rim-Sîn escaped but was soon found and taken prisoner, and he died soon afterwards, around 1763 BCE.
rim-sin-ii: Rim-Sin II, also written Rīm-Sîn II, ruled the city-state of Larsa and was the last of the Dynasty of Larsa. He was a contemporary of Samsu-iluna of Babylon, and his reign is now thought to have lasted less than two years. He is mentioned as a son of one Warad-Sin, but it is unclear whether this was the earlier ruler of Larsa of that name, and it is not even clear that he came from Larsa. One of his letters suggests that his family came from Kesh, which he calls the city of the one who bore him.

His name was sometimes preceded by the dingir, the sign for a god, though there is no record of his being deified. In a letter he wrote that the great gods had set the foundation of his throne firmly in Kesh to bring light to Emutbalum and gather its scattered people. Several of his year names survive. They record the laying of foundations for the Emudkur temple at Ur and his raising to kingship over the land by the goddess Ninmah in the Kesh temple; one version adds that the evil Kassites had not retreated from the land.

The rebellion began in the eighth regnal year of Samsu-iluna. The rebellious cities included Ur, Uruk, Larsa, Girsu, Umma, Nippur, Kazallu, Kutalla and Bad-tibira, with Eshnunna in the north, and among Rim-Sin's fellow rebels were Ilūni of Eshnunna, Rim-Šara of Umma and Rîm-Anum of Uruk. Kassite troops served in his forces. For a time he controlled Nippur and Ur: documents at Nippur were dated by his reign after Samsu-iluna's year 8 and by Samsu-iluna's again from his year 11.

About 18 months after it began, the rebellion ended for Rim-Sin II with his death and the fall of Larsa to Samsu-iluna. In Samsu-iluna's own account, written from his side, the year was not half over when he killed Rim-Sin, the suborner of Emutbalum, and heaped up a burial mound over him in the land of Kiš; he also captured Iluni of Eshnunna and had his throat cut. The wider revolt went on until Samsu-iluna's fourteenth year. The conflict is mentioned in the much later, fragmentary Chronicle of Ancient Kings.
rimac-river: The Rímac begins on the western slope of the Andes at about 5,508 metres above sea level, on the Nevado Paca, in the highlands of Huarochirí Province. It runs through the provinces of Huarochirí and Lima and reaches the sea at Callao, near Jorge Chávez International Airport. The river is 204 km long and drains a basin of 3,312 km². Its main tributaries are the Santa Eulalia, the San Mateo or Alto Rímac and the Blanco. Like the Chillón to the north and the Lurín to the south, it belongs to the Pacific slope.

Lima stands on the delta-shaped lower valley, one of the city's three valleys. Towns such as Matucana, Ricardo Palma, Chosica, Chaclacayo and Vitarte lie along it and link the coast with the central mountains. The Central Highway and a railway run beside the river from Callao to La Oroya, passing the Abra de Anticona, known as Ticlio, at 4,840 metres.

The name comes from the Quechua word rimaq, 'speaker', and the river was nicknamed El Río Hablador, 'the talking river'. One explanation is that people of the Lima area built galleries at the river's edge with a space where a priest could enter unseen. The inhabitants approached the river, which they regarded as an apu, or deity, and put their questions to it, and the priest answered from inside. A legend instead derives the name from the sacrifice of Rímac, a son of the god Inti, and his sister Chaclla, to end a drought.

The Spanish misheard Rímac as Lima, and the city took its name from the river. The form Limaq seems to have been the original in coastal Quechua and in the Mochica language that preceded it. The best known of the bridges at Lima is the Puente de Piedra, built in 1610 under the viceroy Juan de Mendoza y Luna, Marquis of Montesclaros.

The Rímac is the main source of drinking water for the Lima and Callao metropolitan area. The largest discharge recorded at the Chosica station was 385 cubic metres a second, in 1941. In 1962 water was brought into the basin from the Marcapomacocha lagoon, in the Mantaro basin, through a siphon-shaped tunnel about 10 km long at 4,000 metres. The basin holds a water treatment plant, La Atarjea, and several hydroelectric plants. In 1998 a reserved zone of the river valley was created along a 28 km strip between Lima, Chaclacayo, San Juan de Lurigancho and Ate.
rimbert: Little is known directly about Rimbert. Most of what survives comes from the Vita Rimberti, a hagiography by an unknown author, probably written in the 10th century. His birthplace is uncertain, but historians widely accept that he was Danish. He trained as a monk at Turholt (Torhout) and then shared a missionary journey to Scandinavia with his mentor Ansgar, Bishop of Hamburg. When Ansgar died in 865, Rimbert was elected unanimously to succeed him, and he was consecrated by Archbishop Liudbert of Mainz on the orders of Louis the German.

Rimbert carried on the missionary work begun under Ansgar despite a lack of royal or papal support. He kept up the poorhouse Ansgar had founded in Bremen, founded a monastery at Bücken and went on preaching to the Danes at Hedeby. In 884 he led a Frisian army against the Vikings and, after the victory at the Battle of Norditi, drove them out of East Frisia for good. In 888 he obtained market, coinage and toll rights for Bremen from Emperor Arnulf of Carinthia, which much improved the finances of the see. The Vita Rimberti credits him with miracles, yet the conversion of the Scandinavians brought modest results.

In a letter answering a lost letter of Rimbert, the theologian Ratramnus of Corbie held that the cynocephali, the dog-headed people reported in the north, were human and should be converted. The exchange shows Rimbert's ties with the monks of Corbie and with Charles the Bald in West Frankia, and his sympathy with the ideas on predestination of Gotschalk of Orbais, which set him against Hincmar of Rheims.

Historians read the Vita Ansgari partly as a defence of the see itself. Before Rimbert, an archiepiscopal see of Hamburg-Bremen had not technically existed: Hamburg was only a bishopric, and the Archbishop of Cologne threatened to claim Bremen. Several of Rimbert's accounts of earlier grants are at odds with the surviving documents, and in the Vita he gave a believable setting for the forged documents used to claim Bremen as well as Hamburg. He is revered as a saint, particularly in Frisia, with a feast day on 4 February, and is called the Second Apostle of the North.
rime-movement: According to Sam van Schaik, non-sectarianism was the norm in Tibet's golden age of the 14th and 15th centuries, when figures such as Longchenpa and Tsongkhapa studied with teachers of different schools. Sectarian wars in Central Tibet in the 16th and 17th centuries set the Kagyu schools against the Gelug, whose victory with the help of the Qoshot Mongol armies left the Gelug politically dominant and the minority lineages at risk of losing their traditions. Some Gelug figures kept a broader outlook, among them the Fifth Dalai Lama, who revered the Nyingma, and the yogi Shabkar Tsokdruk Rangdrol.

In the 19th century Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo (1820–1892), raised in the Sakya order, and Jamgön Kongtrül (1813–1899), of the Nyingma and Kagyu, gathered and printed teachings of their schools, including many near-extinct ones, in compilations such as the Rinchen Terdzod and the Sheja Dzö.

The name joins ris, side or bias, and med, absence, and means without distinction. Only in the 20th century did it become a name for the ideas of the 19th-century scholars, who did not form a conscious unified movement. The scholar Seyfort Ruegg called it universalistic and encyclopaedic rather than eclectic. As the teacher Ringu Tulku explains it, Rimé is not a new school and does not unite the schools by their similarities; it values their differences, and its followers usually keep one lineage as their main practice while respecting the others. Kongtrul warned that without a firm grounding in one's own tradition a student would become tangled, like a bad weaver.

Early Rimé writers often criticised Gelug tenets, which Georges Dreyfus reads as support for marginalised minority views. In the 20th century Phabongkha Rinpoche and his disciples, promoting the cult of Dorje Shugden and Gelug exclusivism, destroyed objects linked to Padmasambhava and forcibly converted Nyingma monasteries in Kham. Rimé ideals have since been promoted by the 13th and 14th Dalai Lamas, the 15th and 16th Karmapas and Sakya Trizin, and taking teachings from several lineages has become common.
rimush: Rimush, also written Rimuš, was the second king of the Akkadian Empire and a son of Sargon of Akkad. His brother Manishtushu succeeded him, and Naram-Sin of Akkad was his nephew. His sister was Enheduana, considered the earliest known named author in world history. Naram-Sin deified Sargon and Manishtushu after their deaths but not his uncle. The city of Dur-Rimuš, the Fortress of Rimush, stood near Tell Ishchali and Khafajah and was a cult centre of the storm god Adad.

According to the Sumerian King List his reign lasted nine years, though variant copies read seven or fifteen. Most of it went to consolidating the empire Sargon had made, which reached Syria in the west, Elam in the east, southern Anatolia in the north and the lower sea in the south. His inscriptions record widespread revolts, and he had to reconquer the cities of Ur, Umma, Adab, Lagash, Der, KI.AN and Kazallu from rebellious governors.

One inscription claims that at Adab and Zabalam he struck down 15,718 men and took 14,576 captives, and another that at Umma and KI.AN he struck down 8,900 and took 3,540. These accounts say he destroyed city walls and expelled and annihilated thousands more, and they speak of enormous Sumerian losses.

He also campaigned against Elam and Marhashi. After the conquest of Elam he dedicated 30 mana of gold, 3,600 mana of copper and 360 slaves to Enlil at Nippur. Under Manishtushu, Elam was ruled by Akkadian military governors. Votive offerings of Rimush have been found in temples at Ur, Sippar, Khafajah and Brak, and an inscription records a statue of himself that he placed before Enlil at Nippur; its metal is variously read as tin, bronze or meteoric iron. A victory stele in fragments from Girsu, attributed to him on stylistic grounds although some propose the time of Naram-Sin, shows Akkadian soldiers slaughtering prisoners and records land grants taken from Lagash for the Akkadian nobility.

Tradition holds that Rimush was assassinated. A first-millennium BCE compendium of omens, the Bārûtu, records an omen of King Rimush, whom his courtiers killed with their cylinder seals. He was succeeded by his brother Manishtushu.
ringstrasse: The boulevard replaced the city walls of Vienna, which had been built in the 13th century and first funded by the ransom paid for the release of Richard the Lionheart, captured near Vienna on his return from the Third Crusade. They were reinforced after the Ottoman Siege of Vienna in 1529 and the Thirty Years' War, and were surrounded by a glacis about 500 metres wide where building and planting were forbidden. By the late 18th century the fortifications were obsolete, and under Emperor Joseph II streets and walkways were laid out in the glacis.

In 1850 the suburbs were incorporated into the city, and the walls became an obstacle to traffic. In 1857 Emperor Franz Joseph I issued the decree Es ist Mein Wille, ordering the demolition of the walls and moats and setting out the dimensions of the new boulevard and the locations and functions of the planned buildings.

The Ringstrasse is a circular boulevard of 5.3 km running clockwise from the Urania to the Schottenring, in nine sections, most named after a prominent structure. Aristocrats and wealthy individuals hurried to build Ring Road palaces in the historicist style. Buildings along it include the Vienna State Opera, the Hofburg, the Kunsthistorisches Museum, the Naturhistorisches Museum, the Austrian Parliament Building, the Burgtheater, the University of Vienna and the Votivkirche. Because the Ring was designed for appearance, a parallel street for freight, the Lastenstraße, later called Zweierlinie, was built beyond it.

Work was not finished until 1913 with the Ministry of War, when the historicist style was already unfashionable, as the Art Nouveau Postal Savings Bank by Otto Wagner, built opposite in 1906, shows. The Ringtheater fire of 1881 killed several hundred people.

The Ring and its buildings were meant as a testament to the grandeur and glory of the Habsburg Empire. On a practical level, the project was influenced by Emperor Napoléon III's planning in Paris, where wider streets had proved effective in preventing revolutionary barricades and in allowing artillery control. The Ringstrasse is designated by UNESCO as part of the Historic Centre of Vienna World Heritage Site. It remains a major route through the city's road network, with trams, two bike lanes, shops and hotels, and a route that tourists walk to see its sights.
rinteln: Rinteln is a small town in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the banks of the Weser river north of the Porta Westfalica. It lies in the broad valley between the hills of the Weserbergland and the North Lippe Bergland, 60 kilometres west of Hanover and 20 kilometres from Hamelin. Its population is about 28,500, and it is reached by the A2 autobahn. The town includes a number of villages, among them Deckbergen, Engern, Exten, Steinbergen and Todenmann.

The settlement of Rinteln was founded about 1150 on the northern bank of the Weser. In 1235 the village of Neu-Rinteln, or New Rinteln, was founded on the southern bank. It is the origin of the modern town, since the northern village was abandoned in 1350 because of the plague. The village grew into a fortified town that served as a southern stronghold of the Counts of Schaumburg.
