From 1621 until its dissolution in 1810, during the Westphalian rule of Jérôme Bonaparte, Rinteln was the seat of the Ernestina University. When the County of Schaumburg was divided, Rinteln became the capital of the eastern part, which kept the name Grafschaft Schaumburg hessischen Anteils, and the Eulenburg in Rinteln became the seat of the counts. It remained the capital of the county and later of the district until the district was merged with the neighbouring district of Schaumburg-Lippe in 1977. The railway station was opened in 1875, and a British Forces hospital stood in Rinteln during the 1960s.

Rinteln is twinned with Kendal in Cumbria and with Sławno in Pomerania. Among people born there are Friedrich Wilhelm von Lossberg (1720–1800), a Hessian lieutenant general who fought with the British-allied German contingents in the American Revolutionary War; Philip II, Count of Schaumburg-Lippe (1723–1787), a ruler of the counties of Lippe-Alverdissen and Schaumburg-Lippe; the Dutch goldsmith Diederik Lodewijk Bennewitz (1764–1826); and the physicist Friedrich Kohlrausch (1840–1910), who investigated the conductive properties of electrolytes.
rio-de-janeiro: Rio de Janeiro lies near the west end of a strip of Brazil's Atlantic coast, close to the Tropic of Capricorn, where the shoreline runs east and west, so the city faces largely south. It was founded at the entrance to an inlet, Guanabara Bay, which is marked by a point of land called Sugar Loaf. The city occupies 1,182.3 square kilometres, and its residents are known as cariocas. Its parks include the Tijuca National Park, a national park since 1961, and the Passeio Público, described as the first public park in the Americas.

The region was inhabited by the Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí peoples. Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 during a Portuguese expedition, which gave the bay and then the city its name, meaning January River. In 1555 some 500 French colonists under Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon occupied an island in the bay and built Fort Coligny, attempting to found the colony of France Antarctique. The Portuguese saw it as a threat, and from 1560 a long military campaign led by Governor General Mem de Sá and later his nephew Estácio de Sá ended on 20 January 1567 in the defeat and expulsion of the French.

Estácio de Sá founded the city proper on 1 March 1565 and named it São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro, after the patron saint of the Portuguese king Sebastião. Until early in the 18th century it was threatened or invaded by pirates and buccaneers, mostly French. In 1763 it became the capital of the State of Brazil, and in 1808 the Portuguese royal court moved there. Rio remained the capital of the Portuguese monarchy until 1822, the only instance in modern history in which the capital of a colonising country officially shifted to one of its colonies. It then served as capital of the Empire of Brazil until 1889, and of republican Brazil until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília.

Rio de Janeiro is the capital of the state of Rio de Janeiro, with about 6 million people in the city proper. It is known for its carnival, samba and bossa nova, and for beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema. Landmarks include the statue of Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain and the Maracanã Stadium.
rio-de-la-plata: The Río de la Plata, in English the River Plate, is the estuary formed by the confluence of the Uruguay River and the Paraná River at Punta Gorda. It flows east into the Atlantic Ocean in a funnel-shaped indentation on the south-eastern coast of South America. It is about 290 km long and widens from about 2 km at its head to about 220 km at its mouth. Geographers disagree whether to call it a river, an estuary, a gulf or a marginal sea. Its drainage basin covers about a quarter of the continent. Part of the border between Argentina and Uruguay runs along it, and its coasts hold the port cities of Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

Nomadic aboriginal peoples lived in the region for thousands of years before European settlers arrived. The Portuguese first explored the estuary in 1512–13. In 1516 the Spanish navigator Juan Díaz de Solís crossed it in search of a passage between the Atlantic and the Pacific. Sebastian Cabot explored the Paraná and Uruguay rivers between 1526 and 1529 and obtained silver trinkets from the Guaraní, which, with legends of a Sierra de la Plata, led him to rename it Río de la Plata, the river of silver. Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires on 2 February 1536, but the settlement was soon abandoned, and Juan de Garay refounded it on 11 June 1580.

The region became the Governorate of the Río de la Plata. Buenos Aires became a centre of trade outside the Spanish fleet system, exporting silver from Potosí and importing European goods, slaves and sugar. In 1776 the Bourbon Crown raised the governorate to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. A British invasion in 1806 and 1807 was defeated by the local garrison and population.

After independence in the early nineteenth century, interests in the territories and navigation rights on the river played a major part in many conflicts, including the Cisplatine and Platine wars and the Paraguayan War. Brazil blockaded the river from 1826 to 1828, the French from 1838 to 1840 and an Anglo-French alliance from 1845 to 1850.

In December 1939 the German pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee fought British and New Zealand cruisers off the estuary in the first naval battle of the Second World War. She put into Montevideo, where her captain scuttled her a few days later.
rio-grande: The Rio Grande, called the Río Bravo in Mexico, is 1,896 miles (3,051 km) long. It rises in Colorado, in the San Juan Mountains, flows through the San Luis Valley and the Rio Grande Gorge into New Mexico, passes Albuquerque and Las Cruces, and reaches El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua. South of El Paso it forms the border between the United States and Mexico as far as the Gulf of Mexico. Its largest tributary by discharge is the Rio Conchos, and the Pecos River drains the largest area. The name means Big River in Spanish; the Navajo call it Tó Baʼáadi.

The earliest traces of people in the valley include Folsom sites near Albuquerque, possibly from about 10,800 to 9,700 BCE. Drought brought the collapse of the Ancestral Puebloan culture at Chaco Canyon around 1130 CE, and many Ancestral Puebloans migrated to the Rio Grande valley, where most of the Tanoan and Keresan pueblos were founded. In autumn 1540 an expedition under Francisco Vásquez de Coronado reached the Tiwa pueblos along the river, and on 12 July 1598 Juan de Oñate y Salazar founded the Spanish colony of New Mexico beside the Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo.

In the late 1830s and early 1840s the river marked the disputed border between Mexico and the Republic of Texas, which Mexico placed at the Nueces River. The disagreement was part of the reason for the Mexican–American War in 1846, and since 1848 the river has marked the boundary from El Paso and Ciudad Juárez to the Gulf. In the nineteenth century over 200 steamboats worked between its mouth and Rio Grande City, and during the American Civil War the Mexican port of Bagdad at its mouth was the Confederacy's only legitimate port.

The river is a vital source of water for seven American and Mexican states and flows mostly through arid and semi-arid land. Its water is shared under treaties signed in 1906 and 1944 and under the Rio Grande Compact of 1938 between Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. Dams include Elephant Butte, Amistad and Falcon. A stretch of 260 miles in New Mexico and Texas is designated the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River. The main border crossings include Ciudad Juárez and El Paso, Laredo and Nuevo Laredo, and Brownsville and Matamoros.
rio-grande-do-norte: Rio Grande do Norte forms the north-eastern tip of the South American continent. Its name means Great Northern River and refers to the mouth of the Potengi river. The coast, about 410 kilometres of sandy beaches, dominates the state, and two climates meet there: humid tropical on the eastern coast and semi-arid over most of the rest, where much of the interior lies in the Polygon of Droughts. The state also includes Rocas Atoll, 260 kilometres north-east of Natal, the only atoll in the South Atlantic.

The first European to reach the region may have been the Spaniard Alonso de Ojeda in 1499. Cape São Roque, to the north of Natal, was visited in 1501 on the Portuguese expedition led by Amerigo Vespucci, which also named the Potengi river and the Rio Grande after which the captaincy and later the state were named. For decades no permanent European settlement was made among the Potiguara, who lived there, and between 1535 and 1598 French pirates came in search of brazilwood. The Portuguese built the Forte dos Reis Magos in 1598 and founded Natal the next year. Cattle and sugarcane then drove the local economy.

In 1633 the area became a battleground between the Portuguese and the Dutch. When sugar prices fell in Amsterdam, a crisis led settlers and native Brazilians to revolt against the Dutch, in what are known as the massacres of Cunhaú and Uruaçu. Religious conflict between Portuguese-Brazilian Catholicism and Dutch Calvinism, Portugal's restoration of its throne in 1640 and the reconquest of Maranhão in 1643 led to the uprising of 1645 under André Vidal de Negreiros and João Fernandes Vieira, in which most of the rebels were Africans and Amerindians. The Dutch were finally driven out in 1654. In the Second World War the state served as an Allied airbase, and in 1964 Latin America's first space launch site, Barreira do Inferno, was built there.

Natal is the capital and largest city, and the state has 167 municipalities and an estimated 3,568,765 inhabitants in 2021. Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has relied on sugar and cattle, and now also on tourism, petroleum, fruit, sea salt, cashew and carnauba wax. The sixteenth-century Forte dos Reis Magos still stands, and the folklorist Luís da Câmara Cascudo was born and worked in the state.
rio-grande-do-sul: Rio Grande do Sul, meaning Great River of the South, lies in the southernmost part of Brazil. It is bordered by Santa Catarina to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, Uruguay to the south and southwest, and the Argentine provinces of Corrientes and Misiones to the west. Its climate is predominantly humid subtropical, and in winter a cold southwesterly wind called the minuano sometimes lowers the temperature below freezing.

Before the arrival of Portuguese and Spanish settlers the area was inhabited mostly by the Guarani and Kaingang peoples. The first Europeans there were Jesuits, followed by settlers from the Azores. By the Treaty of Tordesillas the region was to be Spanish, but Spain's interest lay on the Pacific coast and the River Plate, and the Spanish introduced livestock that escaped into the plains and attracted gauchos. The colonial province saw small wars and border skirmishes between Portugal and Spain. The Portuguese Crown distributed land in enormous latifundia, where cattle raising predominated, while Azorean settlers on smaller properties introduced wheat, the main export until the early 19th century.

In the 19th century the state was the scene of the Ragamuffin War, wars with Argentina and Uruguay, and the Paraguayan War. In the war against the Argentine dictator Juan Manuel Rosas, 75 percent of the Brazilian troops were gaúchos. In 1865 a Paraguayan division occupied Uruguaiana, and troops of the Triple Alliance besieged it until the Paraguayans surrendered. In 1930 Getúlio Vargas, then state president, led a revolt that overthrew the federal government.

Rio Grande do Sul is a state of Brazil divided into 497 municipalities, with Porto Alegre as its capital and largest city. It shares a gaucho culture with Argentina and Uruguay, and its people are known for drinking chimarrão, a local version of mate, and for eating churrasco. Large waves of German and Italian migration have shaped the state.
rio-protocol: In May 1941, as tension mounted on the border and war seemed near, the United States, Brazil and Argentina offered to mediate between Ecuador and Peru. They could not prevent the fighting that began on 23 July 1941, but their intervention brought a ceasefire on 31 July, though skirmishes went on through August and September in the Ecuadorian provinces of El Oro and Loja and in the Amazonian lands. On 2 October, before military observers of the three mediators, the two countries signed the Talara Accord, which set up a demilitarised zone in El Oro and Loja until a peace treaty was made. Chile then joined the mediation.

The protocol was signed on the last day of the third Pan-American Summit in Rio de Janeiro by the foreign ministers Julio Tobar Donoso of Ecuador and Alfredo Solf y Muro of Peru, and co-signed by the four guarantors. Both congresses ratified it on 26 February 1942. Ecuador withdrew its long-standing claim to direct land access to the Marañon and Amazon rivers, and Peru agreed to withdraw its forces from Ecuadorian territory.

About 200,000 square kilometres of disputed land in the Maynas region of the Amazon basin went to Peru. The line was based on the status quo line of the 1936 Lima Accord, which had recognised possession but not sovereignty: against that line Ecuador ceded 18,552 square kilometres it had held, and Peru 5,072 square kilometres.

The protocol was meant to end the long dispute and formally closed the Ecuadorian–Peruvian War of 1941–1942, but it left the boundary incomplete. War broke out twice more, in 1981 and in 1995: the Paquisha Incident and the Cenepa War revived the dispute before the Itamaraty Peace Declaration brought it to its final resolution.
rio-tinto: The Río Tinto rises in the Sierra Morena of Andalusia and flows south-south-west for about 100 kilometres to the Gulf of Cádiz at Huelva. Its name means coloured river, though tinto is also the Spanish word for red wine. It keeps its orange and red colour for about 50 kilometres, because of very high levels of iron and heavy metals in its acidic water, with a pH of about 2. The acid begins to be neutralised near Niebla. The river lies within the Iberian Pyrite Belt, a region of large ore and sulphide deposits that formed by hydrothermal activity on the sea floor in the Carboniferous period. Scientists are unsure how much of its acidity is natural and how much comes from mining.

The area has about 5,000 years of mining, for copper, silver and gold and later for iron and manganese, from as far as 20 kilometres from the river. Mining is traced to the Tartessans and Iberians from around 3000 BCE, followed by the Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Visigoths and Moors, and it greatly changed the region's landscape. After a period of abandonment the mines were rediscovered in 1556, and the Spanish government began operating them again in 1724.

In the 19th century companies from the United Kingdom began large-scale mining, and the Río Tinto Company was formed in 1873 to operate the mines. Output peaked in 1930. Copper mining ended in 1986, silver and gold mining in 1996, and all remaining activity in 2001. The mine had once employed as many as 20,000 people. After a permit was granted in January 2015, Atalaya Mining, formerly EMED Mining, restarted commercial copper production in February 2016.

Little lives in the river besides microorganisms and algae, which make up over half its biomass. Its extreme chemistry, which resembles conditions on Mars described by scientists, has drawn interest from astrobiologists studying the limits of life.
riobamba: The country around Riobamba was inhabited by the Puruha before the Inca advanced into it in the late 15th century. The Puruha fiercely resisted the Inca conquest of what is now northern Ecuador, and the Inca Huayna Capac had to make an alliance to pacify the tribes that followed Condorazo, the Puruha general. He allied with the Schyris confederation, also called the Caran-Quitu people, who are believed to have developed the Kingdom of Quito. The 18th-century Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco described the confederation as ruled by the Duchicela dynasty. Huayna Capac married the princess Paccha, and their son Atahualpa became the last king of the Inca.

After the Spanish invasion Diego de Almagro founded Riobamba on 15 August 1534 on the plains of San Miguel. It is considered the first city founded in what is now Ecuador, and in 1563 it became part of the newly formed Royal Audience of Quito. An earthquake destroyed it completely in 1797, and it was rebuilt a few years later 14 km from its original site, near the village of Cajabamba. During the Ecuadorian War of Independence the city first declared independence on 11 November 1820 but was soon retaken by Crown forces. In 1822 it became part of Gran Colombia, and in 1830 the Republic of Ecuador established its own independence.

Riobamba is the capital of Chimborazo Province, in the Chambo River Valley of the Andes, 200 km south of Quito at an elevation of 2,754 m, close to the Chimborazo volcano. The name joins the Spanish rio, "river", with the Quechua rispampa, "plain". The city keeps much architecture from the Spanish colonial period, and its historic centre has a number of well-preserved churches. Its economy rests on the agriculture of the surrounding region and on cattle ranching, and indigenous artisans sell textiles, leather goods and dairy products at its open-air market.
rionegro: The territory was first mentioned in 1541 by the Spanish lieutenant Álvaro de Mendoza, and Jorge Robledo is said to have been the first Iberian to reach the Valley of San Nicolás on 2 September 1541. On 8 November 1581 Juan Daza took possession of the land by nailing his sword in the ground, in accordance with the rituals of the laws of Indias, and began building a farm. Settlers came from many parts of the country, among them the provincial capital Santa Fe de Antioquia, and the farm grew into a village and then a town in the first half of the 17th century. The chapel of San Nicolás el Magno was built as early as 1642.

For most of the 18th century Rionegro was isolated by jungle and mountains. By 1783 it had enough population to be treated as a municipality, and in 1786 it became the City of Santiago de Arma de Rionegro under a certificate of King Carlos III. The bishop of Popayán visited in 1793, found the chapel in a poor state and ordered a new one, which was inaugurated in 1803. In the 19th century Rionegro was an important centre at the end of Spanish rule and in the early years of independence, and it rivalled Santa Fe de Antioquia for the capital of Antioquia until Medellín grew far beyond both. The 1863 constitution was written in the city, which is sometimes called the Cradle of Democracy.

Rionegro is a city and municipality in the subregion of Eastern Antioquia, in the central range of the Andes, at an average elevation of 2,125 metres. It covers 196 square kilometres and takes its name, meaning Black River, from a river that looks black because of the shadows the trees cast on it. The population was 101,046 at the 2005 census. It is a trading centre for the region, with industry and flower growing, and José María Córdova International Airport, which serves Medellín, stands within it. Its historic sites include the Concatedral de San Nicolás el Magno and the Casa de la Convención.
ripon: Ripon lies at the confluence of two tributaries of the River Ure, the Laver and the Skell, in North Yorkshire, and was originally known as Inhrypum. The area was once under the Brigantes, who built a large circular earthwork at Hutton Moor. The Romans did not settle at Ripon but kept a military outpost about 8 km away at North Stainley.

Solid evidence for Ripon begins in the 7th century, under the Anglian kingdom of Northumbria. King Alhfrith of Deira gave land to Eata of Hexham for a monastery, with monks including the young Cuthbert as guest-master. When Alhfrith drove Eata out, the abbey passed to Wilfrid, who replaced the timber church with one of stone, using stonemasons, glaziers and plasterers from Lyon and Rome. In 937 King Athelstan granted the church sanctuary for a mile around, and after the Northumbrians rebelled in 948 King Edred had the buildings burned. Prosperity returned by the end of the 10th century, when the body of Saint Cuthbert was moved to Ripon for a time because of the threat of Danish raids.

After the Harrying of the North that followed the rebellion of 1069, Ripon is thought to have shrunk to a small community around the church, and a Gothic Collegiate Church was built over Wilfrid's building. In the 12th century a wool trade drew Florentine merchants, and after 1326 a cloth industry grew that was the third largest in Yorkshire after York and Halifax. The Reformation badly affected the town, and 300 rebels of the Rising of the North were hanged at Gallows Hill in January 1570. In the 16th and 17th centuries Ripon was known for its spurs, which gave rise to the proverb as true steel as Ripon Rowels. A treaty ending the Bishops' Wars was signed there in 1640.

In 1836 Ripon's church became a cathedral when the diocese was created, the first of the Church of England after the Reformation. The council presumed this made the town a city, and the City of Ripon Act of 1865 recognised the status.

The cathedral, an English Gothic building, has been rebuilt many times, and only the Saxon crypt is original. It holds the grave of Wilfrid. The Ripon Hornblower tradition is said to date from 886, and the Ripon Obelisk in the market square was erected in 1702. Nearby are Studley Royal Park and Fountains Abbey, a World Heritage Site.
ripuarian-franks: The Ripuarian Franks, also called Rhenish or Rhineland Franks, were the Franks who established themselves in and around the formerly Roman city of Cologne. Until the 1950s they were seen as the easternmost of two distinct sub-tribes of the Franks, ruling much of what later became Austrasia, while their western counterparts, the Salians, took northern France. This view rested on two 7th-century codes, the Lex Ripuaria and the Lex Salica. Since the 1950s the term Ripuarian is no longer seen as having begun as a tribal name, even if it came to name a specific population based at Cologne.

The origin of the word is debated. A traditional explanation derives it from the Latin ripa, riverbank, referring to the Rhine, but the second part of the name resembles the Germanic suffix -varii, meaning inhabitants, found in tribal names such as the Ampsivarii. Springer proposed that the people of Cologne owed the name to a unit of Roman border police posted there before the Franks took over.

The kingdom of Cologne lost its independence almost as soon as it entered the record. According to Gregory of Tours, Cologne was ruled by Sigobert the Lame, who had fought beside the Salian Frank Clovis against the Alamanni and was lamed by a wound at the Battle of Tolbiac in 496. In 509, Gregory says, Clovis sent word to Sigobert's son Chloderic that he would ally with him if his father died. Chloderic had his father killed by hired assassins in his tent across the Rhine from Cologne, and then offered Clovis part of the treasury. Chloderic was killed by an axe blow as he showed it to Clovis's messengers.

Clovis then came to Cologne, denied any part in the murders and advised the citizens to place themselves under his protection. They acclaimed him by voice vote and raised him on their shields, and the independent kingdom of the Cologne Franks ended at a single assembly in 509.

In the first half of the 7th century the Ripuarians received the Ripuarian law, the Lex Ripuaria, from the dominant Salian Franks, who mainly re-authorized laws the Ripuarians already used so that they kept a local constitution. It is now seen mainly as a law code of the Cologne Rhineland, covering neighbouring towns such as Bonn, Zülpich, Jülich and Neuss. The earliest narrative source clearly using the word for the people of Cologne is the Liber Historiae Francorum, completed about 726/27. The term was later used of larger areas: the Annals of Xanten called Lothar II king of the Ripuarians.
risan: Risan lies in the innermost part of the Bay of Kotor, protected from the interior by the limestone cliffs of the Orjen mountain, the highest range of the eastern Adriatic, and from the open sea by several narrow straits. The Krivošije karst plateau above it receives over 5,000 millimetres of rain a year, and karst springs collect in a narrow cultivable belt at the shore. The Latin name was Risinium, which may be related to the Albanian rrjedh, meaning flow or stream. It is in the northern part of the Municipality of Kotor.

The earliest mention of Rhizon dates from the 4th century BCE, as the main fortress of the Illyrian state where Queen Teuta took refuge during the Illyrian Wars. Hellenization there was very high. In Roman times Rhizinium was an oppidum of Roman citizens, and it was most prosperous in the 1st and 2nd centuries, when large villas were built and the city had 10,000 inhabitants. Five mosaics from that period are the most valuable remains, for Montenegro as well as for Risan. Around 500 it became the see of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Risano, but invasions by the Avars and Slavs left it deserted, and the last Roman bishop recorded there dates from 595.

In the 10th century Constantine Porphyrogenitus listed Risan among the inhabited towns of Travunia. In the Middle Ages it lost its ancient importance, though a series of Latin Catholic bishops of Risano continued until about 1630. In the mid-15th century it belonged to Herceg Stjepan, and in 1482 the Ottomans took it from his son Vlatko, using it as a base for corsairs against Venetian shipping. It became Venetian in 1688, and in the 1627 census had 800 inhabitants, of whom 570 were Muslim, 150 Orthodox and 80 Catholic.

Risan is a small port of roughly 2,000 inhabitants, from which logs from the forests of the Bijela gora are shipped, mostly to Italy. On the Gradina hill above the archaeological site of Carine stands a fortification with the remains of an Illyrian acropolis and medieval and Turkish layers. During World War II it was for a few years part of the Italian Governatorate of Dalmatia, and it is now in independent Montenegro.
rites-of-zhou: The Rites of Zhou, originally titled Officers of Zhou, appeared in the middle of the 2nd century BCE, when it was found and added to the Old Texts in the library of Prince Liu De, a younger brother of the Han emperor Wu. Its first editor was Liu Xin, who credited it to the Duke of Zhou and renamed it to distinguish it from a chapter of the Book of History with the same title. Tradition continued this attribution at least from the Song dynasty.

The book could not have been composed in the Western Zhou. Following Kang Youwei, writers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries often took it for a forgery by Liu Xin. Most scholars now follow Qian Mu and Gu Jiegang in dating it to about the 3rd century BCE, and Yu Yingshi argues for the late Warring States period, reading Zhou in the title as the small royal state of that name. Mark Edward Lewis links it to the administrative reforms of that age.

The work is divided into six chapters on the offices of Heaven, Earth, Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter. They cover general governance and the royal household, local government, agriculture and taxation, ceremonies, music and ritual, the army, justice and punishments, and public works and crafts. Within each department officials come in five ranks, from a single minister down to junior clerks. Most of the text is a schematic list of what each office does and who may hold it, interrupted now and then by exposition on how an office serves social harmony.

The Winter chapter holds the Record of Trades, with information on technology, architecture and city planning. It describes a capital that is nine li square, with three gates on each side and nine streets running each way.

The Rites of Zhou became one of the Three Rites, the ancient ritual texts among the Confucian classics, alongside the Book of Rites and the Etiquette and Ceremonial. In the 12th century it was placed among the Five Classics in place of the long-lost Classic of Music. It was translated into French by Édouard Biot in 1850, and an abridged English version appeared in 1852.
ritsurin-garden: In 1625 Ikoma Takatoshi, the feudal lord of Takamatsu in Sanuki Province, began building a garden around the South Pond, with the greenery of Mount Shiun, Purple Cloud Mountain, as its backdrop. After Matsudaira Yorishige took control of the province he continued the work, and successive lords improved and extended the garden until the fifth lord, Yoritaka, completed it in 1745 as a private strolling garden and villa.

Ritsurin covers 750,000 square metres of a former river bed on the east side of Mount Shiun and is one of the largest strolling gardens in Japan. Numerous ponds and small artificial hills dot it, among them the Western Lake, Sai-ko, the Southern Lake, Nan-ko, and the two artificial mountains Hiraiho and Fuyō-ho, and there is a Wild Duck Hunting Moat. The southern part keeps the traditional Japanese style, with historic teahouses such as the Kikugetsu-tei, the Moon Scooping Pavilion, built around 1640, and the hakomatsu, black pines whose branches and needles are trimmed into geometrical shapes. Koi fill the ponds and streams.

The Meiji government, which came to power in 1868, requisitioned the garden. A silk mill was at first proposed, but Ritsurin was designated a prefectural garden and opened to the public on 16 March 1875. Its northern part was then redesigned in Western style, and a large museum, later the Commerce and Industry Promotion Hall, and folk craft galleries were built at its centre; for a time the garden also held a zoo and a swimming pool, since removed. In 1953 it was designated a Special Place of Scenic Beauty.
ritsuryo: The Taika reforms of 645 were the first signs of the system. The court then issued a series of codes: the Ōmi-ryō of 669, an administrative code of 22 volumes whose existence is disputed; the Asuka-kiyomihara-ryō of 689, also of 22 volumes; the Taihō-ritsuryō of 701, with 11 volumes of administrative and 6 of criminal law; and the Yōrō-ritsuryō, a revision of the Taihō code compiled in 720 and enacted in 757. Later amendments were called kyaku and enactments shiki.

The country was divided into provinces (kuni), districts (gun) and neighbourhoods of 50 homes; a variant with townships, introduced in 715, was abandoned in 740. At the centre stood the Jingi-kan, the Department of Worship, and the Daijō-kan, the Department of State with its eight ministries. Every post had four grades, from the kami at the head to the sakan, a pattern repeated even for court musicians and apothecaries. Income rose steeply with rank: an official of the sixth rank might receive 22 koku of rice a year, one of the third rank as much as 6,957.

Households were registered every six years and a yearly tax book was kept, on which the so-yō-chō taxes on rice and local products rested, along with corvée and military service. The criminal code set five grades of punishment, from caning to exile and death by hanging or beheading, and eight grave crimes, among them plots against the emperor and acts of unfilial piety, which no amnesty could pardon. It followed the Ten Abominations of the Tang code but left out two crimes concerning family life.

Under the Handen-Shūju system every registered person over six received a taxable rice field, 2 tan for a man and two thirds of that for a woman, returned at death. Laws of 723 and 743 let those who cleared new land keep it, first for three generations and then without limit, which gave rise to the first private estates, the shōen. Emperor Kanmu stretched the interval between redistributions to 12 years, and the last took place in 902 and 903.
river-avon-hampshire: The Avon begins as two separate streams. The western arm rises east of Devizes and drains the Vale of Pewsey, while the eastern arm rises at Easton Royal, east of Pewsey. They merge at Upavon and flow south across Salisbury Plain through Durrington, Amesbury and Salisbury, where the Nadder, Wylye, Bourne and Ebble converge. South of Salisbury the river flows along the western edge of the New Forest through Fordingbridge and Ringwood to Christchurch, where it meets the River Stour and enters Christchurch Harbour. About half of the river is in Wiltshire; the rest is split between Hampshire and, since 1974, Dorset. Its name is a tautology, since Avon is the Proto-Brythonic word for river.

Many prehistoric sites lie on either side of the valley, the largest being the World Heritage Site zone of Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites, followed by the fortified knoll of Old Sarum. Long-farmed pastures and arable fields line much of the valley, and the wealth they brought to landowners is shown by ten large listed houses with protected parks, among them Wilton House, Longford Castle and Breamore House.

A navigation from Salisbury to Christchurch was authorised by an Act of 1664. Work began in 1675 and the route was completed in 1684, but it fell out of use around 1715. Canalised channels were dug to straighten sections of the river, and a lock near Longford Castle survives, rebuilt in brick as a pound lock after flooding damaged the original in the early 18th century. In 1699 the freeholders of Ibsley and Fordingbridge petitioned the House of Commons that they could not comply with the Act, and court cases to enforce a right of navigation in 1737 and 1772 were indecisive.

The Avon is thought to contain more species of fish than any other river in Britain. In 1993 the valley in Hampshire between Bickton and Christchurch was designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest, and in 1996 almost the whole river, with its tributaries, was designated the River Avon System SSSI. A four-year project called STREAM began in September 2005 to benefit species such as Atlantic salmon and water-crowfoot, followed by a project called Living River from 2006 to 2010. The Pewsey Avon Trail and the Avon Valley Path follow much of its length.
river-avon-warwickshire: The Avon is a major left-bank tributary of the River Severn and the easternmost of its main tributaries. It is also called Shakespeare's Avon, to distinguish it from other rivers of the same name. It rises from a spring near Naseby in Northamptonshire, forms the border between Northamptonshire and Leicestershire for its first few miles, and enters Warwickshire at Dow Bridge on Watling Street. It then flows west-south-west past Rugby, Warwick, Stratford-upon-Avon, Evesham and Pershore to join the Severn at Tewkesbury. Its catchment is 2,670 square kilometres. The name comes from the British word abona, 'river', so River Avon says the same thing twice.

In prehistory the Avon was a small river that drained north to the Trent. During the Wolstonian glacial period, ice blocked its flow and trapped the waters in a large glacial lake, Lake Harrison, which at its maximum covered the whole of Warwickshire and was over 200 feet deep. After about 10,000 years the retreating glacier let the water cut through the old watershed and escape to the south-west, giving the river its present course.

Works for navigation were authorised in 1635 by an Order in Council and letters patent of Charles I naming William Sandys, who built pound locks with two sets of gates. By 1641 the river was navigable to within 4 miles of Warwick. From 1664 a syndicate led by Andrew Yarranton improved the river above Evesham, so that barges of 30 tonnes could reach Stratford. The navigation was divided at Evesham into the Upper and Lower Avon, and George Perrott leased the lower river in 1758 and had it improved for 40-ton barges by 1768. The Stratford Canal joined the river at Stratford on 24 June 1816.

The tortuous Upper Avon, prone to flooding, was abandoned as a navigation in 1877, and by 1945 the Lower Avon was navigable only below Pershore. Restoration of the lower river began in 1950 and was completed in 1962. On the upper river work began in 1965 on nine new locks and 17 miles of river, mainly by volunteers, and was completed in 1974, when Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother opened it.

Traffic on the river is now exclusively for leisure. The Avon meets the Stratford-upon-Avon Canal in the centre of Stratford and forms part of the Avon Ring, a circular cruising route of 109 miles with 129 locks. A long-distance footpath, Shakespeare's Avon Way, follows the river for 88 miles from Naseby to Tewkesbury.
river-bann: The River Bann, from the Irish An Bhanna, the goddess, runs for 129 km as the Upper and Lower Bann combined, or 159 km counting its course through the 30 km of Lough Neagh. It winds from the southeast corner of Ulster to the northwest coast. The Upper Bann rises at Slieve Muck in the Mourne Mountains and after 64 km joins Lough Neagh at Bannfoot in County Armagh. The Lower Bann, also 64 km long, leaves the lough at Toome and reaches the Atlantic at Barmouth, between Portstewart and Castlerock. It forms most of the border between County Antrim and County Londonderry, and its only commercial port is Coleraine.

Ptolemy's Geography of the 2nd century CE describes a river mouth called Argita, shining, which refers to the Bann. The Lower Bann is the only outlet of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles, and the land around it was prone to flooding. A shoal of rock at Portna reduced the outflow, and in 1738 Francis Hutchinson, Bishop of Down and Connor, petitioned the Irish Parliament to deal with it, without result. In 1822 the engineer Alexander Nimmo proposed a second outlet to the sea, but his plan was thought too ambitious.

The Drainage (Ireland) Act 1842 authorised the Board of Works to improve navigation, drainage and milling in the Lough Neagh basin. Work on the Lower Bann began in 1847 under the chief engineer Charles Ottley, who found it hard to recruit labour after famine and emigration. It took eleven years. A double-chambered lock was built at Portna, where the shoal was removed, with four other locks. It was one of four navigations part funded by the Treasury in the famine years, and the adjoining counties had to cover its annual deficit. The Upper Bann was abandoned as a navigation in 1954.

The river played an important part in the industrialisation of Northern Ireland, especially the linen industry, and salmon and eel fisheries are its chief economic feature. The Lower Bann is canalised and is used by water sports enthusiasts, anglers and cruisers. A barrage at Toome regulates the level of the lough. The river is often used as a dividing line between the eastern and western areas of Northern Ireland, called the Bann divide.
river-barrow: The Barrow, in Irish An Bhearú, rises at Glenbarrow in the Slieve Bloom Mountains in County Laois. Before reaching Waterford it passes through Portarlington, Monasterevin, Athy, Carlow and Graiguecullen, Bagenalstown, Goresbridge, Graiguenamanagh and New Ross. Its catchment is 3,067 square kilometres before the River Nore joins it a little over 20 kilometres from its mouth, and about 5,500 square kilometres after the junction. The river forms a natural border between County Kilkenny and County Waterford on its right bank and County Carlow and County Wexford on its left.

The Irish name Bearú has been derived from a Proto-Celtic root meaning boil or brew, which would make it cognate with Borvo, the Celtic god of mineral and spring waters. Ptolemy's Geography, in the 2nd century CE, describes a river called Birgu, which may refer to Waterford Harbour as a place of refuge. Legend ties the name to Dian Cecht, who slew three serpents found in the heart of the Morrígan's infant son and threw them into the Barrow, making it boil.

The Barrow historically formed a natural boundary between the kingdom of Laigin on its eastern shore and Osraige on its western. The Irish annals record a Leinster campaign in which Domnall ua Néill plundered from the Berbha eastwards to the sea, carried off a great prey of cattle and besieged the Norsemen and the Leinstermen for two months. Sir John Davies quoted a proverb that whoever lives west of the Barrow lives west of the law.

The river forms a major part of Ireland's inland waterways, linking the port of Waterford with the Grand Canal, which connects Dublin to the River Shannon. Its navigation has three parts: 88 kilometres of tidal river together with the tidal reaches of the Suir and the Nore; 66 kilometres of non-tidal river with 23 locks from St Mullin's to Athy; and the Barrow Line of the Grand Canal, which continues 45 kilometres north from Athy with 9 locks to Lowtown.

Parts of the Barrow attract kayakers and swimmers, mainly in summer. The Barrow Way, a 120-kilometre long-distance walk along the Barrow Line and the towpaths of the non-tidal river, is one of Ireland's National Waymarked Trails and ends at St Mullins.
river-boyne: The Boyne, in Irish An Bhóinn, rises near Carbury in County Kildare and flows north-east along the border with County Offaly before entering County Meath. It reaches the Irish Sea between Mornington in Meath and Baltray in County Louth. It is a lowland river in the Boyne Valley. The River Deal joins it near Donore Castle, carrying water from Lough Lene, and the Kells Blackwater joins it at Navan. Its catchment is 2,695 square kilometres, and west of Drogheda it is crossed by the Mary McAleese Boyne Valley Bridge on the M1 motorway and by the Boyne Viaduct on the Dublin–Belfast railway.

In the 2nd century CE Ptolemy mapped the river as Bouwinda, a Celtic name meaning white cow. Irish mythology says the goddess Boann created it, and in other legends Fionn mac Cumhail caught the Salmon of Knowledge in it. Its estuary, Inber Colpa, is tied by tradition to Colpa of the Sword, a son of Míl Espáine, who drowned trying to land there.

Despite its short course the Boyne has great historical and archaeological weight. It passes Trim and Trim Castle, the Hill of Tara, the ancient capital of the High King of Ireland, Navan, the Hill of Slane, Brú na Bóinne, a complex of megalithic monuments, Mellifont Abbey and the medieval town of Drogheda. Loughcrew, Kells, Celtic crosses and castles also lie in the valley. An annal entry for the year 770 records a battle of Bolg Bóinne won by the Laigin against the Uí Néill.

In 1690, during the Williamite war in Ireland, the Protestant King William III defeated the Catholic King James near Drogheda. The Ulster Protestant ballad The Boyne Water recalls these events. A prehistoric log-boat, which experts believed might be 5,000 years old, was found near Drogheda in May 2013, and in 2006 dredging in Drogheda turned up the remains of a Viking ship.

The Boyne Navigation, a series of canals running roughly parallel to the river from Oldbridge to Navan, is owned by An Taisce and mostly derelict, and the Inland Waterways Association of Ireland is restoring it; the canal at Oldbridge, on the battle site, was restored first. Much of the river is a Special Protection Area for the kingfisher and a Special Area of Conservation for Atlantic salmon, European river lamprey, Eurasian otter, alluvial woodland and alkaline fen.
river-clyde: The Clyde is formed where the Daer Water and the Potrail Water meet at Watermeetings. It runs north-east, then west, past Lanark, where David Dale and Robert Owen built the mills and model settlement of New Lanark beside the Falls of Clyde. It continues north-west past Hamilton and Bothwell into Glasgow, where it becomes tidal below the Tidal Weir, and then west past Renfrew and Dumbarton to the Tail of the Bank off Greenock, where it merges into the Firth of Clyde. Its drainage basin closely resembles the borders of historic Lanarkshire, once known as Clydesdale.

People have lived along the river since the Paleolithic, and artifacts from about 12,000 BCE have been found near Biggar. The earliest recorded form of the name is Klōta, given by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. Roman forts stood on the river at Castledykes, Bothwellhaugh and Old Kilpatrick, and the Antonine Wall lay a few miles away. Later the kingdom of Alt Clut, which became Strathclyde, was ruled from Dumbarton Rock. Norse-Irish raiders from Dublin sacked it in 870, and in the 11th century the kingdom was annexed by the Kingdom of Alba. In the 7th century Saint Mungo founded a Christian community on the Molendinar Burn, which became Glasgow.

Glasgow built its first bridge over the river in the 13th century. Shoals meant only small vessels could use the river, so in 1688 Glasgow merchants built Port Glasgow downstream for seagoing ships. Tobacco and cotton trade drove the economy in the early 18th century. From 1768 engineers built jetties and training walls and dredged the channel, removing much of the Elderslie Rock; the work was not completed until the 1880s. Shipbuilding then replaced trade as the main activity, and the Clyde became the world's pre-eminent shipbuilding centre, with over 370 ships completed in 1913 alone. After the Second World War the yards declined, and Upper Clyde Shipbuilders collapsed in 1971.

The Clyde is about 170 km long, the second longest river in Scotland. The former docklands in Glasgow have been redeveloped as housing and public attractions, among them the Glasgow Science Centre and the Riverside Museum. New Lanark is a World Heritage Site, and the Clyde Walkway follows the river between Glasgow and New Lanark.
river-conwy: The Conwy is 34 miles (55 km) long from its source to Conwy Bay and drains an area of 262 square miles (678 km²). Its name comes from the old Welsh words cyn, 'chief', and gwy, 'water', and the river was originally the Cynwy; it was formerly anglicised as Conway. It rises on the Migneint moor, where small streams feed Llyn Conwy, and flows north, joined by the Machno and the Lledr before Betws-y-coed, where the Llugwy joins it. It then passes Llanrwst, Trefriw and Dolgarrog. At spring tides it is tidal as far as Tan-lan, near Llanrwst.

The river has two different banks. Silurian mudstone hills lie to the east, covered in moor and, in places, planted conifers. Harder Cambrian rocks lie to the west, where the river falls in cascades and waterfalls at Conwy Falls and in the Lledr Gorge. Copper, lead and silver have been mined in the valley since Roman times. Below Betws-y-coed the valley is wide and fertile and supports dairying and sheep, and in winter the pastures take sheep brought down from the mountains.

There is evidence of settlement in the valley back to the Stone Age, and the Romans occupied the area until about 400 CE. The churches of Llanrhychwyn and Llangelynnin, among the oldest in Wales, date from the 11th and 12th centuries. In 1466, after a Lancastrian attack on Denbigh, the Earl of Pembroke laid waste much of the valley during the Wars of the Roses, on the orders of the Yorkist king Edward IV.

Deganwy Castle, on the estuary, was the original defensive position of the area. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, destroyed it in 1263, and its problems of resupply in a siege led to a new castle being built across the water at the town of Conwy.

Conwy Castle, a World Heritage Site, stands at the river's mouth, beside two well-known bridges: Thomas Telford's early suspension bridge, now a footpath, and Robert Stephenson's tubular iron bridge, which still carries the Holyhead to London railway line. A third bridge carries road traffic, and the A55 passes under the estuary in the Conwy Crossing, an immersed tube tunnel opened in October 1991. Aber Afon Conwy is a site of special scientific interest, and the river is noted for salmon and sea trout.
river-dee-aberdeenshire: The Dee rises from a spring on the Braeriach plateau in the Cairngorm Mountains at about 1,220 metres, the highest source of any major river in the British Isles. It emerges in pools called the Wells of Dee, crosses the plateau and plunges over the Falls of Dee into An Garbh Choire, then flows south down the Lairig Ghru between Ben Macdui and Cairn Toul before turning east at the confluence with the Geldie Burn. At Linn of Dee it passes through a 300-metre rock gorge, and it then runs past Braemar, Balmoral Castle, Ballater, Aboyne and Banchory to the North Sea at Aberdeen.

Evidence of human activity as far back as about 8,200 BCE has been found at a complex of sites along the banks of the Dee. The New Statistical Account of Scotland attributed the name to the second-century geographer Ptolemy, who wrote it as Deva, 'goddess', which would show that the river had divine status for its ancient inhabitants. The Gaelic name Uisge Dhe means 'Water of God', and other rivers in Great Britain have similar names.

Queen Victoria visited in 1848 and greatly enjoyed herself, and she and Prince Albert built Balmoral Castle, which replaced an older castle. She opened the bridge over the Dee at Linn of Dee in 1857. The Deeside Railway, run by the Great North of Scotland Railway, opened from Aberdeen to Banchory in 1853, reached Aboyne in 1859 and Ballater in 1866. It was not extended to Braemar because it would have run close to Balmoral, to which Victoria objected, and it closed in 1966. Bridge of Dee, near the tidal limit, was built about 1720, and an artificial channel was cut in 1872 to straighten the river's flow into the sea.

The area between Braemar and Banchory is known as Royal Deeside, and the British royal family have spent their summers at Balmoral since Victoria's reign. The upper catchment lies in the Cairngorms National Park, and the whole length of the Dee is a Special Area of Conservation for salmon, otters and freshwater pearl mussels. It is one of the best-known salmon rivers, fished on a catch-and-release basis, and before reaching the sea it passes through Aberdeen Harbour.
river-dee-wales: The River Dee, in Welsh Afon Dyfrdwy, has its source on the slopes of Dduallt above Llanuwchllyn in Snowdonia. It runs northeast through the Vale of Edeyrnion to Corwen, then through the forested valley past Llangollen, where it flows under a 16th-century bridge counted among the Seven Wonders of Wales and, further east, below Thomas Telford's Pontcysyllte Aqueduct of 1805. Beyond that it forms the border between Wales and England and meanders across the Cheshire Plain to Chester. The section from Bala to Chester is 113 kilometres long, and the catchment down to Chester Weir covers 1,816.8 square kilometres.

The Dee was the traditional boundary of the Kingdom of Gwynedd for centuries, possibly since its founding in the 5th century. A 13th-century form of the name, flumen Dubr Duiu, appears to derive from the Brythonic dēvā, River of the Goddess or Holy River, and the river is personified as the goddess Aerfen. Its name inspired that of the Roman fortress Deva Victrix.

At Chester the Old Dee Bridge dates from about 1387, on the site of wooden predecessors reaching back to the Roman period. Chester Weir was built by Hugh Lupus to power corn mills, and the Roodee racecourse stands on the site of the Roman harbour, which silted up. From the end of the 17th century sediment kept larger ships from the city and its trade declined. Between 1732 and 1736 the Dee Navigation Company, using engineers from the Netherlands and local money, dug a straight channel west of Chester and diverted the river into it.

Below Chester the canalised river passes Deeside, a region of heavy industry, before widening into an estuary 23 kilometres long that enters the Irish Sea. Its mudflats and saltmarsh make it important for birdlife, and it is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Ramsar site. The river is also a Special Area of Conservation for Atlantic salmon and floating water plantain. A system of reservoirs, the Dee Regulation Scheme, stores winter water and releases it in summer.
river-don-aberdeenshire: The River Don rises in the Grampians, in the peat flat beneath Druim na Feithe and in the shadow of Glen Avon, and drains a catchment of 1,312 square kilometres. Several streams, among them the Dhiver, Feith Bhait and Allt nan Aighean, merge to form its headwaters. Water from the north of Brown Cow Hill drains into the Don, while water from the west side runs into the River Spey and that from the south side into the River Dee.

The river follows a circuitous route eastwards past Corgarff Castle, through Strathdon and the Howe of Alford, passing Alford, Kemnay, Inverurie, Kintore and Dyce. Its main tributary, the River Ury, joins it at Inverurie. It enters the North Sea at Bridge of Don, just north of Old Aberdeen.

Near Kintore, not far from the river, lies the Deers Den Roman Camp. In 1750 the Don's lower reaches were channelled towards the sea, which moved its mouth northwards. River levels have been measured at gauging stations since 1969. The lowest, at Parkhill near Dyce, records a mean flow of 20.64 cubic metres per second.

Until 2016 the highest levels were those of the floods of November 2002, when the river reached 5.07 metres at Haughton near Inverurie. These were exceeded in January 2016, when levels at Haughton reached 5.6 metres and those at Parkhill were over a metre higher than before, at 5.5 metres. Residents along the river had to leave their homes, in some cases with the help of local rescue teams, and care homes in Donside in Aberdeen were evacuated as a precaution.
Strathdon attracts visitors for salmon and trout fishing as well as for its castles and scenery. A 100 kW hydro scheme at Tillydrone stands on the former site of the Donside Papermill.
river-dyfi: The Welsh spelling Dyfi is widely used locally and by the Welsh Government, Natural Resources Wales and the BBC, while some still use the anglicised Dovey. The river ends in a large estuary, known for its saltmarshes, which forms the boundary between the counties of Gwynedd and Ceredigion. Its tributaries include the Afon Cerist at Dinas Mawddwy, the Afon Cleifion at Mallwyd, the Afon Twymyn upstream of Cemmaes Road, the South Dulas east of Machynlleth and the Afon Leri at Ynyslas. Pont Minllyn and the Dyfi Bridge, Pont ar Ddyfi, are its best-known bridges.

The lower reaches of the river have historically been considered the border between North Wales and South Wales. The 14th-century poet Dafydd ap Gwilym wrote Y Don ar Afon Dyfi (The Wave on the River Dyfi), in which, travelling home from North Wales, he finds the river in spate and cannot cross to meet Morfudd. The 15th-century poet Dafydd Llwyd ap Llywelyn, born at Mathafarn on its banks, also addressed a poem to the river, which David Myrddin Lloyd called a work of great beauty.

The estuary appeared in Led Zeppelin's film The Song Remains the Same (1976), in the scene in which Robert Plant comes ashore from a boat before riding to Raglan Castle; the band's Bron-Yr-Aur cottage stands on the edge of Machynlleth.

The area around Aberystwyth and the Dyfi Valley forms the Dyfi Biosphere, designated by UNESCO in 1978, which takes in Special Areas of Conservation and Sites of Special Scientific Interest such as Cors Fochno and Coed Cwm Einion. In March 2021 Natural Resources Wales licensed the Montgomeryshire Wildlife Trust to release a family of beavers into an enclosure at the Dyfi Wildlife Centre, the first officially licensed release of beavers in Wales. A small wild population of unclear origin already lives in the catchment.
river-eden-cumbria: The River Eden rises on Black Fell Moss in Mallerstang, near the village of Outhgill, on high ground between High Seat and Hugh Seat. There it forms the boundary between Cumbria and North Yorkshire. Two other rivers, the Swale and the Ure, rise within a kilometre of it in the same peat bogs. The Romans knew the river as the Itouna, a name recorded by Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE and derived from a Celtic word meaning water or rushing, so it has no connection with the biblical Garden of Eden. The river later gave its name to the former Eden district of Cumbria.

It begins as Red Gill Beck, becomes Hell Gill Beck and joins Ais Gill Beck to become the Eden. Hell Gill Force is the highest waterfall on its course. The steep-sided dale of Mallerstang opens into the Vale of Eden, and the river flows through Kirkby Stephen and Appleby-in-Westmorland, receiving becks from the Pennines to the east and the Lyvennet, Leith and Eamont from the west. The Eamont reaches it by way of Ullswater and Penrith.

Heading north, the Eden formed the eastern boundary of Inglewood Forest and passes close to the ancient stone circle of Long Meg and Her Daughters. At Wetheral it is crossed by Corby Bridge, a railway viaduct of 1834 now listed Grade I. The Irthing joins it from the east, then the Petteril and the Caldew from the south as it winds through Carlisle. Its junction with the Caldew in north Carlisle marks the point where Hadrian's Wall crosses the river, five miles before it reaches the tidal flats.

The Eden enters the Solway Firth near the mouth of the River Esk after about 81 miles, or 130 kilometres. It runs through sparsely populated beef and dairy farming country on the Solway Plain. The river supports Atlantic salmon and Eurasian otter, and it and its tributaries form a Special Area of Conservation that includes Ullswater. It is also the core of the River Eden and Tributaries SSSI.
river-great-ouse: The Great Ouse flows mostly north and east from Syresham in Northamptonshire through Buckinghamshire, Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Norfolk, before draining into the Wash near King's Lynn. Authorities disagree about both its source and its length. Its best-known tributary is the Cam, which runs through Cambridge. The river passes Buckingham, Bedford, St Neots, Huntingdon and St Ives, and at Earith it enters a short tidal section before the artificial Old and New Bedford rivers carry water north-east towards Denver. The name Ouse comes from a Celtic or pre-Celtic word that probably means simply 'water'.

In prehistory the river flowed from Huntingdon straight to Wisbech and the sea. Its lower reaches silted repeatedly, and in times of flood the waters breached neighbouring watersheds and made new courses, generally progressively eastward. After major floods in the early 13th century it breached another watershed near Denver and took over the channel of the old Wiggenhall Eau, so that it joined the Wash at King's Lynn. The upper course, from Bedford to Stony Stratford, marked the boundary between English territory and the Danelaw under the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum.

The Land Drainage Act 1601 allowed 'adventurers', who paid for drainage schemes themselves, to be repaid in land. Below Earith, thirteen Adventurers working with the Earl of Bedford formed a corporation to drain the Bedford Levels, with Cornelius Vermuyden as engineer. The Old Bedford River, a straight cut from Earith to a new sluice near Salters Lode, was completed in 1637, and the New Bedford River, authorised by an act of 29 May 1649, in 1652. Ports and towns on the river strongly opposed the works, and there were attempts to destroy them during the English civil wars. Above Earith, navigation was extended to Bedford in 1689.

The sluice at Denver failed in 1713 and was rebuilt by 1750. With the coming of the railways the river declined and its navigation was declared derelict in the 1870s. Responsibility was divided among many bodies until the Great Ouse Catchment Board was created under the Land Drainage Act 1930.

The Ouse Washes, between the Old and New Bedford rivers, are the largest area of washland in the United Kingdom: pasture in summer that floods in winter, a breeding ground for lapwings, redshanks and snipe, and a winter home of ducks and swans. The river is navigable from the Wash to Kempston Mill near Bedford, 72 miles with 17 locks.
river-lea: The Lea is usually said to rise at Well Head inside Waulud's Bank, a Neolithic henge at Leagrave Common in Luton, in the Chiltern Hills. It enters Hertfordshire six miles from its source, passes Harpenden and Wheathampstead, once the capital of the Catuvellauni, and reaches Hertford, where its tributaries gather. Below Hertford the river has been altered since medieval times to carry boats as the Lee Navigation, and the navigable River Stort, its main tributary, joins it near Hoddesdon. It flows through Enfield, Tottenham, Walthamstow and Hackney to meet the Thames at Bow Creek. The name, first recorded in the 9th century, probably comes from a Celtic root meaning bright.

The Lea and the Stort long served as a boundary. In the Iron Age their valleys were a contested frontier between the Catuvellauni to the west and the Trinovantes to the east, and they probably bounded the core territory of the East Saxons. Between 878 and 890 the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum used the Lea to mark the border between the English and the Danes. In 894 a force of Danes sailed up to Hertford and built a fortified camp, and Alfred the Great dug a new channel to lower the water and leave them stranded. The river later divided Essex from Hertfordshire and Middlesex.

Queen Matilda, wife of Henry I, is reputed to have ordered a three-arched bridge at Bow in 1110, the first over the lower Lea. Medieval mills at Temple Mills, Abbey Mills, Old Ford and Bow supplied flour to London, and Ware was a brewing and malting centre whose barges carried malt to the city. In 1613 the New River was cut to bring clean water to London, and from 1577 locks improved navigation. Armaments factories at Waltham Abbey and Enfield, and A. V. Roe's powered flight of 1909 on the Walthamstow Marshes, belong to its later industrial story.

Much of the river lies within the Lee Valley Park, a green corridor reaching deep into London, and its upper stretch and tributaries are chalk streams that supply drinking water to the capital. The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, built for the 2012 Summer Olympics, stands on its banks.
river-liffey: The Liffey rises in the Liffey Head Bog, between the mountains of Kippure and Tonduff in the northern Wicklow Mountains, forming from many streamlets near the Sally Gap. It flows for 132 km through counties Wicklow, Kildare and Dublin, crossing from Wicklow into Kildare at Poulaphouca and from Kildare into Dublin at Leixlip, with most of its length in Kildare. Its mouth lies at the midpoint of Dublin Bay. The catchment covers 1,256 square kilometres.

Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle and the River Camac. Towns along it include Blessington, Ballymore Eustace, Kilcullen, Newbridge, Clane, Celbridge, Leixlip and Lucan, before it passes Chapelizod and runs through the centre of Dublin.

The river was earlier called An Ruirthech, meaning fast or strong runner. The name Life or Liphe first belonged to the plain of Kildare through which it runs, and later came to mean the river itself. A legend derives the plain's name from Life, daughter of Canann Curthach, who eloped with Deltbanna mac Druchta, the cup-bearer of the High King Conaire Mór. Scholars have offered other origins, one linking it to the Welsh llif, meaning flood, another to a language spoken in Ireland before the Celts. The Annals of Inisfallen record under 808 a defeat inflicted by the Laigin on Áed, son of Niall, at the river of Liphe.

The river has carried trade since the Viking beginnings of Dublin. The earliest stone bridge of which there is solid evidence was the Bridge of Dublin, which replaced an 11th-century wooden bridge, Dubhghall's Bridge. The Dominicans built it in 1428, with four arches and buildings including a chapel and bakehouse. Island Bridge followed in 1577, and four more bridges were added between 1670 and 1684 as commercial Dublin grew. Floods repeatedly took bridges: one in 1763 destroyed Arran Bridge, and one in December 1801 destroyed the oldest of all, replaced by Whitworth Bridge in 1816. The oldest bridge still standing is Mellows Bridge, built in 1764, and the first iron bridge was the Ha'penny Bridge of 1816.

The Liffey divides the Northside of Dublin from the Southside and is crossed by many bridges. Around 60 per cent of its flow is taken for drinking water and industry, and hydroelectric stations stand at Poulaphouca, Golden Falls and Leixlip. The Liffey Descent canoe race has run each year since 1960. James Joyce made the river the allegorical heroine of Finnegans Wake as Anna Livia Plurabelle.
river-medway: The Medway rises in the High Weald and flows through Tonbridge, Maidstone and the Medway conurbation before emptying into the Thames Estuary near Sheerness, a distance of 70 miles. About 13 miles of it lie in East Sussex and the rest in Kent. Its catchment of 930 square miles is the second largest in southern England after the Thames, fed by tributaries that include the Eden, the Teise, the Beult and the Len. At first it runs west to east south of the North Downs; at the confluence of the Beult it turns north and breaks through the North Downs at the Medway Gap, a steep narrow valley near Rochester.

Until 1746 the river was not navigable above Maidstone, and each village below, among them Halling, Snodland, New Hythe and Aylesford, had its wharf for corn, fodder, fruit, stone and timber. Improvements in 1746 let barges of 40 long tons reach Tonbridge, and in 1828 the channel was improved up to Leigh. Eleven locks stand on the river, the lowest, at Allington, opened in 1792 and marking the tidal limit.

Ancient sites lie all along the river. Around Aylesford are the Medway megaliths, Neolithic chamber tombs including the Coldrum Stones and Kit's Coty House. Bronze Age ornaments and beakers, Iron Age burials and Roman villas have been found in the valley, and later Jutish burials too. The Domesday Book records many manors there, and castles at Rochester, Allington, Leeds and West Malling became features of the landscape. A bridge has stood at Rochester since Roman times, and in the 14th century Sir John de Cobham instituted the Wardens and Commonalty of Rochester Bridge to pay for its rebuilding and upkeep.

Two military actions are named after the river: the Battle of the Medway during the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 CE, and the Raid on the Medway in 1667 during the Second Anglo-Dutch War. The Thames and Medway Canal, linking Strood to Gravesend, was completed in 1824 but was not a commercial success. In 1914 HMS Bulwark exploded at Kethole Reach near Sheerness with the loss of 741 men, and the next year HMS Princess Irene exploded in Saltpan Reach with 352 lives lost. In 1942 a submarine oil pipeline laid across the Medway in Operation Pluto was the first of its kind to be tested.

Rochester's bridge remained the lowest public crossing until the Medway Tunnel opened in 1996 between Gillingham and Strood. The Medway Valley Walk follows the river from Rochester to Tonbridge, and the Maidstone River Festival has been held annually since 1980. Tradition holds that those born east of the river are Men of Kent and those born west Kentish Men, though the basis of the distinction is disputed.
river-mersey: The Mersey is 69 miles (111 km) long. It is now regarded as beginning at the confluence of the River Tame and the River Goyt in the centre of Stockport, though older definitions and maps place its start near Marple, where the Etherow meets the Goyt. It flows west through south Manchester and, near Irlam Locks, into the Manchester Ship Canal, which obliterated its old course for part of the way. After leaving the canal it runs to Warrington and through the Runcorn Gap between Runcorn and Widnes.

Below it a large estuary opens, 3 miles (4.8 km) across at its widest near Ellesmere Port, then narrows to 0.7 miles (1.1 km) between Liverpool and Birkenhead before it empties into Liverpool Bay. Its tidal range is the second highest in Britain, after the Severn.

The name comes from the Anglo-Saxon words mǣres, of a boundary, and ēa, a river, and may refer to its having been the border between the kingdoms of Mercia and Northumbria. For centuries it has formed part of the boundary between Lancashire and Cheshire. Before the Anglo-Saxon conquest the river had a Celtic name, recorded by Ptolemy as Seteia, as the southern border of the Setantii tribe.

The lowest bridging point was at Warrington, where there has been a bridge since medieval times. Monks from Birkenhead Priory introduced the first ferry across the estuary in the Middle Ages and sheltered travellers at the priory in bad weather.

Birkenhead grew quickly in the 19th century after the paddle steamer Elizabeth of 1815, with docks, shipbuilding, flour milling and soap manufacture. In 1836 Captain William Gill of the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company charted a safe channel, the Victoria Channel, through the estuary. The Mersey Railway tunnel between Birkenhead and Liverpool opened in 1886, and the Queensway Tunnel in 1934.

Liverpool's docks stretch over 7.5 miles (12.1 km). Industrialisation badly polluted the river, and in 1985 the Mersey Basin Campaign began to improve water quality; in 2002 oxygen levels able to support fish were recorded along its whole length for the first time since industry began.

Most of the conurbation on both sides of the estuary is known as Merseyside. The Mersey Ferry still runs from Liverpool to Birkenhead and Seacombe. The wetlands of the estuary are a Ramsar site. The river gave its name to Merseybeat, developed by Liverpool bands including the Beatles.
river-nene: The River Nene flows through Northamptonshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Lincolnshire in eastern England and into the Wash. One of its sources lies near Arbury Hill in Northamptonshire, and its mouth is at Lutton Marsh. It is about 105 miles (169 km) long and, with its tributaries, drains some 2,270 square kilometres. The main tributaries include the River Ise, Wootton Brook, Willow Brook and Harper's Brook. Below Northampton the river runs through a broad, flat valley formed by meltwater at the end of the Ice Age, with floodplains and the gravel deposits that later became gravel pits. The river is tidal for 45 kilometres, up to the Dog-in-a-Doublet sluice near Peterborough, and forms part of the boundary between Cambridgeshire and Norfolk.

The origin of the name is unknown. The earliest forms date from the 10th century, and the toponymist Victor Watts called the name certainly pre-English and possibly pre-Celtic. The pronunciation changes along the river, with Nene rhyming with 'keen' around Peterborough and with 'ten' in Northampton.

Along its banks lie traces of the Roman past, among them the remains of the Roman town at Irchester and the point near Oundle where the Romans carried Ermine Street over the river in the first century. Hardwater Watermill near Doddington is mentioned in the Domesday Book and ground flour for almost a thousand years. Thomas Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, is said to have used it as a hiding place in 1164 after escaping from Northampton Castle and fleeing down the river.

Efforts to make the river navigable began with surveys in 1567 and 1606. An Act of Parliament of 1713 found no taker, and a second Act in 1724 allowed work in stages at the contractor's cost. Robert Wright and Thomas Squire finished the stretch from Peterborough to Oundle by 1730 and the section to Thrapston by late 1737. Below Peterborough Bishop Morton built Morton's Leam, a straight channel to Wisbech, in the 1470s, and the Bedford Level Corporation cut Smith's Leam in 1728. By the time the Nene Catchment Board took over after the Land Drainage Act 1930 the river was described as in unparalleled decay. The board rebuilt the locks, and the floods of 1947 showed the benefit.

The river is navigable for 88 miles (142 km) from Northampton to the Wash, through locks that take boats up to 78 by 13 feet, and most leisure use lies between Northampton and Peterborough. Its valley is largely occupied by mature gravel-pit lakes, and Titchmarsh Nature Reserve, designated in 1989, lies beside it north of Thrapston. Serious floods struck Wisbech in January 1978 and Northampton and other riverside towns at Easter 1998.
river-ness: The River Ness, in Scottish Gaelic Abhainn Nis, is a short river in the Great Glen of Scotland, about six miles (10 km) long. It begins at Loch Dochfour, at the northern end of Loch Ness, and flows north-east towards Inverness, where it empties into the Moray Firth. For the first half of its course it runs parallel to the Caledonian Canal. At Inverness it contains a group of wooded islets known as the Ness Islands, some of which are linked to the shore by footbridges.

According to Adomnán, Saint Columba visited King Bridei I of Pictland at his house on the River Ness. There he met a wizard named Broichan, who held an Irish slave-girl and refused to release her. Columba picked up a white pebble from the river and said that it would heal many sick people in Pictland. Broichan then fell ill, and the king's messengers asked for help. Columba told them to dip the stone in water and give it to Broichan if he would free the girl. He agreed, the stone floated, and he drank and was healed. Bridei kept the stone in his treasury, and people who came for healing were given water with the stone floating in it.

The first claimed sighting of the Loch Ness Monster was in the River Ness in 565, when Columba is said to have banished a water monster back into the river after it tried to attack a disciple who was swimming across. Scottish folklore also holds that kelpies live in the river, water spirits that take the form of horses or people and lure travellers into the water.

The Ness Bridge has been the main crossing of the river since at least the 15th century. Its timber predecessor was rebuilt in 1685, the next bridge, which included a small prison cell, stood for 164 years until a flood in January 1849, and a suspension bridge of 1850 was demolished in 1960. The present bridge was completed on 7 August 1961. The Black Bridge of 1889 replaced a wooden bridge of 1808. Joseph Mitchell built the Ness Viaduct for the railway in 1862, and floods washed most of it away in 1989. Two suspension footbridges of 1890, the Greig Street Bridge and the Infirmary Bridge, are known locally as the Bouncy Bridges, and the Friars Bridge opened on 23 December 1986.
river-nore: The River Nore, in Irish An Fheoir, is one of the principal rivers of the south-east of Ireland, with the Suir and the Barrow. It is 140 kilometres long and drains about 2,530 square kilometres of Leinster and Munster, in parts of Tipperary, Laois and Kilkenny. It rises on the eastern slopes of the Devil's Bit Mountain, in the townland of Borrisnoe, and flows south-east and then south. It passes near Durrow, then Ballyragget, the city of Kilkenny, Bennettsbridge and Thomastown, and forms a V-shaped valley near Inistioge, the tidal limit, before joining the Barrow at Ringwood, north of New Ross.

Its main tributaries include the Dinan, the Breagagh, the King's River, the Little Arrigle and the Black Water. The catchment rises on sandstone but soon turns to limestone, and the river has a fairly steep gradient checked by innumerable weirs.

The name is an anglicisation of the Old Irish An Eoir, thought to derive from feórann, meaning green bank or shoreland. The Martyrology of Oengus, written before 824, mentions the river as the cold-pure Eoire, and a Middle Irish reference from before 1420 calls it the fair wide plain of the Feoir.

Before the Famine many water-powered industries stood in the valley, particularly in the ten-mile stretch between Kilkenny city and Thomastown, including breweries, woollen mills, sawmills, marble works, distilleries and grain mills. Flax and linen were produced just north of Kilkenny. Salmon runs were interrupted in 2005 and 2006 by a flood relief scheme in Kilkenny, which was built without suitable fish passes; the omission was later put right.

The countryside along the river is one of mixed farming, with tillage, pasture, dairying and some bloodstock. Much of the river's length is designated a Special Area of Conservation, and it is home to a population of the Nore freshwater pearl mussel, a critically endangered species. Its brown trout and salmon attract anglers, and some of its weirs are used for playboating.
river-severn: The Severn rises at an altitude of 610 metres on the Plynlimon massif in the Cambrian Mountains of mid Wales and runs through Shropshire, Worcestershire and Gloucestershire. Its average flow of 107 cubic metres per second at Apperley makes it by far the most voluminous river in England and Wales. Its main tributaries are the Vyrnwy, the Tern, the Teme, the Warwickshire Avon and the Worcestershire Stour. By convention the river ends and the Severn Estuary begins after the Prince of Wales Bridge. The estuary leads into the Bristol Channel, which was known until Tudor times as the Severn Sea.

A tidal bore forms upstream of the port of Sharpness: at the highest tides the rising water is funnelled into a wave that travels upstream against the current. The Romano-British name was Sabrina, the Welsh name Afon Hafren is recorded as Habren about 800, and the English name comes from Old English Sæfern.

In the summer of 893 a coalition of the Danish armies in England made a determined attempt to annex western Mercia to Danish Mercia, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the Battle of Buttington. Welsh tradition made the river a drowned princess, Hafren, who in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae is the daughter of Locrin and the captive Germanic princess Estrildis. Her name was later taken for the nymph Sabrina in Milton's masque Comus of 1634.

The Severn Navigation between Gloucester and Stourport was managed by the Severn Commissioners, created by an Act of 1842 and dissolved in 1948, who took tolls and built locks and weirs. Canals joined the river, among them the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal at Stourport, the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at Worcester and the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, which avoids a dangerous stretch of the tidal river.

A three-mile stretch in Shropshire, the Ironbridge Gorge, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 as the centre of the iron industry in the early Industrial Revolution. It takes its name from the Iron Bridge of 1779, the first cast-iron arch bridge ever built. The Severn Tunnel, completed in 1886 by John Hawkshaw for the Great Western Railway, carries the South Wales Main Line under the channel. The Severn Bridge opened in 1966, replacing the Aust Ferry, and the Prince of Wales Bridge opened in 1996. Shrewsbury, Worcester and Gloucester lie on the river.
river-shannon: The Shannon drains a basin of 16,900 square kilometres, about one fifth of the island of Ireland. By tradition it rises in the Shannon Pot, a small pool on the slopes of Cuilcagh Mountain in County Cavan, flows through or between 11 counties and enters the Atlantic through a tidal estuary 102.1 km long, at the head of which stands Limerick. Its fall is slight: it rises only 76 metres above sea level, and it is shallow in places. It divides the west of Ireland, principally Connacht, from the east and south, and there are fewer than thirty-five crossing points between Dowra in the north and Limerick. Many different lengths have been given for it, since an estuary has no definite end.

Ptolemy's Geography of the 2nd century CE already names the river, which had been an important waterway since antiquity.
