Vikings settled in the region in the 10th century and used the river to raid monasteries deep inland; in 937 the Limerick Vikings clashed with those of Dublin on Lough Ree and were defeated.

In the 17th century the river formed a strategic boundary. In the Irish Confederate Wars the Irish retreated behind the Shannon in 1650 and held out for two more years against English Parliamentarian forces. Oliver Cromwell reputedly said the remaining Irish landowners would go "to Hell or Connacht", meaning west across the river. In the Williamite War the Jacobites also withdrew behind it after the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, and Athlone and Limerick, which command bridges, saw bloody sieges.

Navigation was improved from 1755, when Thomas Omer began lateral canals and locks between Lough Derg and Lough Ree. The Limerick stretch was opened in 1799, and paddle steamers arrived in the 1820s; by 1831 they carried 14,600 passengers and 36,000 long tons of freight. A railway from Dublin to Limerick opened in 1849 and passenger numbers fell sharply. One of the first projects of the Irish Free State in the 1920s was the Shannon hydroelectric scheme at Ardnacrusha, which replaced the old canal from Killaloe to Limerick.

The Royal Canal and the Grand Canal connect the Shannon to Dublin and the Irish Sea, and the Shannon–Erne Waterway links it to Lough Erne. Commercial traffic fell from the 1950s, but leisure boating has since grown steadily. The Shannon Callows, lowland areas along the river, are a Special Area of Conservation. Irish mythology names the river after Sionann, a granddaughter of Manannán mac Lir, drowned when the waters of Connla's Well burst forth after she sought wisdom there.
river-tamar: The Tamar rises at Woolley Moor, about 5.6 kilometres from the north Cornish coast, and flows south to the Hamoaze, which opens into Plymouth Sound. Its tributaries include the Inny, Ottery, Kensey and Lynher on the Cornish side and the Deer and Tavy on the Devon side. Ptolemy mentioned the name in the second century CE, and it is said to mean "great water". The Ravenna Cosmography names a Roman settlement called Tamaris, though it is unclear which town along the river is meant.

According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Vikings sailed up the Tamar and the Tavy in 997 as far as Lydford and burned the monastery at Tavistock. In the 11th century several villages north of Launceston passed to Devon when the border was drawn along the River Ottery instead of the Tamar, and the line was restored to the Tamar in 1966. In the English Civil War Cornwall was loyal to Charles I while Devon was mostly Parliamentarian, so each side needed the river crossings to invade or defend.

The valley was worked almost continuously for silver, tin, lead and arsenic, from the Bronze Age to the modern era. Tavistock was one of the three stannary towns of Devon, and refined tin was exported through Morwellham from the 12th century until 1838. The royal mines on the Bere peninsula produced much lead and silver in the 13th century. In the 19th century copper was shipped from Morwellham, Calstock and New Quay to south Wales for smelting, and arsenic went to the southern United States as an insecticide for cotton. Railways reached the valley from 1859, and traffic on the river fell as the mines were exhausted.

The tidal river runs for 19.2 miles, to a weir near Gunnislake. It has 22 road crossings, the oldest surviving being the bridge at Horsebridge, dating from 1437. The Royal Albert Bridge of 1859 carries the railway between Saltash and Plymouth, beside the Tamar Bridge opened in 1962, and the Calstock Viaduct was built between 1904 and 1907. The lower valley is a National Landscape, designated in 1995, and was added to the World Heritage List in July 2006 as part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape.
river-tay: The Tay rises on the slopes of Ben Lui, about 40 km from the west coast town of Oban in Argyll and Bute. In its upper catchment it carries several names, the River Cononish, the River Fillan and the River Dochart, before it flows into Loch Tay at Killin. It leaves the loch at Kenmore and runs to Perth, which was its lowest bridging point in historical times, and below Perth it becomes tidal and enters the Firth of Tay, south of Dundee.

Over its 190 km from west to east it drains much of the lower Highlands, and, unusually among Scottish rivers, it has several major tributaries: the Earn, the Isla, the Tummel, the Almond and the Lyon. Its name is thought to come from a conjectured Brythonic word, Tausa, possibly meaning silent one or strong one.

The highest flood recorded at Perth occurred in 1814, when the river rose 7 m above its usual level, partly because of a blockage of ice under Smeaton's Bridge. In January 1993 a flow of 2,268 cubic metres a second brought extensive flooding to the city, although hydroelectric schemes upstream held back runoff.

In the 19th century the Tay Rail Bridge was built across the firth at Dundee as part of the East Coast Main Line, designed by Sir Thomas Bouch and opened in May 1878. On 28 December 1879 it collapsed as a train passed over, and the whole train fell into the firth with the loss of 75 passengers and crew. The disaster was commemorated in a poem by William McGonagall and in another by Theodor Fontane. The replacement bridge opened on 11 June 1887. A ferry for passengers and vehicles ran between Craig Pier in Dundee and Newport-on-Tay in Fife until the Tay Road Bridge opened on 18 August 1966.

The river is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Area of Conservation, important for salmon, otters, lampreys and freshwater pearl mussels. It is known for salmon fishing, and the largest rod-caught salmon in Britain, 64 pounds, was caught on the Tay by Georgina Ballantine in 1922. The stretch around Dunkeld is one of Scotland's 40 national scenic areas and covers 5,708 hectares. Dundee is the largest city on the river, which has a catchment of about 5,200 square kilometres and the largest measured discharge of any river in the United Kingdom.
river-tees: The Tees rises at Teeshead, just below Cross Fell, at an elevation of about 732 metres, and drains some 1,800 square kilometres. Its tributaries include the Greta, Lune, Balder, Leven and Skerne. Below the Cow Green Reservoir, built to store water for the industries of Teesside, it crosses hard basalt and dolerite at Cauldron Snout and drops over the 21-metre High Force and the smaller Low Force.

It then passes Middleton-in-Teesdale, Barnard Castle, Egglestone Abbey and Rokeby Park, known through Sir Walter Scott's poem Rokeby, before meandering across the plain by Darlington, Yarm, Stockton-on-Tees and Middlesbrough. In its highest reach it divided the historic counties of Westmorland and Durham. The name is possibly of Brittonic origin, perhaps from a word meaning warmth.

Before the Industrial Revolution the lower river wandered in wide loops between Stockton-on-Tees and Middlesbrough, and a journey by sailing barge from Thornaby to the mouth could take as long as seven days. A proposal of 1769 to cut through the loops led to the Mandale Cut in 1810 and the Portrack Cut in 1831. Later work deepened the channel and made it narrower: ship's ballast and ironworks slag were dumped along the banks, and a river that before 1900 ran in places 300 metres wide now varies between about 100 and 200 metres.

The river carried coal from the Durham coalfields, and as ships grew larger the docks at Yarm and Stockton were superseded by deeper ones at Middlesbrough and later at Teesport. That trade drove the growth of Middlesbrough and of the railway between Stockton and Darlington, where George Stephenson developed the locomotive Locomotion; it was the first steam railway to carry passengers, and its shareholders first met in a public house in Yarm. The steelworks of the late 19th century gave the river the nickname The Steel River, and in the 20th century its banks served the chemical industry, notably Imperial Chemical Industries.

The Tees turns tidal below the Tees Barrage, which stands near the site of the Mandale Cut. Teesport lies on reclaimed land on the south side of the estuary below Middlesbrough and is owned by PD Ports. Common seals were absent from the flats at Seal Sands for about a century of heavy industrialisation but have returned, and the area is now the Teesmouth National Nature Reserve. In its upper reaches the valley lies within the North Pennine Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
river-teifi: The river's source is Llyn Teifi, the second-largest of the five Teifi lakes after Llyn Egnant, lying in Elenydd at 455 metres. It flows past Strata Florida Abbey and through Pontrhydfendigaid, then turns southwest across Cors Caron, an extensive peat bog also called Cors Goch Glanteifi, the red bog on the banks of the Teifi. It meanders in a gentle arc past Llanddewi Brefi, Llanybydder, Llandysul, Newcastle Emlyn and Cenarth, and is tidal below Llechryd.

Below Llechryd it runs through the steep, wooded Cilgerran Gorge, and west of Cardigan and St Dogmaels it widens into an estuary between Poppit Sands and Gwbert. For its last 4.8 kilometres it divides Ceredigion from Pembrokeshire. Its catchment of 1,008 square kilometres lies on Ordovician and Silurian mudstones, shaped by glaciation into rolling hills given to sheep and dairy farming. The river floods easily: when a swollen river meets a high tide, water reaches Cardigan and as far upstream as Llechryd, as it did in 2007, 2008 and December 2015.

The valley has been inhabited since prehistory, and cromlechs and standing stones of the Stone Age and Iron Age survive along it. Gerald of Wales wrote that the Teifi was the only river in Wales where beavers lived in his time, and that it surpassed all other rivers in the abundance and delicacy of its salmon. The remains of the medieval abbey at Strata Florida keep examples of encaustic floor tiles. Cardigan's Welsh name, Aberteifi, means mouth of the Teifi, and the river was once also called the Tivy.

Between Cenarth and Cardigan an old tradition of fishing and travel by coracle continues: light boats of bent sticks covered with waterproofed hide, worked by a single paddle at the front and used chiefly for netting salmon. Few licences are now issued to coracle fishermen. Near the river at Lampeter stood the University of Wales, Lampeter, founded in 1822 as the oldest university established in Wales.

The Teifi has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since December 1997, notified for both its geology and its wildlife and covering 772.6 hectares managed by Natural Resources Wales. Llyn Teifi serves as a reservoir, and the river is the whole water source for Mid and South Ceredigion. The Lampeter campus of the University of Wales Trinity Saint David stands near its banks.
river-thames: The Thames rises at Thames Head in Gloucestershire, about 1.5 miles north of the village of Kemble in the Cotswolds, and flows into the North Sea near Tilbury in Essex and Gravesend in Kent via the Thames Estuary. It passes through Oxford, where it is sometimes called the Isis, and Reading, Henley-on-Thames and Windsor, and it drains the whole of Greater London. Its lower reaches, the Tideway, extend up to Teddington Lock. Along its course are 45 navigation locks, and the river contains over 80 islands.

Researchers have identified the Thames as a discrete drainage line as early as 58 million years ago. About 450,000 years ago, in the Anglian ice age, the ice sheet dammed the river in Hertfordshire, and the large ice lakes that formed eventually burst and diverted the river onto its present course through the area of London. The name derives from the Brittonic Tamesas, recorded in Latin as Tamesis.

Some of the earliest written references occur in Julius Caesar's account of his second expedition to Britain in 54 BCE, when the river presented a major obstacle and he met the Belgic tribes of the Catuvellauni and Atrebates along it. Until enough crossings existed the river was a formidable barrier, and Belgic tribes and Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were defined by which side of it they lay on. When English counties were established, their boundaries were partly set by the Thames.

In the early modern period the Stuart monarchs and the City of London organised pageants on the river. During cold winters it froze above London Bridge, and a tent city stood on it at the first Frost Fair in 1607. Four serious cholera outbreaks killed tens of thousands of people between 1832 and 1865, and in the Great Stink of 1858 sittings of the House of Commons had to be abandoned. A flood on 7 January 1928 drowned fourteen people in London, and together with the North Sea flood of 1953 helped lead to the Thames Barrier, built in the 1970s.

At 215 miles (346 km) the Thames is the longest river entirely in England and the second-longest in the United Kingdom, after the Severn. It is maintained for navigation by powered craft from the estuary as far as Lechlade, and it supplies drinking water, including through the Thames Water Ring Main in London. The river is the historic heartland of rowing in the United Kingdom. Handel's Water Music premiered on the river on 17 July 1717 for King George I.
river-trent: The Trent rises in the Staffordshire Moorlands, near Biddulph Moor, and flows south past Stoke-on-Trent, Stone, Rugeley, Burton upon Trent, Nottingham, Newark-on-Trent and Gainsborough. At Trent Falls it joins the Yorkshire Ouse to form the Humber estuary, which has often been characterised as the boundary between the Midlands and the North. Its largest tributary is the Tame, which supplies nearly a quarter of its flow, followed by the Derwent, Soar, Dove and Sow.

The name is possibly Romano-British and meant strongly flooding. Another derivation, from Trisantona, gives great thoroughfare. Izaak Walton's explanation of 1653, that the river was named for thirty kinds of fish, is almost certainly wrong.

The river changed its channel during historic times, and has been compared to the Mississippi in this respect. At Repton an abandoned channel was once the main navigable route until the river moved to a more northerly course in the 18th century, and at Hemington archaeologists found a medieval bridge across another abandoned channel. Before the mid-18th century there were only four bridges downstream of the Tame, at Burton, Swarkestone, Nottingham and Newark, all first built by 1204, and over thirty ferries.

Fishing along the river goes back to the Neolithic period, to which a possible fish weir at Hemington may belong. Domesday records mills and fisheries along it, and in the 12th century landlords at Burton upon Trent were paid in salmon in place of rent. Nottingham seems to have been the ancient head of navigation until the Restoration. The Trent Navigation Act 1773 authorised locks at Newark, and tolls fell from £11,344 in 1839 to £3,111 in 1855 as railways took the traffic. The Ministry of Transport took over the navigation on 24 September 1920, and Neville Chamberlain opened Hazelford lock on 25 June 1926.

The Trent also marked the boundary between northern and southern England. Royal forests had different justice in eyre north and south of it, the medieval Council of the North's jurisdiction began there, and Oxford University divided its students into northern and southern nations by it. Industrial growth polluted the river: a salmon fishery taking some 3,000 fish a year in the late 1880s had fallen to 100 a decade later.

The river is known for flooding, with a well-documented flood history of some 900 years, and its tidal lower reaches have a bore called the Trent Aegir, up to 1.5 metres high, which travels as far as Gainsborough. Twelve large power stations were built along its banks from the 1940s, using its cooling water, and at one time supplied a quarter of the electricity of the United Kingdom, giving the valley the name Megawatt Valley. The Trent Valley Way, a long-distance footpath, was created in 1998.
river-tummel: The Tummel runs 93 kilometres from its source on Stob Ghabbar, 1,087 metres high, to the River Tay. Leaving Loch Rannoch it flows east to a point near the Falls of Tummel, then bends south-east and keeps that direction to the Tay. Its only considerable tributary is the Garry, an impetuous river 39 kilometres long that issues from Loch Garry, 407 metres above sea level.

Some 2 miles below Loch Rannoch the river widens into Dunalastair Water, a man-made loch formed by a weir, and about midway along its course into Loch Tummel. Between the loch and the meeting with the Garry lie the Pass and Falls of the Tummel, more rapids than falls, with a total descent of 4.6 metres. The Clunie Dam of 1950 raised Loch Tummel by 4.5 metres, lengthening it from 4.43 kilometres to about 11.

The ancient name of the river, at least in its upper reaches, was the Dubhag; in Scottish Gaelic it is Uisge Theimheil. Above the eastern end of Loch Tummel is the viewpoint known as the Queen's View, which Queen Victoria made widely known in 1866, though it is said to be named after Queen Isabel, wife of Robert the Bruce. The rocky hill of Dunalastair, the stronghold of Alexander, takes its name from Alexander Robertson of Struan, the Jacobite and poet, who did much to embellish its wooded grounds.

Water from the river is used in the Tummel hydro-electric power scheme. As a tributary of the Tay it is part of the River Tay Special Area of Conservation, designated for the river system's salmon, otters and brook, river and sea lampreys. Kinloch Rannoch, Foss, Pitlochry and Ballinluig are among the places along its course.
river-tweed: The River Tweed, or Tweed Water, is 97 miles (156 km) long and flows east across the Border region of Scotland and northern England. It rises in the Lowther Hills at Tweed's Well, close to the sources of the Clyde, which drains northwest, and of the Annan, which drains south. A saying of the Border region records this: Annan, Tweed and Clyde rise out of one hillside. The name may represent an Old Brittonic word meaning border, though a proposal deriving it from an Indo-European root meaning swell or grow powerful is doubtful. Tweed cloth takes its name from its association with the river.

East of the settlements of Birgham and Carham, which stand on opposite banks, the river forms the historic boundary between Scotland and England. East of Kelso it becomes part of the eastern border. For only 7 km of its course is it wholly in England, and for 30 km it forms the border. It enters the North Sea at Berwick-upon-Tweed in Northumberland.

The Tweed flows through the Borders region of Scotland, passing Innerleithen, Peebles, Galashiels, Melrose, Kelso, Coldstream and Berwick-upon-Tweed. Its tributaries include the Teviot Water, the Ettrick Water, the Yarrow Water, the Gala Water, the Whiteadder Water, the River Till and the Eden Water. East of St Boswells it runs through a drumlin field, the relic of a former ice stream that flowed through the area during the last glaciation.

The upper catchment is known as Tweeddale, part of which is protected as the Upper Tweeddale National Scenic Area, one of 40 such areas in Scotland. Although the catchment straddles the border, a single body, the River Tweed Commission, oversees water quality, bio-security and the protection of the river's salmon. The Tweed is among the great salmon rivers of Britain and the only river in England where an Environment Agency rod licence is not needed for angling. Historical flooding in the catchment has been studied from documentary records: a study of 1990 by Lindsey J. McEwen reconstructed chronologies of major floods in four sub-catchments of the middle Tweed basin.
river-tyne: The River Tyne is 73 miles (118 km) long, excluding its tributaries. It is formed by the North Tyne and the South Tyne, which meet at Warden near Hexham in Northumberland. The North Tyne rises at Deadwater a few tens of metres short of the Scottish border and flows through Kielder and past Bellingham, passing Hadrian's Wall near Chollerford. The South Tyne rises at Tyne Head on Alston Moor in Cumbria, close to the sources of the Tees and the Wear, and runs beside Hadrian's Wall through the low east-west corridor across the Pennines known as the Tyne Gap.

Below Warden the river flows east by Hexham, Corbridge and Prudhoe, and for 13 miles forms the boundary between Newcastle upon Tyne on the north bank and Gateshead on the south, passing under ten bridges. It then divides Hebburn and Jarrow from Walker and Wallsend, and reaches the North Sea between South Shields and Tynemouth. Before the last ice age the Wear is thought to have followed the course of the lower Team and joined the Tyne at Dunston; ice diverted it to flow east to Sunderland.

Nothing definite is known of the origin of the name, and the river is not known by it until the Saxon period; Tynemouth is recorded in Anglo-Saxon as Tinanmuðe. Because of its closeness to the coalfields the Tyne was a major route for the export of coal from the thirteenth century until mining declined in the later twentieth century. The largest coal staithes stood at Dunston, Hebburn and Tyne Dock. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the lower reaches were also one of the world's most important centres of shipbuilding.

The River Tyne Improvement Act of 1850 created the Tyne Improvement Commission, which lasted until 1968. Over its first seventy years the river was deepened from 6 to 30 feet and 150 million tonnes were dredged from it; the two Tyne piers and the Northumbrian, Tyne and Albert Docks were built, and by 1910 the port handled millions of tonnes of cargo. Islands were removed and meanders straightened. The period from 1850 to 1950 was the worst for pollution of the river. The Port of Tyne Authority has managed the tidal river since 1968.

The wooden coal staithes at Dunston, built in 1890, have been preserved. A bronze figure, River God Tyne, by David Wynne, was unveiled in 1968 at Newcastle's Civic Centre. The Tyne Rivers Trust, a community organisation founded in 2004, works to improve habitat across the catchment.
river-usk: The Usk rises on the northern slopes of the Black Mountain range, in the western part of the Brecon Beacons National Park, and drains a basin of 1,160 square kilometres. It flows through Brecon, Crickhowell, Abergavenny, Usk, Caerleon and Newport to the Severn Estuary at Uskmouth. The Encyclopaedia of Wales gives its length as 137 kilometres and calls it the longest river flowing wholly within Wales. The name comes from a Common Brittonic word meaning abounding in fish, or possibly water, a root also found in the Exe, Axe and Esk. The whole river is a Site of Special Scientific Interest, with Atlantic salmon, otters, twait shad and lampreys, and it has long been noted for salmon and trout.

The valley has been a route for settlement and trade since prehistoric times, and an avenue into Wales for invaders such as the Romans and the Normans. For much of the last millennium its tidal reaches have served as a port, thanks to a wide, deep mouth with good access from the Severn Estuary and the Bristol Channel. The remains of the Newport Ship, discovered in 2002 and dated to around 1465, were probably a trading vessel. Watermills, mostly grinding corn, stood along its banks, the uppermost a mill of medieval origin at Cwm-wysg.

Many historic bridges cross it. The Brecon bridge dates from 1563, and the bridge at Usk was built by William Edwards in the late 1740s and that at Newbridge-on-Usk is probably also his work, of 1779. Caerleon Bridge dates from 1806, and the Newport Transporter Bridge, completed in 1906, is one of fewer than ten such structures in use in the world. The river also features in medieval Welsh and Arthurian literature. Geoffrey of Monmouth, in the mid 12th century, described Caerleon as a delightful place on the Usk, wealthy and suited to a great ceremony because kings and princes could arrive by ship along the river, and a medieval Latin tale, De Ortu Waluuanii, has Gawain push Arthur into the Usk.

The Usk remains a noted fishing river, and in 1999 it had the highest estimated salmon egg deposition of any river south of Cumbria and the Scottish rivers. Its normal tidal limit lies just below the bridge at Newbridge-on-Usk, about five miles north of Newport.
river-welland: The Welland is a lowland river some 65 miles (105 km) long. It rises in the Hothorpe Hills at Sibbertoft and reaches The Wash near Fosdyke, where its banks become sea embankments and it ends as a tidal channel, the Welland Outfall. Its catchment covers 609 square miles, of which 179 square miles lie below sea level and would flood without defences. The ground runs from Lias clays in the west through Lincolnshire limestone to alluvial soils in the east. Below Spalding it crosses the Fens of South Holland between widely spaced embankments that leave washlands for flood water.

The name appears to be older than English, and the river is first mentioned, as the Weolud, in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 921. The Romans used it for navigation as far as Stamford, where Ermine Street forded it, as part of a system that included the Car Dyke. Under William the Conqueror, Richard de Rulos, lord of Deeping Fen, built an embankment against floods. A Welland Navigation Act of 1571 complained that mills had made the river impassable, though no work under it is recorded.

In the 1660s a new cut with 10 locks, the Stamford Canal, was built between Stamford and Market Deeping; it was the longest canal with locks in Britain at the time. The Draining Deeping Fen Act 1664 granted the Earl of Manchester and others 10,000 acres for drainage works, and from 1730 John Perry built scouring sluices. Drainage succeeded fully only after a steam pumping station was built at Pode Hole in 1827. Traffic on the upper river ended by April 1863, after the railways came, but Spalding remained a port until the end of the Second World War.

The Environment Agency is the navigation authority, and the river is navigable up to Crowland. After the floods of 1947 the Coronation Channel was built to protect Spalding, whose silt soils supported large bulb fields from the 1880s. Pinchbeck Marsh Pumping Station, built in 1833, now houses a museum of land drainage. For much of its length the river forms county boundaries, between Northamptonshire and Leicestershire or Rutland and lower down between Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire.
river-witham: The Witham rises on high ground near South Witham at about 100 m above ordnance datum, flows north through Colsterworth and Grantham, and near Barnby in the Willows forms the border between Lincolnshire and Nottinghamshire for about 3 miles. At Lincoln it flows into Brayford Pool and leaves beneath the medieval High Bridge, then turns east and south through the Lincoln Gap towards Boston and The Haven, a tidal arm of The Wash. Its course may be the result of glaciation redirecting older rivers. The name is very old and of unknown origin; John Leland noted in the 16th century that it was also called the Lindis.

Finds such as the Iron Age Witham Shield, found near Washingborough in 1826, and the Fiskerton Boat, a log boat found in 2001, point to navigation since the Iron Age. The Romans improved the river from Lincoln to The Wash and built the Fossdyke from Lincoln to Torksey on the River Trent, giving Lindum, one of only four colonia in Britain, access to the east coast and the Humber. Severe flooding in 1014 diverted the river from Bicker Haven to The Haven at Boston.

Silting hampered trade despite sluices built from 1142 onwards. After surveys by John Grundy, Sr. and his son John Grundy, Jr., and a joint report with John Smeaton and Langley Edwards, an Act of 1762 created the Witham Navigation Commissioners and the Witham Drainage General Commissioners. Edwards's Grand Sluice at Boston, completed in 1766, held the river above it near high-tide level and scoured the channel below, and the drainage network that followed transformed much of northern Lincolnshire from fen to farming land.

Steam packet boats ran from 1816. The Great Northern Railway leased the navigation for 999 years, opened its line from Lincoln to Boston along the bank on 17 October 1848 and drew the traffic away, and by 1863 the packets had stopped.

Commercial traffic above Boston has ceased, and pleasure craft use the river from Brayford Pool in Lincoln to Boston, with locks at Lincoln, Bardney and the Grand Sluice. Lincoln's High Bridge, whose arch was built in c1160, is the only British bridge that still has secular medieval buildings standing on it and is a Grade I listed building. Since 2 July 2012 the navigation has been managed by the Canal & River Trust.
river-wye: 2 kilometres from the source of the Severn. Although the source lies about 19 kilometres from the Irish Sea, the river at first runs inland. It passes Rhayader, Builth Wells, Hay-on-Wye, Hereford, the only city on the river, Ross-on-Wye, Symonds Yat, Monmouth and Tintern, and meets the Severn Estuary just below Chepstow. The lower 26 kilometres, from Redbrook to Chepstow, form part of the border between England and Wales.
The Welsh name is Afon Gwy, and a mention of Guoy in the Historia Brittonum of the early 9th century may be the earliest reference to the name, whose meaning is not clear.

The Romans built a bridge of wood and stone just upstream of present-day Chepstow. The river is tidal for about 24 kilometres up to Bigsweir, where hard rock forms a natural weir, and spring tides can raise the water by as much as 15 metres. Since Roman times it has carried coal from the Forest of Dean, cider from Hereford, wine, iron, stone and timber.

Early records are fragmentary, but iron appears to have been shipped down the river for the ships of Edward the Confessor in the 11th century. In 1171 and 1172 iron was supplied to Henry II for his invasion of Ireland. Under Edward I a common right of navigation was recorded, with the channel to be kept free of weirs.

Schemes to improve navigation followed. Sir William Sandys was appointed in 1662 to make the Wye and the Lugg navigable with flash locks, but the Wye ran too fast, the locks proved impracticable and costly, and the scheme was abandoned by 1668. The Rivers Wye and Lugg Navigation Act of 1695 authorised Herefordshire to buy and demolish the weirs and declared the rivers free and common. A towing path for horses from Lydbrook to Hereford was authorised in 1809, and barges reached Hereford in January 1811. Passenger boats ran from 1835. Trade declined after the Herefordshire and Gloucestershire Canal reached Hereford in 1845 and railways opened.

The lower valley is a National Landscape, and the river is protected by two Sites of Special Scientific Interest and designated a Special Area of Conservation. It was once known for its large spring salmon, the largest recorded weighing 59 lb 8 oz, caught in 1923. The river is used for canoeing, rowing and walking, and the Wye Valley Walk follows it from near Plynlimon to Chepstow.
rivonia-trial: Liliesleaf Farm, owned by Arthur Goldreich, had served as a hideout for the African National Congress, the Communist Party and others. Nelson Mandela lived there from October 1961 disguised as a gardener and cook called David Motsamayi, and was arrested on 5 August 1962 without the farm being found. On 11 July 1963 the South African Police raided it and arrested Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki, Ahmed Kathrada, Denis Goldberg, Lionel Bernstein, Raymond Mhlaba and others, holding them incommunicado under a law that allowed 90 days' detention without trial. On 11 August Goldreich, Abdulhay Jassat, Moosa Moolla and Harold Wolpe escaped from The Fort prison in Johannesburg after bribing a guard.

The prosecutor was Percy Yutar, deputy attorney-general of the Transvaal, and the judge Quartus de Wet. The defence, led by Bram Fischer with Joel Joffe as instructing attorney and George Bizos, Arthur Chaskalson and Vernon Berrangé among the advocates, had the first indictment quashed. The second charged ten men with recruiting for sabotage and guerrilla warfare, conspiring to aid a foreign invasion, furthering communism and receiving money from abroad. James Kantor, Wolpe's brother-in-law, was discharged at the end of the prosecution's case.

On 20 April 1964 Mandela spoke from the dock for three hours. He explained why the movement had turned from non-violent methods to sabotage against property, set out its relationship with the Communist Party and declared his support for constitutional democracy. He closed with the words that the ideal of a free society was one for which, if needs be, he was prepared to die.

On 12 June 1964 Bernstein was acquitted; the rest were sentenced to life imprisonment, although observers had expected the prosecution to seek death. Goldberg served 22 years in Pretoria Central Prison, while most of the others were held on Robben Island. Goldberg was freed in 1985, Mbeki in 1987, Sisulu and four others in 1989 and Mandela on 11 February 1990. The trial was condemned by the United Nations Security Council, and in 2007 UNESCO added its records to the Memory of the World Register.
riyadh: Riyadh is the largest city on the Arabian Peninsula. It lies in the eastern part of the Najd plateau, at an average elevation of 600 metres above sea level. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers and short, cold winters. The city is known for dust storms so thick that visibility can fall under 10 m. The old town within the walls did not exceed an area of 1 km2, and the city is now divided into fourteen branch municipalities and the Diplomatic Quarter.

In the pre-Islamic era the city on the site was called Hajr and was reportedly founded by the tribe of Banu Hanifa. It was the capital of the province of Al-Yamama, whose governors were responsible for most of central and eastern Arabia under the Umayyad Caliphate and Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Yamama broke away from the Abbasid Caliphate in 866, and the Banu Ukhaidhir, who then ruled the area, moved the capital to nearby Al-Kharj. Hajr went into a long decline. In the 14th century Ibn Battuta visited it, and described it as the main city of Al-Yamama, a city of canals and trees whose inhabitants mostly belonged to the Banu Hanifa.

Hajr later broke up into separate settlements and estates, the most notable being Migrin and Mi'kal. The earliest known reference to the area as Riyadh, meaning gardens, comes from a 17th-century chronicler describing an event of 1590. Dahham ibn Dawwas, a refugee from neighbouring Manfuhah, took control and built a single wall around the various oasis towns, making them in effect one fortress city. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the Emir of Diriyah, Muhammad bin Saud, then took the town from him, but the First Saudi state they formed collapsed in 1818. Turki ibn Abdullah founded the Second Saudi state in the early 19th century and made Riyadh his capital, though a joint Ottoman and Rashidi alliance disrupted his rule.

Ibn Saud retrieved his ancestral rule in 1902 with the Emirate of Riyadh and consolidated it by 1926 with the conquest of the Hejaz. In September 1932 he named his kingdom Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh as the capital. The first major construction beyond the walls was his Murabba Palace, built in 1936-1938, and the government moved there in 1938. In the 1950s the walls were dismantled and the modern city expanded from the old town. The population was 40,000 in 1935 and 83,000 in 1949. Of the old town the Al-Masmak Palace and parts of the wall and its gate survive, restored.
rizal-province: Rizal lies in the Calabarzon region of Luzon, about 16 kilometres east of Manila. It is bordered by Metro Manila to the west, Bulacan to the north, Quezon to the east and Laguna to the southeast, and its southern towns stand on the northern shores of Laguna de Bay, the largest lake in the country. The province is mountainous, set on the western slopes of the southern part of the Sierra Madre. Talim Island, the largest island in the lake, belongs to it and is shared by Binangonan and Cardona.

Tagalog settlement arrived in the pre-Spanish period, and under Spanish rule the territory fell within the provinces of Tondo and Laguna. In 1853 a Political-Military District of the San Mateo Mountains was formed, taking Antipolo, Cainta and Taytay from Tondo and Morong, Baras, Tanay and other towns from Laguna, with Morong as its capital. Four years later it became the Political-Military District of Morong. In 1859 the Province of Tondo became the Province of Manila.

On 5 June 1901 a meeting of 221 delegates at the Pasig Catholic Church discussed organising civil government under the First Philippine Commission, headed by William Howard Taft. Delegates from Morong objected to joining Manila, while Juan Sumulong of Antipolo argued strongly for the move. On the suggestion of Trinidad H. Pardo de Tavera the body agreed on a new province, named after José Rizal. Act No. 137 created it on 11 June 1901 from 32 municipalities, 19 from the old Province of Manila and 13 from the District of Morong, with Pasig as its seat.
On 7 November 1975 Presidential Decree No. 824 partitioned the province to form Metropolitan Manila. Twelve municipalities and three cities were taken out of it, and 14 towns remained in Rizal.

Rizal has 13 municipalities and one city, Antipolo, which became the provincial capital by law in 2020; Pasig had been the capital before. Almost all residents speak Tagalog, with English and Filipino as second languages, and Roman Catholicism is the predominant religion, followed by about 80 percent of the people. The Iglesia Ni Cristo is the largest minority.
roald-amundsen: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on 16 July 1872 in Borge, Østfold, into a family of Norwegian shipowners and captains. His mother wanted him to avoid the maritime trade and become a doctor, a promise he kept until she died when he was 21, after which he quit university for a life at sea. At fifteen he had been enthralled by Sir John Franklin's narratives of his Arctic expeditions. In 1897 he joined the Belgian Antarctic Expedition of Adrien de Gerlache as first mate; its ship Belgica became locked in sea ice and the first expedition to overwinter in Antarctica endured a winter for which it was poorly prepared.

In 1903 Amundsen led the first expedition to traverse the Northwest Passage, in the 45-ton sloop Gjøa with a crew of six. They spent two winters at King William Island, where the Netsilik Inuit taught them Arctic survival skills, such as using sled dogs and wearing animal skins instead of woolen parkas. The ship cleared the Canadian Arctic Archipelago on 17 August 1905, and the crew returned to Oslo in November 1906.

In 1909, hearing of the claims of Frederick Cook and Robert Peary to the North Pole, Amundsen turned to Antarctica without making clear his intentions, and Robert F. Scott felt misled. He left Oslo in the Fram on 3 June 1910 and set up base at Framheim in January 1911. Five men, Amundsen, Olav Bjaaland, Helmer Hanssen, Sverre Hassel and Oscar Wisting, left on 19 October with four sledges and 52 dogs and reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, a month before Scott's group. His success rested on careful preparation, skis, dogs and Inuit-style furred clothing.

From 1918 to 1925 Amundsen led an expedition in the ship Maud through the Northeast Passage, aiming to drift towards the North Pole as Fridtjof Nansen had; the ship froze in the ice and the goal was not achieved. On 12 May 1926 he and 15 other men in the airship Norge became the first explorers verified to have reached the North Pole. In June 1928 he disappeared while flying on a rescue mission for the airship Italia in the Arctic. The search for his remains, which have not been found, was called off that September.
roanoke-river: The Roanoke River is 410 miles (660 km) long and drains a largely rural area from the eastern edge of the Appalachian Mountains across the Piedmont to Albemarle Sound. It begins at Lafayette in Montgomery County, Virginia, where the North Fork and South Fork meet, and flows through the Roanoke Valley and past the city of Roanoke.

It then crosses the Piedmont and enters North Carolina north of Roanoke Rapids at the fall line, before zigzagging across the coastal plain to Batchelor Bay. An 81-mile stretch of its lower course in Virginia, between Leesville Lake and Kerr Lake, is known as the Staunton River. The river is impounded in six places, among them Smith Mountain Lake, Kerr Lake and Lake Gaston.

The valley was the homeland of Native peoples such as the Moratoc, Occaneechi, Tuscarora and Tutelo, and its deadly spring floods earned it the name River of Death. Virginians began settling its lower course about the middle of the 17th century, in what were called the Albemarle Settlements.

Fur trading parties sent by Abraham Wood explored its upper reaches in the late 17th century, but the English did not settle them until the early 18th century. In 1883 the town of Big Lick was chosen as a major shops and terminal point of the Norfolk and Western Railway and was renamed Roanoke after the river, as Roanoke County had been in 1838.

The river flooded severely until the John H. Kerr Dam was completed in 1953, a project prompted by the record floods of the 1940 South Carolina hurricane. The Niagara Dam near Roanoke, built in 1906 to power the city's streetcars, is the first of its dams. A paddle trail, the Roanoke River State Trail, follows the lower river from Roanoke Rapids to Albemarle Sound. It was developed from 1997 by the non-profit Roanoke River Partners and became North Carolina's twelfth state trail by a law passed on 18 November 2021.
roatan: Roatán lies about 65 kilometres off the northern coast of Honduras, between Utila and Guanaja. It is about 59 kilometres long and less than 8 kilometres across at its widest. A coral island set on an exposed ancient reef, it rises to about 270 metres. It has two municipalities, José Santos Guardiola in the east and Roatán in the west, where most of the infrastructure lies, and its most populous town is Coxen Hole. It lies on the southern edge of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and was formerly known in English as Ruatan and Rattan.

The first inhabitants are believed to have been related to the Paya, Maya, Lenca or Tolupan of the mainland. The Spanish began trading in the islands for slave labour, and smallpox and measles were even more devastating. The English occupied the Bay Islands on and off between 1550 and 1700, and pirates settled there. A British detachment under John Caulfield garrisoned Roatán from 1742 to 1749.

In 1797 the British defeated the Garifuna, who had French support, in the Second Carib War on St. Vincent and deported them to Roatán. Most went on to Trujillo on the mainland, but some founded Punta Gorda on the northern coast, becoming the islands' first permanent post-Columbian settlers. From there the Garifuna spread along the coast of Central America. In the 19th century settlers from the Cayman Islands, former slaveholders and former slaves, arrived and became the largest cultural group. Britain made the Bay Islands a colony in the 1850s and ceded them back to Honduras within a decade.

In the 2013 census Roatán municipality had 41,831 people, of whom 52.06 per cent were Mestizo. The English-speaking Islanders, of European and British-Afro-Caribbean descent, speak Bay Island English and differ culturally from mainland Hondurans. Fishing and later diving laid the foundation of a tourist trade, and cruise ships call at Coxen Hole and Dixon Cove. Hurricane Mitch damaged the island in 1998, and the Roatán Marine Park, formed in 2005, works to protect its reefs.
robben-island: Robben Island lies in Table Bay, 6.9 kilometres west of the coast of Bloubergstrand and north of Cape Town. It is roughly oval, 3.3 kilometres long and 1.9 kilometres wide, and so flat that it stands only a few metres above sea level. Its name comes from the archaic Dutch word for seals, robben. Jan van Riebeeck had bonfires lit on its highest point in the 1650s to warn ships, and a lighthouse was completed on Minto Hill in 1865.

The island is said to have been found by Bartolomeu Dias in 1488, and Portuguese, English and Dutch sailors used it as a refuelling station. In 1654 the settlers of the Dutch Cape Colony sheltered livestock there. From the end of the 17th century it was used to imprison mainly political prisoners, with Autshumato probably the first, in the mid-17th century. Political leaders from other Dutch colonies were held there, among them Massavana and Koesaaij, two surviving Malagasy leaders of the mutiny aboard the slave ship Meermin. After the failed uprising at Grahamstown in 1819 the British sentenced the African leader Makanda Nxele to life imprisonment on the island; he drowned in Table Bay after escaping.

From 1845 people with leprosy were moved to the island, at first voluntarily, and after the Leprosy Repression Act of May 1892 admission was compulsory. From 1961 to 1996 the South African government used it to imprison political dissidents, among them the future presidents Nelson Mandela, Kgalema Motlanthe and Jacob Zuma. The maximum security prison closed in 1991 and the medium security prison for criminal prisoners in 1996.

In 1997 the island became a museum and a national monument, and in 1999 it was recognised as a World Heritage Site. The Robben Island Museum runs it as a living museum, and many of the guides are former prisoners. Visitors reach it by ferry from Cape Town's Victoria & Alfred Waterfront and see the maximum security prison, Nelson Mandela's cell, the lime quarry, Robert Sobukwe's house and the Moturu Kramat, a shrine built in 1969 that is a sacred site for Muslim pilgrimage. Administratively it is a suburb of the City of Cape Town.
robert-baldwin: Baldwin came of a prominent family: his grandfather, also Robert Baldwin, moved to Upper Canada from Ireland in 1799, and his father was William Warren Baldwin, to whom with his son the idea of responsible government has been attributed. In 1827 he married his cousin Augusta Elizabeth Sullivan, with whom he had two sons and two daughters; her death in 1836 ended the marriage. Described as melancholy and awkward in public, he won a by-election for the town of York in 1830 but lost his seat in the general election later that year.

In 1836 the new Lieutenant Governor, Sir Francis Bond Head, appointed Baldwin to the Executive Council; when Bond Head would not confirm in writing a commitment to responsible government, Baldwin resigned within a month and persuaded the other councillors to go with him. Bond Head then won an election marked by Orange Order violence. Baldwin disapproved of the rebellion of 1837, carried a flag of truce to the rebel camp north of Toronto on 5 December 1837, and with his father advised Lord Durham to recommend responsible government.

Named Solicitor General in 1840, he was elected for 4th York and Hastings. Orange violence kept Louis-Hippolyte LaFontaine from a seat in Canada East, so Baldwin had him nominated for 4th York; when Baldwin lost Hastings, LaFontaine arranged his election at Rimouski in 1843. Their first ministry, formed in September 1842, ended in November 1843 in a year-long crisis with Governor Sir Charles Metcalfe, who rejected Baldwin's Secret Societies Bill against the Orange Order. Baldwin founded a Reform Association in February 1844.

Lord Elgin was sent to accept responsible government, and the second Baldwin-LaFontaine administration, formed on 11 March 1848, passed the Amnesty Act, the Baldwin Act on municipal government and the Rebellion Losses Bill of 1849, after which rioters burned the Parliament buildings in Montreal. Baldwin resigned in 1851 after most Upper Canada members backed abolishing the Court of Chancery, and he lost York after refusing a pledge on the Clergy Reserves. He died at Spadina on 9 December 1858. John Ralston Saul credited Baldwin and LaFontaine with Canada's non-violent political tradition.
robert-barclay: Barclay was born at Gordonstoun in Moray on 23 December 1648, the son of David Barclay, first laird of Ury, who had served under Gustavus Adolphus, and of Katherine Gordon, daughter of Sir Robert Gordon, 1st Baronet of Gordonstoun. He finished his education at the Scots College in Paris, where his uncle was Rector; the uncle offered to make him his heir if he stayed in France and joined the Roman Catholic Church. Instead, after returning to Scotland, he followed his father into the Religious Society of Friends in 1667.

Barclay began writing in defence of the Friends with Truth cleared of Calumnies (1670), a reply to William Mitchell, and A Catechism and Confession of Faith (1673). His central view was that all people can be illuminated by the Inward Light of Christ. His fifteen Theses Theologiae, which set that light above reason and scripture, led to a public debate in Aberdeen in which each side claimed victory. The Apology appeared in Latin at Amsterdam in 1676 and in his own English translation in 1678. He supported George Fox in the controversies of the 1670s.

In 1670 he married the Quaker Christian Mollison, daughter of Gilbert Mollison of Aberdeen; they had three sons and four daughters. He travelled in Europe, once with William Penn and George Fox, met Elisabeth, Princess Palatine, and was imprisoned several times, though each time he soon regained his liberty.

Barclay had much influence with James II, and he is said to have visited the king to seek terms with William of Orange. As absentee governor of East Jersey he governed through deputies: Thomas Rudyard from 16 September 1682, Gawen Lawrie from 27 July 1683, Lord Neill Campbell in 1686 and Andrew Hamilton from 10 December 1686. Under Rudyard the counties of Bergen, Essex, Middlesex and Monmouth were set up, and in 1686 the assembly rejected the Fundamental Constitutions drafted by the proprietors. Barclay died at Ury on 3 October 1690. His grandson David Barclay of Youngsbury was one of the founders of what became Barclays Bank.
robert-bosch: Robert Bosch was born on 23 September 1861 at Albeck in the Swabian Highlands near Ulm, one of twelve children of Servatius Bosch, who ran a large progressive farm with a brewery. He attended the Realanstalt in Ulm until 1879, with an apprenticeship as a precision-instrument maker. In 1883 and 1884 he studied at the Stuttgart Technical University. On 24 May 1884 he sailed for the United States and worked as an engineer under Thomas Edison and Sigmund Bergmann in New York; in 1885 he went to London, where he found employment with Siemens Brothers.

On 15 November 1886 Bosch opened his own Workshop for Precision Mechanics and Electrical Engineering in Stuttgart. In 1887 Gottlieb Daimler asked whether he could build a device like the low-voltage magneto with firing points used by the Gasoline Engine Factory Deutz, to produce the spark that ignites the air-fuel mixture at maximum compression, and Bosch made four. In 1893 Frederick Richard Simms proposed adapting the stationary-engine magneto for motor vehicles. Arnold Zähringer and Gottlob Honold modified it to raise the speed of sparks from 250 to 1800 rpm, and orders from Daimler followed after a demonstration in January 1898.

By 1913 the company had branches in America, Asia, Africa and Australia and made 88% of its sales outside Germany. After the First World War Bosch introduced diesel fuel injection in 1927, and in the 1920s he modernised and diversified, turning a small automotive supplier into a multinational electronics group.

Bosch was one of the first German industrialists to introduce the eight-hour day, and he promoted occupational training. He did not wish to profit from armaments contracts of the First World War and gave several million marks to charity, including the Robert Bosch Hospital in Stuttgart. As a liberal he devoted energy and money to reconciliation between Germany and France. His relationship with Nazism is described as complex: as much as 60% of the firm's revenue came from Wehrmacht contracts in the 1940s, yet he worked with Carl Friedrich Goerdeler, central to the plot of 20 July, and his managers joined the Nazi party to keep committed Nazis out of the company.

In 1937 he made the company a private limited company, and his will required that its earnings go to charitable causes. He died on 12 March 1942, survived by four children from two marriages, and was inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame in 1984.
robert-boyle: Robert Boyle was born at Lismore Castle in County Waterford on 25 January 1627, the seventh son and fourteenth child of Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Cork, and Catherine Fenton. After his mother's death, when he was eight, he and his brother Francis were sent to Eton College. He then travelled abroad with a French tutor and spent the winter of 1641 in Florence, studying the paradoxes of the elderly Galileo Galilei. He returned to England in 1644, a year after his father's death, and lived at the manor of Stalbridge in Dorset until 1652, working in a laboratory and joining the band of enquirers known as the Invisible College.

Boyle moved to Ireland in 1652 but, frustrated in his chemical work, went to Oxford in 1654. Having read in 1657 of Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump, he set about improving it with Robert Hooke, and his Pneumatical Engine was finished in 1659. In answering the Jesuit Francis Line's objections to his account of the experiments he first mentioned the law that the volume of a gas varies inversely to its pressure. In continental Europe it is sometimes attributed to Edme Mariotte.

In 1663 the Invisible College became the Royal Society of London, and Charles II's charter named Boyle to its council. In 1680 he was elected president but declined from a scruple about oaths. From 1668 he lived in London in the house of his sister Katherine Jones, Lady Ranelagh, with whom he kept a lifelong intellectual partnership. He died on 31 December 1691, a week after her, and was buried at St Martin-in-the-Fields.

Boyle held that knowledge should rest on experiment, writing that he did not love to believe anything upon conjectures when a not over-difficult experiment could test it. He was also an alchemist who thought the transmutation of metals possible. In The Sceptical Chymist he criticised the Spagyrists who held that salt, sulphur and mercury were the true principles of things. He took elements to be the undecomposable constituents of bodies, distinguished mixtures from compounds and gave the name analysis to the detection of their ingredients.

A devout Anglican, he refused holy orders on the ground that his religious writings would carry more weight from a layman, and he argued that the design visible in nature showed God's involvement with the world. From 1680 to 1685 he paid for the printing of the Bible in Irish.
robert-clive: Robert Clive was born at Styche, the family estate near Market Drayton in Shropshire, the eldest of thirteen children of Richard Clive, a lawyer and member of Parliament. His father obtained for him a post as a writer, or clerk, with the East India Company, and in 1743 he sailed for India. After the French took Madras in 1746, during the First Carnatic War, Clive joined the Company's army. He served in a failed expedition to Tanjore and nearly lost his small force at Devikottai.

The death of the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1748 began the Second Carnatic War, in which the French governor Dupleix used small disciplined forces to tip the balance among Indian rulers. He returned in 1755 as deputy governor of Fort St. David. In 1756 the new Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, took Calcutta, and prisoners were put in the cell known as the Black Hole, where 43 of 64 were reported to have died. Clive retook the city and besieged the French colony of Chandannagar. He agreed with Mir Jafar, who led a conspiracy against the nawab, to make him viceroy in return for payments to the Company. Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757 followed.

He went home in 1760 with a fortune, entered Parliament and was made an Irish baron. He returned to Bengal in 1765 and on 12 August of that year obtained from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, which made the Company the real ruler of some thirty million people. He raised civil servants' pay and forbade gifts from Indians, though corruption continued. He left India for the last time in February 1767.

Back in England he bought Claremont in Surrey, where Capability Brown remodelled the house and garden. Parliamentary debate on the great Bengal famine, which Adam Smith and others blamed on Company officials, reduced his political popularity. On 22 November 1774 Clive died at his house in Berkeley Square after cutting his throat with a paper knife; no inquest was held, and newspapers reported an apoplectic fit.

Clive remains one of Britain's most controversial colonial figures. Lord Macaulay admired him, but modern historians criticise his management of Bengal's revenue, which raised demands on the rural population and increased poverty before the famine of 1770. His statue stands in Shrewsbury and in King Charles Street in London.
robert-conquest: Conquest was born in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, to an American father and an English mother. He was educated at Winchester College and won an exhibition to study philosophy, politics and economics at Magdalen College, Oxford, after a year at the University of Grenoble and in Bulgaria. Back at Oxford in 1937 he joined the Communist Party of Great Britain, but he broke with it when it denounced the war of 1939 as imperialist, and he was commissioned in the Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry in 1940. In 1944 he went to Bulgaria as a liaison officer and later served as press officer at the British Legation in Sofia. He said later that he first learned the realities of a Stalinist takeover there.

In 1948 Conquest was recalled to London and joined the Foreign Office's Information Research Department, a unit created by the Attlee government to collect information on Soviet and communist misdoings and to support anticommunist publications. He worked there until 1956, when he left to write as a freelancer and historian. In the 1960s he edited eight volumes produced by the department, published by the Bodley Head as the Soviet Studies Series. He was literary editor of The Spectator in 1962 and 1963. In 1981 he moved to California as a research fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, where he remained. He died at Stanford in 2015, aged 98.

Conquest's The Great Terror (1968) was based mainly on information made public during the Khrushchev Thaw, on émigré accounts and on official Soviet documents. It widened the understanding of the purges beyond the Moscow trials, which he treated as a minor detail. After the Soviet archives opened he revised it as The Great Terror: A Reassessment (1990). J. Arch Getty wrote in 1993 that the archives did not support his casualty figures, and Stephen G. Wheatcroft holds his totals too high. In 1996 Eric Hobsbawm called the book a pioneering effort that archival sources had made obsolete.

The Harvest of Sorrow (1986) treated collectivisation and the famine that followed in Ukraine and elsewhere. Conquest described the famine as a planned act of genocide, though in a letter of 2003 he wrote that Stalin could have prevented it but put Soviet interest first. He was also a poet, associated with the group known as The Movement, and with Kingsley Amis he wrote the novel The Egyptologists (1965).
robert-curthose: Robert was the eldest son of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders. His birth has been dated to between 1051 and 1053. The epithet Curthose comes from the Norman French courtheuse, 'short stockings'; the chroniclers William of Malmesbury and Orderic Vitalis wrote that his father derisively called him brevis-ocrea, 'short boot'. In 1063 his father made him Count of Maine, in view of his betrothal to Margaret, the heiress of Maine, who died before they could marry. In 1077 a quarrel with his younger brothers William Rufus and Henry led him to attempt to seize Rouen Castle, and he spent the following years in exile, at one point wounding his father in battle in January 1079.

When William died in 1087 he gave Normandy to Robert and England to William Rufus, and Henry received money to buy land. Robert was generous to his barons and the clergy but was almost perpetually short of funds, and the central authority of the duchy weakened. William Rufus bribed many of his vassals away. Robert's support for the Rebellion of 1088 against Rufus failed, and he never joined the English rebels himself.

In 1096 Robert left to join the First Crusade, mortgaging his duchy to Rufus for 10,000 marks. He fought at the Battle of Dorylaeum on 1 July 1097, took part in the siege and battle of Antioch, and was among the crusaders who captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. At Ascalon on 12 August 1099 he commanded part of the crusader centre. On the way home he married Sybil of Conversano, whose dowry helped him buy back his duchy.

Rufus died on 2 August 1100 while Robert was still returning, and Henry seized the English crown. In 1101 Robert landed at Portsmouth with a fleet, but he and Henry agreed the Treaty of Alton, by which Robert recognised Henry's crown in exchange for 3,000 livres. His position in Normandy then deteriorated amid private wars among the barons.

In 1106 Henry decisively defeated Robert's army at the Battle of Tinchebray and claimed Normandy for the English crown, a situation that lasted almost a century. Robert was captured and held at Corfe Castle, then at Devizes Castle and finally at Cardiff Castle, where he died probably on 3 February 1134. He was buried at Gloucester Abbey, where an effigy of bog oak, carved about a century after his death, lies on a mortuary chest. His reputation rests largely on his conduct on the crusade, described as the one period of clear distinction in his career.
robert-dudley-1st-earl-of-leicester: Robert Dudley was the fifth son of John Dudley, 1st Duke of Northumberland. His tutors included John Dee, Thomas Wilson and Roger Ascham. When Edward VI died on 6 July 1553 and Northumberland tried to give the crown to Lady Jane Grey, Dudley led a force of 300 into Norfolk against Mary. He took King's Lynn and proclaimed Jane there, but the townsmen seized him, and he was condemned to death. He was released in 1554 and was rehabilitated after taking part in the Battle of St. Quentin under Philip.

On the morning after Elizabeth's accession in November 1558, Dudley witnessed the surrender of the Great Seal to her and became Master of the Horse. He became a privy councillor in October 1562 and Earl of Leicester in 1564, and the queen granted him Kenilworth and the lordships of Denbigh and Chirk. His wife Amy Robsart was found dead at Cumnor Place near Oxford on 8 September 1560. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of accident, but rumours that he had arranged it lasted all his life and damaged his suit for Elizabeth's hand. In July 1575 he staged a 19-day festival at Kenilworth for the queen.

He worked with William Cecil and Francis Walsingham and patronised Puritans, the arts and the theatre. He backed Francis Drake's circumnavigation. In 1585, under the Treaty of Nonsuch, he led the English campaign in support of the Dutch Revolt and mortgaged his estate for £25,000 to equip it. His acceptance of the post of governor-general of the United Provinces infuriated Elizabeth, and the expedition was a military and political failure that ruined him financially.

In July 1588 Leicester was appointed lieutenant and captain-general of the queen's armies. He set up a camp at Tilbury for the defence of London against the Spanish Armada, and he walked bare-headed beside the queen's horse on the day she addressed the troops. He died on 4 September 1588.

A libel printed in Paris in 1584, later known as Leicester's Commonwealth, was written by Catholic exiles who wanted Mary, Queen of Scots to succeed Elizabeth. It presented him as an atheistic and hypocritical poisoner who aimed at the crown, and it was the origin of much of his later reputation. More recent research has led to a reassessment of his place in Elizabethan government and society.
robert-e-lee: Robert Edward Lee was born on 19 January 1807 at Stratford Hall Plantation in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the fourth child of the Revolutionary War officer Henry Lee III and Anne Hill Carter Lee. A top graduate of the United States Military Academy, he served 32 years in the United States Army as an officer and military engineer. In 1831 he married Mary Anna Randolph Custis, a great-granddaughter of Martha Washington, and they eventually had seven children.

In the Mexican–American War he was one of Winfield Scott's chief aides, finding routes of attack the Mexicans had left undefended, and he was wounded at Chapultepec. From 1852 he was Superintendent of the Military Academy at West Point. After his father-in-law died in 1857, Lee took leave to run the Arlington estate, which held hundreds of enslaved people. In October 1859 he commanded the force that captured John Brown's raiders at Harpers Ferry.

Lee privately opposed secession, calling it nothing but revolution, but when Virginia seceded in 1861 he followed his state and resigned from the army. He took command of the Army of Northern Virginia in June 1862 and drove George B. McClellan's Army of the Potomac from Richmond in the Seven Days Battles. He defeated John Pope at the Second Battle of Bull Run, and then won at Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville. His invasion of Maryland ended in the inconclusive Battle of Antietam, and his second invasion of the North ended in decisive defeat at Gettysburg in 1863.

In 1864 Ulysses S. Grant fought him at the Wilderness, Spotsylvania Court House and Cold Harbor and pinned him at Richmond, and the Siege of Petersburg followed. Lee became General in Chief of the Confederate armies on 6 February 1865. After the capture of Richmond and the destruction of most of his army, he surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865.

After the war Lee was indicted but not punished, though he lost the right to vote and some property. He became president of Washington College, now Washington and Lee University, in Lexington, Virginia, and supported reconciliation between North and South. He accepted the end of slavery but opposed racial equality for African Americans. He died of pneumonia in Lexington on 12 October 1870, after a stroke.

Among supporters of the Confederacy he was revered more after the surrender than during the war. Historians note contradictions in his views on slavery, which he called a moral and political evil while defending its legality. Promoters of the Lost Cause made him an icon, and after the civil rights movement historians reassessed his failure to support rights for freedmen and his strategic choices.
robert-emmet: Robert Emmet was born on 4 March 1778 at 109 St Stephen's Green in Dublin, the youngest son of the physician to the Lord Lieutenant and a member of a comfortable Protestant Ascendancy family. His father supported American independence, and his elder brother Thomas Addis Emmet was a friend of Theobald Wolfe Tone. He entered Trinity College Dublin in October 1793 at fifteen and excelled in history and chemistry. In April 1798 he was exposed as secretary of a secret college committee backing the Society of United Irishmen and withdrew from Trinity rather than be questioned under oath.

Emmet took no part in the uprising of May 1798, but afterwards he joined William Putnam McCabe in rebuilding the United Irish organisation on a military basis, hoping again for French help. In 1800 he went to Paris as secretary to Malachy Delaney and, with Delaney, presented Napoleon with a memorial arguing that the Union had not eased Ireland's discontent. Back in Dublin from October 1802, he prepared a rising with a legacy of £2,000 from his father and the help of his housekeeper Anne Devlin, having come to doubt that France would put Ireland's interests first.

A gunpowder explosion at the rebels' depot in Patrick Street on 16 July 1803 forced his hand, and he brought the date forward to 23 July. His proclamation of a provisional government called on the Irish to rely on their own strength, and announced the abolition of tithes and the nationalisation of the land of the Church of Ireland. Many veterans of 1798 stayed away. The plan to storm Dublin Castle was botched; by evening he had only about 80 men outside his Thomas Street arsenal and told them to disperse. In the night's clashes the Lord Chief Justice, Lord Kilwarden, was dragged from his carriage and killed with pikes.

Emmet was captured on 25 August, tried for high treason on 19 September and convicted, offering no defence. His Speech from the Dock, of which over seventy versions exist, ends by asking that no man vindicate or calumniate his character until other times and other men could do it justice. He was hanged on 20 September 1803, and his burial place is unknown. Daniel O'Connell condemned the resort to physical force, but the Young Irelanders began his political rehabilitation in the 1840s. Thomas Moore's ballads made him an icon, W. B. Yeats observing in 1904 that Emmet died and became an image, and in 1916 Patrick Pearse again proclaimed a provisional government in Dublin.
robert-f-kennedy: Kennedy was born in Brookline, Massachusetts, on 20 November 1925, the seventh of the nine children of Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., a politician and businessman, and Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy. All four of his grandparents were children of Irish immigrants, and both parents came from prominent Irish-American families active in the Massachusetts Democratic Party. He enlisted in the United States Naval Reserve in 1943, entered Harvard University as a junior in 1946, and graduated in 1948 with a degree in political science.

After Harvard, Kennedy toured Europe and the Middle East as a correspondent for The Boston Post. He earned his law degree at the University of Virginia, worked at the Department of Justice, and resigned on 6 June 1952 to manage his brother John F. Kennedy's campaign for the United States Senate. He was chief counsel of the Senate Labor Rackets Committee from 1957 to 1959, where he publicly challenged the Teamsters president Jimmy Hoffa.

President-elect John F. Kennedy appointed him attorney general in 1961, over criticism that he was inexperienced. He built the first coordinated program involving all 26 federal law enforcement agencies against organized crime, and convictions of organized crime figures rose by 800 percent during his term. He authorised the Federal Bureau of Investigation to wiretap Martin Luther King Jr. on a limited basis. He resigned on 3 September 1964 and won a New York Senate seat, defeating the Republican incumbent Kenneth Keating.

In the Senate Kennedy opposed American involvement in the Vietnam War and sponsored legislation to draw private business to poor communities. After the Tet Offensive of early 1968 he entered the race for the Democratic presidential nomination. He won the California and South Dakota primaries on 4 June. Shortly after midnight he left a speech at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles through the kitchen, where Sirhan Sirhan, a 24-year-old Palestinian, shot him three times. He died 25 hours later and was buried near his brother at Arlington National Cemetery.
He married Ethel Skakel in 1950, and they had eleven children. His books include The Enemy Within (1960) and Thirteen Days, an account of the Cuban Missile Crisis published after his death.
robert-f-stockton: Robert Field Stockton was born on 20 August 1795 at Morven, in Princeton, New Jersey, into a political family: his father Richard Stockton was a senator and representative, and his grandfather, Judge Richard Stockton, signed the Declaration of Independence. He was appointed a midshipman in September 1811, just after his 16th birthday, and served in the War of 1812. As a lieutenant he served in the Mediterranean, the Caribbean and off West Africa, where he captured several slave ships.

In December 1821 he negotiated the treaty that led to the founding of Liberia, and one account says that he levelled a pistol at King Peter's head to persuade him to sell land. He married Harriet Maria Potter in Charleston on 4 March 1823, and they had ten children.

Returning to active service as a captain in 1838, Stockton declined President John Tyler's offer of the post of Secretary of the Navy in 1841 and promoted instead an advanced steam warship. The result, USS Princeton, designed by John Ericsson and completed in 1843, was the Navy's first screw-propelled steamer. In February 1844 one of its heavy guns, the Peacemaker, which Stockton had devised, exploded and killed two cabinet secretaries and several others; his political influence saw him cleared. President James K. Polk then sent him to Texas with the offer of annexation.

On 23 July 1846 he arrived at Monterey and took over the Pacific Squadron from the ailing Commodore John D. Sloat, becoming senior commander and military governor in California. General Castro retreated before him from Los Angeles, and in December he led a relief column for General Stephen Kearny after the Battle of San Pasqual. After the battles of Rio San Gabriel and La Mesa in January 1847 the Californios signed the Treaty of Cahuenga, and Stockton appointed John C. Fremont to succeed him before handing control to Kearny.

Stockton resigned from the Navy in May 1850. Elected to the Senate as a Democrat in 1851, he sponsored a bill to abolish flogging in the Navy, then resigned on 10 January 1853 to head the Delaware and Raritan Canal Company. He attended the Peace Conference of 1861 and commanded the New Jersey militia in 1863. He died at Princeton on 7 October 1866. Stockton, California, four Navy ships and Stockton Creek in Monrovia bear his name.
robert-fitzhamon: Robert Fitzhamon, Seigneur de Creully and Torigny in Normandy, was probably born in the 1040s or 1050s, the son of Hamo Dapifer, Sheriff of Kent, and grandson of Hamon Dentatus. His grandfather held Torigny, Creully, Mézy and Évrecy, but after his death at the Battle of Val-ès-Dunes in 1047 the family may have lost these lordships. Robert is said to have been a kinsman of William the Conqueror, though how is unknown. He probably did not fight at the Battle of Hastings and does not appear in the Domesday Book of 1086.

Robert first appears as a supporter of King William Rufus in the Rebellion of 1088. As a reward he received the feudal barony of Gloucester, more than two hundred manors that had belonged to Queen Matilda. He refounded Tewkesbury Abbey, apparently under the influence of his wife Sybil de Montgomery, a daughter of Roger of Montgomery, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury. A 16th-century legend, the Twelve Knights of Glamorgan, tells that Iestyn called in his help against Rhys ap Tewdwr and was then dispossessed. Whatever its truth, Robert took the lowlands of Glamorgan and Gwynllwg, holding Cardiff Castle on the site of a Roman fort and new castles at Newport and Kenfig.

He stayed loyal to Henry I in his conflicts with his brother Robert Curthose and was one of three barons who negotiated their truce of 1101. Legend says he wept over the body of William Rufus and covered it with his cloak.

In 1105 Robert was captured fighting near his family's estates by Bayeux, one reason Henry I crossed to Normandy with a large force that year. Freed, he joined the siege of Falaise, where he suffered a severe head wound; he lived two more years but was never the same in mind. He was buried in the chapter house at Tewkesbury. His eldest daughter Mabel inherited his estates and married Robert de Caen, a natural son of Henry I, who was made 1st Earl of Gloucester in 1122.
robert-guiscard: Robert was the sixth of the twelve sons of Tancred of Hauteville and his second wife Fressenda, and was born in Normandy. From 999 to 1042 Normans had been migrating to Italy, mostly as mercenaries serving Byzantines and Lombard nobles. His elder brothers William Iron Arm and Drogo arrived in 1038 and joined a Lombard revolt against Byzantine rule in Apulia. Robert came in 1047; the Byzantine historian Anna Komnene, who disliked him, says that he left Normandy with five mounted riders and thirty men on foot and became chief of a roving band of robbers.

His sobriquet Guiscard, in contemporary Latin Viscardus, is often rendered as the Resourceful, the Cunning or the Fox. In Calabria he married Alberada of Buonalbergo in 1051. In 1053 he fought in the Battle of Civitate, where the Normans under Humphrey defeated the coalition raised by Pope Leo IX.

When Humphrey died in 1057 Robert succeeded him as count, passing over his elder half-brother Geoffrey. His marriage to Alberada was annulled for consanguinity, probably in 1058, and he married Sikelgaita. By the Treaty of Melfi in 1059 he swore fealty to Pope Nicholas II, who invested him as Duke of Apulia and Calabria and future Lord of Sicily, at a time when the papacy wanted Norman allies against the Holy Roman Emperor.

In Sicily he and his brother Roger took Messina by surprise in 1061. The County of Sicily was created for Roger in 1071, and Palermo fell a year later. Meanwhile Robert besieged Bari by land and water for four years until it surrendered in 1071. He took Salerno in December 1076 and the principality of Benevento in 1078, which he returned to the papacy in 1081. In 1081 he crossed to the Balkans and defeated Alexios I Komnenos at the Battle of Dyrrachium in October. In May 1084 he entered Rome to relieve Pope Gregory VII, besieged by Emperor Henry IV.

Robert died of a fever on 17 July 1085 at Atheras on Cephalonia and was buried in the Hauteville family mausoleum, the Abbey of Santissima Trinità at Venosa. His eldest son Bohemond, made illegitimate when the first marriage was annulled, received land around Taranto and later became a leader of the First Crusade and first prince of Antioch. The dukedom passed to Roger Borsa, his eldest son by Sikelgaita.

His conquests of Calabria and Sicily brought Latin Christianity to regions that had followed the Byzantine rite, and the descendants of his brother Roger I later created the Kingdom of Sicily. Dante places his spirit in the Heaven of Mars.
robert-henryson: Almost nothing is known of Henryson outside his surviving writing, and there is no record of when or where he was born or educated. On 10 September 1462 a man of his name with licence to teach took a post at the recently founded University of Glasgow; if this was the poet, as is usually assumed, he had completed studies in both arts and canon law. In 1478 his name appears as a witness on charters of Dunfermline Abbey, which would make him a notary for the abbey.

Early references almost all link him with Dunfermline, and the name schoolmaster is usually taken to mean that he ran the grammar school of the abbey's burgh; a confirmatio of 1468 provided for a house there for a priest, as master of grammar, and scholars, including poor scholars taught free. The court often visited Dunfermline, so he probably knew the royal household. He was active under James III and James IV, both keen on literature.

His surviving work, almost 5000 lines in Middle Scots, consists of three long poems and about twelve shorter ones.
