The Morall Fabillis, a cycle of thirteen fables running just short of 3000 lines, joins seven Aesopian fables from the elegiac Romulus texts with six Reynardian ones, and internal evidence suggests it was composed in the 1480s. The Tale of Orpheus and Erudices his Quene and The Testament of Cresseid each run to a little over 600 lines; the Orpheus may be early, from his time in Glasgow, since one of its main sources was in the university library.

The shorter works include the pastourelle Robene and Makyne, a comic flyting on the medicine of his day, a poem of Marian devotion, allegories, philosophical meditations and a prayer against the pest. He usually writes in a familiar first-person voice, in a concise Scots that shows he knew Latin, with closely observed Scottish settings.

According to William Dunbar, Henryson died in Dunfermline: Dunbar's Lament for the Makaris, usually dated to about 1505, says that death had whispered there with Maister Robert Henrysoun. The year of his death is unknown, though about 1498-9, a time of plague in the burgh, has been suggested. In 2010 Faber and Faber published Seamus Heaney's adaptation of the fables, which were made into short animated films with Billy Connolly and broadcast on the BBC in 2014.
robert-i-count-of-flanders: Robert was the older son of Baldwin V of Flanders and his first wife, whose name the sources do not give. His younger brother Baldwin VI succeeded their father as count in 1067, and his sister Matilda married William the Conqueror, duke of Normandy and later king of England, in 1051/2. In 1063 Robert married Gertrude of Saxony, dowager countess of West Frisia. He gained his nickname, apparently, by acting as regent for his stepson Count Dirk V of West Frisia. Robert twice swore to renounce his claims to Flanders and received a large payment.

When Baldwin VI died in 1070, he left Flanders and Hainaut to his elder son Arnulf III, with Richilde, Arnulf's mother, as regent. Robert disputed the succession despite his oaths and recruited support in Maritime Flanders and Ghent. Richilde appealed to King Philip I of France, who brought an army to Flanders with the counts of Boulogne, Saint-Pol and Ardres. At the Battle of Cassel on 22 February 1071 Philip fled and Robert and Richilde were both captured, but Robert won. Arnulf III was among the dead. Robert claimed Flanders, and Richilde's son Baldwin became count of Hainaut. After more fighting Robert was the unchallenged ruler.

He made peace with Philip, who married his stepdaughter Bertha of West Frisia, and relations stayed friendly until Philip repudiated her in 1092. Flanders became a refuge for enemies of William the Conqueror, including Edgar Ætheling in 1075. In 1080 Robert married his daughter Adela to Canute IV of Denmark, and in 1085 the two planned a large naval attack on England, which ended with Canute's assassination. Around 1077 Robert was excommunicated for failing to act against Bishop Drogo of Thérouanne, an act probably lifted after September 1079.
In 1086 Robert made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem with a large escort and on the way home helped the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos against the Seljuq Turks. He died on 13 October 1093.
robert-ii-count-of-artois: Robert was born in September 1250, the posthumous son and heir of Robert I and Matilda of Brabant. He was a nephew of two kings, Louis IX of France and Charles I of Sicily, and became a close confidant of the Capetian royal family, a capable military commander and an administrator. In 1262, in Paris, he married Amicie de Courtenay, daughter of Pierre de Courtenay. Their children were Mahaut, born in 1268, Philip, who lived from 1269 to 1298, and a second Robert who died young. After Amicie's death he married Agnes of Dampierre in 1277 and, on 18 October 1298, Margaret, daughter of John II, Count of Hainaut.

Robert served his cousin Philip III of France and then Philip's son Philip IV. Philip III sent him with an army to Iberia to suppress a rebellion in Navarre. At the request of his uncle Charles I of Anjou he led Angevin troops against Ghibelline and Genoese forces in Piedmont, and Charles named him Vicar in Provence, but he was defeated and forced to withdraw.

In 1285 he became regent of the Angevin Kingdom of Naples during the War of the Sicilian Vespers against Aragon, when Charles II was an Aragonese prisoner. He rebuilt the treasury and worked on the kingdom's navy. That year he also took part in the French-led Aragonese Crusade, which ended in defeat, and in 1287 he attempted an invasion of Sicily. The release of Charles II that year ended his regency. In 1288 he began a great park at Hesdin Castle, with a menagerie, aviaries, fishponds, orchards, an enclosed garden, facilities for tournaments and mechanical statues, among them waving monkeys draped in skins.

In 1297 Robert commanded the French army that ambushed and defeated a larger English relief force at Bonnegarde in the Gascon War, and a few months later he defeated the Flemings at Furnes. In July 1302 he returned to Flanders, ravaged the countryside and tried to take Courtrai.

At the Battle of the Golden Spurs his infantry advanced successfully, but he recalled it so that his cavalry could make the final charge. On the broken, marshy ground the knights could not gain enough momentum to break the Flemish shieldwall and were knocked down. Robert led some of the reserves in a second charge, was unhorsed by Willem van Saeftinghe and was cut down on 11 July 1302. His daughter Mahaut inherited Artois, and his grandson Robert III tried unsuccessfully to claim it.
robert-ii-of-france: Robert II was the only son of Hugh Capet and Adelaide of Aquitaine, and was named after his ancestor Robert the Strong, who died fighting the Vikings in 866. His exact birth date and birthplace are unknown, though historians favour the year 972 and the city of Orléans. He was educated at Reims by Gerbert of Aurillac, the future Pope Sylvester II, and as junior king he presided over episcopal synods, including the Council of Saint-Basle de Verzy in 991.

Sole ruler from 996, Robert kept the alliance with Normandy and Anjou and so contained the ambitions of Count Odo II of Blois. His first marriage, to Rozala of Italy, ended in repudiation after three or four years, as she was about 22 years his elder and had borne him no child. A second marriage, to Bertha, daughter of King Conrad I of Burgundy, was also childless. He then married Constance of Arles, who bore seven children.

When Duke Henry I of Burgundy died on 15 October 1002 without a legitimate heir, Robert claimed the duchy as his nearest male kinsman. Henry's stepson Otto-William of Ivrea resisted, but the war ended in Robert's favour in 1005. Around 1007 Robert accused the Jews of complicity with the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, who had persecuted Christians, and chroniclers report spoliations, massacres and forced conversions; Pope John XVIII and his successor Sergius IV demanded an end to them.

Helgaud of Fleury, in his Life of King Robert the Pious, presents Robert as a model of charity and generous giving to religious houses; he was the first sovereign regarded as a miracle worker. After the early death of his eldest son Hugh in 1025, Constance opposed the crowning of Henry and favoured her son Robert, but the king imposed his will and Henry was consecrated junior king at Reims on 14 May 1027. Henry and his brother Robert later revolted against their father. Robert II died on 20 July 1031, after a reign of 35 years, and Henry I succeeded him.
robert-iii-of-artois: Robert was the son of Philip of Artois, lord of Conches-en-Ouche, and Blanche, daughter of Duke John II of Brittany. His father died on 11 September 1298 of wounds received fighting the Flemish at the Battle of Furnes on 20 August 1297. When his grandfather, Count Robert II of Artois, was killed at the Battle of Courtrai in 1302, the county passed by custom to Robert's aunt Mahaut, who stood closer to the dead count. Robert was then too young to contest the succession.

Robert played an important part in the accession of his brother-in-law Philip VI of France and was for a time his trusted adviser. Through this influence he was granted the County of Beaumont-le-Roger in compensation for Artois. When Mahaut died in 1329 and Artois passed to her daughter, Countess Joan II of Burgundy, Robert reopened the question of the succession, following the example of the county of Flanders.

In 1331 he was found guilty of forgery: his claim rested on thirty-four perjured depositions and a fake document made by Jeanne de Divion, who was burned at the stake. Robert ignored a fourth summons to appear before the king and on 8 April 1332 was sentenced in absentia to exile and the confiscation of his estates. He fled to his nephew, Marquis John II of Namur, and, when Philip asked the Bishop of Liège to attack Namur, to his nephew-in-law Duke John III of Brabant. Philip compelled the duke to abandon Robert, who crossed the Channel to the court of Edward III of England.

In England Robert sat on Edward's royal council and gave the king detailed information about the French court. Later legends held that he urged Edward to claim the French crown, and many contemporary chroniclers traced the Hundred Years' War to his influence: Philip VI named Edward's refusal to expel him as the reason for confiscating the Duchy of Guyenne in May 1337. Robert was briefly Earl of Richmond in 1341 and commanded the Anglo-Flemish army at the Battle of Saint-Omer in 1340.

Wounded during the retreat from Vannes in the War of the Breton Succession, he died of dysentery in November 1342. He was buried in Blackfriars Church in London; his tomb is now in St Paul's Cathedral. In the late 1340s the poem Voeux du héron (Vow of the Heron) presented Edward's invasion of France as the fulfilment of an oath sworn to Robert, and he is a leading character in Maurice Druon's novels Les Rois maudits.
robert-king-of-naples: Robert of Anjou was born around 1276, the third son of the future Charles II of Naples and Mary of Hungary. His grandfather Charles of Anjou had established the Angevin realm in 1266. The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 and the war that followed shaped his youth: his father was captured in 1284, and Robert was sent to the Aragonese court as a hostage. He became heir after his elder brother Louis, later Saint Louis of Toulouse, renounced his inheritance to take holy orders. In 1298 he led an Angevin invasion of Sicily, which stalled, and the Peace of Caltabellotta of 1302 left the Angevins without Sicily for good.

Robert succeeded Charles II in 1309, and Pope Clement V made him papal vicar in Romagna and Tuscany. As leader of the Guelph party he opposed Emperor Henry VII's stay in Italy from 1311 to 1313. In 1313 the pope named him Senator of Rome, and from 1314 he held the title of imperial vicar of all Italy during the empire's vacancy. He was lord of Genoa from 1318. In 1328 he fought Louis IV of Bavaria, and in 1330 he forced John of Bohemia to leave northern Italy. The House of Barcelona, which held Sicily and Aragon, limited his hegemony.

With his second wife, Sancha of Majorca, he made Naples a centre of early Renaissance culture. Giotto painted works for him, and Dante dismissed him as a king of words. Robert himself preached hundreds of sermons at universities and religious houses, an oratory usually reserved for clerics.

Robert died on 20 January 1343. His son Charles of Calabria had died in 1328, so Robert left the throne to his 16-year-old granddaughter Joanna I and excluded the claims of her betrothed, Andrew of Hungary. The story that Andrew was meant to be crowned comes largely from Hungarian royal propaganda after Andrew's murder in 1345. That propaganda and the invasion of Louis I of Hungary led to the end of Angevin rule in Naples. Petrarch asked to be examined by Robert before his coronation as poet in Rome in 1341. Robert was nicknamed the peace-maker of Italy.
robert-ley: Robert Ley was born in Niederbreidenbach in the Rhine Province, the seventh of eleven children of a farmer. He studied chemistry at Jena, Bonn and Münster. He volunteered for the army in 1914, served in artillery on both the eastern and western fronts, and in July 1917 was taken prisoner when his aircraft was shot down over France. It has been suggested that he suffered a traumatic brain injury in the crash; for the rest of his life he spoke with a stammer and had bouts of erratic behaviour, worsened by heavy drinking.

Released in January 1920, he took a doctorate and worked as a food chemist for a branch of IG Farben. Enraged by the French occupation of the Ruhr, he became an ultra-nationalist and joined the Nazi Party soon after reading Adolf Hitler's speech at his trial after the Beer Hall Putsch. He rejoined the re-founded party in March 1925 and became Gauleiter of the Southern Rhineland that July.

Ley edited a virulently anti-Semitic newspaper, the Westdeutscher Beobachter, from 1928 and sat in the Reichstag from September 1930 until May 1945. Although sympathetic to the working-class wing around Gregor Strasser, he always sided with Hitler in party disputes. When Strasser resigned in December 1932, Hitler took over party organisation and made Ley his chief of staff.

On 10 May 1933, after the suppression of the trade unions, Hitler appointed him head of the new German Labour Front, which became an arm of the state for deploying and disciplining labour, particularly for rearmament. In November 1933 it founded Strength Through Joy, which offered subsidised holidays, cruises, concerts and sport and was among the regime's most popular programmes. The Front also took over the Volkswagen project; the first models appeared in February 1939, but none of the 340,000 workers who paid for a car received one. Ley became notorious for drunkenness and for embezzling the Front's funds.
After the outbreak of war in 1939 his influence declined, as Fritz Todt and later Albert Speer took over direction of the workforce, but he stayed in Hitler's inner circle.

American paratroopers captured Ley on 16 May 1945 in the village of Schleching, where he had given a false name. He was indicted at the Nuremberg trials for conspiracy, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Three days after receiving the indictment, in October 1945, he killed himself in his cell, one of two of the 22 leaders at Nuremberg to do so, the other being Hermann Göring. The psychiatrist Douglas Kelley believed his behaviour came from organic brain damage.
robert-louis-stevenson: Stevenson was born at 8 Howard Place, Edinburgh, on 13 November 1850 and christened Robert Lewis Balfour Stevenson. His father, Thomas Stevenson, was a leading lighthouse engineer, and lighthouse design was the family's profession. About the age of 18 he changed the spelling of Lewis to Louis. Serious bronchial trouble kept him from school for long periods. In November 1867 he entered the University of Edinburgh to study engineering but showed no enthusiasm, and in April 1871 he told his father he would pursue a life of letters. It was agreed that he should read law instead.

In late 1873 he met Sidney Colvin, who became his literary adviser. In 1876 he met Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne, an American and a magazine short-story writer, at Grez-sur-Loing. In 1884 the couple settled in Bournemouth. He is best known for Treasure Island (1883), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Kidnapped (1886) and A Child's Garden of Verses (1885). W. E. Henley may have provided the model for Long John Silver.

In June 1888 he chartered the yacht Casco and sailed with his family from San Francisco. For nearly three years he wandered the eastern and central Pacific, staying in the Hawaiian Islands, where he befriended King Kalākaua, and visiting the Gilbert Islands, where he spent months on Abemama with the chief Tem Binoka, whom he described in In the South Seas. In December 1889 the family arrived at Apia in Samoa and decided to settle, buying land at Vailima in January 1890. Alarmed at growing European and American influence in the islands, he turned from romance toward realism, notably in The Beach of Falesá.

On 3 December 1894, at Vailima, Stevenson collapsed while talking to his wife and died within a few hours at the age of 44, possibly of a brain haemorrhage. He was a celebrity in his lifetime, admired by writers including Henry James and Rudyard Kipling, and half his original manuscripts, among them that of Treasure Island, are lost.
robert-menzies: Robert Gordon Menzies was born on 20 December 1894 at his parents' home in Jeparit, Victoria, the fourth of five children. He was the first Australian prime minister with two Australian-born parents. At 13 he came first in the state-wide scholarship examinations, which paid for his secondary education. He studied law at the University of Melbourne, was admitted to the Victorian Bar in 1918, specialised in constitutional law, and became a King's Counsel in 1929.

He entered the Victorian Legislative Council in 1928 for the Nationalist Party and was Deputy Premier of Victoria from 1932 to 1934. In 1934 he moved to federal politics as member for Kooyong and became Attorney-General in the government of Joseph Lyons.

After Lyons died on 7 April 1939, Menzies was elected leader of the United Australia Party and was sworn in as prime minister eight days after his election on 18 April. On 3 September 1939 he announced that Australia was at war alongside Britain. With his position in his party weakening, he resigned on 27 August 1941. In opposition he spoke on radio to those he called the Forgotten People, and in October 1944 he called a conference in Canberra at which fourteen anti-Labor parties agreed to merge as the Liberal Party of Australia.

He returned as prime minister on 19 December 1949 and won seven consecutive elections. His government signed the ANZUS treaty on 1 September 1951, sent troops to the Korean War, maintained the post-war immigration scheme, introduced Commonwealth scholarships in 1951 and established the National Capital Development Commission in 1957. A 1950 bill to ban the Communist Party was ruled unconstitutional, and a 1951 referendum on the question was narrowly defeated. He retired in January 1966.

Menzies suffered strokes in 1971 and 1972 and used a wheelchair outside his home. He died of a heart attack at his home in Malvern, Melbourne, on 15 May 1978. His combined term of 18 years and 163 days is the longest in Australian history, and his second period is the longest unbroken tenure in the office. He lost the two-party-preferred vote at three elections, in 1940, 1954 and 1961, while retaining government each time.
robert-mugabe: Robert Gabriel Mugabe was born on 21 February 1924 at the Kutama Mission village in Southern Rhodesia. His father was a carpenter and his mother a Christian catechist for the village children, and the family belonged to the Zezuru clan, one of the smallest branches of the Shona people. He worked as a schoolteacher, and in 1949 won a scholarship to the University of Fort Hare in South Africa. There he joined the youth league of the African National Congress and met Jewish South African communists who introduced him to Marxist ideas, though he later said his biggest influence was Mahatma Gandhi. He left in 1952 with a degree in history and English literature.

Mugabe returned to Southern Rhodesia in May 1960. He was arrested in December 1963 and sentenced in March 1964 for subversive statements. He remained in prison for eight years in Salisbury, studying and gaining several degrees from the University of London. In March 1975 he left for Mozambique, where President Samora Machel at first doubted his leadership and kept him under partial house arrest for almost a year before accepting him as head of ZANU. After the Lancaster House Agreement he returned to Salisbury in January 1980 and campaigned without Marxist or revolutionary rhetoric, as Machel had advised. ZANU-PF won the election.

Zimbabwe gained internationally recognised independence on 18 April 1980, and Mugabe took the oath as prime minister. He pledged racial reconciliation and invited members of rival parties into his cabinet. Relations with Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU deteriorated, and in the Gukurahundi of 1982 to 1987 the 5th Brigade crushed ZAPU-linked opposition in Matabeleland in a campaign that killed at least 20,000 people. On 30 December 1987 parliament made him executive president, with power to dissolve parliament and run for an unlimited number of terms.

From 2000 he encouraged black Zimbabweans to seize white-owned farms, and food production fell, followed by famine and hyperinflation. On 6 November 2017 he dismissed Vice-President Emmerson Mnangagwa, and on 15 November the army placed him under house arrest. He resigned, and Mnangagwa succeeded him. Mugabe died in Singapore on 6 September 2019.
robert-muldoon: Robert David Muldoon was born in Auckland on 25 September 1921. When he was eight his father was admitted to Auckland Mental Hospital, and he was raised by his mother under the strong influence of his maternal grandmother Jerusha, a committed socialist whose creed he never accepted but who left him with an interest in politics and a respect for the welfare state. He left Mount Albert Grammar School at 15 and studied accountancy by correspondence. In the Second World War he served in the South Pacific and in Italy, where he sat his final accountancy examinations.

After two unsuccessful bids, he won the Auckland seat of Tamaki for the National Party in 1960 and held it for 32 years. As under-secretary to the finance minister Harry Lake he oversaw the introduction of decimal currency in July 1967. On Lake's death in February 1967 Keith Holyoake made him Minister of Finance, at 45 the youngest since the 1890s; he met a slump in wool prices with mini-budgets, spending cuts and higher indirect taxes. He became deputy prime minister in 1972 and, after National's defeat that year, was elected unopposed as Leader of the Opposition on 9 July 1974, drawing loyal crowds known as Rob's Mob.

Sworn in on 12 December 1975, he named himself Minister of Finance and promised a government of the ordinary bloke. A recession from June 1976 to March 1978 shrank the economy by 4.1%, and his years in power saw stagnation, high inflation, rising unemployment and heavy borrowing. His government introduced national superannuation and industrial incentives, revived and intensified the Dawn Raids against Pasifika overstayers, and kept close to the United States and Australia under ANZUS. His refusal to stop the Springbok rugby tour of 1981 brought civil disorder on a scale the country had not seen.

National won again in 1978 and 1981 while losing the popular vote. In 1982 Derek Quigley resigned from the Cabinet after criticising Think Big, and the businessman Bob Jones founded the New Zealand Party in 1983. Muldoon lost the snap election of 1984 and was then replaced as leader by his deputy Jim McLay. Heavy legal costs led him to appear in The Rocky Horror Show. He stayed in parliament until 1992 and died on 5 August that year; Black Power performed a haka at his funeral.
robert-of-belleme: Robert was the eldest surviving son of Roger of Montgomery, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, and Mabel de Bellême, through whom he was heir to the lordship of Bellême. William the Conqueror knighted him at the siege of Fresnay castle in 1073, and in 1077 he joined the revolt of the young Robert Curthose against Duke William. On his mother's killing around 1079 he inherited her vast estates, and on hearing of the Conqueror's death in 1087 he expelled the ducal garrisons from his castles.

He took part in the Rebellion of 1088 against William II and was among the rebels at Rochester Castle who won a guarantee of life and limb. Returning to Normandy with Count Henry, the future Henry I, he was seized at Bishop Odo of Bayeux's prompting and imprisoned, until his father's pressure on Duke Robert freed him. By 1090 Orderic Vitalis calls him a principal councillor of the duke. On his father's death in 1094 he received the Norman lands, and in 1098, on his brother Hugh's death and a payment of £3,000, the English lands and the earldom; with Ponthieu, held through his wife Agnes, and the honour of Tickhill, this made him the wealthiest magnate in England and Normandy.

In 1098 he captured Elias I, Count of Maine, for William II. He joined Curthose's invasion of England in 1101, and after Henry I's charges in 1102 lost his English lands and titles. He commanded the rear at the Battle of Tinchebrai in 1106 and fled, then submitted. Sent in 1112 as the French king's envoy to Henry's court at Bonneville, he was seized despite his status, and the rebellion of 1110–12 collapsed.

The date of his death in prison is not known. Orderic called him grasping, cruel and unequalled for iniquity in the whole Christian era, but historians note the chronicler's abbey of Saint-Evroul was patronised by the Giroie family, long feuding with the Bellêmes, and that Robert's dealings with the Church were typical of his peers. Stories of his brutality may have inspired the legend of Robert the Devil.
robert-of-molesme: Robert was born near Troyes, a younger son of Thierry and Ermengarde, nobles of Champagne. At fifteen he entered the Benedictine abbey of Montier-la-Celle near Troyes and rose to be its prior. Around 1070 he became abbot of Saint Michel-de-Tonnerre, but found the monks quarrelsome and disobedient and returned to Montier-la-Celle.

Two hermits from a group of monks settled at Collan went to Rome and asked Pope Gregory VII to appoint Robert as their superior. The pope agreed, and by 1074 Robert led them. He soon moved the community to Molesme, in the valley of Langres in Burgundy, where at first there were only huts of branches around a chapel dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The abbey became known for its piety, and in 1082 Bruno of Cologne came to Robert for advice before founding the Grande Chartreuse, the first Carthusian monastery.

By 1098 Molesme had 35 dependent priories, other annexes and some houses of nuns. Donors competed to help the monks, who soon had more than they needed and became lax. Benefactors sent their children to be educated there, and the large landholdings required many employees. Men who sought entry for the wrong reasons divided the community and challenged Robert's severity. He twice tried to leave and was ordered back by the pope. In 1098 he left with twenty-one monks, and Renaud, Viscount of Beaune, gave them a desolate forest valley where they founded Cîteaux Abbey. Stephen Harding and Albéric were pivotal in founding it, and Odo I, Duke of Burgundy, paid for the building and gave land and cattle.

In 1099 the monks of Molesme asked Robert to return and promised to follow his reading of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the local bishop pressed him too. He agreed, and Molesme became a major centre of Benedictine life under him. Albéric succeeded him at Cîteaux, with Stephen Harding as prior. Robert died on 17 April 1111 and was canonised by Pope Honorius III in 1222. His feast day is 17 April, and Benedictines keep it with Albéric and Stephen Harding on 26 February. His life was written by Guy, his successor as abbot of Molesme.
robert-owen: Robert Owen was born on 14 May 1771 in Newtown, Montgomeryshire, Wales, the sixth of seven children of a saddler, ironmonger and local postmaster. He received little formal schooling but read avidly. He left school at ten to work four years as an apprentice draper in Stamford, then worked in London drapery shops before moving at about eighteen to Manchester, where he spent twelve years.

In Manchester he borrowed £100 from his brother William to go into spinning mules, then newly invented for cotton thread. In 1792 the mill-owner Peter Drinkwater made him manager of the Piccadilly Mill, and he later helped found and manage the Chorlton Twist Mills. In 1793 he became a member of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society. He married Ann Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, the proprietor of the New Lanark Mills, on 30 September 1799.

At New Lanark Owen tested his ideas on conditions for workers and their children. Visitors including the future Tsar Nicholas I of Russia came to study the mills. He devised a silent monitor, a block hung over each worker's place whose four colours showed the quality of their work, as an alternative to corporal punishment. In 1813 his partners, among them Jeremy Bentham and William Allen, bought out his share, and in the same year he published A New View of Society. He supported the Cotton Mills and Factories Act 1819.

Owen held that character is formed by conditions beyond the individual's control, so that people should be placed under proper influences from the earliest years. In 1824 he sailed to the United States with his son William and in January 1825 bought the town of Harmony on the Wabash River in Indiana from George Rapp's Harmony Society, renaming it New Harmony. At least 16 of about 130 communitarian experiments in the United States before the Civil War were Owenite or Owenite-influenced.

Back in London from 1828, Owen opened the National Equitable Labour Exchange in 1832, a system of labour notes that lasted in London until 1833. He formed the Association of all Classes of all Nations in 1835, in discussions of which socialism first became current in British usage. By 1846 the only lasting result of his agitation remained the Co-operative movement.

In 1817 Owen publicly declared all religions false; in 1854, aged 83, he turned to spiritualism after sittings with the American medium Maria B. Hayden. He died on 17 November 1858. His tomb stands in St Mary's Churchyard in Newtown, with railings added by the co-operative movement in 1902. Critics held his plans unachievable because he set no rules for property and membership, and opponents called him a dictator and a blasphemer.
robert-peel: Robert Peel was born on 5 February 1788 at Chamber Hall in Bury, Lancashire, the son of Sir Robert Peel, 1st Baronet, one of the richest textile manufacturers of the early Industrial Revolution, and of Ellen Yates. He took a double first in classics and mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford, and entered Parliament in 1809, aged 21, for the Irish rotten borough of Cashel, where he was elected unopposed by 24 electors. His sponsor was Sir Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington. His maiden speech in 1810 was described by the Speaker, Charles Abbot, as the best first speech since that of William Pitt the Younger.

Peel became Under-Secretary of State for War and the Colonies in 1810 and Chief Secretary for Ireland in 1812. His Peace Preservation Act 1814 allowed paid special constables to be appointed in disturbed counties, later called peelers, and laid the basis for the Royal Irish Constabulary. He entered the cabinet as Home Secretary in 1822. He cut the number of crimes punishable by death, consolidated criminal statutes into what are called Peel's Acts, and in the Gaols Act 1823 introduced pay for gaolers and education for inmates.

In 1829 he established the Metropolitan Police for London at Scotland Yard, with about 1,000 constables nicknamed bobbies or peelers. Unpopular at first, they cut crime, and by 1857 every British city had to form its own force. The nine Peelian Principles often credited to him were written by Charles Reith in 1948 as a summary of the force's 1829 Instructions. Peel, once a supporter of legal discrimination against Catholics, backed the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829, judging civil strife a greater danger than emancipation.

William IV invited Peel to form a government in December 1834, when he was in Italy, so Wellington acted as caretaker for three weeks. His minority ministry issued the Tamworth Manifesto, pledging modest reform, and was defeated in the Commons on 7 April 1835 by 285 votes to 258 over Church of Ireland revenues. It resigned having established the Ecclesiastical Commission.

He won a majority in the election of July 1841, in a recession with a budget deficit of £7.5 million. His second ministry passed the Mines and Collieries Act 1842, the Income Tax Act 1842, the Factories Act 1844 and the Railway Regulation Act 1844. Historians note that he was an intellectual convert to free trade from the 1820s. The Corn Laws were repealed on 29 June 1846 and he resigned. Leading the Peelites, he stayed influential until his death on 2 July 1850, and was said by some critics to be a traitor to Toryism and by others, like Thomas Carlyle, a reforming Hercules.
robert-schuman: Schuman was born on 29 June 1886 in Clausen, Luxembourg, and inherited his father's German citizenship. His father, a native of Lorraine, had become a German citizen when Germany annexed Lorraine in 1871 and had settled in Luxembourg. Schuman's mother was a Luxembourger, and he grew up in Luxembourg City speaking Luxembourgish. From 1904 to 1910 he studied law, economics, political philosophy, theology and statistics at universities in Berlin, Bonn and Strasbourg, and took a law degree at Strasbourg with the highest distinction. In 1912 he set up as a lawyer in Metz. After Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, he became a French citizen in 1918.

Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1919, Schuman sat for Thionville until 1958, with an interval during the war. He contributed to the reintroduction of the French Civil and Commercial Codes in Alsace-Lorraine, a harmonisation known as the Lex Schuman, and exposed corruption in the Lorraine steel industries and in the region's railways. In 1940 he joined Paul Reynaud's wartime government in charge of refugees and kept the post under Pétain. On 10 July 1940 he voted to give Pétain full powers, though he refused to stay in the government.

Arrested in Metz on 14 September 1940, he was placed under house arrest and escaped to the unoccupied zone in August 1942. After the liberation he was declared ineligible for public office because of his vote of 1940, and regained his civic rights on 15 September 1945 after Charles de Gaulle answered his appeal favourably.

Schuman was Minister of Finance in 1946 and Prime Minister from 1947 to 1948, then Foreign Minister from 1948 until early 1953. His first government proposed a European Assembly, which became the Council of Europe, whose statutes were signed in London on 5 May 1949. He also signed the North Atlantic Treaty for France. On 9 May 1950 came the Schuman Declaration, prepared by Paul Reuter, Bernard Clappier, Jean Monnet and others, inviting West Germany and other countries to manage their coal and steel industries jointly. Six founder members signed the Treaty of Paris on 18 April 1951, creating the European Coal and Steel Community, and 9 May is observed as Europe Day.

He later served as Minister of Justice and became the first President of the European Parliamentary Assembly, which gave him the title Father of Europe. In 1958 he received the Karlspreis of Aachen. He was a devout Catholic, and in 2021 Pope Francis declared him venerable. He died on 4 September 1963.
robert-schumann: Robert Schumann was born on 8 June 1810 in Zwickau, in the Kingdom of Saxony, the fifth and last child of August Schumann and his wife Johanna Christiane. His father was a bookseller, lexicographer, author and publisher who made considerable sums from German translations of Cervantes, Walter Scott and Lord Byron, and Robert, his favourite child, spent many hours exploring the classics in his father's collection. August died in 1826, and Schumann's mother, less enthusiastic about a musical career, persuaded him to study law. He entered Leipzig University in 1828, but reading and playing the piano occupied much of his time. He discovered the works of Franz Schubert, whose death in November 1828 made him cry all night.

Schumann published his Op. 1, piano variations on a theme spelled from the name of Countess Pauline von Abegg, who was almost certainly his own invention. The use of a musical cryptogram became a recurrent feature of his later music. In 1832 he published Papillons, a programmatic piano piece. He came to regard himself as having two sides to his personality and art, and named his introspective self Eusebius and his impetuous alter ego Florestan. In 1840 he turned to song, producing more than half his total output of Lieder, including Myrthen, a wedding present for Clara, Frauenliebe und Leben and Dichterliebe.

In 1841 he focused on orchestral music. His First Symphony, The Spring, was premiered by Mendelssohn at the Gewandhaus on 31 March, at a concert where Clara also played. In 1842 he wrote three string quartets, a Piano Quintet, written for Clara, and a Piano Quartet. His opera Genoveva, premiered in Leipzig in June 1850, was not the success he hoped for, and Franz Liszt revived it at Weimar in 1855, the only other production in Schumann's lifetime. Schumann wrote more than 300 songs for voice and piano, favouring such later Romantic poets as Heine, Eichendorff and Mörike.

Schumann moved to Düsseldorf in 1850 as the city's director of music but resigned after three years, since his shyness and mental instability made it hard to work with his orchestra. In 1853 he met the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms and praised him in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The following year his mental health deteriorated gravely. He threw himself into the Rhine, was rescued and was taken to a private sanatorium near Bonn, where he died on 29 July 1856.

His reputation rests chiefly on the piano works and songs of the 1830s and 1840s. Later composers drew on him, among them Mahler, Richard Strauss, Arnold Schoenberg, Bizet, Fauré, Debussy and Ravel. Elgar called him his ideal, and Tchaikovsky, though critical of his orchestration, described him as a composer of genius.
robert-sherley: Robert Shirley, as the name is also written, was the third son of Thomas Shirley of Wiston, West Sussex, and Anne Kempe, daughter of Thomas Kempe of Olantigh in Wye, Kent. His elder brothers were Thomas Shirley and Anthony Shirley, and six of his sisters survived infancy. In 1598 he went to Persia with Anthony, who had been sent to Safavid Iran to train its army in the manner of the English militia and to reform its artillery. When Anthony left, Robert stayed on with fourteen other Englishmen.

In February 1607 he married Sampsonia, a Circassian Orthodox Christian slave related to Abbas the Great; baptised a Catholic by the Carmelites, she took the name Teresa after Teresa of Ávila and became known in the west as Lady Shirley, Teresa Sampsonia. The modernisation of the Safavid army by Robert and his men is credited with the first decisive Safavid victory over the Ottomans, in the Ottoman–Safavid War (1603–1612), which ended on terms highly favourable to Persia.

In 1608 Abbas sent him to James VI and I and other European princes to unite them in an alliance against the Ottoman Empire. Sigismund III Vasa received him in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; in Germany Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor, made him a count palatine and a Knight of the Holy Roman Empire, and Pope Paul V also made him a count. He entered Rome with a suite of eighteen on 27 September 1609, then went by Milan and Genoa to Spain, reaching Barcelona in December 1609, and stayed there with his wife, mainly in Madrid, until the summer of 1611.

He returned to Persia in 1613 and to Madrid in 1615, when his caravan met the travel writer Thomas Coryate in the desert basins of central Persia. In 1627 he went to Persia a third time with Dodmore Cotton, the first English ambassador to the Safavids, and died of dysentery at Qazvin soon after arriving. Teresa, who retired to a Carmelite convent attached to Santa Maria della Scala in Rome, had his remains moved there in 1658 and died in 1668.

The brothers' exploits were dramatised in 1607 in The Travels of the Three English Brothers by John Day, William Rowley and George Wilkins, and Thomas Middleton translated a Latin panegyric of Robert as Sir Robert Sherley his Entertainment in Cracovia. Van Dyck painted a double portrait of him and his wife, now at Petworth House.
robert-sobukwe: Sobukwe was born in Graaff-Reinet in the Eastern Cape on 5 December 1924, the youngest of six children. His father, from Lesotho, was a general store clerk and part-time woodcutter, and his Xhosa mother worked as a domestic worker and as a cook at the local hospital. After a mission school he spent six years at the Healdtown Institute, a Methodist school, with financial help from George Caley, and then trained as a primary teacher. Tuberculosis interrupted his studies in 1943.

In 1947 he enrolled at the South African Native College at Fort Hare, majoring in English, Xhosa and Native Administration. Under the influence of his lecturer Cecil Ntloko, a follower of the All-African Convention, he turned to politics, joined the African National Congress Youth League in 1948 and in 1949 became the first president of the Fort Hare Students' Representative Council. He married Veronica Mathe in 1950.

In 1950 Sobukwe became a teacher at a high school in Standerton, a post he lost for speaking in favour of the Defiance Campaign in 1952, though he was later reinstated. In 1954 he moved to Johannesburg, where he lectured in African Studies and was nicknamed The Prof. As editor of The Africanist he criticised the ANC for letting itself be dominated by what he called liberal-left-multi-racialists, and as an anticommunist he rejected its alliance with the South African Communist Party. The PAC's inaugural congress met in Orlando from 4 to 6 April 1959 and elected him unanimously. In his speech he declared that there is only one race, the human race.

On 21 March 1960 he led a march to the police station at Orlando, Soweto, and presented himself for arrest under the pass laws. On the same day police at Sharpeville killed 69 PAC supporters. He served his sentence in Witbank Prison and Pretoria Gaol.

On Robben Island he was kept apart from other prisoners but allowed books, newspapers and civilian clothing, and he took a degree in economics from the University of London. In Kimberley he was refused permission to take up a teaching post at the University of Wisconsin, completed a law degree and opened a practice in 1975. He was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1977, died on 27 February 1978 and was buried in Graaff-Reinet. Streets in Pretoria and Cape Town and a block of the University of the Witwatersrand bear his name, and in January 2026 the renaming of Graaff-Reinet as Robert Sobukwe Town was approved.
robert-surcouf: Surcouf was born on 12 December 1773 in Saint-Malo to a family of ship-owners; his great-grandfather had captained a privateer under Louis XIV. Sent to college at Dinan to become a priest, he fled at thirteen to sea. In 1789 he joined the slave ship Aurore, which was wrecked in the Mozambique Channel, drowning 400 enslaved Africans chained below deck. He served on further slave ships and, as captain of the brig Créole, traded in slaves off Africa and Madagascar in 1794 although the National Convention had prohibited it.

In 1795 Governor Malartic refused him a letter of marque, yet on the schooner Émilie Surcouf seized British ships off the Ganges Delta and, with 26 men, boarded and took the East Indiaman Triton. Because Émilie was not a licensed privateer, the prize court sold his prizes for the state; in France the government granted him 660,000 francs, of which he received only 80,000. Commanding Clarisse from 1798 with a proper commission, he took British, American, Portuguese and Danish ships, among them Auspicious, with a cargo worth 1,032,580 francs.

On Confiance he boarded Kent, whose 437 people included rescued crew and passengers; after more than an hour and a half of fighting the British had fourteen killed, among them the captain, and the French five. The British Admiralty put a reward on his capture. He declined a navy commission and received the Legion of Honour on 19 May 1802. Sailing again in 1807 on Revenant, built to his own design, he took 16 British merchantmen before Governor Charles Decaen requisitioned the ship in 1808.

From 1809 Surcouf armed privateers from Saint-Malo; all those sent into the Channel were captured except Renard, which defeated HMS Alphea in 1812. After Waterloo he organised over 116 commercial expeditions, many to Newfoundland, and in 1815 and 1819 sent the Africain to carry enslaved Africans from Gabon. He died on 8 July 1827 and was buried in Saint-Malo with military honours. Five French Navy ships have borne his name, among them a submarine cruiser that was the largest submarine in the world at its launch. Legends that he was made a baron, or threw gold from Kent overboard, are untrue.
robert-the-bruce: Robert was born on 11 July 1274, most likely at Turnberry Castle in Ayrshire, the eldest of ten children of Robert de Brus, 6th Lord of Annandale, and Marjorie, Countess of Carrick. From his mother he inherited the Earldom of Carrick and from his father the Lordship of Annandale and a descent from David I that gave a claim to the Scottish throne. In 1298 he became a Guardian of Scotland, and he resigned in 1300 after quarrelling with his rival John Comyn.

Comyn was killed in Dumfries in February 1306, and Bruce was excommunicated by Pope Clement V, though Robert Wishart, Bishop of Glasgow, absolved him. Six weeks later, on Palm Sunday 25 March 1306, Bishop Lamberton inaugurated him as King of Scots at Scone, and the next day Isabella MacDuff, Countess of Buchan, crowned him a second time. After defeat at Methven he went into hiding and returned in 1307 to win at Loudoun Hill. Victories between 1310 and 1314 won him much of Scotland, and he took Berwick, the last English stronghold, in 1318.

After Bannockburn his armies raided Yorkshire and Lancashire. In 1315 he sent his brother Edward to Ireland to open a second front and secure a second crown, and Edward was crowned High King of Ireland in 1316. The Declaration of Arbroath of 1320 strengthened his position with the papacy, and Pope John XXII recognised him in 1324 and eventually lifted his excommunication. The Treaty of Corbeil renewed the Franco-Scottish alliance in 1326, and the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton in 1328 had Edward III renounce all claims to sovereignty over Scotland.

Robert died on 7 June 1329 at the Manor of Cardross, near Dumbarton, leaving his infant son David II in the care of Moray. His body was buried in Dunfermline Abbey beneath a box tomb of white Italian marble bought in Paris, his heart in Melrose Abbey, and his viscera in the chapel of Saint Serf. The tomb was destroyed at the Reformation, and ten alabaster fragments are in the National Museum of Scotland. He is regarded in Scotland as a national hero, and all later Scottish monarchs descend from him. A legend tells that while hiding after Methven he watched a spider fail twice and succeed on a third attempt to span a cave.
robert-the-strong: Robert's parentage is obscure. One proposal makes him a son of Robert III of Worms; others, based mainly on the recurrence of the name, point to the Hesbaye region of present-day eastern Belgium or to the family of Chrodegang of Metz, though these are unproven. According to the Worms proposal, the family emigrated from East Francia to West Francia in the time of Louis the German, and Charles the Bald rewarded them for leaving his enemy by giving Robert the lay abbacy of Marmoutier in 852.

In 853 Charles made him missus dominicus in Maine, Anjou and Touraine, giving him de facto control of the old ducatus Cenomannicus, centred on Le Mans. His rise came at the expense of the established family of the Rorigonids and was meant to curb their regional power and to defend Neustria against Viking and Breton raids.

In 858 Robert joined a rebellion against Charles. With the Bretons under Salomon he led the Neustrian nobles and invited Louis the German to invade West Francia. The revolt followed a marriage alliance between Charles and Erispoe, King of Brittany, and the investment of Charles's son Louis the Stammerer with the regnum Neustriae, which curtailed the powers of both Salomon and Robert. In 861 Charles made peace with Robert and appointed him Count of Anjou, and Robert then defended the northern coast against a Viking invasion.

In 862 two Viking fleets converged on Brittany, and Salomon hired one to ravage the Loire valley. Robert captured twelve of its ships and then hired the former Seine Vikings, for 6,000 pounds of silver, to attack Salomon's realm. Peace did not last: when Salomon made peace in 863 the Vikings, deprived of enemy lands to loot, ravaged Neustria. Charles made Robert lay abbot of Saint Martin at Tours. He also fought Pepin II of Aquitaine and defended Autun against Louis the German in 856 and 863.

On 2 July 866 Robert was killed at the Battle of Brissarthe, defending Francia against a joint Breton and Viking raiding party led by Salomon and the Viking chieftain Hastein. The Viking commander was trapped in a nearby church, and Robert took off his armour to besiege it. The Vikings launched a surprise attack and he died in the melee. The Annales Fuldenses called him a second Maccabaeus. He left a nine-year-old son, Odo, later king of West Francia (888–898); his younger son Robert I reigned in 922–923. His descendants are called the Robertians, and through his great-grandson Hugh Capet he is the ancestor of all the Capetians.
robert-walpole: Walpole was born at Houghton, Norfolk, in 1676, one of 19 children and the third son of Robert Walpole, a local gentleman and Whig member of Parliament. He entered Eton College in 1690 as a King's Scholar and matriculated at King's College, Cambridge, in 1696. He left Cambridge in 1698 after the death of his last older brother to help his father run the estate, and abandoned his plan to become a clergyman. His father died in November 1700 and he inherited the estate. In January 1701 he won a seat at Castle Rising, and from 1702 he sat for King's Lynn.

Walpole rose under Queen Anne and was Secretary at War from 1708. After the accession of George I in 1714 the Whigs held power for fifty years, and Walpole became Paymaster of the Forces. When the South Sea Bubble collapsed in 1720, he was recalled to the Cabinet. A committee found corruption among ministers, and Walpole shielded Lords Stanhope and Sunderland, which earned him the nickname the Screen. In 1721 he began his premiership.

When George II succeeded in 1727 it seemed for a few days that Walpole would be dismissed, but Queen Caroline advised the King to keep him. Charles Townshend retired on 15 May 1730, leaving Walpole the dominant partner. Lord Bolingbroke and William Pulteney attacked him in the periodical The Craftsman. Walpole tried to prevent war with Spain but was opposed by the King, the Commons and part of his Cabinet, and in 1739 the War of Jenkins' Ear began.

Walpole resigned in 1742 and became Earl of Orford. A committee inquired into his ministry but found no substantial evidence of wrongdoing. He kept influence with George II as the Minister behind the Curtain. He died on 18 March 1745.

Under Walpole the Tories became a minor faction and the Whigs a dominant party. He is regarded as Britain's first prime minister, though his power rested on the favour of the King and on personal influence rather than on the office, and several decades passed before the premiership became the country's most powerful post. His policy of peace contributed to prosperity and he secured the Hanoverian dynasty.
robert-william-wilcox: Wilcox was born on Maui on 15 February 1855, the son of Captain William Slocum Wilcox of Newport, Rhode Island, and Kalua, a Hawaiian of Maui, through whom he descended from the late-17th-century king Keaweʻīkekahialiʻiokamoku. After Haleakala Boarding School he taught at a country school and in 1880 was elected to the House of Representatives for Wailuku. In 1881 King David Kalākaua chose him for the Education of Hawaiian Youths Abroad programme at the Royal Military Academy at Turin, where he became a sublieutenant of artillery. He married Gina Sobrero, an Italian baroness.

The Reform Party ended his training, and he returned to Hawaii in October 1887. On 30 July 1889 he led a rising to force Kalākaua to sign a new constitution; confronted by the Honolulu Rifles, he surrendered after a pitched battle and was acquitted of treason in October 1889. He sat in the legislature from 1890 to 1893, formed the National Liberal Party in November 1891 and ran the newspaper The Liberal. When the Committee of Safety seized the palace on 17 January 1893, Queen Liliʻuokalani gave him command of the Royal Guard's field pieces, but she surrendered before any shots were fired.

In January 1895 royalists asked him to lead their counter-revolution. The forces met at Diamond Head, Mōʻiliʻili and Mānoa, and the royalists were quickly routed. Convicted on 23 February 1895, he had his sentence reduced to 35 years and was pardoned by Sanford B. Dole on 1 January 1898.

Founding the Home Rule Party, he won the 1900 election under the slogan Equal rights for the People and sat in the 57th Congress until 3 March 1903, an outsider whose English was his second language. He lost in 1902 to Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole, and while campaigning for high sheriff of Honolulu he suffered a hemorrhage and died on 23 October 1903. A bronze statue unveiled in 1993 stands in Wilcox Park in downtown Honolulu.
robertians: The Robertians, sometimes called Robertines in modern scholarship, are a proposed family whose members appear in the records as powerful nobles under the Carolingian rulers, mainly in West Francia. The ancestry of Robert the Strong, who died in 866, is uncertain, and medieval records hint at an origin in Austrasia or East Francia. Regino of Prüm states that Robert's son Odo was said to be a relative of Count Meingaud, a count near Worms who died in 892.

Modern proposals rest on the idea of one family that often named its sons Robert, including Robert III of Worms, Robert the Strong and Robert I of France. The oldest known members probably came from the county of Hesbaye, around Tongeren in present-day Belgium. Robert the Strong is probably the son of Robert III of Worms and nephew of Ermengarde of Hesbaye, wife of Louis the Pious. Related figures include Cancor, founder of Lorsch Abbey, and his nephew Saint Chrodogang, Archbishop of Metz.

The family married into the Carolingian house. Robert the Strong's sons Odo and Robert both became kings of West Francia: Odo reigned from 888 to 898 and Robert from 922 to 923. The family became Counts of Paris under Odo, in 882, and Dukes of the Franks under Robert, holding large parts of ancient Neustria. Robert's son Hugh the Great quarrelled with Louis IV of France, but the quarrels were mended when Lothair came to the throne in 954. Lothair greatly enlarged the Robertian lands by granting Hugh Aquitaine and much of Burgundy.

The Carolingians ceased to rule France with the death of Louis V in 987. Hugh Capet, son of Hugh the Great, was chosen king and crowned at Noyon on 3 July 987 with the support of the Holy Roman Emperor Otto III. He ruled from Paris, and historians count him as the first king of France.

Hugh's descendants took the name Capetians from him and ruled France as Capetians, Valois and Bourbons until the French Revolution. They returned after 1815 and reigned until Louis Philippe was deposed in 1848. Through the Bourbon branch the family has continued to rule Spain, apart from two republican interruptions, and both King Felipe VI of Spain and Grand Duke Henri of Luxembourg descend from it.
roberto-daubuisson: Roberto D'Aubuisson Arrieta was born on 23 August 1943 in Santa Tecla, the son of Roberto d'Aubuisson Andrade and Joaquina Arrieta Alvarado, a career civil servant. The family descended from Jacques Marie Germain Gustave d'Aubuisson, born in Toulouse in 1822, who settled in El Salvador as an ironmonger. He entered the Captain General Gerardo Barrios Military School in 1958, at fifteen, and joined the National Guard. In 1972 he trained in communications at the School of the Americas, then joined military intelligence; he also studied at Fu Hsing Kang College in Taiwan.

In the mid-1970s he became associated with the White Warriors Union, the second death squad to emerge in the country. After progressive officers deposed Carlos Humberto Romero in October 1979 and set up the Revolutionary Government Junta, he was forced out of the army for his death squad connections, though he kept working secretly for senior commanders. On television he denounced alleged traitors and communists, who were then murdered by death squads. On 7 May 1980 he was arrested on a farm with civilians and soldiers, weapons and documents naming them as death squad organisers planning a coup; eight of the fourteen garrison commanders voted for his release.

In August 1981 The Washington Post reported that he spoke openly of the need to kill 200,000 to 300,000 people to restore peace, and on 30 September he founded ARENA. Contemporaries and historians widely saw him as a neo-fascist; he praised Hitler to West German journalists. After the 1982 election, pressure from the United States kept the assembly from making him president of the country, and Álvaro Magaña was chosen instead. In 1984 he lost the presidential run-off to José Napoleón Duarte, 46.4 percent to 53.6, and claimed fraud and American interference. He was returned as a deputy in 1985, 1988 and 1991.

He died of esophageal cancer and bleeding ulcers on 20 February 1992. Documents released by the United States government in November 1993 showed that the administrations of Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush knew of the killings he directed and worked with him regardless. ARENA supporters honour him for his opposition to communism, while FMLN supporters condemn him for human rights abuses; in 2007 President Antonio Saca paid him homage, but an attempt to name him a meritorious son of El Salvador failed against protests by Church leaders and human rights workers. Political prisoners knew him as Blowtorch Bob.
roberto-de-nobili: Born in Montepulciano in Tuscany in September 1577, de Nobili reached the Portuguese ports of Goa and Bombay on 20 May 1605. There he probably met Thomas Stephens, a Jesuit in India since 1579 who was likely then composing his Khristapurana, a poem telling the life of Christ in Hindu literary forms. After a short stay in Cochin in Kerala he settled at Madurai in November 1606, called himself a teacher of wisdom and shaved his head but for a small tuft. He wore a three-stringed thread across his chest, which he took to stand for the Holy Trinity.

Claiming noble parentage, he approached high-caste people as an equal and debated with Hindu scholars. The Portuguese missionaries before him had found their converts among the lower classes, which had earned them the scorn of the brahmins, and his methods were an implied criticism of theirs. Fellow Jesuits and the Archbishop of Goa, Cristóvão de Sá e Lisboa, opposed him. Pope Gregory XV's apostolic constitution Romanæ Sedis Antistes of 31 January 1623 allowed the thread, the tuft, sandalwood paste on the forehead and ritual baths where they implied no superstition, and urged converts to overcome caste feeling and contempt for pariahs.

With his teacher Shivadharma, de Nobili mastered the languages and literature of Sanskrit, Telugu and Tamil; Max Muller, a key figure in the study of Orientalism, called him the first European Sanskrit scholar. In explaining Christian doctrine in Tamil he took over Hindu words: kovil for a place of worship, arul and prasadam for grace, guru for priest, Vedam for the Bible and poosai for the Mass. He wrote catechisms and philosophical discourses in Tamil and contributed to the growth of modern Tamil prose.

Known as the White Brahmin, de Nobili died at Mylapore near Chennai on 16 January 1656, aged 79. The Telugu novelist Viswanatha Satyanarayana appears to have based the ascetic preacher of his historical novel Ekaveera on him, and eight Jesuit schools in Jharkhand bear his name. He was once named as the author of the Ezourvedam, a spurious French version of a supposed Sanskrit scripture, but Max Mueller rejected this, Ludo Rocher showed its author must have been a French missionary, and Urs App has argued for Jean Calmette.
roberts-international-airport: In 1942 Liberia signed a defence pact with the United States, which began a period of strategic road building and other construction serving American military interests in checking the expansion of the Axis powers. The airport was built by the United States government as an air force base as part of this work. Its runway was made long enough for B-47 Stratojet bombers to land for refuelling, which gave Liberia for many years the longest runway in Africa.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt lunched with President Edwin J. Barclay at Roberts Field during his visit to Liberia in January 1943. From 1943 to 1945 it was an alternative base for a contingent of 26 Squadron of the South African Air Force, whose Vickers Wellington bombers flew anti-submarine and convoy escort patrols over the Atlantic.

From the end of the Second World War until 1985 Pan American World Airways administered and operated the airport under contract with Liberia's Ministry of Transport. Monrovia was an intermediate stop on its African network between Accra and Dakar, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s Robertsfield became Pan Am's principal African hub, with a nonstop Boeing 747 service from New York. European and African airlines also called there from the mid-1960s to the mid-1980s, and Varig used it as a stop between Brazil and Europe. A Varig DC-8 from Rome crashed on approach on 5 March 1967, killing 51 of the 90 on board and five on the ground, the worst aviation accident in Liberia.

The Second Liberian Civil War badly damaged the main terminal, which stood burnt out and vacant for nearly fifteen years. Commercial service returned slowly after 2003. Delta Air Lines began flights in 2010 and ended them on 31 August 2014, and the Ebola outbreak of that year suspended most scheduled services. An overhaul begun in 2018 renewed the runway and apron and rebuilt the terminal on the salvaged structure of the original, at a reported cost of 80 million US dollars, with a first set of jet bridges. The terminal was fully operational by September 2019.

The airport takes its name from Joseph Jenkins Roberts, the first president of Liberia. Its 11,000-foot runway served as an emergency landing site for the American Space Shuttle programme. It is one of only two paved runways in the country.
rochefort-charente-maritime: Rochefort lies on the river Charente, close to its outflow into the Atlantic Ocean, about 30 kilometres southeast of La Rochelle. It is a port on the Charente estuary and a subprefecture of the department of Charente-Maritime. Jean-Baptiste Colbert chose it as a place of refuge, defence and supply for the French Navy.

It is a notable example of a 17th-century ville nouvelle, a new town whose design and building resulted from a political decree. The reason for building it was in large part that royal power could hardly depend on rebellious Protestant La Rochelle, which Cardinal Richelieu had had to besiege a few decades earlier.

The Arsenal de Rochefort served as a naval base and dockyard until it closed in 1926. In September 1757 the town was the target of an ambitious British raid during the Seven Years' War. From 1766 it also had a bagne, a high-security penal colony with hard labour, such as existed at military harbours and naval bases like Toulon and Brest because they provided free labour.

During the Jacobin period of the French Revolution over 800 Roman Catholic priests and other clergy who refused the oath of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy were put aboard prison ships in Rochefort harbour, and most died of the conditions.

On 17 July 1815 Napoleon Bonaparte, who had spent several days on the Île-d'Aix hoping to flee to America, surrendered to Captain F. L. Maitland aboard HMS Bellerophon off Rochefort, ending the Hundred Days. Well into the 20th century Rochefort remained primarily a garrison town.

The buildings of the original naval establishment include a hospital with a School of Naval Medicine, now a museum, and the Arsenal with a monumental gateway and the National Navy Museum. The Rope Factory, the corderie, at over 370 metres long was for centuries the longest manufacturing building in the world. Three dry docks for shipbuilding and repair and a cannon foundry also survive. The Rochefort-Martrou Transporter Bridge, built in 1900, is the only remaining one in France. L'Hermione, a replica of a frigate of 1779, was completed in the town in 2014. The Hôtel de Ville on Place Colbert was completed in around 1770.
rochester-kent: Rochester is a port town at the lowest bridging point of the River Medway, in the unitary authority of Medway in Kent, about 50 km east-southeast of London. It forms a conurbation with Chatham, Rainham, Strood and Gillingham. The Romano-British name Durobrivae is commonly explained as 'stronghold by the bridge' or as a Latinisation of a British word meaning 'swiftstream'. Bede, writing around 730, calls it Hrofes cæster, and from this came the later forms Hrofescester, Rovescester and Rochester. Its street plan was fixed in the Middle Ages by the Medway, Watling Street, Rochester Priory and Rochester Castle.

Remains from the Neolithic have been found near Rochester, which was one of the two administrative centres of the Cantiaci tribe in the Celtic period. During the Roman conquest a decisive battle was fought on the Medway somewhere near it, and the first bridge was built early in the Roman period. In the later Roman period the settlement was walled in stone. King Æthelberht of Kent established a legal system that survives in the 12th-century Textus Roffensis, and in 604 the bishopric and Rochester Cathedral were founded.

The present cathedral was built between 1080 and 1130, with further work in 1227 and 1343. Rochester Castle, built by Bishop Gundulf to guard the river crossing, has one of the best-preserved keeps in England or France. In the First Barons' War baronial forces took it from Archbishop Stephen Langton and held it against King John, who besieged it in 1215. In 1667 a Dutch fleet under de Ruijter broke through the chain at Upnor and sailed to Rochester Bridge, where it captured and burned part of the English fleet.

Rochester was a city from 1211 until 1998, when it lost that status as its local government district was abolished. The Royal Navy dockyard at Chatham closed in 1984 and caused a surge in local unemployment. Rochester has long been tied to Charles Dickens, who owned nearby Gads Hill Place and based many of his novels on the area. The King's School, which grew out of the cathedral's foundation of 604, is recognised as the second-oldest continuously running school in the world.
rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela: The eleven rock-hewn churches stand in the Ethiopian Highlands near the town of Lalibela, named after King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, who is said to have commissioned them to recreate the holy city of Jerusalem in his own kingdom. According to local tradition, Lalibela, traditionally known as Roha, was founded by an Agew family called the Zagwa or Zagwe in 1137 CE. Tradition also holds that before he became king, Lalibela was guided by Christ on a tour of Jerusalem and told to build a second Jerusalem in Ethiopia.

The king reigned about 1181 to 1221 and the work is said to have taken 24 years, though the churches more likely reached their present form over several phases of construction and alteration of earlier structures.

The site lies at an altitude of around 2,480 metres. Five churches stand north of the town's river Jordan, five south of it, and one, Biete Giorgis, stands apart and is joined to the others by trenches. Tunnels and trenches connect the churches of each group. The northern churches are Biete Medhane Alem, Biete Maryam, Biete Golgotha Mikael, Biete Meskel and Biete Denagel, and the southern are Biete Amanuel, Biete Qeddus Mercoreus, Biete Abba Libanos, Biete Lehem and Biete Gabriel-Rufael.

The churches were made by taking material away. Workers used hammers and chisels to cut trenches round the monolithic and semi-monolithic structures out of scoriaceous basalt, working from the top down. Four are free-standing and seven share a wall with the mountain. Each is distinct, with human figures in bas-relief inside Bet Golgotha and coloured paintings of geometrical designs and biblical scenes in Bet Mariam.

The churches are of great religious significance to Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, and their layout represents Jerusalem. The site is still used for daily worship and prayer, for festivals such as Timkat and Genna, and as a home for clergy, and it remains a place of pilgrimage. UNESCO first placed it on the World Heritage List in 1978. In 2008 four shelters were put up to cover five of the churches as a temporary protection.
rock-of-cashel: The Rock of Cashel, also called Carraig Phádraig or St. Patrick's Rock, rises above a plain at Cashel in County Tipperary. Local legend says the Rock fell there from the Devil's Bit, a mountain 30 kilometres to the north, when Saint Patrick banished Satan from a cave. According to the Tripartite Life of Saint Patrick, Cashel is the reputed site of the conversion of the King of Munster by Patrick in the 5th century. The whole plateau on which the buildings and graveyard stand is walled, and the graveyard holds a number of high crosses.

The Rock was the traditional seat of the kings of Munster as early as the 4th century, before the Norman invasion. In the 5th century the Eóganachta built a fortress at Cashel and kept their supremacy there for hundreds of years. In 977 Brian Boru was crowned king there and made Cashel his capital, and in 1101 the King of Munster, Muirchertach Ua Briain, gave his fortress on the Rock to the Church. Few remnants of the early structures survive; most buildings on the site date from the 12th and 13th centuries.

In 1647, during the Irish Confederate Wars, Cashel was sacked by English Parliamentarian troops under Murrough O'Brien, Earl of Inchiquin. The Irish Confederate troops there were massacred, as were Catholic clergy including Theobald Stapleton, and many religious artefacts were looted or destroyed. During or after the mid-1730s the Anglican Archbishop of Cashel, Arthur Price, had the cathedral roof removed, a decision that was criticised then and since. In 1763 a large number of Whiteboys levelled the wall surrounding the Rock, during a period of their activity in Tipperary between 1763 and 1765.

The round tower, about 28 metres high, is the oldest and tallest structure and dates from about 1100. Cormac's Chapel was begun in 1127 and consecrated in 1134. It has vaulted ceilings, carved tympana, an arcaded interior and exterior, the oldest stairs in Ireland and the only surviving Romanesque frescoes in Ireland. Twin towers at the junction of nave and chancel suggest German influence, and the Irish abbot Dirmicius of Regensburg sent two carpenters to help with the work. The sandstone has become waterlogged over the centuries, so the chapel has been enclosed in a rain-proof structure with dehumidifiers.

The cathedral, built between 1235 and 1270, is an aisleless cruciform building with a central tower and a massive residential tower house at the west end. The 15th-century Hall of the Vicars Choral holds St. Patrick's Cross and was restored by the Office of Public Works in 1975; visitors now enter the site through it. Scully's Cross, put up in 1860, was destroyed in 1976 when lightning struck a metal rod running the length of the cross.
roderic: Roderic, also spelled Ruderic, Roderik or Rodrigo (in Arabic Ludharīq), is an obscure figure about whom little can be said with certainty. According to the late Chronicle of Alfonso III, he was a son of Theodefred, himself a son of King Chindaswinth and Queen Recciberga, and of a woman named Riccilo. His date of birth is unknown but was probably after 687.

According to the Chronicle of 754, Roderic tumultuously invaded the kingdom with the encouragement of the senate. Historians have long debated the words. It was not a typical palace coup but a violent invasion of the palace that sharply divided the kingdom. Scholars disagree whether the legitimate king, Wittiza, was deposed or assassinated or had recently died naturally, and some believe that Achila, who ruled in opposition to Roderic, was Wittiza's son and successor.

Archaeological and numismatic evidence confirms that the southwest around Toledo was in Roderic's hands and the northeast in Achila's. Roderic's twelve surviving coins, all bearing the name Rvdericvs, were minted at Toledo, probably his capital, and at Egitania, probably Idanha-a-Velha. The two rulers never appear to have come into conflict, probably because Roderic was preoccupied with Arab raids. He also faced a rebellion from the Basques.

After several expeditions against the invaders Roderic was deserted by his troops and killed in battle in 711, probably near the mouth of the Guadalete river. The Chronicle of 754 says some nobles who accompanied him did so out of ambition for the kingdom, perhaps intending to let him die. Other historians suggest that low morale caused by his disputed succession explains the defeat. His widow, Egilo, later married the governor Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa.

A legend, treated for centuries as historical fact, has Roderic seduce or rape the daughter of Count Julian, known in late accounts as Florinda la Cava. It inspired William Rowley's tragedy All's Lost by Lust, Walter Scott's The Vision of Don Roderick (1811), Robert Southey's Roderick the Last of the Goths (1814) and Washington Irving's Legends of the Conquest of Spain (1835). He was the last Goth to rule from Toledo, but not the last Gothic king, a title that belongs to Ardo.
rodez: Rodez lies about 150 kilometres north-east of Toulouse, in the western foothills of the Massif Central, between the high limestone plateaus of the Grands Causses and the damp hills of the Ségala. The city was built on an isolated conical hill known as Le Piton and gradually spread over the surrounding slopes. The Aveyron crosses the commune. Its altitude is about 550 metres, and it has an oceanic climate that is colder than that of other cities in the south of France.

The name has Gaulish roots. In antiquity the settlement was Segodunum, from sego, strong, and dunum, hill, so that the name means high hill or stronghold. In late Imperial times it was Civitas Rutenorum, the city of the Ruteni, from which the modern name derives. Its inhabitants are called Ruthénois in French.

Rodez has existed from at least the 5th century BCE, when the Ruteni, a Celtic tribe, are said to have founded one of the oppida characteristic of Gallic civilisation here. Elements of its heritage testify to the later Romanisation of Segodunum. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was occupied by the Visigoths and then the Franks. The Moors seized it in 725 and damaged the ancient church. It was later held by the armies of the Dukes of Aquitaine and the Counts of Toulouse, and English troops captured it during the Hundred Years' War.

At the beginning of the 16th century Bishop François d'Estaing finished the Cathedral of Our Lady of Rodez. He added the bell tower, 87 metres high and topped by a Virgin, still the highest bell tower without a spire in France. The work was completed between 1510 and 1526 despite plague in the city. The old rival of Rodez was Villefranche-de-Rouergue, but the French Revolution gave Rodez the role of administrative centre, because of its central position, as prefecture of the new department of Aveyron.

Rodez is the prefecture of the Aveyron department in the Occitania region and the capital of the former province of Rouergue. It is also the seat of the Diocese of Rodez and Vabres. Its population reached a maximum of 25,550 in 1975 and has stayed around 24,000 since. The old town, Vieux-Rodez, keeps the remains of its ramparts, narrow streets and squares such as the Place du Bourg and the Place de la Cité, where markets are held.

The cathedral was made a Historic Monument in 1862. The city has long been a centre of Occitan culture, and troubadours are said to have found refuge there. The Musée Soulages is among its three museums.
rodolfo-graziani: Rodolfo Graziani was born on 11 August 1882 in Filettino, in the province of Frosinone, the son of the village doctor. He was educated at a seminary in Subiaco and at a Rome lyceum, and studied law because he could not afford the Military Academy of Modena. He joined the Royal Italian Army as a reserve officer cadet in 1903, became a regular second lieutenant in 1906 and was first posted to Eritrea, where he learned Arabic and Tigrinya. In 1918 he became the youngest colonel in Italian history.

After the First World War Graziani served in Libya, in the pacification of Tripolitania and then of Cyrenaica, where he was vice-governor from January 1930. In 1931 he was sent to put down the revolt led by ʿOmar al-Mukhtar. On the orders of Pietro Badoglio, the population of the Gebel el-Achdar, where al-Mukhtar found refuge, was moved to concentration camps on the coast, among them Marsa Brega, Soluch and Agedabia. The measure, which was decisive in defeating the rebellion, raised controversy throughout the Arab world.

In the Second Italo-Ethiopian War he commanded the southern front. The first chemical attack of the war was carried out against the fort of Gorrahei on 10 October 1935, and in December he asked for freedom to use poison gas, which Mussolini authorised. In February 1937, after an assassination attempt against him at a ceremony in Addis Ababa, he ordered a period of brutal retribution now known as Yekatit 12. In 1940 he commanded Italian North Africa and invaded Egypt on 9 September under pressure from Mussolini; the British counteroffensive of 9 December 1940 routed his forces. After 1943 he was Minister of National Defence of the Italian Social Republic.

Graziani was included on the United Nations War Crimes Commission's list of Italians eligible for prosecution, with a prima facie case found against eight Italians including him, but Allied opposition and indifference to prosecuting Italian war criminals frustrated Ethiopian attempts to bring him to justice. In 1950 an Italian court sentenced him to 19 years in prison for collaborating with the Nazis, and he served four months. He became Honorary President of the Italian Social Movement in 1953 and resigned from it in the summer of 1954. He died in Rome on 11 January 1955, and more than 100,000 people attended his funeral. In 2012 a monument was built over his tomb at Affile, which drew criticism from Ethiopia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
rodrigo-of-castile: Rodrigo's parentage is not documented. Some Iberian Muslim writers mention a brother or brother-in-law of Ordoño I active in Castile, and his missions suggest he was close to the royal house. Fernández de Béthencourt made him a son of Ramiro I of Asturias by his second wife, Paterna, but since they did not marry until around 842 he would then have become count as a child, and many historians think this unlikely; Barrau-Dihago rejected it for lack of support in the primary sources. Another reconstruction makes him the brother of Ordoño's wife Munia.
