Rodrigo governed the eastern march of the realm, which the Arabs called al-Qila and which later became the county of Castile, named for the castles built in a land with few natural defences. His territory, Bardulia, was then small, bounded by the Ebro, Brañosera, the Cantabrian Mountains and a line of fortifications. Castilian soldiers took Haro in 854, and in 859 Rodrigo fought at the Battle of Monte Laturce, where the armies of Ordoño and García Íñiguez of Pamplona defeated Musa ibn Musa. Many of his settlers at Amaya were Mozarabs fleeing persecution in the Emirate of Córdoba, and in 863 he raided as far as Talamanca de Jarama.

Emir Muhammad I struck back. In 863 his son Abd ar-Rahman and the commander Abd al-Malik ibn Abbas broke Rodrigo's defence of the gorge near Pancorbo, and in 865 an army of 20,000 took the border fortresses and defeated him at the Battle of the Morcuera near Añana. When Alfonso III was overthrown by Count Fruela Bermudez of Lugo in 866, Rodrigo raised an army that restored him in Oviedo, and he became one of the king's closest advisers. After ending the rebellion of the Basque magnate Eglyón without a fight, he was made count of Álava, holding it until 870, the year he retook Pancorbo.

Rodrigo last appears in a document of 18 April 873 and died on 4 October or 5 November that year. His son Diego Rodríguez succeeded him with the king's approval, the first count in Asturias to inherit his possessions. His standing as the probable founding count of Castile led later writers to enlarge his deeds: forged charters push his rule a decade earlier than can be traced, and earlier counts named Rodrigo and Diego were invented.
roermond: Roermond lies on the lower Roer, on the east bank of the Meuse, in the middle of the province of Limburg. Celtic inhabitants lived on both sides of the Roer. The Romans built a bridge, now called the Steene Brök, and founded the first town there, now the suburb of Voorstad Sint Jacob. Roermond received town rights in 1231.

From about 1180 to 1543 Roermond belonged to the Duchy of Guelders. Otto IV of Brunswick destroyed it in 1213, but by 1232 it had been rebuilt and given its own seal, mint and court. A charterhouse was founded in 1376. Around 1350 it became capital of the Upper Quarter of Guelders. The French besieged it in 1388, it joined the Hanseatic League in 1441, and by 1472 it had the right to coin money.

From 1543 to 1702 the area was part of the Spanish Netherlands. The Battle of Rheindalen, fought near Roermond on 23 April 1568, signalled the start of the Eighty Years' War. William the Silent occupied the town in 1572, and on 23 July of that year Calvinists murdered 13 Catholic clerics there. Under Spanish rule Roermond became a bastion of the Counter-Reformation, and in 1613 64 witches were burnt on the Galgeberg, the largest witch trial in the Netherlands. The Germans occupied it from 1940 to 1945, and by its liberation on 1 March 1945 about 90 per cent of its buildings were damaged or destroyed.

Roermond has been the seat of a Catholic diocese since 1559. Its skyline is dominated by the towers of St. Christopher's Cathedral and the Munsterkerk, and the town centre is a designated conservation area. Other monuments include the Carolus Chapel, the Cuypershuis and the Rattentoren.
roger-bernard-iii-of-foix: Roger-Bernard was the son of Roger IV of Foix and Brunissende of Cardona. In 1252 he married Margaret of Béarn, daughter of Gaston VII of Béarn and Martha of Marsan. Gaston first named Margaret his heir and later his third daughter Guillemette, but when he died in 1290 Roger-Bernard at once took possession of his counties and quartered the arms of Béarn with those of Foix. The claim led to a long war with the house of Armagnac, which had married Gaston's second daughter, Mathe.

In 1272 Roger-Bernard and Gerald VI, Count of Armagnac, attacked the lord of Sompuy, who appealed to the king. Philip III of France invaded Languedoc, began the siege of Foix on 3 June, and took the citadel two days later; Roger-Bernard surrendered and was imprisoned at Carcassonne. Released before the end of 1273, he did homage and recovered part of his lands, and in December 1277 Philip called him his most loyal and faithful vassal. In September 1276 he led a French army into Navarre for Joanna, heiress of Henry I of Navarre, and took and razed Pamplona.

In spring 1280 he led Catalan nobles, among them Ermengol X of Urgell, in revolt against Peter III of Aragon. Besieged in Balaguer, he surrendered on 22 July and stayed in an Aragonese prison until December 1283, then sided with the French in the Aragonese Crusade, negotiating the surrenders of Elne and Girona in 1285.

Under Philip IV he quarrelled with the royal seneschals over justice and taxes, and the king confiscated two of his castles in 1290, returning them in 1295, when he made the count Governor of Gascony. In 1297 Roger-Bernard was one of three commanders of the army that defeated Henry de Lacy, Earl of Lincoln, at the Battle of Bonnegarde. He refused to lead the revolt that Bernard Saisset, bishop of Pamiers, was stirring in Toulouse. He died at Tarascon-sur-Ariège on 3 March 1302 and was buried at Boulbonne, and his son Gaston I succeeded him.
roger-borsa: Roger was the son of Robert Guiscard and Sikelgaita, a Lombard noblewoman. His mother arranged for him to succeed his father in place of Guiscard's eldest son by another wife, Bohemond of Taranto. His nickname Borsa means purse and came from his early habit of counting and recounting his money. In 1073 Sikelgaita had Roger proclaimed heir after Guiscard fell ill at Trani. Only his cousin Abelard dissented, claiming to be the rightful heir to the duchy.

Roger accompanied his father on the campaign to Greece in 1084 and was still there when Guiscard died on 17 July 1085 on Cephalonia. Bohemond was meant to take the Greek possessions and Roger the Italian ones, but Bohemond was in Salerno and Roger in Greece. Roger returned to Italy with his mother, and with the support of his uncle Roger I of Sicily was recognised as duke in September. His Lombard descent made him a more attractive candidate than his Norman half-brother, who fled to Capua.

With the support of Jordan I of Capua, Bohemond rebelled and took Oria, Otranto and Taranto. Peace came in March 1086 and the brothers acted as co-rulers, but Bohemond renewed the war in late summer 1087 with some of Roger's vassals and defeated him at Fragneto. Pope Urban II mediated and Bohemond received Taranto and other possessions, together with the homage of Geoffrey of Conversano. In September 1089 Urban invested Roger with the Duchy of Apulia at the Synod of Melfi. He allowed some barons to mint coins and planned to build up towns in southern Italy by granting charters.

In May 1098 Roger and his uncle Roger I of Sicily besieged Capua at the request of Prince Richard II of Capua, who then did homage to the duke, though his successors ignored it. In October 1104 Roger besieged William, Count of Monte Sant'Angelo, who had pledged himself to the Byzantines, and abolished the county. In 1092 he had married Adela, daughter of Robert I, Count of Flanders and widow of Canute IV of Denmark. He died on 22 February 1111 and was buried in Salerno cathedral. His children included a son William, and Adela's son Louis died young in 1094.
roger-casement: Roger David Casement was born in Dublin on 1 September 1864. His mother, Anne Jephson, had him secretly baptised as a Catholic at the age of three, but he was raised a Protestant and remained one as an adult. In 1884 he went to the Congo to work for Henry Morton Stanley and the African International Association, a front for Leopold II of Belgium. He helped survey and build a railway to bypass the cataracts of the lower Congo, and learned African languages.

Casement became a British consul in 1891. His Casement Report on the Congo Free State was honoured in 1905. In 1906 the Foreign Office sent him to Brazil, and there he joined a commission investigating an enslaved workforce collecting rubber for the Peruvian Amazon Company, a firm registered in Britain. He was knighted in 1911 for his investigations of abuses in Peru. The Second Boer War and the colonial atrocities he investigated made him mistrust imperialism, and he retired from consular service in 1913.

He joined the Gaelic League in 1904 and Sinn Féin in 1905. In July 1914 he went to the United States to raise money for the Irish Volunteers and helped organise and finance the Howth gun-running. During the First World War he sought German military aid for the Easter Rising of 1916, but believed the Germans were giving inadequate aid that doomed a rising.

Casement's trial opened on 26 June 1916. The Treason Act 1351 seemed to cover only acts on English soil, and the court read a comma into its text so that in the realm or elsewhere described where acts were done. Casement wrote that he was to be hanged on a comma. He was hanged on 3 August 1916 and buried in quicklime at Pentonville Prison, though he had wished to lie at Murlough Bay in County Antrim. British governments refused requests for the return of his remains for decades.

In 1916 British officials showed typescripts said to copy private journals, the Black Diaries, which described homosexual activity, to influential people to undermine support for clemency. Whether the diaries are genuine has been much disputed: Roger McHugh and Angus Mitchell regard them as forged, while Jeffrey Dudgeon finds the evidence convincing.
roger-i-of-sicily: Roger was born in Normandy, probably in Hauteville-la-Guichard, the youngest son of Tancred de Hauteville and his second wife Fressenda. Little is known of his life before the expeditions to southern Italy, where he arrived as a young man in the summer of 1057. His brother Robert inherited the main title, and Roger became his vassal as holder of the newly conquered County of Calabria. The monk Goffredo Malaterra described him as a youth of great beauty, eloquent in speech and cool in counsel. He established his court at Mileto.

In May 1061 the brothers crossed from Reggio and captured Messina, invited by Ibn al-Thumna, emir of Catania, who was at war with his brother-in-law, the emir of Agrigento. In June 1063 Roger defeated a Muslim army at the Battle of Cerami, and he won another victory at Misilmeri in 1068. In 1071 he was made Grand Count of Sicily, and on 10 January 1072 Palermo was taken after a siege of five months.

In 1086 he attacked Syracuse, where the emir Benavert drowned in the night attack on his fleet, and the city surrendered in October. Agrigento fell in 1087, Butera in 1090, and by 1091 Roger controlled the whole island. That year he also took Malta, whose qadi agreed to continue administering the islands as a tributary of the count.

Roger made himself master of the island's church. In 1098 the papacy granted him and his heirs the apostolic legateship, and he created new Latin bishoprics at Syracuse, Girgenti and elsewhere. He practised general toleration towards Arabs and Greeks and sponsored over twelve Greek monasteries. In the cities Muslims who had secured such terms kept their mosques, qadis and freedom of trade, but in the countryside they became serfs, and Roger drew most of his infantry from them. No feudal revolt of importance arose against him.

Roger died on 22 June 1101 at Mileto and was buried at the Benedictine Abbey of the Holy Trinity. His son Simon became count with his mother Adelaide del Vasto as regent. After Simon died in 1105, aged 12, the title passed to Roger II of Sicily.
roger-ii-of-sicily: Roger was born at Mileto in Calabria in 1095, the youngest son of Roger I of Sicily. By then Norman adventurers, who had reached southern Italy by 999, had become the rulers of the major polities south of Rome. His father died in 1101, and his elder brother Simon died in 1105 at the age of twelve. Roger, aged nine, inherited the County of Sicily under the regency of his mother, Adelaide del Vasto, and his brother-in-law Robert of Burgundy. In 1112, at sixteen, he began his personal rule.

When William II of Apulia died childless in July 1127, Roger claimed the Hauteville possessions on the peninsula. Pope Honorius II opposed the union of Sicily and Apulia, but in August 1128 he invested Roger as Duke of Apulia at Benevento. In 1130 Roger supported Antipope Anacletus II against Innocent II, and Anacletus made him king of Sicily by a bull of 27 September. He was crowned at Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. This brought a ten-year war, in which Bernard of Clairvaux, Louis VI of France, Henry I of England and the emperor Lothair III stood against him, and the southern nobility rebelled.

Roger lost the Battle of Nocera in 1132 and suffered his worst defeat at Rignano in 1137, but he wore down his enemies. In July 1139 his son captured Innocent II at Galluccio, and by the Treaty of Mignano the pope recognised him as king. He then issued the Assizes of Ariano, which gave the king and his officials wide powers over the vassals, and introduced a new coinage, the ducat.

His court at Palermo drew men of several cultures, among them the geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi, and George of Antioch, whom he made ammiratus ammiratorum, the origin of the word admiral, commanded his fleet. George took Tripoli in 1146 and Cape Bona in 1148, and in 1147 raided Corfu, Athens, Thebes and Corinth.

Roger died at Palermo on 26 February 1154 and was buried in the cathedral there. His fourth son, William, succeeded him; the African conquests were lost in William's reign and never became an integral part of the kingdom. The lands Roger gathered formed the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily for the next seven centuries. His royal mantle, dated to 1133-34 by its Arabic inscription, was made in a royal workshop at Palermo and was later used as a coronation cloak by the Holy Roman Emperors. It is now in the Imperial Treasury in Vienna. Karol Szymanowski's opera King Roger of 1926 takes him as its subject.
roger-of-lauria: Roger was born at Lauria, or perhaps Scalea, in southern Italy, the son of Richard of Lauria, Great Justiciar of the Kingdom of Sicily, and Donna Bella, a nurse of Constance of Sicily. His father had served King Manfred of Sicily of the Hohenstaufen. After Conradin of Swabia, the last of that family, was beheaded at Naples in 1268, Roger and his mother joined other Ghibelline exiles at Barcelona. King Peter III of Aragon, husband of Constance, knighted him together with Corrado Lancia, and in 1273 arranged Roger's marriage to Corrado's sister Margherita.

Named commander of the Aragonese fleet in 1282, Roger kept the post under Peter's successors James II and Frederick III. In the war that followed the Sicilian Vespers he won six galley battles. He defeated the Angevins in the Grand Harbour at the Battle of Malta on 8 July 1283 and, on 5 June 1284, beat the Neapolitan fleet at the Battle of Castellammare, capturing its commander, Charles of Salerno, the future Charles II of Naples. On 4 September 1285, during the Aragonese Crusade, his victory over the French at the Battle of Les Formigues broke French naval power in the Mediterranean for a long time.

On 23 June 1287 he won the Battle of the Counts near Naples with forty ships against eighty, then made a truce with the Neapolitans without King James's authority. Frederick III granted him the fief of Aci, but the two fell out. When Roger went over to the Angevins, Frederick took Aci; Roger escaped arrest at Palermo and lost all his fiefs. He defeated the Sicilian fleet at the Battle of Cape Orlando on 4 July 1299 and again at the Battle of Ponza on 14 June 1300. After the Peace of Caltabellotta he was pardoned, and he died at Cocentaina in the Kingdom of Valencia.

Roger drew enemy fleets out of defended ports by feigning retreat, then turned in formation on the disordered pursuers. He kept closer control of his captains than his opponents did, opened battle with archers and crossbowmen while oarsmen and lightly armed Almogavars stayed under cover, disguised the size of his force and sometimes held galleys back to strike the enemy's rear.
roger-williams: Roger Williams was born in London, probably in 1603. His birth records were destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666, and he gave contradictory information about his age during his life. His father was a merchant tailor in Smithfield. As an adolescent he apprenticed under the jurist Sir Edward Coke, who paid for his schooling at Charterhouse, and he received a Bachelor of Arts from Pembroke College, Cambridge, in 1627. He knew Latin, Hebrew, Greek, Dutch and French. He took holy orders in the Church of England but became a Puritan at Cambridge, then a Separatist, and he and his wife Mary Bernard sailed from Bristol on the Lyon in December 1630.

The Lyon anchored at Nantasket on 5 February 1631. Williams declined a post at Boston because it was 'an unseparated church', and he argued that civil magistrates must not punish breaches of the first table of the Ten Commandments and that individuals should be free to follow their convictions in religion. He lived at Plymouth Colony and at Salem, and in December 1632 he wrote a tract condemning the king's charters and questioning the right to the land without purchase from the Native Americans. In October 1635 the General Court of Massachusetts Bay convicted him of sedition and heresy and ordered him banished.

When the sheriff came in January 1636, Williams had slipped away three days earlier during a blizzard. He reached a Wampanoag winter camp at Raynham, where the sachem Massasoit sheltered him for three months. In spring 1636 he and four companions founded Providence on land acquired from the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi. A majority of heads of households governed it, only in civil matters. In 1638 Williams and about twelve others formed a congregation now recognised as the First Baptist Church in America. In July 1644 he obtained a charter from Parliament, and in 1647 Providence, Portsmouth, Newport and Warwick united as the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations.

In 1643 Williams published in London A Key into the Language of America, the first book-length study of a Native American language in English. His The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution for Cause of Conscience, published in 1644, caused a great uproar: at least 60 pamphlets addressed it between 1644 and 1649, and Parliament ordered the public hangman to burn all copies. Williams held that citizenship and religion should be separate, and Rhode Island is described as the first government in the Western world to guarantee religious freedom in its founding charter. He later became a 'seeker' who belonged to no specific church, and he mediated for nearly 40 years between the Native Americans and the colony.
rogier-van-der-weyden: Few certain facts of Rogier's life survive, because archives were lost in 1695 and again in 1940. He was born Rogelet de le Pasture in Tournai in 1399 or 1400, the son of Henri de le Pasture, a knife maker, and Agnes de Wattrélos. In 1426 he married Elisabeth, daughter of a Brussels shoemaker. On 5 March 1427 the painters' guild records show Rogelet de le Pasture entering the workshop of Robert Campin with Jacques Daret, and on 1 August 1432 he obtained the title of master painter. The close stylistic link between Daret, Campin and Van der Weyden is the main argument for seeing him as Campin's pupil.

By 21 October 1435 the family had settled in Brussels, where he took the Flemish form of his name. From 2 March 1436 he held the post of painter to the town, created for him and linked to a commission for four justice scenes for the Golden Chamber of the city hall.

The Justice of Trajan and Herkinbald panels, each about 4.5 metres across, were finished before 1450 and destroyed in the French bombardment of Brussels in 1695. They are known from descriptions and a tapestry copy at Bern. His Descent from the Cross, painted for Notre-Dame-hors-des-Murs in Leuven, was sent to the King of Spain, and when the ship sank the painting floated. King Juan II of Castile gave the Miraflores Altarpiece to the Charterhouse of Miraflores in 1445.

According to some sources he went to Italy in 1449, and the House of Este and the Medici family commissioned paintings from him. His portraits include those of Philip the Good, Isabella of Portugal and Charles the Bold. He died on 18 June 1464 in Brussels and was buried in St. Catherine's Chapel of the cathedral.

He worked from life models and often idealised their features, enlarging the eyes and strengthening the jaw. He introduced new religious iconography, showing patrons taking part in sacred events and joining half-length portraits of the Madonna with portraits of people at prayer to form diptychs.

No work can be attributed to him with certainty from fifteenth-century documents alone, and later writers confused his identity: Van Mander, misled by Vasari, took Rogier of Bruges and Rogier of Brussels for two painters. Erwin Panofsky established in 1953 that there was only one painter with two names. His influence reached France, Germany, Italy and Spain, and Hans Memling and Martin Schongauer were among those who followed him.
rogneda-of-polotsk: Rogneda, also called Ragnhild, is mentioned in the Primary Chronicle as a princess of Polotsk, the daughter of Rogvolod, or Ragnvald, who came from Scandinavia and established himself at Polotsk in the middle of the 10th century. Her Christian name was Anastasia.

The Primary Chronicle says that Vladimir, then prince of Novgorod, was entangled in a war of succession with his brother Yaropolk, prince of Kiev. Seeking allies, he proposed marriage to Rogneda through her father. She replied that she did not wish to take off a slave's son's shoes, but wanted to take off Yaropolk's. Vladimir then led an army to devastate Polotsk, killed Rogvolod and his two sons and took her as a wife. Jonathan Shepard and Simon Franklin think he was most likely seeking to strengthen his political legitimacy rather than acting from revenge alone.

The Primary Chronicle names Iziaslav, Mstislav, Yaroslav and Vsevolod as her sons by Vladimir. Aleksandr Koptev comments that she is presented as his most significant wife because she was the mother of Yaroslav. Other evidence suggests Yaroslav may have been a son of Anna rather than Rogneda. When Vladimir adopted Christianity and married Anna Porphyrogeneta, he had to divorce all his earlier wives, and Rogneda entered a convent as Anastasia.

The later Suzdalian Chronicle tells a related story, probably taken from a Norse saga, of a daughter of Rogvolod called Gorislava. Vladimir rapes her before her parents, kills her father and takes her as wife, and she plots his death through her elder son Iziaslav. Iziaslav's line continued to rule Polotsk. Scholars such as Francis Butler believe the two women were first named differently, and the first source to identify them is a chronicle of 1479, some 500 years after the events. Around 1823 Kondraty Ryleev wrote a poem, Rogneda, which was a source for Alexander Serov's opera Rogneda, first performed in 1865.
rognvald-eysteinsson: Rognvald, Ragnvald Mørejarl in modern Norwegian, is sometimes given bynames meaning the Wise or the Powerful. The sources about him contradict one another and were compiled long after his death. The best known are the sagas, the Orkneyinga saga, which most scholars date between 1170 and 1220, and Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla of about 1230. Some scholars prefer the older Fragmentary Annals of Ireland, though it is not certain that the Ragnall they name is Rognvald.

His parentage is disputed. The Irish annals make Ragnall a son of Halfdan, King of Lochlann, usually taken as Halfdan the Black, which would make him a brother of Harald Fairhair; the Orkneyinga saga calls him the son of Eystein Ivarsson. Both sagas give him six sons, three born of concubines and three, Ivar, Hrólfr and Thorir the Silent, born in marriage.

In the Orkneyinga saga Harald Fairhair made Rognvald Earl of Møre, and Heimskringla says Rognvald gave the king his byname by cutting his hair, left uncut for ten years under a vow. The sagas tell of a great expedition that cleared Orkney and Shetland of vikings raiding Norway and went on to Scotland, Ireland and the Isle of Man; Rognvald's son Ivarr was killed in it.

Most historians now doubt that Rognvald led this voyage, and many reject Harald's western expeditions as historical, seeing the account as shaped by 13th-century rivalry between Norway and the kings of Scots over the Hebrides and the Isle of Man, and by the later expeditions of Magnus Barefoot. The view that members of the Møre family created the Orkney earldom still has academic support, but Smyth (1984) regarded Torf-Einarr as the first historical earl.

According to the sagas, Harald's son Halfdan Hålegg and Gudrod Gleam surrounded the house where Rognvald was staying and burned it with the earl and 60 of his men inside. Harald banished Gudrod, Torf-Einarr later killed Halfdan on North Ronaldsay, and Rognvald's son Thorir became Earl of Møre. The sagas make Rognvald the ancestor of the Norse earls of Orkney, who held the islands until the early 13th century, and of important Icelandic families; French sources, however, give Rollo another father.
rognvald-kali-kolsson: Rögnvald's father was the lendmann Kolr Kalisson and his mother Gunnhildr Erlendsdottir, a sister of Magnus Erlendsson, Earl of Orkney. It was through his mother that he had a claim to the earldom. His birthplace is uncertain: some researchers place it near the medieval Fjære Church in the present-day Grimstad Municipality, others at the king's estate at Lista in Agder, where his family owned several farms.

King Sigurd I of Norway appointed him Earl of Orkney and Shetland in 1129. Kali then took the name Rögnvald, after Earl Rögnvald Brusason, whom his mother thought the ablest of the earls of Orkney, in the hope that the name would bring him luck. He should have held half of Orkney, as Magnus had, but his second cousin Paul Haakonsson had made himself sole ruler of the islands and would not give up any of them.

Rögnvald remained in Norway as one of the leading men of King Harald Gille and was hailed as jarl in 1136. In 1137 he began the building of St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall. He was guardian of Harald Maddadsson, the five-year-old nephew of Paul Haakonsson, and in 1138 made him earl alongside himself. Harald had inherited Caithness in Scotland, which brought that area under Rögnvald's control as well.

In 1151 he set out on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, which takes up five chapters of the Orkneyinga saga. The saga says little of the stay in the Holy Land itself and dwells on fighting and feasting during the voyage. It credits the idea to Eindridi Ungi, a distant relative, who named prestige as a reason for the expedition. With Hallr Þórarinsson, Rögnvald composed the learned skaldic poem Háttalykill inn forni, and other verses of his record the journey, among them five weeks spent in the mud of Grimsby and a swim across the River Jordan.

While he was away, King David I of Scotland granted half of Caithness to Erlend Haraldsson, who was later driven out by Harald and killed in 1156. In August 1158 Rögnvald and his company of eight men were cut down by Thorbjorn Klerk, a former friend and counsellor of Harald, whom he had outlawed for a murder in Kirkwall. He was buried in St Magnus Cathedral, and miracles were reported at his grave and at the stone where he died. He is said to have been canonized by Pope Celestine III in 1192, though no surviving record confirms it. North Ronaldsay and South Ronaldsay in Orkney are named after him.
rogun-dam: The Rogun Dam was first proposed in 1959 and a technical scheme was developed by 1965. It stands on the Vakhsh River about 110 km from Dushanbe as one of the planned plants of the Vakhsh Cascade. Construction began in 1976 but stalled after the collapse of the Soviet Union and was abandoned in 1993, when a flood destroyed the early works, and only preliminary construction had been done over three decades.

An agreement with Russia in 1994 was never implemented and was denounced by the Tajik parliament. In 2004 an agreement was signed with RUSAL to finish the dam, and in 2007 a partnership with Russia was announced, but Russia later refused it over a dispute about the controlling stake.

The dam was long listed as the highest in the world at 335 metres, but this was only ever the projected height; the structure stood only about 200 feet high until 1993. In 2014 three designs were under consideration: the original 335 metres and alternatives of 300 and 265 metres. The power plant is planned to have six turbines with a combined capacity of 3600 MW and to produce about 17 terawatt-hours a year.

In 2010 Tajikistan launched a public share offering to raise US$1.4 billion and collected US$184 million. Work was suspended in August 2012 pending World Bank studies, whose environmental assessment of 2014 stated that most impacts were small and easily mitigated.

On 1 July 2016 the state commission chose the Italian company Salini Impregilo for a contract of US$3.9 billion. On 29 October 2016 President Emomali Rahmon launched construction and the river was diverted through reconstructed tunnels. The first unit was commissioned in November 2018 and the second in September 2019, both at a lower head, and concrete pouring on the main dam core began in July 2022.

Uzbekistan, which feared for its irrigated cotton, opposed the project from Soviet times. In 2010 its president, Islam Karimov, called it a stupid project, but in July 2018 its foreign minister said that Uzbekistan would not oppose it, provided that guarantees under signed conventions were kept.
rohilkhand: Rohilkhand lies in the upper Ganges Plain and centres on the Bareilly and Moradabad divisions of Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, call the region Madhyadesh and Panchala. Its name means the land of the Rohilla: the term became common in the 17th century for people from Roh, a mountainous region stretching from Swat and Bajaur to Sibi and from Attock to Kabul and Kandahar, a name traced to the Sanskrit Rohitagiri, red hills.

Under orders of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, the Rohilla leader Daud Khan led a settlement in the Katehar region to put down risings of the Katheria Rajputs. Some 20,000 soldiers from Pashtun tribes were first hired, then a further 25,000 recruited, and most settled there with their families. A new wave during Nadir Shah's invasion of 1739 raised their number to over 1,000,000, and Katehar became known as Rohilkhand, with Bareilly as its capital and Moradabad, Rampur, Shahjahanpur and Badaun as other chief towns.

In 1752 the Nawab of Oudh, Safdar Jang, called in the Marathas against the Rohillas. After taking Delhi, the Marathas sent a large army in 1772 to punish the Rohillas for their part at Panipat, desecrated the grave of Najib ad-Dawla and burnt much of the country. On 15 June 1772, in the presence of Robert Barker of the East India Company, Hafiz Rahmat Khan agreed to pay Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula Rs 40 lakh for protection against the Marathas.

When the Marathas came again in 1773 and were driven off, Hafiz Rahmat Khan refused to pay, pleading internal strife. Awadh and its British allies invaded, and he was killed at the Battle of Miranpur Katra in 1774. The country was plundered and occupied, most Rohillas fled across the Ganges, and a Rohilla state under British protection was set up at Rampur under Faizullah Khan. By the treaty of 10 November 1801 Saadat Ali Khan II surrendered the whole of Rohilkhand to the East India Company.
rohillas: The name comes from Roh, the hill country that came to mean the Pashtun homeland, from Swat and Bajaur in the north to Sibi in the south and from Hasan Abdal to Kabul and Kandahar. Landless villagers and men seeking trade left Roh for northern India, and the flow grew with the collapse of Mughal authority and the invasion of Nadir Shah. Through new marriage alliances they formed a community of Indian Pathan families, converted Hindus and newcomers from the north-west, called Vilayati.

The first immigrant to the Katehr region was Shah Alam Khan, who settled there in 1673 with a band of the Barech. His son Daud Khan gained villages by serving the Mughals and Rajput zamindars, and adopted two Hindu boys, raised them as Muslims and trained them as soldiers. One of them, Ali Mohammed Khan, succeeded to Daud Khan's jagirs in 1721.

Ali Mohammed Khan helped suppress a rising of the Barah Sayyid tribe and was made Nawab by the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in 1737. He stopped sending revenue to Delhi and invaded Kumaon, where a combined Garhwal and Kumaon army defeated him at the battle of Kairarau. Warned by Safdar Jang, Nawab of Oudh, the emperor sent an expedition that forced his surrender; pardoned, he returned with Bareilly as his capital.

After his death power passed to other Rohilla chiefs, among them Hafiz Rahmat Khan Barech. With Shuja-ud-Daula they drove the Marathas across the Ganges in November 1759, and at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 Najib-ud-Daula brought 40,000 Rohilla troops to Ahmad Shah Abdali. When the Marathas struck back, Hafiz Rahmat Khan promised Oudh four million rupees for help but did not pay. Oudh, aided by an East India Company force under Colonel Alexander Champion, then attacked in the Rohilla War. Hafiz Rahmat Khan was killed in April 1774 and Rohilkhand was annexed by Oudh, though Faizullah Khan founded the Rohilla State of Rampur on 7 October 1774.

After 1774 most Rohillas lived in villages, often owning and farming the land, some in large brotherhoods like those of the Jats and Rajputs. In the late 19th century Urdu became their native language and the name Pathan gradually replaced Rohilla. Ahmad Raza Khan, founder of the Barelvi movement, was born among them. They live today throughout Uttar Pradesh, most densely in Rampur, Bareilly and Shahjahanpur, and some moved to Karachi after the Partition of India in 1947.
rohingya: The Rohingya are an Indo-Aryan ethnolinguistic group from Rakhine State, historically Arakan, a coastal region on the Bay of Bengal between South and Southeast Asia. By the 4th century Arakan was one of the earliest Indianised kingdoms in Southeast Asia. Arab merchants are recorded on the coast of south-eastern Bengal from the 9th century, and the Rohingya trace their history to this period. Early evidence of Bengali Muslim settlement in Arakan dates from the reign of Min Saw Mon (1430–34) of the Kingdom of Mrauk U, who regained his throne in 1430 with military help from the Bengal Sultanate.

The Rohingya maintain that they are indigenous to western Myanmar, with a heritage of over a millennium; the Myanmar government regards them as migrants from Chittagong in the colonial and postcolonial periods. After the Konbaung Dynasty conquered Arakan in 1785, as many as 35,000 people fled to the Chittagong region in 1799. Under British rule, thousands of Bengalis from Chittagong settled in Arakan in the early 19th century as farm labourers. A separate administrative zone for the Rohingya-majority north, the Mayu Frontier District, existed from 1961 to 1964.

After the coup of 1962 the Rohingya were increasingly deprived of political rights. A military operation in 1978 sent an estimated 200,000 refugees into Bangladesh, most of whom later returned. A citizenship law of 1982 did not list the Rohingya among Burma's 135 national races, which left much of the population stateless. Further crackdowns followed in 1991–1992 and 2012, and from 2016 most Rohingya in Myanmar were driven into Bangladesh. The International Criminal Court began an investigation of crimes against humanity, and the International Court of Justice heard a case alleging genocide.

Before that crackdown about 1.4 million Rohingya lived in Myanmar, chiefly in the northernmost townships of Rakhine, where they formed 80 to 98 per cent of the people. Their language is Indo-Aryan and related to Chittagonian, and both are related to Bengali but are not mutually intelligible with it. It has been written in Arabic, Urdu, Roman and Burmese scripts and in Hanifi, a newer alphabet derived from Arabic. Most Rohingya are Muslim, following a blend of Sunni Islam and Sufism, with Hindu and Christian minorities. Myanmar's governments have rejected the name Rohingya and call the community Bengali.
rohtak: Rohtak is the administrative headquarters of Rohtak district in Haryana. It lies 70 kilometres north-west of New Delhi and 250 kilometres south of the state capital Chandigarh, and forms part of the National Capital Region. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with an average annual rainfall of about 613 millimetres, 80 percent of it falling between July and September, so that farming in the district depends largely on canal irrigation and tubewells. The name is derived from an earlier form, Rohtasgarh, the fort of Rohtas, after a Rajput chieftain associated with the early settlement. The older form Rauhītaka occurs in the 12th-century Rājataraṅgiṇī.

Excavations at Khokhrakot have uncovered clay moulds for casting coins of the Yaudheyas, dated to the 3rd or 4th century CE, with clay seals of that and later periods and Gupta terracotta from the 4th to 6th centuries. The astronomical text Surya Siddhanta, of the 4th century CE, placed a prime meridian between Avanti (Ujjain) and Rohitaka, taken to be Rohtak. A 7th-century statue of Parshvanatha, the 23rd Jain tirthankara, was found at the village of Asthal Bohar, and Jain sources of the 9th century show the prominence of Parshvanatha in the area.

The town flourished until the 10th century, as coins of Samanta Deva of the Hindu Shahi found there show, and the Ghaznavids under Mahmud of Ghazni conquered it between 1020 and 1030. Chahamanas ruled the region in the 12th century.

The Ain-i-Akbari lists Rohtak as a Mughal pargana under the Delhi sarkar, dominated by the Jats, with a brick fort, a revenue of 8,599,270 dams and a force of 2,000 infantry and 100 cavalry. A fort in what is now Qilla Mohallah was besieged by Syed Khizer Khan in 1410 and fell only after six months. In 1762 Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, sent his sons Jawahar Singh and Nahar Singh to capture what is now Haryana, and they took the Rohtak pargana. British officers lived there from 1810, and All Saints Church was completed in 1867.

Rohtak had 373,133 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It is home to Maharshi Dayanand University, founded in 1976, and to the Pandit Bhagwat Dayal Sharma Post Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences, which began as a medical college in 1960. The Baba Mast Nath monastery was founded in 1731, and the town has havelis, mosques and temples in traditional Indian and Mughal styles. It lies on national highways and has a railway junction with connections to Delhi.
rohtas-fort: Sher Shah Suri, founder of the Sur Empire, commissioned the fort on the advice of his finance minister Todar Mal. He adopted a scorched-earth strategy against the Gakhar, a local tribe near the Salt Range that gave the Surs bold resistance. The fort stood between the mountains of Pothohar and the plains of Punjab, and it was meant to prevent Humayun from returning to India from his exile in Persia.

Todar Mal supervised the work from 1541, but it stalled when the Gakhars, whose men had vowed not to cooperate with the Surs, refused to labour. It resumed only after Sher Shah raised wages so far that many Gakhars agreed to work. Sher Shah died in 1545, before the fort was finished.

The fort covers 70 hectares on a hill in the Tilla Jogian Range, 91.5 metres above its surroundings, and follows the contours of the hill as an irregular triangle. Its sandstone walls, laid in lime mortar mixed with brick, are between 10 and 18 metres high and 10 to 13 metres thick, with 68 bastion towers. Hundreds of machicolations allowed defenders to pour molten lead or other hot liquids on attackers. A citadel in the north-west corner could hold up to 30,000 men.

The designers valued function over form, drawing on Turkish, Middle Eastern and South Asian traditions. The Sohail gate has some of the best masonry of the Sur Empire and is named after a local saint, Sohail Bukhari. The Shishi gate takes its name from the glazed blue tiles of its outer arch, the earliest known examples of the technique, and bears a Persian inscription giving the date of the fort as 948 in the Hijri year, 1541 CE. There are three stepwells.

After Sher Shah's death Humayun returned, and the fort was ceded to him in 1555. It lost much of its defensive importance and was never popular with the Mughals, who disliked its plain military style and lack of gardens. In the 1580s Akbar built Attock Fort nearby. Akbar stayed at Rohtas for only one night. In 1767 Charat Singh captured it from its Durrani governor, and the Sikh Empire used it for administration until the British took over the region in 1849.

UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1997, calling it an exceptional example of Muslim military architecture of Central and South Asia in the 16th century, and a model for later Mughal architecture. More than a third of its area is occupied by Rohtas village, inhabited continuously since the time of Islam Shah Suri.
rollo: Rollo, in Old Norse Hrólfr, was almost certainly born in Scandinavia, in either Norway or Denmark, but his origin is heavily disputed. Dudo of Saint-Quentin, writing in the late 10th century at the request of Rollo's grandson Richard I of Normandy, called him Danish and said he left after a hostile Danish king killed his brother Gurim. Medieval Norwegian and Icelandic writers identified him with Hrólfr the Walker, son of the jarl Rognvald Eysteinsson of Møre in western Norway.

The debate was begun in the late nineteenth century by the Danish historian Johannes Steenstrup and partly followed national lines. British, French and Norwegian scholars have generally accepted the Norwegian-Icelandic tradition, while Danish, Swedish and German historians have tended to follow Dudo. The question cannot be settled conclusively. Dudo's work was an official biography, and many of his genealogical claims may have been invented to legitimise Rollo's line.

The earliest well-attested event associated with Rollo is the siege of Paris in 885 and 886, in which he was a prominent leader of the Vikings, fended off by Odo of France. In 911 Robert I of France defeated another Viking band at Chartres with his horsemen, which paved the way for Rollo's baptism and settlement. Under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, Charles III recognised the lands Rollo held in return for baptism and help in defending the realm. Rollo took the baptismal name Robert after his godfather, Robert I, and the agreement was to be sealed by his marriage to Gisela, Charles's daughter.

After his oath Rollo divided the lands between the Epte and the Risle among his chieftains and made Rouen his capital. The earliest record of him is a charter of 918 mentioning Rollo and his associates, and a later agreement under Rudolph of France conceded the Bessin and Maine to a group of Norsemen presumed to be his. He died between a last mention in 928 and 933.

His son and successor William Longsword and his grandson Richard the Fearless forged Normandy into West Francia's most cohesive principality. The descendants of Rollo and his men assimilated with Frankish culture and became known as the Normans. Rollo was the great-great-great-grandfather of William the Conqueror, and his direct male descendants ruled Normandy until Stephen of Blois became King of England and Duke of Normandy in 1135.
romagna: Romagna is traditionally bounded by the Apennines to the south-west, the Adriatic to the east and the rivers Reno and Sillaro to the north and west. To the south-east the valley of the River Conca has historically formed a buffer between Romagna and the Marche. Its major cities are Cesena, Faenza, Forlì, Imola, Ravenna and Rimini. The name comes from the Latin Romania, first the generic name for land inhabited by Romans and later the territory under Eastern Roman rule administered by the Exarchate of Ravenna, as distinct from the Lombard lands of Langobardia.

The first traceable inhabitants were the Umbri, and Etruscans also lived in parts of the region. In the 5th century BCE Gaulish tribes moved south, and the Senones settled in Romagna. Rome defeated a coalition at the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE, founded the colony of Ariminum in 268 BCE and completed the Via Aemilia in 187 BCE, with colonies along it at Forlì, Imola and Forlimpopoli. In 49 BCE Julius Caesar, residing at Ravenna, led the Legio XIII across the Rubicon. In 402 Emperor Honorius moved the capital of the Western Roman Empire to Ravenna, and in 476 Odoacer deposed Romulus there.

Theodoric the Great entered Ravenna in 493 and had Odoacer murdered. After Justinian I's Gothic War an exarch ruled Italy from Ravenna, until the Lombard king Aistulf conquered Romagna and ended the exarchate in 751. King Rudolf I of Germany ceded Romagna to the Papal States in 1278, but papal control stayed nominal for long, and the region was divided among lords such as the Ordelaffi of Forlì and the Malatesta of Rimini. Cesare Borgia carved out a short-lived Duchy of Romagna in 1500, and Pope Julius II took it from him. Romagna was first recognised as an entity under Napoleonic rule, and it joined the unification of Italy in 1860.

Romagna approximately corresponds to the south-eastern part of the present-day region of Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy. It has its own language, Romagnol, and its culture exerts a considerable influence over the historical region of Montefeltro.
roman-catholic-relief-act-1829: The act closed a fifty-year process of relief from the penal laws. The Papists Act 1778 let Catholics in Great Britain again own property and inherit land, and the Roman Catholic Relief Acts of 1791 in Great Britain and 1793 in Ireland removed many other restrictions. The Oath of Supremacy still barred Catholics from Parliament and the higher offices of state. Daniel O'Connell built his Catholic Association into a mass movement funded by a Catholic rent of a penny a month and holding rallies of over 100,000 people. In July 1828 he defeated William Vesey Fitzgerald in the County Clare by-election by 2057 votes to 982.

Wellington and his Home Secretary, Robert Peel, concluded that without concessions a confrontation was inevitable. Peel, fearing insurrection in Ireland, drafted the bill and guided it through the Commons. To overcome the opposition of George IV and the House of Lords, Wellington threatened to resign. The king at first accepted his resignation, and the Duke of Cumberland, the king's brother and Grand Master of the Orange Order, tried to form a government against emancipation, but with little support in the Commons he gave up, the king recalled Wellington and the bill passed the Lords.

The act repealed the declarations against transubstantiation, the invocation of saints and the sacrifice of the mass, and replaced the Oath of Supremacy with a pledge of true allegiance to the King that recognised the Hanoverian succession, rejected any temporal or civil jurisdiction of the Pope within the United Kingdom and abjured any intention to subvert the established church. It forbade the Catholic Church to take episcopal titles already used by the United Church of England and Ireland. The Parliamentary Elections (Ireland) Act 1829, which received royal assent the same day, cut the Irish electorate from 216,000 voters to 37,000.

The historian J. C. D. Clark sees emancipation as the shattering of a whole social order resting on Anglican supremacy; others stress continuity, and Eric J. Evans argues that it split the anti-reformers beyond repair, easing the way for the Reform Act 1832. In Ireland it is generally regarded as having come too late to win Catholic opinion to the union. Some sectarian clauses were repealed by the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1926, and the university tests that the act left in place were abolished in 1871 and 1873.
roman-concrete: Many bridges, reservoirs and aqueducts built with Roman concrete still stand. Some scholars believe it was developed a century before its widespread use from about 150 BCE. The Romans first used hydraulic concrete in coastal underwater structures, probably in the harbours around Baiae before the end of the 2nd century BCE. The harbour of Caesarea, built between 22 and 15 BCE, is a large-scale example, for which enormous quantities of pozzolana were imported from Puteoli.

Vitruvius, writing around 25 BCE in his Ten Books on Architecture, recommended pozzolana, the volcanic sand of Pozzuoli, for structural mortars, in a ratio of 1 part lime to 3 of pozzolana for buildings and 1 to 2 for underwater work. After the fire of 64 CE destroyed large parts of Rome, Nero's new building code largely called for brick-faced concrete, which seems to have encouraged the brick and concrete industries.

Like any concrete, it consists of an aggregate and a hydraulic mortar, a binder mixed with water that hardens over time. The aggregate varied and included rock, ceramic tile, lime clasts and brick rubble from demolished buildings; in Rome tuff was often used. Gypsum and quicklime served as binders, and volcanic dusts were favoured where they could be had. Roman concretes could usually set underwater, and they were laid rather than poured because their aggregates were often larger.

Builders also adapted it to an earthquake-prone land. Interruptions and internal constructions within walls and domes created discontinuities, so that parts of a building could shift slightly in a tremor. In the Pantheon the aggregate of the upper dome alternates layers of light tuff and pumice, giving a density of 1,350 kilograms per cubic metre, while the foundation uses travertine at 2,200. Interiors were finished with stucco, fresco or coloured marble.

It was long thought that pozzolanic ash gave the concrete its strength. Research in 2023 found that lime clasts, once taken as a sign of poor technique, react with water seeping into cracks and let new calcium carbonate crystals reseal them, probably the result of mixing with quicklime while hot. Seawater reacting with volcanic ash and quicklime forms a rare crystal, tobermorite, which may resist fracturing. In 2013 the University of California, Berkeley described how a calcium-aluminium-silicate-hydrate compound binds the material. Since 2010 companies and municipalities in North America have begun to explore Roman-style concrete using coal fly ash in place of volcanic ash.
roman-conquest-of-britain: Julius Caesar's expeditions of 55 and 54 BCE left some southern British chiefdoms as allies of Rome, and for the next century the island stayed in a relationship of tribute, hostages and client states without direct occupation. By 40 CE the Catuvellauni had become the strongest kingdom in the south-east and under Caratacus conquered the kingdom of the Atrebates, whose king Verica, recognised by Rome, was expelled. His exile gave Claudius a pretext for invasion.

In 43 the invasion force under Aulus Plautius crossed in three divisions. The port of departure and the landing place are uncertain, though Richborough in Kent is the usual choice. Togodumnus and Caratacus, sons of the late king Cunobeline, led the resistance, and the Battle of the Medway lasted two days. Claudius joined the army for the final march on Camulodunum, and eleven British kings are recorded as surrendering to him. Vespasian then took a force westward as far as Exeter, and by 47 the Romans probably held the land south-east of a line from the Humber to the Severn.

The governor Publius Ostorius Scapula fought the tribes of Wales from late 47, and Caratacus, defeated, fled to the Brigantes, whose queen Cartimandua handed him over. Gaius Suetonius Paulinus attacked the druids on Anglesey in 60, but the rising of Boudica, in which Camulodunum, Verulamium and Londinium were destroyed, called him back to the south-east. It was put down by 61. Wales was finally subdued by about 77, and Cerialis and Frontinus advanced against the Brigantes. Gnaeus Julius Agricola, governor from 78, pushed into Scotland, defeated a Caledonian army led by Calgacus at Mons Graupius and was recalled in 84.

Agricola's successors abandoned much of what he had taken, and the fortress at Inchtuthil was dismantled before it was finished. By 87 the frontier was settled on the Stanegate road between Carlisle and Corbridge. Hadrian's Wall was begun from around 122, and the Antonine Wall, built by 142, was given up in 162. Septimius Severus campaigned against the Caledonian Confederacy in 209, and Constantius led an army north in 306.
roman-empire: By 100 BCE the city of Rome had expanded its rule from the Italian peninsula to most of the Mediterranean, but civil wars severely destabilised the Republic. They culminated in the victory of Octavian over Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Roman Senate granted Octavian overarching military power (imperium) and the title of Augustus, marking his accession as the first Roman emperor. The first two centuries of the Empire saw stability and prosperity known as the Pax Romana, and Rome reached its widest extent under Trajan (r. 98 to 117 CE).

Decline began under Commodus (r. 180 to 192). In the 3rd century a 50-year crisis of civil war, plagues and invasions threatened the Empire; the Gallic and Palmyrene empires broke away, and the Empire was reunified under Aurelian (r. 270 to 275). Diocletian (r. 284 to 305) set up two imperial courts, in the Greek East and the Latin West, and Constantine (r. 306 to 337), the first Christian emperor, moved the imperial seat to Byzantium in 330 and renamed it Constantinople. The Western Empire collapsed in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustus. The Eastern Empire survived until the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Provinces were either senatorial, governed by proconsuls appointed by lot each year, or imperial, belonging to the emperor and governed by legates. The Romans lacked the manpower to rule by force alone, so they cooperated with local elites, and communities that showed loyalty kept their own laws and could collect their own taxes. Latin and Greek were the main languages, and the Empire was deliberately multilingual. By the time of Nero it was not unusual to find a former slave richer than a freeborn citizen. Roman religion rested on correct ritual and sacrifice rather than faith or dogma, and as many as 135 days of the calendar were given to festivals and games.

Several states claimed to be the Empire's successor. The Holy Roman Empire was established in 800 when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor, and the Russian Tsardom counted itself the Third Rome, Constantinople having been the second. When the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II made it his capital and claimed to sit on the throne of the Roman Empire. Rome's republican institutions influenced the Italian city-state republics, the early United States and modern democratic republics.
roman-forum: The Forum lies in the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills. Its long axis runs northwest to southeast, from the foot of the Capitoline to that of the Velian Hill. The site was originally a marshy lake where water drained from the surrounding hills, and tradition says the Tarquins drained it with the Cloaca Maxima.

Sediment from Tiber floods and from the eroding hills kept raising the ground, and residents paved over debris too great to remove; the final travertine paving, still visible, dates from the reign of Augustus. By the imperial period the large buildings around it had reduced the open space to a rectangle of about 130 by 50 metres, with the Basilica Aemilia on the north and the Basilica Julia on the south.

Pottery shows that people occupied the Forum, Palatine and Capitoline in the Final Bronze Age. In the early Iron Age part of the future Forum was a cemetery, probably until the late 9th century BCE, and in the 8th century BCE it began to change into a public site. Roman tradition links its beginnings to an alliance between Romulus and Titus Tatius, and credits Numa Pompilius with the cult of Vesta and the Regia.

In the Republic the Comitium was the centre of judicial and political life. The earliest Forum temples of known date are those of Saturn (497 BCE) and of Castor and Pollux (484 BCE). Gaius Gracchus is said to have turned from the Senate to speak to the people from the Rostra, as the tribune Caius Licinius had two centuries before.

Julius Caesar built the Basilica Julia and the Curia Julia, and Augustus completed the Forum's final form, adding the Temple of Caesar in 29 BCE. In 69 CE Galba was killed there by Otho's cavalry. Business and legal affairs moved north to Trajan's Forum and the Basilica Ulpia, and the Basilica of Maxentius of 312 CE was the last major expansion.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the population of Rome shrank and the Forum was largely abandoned. The Column of Phocas, erected on 1 August 608, was the last monumental addition. Old buildings were turned into churches, and the Forum became known as the Campo Vaccino, the cattle field.

In the 16th century Pope Paul III used it as a quarry for the new Saint Peter's Basilica. Carlo Fea began clearing the debris in 1803, and the Italian government began official excavations in 1898, led by Giacomo Boni until his death in 1925. Excavations continue. Artists including Claude Lorrain, Turner and Piranesi drew the site, whose ruins today attract more than four million visitors a year.
roman-inquisition: The Roman Inquisition drew on medieval procedures against heresy. Pope Lucius III's bull Ad abolendam had set out penalties for heretical clerics and laymen and a system of inquiry by bishops, and the third canon of the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 laid down how heretics and their accomplices were to be pursued. Founded in 1542 as part of the Counter-Reformation, the new body was formally the Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Roman and Universal Inquisition. In 1588 Pope Sixtus V made it one of fifteen congregations of the Roman Curia in the bull Immensa Aeterni Dei.

A cardinal appointed by the pope presided over its meetings; historians often call him Grand Inquisitor, though his office differed from the Spanish post of that name. Usually ten other cardinals sat with him, with a prelate and two assistants from the Dominican Order, and scholars of theology and canon law advised on particular questions. The Congregation directed the local tribunals.

In 1616, answering complaints against Galileo Galilei, the Inquisition's consultants judged the view that the sun stands still at the centre of the universe formally heretical. Unexpurgated copies of Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium were placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632 alienated Pope Urban VIII; tried in 1633, Galileo was found vehemently suspect of heresy, forced to recant and kept under house arrest at Arcetri near Florence for the rest of his life. Giordano Bruno was executed in 1600, the miller Domenico Scandella in 1599 and the friar Fulgenzio Manfredi in 1610, and Tommaso Campanella was also investigated.

The Italian historian Andrea Del Col estimates that of 51,000 to 75,000 cases judged in Italy after 1542, about 1,250 ended in a death sentence. Older writers such as Henry Charles Lea stressed the use of torture, and some feminist writers blamed the Inquisitions for hundreds of thousands of deaths in the witch-hunts. Historians including John Tedeschi, Brian P. Levack and Christopher F. Black have argued instead that most witch trials were held by local and secular courts and that its procedures restrained witch-hunting in Italy. The Congregation was renamed in 1908, 1965 and 2022.
roman-law: Before the Twelve Tables, Roman private law was the ius civile, which applied only to Roman citizens, was bound to religion and was strictly formal. According to Livy's traditional account, the plebeian tribune C. Terentilius Arsa proposed that the law be written down to stop magistrates applying it arbitrarily. Ten men, the decemviri, were chosen in 451 BCE and produced ten tablets in 450 BCE; a second board is said to have added two more in 449 BCE. Modern scholars doubt that a second decemvirate took place and consider it unlikely that an official delegation went to Greece.

The original text was probably destroyed when the Gauls burned Rome in 387 BCE. The surviving fragments show that the Tables were not a code in the modern sense but specific provisions altering customary law, mostly on private law and civil procedure. The Lex Hortensia of 287 BCE later made the decisions of plebeian assemblies binding on all.

Rome's most important contribution, in this view, was a class of professional jurists and a legal science, rather than well-drafted statutes. Between about 201 and 27 BCE the praetors' edicts created a body of praetoric law that supplemented the formal ius civile and drew on the ius gentium, the law of peoples. Around 130 CE the jurist Salvius Iulianus drafted a standard form of the praetor's edict, which later jurists such as Paulus and Ulpian commented on.

Gaius's Institutes divided private law into persons, things and legal actions, a scheme later reflected in Blackstone's Commentaries, the French Code civil and the German BGB. A person's rights depended on status: citizen or foreigner, free or slave, head of a family or a member under another's authority.

By the middle of the 3rd century jurisprudence had all but ended in the West, and classical law gave way to a vulgar law. In the East, Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis of 529 to 534 remained the basis of legal practice. In the West the Digest was largely ignored until a manuscript was rediscovered in Italy around 1070. Glossators then studied it at Bologna, whose law school gradually became Europe's first university.

By the middle of the 16th century Roman law, mixed with canon law and feudal custom, formed the ius commune of continental Europe. Only England and the Nordic countries did not take part in its wholesale reception. National codes, beginning with the French civil code of 1804 and ending with the German BGB in 1900, brought this practice to an end. The legal systems of South Africa and San Marino are still based on the old ius commune, and the civil law system spread through colonial expansion.
roman-parthian-war-of-58-63: Armenia, the largest of the states between Rome and Parthia, had been a Roman protectorate since Augustus enthroned Tigranes III in 20 BCE. After Rhadamistus of Iberia seized the throne in 51, the new Parthian king Vologases I took the capitals Artaxata and Tigranocerta and made his younger brother Tiridates king, and by 54 Tiridates was established in the country. In that year Nero succeeded Claudius, and the Parthian move was seen as a test of the new emperor. He gave the supreme command in the East to Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, who spent two years restoring the discipline of the eastern legions, wintering them under canvas on the Anatolian plateau.

War broke out in the early spring of 58, while Vologases was held down by a revolt of the Hyrcanians. Tiridates avoided pitched battle, so Corbulo stormed his strongholds, among them Volandum, and marched on Artaxata in a hollow square that the Parthian horse archers could not break. Tiridates abandoned the city, which was burned. In 59 the Romans took Tigranocerta and installed Tigranes VI, and Corbulo became governor of Syria in 60.

When Tigranes raided the Parthian province of Adiabene in 61, Vologases crowned Tiridates king of Armenia and sent Monaeses to besiege Tigranocerta, without success. War resumed in 62 under a new commander in Armenia, Lucius Caesennius Paetus, whose relations with Corbulo were strained. Paetus dispersed his forces, was besieged in camps near Rhandeia and capitulated before Corbulo's relief arrived. The Romans agreed to leave Armenia and to build a bridge over the Arsanias for Vologases' triumph, and Tacitus reports a rumour that they were made to pass under the yoke.

When a Parthian embassy reached Rome in the spring of 63, Nero recalled Paetus and gave Corbulo extraordinary command. Corbulo crossed the Euphrates, and Tiridates agreed to meet him at Rhandeia, where he laid his diadem at the foot of a statue of Nero and agreed to receive his crown in Rome. Nero hailed the peace as a major achievement and closed the gates of the Temple of Janus, but the compromise left Armenia to an Arsacid king under growing Parthian influence. Corbulo, suspected as a rival, killed himself on Nero's order in 67, and Rome went on to annex Pontus, Colchis, Commagene and Lesser Armenia.
roman-parthian-wars: After the Seleucid–Parthian Wars the Parthians annexed much of the Seleucid Empire and began to look west. Under Mithridates I the Arsacids extended their rule into Armenia and Mesopotamia. Contact with Rome was restored when Lucullus invaded southern Armenia and defeated Tigranes in 69 BCE. When Pompey took charge in the East he reached an agreement with Phraates III, and Roman and Parthian troops invaded Armenia in 66 or 65 BCE, but a dispute soon arose over the Euphrates boundary.

In 53 BCE Crassus invaded Mesopotamia and was defeated and killed with his son Publius at Carrhae by a Parthian army under Surena. Of 42,000 men about half died, a quarter returned to Syria and the rest were taken prisoner, and the Parthians captured several legionary eagles. In 40 BCE Pacorus and Quintus Labienus overran Syria and put Antigonus on the throne of Judea, but Ventidius defeated them, and Pacorus was killed in 38 BCE. Mark Antony's own campaign in 36 BCE ended in a withdrawal with heavy casualties.

A new crisis began in 58 CE, when Vologases I installed his brother Tiridates in Armenia and Corbulo overthrew him. The war ended in 63 when Rome let Tiridates rule on condition that he received the crown from the emperor. In 113 Trajan began a campaign that annexed Armenia, overran northern Mesopotamia and captured Ctesiphon, but revolts forced him to install Parthamaspates as client ruler and withdraw, and he died in 117. Hadrian gave the conquered lands back. In 165 Avidius Cassius sacked Ctesiphon, though an epidemic forced the Romans to withdraw. Septimius Severus occupied Seleucia and Babylon from 195 and sacked Ctesiphon in 197, gaining northern Mesopotamia as far as Nisibis and Singara.

Caracalla sacked Arbela in 216, but after his assassination his successor Macrinus lost a battle against the Parthians at Nisibis and had to pay tribute; this was the last engagement of the Parthian wars. Ardashir I entered Ctesiphon in 226 and destroyed Parthia. The conflict continued as part of 682 years of Roman–Persian wars, and Armenia remained a constant bone of contention between Rome and its Persian rivals.
roman-persian-wars: The Romans and the Parthians came into contact through their conquests of parts of the Seleucid Empire. The Parthians, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty, had by the early first century BCE conquered Persia, Mesopotamia and Armenia. In 64 BCE Pompey conquered the remaining Seleucid territories in Syria and advanced the Roman frontier to the Euphrates, where it met Parthian territory.

In 53 BCE the Roman general Marcus Licinius Crassus invaded Mesopotamia and was killed with his son Publius at the Battle of Carrhae by Parthians under Surena, the worst Roman defeat since Arausio. Rivalry over Armenia led to war from 58 CE, ended in 63 CE when Tiridates and his descendants were allowed to rule Armenia on condition that they received the crown from the Roman emperor. In 114 and 115 the Emperor Trajan annexed Armenia and Mesopotamia and captured the Parthian capital Ctesiphon, but revolts forced him to withdraw, and he died in 117.

After Ardashir I founded the Sasanian Empire, he raided Mesopotamia and Syria in 230. The Emperor Gordian III was defeated at Misiche in 244 and Philip paid 500,000 denarii for peace. The Anastasian War began in 502 when Kavadh I seized Theodosiopolis and besieged Amida. Khosrau I broke the Treaty of Eternal Peace in 540, invaded Syria and deported the people of Antioch to Persia; the Lazic War that followed was ended by a truce in 545 secured by Roman payments. A new war from 571 turned on the Caucasus.

In 602 the army mutinied under Phocas, who killed the Emperor Maurice. Khosrau II used the murder as a pretext, and in the following years the Persians took the fortress cities of Mesopotamia one by one, then overran Syria in 611 and entered Anatolia. Heraclius took the throne in 610 but was decisively defeated outside Antioch in 613.

The final war and a century of almost continuous conflict left both empires crippled. Persia fell into dynastic turmoil and civil war after Kavadh II died only months after coming to the throne, and was weakened by economic decline, heavy taxation, religious unrest and the power of provincial landholders. The Byzantine Empire had exhausted its financial reserves, and the Balkans were largely in Slav hands. Both were then attacked by the Rashidun Caliphate, which conquered Persia and took the Levant, Egypt and the rest of North Africa.

Historians note that the frontier in upper Mesopotamia stayed more or less constant for centuries, although Nisibis, Singara and Dara changed hands. Cassius Dio observed a never-ending cycle of armed confrontations.
roman-republic: Rome had been ruled by monarchs elected for life by the Senate. Traditional histories say the last, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled in 509 BCE after his son Sextus Tarquinius raped a noblewoman, Lucretia, and that a revolution led by the semi-mythical Lucius Junius Brutus transferred the king's powers to two consuls elected for one year, each able to veto his colleague. Most modern scholarship describes these accounts as the quasi-mythological detailing of an aristocratic coup within Tarquin's own family, or a consequence of an Etruscan occupation of Rome, rather than a popular revolution.

Republican Rome was in a state of near-perpetual war. After the Gallic sack of Rome it conquered most of the Italian peninsula in a century. It fought three wars against Carthage and defeated it at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, then defeated Philip V and Perseus of Macedon, Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire and Vercingetorix of the Arverni. At home the plebs achieved political equality with the patricians by the 4th century BCE, ending the Conflict of the Orders peacefully.

From 133 BCE the late Republic saw substantial domestic strife. The Social War between Rome and its Italian allies over citizenship expanded civil violence, and mass slavery contributed to three Servile Wars. Powerful semi-autonomous generals led to civil wars, first between Marius and Sulla and in 49 BCE between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Erich S. Gruen holds that civil war caused the fall of the republic, not the reverse. It ended in 27 BCE with the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The constitution was an unwritten, evolving set of principles passed down through precedent. There were annual elections, but the system was an elective oligarchy, with powerful families largely monopolising the senior magistracies. The Senate's decrees were officially advice, yet magistrates usually followed them, and it came to control finances and external affairs. Consuls and praetors held imperium, the authority to command an army. Census figures report 130,000 Romans in 509 BCE and 4,937,000 in 14 CE. From 107 BCE all citizens, whatever their wealth, could enter the army, which became paid and attracted the poorest.
roman-seleucid-war: A "cold war" between Rome and the Seleucid Empire had begun in 196 BCE. Rome saw Greece as its sphere of influence and Asia Minor as a buffer, while Antiochus III saw Asia Minor as a core part of his empire and Greece as the buffer. After the Second Macedonian War, Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks, including those under Antiochus in Asia Minor, and in 195 BCE Roman forces largely withdrew from Greece.

Antiochus campaigned against tribes in Thrace and read the withdrawal as a retreat. In late 193 BCE the Aetolian League, hoping to draw both powers into a war for its own advantage, invited Antiochus to liberate Greece. He landed at Demetrias and said he would free the Greeks from Roman subjugation.

Antiochus was received coolly in Greece, and the Achaean League declared war on him. In the spring of 191 BCE the Macedonians entered the war against the Aetolians, and the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio marched into Thessaly. Antiochus chose to fight at Thermopylae, was overwhelmingly defeated and fled to Ephesus, less than six months after his arrival at Demetrias. Roman fleets then defeated his navy off Corycus and at the Battle of Myonessus, and the Rhodians stopped Hannibal's fleet at the Eurymedon. The consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio and his legate Scipio Africanus crossed the Hellespont without opposition.

Antiochus offered to pay half the Roman costs and give up Smyrna, Lampsacus and Alexandria Troas, but the Scipios demanded all of Asia Minor north-west of the Taurus Mountains and the whole cost of the war. Around the middle of December 190 BCE the armies met near Magnesia ad Sipylum. Livy gives Antiochus 60,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry against about 30,000, though John Grainger argues both had about 50,000. Eumenes II of Pergamum led a cavalry charge, and when the Seleucid infantry was thrown into disorder by its own elephants Eumenes annihilated the phalanx from the flank.

At Sardis Antiochus accepted terms later settled at Apamea in 188 BCE. He ceded his lands beyond the Taurus Mountains, paid 15,000 Euboeic talents over twelve years, gave twenty hostages, including his youngest son, and was to surrender enemies of Rome such as Hannibal. His navy was limited to ten large ships and he was to give up war elephants. The senate gave Rhodes Lycia and Caria south of the Maeander and Eumenes the rest, and wished to keep no army in Asia Minor. The Aetolians, who made a separate peace in 189 BCE, were reduced to a Roman client state. Hannibal fled and killed himself in 183 or 182 BCE, and Antiochus died on 3 July 187 BCE.
roman-senate: The word senatus comes from senex, 'old man', and means an assembly of elders. In the Roman Kingdom, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, the heads of the leading clans formed a board of elders. The senate is said to have been created by Rome's first king, Romulus. It served as the king's council, and its most important function was to choose new kings: the interrex nominated a candidate, the senate approved him, the people elected him and the senate approved him again. After the last king was overthrown, Lucius Junius Brutus and Publius Valerius Publicola are said to have raised the senate to 300 members in 509 BCE.

In the Republic the senate had 300 to 500 members who served for life, at first only patricians. Its decrees, the senatus consulta, were formally advice to a magistrate and had no legal force, but they were usually obeyed. Only the senate could authorise spending from the treasury, and it decided which magistrate governed which province. After 202 BCE the senatus consultum ultimum replaced the dictatorship in emergencies.

Senators wore a toga with a broad purple stripe and an iron, later gold, ring. They could not engage in banking or public contracts, could not leave Italy without permission and were paid no salary. Meetings opened with a sacrifice and a search for omens and had to end by nightfall, so a determined senator could talk a proposal to death.

The senate reached the apex of its republican power in the middle Republic and declined in the late Republic after the reforms of the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. Under the Principate it kept its legal position but little real authority, though the assemblies' powers passed to it. Around 300 CE Diocletian's reforms ended any illusion that it had independent powers, and Constantine created a second senate in Constantinople.

The Western senate worked under Odoacer and the Ostrogothic kings and was restored after Justinian I's reconquest of Italy, but the long war had mortally weakened it, and it had disappeared by the early 7th century. The Eastern senate lasted into the early 13th century; its last known act was to elect Nicholas Kanabos as emperor in 1204.
roman-the-great: Roman was the son of Mstislav Iziaslavich, Grand Prince of Kiev, and Agnes of Poland, and his maternal grandfather was the Polish prince Boleslaw the Wrymouth. Invited by the locals to rule Novgorod in 1168, he was opposed by Andrey Bogolyubsky, the ruler of Vladimir and Suzdal, and in 1170 he defeated Andrey's son Mstislav in battle.

After his father died that year he was expelled from Novgorod and went to Volhynia, where he inherited the city of Volodymyr. In 1188 he married Predslava, daughter of the future Kyivan prince Rurik Rostislavich, and in the same year he took Halych after the death of Yaroslav Osmomysl, but the Hungarian king Bela III soon expelled him.

After Rurik inherited Kyiv in 1194 he granted Roman several towns, then withdrew the grant under pressure from Vsevolod the Big Nest. Roman allied with Yaroslav II Vsevolodovich of Chernigov and with the Polish dukes Leszek the White and Konrad of Masovia, and was wounded fighting in a Polish quarrel. In 1196 he raided the Jotvingians, who were attacking his borders, and divorced his wife to marry a woman named Anna, whose ancestry is unclear; some theorise that she was a daughter of the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos.

In 1199 he took Halych for the second time, creating the Principality of Galicia-Volhynia. He suppressed local boyar clans and had the support of the townspeople. In 1201–1202 and 1203–1204 he led two successful campaigns against the Cumans, who were then allied with Rurik, and captured Kyiv, installing his brother-in-law Rostislav Rurikovich as prince. Byzantine chroniclers applied the title autocrate to him, though there is no evidence that he took it officially.

In 1205 Roman broke with Leszek and Konrad for reasons that are unknown and invaded Poland. The Galician-Volhynian Chronicle says the boyar Volodyslav Kormylchych advised it. At the Battle of Zawichost his force was attacked by Polish knights and he was killed. His young sons Daniel and Vasylko were expelled from Halych by the boyars, and the throne passed to Vladimir III Igorevich. His death led to the War of the Galician Succession (1205–1245). The Galician-Volhynian chroniclers praised him as a wise ruler, while the Polish historian Jan Długosz saw a tyrant. He founded the Romanovichi branch of the Rurikids, which ruled Galicia–Volhynia until 1340.
roman-triumph: Roman historians placed the first triumph in the mythical past. Plutarch and some Roman sources traced it, and the kingly garb of the triumphator, to Rome's first king Romulus, whose defeat of King Acron of the Caeninenses was thought to date from the foundation of Rome in 753 BCE. Roman etymologists thought the soldiers' chant of triumpe came through Etruscan from the Greek thriambus, cried out in Dionysian processions.
