Like much in Roman culture, the triumph drew on Etruscan and Greek precedents. The purple, embroidered toga picta of the general was thought to derive from the royal toga of Rome's Etruscan kings. The earliest triumphs were probably simple victory parades, ending with some dedication to the gods.

On the day, the general wore a laurel crown, the toga picta and red boots, regalia tied to the monarchy and to the statue of Jupiter Capitolinus. In some accounts his face was painted red. He rode in a four-horse chariot in unarmed procession, with spoils and captives leading the way and his army behind. At the temple of Capitoline Jupiter he sacrificed two white oxen and laid tokens of victory at the statue's feet.

The procession gathered on the Campus Martius, entered the city through a Porta Triumphalis, passed through the Forum along the Via Sacra and climbed the Capitoline Hill, a distance of just under 4 km. Triumphs were notoriously long and slow, and the longest lasted two or three days. Banquets and games, usually paid for by the general from his share of the loot, followed.

In Republican tradition only the Senate could grant a triumph, after a debate and vote confirmed by a people's assembly. No firm evidence shows fixed triumphal laws, although Valerius Maximus listed some, such as a requirement to have killed 5,000 enemies in a single battle. Some triumphs went ahead after the Senate refused, and a lesser honour, the ovation, was granted to Marcus Marcellus in 211 BCE and to Crassus in 71 BCE.

In the Late Republic triumphs grew more frequent and lavish. Triumphal generals minted coins to spread their fame, as Pompey did. Under Augustus the honour became an imperial privilege. The last triumph on the Fasti Triumphales is for 19 BCE, and others received only triumphal ornaments or an ovation.

Later rulers imitated the triumph. In 1325 the city of Lucca gave Castruccio Castracani a Roman-style triumph after the Battle of Altopascio. Petrarch's Triumphs, Andrea Mantegna's Triumphs of Caesar (1484-92) and Maximilian I's Triumphal Procession (1512-19) drew on it. Charles V's royal entry into Rome on 5 April 1536 followed the ancient route and was described as a triumph over the infidel.
roman-von-ungern-sternberg: Ungern-Sternberg was born in Graz to a noble Baltic German family that had settled in present-day Estonia in the Middle Ages. His first language was German, and he became fluent in French, Russian, English and Estonian. His parents divorced in 1891 and he grew up on the estate of his mother's second husband near Reval (Tallinn). He claimed descent from Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and this played a part in his dream of reviving the Mongol Empire.

In the First World War he served with Cossack regiments on the Eastern Front and won several Russian decorations, but he was also known as reckless and unstable and was sentenced to two months in prison after a drunken attack on another officer in October 1916.

An ultraconservative monarchist, Ungern saw the February Revolution as the beginning of the end of Russia. In the Caucasus he met the Cossack captain Grigory Semyonov, and after the October Revolution the two declared allegiance to the Romanov dynasty and joined the White forces in the Transbaikal region. Semyonov refused to recognise Admiral Alexander Kolchak and was supported by the Japanese. Ungern believed monarchs were accountable only to God and wanted the monarchy restored as before 1905. In August 1920 he broke with Semyonov and led his Asiatic Cavalry Division, about 1,500 men, into Outer Mongolia. Assaults on Urga in October and November 1920 failed with heavy losses.

On 21 February 1921, Ungern, with Mongolian lamas and princes, brought the Bogd Khan back to Urga, and on 22 February Mongolia was proclaimed an independent monarchy. The Bogd Khan gave Ungern the title darkhan khoshoi chin wang. During his five-month occupation he kept order in the capital by fear and brutal violence against Bolsheviks and Chinese. Soviet, Far Eastern Republic and Mongolian forces advanced against him in 1921. He was defeated between 11 and 13 June near Troitskosavsk, and the Red and Mongol forces entered Urga on 6 July.

He was taken prisoner by the Red Army and tried for counter-revolution in Novonikolayevsk, now Novosibirsk. After a six-hour show trial he was executed on 15 September 1921. His attraction to Vajrayana Buddhism and his violence towards enemies and his own men earned him the names the Mad Baron and the Bloody Baron. The historian John Jennings argues that his Mongolian campaign removed the one force in the region that might have matched the Red Army and made a Soviet invasion inevitable. Ossendowski's book Beasts, Men and Gods, published in 1922, made his story widely known.
romance-of-the-three-kingdoms: Stories about the heroes of the Three Kingdoms were the basis of entertainment from the Sui and Tang dynasties. By the Song dynasty, professional oral storytellers specialised in them. The earliest written work to combine these stories was a pinghua, the Sanguozhi Pinghua, published between 1321 and 1323. The novel draws on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, Pei Songzhi's annotations, earlier chronicles and Liu Yiqing's A New Account of the Tales of the World, and it combines historical figures and events with fictional scenes, speeches and supernatural episodes.

Luo Guanzhong, a playwright who lived sometime between 1315 and 1400, is the traditional author. The novel was first printed in 1522 as Sanguozhi Tongsu Yanyi, in an edition with a preface dated 1494, and it may have circulated earlier in manuscript. The standard text most readers know is a recension by Mao Lun and his son Mao Zonggang.

The narrative runs from the decline of the Han dynasty and the Yellow Turban Rebellion to the reunification of China under the Western Jin in 280. It has 120 chapters, about 800,000 words and nearly a thousand characters, most of them historical. Its early episodes include Dong Zhuo's seizure of the capital Luoyang, and the oath of Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei in the Peach Garden. Liu Bei visits Zhuge Liang three times to recruit him; the visits are documented in other sources, but the novel expanded them into a dramatic story.

The Battle of Red Cliffs in 208, won by the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei over Cao Cao, is followed by Liu Bei's takeover of Yi Province. Sun Quan then takes Jing Province, and Guan Yu is captured and executed. Liu Bei is defeated at the Battle of Yiling by Lu Xun. The narrative gives particular moral and political weight to Liu Bei and Shu Han.

The novel is counted among the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature and is arguably the most widely read historical novel in late imperial and modern China. Its writing belongs to the emergence of written vernacular in the Ming period. Many Chinese proverbs derive from it. Nurhaci is said to have learned Chinese military and political strategy from it, and it was among the first Chinese books translated into Manchu. It has canonical status in Korea, Japan and Vietnam, and has been called the national novel of Korea.

The novel also shaped religious practice. Guan Yu, already honoured in a local cult near a monastery in Hubei, appears in the novel as a spirit asking the monk Pujing for his head; he is still revered as a Bodhisattva in Buddhist tradition. The story has been retold in television series, manga and video games.
romance-of-the-western-chamber: The play is set in the Tang dynasty and divided into five parts. Cui Yingying, daughter of a chief minister of the Tang court, is resting at a Buddhist monastery with her mother while escorting her father's coffin home, and the young scholar Zhang Sheng falls in love with her at first sight. When the bandit Sun the Flying Tiger surrounds the monastery to seize her, her mother promises her hand to whoever drives him away. Zhang's childhood friend General Du subdues the bandits, but the mother breaks her word, claiming Yingying is betrothed to another official's son.

The maid Hongniang brings the lovers together in secret. On discovering this, the mother consents to a marriage on condition that Zhang pass the civil service examination in the capital. He proves a brilliant scholar, is appointed to high office, and the play ends with the wedding.

The story first appeared in Yingying's Biography, a short story in literary Chinese by Yuan Zhen of the Tang dynasty, in which Zhang Sheng breaks with Yingying and never asks for her hand. The tale stayed popular, recited versions accumulated, and the ending gradually became a happy one. The first example of the new ending is a chantefable, or zhu gongdiao, by Master Dong of the Jin dynasty, Dong Jieyuan, on which Wang Shifu closely modelled his play.

Because it shows the lovers uniting outside marriage, moralists long called the work licentious and placed it high on lists of forbidden books; Gui Guang (1613–1673) called it a book teaching debauchery, while the critic Jin Shengtan defended it. It gave rise to sequels, parodies and rewritings, shaped The Peony Pavilion and Dream of the Red Chamber, in which Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu read it together, and made Hongniang a byword for a matchmaker. It is still performed in Kun Opera and Beijing Opera.

Painters such as Qian Gu, Tang Yin and Chen Hongshou illustrated it, and Min Qiji published a series of colour woodblock prints of it in 1640. Its scenes decorated porcelain over many centuries. It was translated into French by Stanislas Julien in 1872 and filmed as a silent film by Hou Yao in 1927.
romanesque-architecture: Romanesque was the first distinctive style to spread across Europe since the Roman Empire. After the decline of Rome, Roman building methods survived to an extent in western Europe, where Merovingian, Carolingian and Ottonian architects went on building large stone monastery churches and palaces. The round arch stayed in use, but the engineering skills needed to vault large spaces and build large domes were lost. The style emerged nearly simultaneously in several countries, combining features of ancient Roman and Byzantine buildings with local traditions. Rulers founded churches as seats of power and as places of coronation and burial, among them the Abbey of Saint-Denis, Speyer Cathedral and Westminster Abbey.

The general impression is one of massive solidity. Unlike Roman and Gothic building, where the load is carried by columns and arches, Romanesque, like Byzantine architecture, relies on its walls and on sections of wall called piers. The walls are very thick, often double shells filled with rubble, with few and small openings, and are built of local material: brick in Italy, Poland and much of Germany, and limestone, granite and flint elsewhere. Arches are nearly always semicircular, and arcading is the most significant decoration.

Most buildings have wooden roofs. Stone vaults developed from barrel and groin vaults into the ribbed vault, the main structural innovation of the period. A Romanesque doorway has receding planes with a circular shaft in each, sometimes as many as twelve, symbolic of the apostles.

Churches greatly outnumber the castles built in this period, and the late 11th and 12th centuries saw an unprecedented growth in the number of churches, among them Santa Maria in Cosmedin in Rome, San Zeno Maggiore in Verona, Mont Saint-Michel and the abbeys of the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. The Gothic style then rebuilt most Romanesque churches wholly or partly in prosperous areas such as England and Portugal, so the largest groups survive in regions less prosperous later, such as southern France and rural Spain, Portugal and Italy. The term Romanesque, meaning in the manner of Romans, has been used since early in the 19th century.
romani-people: Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests that the Romani originated in north-western regions of the Indian subcontinent, particularly in present-day Punjab, Rajasthan and Sindh. Because the Romani did not chronicle their history, most hypotheses about early Roma rest on linguistic data. Genetic findings published in 2012 suggest that the ancestors of present-day scheduled caste and scheduled tribe populations of northern India, traditionally called the Doma, are the likely ancestral populations of European Roma.

Historians now believe the westward migration, possibly in waves, occurred around 1000 CE, perhaps in the context of the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. The Romani moved west into the Ghaznavid Empire and later the Byzantine Empire. Armenian-origin words in Romani indicate that they passed through Armenia.

The Romani arrived in Europe through the Balkans, probably in the twelfth century. A document of 1068 from Constantinople mentions Atsingani, probably meaning Roma. The English word Gypsy comes from Egipcien, the medieval belief that they were itinerant Egyptians. Their reception was mixed. The first recorded transaction for a Romani slave in Wallachia dates to 1385, while Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund issued them safe conduct in 1417.

Expulsions followed: from the Meissen region of Germany in 1416, Lucerne in 1471, Milan in 1493, France in 1504, Catalonia in 1512, Sweden in 1525, England in 1530 and Denmark in 1536. From 1510 any Roma found in Switzerland were to be executed, and Portugal began deporting Roma to its colonies in 1538. Large-scale emigration to the Americas began in the 1860s. In the mid- to late twentieth century forced sterilisation in several European countries reduced Roma populations.

The Romani traditionally led a nomadic, itinerant life. Many subgroups and clans name themselves, among them the Sinti, Kalderash, Lovari and Manouche. The Romani language is Indo-Aryan with strong Persian, Armenian, Greek and South Slavic influence, and its dialects have more than 2 million speakers. Romanipen is the totality of the Romani spirit, culture, law and identity. The first World Romani Congress in 1971 voted to reject all exonyms for the Romani, including Gypsy.
romania: Romania lies on the lower course of the Danube and on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It covers 238,397 square kilometres, and its terrain is distributed roughly equally between mountains, hills and plains. The Carpathian Mountains dominate the centre, with 14 ranges reaching above 2,000 metres; the highest is Moldoveanu Peak at 2,544 metres. They are surrounded by the Moldavian and Transylvanian plateaus, the Pannonian Plain and the Wallachian plains.

The Danube flows into the Black Sea and forms the Danube Delta, the second-largest and best-preserved delta in Europe. At 5,800 square kilometres it is the largest continuous marshland in Europe. Romania has one of the largest areas of undisturbed forest in Europe, covering almost 27% of its territory, and about 50% of Europe's brown bears outside Russia.

Human remains from Peștera cu Oase, about 40,000 years old, are the oldest known Homo sapiens in Europe. Salt production at the Poiana Slatinei site began between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE, the earliest evidence for salt exploitation in Europe, and the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture flourished in the 3rd millennium BCE. Greek colonies were established on the Black Sea coast in the 7th century BCE. Burebista, the first Dacian ruler to unite the local tribes, conquered the Greek colonies in Dobruja between around 55 and 44 BCE, and his kingdom collapsed after he was murdered in 44 BCE.

Part of the territory became the Roman province of Dacia after Trajan's Dacian Wars. The modern state was formed in 1859 through the union of Moldavia and Wallachia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza and took the name Romania in 1866. The Great Union of 1918 and the treaties that followed created Greater Romania, which reached its largest territorial extent. King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and the communist Romanian People's Republic followed. The revolution of 1989 ended communism.

Romania is a semi-presidential republic with a bicameral Parliament of a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. It joined the European Union in 2007 and is a member of NATO. The 2021 census counted 19,053,815 people, of whom 89.33% were Romanians, 6.05% Hungarians and 3.44% Roma; the Council of Europe puts the Roma figure higher, at 8.32%.

The name derives from the endonym român, from Latin romanus. The oldest surviving document in Romanian is Neacșu's letter, which mentions Țeara Rumânească, the Romanian Land, meaning Wallachia. About 12 million Romanians and people with Romanian-born ancestors live abroad.
romanians: The lands of present-day Romania and Moldova were inhabited by the ancient Getae and Dacian tribes. King Burebista united the tribes of the Dacian kingdom, and King Decebalus, its last king, saw it conquered by the Roman Empire in 106 CE after two wars with Trajan. Roman administration withdrew between 271 and 275 under Emperor Aurelian. Where the Romanians came from is debated. The Daco-Roman continuity theory holds that they descend from Romans and Romanized Dacians of the province of Dacia. Another holds that their ancestors were Romanized peoples of provinces south of the Danube who later migrated north. Dimitrie Onciul's admigration theory is a compromise between the two.

In the Middle Ages Romanians were mostly known as Vlachs, a term of ancient Germanic origin related to Welsh and Walloon, which Slavs passed on to Hungarians and Greeks. Vlachs lived across the Balkans, in Transylvania, and as far north as Poland and as far west as Moravia. Moldavia and Wallachia stayed autonomous within the Ottoman world, unlike other Ottoman territories in Europe. Transylvania was part of the Kingdom of Hungary until 1541 and later a vassal principality of the Ottomans. The three principalities were united for several months in 1600 under the Wallachian prince Michael the Brave. In 1812 the Treaty of Bucharest gave Russia the eastern half of Moldavia, known as Bessarabia.

During the Second World War the Kingdom of Romania lost Northern Transylvania to Hungary through the Second Vienna Award, while the Soviet Union took Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. After the war the Soviet Union imposed a communist government and King Michael was forced to abdicate. Nicolae Ceaușescu headed the Romanian Communist Party from 1965, and the Romanian Revolution of 1989 ended his rule.

Romanians speak Romanian, a Romance language whose basic vocabulary is Latin, with some words assumed to be Dacian. It borrowed from Slavic languages in the Middle Ages, later from German, Hungarian and Turkish, and in the modern era from French and Italian. The name român comes from Latin romanus; early travellers such as Francesco della Valle in 1532 noted that Romanians called themselves Romans. Closely related peoples are the Aromanians, Megleno-Romanians and Istro-Romanians. The great majority of Romanians belong to the Romanian Orthodox Church. Estimates of their worldwide number range from 24 to 30 million, and large communities live in Italy and Spain.
romanos-i-lekapenos: Romanos took his epithet from his birthplace, Lakape, between Melitene and Samosata. His father was a peasant, Theophylaktos, who had saved the emperor Basil I in battle at Tephrike in 872 and was rewarded with a place in the Imperial Guard and estates. Romanos had no refined education, for which his son-in-law Constantine VII later abused him, but he rose in the army under Leo VI the Wise. He was general of the naval theme of Samos in 911 and later admiral of the fleet. After the Bulgarian victory at the Battle of Acheloos in 917, he sailed to Constantinople and gradually overcame the discredited regency of Empress Zoe Karvounopsina.

On 25 March 919, at the head of his fleet, Romanos seized the Boukoleon Palace and the government. In April his daughter Helena married Constantine VII, and he took the title basileopator. He was named caesar on 24 September 920 and crowned senior emperor on 17 December. He crowned his own sons co-emperors, Christopher in 921 and Stephen and Constantine in 924, but left Constantine VII untouched, and so was called the gentle usurper.

The war with Simeon I of Bulgaria took the first four years of his reign. In 924 he met Simeon at Kosmidion and ended the siege of the capital, in effect by tacitly recognising him as emperor of Bulgaria. After Simeon's death in May 927 his granddaughter Maria, renamed Eirene, married the new Bulgarian emperor Peter I in September.

In the east Romanos' general John Kourkouas campaigned from 926 against the Abbasids and their vassals and won Melitene in 934, often seen as the first major Byzantine territorial recovery from the Muslims. In 944 his withdrawal from Edessa gained the relic called the mandylion. A Kievan raid in 941 was defeated with Greek fire, and in 944 Romanos made a treaty with Prince Igor of Kiev. At home he issued laws protecting small landowners from the dynatoi, increased taxes on the aristocracy and, in 933, made his young son Theophylaktos patriarch.

Romanos grew guilt-ridden over the usurpation of Constantine VII's throne. His eldest son Christopher died in 931. Fearing that Romanos would let Constantine VII succeed, his younger sons Stephen and Constantine arrested him on 20 (or 16) December 944 and forced him to become a monk on the Princes' Islands.

The people of Constantinople rose when the sons threatened Constantine VII, and the sons were also exiled. Romanos died on 15 June 948 and was buried in the church of Myrelaion, the burial church he had built beside his palace. Constantine VII wrote that Romanos was an uneducated man of low descent, and his descendants included every emperor for the next century.
romanos-iii-argyros: Romanos Argyros, born in 968, was the son of Marianos, a member of the Argyros family; his grandfather, another Romanos Argyros, had married Agatha, a daughter of Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos. His siblings included Basil Argyros, a general and governor under Basil II, and Pulcheria Argyropoulina, who reportedly helped him control Zoë's spending. He served as judge in Opsikion, where he persecuted heretics at Akmoneia, then as quaestor and one of the judges of the Hippodrome, appearing in the legal compendium called the Peira. He became patrikios and administrator of the Great Church, and under Constantine VIII was urban prefect of Constantinople, formal head of the Senate.

In late 1028 the dying Constantine VIII, who had no son, summoned Constantine Dalassenos from Antioch to marry his eldest daughter Zoë. The emperor's advisers preferred a less formidable candidate and persuaded him to choose Romanos instead. He was forced to divorce his wife Helena, who was sent to a monastery, and marry Zoë, then 50 to his 60. The marriage took place on 9 November 1028, and Constantine died on 11 November. Romanos idealised Marcus Aurelius and sought to imitate Trajan's military prowess. He spent large sums on buildings and endowed churches and monasteries, and he eased taxation for the aristocracy, abandoning earlier policy against nobles' privileges. Peasants increasingly fell into serfdom, weakening the army's recruiting base.

In 1030 he led an army against the Mirdasids of Aleppo. It camped at a waterless site, its scouts were ambushed and a cavalry attack was defeated; on 10 August it withdrew towards Antioch, discipline broke down and the army fled, with only the imperial bodyguard holding firm. Accounts of the losses differ: John Skylitzes speaks of a terrible rout, Yahya of Antioch of remarkably few casualties. A treaty made Aleppo a tributary. In 1032 George Maniakes captured and defended Edessa. His sister-in-law Theodora was implicated in plots in 1029 and 1031 and was confined at the monastery of Petrion.

Romanos limited Zoë's expenses, which deepened their estrangement; he took a mistress, and Zoë fell in love with Michael, brother of the court eunuch John the Orphanotrophos. Romanos died on 11 April 1034, supposedly poisoned by his wife, and some speculate that he was drowned in a bath on her orders. He was buried in the Church of St Mary Peribleptos, which he had built. Zoë and Michael married the same day, and Patriarch Alexios I crowned Michael IV after receiving 50 pounds of gold. Romanos is recorded as a well-meaning but ineffective emperor who disorganised the tax system and undermined the military.
romanos-iv-diogenes: Romanos was the son of the general Constantine Diogenes and belonged to the Diogenai, a powerful family of the Cappadocian military aristocracy. He rose as a commander on the frontiers, serving in Syria and on the Danubian frontier, and in 1067 became duke of a new province centred on Serdica.

He was then convicted of attempting to usurp the throne of the sons of Constantine X Doukas. While he awaited sentence, the regent Eudokia Makrembolitissa pardoned him and chose him as her husband, since the Seljuk Turks had overrun much of Cappadocia and the army needed an energetic general. They married on 1 January 1068, and he was crowned Emperor of the Romans.

Romanos was brave to the point of recklessness, but he inherited an army weakened by years of neglect and made up largely of ill-disciplined mercenaries. His campaigns of 1068 and 1069 against the Turks and the Emirate of Aleppo brought limited success, and Turkish raiders sacked Amorium and Iconium. At home he cut court spending and the salaries of the court nobility, and he antagonised the Doukas family, led by the Caesar John Doukas. In 1071 the last Byzantine outpost in Italy, Bari, fell into Norman hands.

In the spring of 1071 Romanos marched east to recover Manzikert and divided his army. The Seljuk army of Sultan Alp Arslan approached, and the Uzes mercenaries deserted to the Turks. In the battle of 26 August 1071 the Byzantine army was defeated. Romanos fought on after his horse was killed, was wounded in the hand and was taken prisoner. Byzantine sources say Alp Arslan treated him with kindness and released him after about eight days for a treaty and a ransom, first set at 10,000,000 nomismata and reduced to 1,500,000, with 360,000 more a year. Some Muslim sources describe harsher treatment.

While Romanos was a prisoner, the Doukas family declared him deposed and proclaimed Michael VII Doukas emperor, on about 1 October 1071. Romanos gathered troops but was defeated and surrendered at Adana in Cilicia, on assurances that his life would be spared if he retired to a monastery. John Doukas broke the agreement. Romanos was blinded at Kotyaion on 29 June 1072 and exiled to Prote in the Sea of Marmara, where his untreated wound became infected and he died. Historians connect his defeat at Manzikert with the weakening of Byzantine authority in Anatolia and its gradual Turkification.
romanticism: Romanticism originated in Europe towards the end of the 18th century, in response to the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution. Its first ideas arose from an earlier German Counter-Enlightenment movement, Sturm und Drang (Storm and Stress), which criticised the Enlightenment claim that humans can fully comprehend the world through reason alone. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther, published in 1774, helped to shape its ideals.

The period varies by country and art. Scholars of English literature place it between about 1789 or 1798 and about 1830, and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1798 is often held to mark its start. The consensus is that it peaked between 1800 and 1850.

Romantics rejected the social conventions of their time in favour of individualism, and argued that passion and intuition were crucial to understanding the world. Beauty, they held, was more than form, since it evokes a strong emotional response. Their recurring themes were a reverence for nature and the supernatural, an idealisation of the past as a nobler era, a fascination with the exotic and mysterious, and a celebration of the heroic and the sublime.

They preferred the medieval to the classical, seeing the Middle Ages as an age of chivalry and a more organic relationship between humans and their surroundings, in contrast to an industrial society they thought alienating. The movement shaped literature, painting, music and architecture, and touched politics: Romantic thinking influenced conservatism, liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In Poland it is often taken to begin with Adam Mickiewicz's first poems in 1822 and to end with the suppression of the January Uprising of 1863 against the Russians, and was strongly marked by interest in Polish history.

By the First World War the cultural climate had changed so far that Romanticism had dispersed into later movements. Late Romantic figures such as Rachmaninoff, who died in the 1940s, were widely respected but seen as anachronisms. Romantic nationalism has been judged to have had a largely negative effect on 19th-century history writing, because each nation tended to produce its own version of the past with clear heroes and villains.

Romantic thought and art went on to influence art and music, speculative fiction, philosophy, politics and environmentalism. The modern sense of romanticising something often has little to do with the historical movement.
rome: Rome lies in the Lazio region of central Italy on the Tiber. The original settlement developed on hills facing a ford beside the Tiber Island, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was built on seven hills: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal and Viminal. The city centre is about 24 kilometres inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea, though the city territory extends to the shore at Ostia.

The Aniene, which flows into the Tiber north of the historic centre, also crosses modern Rome. Vatican City, the smallest country in the world, is an independent country within Rome's municipal boundaries, the only existing example of a country within a city.

Evidence of human occupation of the Rome area goes back approximately 14,000 years. The view that Rome grew from pastoral settlements on the Palatine Hill, above the future Roman Forum, is supported by several excavations. Today there is wide consensus that the city developed gradually through the aggregation of several villages around the largest, on the Palatine, and archaeological evidence places this in the mid-eighth century BCE. The view that Rome was founded deliberately then, as the legend of Romulus suggests, remains a fringe hypothesis.

By 550 BCE Rome was the second largest city in Italy after Taras, with an estimated population of 35,000, though other sources suggest nearly 100,000. When the Republic was founded in 509 BCE the census recorded 130,000, and the city surpassed 300,000 by 150 BCE. After the fall of the Western Empire the city slowly fell under the political control of the Papacy, and in the 8th century it became capital of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870. Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871.

Rome is the capital of Italy and a special municipality named Roma Capitale, with a population of 2.7 million. It hosts the country's principal political institutions and several United Nations agencies, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Beginning with Nicholas V (1447 to 1455), almost all popes pursued an architectural and urban programme over four hundred years, and Rome became a major centre of the Renaissance and the birthplace of the Baroque and Neoclassicism. Its first university, La Sapienza, was founded in 1303. In 98 CE, according to Sextus Julius Frontinus, Rome had nine aqueducts feeding 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins.
romsdal: Romsdal lies between Nordmøre and Sunnmøre and traditionally takes in the areas of Aukra, Molde, Rauma and Vestnes municipalities with the old Sandøy and Fræna municipalities. It is named after the valley of Romsdalen, through which the river Rauma flows to the Romsdalfjord; the Old Norse name Raumsdalr probably means the dale of Rauma. The valley is ringed by the Romsdalsalpene range, whose Romsdalhorn, 1,550 metres high, has been compared to the Matterhorn, and Trollveggen, the north face of Trollryggen, is the tallest vertical cliff in Europe.

Legend makes the district the inheritance of Raum the Old, son of Nór, whom Hversu Noregr byggðist names as the founder of Norway, and the Laxdæla saga names it as the home of Ketill Flatnose, a chieftain of the 850s who conquered the Hebrides and the Isle of Man. Before Harald Fairhair, Romsdal was a petty kingdom. Ragnvald Eysteinsson, jarl of Møre and Harald's supporter, probably lived on or near Veøya, the district's Viking Age hub of trade; the Orkneyinga saga claims his son Hrolf Ganger was Rollo of Normandy, which historians dispute.

King Eystein I died at Hustad in 1122. Late in the 12th century Veøy Church was built over an ancient pagan site. In the 1600s the Romsdal market opened at Devold as an outlet for the Lesja ironworks; it moved to Veblungsnes in 1820, and Molde later took over its role. A Scottish mercenary force that landed at Isfjorden on its way to Sweden was stopped at the Battle of Kringen. After the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 ceded the land north of the Romsdalfjord to Sweden, local farmers defied Swedish taxes and conscription until the Treaty of Copenhagen restored the region in 1660.

The largest town, Molde, is the seat of Møre og Romsdal County Municipality. Åndalsnes, near the mouth of the Rauma, is the terminus of the Rauma Line railway from Dombås; British troops landed there in April 1940, after the German invasion, as part of a move to retake Trondheim. The hairpin road of Trollstigen leads south from Åndalsnes.
romulo-betancourt: Rómulo Ernesto Betancourt Bello was born on 22 February 1908 in Guatire, a town near Caracas, the son of Luis Betancourt Bello, of Canary origin, and Virginia Bello Milano. He attended the Liceo Caracas and studied law at the Central University of Venezuela. As a young man he was expelled from Venezuela for agitation and moved to Costa Rica, where he founded and led Communist student groups. He was active in the Communist Party from 1930 until his resignation in 1935. He founded the Partido Democrático Nacional, which became an official party in 1941 as Acción Democrática.

In 1945 Acción Democrática, with the officers Marcos Pérez Jiménez and Carlos Delgado Chalbaud, overthrew the government of Isaías Medina Angarita in the October Revolution. The Revolutionary Government Junta that followed, five civilians and two officers, called a Constituent Assembly in 1946, and the 1947 constitution gave women the vote. The junta halted oil concessions and agreed a profit-sharing arrangement with foreign companies. Betancourt then handed power to his party colleague Rómulo Gallegos, who was overthrown in November 1948, and Betancourt went into exile in New York.

After Pérez Jiménez was ousted he was elected president in 1958 and became the first leader of the Punto Fijo Pact. He kept the state solvent despite low oil prices, built roads and power programmes such as the first phase of the Guri Dam, and sought industrialisation by import substitution. His minister Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonso created the Venezuelan Petroleum Corporation in 1960, and Venezuela helped found OPEC in September 1960 at Baghdad. The left rose in revolts in 1961 and 1962, Betancourt suspended civil liberties, and the guerrilla army FALN, which Fidel Castro was found to be arming, sabotaged pipelines and bombed the United States Embassy in Caracas. The Betancourt Doctrine denied recognition to any regime that came to power by military force.

In 1964 Betancourt was given a lifetime seat in the Venezuelan senate as a former president. He devoted his last years to writing and died on 28 September 1981 at Doctors Hospital in New York City. He is known as the Father of Venezuelan Democracy, and scholars credit him as the founding father of modern democratic Venezuela, with reforms in health, education and housing during his presidency.
romulo-gallegos: Rómulo Ángel del Monte Carmelo Gallegos Freire was born in Caracas to Rómulo Gallegos Osío and Rita Freire Guruceaga, into a family of humble origin. From 1903 he worked as a schoolteacher, writer, journalist and enthusiast of classical music. His novel Doña Bárbara, first published in 1929, criticised the regime of the long-time dictator Juan Vicente Gómez, and he was forced to leave the country. He took refuge in Spain, where he wrote the acclaimed novels Cantaclaro (1934) and Canaima (1935). He returned to Venezuela in 1936 and was appointed Minister of Public Education.

In 1937 Gallegos was elected to Congress, and in 1940–41 he served as Mayor of Caracas. He was involved in the coup of 1945 that brought Rómulo Betancourt and the Revolutionary Government Junta to power, in the period known as El Trienio Adeco. In the general election of 1947 he stood for the presidency as the Acción Democrática candidate and won what is generally believed to have been the country's first honest election, with over 74 percent of the vote, which is still a record for a free election in Venezuela.

He took office on 15 February 1948. His government raised the state's share of oil profits through taxation from 43 percent to 50 percent, a scheme known as fifty-fifty that was later copied in other oil-producing countries such as Saudi Arabia. He also began an open-door policy that brought an influx of Italians, who became the largest European population group in Venezuela. In November 1948 the army officers Carlos Delgado Chalbaud, Marcos Pérez Jiménez and Luis Felipe Llovera Páez overthrew him, and he took refuge first in Cuba and then in Mexico.

Gallegos returned to Venezuela after the fall of the dictatorship of Marcos Pérez Jiménez in 1958. He became a senator for life but took no active part in politics. He received the National Literature Prize in 1958 for La doncella and was elected to the Venezuelan Academy of the Language. From 1960 to 1963 he was a commissioner of the newly created Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and its first president.

He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1960 but lost to Saint-John Perse. The Rómulo Gallegos International Novel Prize was established in his honour in 1964. He died in Caracas on 5 April 1969. He is considered the most important Venezuelan novelist of the 20th century.
romulus: In Roman tradition Romulus and Remus were the sons of Rhea Silvia by the god Mars. Their grandfather Numitor, rightful king of Alba Longa, had been deposed by his brother Amulius, who made Rhea Silvia a Vestal Virgin. When the twins were born, Amulius ordered them thrown into the Tiber, but the river was swollen and the servants left them beneath a fig tree at the foot of the Palatine Hill. A she-wolf suckled them until the royal herdsman Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia found them. The brothers grew up among shepherds, and with the help of friends they killed Amulius and restored Numitor.

They then set out to found a city of their own and disagreed over the site. Remus saw six vultures over the Aventine Hill, Romulus twelve over the Palatine, and the quarrel ended with Romulus or one of his followers killing Remus.

Romulus fortified the Palatine, ploughed a furrow for the city's boundary, and accepted the crown with the people's approval. He divided the people into three tribes, the Ramnes, Titienses and Luceres, chose one hundred men to form the Senate, and set up an asylum for fugitives on the Capitoline Hill. Since the city had few women, he invited neighbouring peoples to a festival and the Romans seized the marriageable women among the Sabine guests. War followed. The Sabines under Titus Tatius took the citadel through the treachery of Tarpeia, and fighting ended only when the Sabine women stepped between the armies. The two peoples formed one community, ruled jointly by Romulus and Tatius.

After Tatius was killed in a riot at Lavinium, Romulus is said to have conquered Fidenae and ravaged the countryside of Veii. The founding of Rome was commemorated each year on 21 April at the Parilia.

After a reign of thirty-seven years Romulus is said to have disappeared in a storm while reviewing his troops on the Campus Martius. Livy reports that he was either murdered by the senators or raised to heaven by Mars, and prefers the latter. He gained a cult, later assimilated to that of Quirinus, and was succeeded by Numa Pompilius, a Sabine.

How far a historical figure lies behind the legend is unclear and disputed. Most modern historians think the name Romulus is a back-formation from the name of the city. A rectangular tuff chest of the 6th century BCE, found by Giacomo Boni in 1899 beside the Lapis Niger and rediscovered in 2020, has been called the Tomb of Romulus, but no remains were found and it is more likely a cenotaph.
romulus-augustulus: Romulus was born between about 460 and 465 and was named after his maternal grandfather, a nobleman from Poetovio in Noricum, a comes who was sent on an embassy to Attila in 449. His father Orestes was a Roman citizen from Pannonia who had once served as secretary to Attila. The name of his mother is not known; it might have been Barbaria. On his accession he took Augustus as a proper name, and his coins read Romulus Augustus. The nickname Augustulus, little Augustus, was a derisive reference to his youth, never in official use, and in Greek his first name was twisted into Momylus, little disgrace.

In 475 the emperor Julius Nepos named Orestes magister militum and sent him against rebelling Visigoths and Burgundians. Orestes instead heeded the grievances of his troops, many of them foederati, and marched on Ravenna, which he entered on 28 August 475; Nepos escaped to Salona in Dalmatia.

After an interregnum of two months Orestes proclaimed Romulus emperor on 31 October 475, when he may have been as young as ten. Romulus was little more than a figurehead, and his father ran much of the administration. The eastern emperor Zeno never recognised him, since Nepos, invested by Leo I, still claimed the title in exile. In 476 the foederati in Italy, mainly Herules, Scirians and Turcilingians, demanded land to settle on. Orestes refused, and under their leader Odoacer they defeated and executed him at Ticinum on 28 August 476.

On 4 September Odoacer captured Ravenna and deposed Romulus. He became the first King of Italy, sent the western regalia to Zeno and ruled without a further emperor in the West, nominally under Zeno's authority. Odoacer spared Romulus, on account of his youth and beauty, with a pension of 6,000 solidi and an estate in Campania, the castellum Lucullanum. Little is known of his later life. He may have helped to found a monastery there around the remains of Saint Severinus, and a letter of Theodoric the Great of 507 or 511 to a Romulus may refer to him. Very few records of his reign survive, and no policies, laws or significant inscriptions are known.
ronald-reagan: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on 6 February 1911 in an apartment in Tampico, Illinois, the younger son of Nelle Clyde Wilson and Jack Reagan. His mother was committed to the Disciples of Christ and led prayer meetings; Reagan credited her spiritual influence. His father focused on making money for the family, a task complicated by his alcoholism. The family lived in several Illinois towns before settling in 1920 in Dixon, where Reagan attended Dixon High School and developed interests in drama and football. He graduated from Eureka College in 1932 with a degree in economics and sociology.

Reagan began as a sports broadcaster in Iowa, and a screen test in 1936 led to a seven-year contract with Warner Bros. Pictures. He arrived in Hollywood in 1937 and made thirty films, mostly B films, before beginning military service in April 1942. His part as George Gipp in Knute Rockne, All American (1940) later led reporters to call him the Gipper while he campaigned for president. He served as an officer in the Army Air Forces, producing over 400 training films, and was discharged on 9 December 1945 as a captain. He began his political life as a Democrat, admiring Franklin D. Roosevelt, and registered as a Republican in 1962 after General Electric dropped him as a speaker.

He was elected governor of California in 1966 and served from 1967 to 1975. He accepted tax increases to balance the budget, and by 1973 the state had a surplus. In 1967 he signed the Mulford Act, which prohibited the public carrying of firearms. After losing the 1976 Republican primaries to President Gerald Ford, he won the nomination in 1980 and defeated President Jimmy Carter. He was inaugurated as the 40th president on 20 January 1981. His economic policy, called Reaganomics, combined deregulation with tax cuts, including the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, and he lifted federal oil and gasoline price controls on 28 January 1981.

Reagan left the presidency on 20 January 1989, at the age of 77, and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library opened in 1991. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 1994, and his capacities gradually deteriorated. He died of pneumonia, complicated by Alzheimer's, at his home in Los Angeles on 5 June 2004. A public funeral was held in the Washington National Cathedral, where Margaret Thatcher, Brian Mulroney, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush gave eulogies, and he was interred at his presidential library. His tenure is regarded as a realignment toward conservative policies in the United States.
ronald-storrs: Ronald Henry Amherst Storrs was born in Bury St Edmunds on 19 November 1881, a son of John Storrs, then vicar of St Peter's Church and later Dean of Rochester, and Lucy Anna Marie Cust. Educated at Temple Grove School, Charterhouse and Pembroke College, Cambridge, he took the Classical Tripos in 1903 and then studied Arabic under Edward Granville Browne.

He joined the Egyptian Finance Ministry in 1904 and five years later succeeded Harry Boyle as Oriental Secretary to the British Agency in Cairo. T. E. Lawrence called him the most brilliant Englishman in the Near East. In the First World War he served in the Arab Bureau and took part in the negotiations with Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, and the organisation of the Arab Revolt; he held that the Sharif asked for more territory than he had a right to and favoured a British-sponsored Egyptian empire taking in Syria and Palestine.

As military governor of Jerusalem, with the rank of colonel, he succeeded Brigadier General Neville Travers Borton and claimed to be the first since Pontius Pilate. The Nebi Musa riots of 1920 came during his term. Trying to support Zionism while protecting the Arab inhabitants, he earned the hostility of both sides. In 1918 he created the post of Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, first held by Kamil al-Husayni, and founded the International Chess Club, which closed within a year. From 1926 to 1932 he governed Cyprus, where Government House was burned in the revolt of 1931, and then Northern Rhodesia until he retired for his health in 1934.

He was a pallbearer at Lawrence's funeral in 1935, published his memoirs Orientations in 1937, served on the London County Council from 1937 to 1945 and broadcast for the Ministry of Information in the Second World War. He died at St Stephen's Hospital in Chelsea on 1 November 1955 and is buried at Pebmarsh in Essex. Moya Tönnies has argued that he in fact acted against political Zionism.
ronda: Ronda sits on the Ronda Depression, a Miocene plateau about 600 to 800 metres above sea level whose fertile land suits wheat, olives and vines. The Guadalevín river divides the city in two and has carved the steep gorge called El Tajo, more than 100 metres deep, above which the town perches. Around it are prehistoric remains from the Neolithic, including the rock art of the Cueva de la Pileta. Ronda is traditionally identified with ancient Arunda, which was populated under Iberians and Romans.

In the fifth century the Suebi, led by Rechila, conquered Ronda. The Eastern Roman Empire retook it in the following century, and the Visigothic king Liuvigild later captured it. In 713 it fell to Umayyad troops, who named it Hisn al-Rundah and made it capital of the province of Takurunna. The polymath Abbas ibn Firnas (810–887) came from the town. After the caliphate of Córdoba broke up, Ronda became the capital of a small kingdom ruled by the Berber Banu Ifran, and most of its Islamic architectural heritage dates from this period. In 1065 the taifa of Seville, led by Abbad II al-Mu'tadid, conquered it.

As part of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, Ronda was seized by the Crown of Castile in 1485 and was granted a fuero copying Seville's. After the conquest Christians were settled in the cities while Muslim majorities stayed in the rural communities. Early in the 16th century edicts required mudéjares of the Crown of Castile to leave or convert. After the Alpujarras revolt, the resettlement of the moriscos de paces in 1570 and thefts and enslavement by Christian militias led by Antonio de Luna, the morisco community of the Serranía de Ronda radicalised and took to guerrilla warfare and banditry.

In the Peninsular War the population fell from 15,600 to 5,000 in three years. The area then became a base for guerrillas and later bandits, whose deeds inspired Washington Irving, Prosper Mérimée and Gustave Doré. In 1918 the Assembly of Ronda designed the Andalusian flag, coat of arms and anthem. The Romero family, from Francisco, born in 1698, to his grandson Pedro, who died in 1839, played a principal role in developing modern Spanish bullfighting.

Three bridges span the Tajo: the Roman or Arabic bridge, the Old Bridge and the Puente Nuevo, whose building began in 1751 and took until 1793; it towers 120 metres above the canyon floor. The Plaza de Toros, built in 1784 by José Martín de Aldehuela, who also designed the Puente Nuevo, is one of the oldest and best-preserved bullrings in Spain. The Arab baths, dating from the 13th and 14th centuries, are among the best preserved in Spain. The railway to Algeciras was built between 1890 and 1892.
rondonia: Rondônia lies in the North Region of Brazil, bordered by Acre to the west, Amazonas to the north, Mato Grosso to the east and Bolivia to the south. Its capital and largest city, Porto Velho, stands on the Madeira River. The state occupies 237,590 square kilometres and has 52 municipalities. It once held over 200,000 square kilometres of rainforest, and by 2003 about 70,000 square kilometres had been cleared. The area around the Guaporé River belongs to the Beni savanna ecoregion, and the Samuel Dam stands on the Jamari River.

Before the arrival of the Portuguese the region was home to Indigenous peoples speaking Arawan, Chapacuran, Macro-Jê, Nambikwaran, Panoan and Tupian languages and several language isolates. Linguists generally accept that the area of Rondônia is the origin of the Tupian languages. The Spaniard Ñuflo de Chávez was the first European explorer to reach the valley of the Guaporé River, between 1541 and 1542, but only passed through. Bandeirantes came around 1650 to seek gold and other minerals, and Jesuit priests founded the first village. After gold was found on the right bank of the Guaporé, the Portuguese Crown founded the Captaincy of Mato Grosso in 1748.

Its governor, Antonio Rolim de Moura Tavares, named Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade its capital in 1752 and directed the border demarcation that followed the Treaty of Madrid of 1750. Forts were built on the Guaporé to hold the frontier against the Spanish, the last being Forte Príncipe da Beira, built in 1776. The decline of mining left the region of little economic importance until rubber came to a peak late in the 19th century.

The definitive establishment of Acre in 1903 gave impetus to the region, since the Treaty of Petrópolis obliged Brazil to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway. Decree-Law No. 5812 of 13 September 1943 created the Federal Territory of Guaporé from parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso, and a law of 17 February 1956 renamed it the Federal Territory of Rondônia in honour of Marshal Cândido Rondon.

Brazil nuts and rubber were the main activities until cassiterite was found. In the 1970s and 1980s tax incentives, federal investment, highways, colonization centres and cheap land drew migrants, largely from the Center-South of Brazil, and in 1982 the territory became a state with 13 municipalities including Porto Velho.

Rondônia has about 1.8 million inhabitants, drawn from all regions of Brazil, with settlers from Paraná, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul prominent. It has 21 Indigenous Territories, the largest being the Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau Indigenous Territory of over 1.8 million hectares. Other cities include Ariquemes, Cacoal, Guajará-Mirim, Ji-Paraná and Vilhena.
rong-people: Rong was less the name of one people than a word for warlike outsiders. The historian Nicola Di Cosmo calls it a vague term for warlike foreigners and places the Rong from the upper Wei River valley along the Fen River to the Taiyuan basin and the Taihang Mountains, a zone of transition between farming and steppe life. Li Feng notes that Western Zhou bronze inscriptions often used the word to mean warfare, so a people called Rong was probably seen as a political and military adversary rather than a cultural other.

With the Dongyi of the east, the Beidi of the north and the Nanman of the south, the Rong were counted among the Four Barbarians, the Siyi. The Record of Rites repeats the stereotypes of its time: the people of the west wore their hair unbound, dressed in skins and in some cases ate no grain. Spade-foot three-legged pottery vessels and pots with one or two handles are counted among their main cultural traits.

The Quanrong are believed to have spoken a Tibeto-Burman language, and ancient Qiang remains associated with the Xirong show a close genetic affinity with present-day Sino-Tibetan peoples and with the ancient Yellow River farmers of the Yangshao culture.

King Mu of Zhou defeated the Quanrong around 964 BCE and attacked the Western Rong the following year. In 859 BCE the Rong of Taiyuan attacked the Zhou capital, and under King Li of Zhou the Western Rong and the Xianyun raided deep into Zhou territory. King Xuan of Zhou sent the State of Qin against the Western Rong, who submitted and ceded land, and the State of Jin against the Northern Rong.

Rong groups later lived among the cities of the North China Plain. Mountain Rong attacked the State of Zheng in 714 BCE and Qi in 706 BCE, Duke Zhuang of Lu fought many wars with them, and in 662 BCE the Beidi drove the Rong out of Taiyuan. After 650 BCE they are rarely mentioned, having been mostly absorbed by Qi and Jin, and in 314 BCE Qin defeated the last hostile Rong tribe.
rongelap: Rongelap is a coral atoll of 61 islets in the Pacific Ocean, forming a legislative district of the Ralik Chain of the Marshall Islands. Its land area is about 21 square kilometres, and it encloses a lagoon of about 2,600 square kilometres. The Marshall Islands were first settled by Micronesians. The first European sighting was by the Spanish navigator Álvaro de Saavedra on 1 January 1528; with Utirik, Ailinginae and Toke it was charted as the Islas de los Reyes, because of its nearness to Epiphany.

Germany claimed the Marshall Islands in 1885, Japan held them under the South Seas Mandate after World War I, and after World War II the atoll passed to the United States as part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands.

From 1946 to 1958 the United States conducted atmospheric nuclear tests, mostly at Bikini Atoll, about 120 kilometres from Rongelap. The Castle Bravo hydrogen device, fired on 1 March 1954, was two and a half times more powerful than predicted and contaminated more than 7,000 square miles of the Pacific. Fallout lay up to two centimetres deep on Rongelap. A United States military medical team visited with Geiger counters the day after but left without telling the islanders of the danger.

Nearly all the inhabitants suffered radiation sickness, with itching, vomiting, burning eyes and swelling of the neck, arms and legs, and they were evacuated and taken to Kwajalein for treatment. A secret project to study the medical effects began six days after the test, and the United States was later accused of using the islanders in research without their consent.

In 1957 the United States declared the atoll clean and safe, and the islanders returned, told to eat canned food and avoid the northern islets. Thyroid tumours appeared, many children died of leukaemia, and miscarriages and stillbirths were twice as common as among unexposed women of the Marshall Islands. The magistrate John Anjain, whose own son died of leukaemia, appealed for help without much response.

In 1985 the Rainbow Warrior of Greenpeace moved about 350 people and 100 tons of building material in three trips to Mejato on Kwajalein Atoll, 180 kilometres away, in Operation Exodus. In 1991 the people of Rongelap and Jeton Anjain received the Right Livelihood Award. A 1996 resettlement agreement with the United States Department of the Interior provided 45 million dollars.

Rongelap is a district of the Marshall Islands, lying about 120 kilometres from Bikini Atoll, and its name is tied to the hydrogen bomb tests of 1954. The Marshall Islands Public School System runs Mejatto Elementary School, which serves descendants of the Rongelap community who settled at Mejato.
ronin: The word rōnin is written with characters meaning 'wave' and 'person', and idiomatically means a vagrant or wanderer, someone who belongs to no one place. It arose in the Nara and Heian periods for a serf who had fled his master's land, and later came to be used of a samurai without a master. A samurai became one on the death of his master or after losing his favour or legal privilege. According to the Bushido Shoshinshu, a samurai was supposed to commit seppuku on the loss of his master, and one who did not was meant to suffer great shame.

Until the Sengoku period peasants made up most of the daimyō armies, so they made up most of the rōnin. In that age the bond between lord and vassal was loose, and a rōnin could serve a new lord. Many warriors served a succession of masters, and some became daimyō: Tōdō Takatora served ten lords, and Saitō Dōsan rose from merchant to daimyō.

The Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 led to the confiscation or reduction of the fiefs of many daimyō on the losing side, and many samurai became rōnin. As many as a hundred thousand joined Toyotomi Hideyori at the Siege of Osaka. Afterwards many turned to farming or became townspeople, and a few, such as Yamada Nagamasa, went overseas as mercenaries. Most lived in poverty, and their number approached half a million under the third shōgun, Tokugawa Iemitsu.

Under the Edo shogunate's rigid class system a samurai could no longer take a new master without his previous master's permission. Some rōnin became mercenaries guarding trade caravans or bodyguards of wealthy merchants. Others became bandits or hired muscle for gangs running gambling rings, brothels and protection rackets, which gave rōnin a lasting reputation for disgrace.

The shogunate at first banished them from the cities and forbade them new masters. After rōnin joined the Keian Uprising of 1651 it relaxed its limits on daimyō inheritance, which meant fewer confiscations, and allowed rōnin to join new masters. The status ended when Emperor Meiji abolished the samurai class in the 19th century.
ronnie-brunswijk: Ronnie Brunswijk was born on 7 March 1961; his birth village was Moiwana. He joined the Suriname National Army at the age of 18, was considered a good soldier and was sent to Cuba for commando training, after which he was appointed a personal bodyguard of Desi Bouterse. In 1984 he asked for a raise; instead he was discharged on 16 April and refused his back pay. He then sought recognition and rights for the Maroons of the interior, descendants of Africans who had escaped slavery and founded independent communities in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Surinamese Interior War began at Stolkertsijver on 22 July 1986, when the Jungle Commando captured twelve soldiers guarding a checkpoint. During the war the group received arms and funding from the Netherlands. On 29 November 1986 the Surinamese army attacked Moiwana, murdered at least 39 villagers, mostly women and children, and burned Brunswijk's house; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights later ordered the government to compensate the survivors. The war caused hundreds of deaths and drove more than 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. A ceasefire was negotiated at Kourou on 21 July 1989, and a final peace treaty was signed on 8 August 1992.

A Dutch court in Haarlem convicted Brunswijk in absentia of cocaine smuggling and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment, reduced to six years on appeal in 2000; he contested the evidence. He chairs the General Liberation and Development Party and has sat in the National Assembly. He owned a gold-mining company, Robruns NV, whose concessions he transferred to a foundation in July 2020 in order to qualify for the vice-presidency.

In the 2020 elections Brunswijk was elected to the National Assembly, and on 29 June 2020 he became its chairman. On 13 July he was elected vice-president by acclamation, with Chan Santokhi as president, and was inaugurated on 16 July. He also owns the football club Inter Moengotapoe and in 2002 built a stadium in Moengo. On 21 September 2021 he played 54 minutes for the club in the CONCACAF League against C.D. Olimpia of Honduras, aged 60 years and 198 days. After a video showed him paying Olimpia players, CONCACAF disqualified both clubs and banned him from its competitions for three years.
roque-dalton: Roque Antonio Dalton García was born on 14 May 1935, the son of Winnall Dalton, an American émigré who had come to El Salvador in the early 1920s, and María García Medrano, the nurse who had cared for him in hospital. He attended Externado San José, a Jesuit school for boys in San Salvador, and studied law at the University of Chile in Santiago, where he befriended leftist students and took a strong interest in socialism.

At the University of El Salvador he and the Guatemalan poet Otto René Castillo founded the University Literary Circle in 1955. A Marxist-Leninist, Dalton joined the Communist Party of El Salvador in 1957 and visited the Soviet Union that year. He was arrested for inciting revolt during the presidency of José María Lemus.

In 1961 Dalton went to Havana, where Casa de las Américas welcomed many exiled Latin American writers and where most of his poetry was published. He returned in secret to El Salvador in 1965 but was caught and held at Cojutepeque; when an earthquake brought down the wall of his cell he escaped, slipped into a religious procession and reached Cuba again.

He then worked in Prague as a correspondent for The International Review: Problems of Peace and Socialism, wrote Taberna y Otros Lugares, which won the Casa de las Américas Poetry Prize in 1969, and a biography of Miguel Mármol, a communist of the 1932 peasant uprising. He trained in Cuban military camps, and in 1973 he joined the People's Revolutionary Army (ERP) after Salvador Cayetano Carpio refused him a place as a fighter, saying his role was that of a poet.

Within the ERP, torn by a bitter factional fight, Dalton criticised its military adventurism and argued for a mass base. Opponents accused him of dividing the organisation and of working for the CIA, a charge the most commonly accepted account holds was false. He was shot dead in a house in the Santa Anita neighbourhood of San Salvador; accounts name Joaquín Villalobos and Jorge Meléndez among his killers. In January 2012 prosecutors declared the statute of limitations expired.

Dalton left almost 15 poetry collections, a novel, a personal testimony, a play, stories and essays. According to Luis Melgar Brizuela his influence was strongest from 1967 until the end of the Salvadoran Civil War in 1992, and the University of El Salvador gave him an honorary doctorate in 2012.
roquebrune-cap-martin: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin lies in the Alpes-Maritimes department of south-eastern France, between Monaco and Menton. It was called simply Roquebrune until 1921, when the name was changed to distinguish it from Roquebrune-sur-Argens in the neighbouring Var. The commune has several parts: the perched village of Roquebrune with its château, the Cap Martin peninsula, the seaside resort of Carnolès bordering Menton, and St. Roman, practically a suburb of Monaco although outside its borders.

Ligurians settled the area before Roman times. The commune, originally Roccabruna, was founded in 971 by Conrad I, Count of Ventimiglia, to protect his western border. In 1355 it came under the control of the Grimaldi family of Monaco, who held it for five centuries and strengthened the castle. It became French in 1793 and returned to Monaco in 1814. In 1804 Napoleon built a road along the coast, which linked the village to the rest of the Côte d'Azur and led to its merger with the smaller town of Cap-Martin.

A revolution related to the Italian Risorgimento in 1848 made Roccabruna and Menton free cities under the protection of the Prince of Savoy. They hoped to join the Italian kingdom of Sardinia, which did not happen; after two years of independence they were administered by the House of Savoy for ten years and were ceded to France by a plebiscite in 1861. Giuseppe Garibaldi complained that the vote was not by universal suffrage. During World War II the coast between Italy and Monte Carlo was occupied by the Kingdom of Italy until September 1943.

The Marseille–Ventimiglia railway made the coast a holiday magnet. Elisabeth of Austria stayed at the Hôtel du Cap Martin from 1894 to 1897, and Eugénie, widow of Napoleon III, owned a villa there. In the 1920s and 1930s buildings such as Coco Chanel's La Pausa and Eileen Gray and Jean Badovici's E-1027 were built. Le Corbusier built a minimalist cabanon and drowned in the sea there on 27 August 1965. The Monte Carlo Country Club, venue of the Monte-Carlo Masters tennis tournament, stands in the commune, not in Monte Carlo.
rosa-luxemburg: Luxemburg arrived in Zurich in early 1889, when Switzerland was the most important centre of Russian and Polish revolutionary Marxism in exile. She enrolled at the University of Zurich in 1890 and from 1892 studied law, public law and political economy under Julius Wolf. When she reached Germany in 1898 the party was divided by the revisionist controversy, begun by Eduard Bernstein, who argued that many of Marx's predictions were outdated and that the party should become a democratic socialist party of reform.

The Russian Revolution of 1905 shaped her theory of the mass strike, set out in a pamphlet published in 1906. On 4 August 1914 the SPD's Reichstag delegation voted unanimously for war credits. With Karl Liebknecht, Clara Zetkin and Franz Mehring she began to organise an opposition, which became the Spartacus League. She was arrested on 18 February 1915 and spent most of the war in prison, where she wrote the Junius Pamphlet.

In Social Reform or Revolution? (1900) she argued that the struggle for reforms was a means to an end, not an end in itself. In The Accumulation of Capital (1913) she held that capitalism could not realise its surplus value within its own closed system and so had to expand into pre-capitalist spheres, above all in colonies abroad. This drive, in her view, was the economic basis of imperialism and militarism. The Junius Pamphlet called the war an imperialist conflict for which all sides were responsible.

She welcomed the Russian Revolution of 1917 but, in a manuscript written in prison in 1918 and published after her death, condemned the Bolsheviks' suppression of the Constituent Assembly and their abolition of democratic freedoms.

Luxemburg was released from prison on 9 November 1918, during the German Revolution of 1918–1919. With Liebknecht she led the Spartacus League and its daily newspaper, Die Rote Fahne. The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 was not a planned putsch by the KPD, and she at first thought it a mistake, but once the masses were on the streets she urged the workers on. After the Freikorps crushed it, she and Liebknecht were captured and killed.

Her death made her a martyr for revolutionary socialists. After Paul Levi published her manuscript on the Russian Revolution in 1922, Lenin answered with a parable that praised her as an eagle while listing her errors. In Germany she and Liebknecht are honoured each January with a demonstration in Berlin.
rosa-parks: Rosa Louise McCauley was born on 4 February 1913 in Tuskegee, Alabama, the daughter of Leona, a teacher, and James McCauley, a carpenter and mason. As a baby she moved with her mother to Pine Level, Alabama, where she attended the African Methodist Episcopal church, to which she belonged all her life. She completed high school in 1933 with the encouragement of her husband, Raymond Parks, at a time when only 7 per cent of Black people in Alabama held a diploma. In 1941 she began work at Maxwell Air Force Base, which was fully integrated, and said it opened her eyes to an alternative to Jim Crow; on her way home she still had to use segregated buses.

Parks joined the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP in 1943 and served as its secretary. After three attempts between 1943 and 1945 she registered to vote despite measures to disenfranchise Black citizens, and she investigated cases of racial and sexual violence, among them those of Recy Taylor and Jeremiah Reeves. Several women had been arrested before her for keeping their seats on Montgomery buses, including Claudette Colvin, aged fifteen, in March 1955, but activists judged Colvin unsuitable as a test case. After Parks's arrest, E. D. Nixon and Clifford Durr favoured her for her standing in the community and her firm quiet spirit.

She agreed after consulting her family, and the lawyer Fred Gray took her case. The Women's Political Council, led by Jo Ann Robinson, had 35,000 leaflets printed announcing a one-day boycott for 5 December 1955, the day of her trial. After she was found guilty the boycott was extended, and the Montgomery Improvement Association ran a network of transport to sustain it.

Parks and her husband lost their jobs and fell into hardship, and in 1957 they moved to Detroit. She took part in the March on Washington in August 1963, and later supported the Free South Africa Movement. She died on 24 October 2005 aged 92. After a service in Montgomery she lay in state in the United States Capitol rotunda, where 40,000 mourners came, and was buried in Detroit. She received the Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Congressional Gold Medal, and was the first Black American memorialised in the National Statuary Hall.
rose-of-lima: Rose was born Isabel Flores de Oliva in Lima on 20 April 1586, one of eleven children of Gaspar Flores, a harquebusier in the Spanish army, and María de Oliva y Herrera, a criolla native of Lima. Her later name came from an incident in infancy, when a servant claimed to have seen her face change into a rose. In 1597 she was confirmed by Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo, who was also later declared a saint, and formally took the name Rosa.

In emulation of Catherine of Siena she began as a girl to fast three times a week and to perform severe penances in secret. When her beauty was admired she cut off her hair and rubbed peppers on her face. She rejected all suitors, against the wishes of her family, and wanted to take a vow of virginity, which her parents opposed. Her father forbade her to become a nun, so she entered the Third Order of Saint Dominic while living at home, and in her twentieth year took the habit of a tertiary and a vow of perpetual virginity.

She abstained permanently from meat, slept at most two hours a night, and wore a heavy silver crown with small spikes inside, in imitation of the Crown of Thorns. She sold needlework, lace and flowers she grew to help her family and to care for the poor, and she brought sick and hungry people to her room. For eleven years she lived this way, with intervals of ecstasy, praying and doing penance in a small grotto she had built.

Rose died on 24 August 1617, aged 31, after a long illness, and is said to have foretold the date. All the public authorities of Lima attended her funeral in the cathedral. She was beatified by Pope Clement IX on 10 May 1667 and canonised by Pope Clement X on 12 April 1671. The Catholic Church holds that many miracles followed her death, among them that she had cured a leper and that Lima smelled of roses at the hour she died.

Her feast entered the General Roman Calendar in 1729 on 30 August, because 24 August is the feast of Saint Bartholomew; Pope Paul VI's revision of 1969 moved it to 23 August. In Peru and some other Latin American countries 30 August remains a public holiday. Her skull, crowned with roses, is displayed in the basilica in Lima, and many places in the New World are named Santa Rosa.
rose-revolution: The Citizens' Union of Georgia, the party of President Eduard Shevardnadze, began to fall apart in 2000 as deputies defected. Mikheil Saakashvili, the Minister of Justice, left it in September 2001 and founded the National Movement a month later. In the 2002 local elections the party won only 70 of about 4,850 seats. Government revenue fell short of projections year after year, the International Monetary Fund suspended its funding in 2002, and unpaid salaries and pensions reached 120 million dollars by the end of 2003. Corruption among officials and police was widespread.

Non-governmental organizations, partly funded from abroad, and the independent channel Rustavi-2 helped the opposition. After a raid on Rustavi-2 in October 2001, thousands of students protested, Shevardnadze dismissed his cabinet, and Saakashvili and Zurab Zhvania left the ruling party.

Parliamentary elections were held on 2 November 2003. On 3 November international observers concluded that they fell short of OSCE commitments and other standards for democratic elections. Saakashvili claimed victory, which independent exit polls and a parallel vote tabulation by the Georgian monitoring group ISFED supported, and the united opposition urged nonviolent civil disobedience. From mid-November large demonstrations spread from Tbilisi to nearly all major towns, with the youth organization Kmara among those active.

On 22 November Shevardnadze tried to open the new session of parliament. Supporters of two opposition parties, led by Saakashvili, burst in with roses in their hands, which gave the revolution its name, and the president was forced to leave with his bodyguards. He declared a state of emergency, but elite military units refused to support him. On the evening of 23 November, after meeting Saakashvili and Zhvania in talks arranged by the Russian foreign minister Igor Ivanov, he announced his resignation. More than 50,000 people gathered in the streets of Tbilisi to mark the victory.

The parliamentary speaker, Nino Burjanadze, became acting president, and the Supreme Court annulled the results of the parliamentary elections. 2 percent of the vote and was inaugurated on 25 January, aged 36. The National Movement - Democrats won a large majority in the parliamentary elections of 28 March 2004.

In May 2004 protests in Batumi, sometimes called the Second Rose Revolution, ended with the resignation of Aslan Abashidze, the leader of the autonomous region of Adjara. The Rose Revolution is counted among the early colour revolutions, and the Orange Revolution, which followed the disputed Ukrainian presidential election of November 2004, is said to have been partly inspired by it.
rosenborg-castle: Rosenborg Castle was built in 1606 as a country summerhouse and is one of the many architectural projects of Christian IV. It is in the Dutch Renaissance style, typical of Danish buildings of the period, and was expanded several times until it reached its present form by 1624. The architects Bertel Lange and Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger are associated with its structural planning. It stands in Kongens Have, the King's Garden, which is the country's oldest royal garden. Christian IV embellished it in the Renaissance style shortly before the castle was built.

Danish rulers used the castle as a royal residence until around 1710. After the reign of Frederik IV it served as a residence only twice, both times in emergencies: after Christiansborg Palace burned down in 1794 and during the British attack on Copenhagen in 1801.

The Long Hall on the third floor was completed in 1624 as a ballroom. Around 1700 it served as the Royal Reception Room and for banquets, and only in the second half of the 19th century did it become known as the Knight's Hall. Christian V had it partly modernised with twelve tapestries showing his victories in the Scanian War of 1675–1679. Its stucco ceiling of the early 18th century shows the Danish coat of arms among the Orders of the Elephant and of Dannebrog. The hall holds the coronation chair of the absolutist kings, the throne of the queens with three silver lions in front, and a large collection of mostly 17th-century silver furniture.

The castle became state property and was opened to the public in 1838. It houses a museum of the Royal Collections, with objects from the late 16th century of Christian IV to the 19th century, some once owned by the nobility. A treasury displays the Crown Jewels and the Danish Crown Regalia, and the Throne Chair of Denmark and a Coronation Carpet are kept there. The Royal Life Guards are garrisoned in barracks beside the castle and guard it.
rosetta-stone: The Rosetta Stone is a stele of granodiorite, a fragment of a larger stele, carved during the Hellenistic period and believed to have been displayed in a temple, possibly at Sais. The decree it carries was issued by a congress of priests gathered at Memphis after the coronation of Ptolemy V and established the divine cult of the new ruler. Its date corresponds to 27 March 196 BCE, the ninth year of Ptolemy V's reign, and it was designed to re-establish the rule of the Ptolemaic kings over Egypt. The stone's rock resembles granodiorite from a small quarry at Gebel Tingar, west of Elephantine near Aswan.

The decree has only minor differences across its three versions. The top register is in Egyptian hieroglyphs, the middle in Demotic and the bottom in Ancient Greek. The damaged top register has suffered most, and only its last 14 lines remain visible. The Demotic text has survived best, with 32 lines, and the Greek has 54 lines, of which the first 27 survive in full. Three other fragmentary copies were found later, and similar bilingual and trilingual inscriptions are known, including the Decree of Canopus of 238 BCE.

French soldiers strengthening Fort Julien near Rashid (Rosetta) found the slab in mid-July 1799, after Napoleon's invasion of Egypt, when they demolished a wall. Lieutenant Pierre-François Bouchard saw that it might be important. A report by Michel Ange Lancret to the Institut d'Égypte noted that it held three inscriptions and rightly suggested that they were versions of the same text.
