After the French defeat the stone was taken to London under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801, and since 1802 it has been on display at the British Museum almost continuously.

The first complete translation of the Greek text appeared in 1803. Johan David Åkerblad and Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy identified names in the Demotic text in 1802. In 1814 Thomas Young found the phonetic characters for Ptolemaios in the hieroglyphic text and noted its similarities to the Demotic. Jean-François Champollion announced the transliteration of the Egyptian scripts in Paris in 1822, though it took longer before scholars could read Egyptian inscriptions and literature confidently. Disputes over precedence between supporters of Young and of Champollion continued long afterwards.

Zahi Hawass, then Secretary-General of Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, asked in 2003 for the stone's return to Egypt. In 2005 the British Museum gave Egypt a full-sized replica. The term Rosetta Stone is now used for the essential clue to a new field of knowledge.
roskilde: Roskilde lies in north-central Zealand at the south end of Roskilde Fjord, the south branch of the Isefjord. The city centre around the cathedral stands about 40 metres above sea level and 1,300 metres south of the fjord, and on the slope down to the harbour there are several springs, the strongest of which is Maglekilde. Saxo Grammaticus and other early sources associate the name, meaning Ro's spring, with King Roar, who possibly lived there in the 6th century.

Roskilde developed as a hub of the Viking land and sea trade routes more than a thousand years ago. From the 11th century until 1443 it was the capital of Denmark, and with the support of kings and bishops it became one of the most important centres in Scandinavia. Adam von Bremen called it Zealand's largest town in 1070. Five Viking ships of the 11th century were scuttled in the fjord to block a channel and protect the city from seaborne attack.

The cathedral was built in the 12th and 13th centuries on the site of a 10th-century wooden church and completed in 1275. It was the first Gothic cathedral in Scandinavia built of brick, a style that spread through northern Europe. At the Reformation in 1536 the town had some 6,000 inhabitants, but war, fire and disease reduced them to only 1,550 by 1753. Fires in the 18th century led to the rebuilding of most of the old town, although the original street plan survives. The first train from Copenhagen arrived on 26 June 1847.

Roskilde is a city 30 kilometres west of Copenhagen. Its cathedral, where 39 Danish monarchs are buried, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. Next to it stands Roskilde Palace, built from 1733 to 1736 on the site of the bishops' residence. The Viking Ship Museum beside the fjord displays the remains of the five ships, excavated in the late 1960s about 20 kilometres north of the city. Roskilde University was founded in 1972, and the Roskilde Festival, a rock music festival, has been held annually since 1971.
ross-on-wye: Ross-on-Wye lies in the south-east of Herefordshire near the border with Wales, on the River Wye and the northern edge of the Forest of Dean, about 11 miles, or 18 kilometres, south-east of Hereford. The name Ross comes from a Welsh or Celtic word for a promontory. The General Post Office renamed the town Ross-on-Wye in 1931 because of confusion with other places of similar name, such as Ross in Scotland.

The town promotes itself as the birthplace of British tourism. In 1745 the rector, Dr John Egerton, began taking friends on boat trips down the valley from his rectory at Ross, to see the river scenery, precipitous landscapes, castles and abbeys that appealed to seekers of the picturesque. William Gilpin's Observations on the River Wye, published in 1782, was the first illustrated tour guide published in Britain. By 1808 eight boats made regular excursions on the Wye, mostly hired from inns in Ross and Monmouth, and by 1850 more than 20 visitors had published accounts of the Wye Tour.

In 1637 plague killed 315 townsfolk, who were buried at night without coffins in a pit near St Mary's church. The Plague Cross in the churchyard was raised that year as their memorial, and it is now a scheduled monument. The Market House of red sandstone was built between 1650 and 1654 to replace a probably wooden Booth Hall. John Kyrle, a philanthropist known as the Man of Ross, rented land in 1696 and turned it into a garden and walkway, the Prospect, which looks over the horseshoe bend of the Wye. The Hereford, Ross and Gloucester Railway opened its station in 1855, and lines to the town closed in stages up to 1964 under the Beeching cuts.

The civil parish had a population of 10,990 at the 2021 census. St Mary's, a church about 700 years old, has a tall spire visible from all directions and holds the alabaster tomb of William Rudhall, who died in 1530, one of the last great works of the Nottingham alabaster masons. Markets are held on Thursday and Saturday at the Market House, and the restored ruins of Wilton Castle west of the town are open to visitors. The A40 bypasses the town, and the M50 motorway ends to the east.
rostam: In the Shahnameh Rostam is the son of Zal and Rudaba, a princess of Kabul, and a native of Zabulistan, a historical region roughly corresponding to Zabul Province in southern Afghanistan. He and his predecessors are marzbans of Sistan. His name derives from a Common Iranian form meaning as strong as a river. According to the story, Rudaba's labour was prolonged by the extraordinary size of the child, and Zal summoned the Simurgh, which instructed him how to perform a Caesarean section. As a young child Rostam killed the maddened white elephant of the king Manuchehr with one blow of his grandfather Sam's mace, and he then tamed his stallion Rakhsh.

Rostam, like his grandfather Sam, serves both as a faithful general and as a maker of kings for the Kayanian dynasty of Persia. His best-known journey is the Seven Quests, or Haft Khan, undertaken to rescue the king Kay Kavus, who had been captured by the Divs of Mazandaran. He is also known for his tragic fight with Esfandiyar and for the story of Sohrab, the son born to him by Tahmineh, princess of Samangan, whom he killed accidentally. He wears a suit named Babr-e Bayan in battle. Scholars have compared his legend with that of the Irish hero Cu Chulainn and the labours of Hercules.

In the poem Rostam has reached the age of six hundred when his envious half-brother Shaghad kills him by throwing him into a well full of poisoned spears. Rakhsh and Rostam's brother Zavareh die with him. Ferdowsi did not invent the character: stories of Rostam were popular in Pars by the seventh century and likely originated earlier in Eastern Iranian territories, and Sogdian manuscripts of the ninth century include a tale of Rostam and demons. Josef Markwart traced his background to Parthian origins, and Ernst Herzfeld connected echoes of the Sistan cycle with the House of Suren. In Persianate cultures Rustam is a byword for physical prowess, especially among wrestlers.
rostam-farrokhzad: Rostam belonged to the House of Ispahbudhan, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran, which claimed Arsacid descent and was acknowledged as kin and partners of the Sasanians. His father Farrukh Hormizd was a first cousin of Khosrow II, and his brother Farrukhzad held high standing at Ctesiphon. The family ruled the north-western quarter of Adurbadagan, where Rostam served as spahbed, or military marshal; his birthplace is variously given as Armenia, Adurbadagan, Hamadan or Ray.

During the war with the Byzantine Empire, as Heraclius advanced into Transcaucasia, Rostam rebelled in Adurbadagan at the head of 10,000 soldiers. In 628 his father, he and Farrukhzad joined the factions that overthrew Khosrow II and placed Kavad II on the throne.

In the civil war of 628 to 632 Farrukh Hormizd led the Pahlav, the Parthian noble families, and was killed on the orders of Queen Azarmidokht after asking her to marry him. Rostam, then in Khorasan, took his place, marched on Ctesiphon, defeated the forces of the Mihranid noble Siyavakhsh and took the city. He had Azarmidokht blinded and killed and restored Boran in June 631; according to Sayf ibn Umar, she entrusted him with rule for ten years. A revolt of the rival Parsig faction ended with Boran's death, after which Rostam and Piruz Khosrow together crowned her nephew Yazdegerd III, ending the civil war.

Yazdegerd gave Rostam the defence of the empire. In 634 he recalled the general Bahman Jaduya from the front after the Battle of the Bridge to put down a revolt in Ctesiphon. Ordered in 636 to meet the Arab armies of Caliph Umar, he urged patience against a single decisive battle, but the young king would not listen. Before fighting he negotiated with the envoys Zuhrah and Mughirah ibn Shubah without result.

All accounts agree that he died in the battle at al-Qādisiyyah, west of the Euphrates. One says he was found in a sandstorm with over 600 wounds; stories of his beheading by Hilal ibn Ullafa or of a duel with Sa'd are probably inventions of later storytellers. Yazdegerd III was murdered in 651. Rostam lives on as a character in the Shahnameh and as a folk hero across greater Iran.
rostom-of-kartli: Rostom was born around 1565 in Isfahan, the illegitimate son of David XI (Daud Khan), who governed part of Kartli on behalf of Persia, and a concubine reportedly from the village of Chindisi; he was raised in the Islamic faith. Taken to the court of Mohammad Khodabanda in 1579, he later fell into poverty and, by some accounts, lived as a beggar in Isfahan. In 1612 the Georgian general Giorgi Saakadze befriended him and raised him out of destitution.

Appointed darugha (prefect) of Isfahan in 1618, a post he kept for life, he became one of the closest advisers of Abbas I. In January 1629 the dying shah named him qollar-aghasi, commander of the imperial guard, renamed him Rostom Khan after the hero of the Shahnameh and charged him with securing the succession of his grandson Sam Mirza, the future Shah Safi.

Already 67 when he took the throne, he governed Kartli on the Safavid model, giving the royal offices Safavid titles and appointing both Persian and Georgian officials. He rebuilt Tbilisi and Gori, where he turned the citadel into a palace, built bridges, roads, caravanserais and bazaars, and in 1639 abolished taxes on Georgian merchants. In 1633 he allied with Levan II Dadiani of Mingrelia, whose sister Mariam he married.

His pro-Persian stance provoked noble revolts and plots, including a conspiracy formed in late 1639 to restore Teimuraz I, which ended with the king's victory in 1642 and the execution of Catholicos Eudemus. In 1648 he defeated Teimuraz again and annexed Kakheti. He paid Persia tribute and sent troops to its wars but enjoyed wide autonomy at home. He signed decrees invoking both Allah and Jesus Christ; Christians were not persecuted, though Persian music and Islamic dress spread in Tbilisi.

Rostom died on 17 November 1658, aged 93. Having no children of his own, he adopted Prince Luarsab in 1641 and, after Luarsab's death, Vakhtang of Mukhrani, who succeeded him as Vakhtang V. David Marshall Lang counted him among the few Georgian monarchs who preferred diplomacy and stability, while Nikoloz Berdzenishvili called him a renegade and a traitor who sacrificed Georgia's independence for Persian financial support.
rotenburg-an-der-wumme: Rotenburg lies on the Wümme river, between the Elbe and the Weser, at about the same latitude as Hamburg and Bremen, with Bremen 40 kilometres to the west. It is the capital of the district of Rotenburg. It is often called Rotenburg (Wümme) to distinguish it from Rotenburg an der Fulda in Hesse and Rothenburg ob der Tauber in Bavaria. Until May 1969 its official name was Rotenburg in Hannover, and in Northern Low Saxon it is Rodenborg.

The town was founded in 1195, when Prince-Bishop Rudolf I of Verden built a castle in the area. The Prince-Bishopric of Verden had been established in 1180. The castle took its name from the colour of its bricks, rot meaning red and Burg castle. The adjoining settlement remained a tiny village until the 19th century.

After the Thirty Years' War the rule of the bishops ended, and Rotenburg became part of the secularised Duchy of Verden under Swedish rule. The new rulers rebuilt the castle as a modern fortress, an outpost protecting the main fortress at Stade. This required the demolition of the western part of the town, so the settlement moved east, and even the parish church was rebuilt on the site of the present town church.

In the Swedish-Brandenburg War of 1675 to 1676 Denmark and several states of the Holy Roman Empire captured the town, which was returned to Sweden after the Treaty of Saint Germain in 1679. The fortress remained in operation until about 1680, then was neglected, and the last ramparts were levelled after 1843. Seven town fires between 1626 and 1835 destroyed much of the town. Denmark captured it in 1712 and in 1715 the Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg acquired the Duchy of Verden by purchase.

After the Congress of Vienna Rotenburg formed the centre of an Office within the Kingdom of Hanover, and after Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866 it lay in the Province of Hanover. The railway station on the Bremen–Hamburg line opened in 1874. Adolf Kottmeier founded the Rotenburger Werke der Inneren Mission in 1880 as facilities for people with intellectual disabilities, and in 1905 the Bethesda Deaconess Motherhouse, founded by Elise Averdieck, moved its headquarters there from Hamburg. The town received city rights in 1929. Its sights include the Lutheran Stadtkirche, built in 1860–1862, half-timbered houses and a museum of local history.
rothenburg-ob-der-tauber: The name means Red castle above the Tauber and describes the town's position on a plateau overlooking the Tauber river. Rothenburg Castle, also called the Alte Burg, gave the city its name. The counts of Comburg-Rothenburg built the castle in 1070, and the line died out in 1116 with Count Heinrich. Emperor Heinrich V then appointed his nephew Konrad von Hohenstaufen to succeed to their properties. Konrad, who became King Konrad III, built a Staufer castle on cheaper land nearby in 1142.

The city was founded in 1170, when the Staufer castle was built, around its marketplace and St. James' Church, and walls and towers followed in the 13th century. In 1274 King Rudolf of Habsburg granted it privileges as a free imperial city, three fairs were established, and it grew.

The Heilig Blut pilgrimage attracted many pilgrims, and the city was one of the 20 largest of the Holy Roman Empire, with about 5,500 people within the walls and another 14,000 in the surrounding territory. Rabbi Meir ben Baruch of Rothenburg, who died in 1293, had a great reputation as a jurist in Europe. An earthquake destroyed the Staufer castle in 1356.

In October 1631, during the Thirty Years' War, the Catholic Count of Tilly wanted to quarter his 40,000 troops in Protestant Rothenburg. The town resisted and was quickly defeated. According to the legend of the Meistertrunk, Tilly offered to spare the city if anyone could drink 3 1/4 litres of wine in one draught, and Mayor Georg Nusch did so; the story is almost certainly apocryphal, since it first appears in a chronicle written more than a century later. The troops left the town poor and nearly empty, and a bubonic plague in 1634 killed many more. Without money or power Rothenburg stopped growing and kept its 17th-century state.

Rothenburg lies in Middle Franconia in Bavaria and is on the Romantic Road. It is one of only four towns in Germany with completely intact city walls. Painters of the Romantic period visited it from 1877, followed by the first tourists, and laws were passed to prevent major changes. On 31 March 1945 bombing destroyed around 275 houses and damaged the walls. S. Assistant Secretary of War John J.

McCloy ordered that artillery not be used, and the local commander Major Thömmes gave up the town, American troops occupied it on 17 April 1945. About 32 percent of the town was rebuilt, and rebuilt walls carry bricks naming donors. The Rathaus has a Gothic rear part of 1250 and a Renaissance front begun in 1572, and St. James' Church holds a Holy Blood altarpiece by Tilman Riemenschneider.
rothschild-family: The family's documented history begins in 16th-century Frankfurt. Its name comes from the German zum rothen Schild, "at the red shield", the sign of the house in which it lived for many generations, built by Isaak Elchanan Bacharach in 1567; a red shield still stands at the centre of the family's coat of arms. The family rose to prominence with Mayer Amschel Rothschild (1744-1812), born in the Judengasse, the ghetto of Frankfurt, the son of a money changer, who became a court factor to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel. Unlike most earlier court factors he managed to pass on his wealth, through five sons whom he installed in Paris, Frankfurt, London, Vienna and Naples.

From London between 1813 and 1815, Nathan Mayer Rothschild was instrumental in financing the British war effort against Napoleon, organising the shipment of bullion to the Duke of Wellington's armies and the payment of British subsidies to the continental allies; in 1815 alone the family provided £9.8 million in subsidy loans. The family dominated international finance in Europe between the 1820s and the 1870s, until joint-stock banks broke its hegemony, and its banks supported railways and complex government financing such as the Suez Canal. In 1816 four of the five brothers were raised to the Austrian nobility by Emperor Francis I, and Nathan in 1818. They were granted the title of Freiherr (baron) on 29 September 1822.

The houses separated over time. The Naples house closed in 1863 after forty-two years, following the unification of Italy and the decline of the aristocrats who had been its main clients. In 1901 the German branch closed after the death of Wilhelm Rothschild without male heirs. By the start of the 20th century national taxation systems had ended the practice of keeping a single set of accounts, and the branches became independent banks. In Austria the family had to surrender its bank to the Nazis and flee during the Second World War; all its members escaped the Holocaust, and in 1999 the Austrian government agreed to return some 250 art treasures looted by the Nazis.

Only the French and British branches still subsist. The family's wealth was divided among many descendants over the 20th century, and its businesses now cover financial services, real estate, mining, energy, agriculture and winemaking; Nathaniel de Rothschild bought Château Mouton Rothschild in 1853 and James Mayer de Rothschild Château Lafite in 1868. The family has often been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories.
rotrou-iii-count-of-perche: Rotrou was the son of Geoffrey II, Count of Perche, and Beatrix de Ramerupt, daughter of Hilduin IV, Count of Montdidier. The Perche was a border region of southern Normandy, and his family was tied to the Anglo-Norman aristocracy and to Spain: his mother's sister Felicia married Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragon. He went on the First Crusade with Robert Curthose, Duke of Normandy. According to the Chanson d'Antioche he was among the first over the walls of Antioch on 3 June 1098 and a front-line commander against the Seljuk relief force two weeks later. He reached Jerusalem, and his father died while he was away.

Back in France he laid a palm frond from Jerusalem on the altar at Nogent-le-Rotrou. He defended the Norman frontier with the Île-de-France and sided with Henry I against Robert Curthose, becoming important in Henry's rule of Normandy after Tinchebrai in 1106. In 1107 a castle he built began a dispute with Hugh II of Le Puiset that tested the Church's new protection of crusaders' goods.

After his wife Matilda, his eldest son and two nephews drowned in the White Ship in 1120, Rotrou returned to Spain. Later chronicles making him conqueror of Tudela have been shown to be false, but charters show him as count in Tudela from 1123, ruling it as a vassal of Alfonso the Battler through his alcalde Robert Burdet until 1131. In the winter of 1124 to 1125 he led an expedition against the fortress of Peña Cadiella.

Sometime before 1144 he went again to the Holy Land and brought relics for La Trappe, the monastery he had founded in 1122 in memory of Matilda, which laid the foundations of the later Trappists. He is credited with bringing Arabian horses to the Perche, giving rise to the Percheron breed. His son Rotrou IV succeeded him; another son, Stephen, became Archbishop of Palermo.
rotterdam: Rotterdam lies in the province of South Holland, in the North Sea mouth of the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta, reached by the New Meuse channel, which was dug to connect first to the Meuse and now to the Rhine. The river Nieuwe Maas divides the city into a northern and a southern part, joined by tunnels and bridges. The Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt give waterway access into the heart of Western Europe, including the industrialised Ruhr, and together with rail and road links they earned the city the nicknames Gateway to Europe and Gateway to the World.

The settlement at the lower end of the fen stream Rotte, then called Rotta from words for muddy water, dates from at least the year 950. Around 1150 large floods ended development and led to the building of protective dikes and dams, including Schieland's High Sea Dike along the northern bank of the Nieuwe Maas. A dam on the Rotte was built in the 13th century, at the present-day Hoogstraat, and in 1340 William IV, Count of Holland, granted Rotterdam city rights.

Rotterdam has always been one of the main centres of Dutch shipping. Its Chamber of the VOC, the world's first multinational, was established in 1602. Since 1795 it has hosted the chief congregation of the liberal Protestant Remonstrants, and its Catholic bishopric dates from 1955. The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus is counted among its former inhabitants. During the First World War, because of Dutch neutrality and the city's position between Britain, Germany and German-occupied Belgium, it was the world's largest spy centre, and MI6 had its main European office on the Boompjes. On average 25,000 Belgian refugees lived there.

In the early stages of the Second World War the German Luftwaffe bombed the city centre and destroyed many of its older buildings. After an initial crisis of reconstruction the centre became a site of ambitious new architecture. Earlier landmarks include the White House of 1898, the tallest office building in Europe in its day, the Van Nelle Factory of 1929, a monument of modern factory design that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and Feyenoord's stadium De Kuip of 1936.

Rotterdam is the second-largest city of the Netherlands by population and the largest by area, and it is Europe's largest seaport. It is the centre of the Rotterdam–The Hague metropolitan area, the most populous in the country. Erasmus University Rotterdam is named after Erasmus. The destruction of the city centre in 1940 gave it a varied architectural landscape, with skyscrapers designed by architects such as Rem Koolhaas, Piet Blom and Ben van Berkel.
rouen: Rouen stands on the River Seine in northwestern France and is the prefecture of the region of Normandy and of the department of Seine-Maritime. The Seine has been central to its prosperity: in the Middle Ages the city had a monopoly on river traffic that reached as far upstream as Paris, and today the Port of Rouen is a major axis for maritime cargo.

Rouen was founded by the Gaulish tribe of the Veliocasses, who called it Ratumacos; the Romans called it Rotomagus. It was considered the second city of Gallia Lugdunensis after Lugdunum (Lyon), and under Diocletian it was chief city of Lugdunensis secunda, with an amphitheatre and baths. In the 5th century it became the seat of a bishopric and later a capital of Merovingian Neustria.

The Normans overran it from 841, and in the early 10th century it became the capital of the Duchy of Normandy until William the Conqueror moved his residence to Caen. It received a charter of self-government in 1150. In the 12th century about 6,000 Jews, a fifth of the population, lived in the town, which had a yeshiva known as La Maison Sublime.

On 24 June 1204 Philip II Augustus of France annexed Normandy, and from the 13th century a textile industry based on English wool made the city prosperous. The mayor was assassinated in 1291, Philip IV expelled the Jewish community in 1306, and the Harelle, a revolt of the underclass, in 1389 was suppressed with the loss of the city's charter. Rouen surrendered to Henry V of England on 19 January 1419 after a long siege.

Joan of Arc was burned at the stake there on 30 May 1431, and Charles VII recaptured the city in 1449. It withstood a five-month siege by Henry IV and an English force in 1591/2, and in the Second World War was heavily damaged and its cathedral almost destroyed by Allied bombs.

Rouen is the seat of an archdiocese, with a university and a court of appeal, and its metropolitan area has 715,239 people. Its monuments include Rouen Cathedral, whose Gothic facade Claude Monet painted in a series, the 14th-century astronomical clock known as the Gros Horloge, and the Church of Saint Ouen and the Gothic Church of St Maclou. The Place du Vieux Marché marks the site of Joan of Arc's pyre.
round-city-of-baghdad: According to Ya'qubi, construction began on 2 August 762 under the supervision of four architects. Arab chroniclers report 100,000 workers and craftsmen and sums of 18 million gold dinars or 100 million silver dirhams. The Palace of the Golden Gate, the main mosque and some offices were apparently finished by 763, so al-Mansur could move in, and the rest was completed by 766. His aim was to replace Harran as the seat of the caliphal government. A city called Baghdad is mentioned in pre-Islamic texts, including the Talmud, and the Abbasid city was likely built on the site of the earlier settlement.

The city was a circle about 1 km in radius, enclosing roughly 3 square kilometres, though the sources disagree about its size. A ring of residential and commercial buildings lay inside the walls, and the final construction added a second ring. The palace, the mosque and the guards' headquarters stood at the centre. It had four gates, Bab al-Kufa, Bab al-Sham, Bab al-Khorasan and Bab al-Basra. The buildings were mostly of brick, sometimes strengthened with reeds.

The circular plan reflected Sasanian urban design, and the city of Gur is nearly identical in layout. The planners hired by al-Mansur were Naubakht, a former Zoroastrian, and Mashallah ibn Athari, a Persian Jewish astrologer. Residents were soldiers settled by the caliph, mostly Persians from Khorasan and Transoxania, and ordinary people who came for economic opportunity, mostly Arabs and local Nabateans. The House of Wisdom stood within its grounds. The Mongols' Ilkhanate breached its walls in February 1258.

None of the structures survives, and what is known rests on literary sources such as Ibn Serapion's description of the canals and Ya'qubi's geography. Guy Le Strange reconstructed a plan in 1900, which Ernst Herzfeld improved between 1905 and 1913. No excavations have taken place at the supposed site, so reconstruction remains hypothetical.

Jacob Lassner argued that al-Mansur, with no known architectural experience, could not himself have designed it, that it showed Abbasid inheritance of Sasanian urban tradition, and that no source supports a cosmological meaning. In his view it was an administrative centre and not a city in the conventional sense.
round-table-conferences-india: Demands for Swaraj, or self-rule, had been growing, and by the 1930s many British politicians believed that India needed to move towards dominion status. The conferences followed a recommendation by Muhammad Ali Jinnah to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, and the report of the Simon Commission in May 1930. Sir Samuel Hoare advised the cabinet that a federal formula would give a semblance of responsible government while keeping the realities of British control.

George V opened the first conference in the Royal Gallery of the House of Lords on 12 November 1930, with MacDonald in the chair. Sixteen delegates represented eight British parties, and 74 came from India, fifty-eight from British India and sixteen from the princely states. Congress stayed away, many of its leaders, Gandhi among them, being in jail for the Civil Disobedience Movement. Tej Bahadur Sapru moved an All-India Federation to the centre of discussion, and every group present supported it, the princely states provided their internal sovereignty was guaranteed.

Gandhi and other Congress leaders were freed on 26 January 1931, and under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact Congress agreed to take part. The second session opened on 7 September 1931 with Gandhi as its sole representative, but MacDonald now headed a National Government dominated by the Conservatives, and Britain left the Gold Standard during the talks. Other Indian participants rejected Gandhi's claims that Congress alone represented political India and that there should be no separate electorates, and he opposed treating the Untouchables as a separate minority, as B. R. Ambedkar demanded.

MacDonald undertook to produce a Communal Award on minority representation, and Gandhi and Ambedkar settled their dispute in the Poona Pact of 1932. The third session, which assembled on 17 November 1932, had only forty-six delegates, as the Indian National Congress and the British Labour Party refused to attend. Under Hoare, Secretary of State for India, the reforms took shape between September 1931 and March 1933, and a Joint Committee's recommendations were enacted as the Government of India Act 1935.
rourkela: Rourkela is a planned city in Sundargarh district in the north of Odisha, about 328 kilometres west of the state capital, Bhubaneswar. It lies in a hilly region at about 219 metres above sea level, encircled by the rivers Koel, Sankha and Brahmani. The South Koel and the Sankha meet at Vedvyas and flow on as the Brahmani. In the local Sadri language the name means Your village. The area is rich in iron ore, with mines at Bolani and Barsuan, and red and laterite soils.

The twin towns of Rourkela and Fertilizer Township stand where dense forest once grew. After India's independence, Jawaharlal Nehru wanted to make the country an industrialised state on a Soviet model of social development, and Biju Pattanaik is credited with persuading him to choose Rourkela for a steel plant. A preliminary survey began in 1952 and the government of Odisha issued a gazette notification on 16 February 1954. The German firms Krupp and Demag provided financial and technical help, and Krupp built the plant drawing on its works in Essen.

The land came at a cost. The state acquired about 80 square miles for the plant, and almost 13,000 people in 2,424 families lost their homes. Later acquisitions for the Mandira Dam and for railway lines to Hatia and Barsuan took more, and the Bondamunda railway junction displaced a further 20,000 people. Many of the tribal people affected were given employment and housing, and were relocated to places such as Jalda and Jhirpani.

Thousands of technical personnel came from West Germany, some with their families, and in the late 1950s and early 1960s the town was the largest German colony outside Germany. They formed the Indo-German Club, which still keeps a library named after Max Muller. Local people, many from coastal and western Odisha, were trained by the German workforce in the plant's technology.

The city is divided into the Steel Township, run by the plant's administration, and the Civil Township, with the Rourkela Municipal Corporation, declared in November 2014, governing most of the rest. Its population was 483,038 at the 2011 census. Besides the steel plant, its industries include a power company, a locomotive shed and Software Technology Parks of India. Rourkela Day is marked every year on 3 March.
roussillon: Roussillon was a historical province of France on the Mediterranean, at the eastern end of the Pyrenees. It largely corresponded to the County of Roussillon and part of the County of Cerdagne in the former Principality of Catalonia, and it belongs to the region called Northern Catalonia or French Catalonia. It covers roughly the present département of Pyrénées-Orientales. The name comes from Ruscino, a small fortified place near Perpignan where Gaulish chieftains met to consider Hannibal's request for a conference.

The region was part of the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis from 121 BCE and passed with the rest of Septimania to the Visigothic king Theodoric II in 462 CE. Pepin the Short defeated the Saracens in 759 and occupied Roussillon, which the Carolingians held from 760. In 893 Sunyer II became the first hereditary count of Roussillon. Count Girard I took part in the First Crusade and was among the first into Jerusalem in 1099. The last count, Girard II, left his lands to Alfonso II of Aragon, who took possession in 1172, and under Aragon the port of Collioure became an important centre of Mediterranean trade.

By the Treaty of Corbeil of 1258 Louis IX of France gave up his claims of sovereignty over Roussillon to the Crown of Aragon. James I of Aragon joined it with the Balearic Isles to form the Kingdom of Majorca, with its capital at Perpignan, and granted it in 1276 to his son James II. In 1344 Peter IV of Aragon seized Majorca and Roussillon, which were reunited with Catalonia within the Crown of Aragon. French troops held the province from 1462, when it was pledged to Louis XI for 300,000 crowns, until 1493.

When the Catalans rose against the Spanish Crown in 1640, Louis XIII joined the revolt, and the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 divided the Principality of Catalonia and gave Roussillon and part of Cerdanya to France. Louis XIV tried to change the cultural identity of his new subjects, succeeding in winning their political loyalty but not in changing their culture. During the French Revolution the province was abolished and replaced by the department of Pyrénées-Orientales, with Fenouillèdes added. Its capital is Perpignan, and the old name survives in the former region of Languedoc-Roussillon.
rova-of-antananarivo: In the early 17th century the Merina king Andrianjaka, grandson of King Andriamanelo, sent a garrison of 1,000 soldiers to take the hill of Analamanga, 1,480 metres above sea level, from its Vazimba inhabitants; according to oral history the encampment of his army alone brought their submission. His men cleared the summit and built a traditional rova with wooden houses, among them Besakana, and he chose the site of the royal tombs called Fitomiandalana, the first of which was his own.

Like every rova, the compound had a central courtyard with a tall sacred stone from which the sovereign gave royal speeches, at least one palace and the tomb of its founders. Andrianampoinimerina, who captured Antananarivo by 1793 and moved his capital there from Ambohimanga the following year, added new buildings, and the Rova remained the seat of the sovereigns of the Kingdom of Madagascar, from Radama I to Ranavalona III, until the French colonisation of 1896.

The compound covers just under one hectare, 116 metres from north to south, and is entered by a north-facing gate built by James Cameron in 1845 and topped by a bronze eagle that Jean Laborde imported from France. Manjakamiadana, the largest palace, was built in wood by Laborde in 1839 and 1840 for Ranavalona I and encased in stone in 1867; it rose 37 metres. Other buildings included Tranovola, the Silver House, Queen Rasoherina's villa Manampisoa, nine royal tombs and a stone chapel inaugurated on 8 April 1880.

After the French conquest the Rova became a museum in 1897. Under General Joseph Gallieni the bodies of sovereigns buried at Ambohimanga were moved to its tombs, an act that Frémigacci sees as a calculated desacralisation meant to break popular belief in the royal ancestors. After independence the compound stayed largely closed to the public.

On the night of 6 November 1995, shortly before the Rova was due to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, fire destroyed or badly damaged every building, leaving only the stone shells of the chapel and Manjakamiadana; about 1,675 of some 6,700 objects were saved. The fire was officially declared an accident, though rumours of arson persist. The chapel, the tombs, Besakana and Mahitsielafanjaka have since been restored.
rowlatt-act: Its official short title was the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act 1919. During the First World War the Defence of India Act, 1915 had given the government emergency powers of preventive detention and imprisonment without trial. As that law was due to lapse, the government feared that revolutionary nationalists would return to the conspiracies of the war years. On the report of the committee headed by Justice Sidney Rowlatt, two bills, soon called the Black Bills, were introduced in the Central Legislature on 6 February 1919. Despite strong opposition from its Indian members, the Imperial Legislative Council in Delhi passed the act on 18 March 1919, and it came into effect on 21 March.

The act extended the wartime measures indefinitely. It allowed the authorities to imprison anyone suspected of terrorism for up to two years without trial and provided for stricter control of the press, arrest without warrant and trials held in camera without a jury for proscribed political acts. The accused were not told who accused them or what evidence was used. Cases went to a panel of three high court judges, from which there was no appeal; habeas corpus was suspended, and the panel could admit evidence barred under the Indian Evidence Act. Those released had to deposit securities and were barred from political, educational and religious activity.

Madan Mohan Malaviya, Mazarul Haque and Muhammad Ali Jinnah resigned from the council in protest; Jinnah called the law a Black Act in his letter to the Viceroy, Frederic Thesiger. Mahatma Gandhi called for satyagraha, and on 6 April Indians closed their businesses, struck, fasted and held public meetings in a hartal. The Delhi hartal of 30 March was followed by rioting in the Punjab, Delhi and Gujarat, and Gandhi suspended the resistance, judging that Indians were not yet ready to keep to nonviolence.

In the Punjab the Congress leaders Dr. Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlew were arrested on 10 April and taken secretly to Dharamsala. Three days later crowds gathered in Amritsar for Baisakhi and to protest at their deportation, and the events ended in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The agitation brought Gandhi into the mainstream of the independence struggle; Jawaharlal Nehru called it the politics of action, not of talk. Accepting the report of the Repressive Laws Committee, the government repealed the act in March 1922.
roxana: Roxana was the daughter of the Bactrian nobleman Oxyartes, satrap of Bactria and Sogdia, who served Bessus and was probably involved in the murder of the last Achaemenid king, Darius III. The date of her birth is unknown, but she was of childbearing age by 326 BCE. After Alexander the Great captured Bessus, Oxyartes and his family fled north and, with the Sogdian warlord Spitamenes, took up position in a fortress known as the Sogdian Rock, where the Macedonians defeated them.

Alexander then reportedly fell in love with Roxana on sight at a celebration. Where it took place is disputed. Arrian states that Oxyartes surrendered when he learned how well Alexander had received his daughter, and A. B. Bosworth raises the possibility that she was captured at the Sogdian Rock and the two married at the fortress of Chorienes.

The marriage took place in 327 BCE and, according to most sources, followed Macedonian rather than Persian custom. Alexander married her despite opposition from his companions, who would have preferred a Macedonian or Greek queen, and the match may also have been political, since the Bactrian and Sogdian armies became more loyal afterwards. According to the Metz Epitome she went with him to India, where their first son died in infancy near the Hydaspes in the autumn of 326 BCE. In 324 BCE Alexander also married Stateira II, a daughter of Darius III.

After Alexander died suddenly at Babylon in 323 BCE, Roxana is believed to have murdered Stateira, and Plutarch says she had Stateira's sister Drypetis killed with the consent of Perdiccas. She was pregnant, and the Macedonians reached a compromise: Philip Arrhidaeus was declared king, and the unborn child was to be king as well if a son. She bore a son, Alexander IV, in 323 BCE.

By 317 BCE the young Alexander had lost his kingship through the intrigues of Philip Arrhidaeus' wife, Eurydice II, and Roxana and her son were protected by Alexander's mother Olympias in Macedonia. After Olympias was assassinated in 316 BCE, Cassander imprisoned them in the citadel of Amphipolis. A peace treaty of 311 BCE confirmed Alexander IV's kingship with Cassander as his guardian, but Cassander ordered Glaucias of Macedon to kill the boy and Roxana, possibly by poison. Scholars disagree on the date of their deaths. Inscriptions at the Acropolis record offerings Roxana dedicated to Athena as Alexander's wife, and the asteroid 317 Roxane is named for her.
roy-welensky: Raphael Welensky was born on 20 January 1907 in Pioneer Street, Salisbury, the thirteenth child of Michael Welensky, a Lithuanian Jewish trader from near Wilno, and Leah, born Aletta Ferreira, an Afrikaner. His parents kept a poor white boarding house, and his mother died when he was eleven. He left school at fourteen, worked for Rhodesia Railways as a fireman, boxed, and rose to locomotive driver. After the failed Rhodesian Railways strike of 1929 he was moved to Broken Hill in Northern Rhodesia, where he chaired the branch of the Rhodesian Railway Workers' Union from 1933.

Elected to the Northern Rhodesian Legislative Council in 1938, Welensky founded the Northern Rhodesian Labour Party in 1941 to seek amalgamation with Southern Rhodesia, and in 1945 succeeded Stewart Gore-Browne as leader of the unofficial members, while still driving trains. When Britain rejected amalgamation he worked for a federation instead. At a conference at the Victoria Falls Hotel in February 1949, attended by neither Africans nor the British government, he proposed the Constitution of Australia as a model and spoke of partnership between black and white, with the whites, he said, as senior partners.

In 1953 he and Sir Godfrey Huggins founded the United Federal Party, which won the first federal election; Welensky took more than 80% of the vote at Broken Hill and became Minister for Transport. He succeeded Huggins as prime minister on 1 November 1956.

Welensky backed Britain in the Suez Crisis, after which British policy turned to faster decolonisation. Hastings Banda returned to Nyasaland in 1958 to organise opposition to the federation, and Welensky called the Monckton Report of October 1960, which proposed African majorities in the Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesian legislatures and an option to secede, the death knell of federation. During the Congo Crisis the Royal Rhodesian Air Force evacuated more than 6,000 refugees, and Welensky supported Moise Tshombe's Katanga as a buffer against Patrice Lumumba.

Under new territorial constitutions the UFP lost each territorial election of 1961 and 1962, and the Rhodesian Front of Ian Smith and Winston Field won Southern Rhodesia. Welensky secured the transfer of federal assets to Southern Rhodesia, and the federation was dissolved on 31 December 1963. He later led the Rhodesia Party against a unilateral declaration of independence, settled at Blandford Forum, Dorset, in 1981, and died there on 5 December 1991.
royal-air-force: The Royal Air Force was formed towards the end of the First World War, on 1 April 1918, by merging the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service. To emphasise the merger of military and naval aviation, many officers' titles were deliberately chosen to be naval in character, such as flight lieutenant, wing commander, group captain and air commodore. Following the Allied victory over the Central Powers in 1918, the new force emerged as the largest air force in the world.

Titles and insignia of other ranks were based on those of the Army, with some changes in terminology. Early in the war British aircraft had carried the Union Flag, which was easily confused with Germany's Iron Cross, so in October 1914 the French system of three concentric rings was adopted, with the colours reversed to a red disc surrounded by a white ring and an outer blue ring.

The service expanded rapidly before and during the Second World War. Under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan of December 1939, the air forces of Commonwealth countries trained and formed Article XV squadrons for service with its formations, and exiles from occupied Europe served with its squadrons.

By the end of the war the Royal Canadian Air Force had contributed more than 30 squadrons, and about a quarter of Bomber Command's personnel were Canadian. At its height in 1944 more than 1,100,000 personnel were serving. It defeated the German Luftwaffe's efforts to win air superiority in the Battle of Britain and played a key role in the Combined Bomber Offensive alongside the USAAF.

After the war jet fighters and bombers arrived and the service was reorganised. In the early Cold War one of its first major operations was the Berlin Airlift, between 26 June 1948 and the lifting of the Soviet blockade on 12 May 1949, in which it provided 17 percent of the total supplies delivered. Its first post-war engagements came during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, when RAF fighters shot down four Egyptian aircraft that had mistakenly attacked an RAF airbase, and in encounters with the Israeli Air Force.

The Royal Air Force has played a significant role in British military history. The Royal Flying Corps had provided the flypast for Trooping the Colour since 1913, and the RAF continues to do so. The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, formed in 1957, flies Spitfire and Hurricane fighters, an Avro Lancaster and a Dakota to commemorate the Second World War. The Red Arrows, its aerobatic team, were formed in late 1964, and the Central Band of the Royal Air Force was established in 1920.
royal-commentaries-of-the-incas: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, the first published mestizo writer of colonial Andean South America, was the natural son of Captain Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas and the Inca princess Isabel Suárez Chimpu Ocllo. He lived with his mother and her people until he was ten and grew up in both his parents' worlds, then went to Spain at 21 and stayed there for the rest of his life. Before the Comentarios he had translated the Dialogos de Amor into Spanish and written La Florida del Inca, a popular account of Hernando de Soto's expedition.

The work rests on the oral tradition handed down to him by relatives and other amauta, wise men, in his childhood and youth, and on written sources including the chronicle of Blas Valera. Its ten books follow the Inca rulers from Manco Capac and the founding of Cuzco to Huayna Capac, the civil war between Atahualpa and Huascar and the Spanish conquest, with chapters on administration, quipus, the festival of the sun, the virgins of the sun, the temples of Cuzco and Titicaca and the Sacsahuaman fortress.

Garcilaso wrote both as a member of the royal family of Cuzco and from Spanish Catholic theology, and he interpreted Inca and Andean religion from the European and Christian point of view in which he had been raised.

The first part was printed in Lisbon in the shop of Pedro Crasbeeck. The second part, on the Spanish conquest, appeared a year after the author's death under the title Historia General del Peru. When the uprising led by Tupac Amaru II gained momentum, Charles III of Spain banned its publication in Lima in Quechua for its dangerous content, but copies circulated in secret, and native people drew pride from their Inca heritage. Sir Paul Rycaut's English translation of 1685 was titled The Royal Commentaries of Peru. The book was not printed again in the Americas until 1918, and Maria Jolas's translation, The Incas, appeared in 1961.
royal-hungarian-honved: The Hungarian word honvéd means defender of the homeland. It first appeared in the revolution of 1848, for volunteers who signed on for several weeks or until victory and were sent to fight the Serbs and Croats. As the fighting turned against the Empire of Austria and some regular imperial regiments went over to the Hungarian side, the name came to cover all Hungarian land forces of 1848-49. Around 40% of their private soldiers came from the country's ethnic minorities, and about half of their officers and generals were of foreign origin. Austria defeated them with Russian assistance.

After the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 the Honvéd was restored for Hungary as one of the four armed forces of Austria-Hungary, beside the Common Army, the Austrian Landwehr and the Imperial and Royal Navy. It answered to the Hungarian Ministry of Defence, which was subordinate only to the Hungarian prime minister and the parliament in Budapest, not to the common War Ministry, and it could join the imperial army only with the Hungarian government's explicit authorisation. The monarch remained the supreme warlord and commander-in-chief.

Its Croatian part, the Royal Croatian Home Guard, used Croatian as its language of command under the Croatian–Hungarian Settlement of 1868 and answered to the Ban in Agram. Its regiments had three battalions instead of the Common Army's four, but its troops were regular and highly trained combat soldiers, not the units of limited fighting power the word Landwehr usually implies.

Officers came from Hungarian regiments of the Common Army or from the Ludovika Military Academy in Budapest, opened in 1872. From 1869 conscripts were assigned by lot to the Common Army or the Honvéd; they enlisted at 21, served 24 months and remained liable until 36. In 1914 the force had six Landwehr districts, 32 infantry regiments, 10 regiments of hussars and 8 field artillery regiments. A Honvéd Memorial to the army of 1848-49 was unveiled in Budapest on 21 May 1893.
royal-marines: The corps traces its origin to 28 October 1664, when the Duke of York and Albany's Maritime Regiment of Foot was formed at the grounds of the Honourable Artillery Company. It soon became known as the Admiral's Regiment and began with 1,200 infantrymen recruited from the Trained Bands of London, as part of the mobilisation for the Second Anglo-Dutch War. James, Duke of York and Albany, brother of Charles II, was Lord High Admiral and Captain-General of the Artillery Company, which trained the Trained Bands. On 5 April 1755 His Majesty's Marine Forces, fifty companies in three divisions at Chatham, Portsmouth and Plymouth, were formed by Order of Council under Admiralty control.

In the 18th century the Marines served in landings across the world, the best known being at Belle Île on the Brittany coast in 1761, and in the American War of Independence at Bunker Hill under Major John Pitcairn. Marine officers had lower standing than their Royal Navy counterparts, and until 1771 none was promoted colonel. George IV granted the Great Globe Itself in 1827 in recognition of their service in engagements across the world.

In the First World War Royal Marines were part of the Royal Naval Division, which landed in Belgium in 1914 to help defend Antwerp and took part in the landing at Gallipoli in 1915, where Royal Marines were the last to leave.

The first Royal Marines commando unit was formed at Deal, Kent, on 14 February 1942. After 1945 the Marines took on the main responsibility for the role and training of the British Commandos, and the Army Commandos were disbanded in 1946. In 1956, during the Suez Crisis, they provided the first military unit to carry out an air assault by helicopter, and they formed part of the land force in the Falklands War of 1982. During the Cold War 3 Commando Brigade trained each year in northern Norway.

The Royal Marines form part of the Naval Service, and the Fleet Commander has full command, but they use the army's rank structure. Officers and other ranks train together at the Commando Training Centre at Lympstone, Devon, where recruit training lasts 36 weeks and officer training 64. Unlike most army regiments, their colours carry no battle honours apart from Gibraltar and the laurel wreath for Belle Île, but the globe as a symbol of the corps, which later inspired the globe in the insignia of the United States Marine Corps. A green beret marks those who have passed the commando course, and a navy blue beret those who have not.
royal-navy: Warships were used by English and Scottish kings from the early medieval period, and the first major maritime engagements were fought in the Hundred Years' War against France. For much of the medieval period fleets, or king's ships, were gathered for specific campaigns and dispersed afterwards, and they were generally merchant ships taken into service. Unlike some European states, England kept no small permanent core of warships in peacetime.

Control of the sea became critical to Anglo-Saxon kings only in the 10th century. The English Royal Navy was formally founded in 1546 by Henry VIII, when a standing Navy Royal with its own secretariat, dockyards and a permanent core of purpose-built warships emerged. The Royal Scots Navy merged with it under the Acts of Union 1707.

Under Elizabeth I, England fought Spain, and privately owned vessels joined the queen's ships in raids on Spanish commerce and colonies. The navy was used in 1588 to repulse the Spanish Armada, but the English Armada was lost the next year.

In the early 17th century England's relative naval power deteriorated until Charles I undertook a major shipbuilding programme, whose financing contributed to the outbreak of the English Civil War. After the Restoration in 1660 the navy took its present title. From the 18th century, voyages commissioned with the Royal Society included three by James Cook, and George Vancouver mapped the western coast of North America.

From the early 18th century until the Second World War it was the world's most powerful navy, and it played a key part in establishing and defending the British Empire, with imperial bases and coaling stations securing its superiority. In the First World War the Grand Fleet confronted the German High Seas Fleet across the North Sea, notably at Jutland in 1916, and the navy ferried the whole British Expeditionary Force to the Western Front without loss of life.

The Washington and London Naval Treaties limited it between the wars. In 1939 it was still the largest in the world, with over 1,400 vessels, and in the Battle of the Atlantic it defended British supply lines against U-boat attack.

After the Second World War the decline of the British Empire and economic hardship forced a reduction in its size and capability, and the United States Navy took on the role of global naval power. During the Cold War it became primarily an anti-submarine force. Royal Navy ships in commission have carried the prefix His Majesty's Ship, abbreviated HMS, since 1789. The navy is known as the Senior Service because it is the oldest of the United Kingdom's armed services, and its uniform is the pattern on which many other navies' uniforms are based.
royal-netherlands-academy-of-arts-and-sc: The institution was founded during the Kingdom of Holland as the Koninklijk Instituut van Wetenschappen, Letterkunde en Schoone Kunsten, the Royal Institute of Sciences, Literature and Fine Arts, by Lodewijk Napoleon on 4 May 1808. After the occupation had ended it was renamed in 1816 the Koninklijk-Nederlandsch Instituut van Wetenschappen, Letteren en Schoone Kunsten. In 1851 it was disbanded and re-established as the Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, and in 1938 it received its present name. Since 1812 it has been housed in the Trippenhuis, a 17th-century building in Amsterdam. It was awarded the Gouden Ganzenveer in 1955.

Members are appointed for life by co-optation, and nominations from persons or organisations outside the academy are accepted; the criterion is scientific achievement. Besides regular members there are foreign and corresponding members, though no new corresponding members have been appointed since a new membership system was introduced in 2011. The academy has two departments with around 500 members in all: Science, covering mathematics, physics, astronomy, life sciences and engineering sciences, and Humanities and Social Sciences, covering the humanities, law, behavioural sciences and social sciences. Each has its own board, and the highest body is the general meeting of members.

The academy advises the Dutch government, parliament, ministries, universities, research institutes, funding agencies and international organisations on scientific matters, provides a forum for the scientific world and promotes international scientific cooperation. It is also an umbrella for research institutes, among them the Hubrecht Institute, the Meertens Instituut, the International Institute of Social History, the NIOD Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies, the Fryske Akademie and the Rathenau Instituut. It awards prizes including the Lorentz Medal in theoretical physics, the Dr Hendrik Muller Prize for Behavioural and Social Science and the Heineken Prizes.

The Young Academy, De Jonge Akademie, was founded in 2005 as part of the academy for researchers aged 25 to 45, with ten members elected each year for five years. It was modelled on the German Junge Akademie and in turn served as a model for the Global Young Academy. In 2014 the academy also established the Society of Arts, Akademie van Kunsten, a society of artists from architecture, visual arts, dance, film, photography, literature, music and the performing arts, which began with 19 members and was meant as a place for debate about the value of art in society.
royal-netherlands-east-indies-army: The KNIL was not part of the Royal Netherlands Army but a separate arm formed for service in the Netherlands East Indies. Its campaigns against indigenous groups included the prolonged Aceh War of 1873-1904, the crushing of resistance on Bali in 1849, the annexation of Lombok and Karangasem in 1894 and the Dutch interventions in Bali of 1906 and 1908. After 1904 the colony was considered pacified, and the army turned mainly to military policing and to defence against invasion.

By December 1941 Dutch forces in the colony numbered around 85,000, the regular troops about 1,000 officers and 34,000 men, 28,000 of them indigenous. In the Dutch East Indies campaign of 1941-42 most of the KNIL was quickly defeated by Japan. Most European soldiers were interned as prisoners of war, and 25% of the prisoners did not survive. Some personnel escaped to Australia and regrouped, and small units saw action in the New Guinea and Borneo campaigns of 1944-45.

After the war the KNIL took part in two large campaigns, in 1947 and 1948, to re-establish Dutch control, and it and its Ambonese auxiliaries have been accused of war crimes. The Netherlands recognised Indonesian sovereignty on 27 December 1949. On 26 January 1950 elements of the KNIL took part in the failed coup in Bandung planned by Raymond Westerling and Sultan Hamid II, and the army was disbanded by 26 July 1950.

At first half the army was European and half indigenous, but from the late 1830s the ratio became one to three, as European volunteers were too few. In the 19th century it also recruited foreign mercenaries, among them Flemish, German, Swiss and French volunteers, and in limited numbers slaves of the Ashanti. In 1884 it counted 13,492 European, 14,982 Indonesian and at least 1,666 Eurasian recruits under a wholly European officer corps. The largest share of the native troops had always been Javanese and Sundanese.

At its disbandment the KNIL numbered 65,000, of whom 26,000 joined the new Indonesian Army. Distrust between the mainly Ambonese KNIL troops and the Javanese-dominated republican army led to clashes at Makassar in April 1950 and the attempted secession of the Republic of South Maluku in July, both suppressed by November. About 12,500 Ambonese KNIL soldiers and their families chose temporary resettlement in the Netherlands. The traditions of the KNIL are kept by the Regiment Van Heutsz of the Royal Netherlands Army.
royal-niger-company: British trade on the lower Niger grew out of the expedition of Richard Lander, who in 1832 tried to found a trading post at the meeting of the Niger and Benue rivers; 40 of its 49 members died. Macgregor Laird, one of the survivors, directed and funded later expeditions until his death in 1861, and the success of the Pleiad in 1854 led to annual voyages and the foundation of Lokoja at the confluence in 1857.

Competition among the British firms that followed cut profits to almost nothing. George Goldie, who arrived in 1877, argued for a single monopolistic chartered company, and by 1879 he had combined four firms, among them James Crowther's West African Company, into the United African Company. The Gladstone government refused it a charter in 1881, fearing international conflict and judging the firm undercapitalised for colonial administration.

Goldie raised a million pounds in investments for a new National African Company, which bought the United African Company in 1882. With 30 trading posts and a two-year price war it forced two French firms and a Liverpool rival to sell out by October 1884. At the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 Goldie argued successfully for placing the company's region in a British sphere. Despite pledges of free trade, its more than 400 treaties with local leaders bound them to trade only with or through its agents, and heavy tariffs and licence fees kept other firms out.

When King Jaja of Opobo organised his own trading network and shipped palm oil to Britain, he was lured onto a British warship and exiled to Saint Vincent on charges of treaty breaking and obstructing commerce. In July 1886 the company received its charter as the Royal Niger Company Chartered and Limited, with Lord Aberdare as governor and Goldie as vice-governor.

A chartered company could not hold its own against the state-supported protectorates of France and Germany, and on 1 January 1900 it transferred its territories to the British government for £865,000. With the small Niger Coast Protectorate these lands were formed into British protectorates, united in 1914 as the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria. The company carried on as the Niger Company Ltd and joined the United Africa Company in 1929, which passed under the control of Unilever in the 1930s and was absorbed into it in 1987.
royal-palace-of-caserta: The palace stands in Caserta, in Campania, 35 kilometres north of Naples. It has a rectangular plan measuring 247 by 190 metres, with two orthogonal arms joining the four sides to form four inner courts. It rises five floors, with a volume of about 2 million cubic metres and a floor area of 130,000 square metres. It has 1,200 rooms, including two dozen state apartments, 1,742 windows, 34 staircases, 1,026 fireplaces, a large library and a theatre modelled on the Teatro San Carlo of Naples. The Palatine Chapel, which Luigi Vanvitelli modelled on the chapel at Versailles, stands inside the palace with direct access from the Upper Vestibule.

Behind the palace stretches a garden of 120 hectares, begun in 1753 and also inspired by Versailles. A long alley with fountains and cascades runs from the back façade, among them the fountains of Diana and Actaeon, Venus and Adonis, the Dolphins, Aeolus and Ceres. In the 1780s Carlo Vanvitelli and the botanist John Graefer designed an English garden in the upper part, an early continental example of the naturalistic taste.

Construction began in 1752 for Charles VII of Naples, later Charles III of Spain, working closely with Vanvitelli. Charles never slept a night there, since he abdicated in 1759 to become King of Spain, and the project was carried only to partial completion for his third son and successor, Ferdinand IV of Naples. Versailles was the model, and the proposal first made by Mario Gioffredo in 1750 envisaged a virtual city housing the court and the elites of the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily.

The king also wanted a court and administrative centre protected from sea attack and distant from the revolt-prone and congested capital. The population of Caserta Vecchia was moved 10 kilometres to provide a workforce, and a silk factory at San Leucio was disguised as a pavilion in the park.

Vanvitelli died in 1773 and his son Carlo and other architects continued the work, but his original project, including a pair of frontal wings, was never finished. From 1923 to 1943 the palace housed the Italian Air Force Academy. In 1943 it became Allied Force Headquarters in the Mediterranean, and on 29 April 1945 the unconditional surrender of German forces in Italy was signed there. An air raid in September 1943 destroyed almost all the paintings of the Palatine Chapel.

The palace was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, together with the park, the Carolino aqueduct and the San Leucio complex. The listing describes it as exceptional for its design, which takes in an imposing palace and park, much of the surrounding landscape and an ambitious new town planned by the precepts of its time.
royal-palaces-of-abomey: The palaces stand at the heart of Abomey, formerly the capital of the West African Kingdom of Dahomey, founded in 1625 by the Fon people. King Houegbadja, who founded the city, was the first to begin building palaces and set the legal framework of the kingdom, including its rules of succession. King Agaja defeated Allada in 1724 and Whydah in 1727, and many prisoners were sold as slaves at Ouidah, which began Dahomey's dominance of the slave trade. In the 19th century King Guézo promoted agriculture, and the kingdom prospered by exporting corn and palm oil.

After the Fon returned to raiding the Ouémé Valley, France declared war, and in the Second Franco-Dahomean War of 1892 to 1894 it seized the Singboji palace. King Béhanzin, the last independent king, was eventually deported to Martinique, and his successor Agooli Agbo to Gabon in 1900.

Twelve kings succeeded one another between 1625 and 1900, and, apart from King Akaba, who used a separate enclosure, each had a palace built within the same cob-wall area in keeping with earlier palaces. A mud wall about 10 kilometres around, with six gates and a ditch of prickly acacia, enclosed villages, fields, a market-place and the barracks. At its peak the complex could hold up to 8,000 people. Earth was used for foundations and floors, and the woodwork was of palm, bamboo, iroko and mahogany.

In the absence of written records, polychrome earthen bas-reliefs recorded the kingdom's official history: each king's victories and power, and the myths and customs of the Fon. They were made of earth from ant-hills mixed with palm oil and coloured with vegetable and mineral pigments.

The palaces of Glèlè and Guézo now house the Abomey Historical Museum, set up in 1943 by the French colonial administration. UNESCO inscribed the site in 1985, calling it a unique reminder of a vanished kingdom. A tornado damaged it in 1984 and it stood on the List of World Heritage in Danger until July 2007. A bushfire on 21 January 2009 destroyed many buildings, among them the tombs of Kings Agonglo and Ghezo. In 2022 twenty-six statues looted by French troops in 1892, returned under a French law of 24 December 2020, went on display in Cotonou.
royal-proclamation-of-1763: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 ended the Seven Years' War and its North American theatre, the French and Indian War. France ceded its lands west of the Mississippi to Spain, and those east of the river and south of Rupert's Land to Great Britain, keeping only Saint Pierre and Miquelon. King George III issued the proclamation on 7 October 1763 to govern the new territories and regulate the settlers' advance. The line had been conceived before Pontiac's Rebellion broke out that year, but the war hastened its becoming law.

Besides Quebec, West Florida and East Florida, the proclamation set up a government for the British Ceded Islands of Grenada, Tobago, Saint Vincent and Dominica, and gave the Labrador coast north-east of the St. John River to Newfoundland. The line followed the Appalachian watershed: land whose rivers ran to the Atlantic was left to the colonies, and land draining to the Mississippi was reserved for Native Americans. It was meant as a temporary boundary that could be moved west in an orderly way, and people could cross it but not settle beyond it. Private purchase of Native land was outlawed; future purchases were to be made by Crown officials at a public meeting of the peoples concerned.

Land speculators such as the owners of the Ohio Company, and veterans with grants beyond the line such as George Washington, lobbied against it, and many colonists settled west regardless; Daniel Boone crossed into Kentucky in 1769, and in 1774 James Harrod founded Harrodstown. The Treaties of Fort Stanwix and Hard Labour in 1768 and of Lochaber in 1770 moved the line, opening much of Kentucky and West Virginia. Historians disagree on how far the proclamation fed the American Revolution.

In the United States it lapsed with the Treaty of Paris of 1783, though later laws followed its pattern, and in Johnson v. McIntosh in 1823 the Supreme Court held that only the government could buy Native land. In Canada it continued to govern land cessions in Upper Canada and Rupert's Land, and the Constitution Act, 1982 recognises it as the first legal recognition of aboriginal title. The historian Colin Calloway notes that scholars disagree whether it recognised or undermined tribal sovereignty.
royal-road: The Royal Road was reorganised and rebuilt for trade in the 5th century BCE by the Achaemenid Empire, to allow fast communication in the western part of the empire between Susa and Sardis. It was probably perfected under Darius I, who improved an existing road network into the road as it is known. Because the route followed neither the shortest nor the easiest line between the empire's main cities and ran through the heart of the old Assyrian empire, archaeologists think its westernmost sections may originally have been built by the Assyrian kings.

Its course has been reconstructed from the writings of Herodotus, archaeological research and other records. Herodotus, an Ionian Greek, saw Persia from the west and did not note the eastern stretches, which can be identified in northern Iran.

The road was above all a post road. It had one hundred and eleven posting stations kept supplied with fresh horses, and relays of swift mounted messengers, called pirradazis, carried messages along it. Mounted couriers of the Angarium were supposed to cover the 2,699 kilometres from Susa to Sardis in nine days, while the journey took ninety days on foot. Stretches across the central plateau of Iran, such as the Great Khorasan Road, coincide with the major trade route known as the Silk Road.
25 metres wide, held within a stone curbing. In 1961 S. F. Starr traced the stretch from Gordium to Sardis, identifying river crossings by the remains of ancient bridge abutments.

Herodotus wrote that nothing in the world travels faster than these Persian couriers. A passage inspired by his praise, that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds, is inscribed on the James Farley Post Office in New York, and is sometimes thought of as the creed of the United States Postal Service, which has no official motto.

The phrase royal road also became a metaphor. Euclid is said to have told King Ptolemy that there is no royal road to geometry, a remark also attributed to Menaechmus in reply to Alexander the Great. Sigmund Freud described dreams as the royal road to the unconscious, and Karl Marx wrote in 1872 that there is no royal road to science.
royal-society: The Invisible College has been described as a precursor group to the Royal Society, consisting of a number of natural philosophers around Robert Boyle. The phrase appears in German Rosicrucian pamphlets of the early 17th century, and Ben Jonson referred to the idea in a masque of 1624/5, related in meaning to Francis Bacon's House of Salomon. In letters dated 1646 and 1647 Boyle writes of "our invisible college" or "our philosophical college". The group's common theme was to acquire knowledge through experimental investigation.

The society's second charter was signed on 22 April 1663. In August 1662 Charles II had told the society that it might use the arms of England as part of its own, and the charter granted the arms, with the motto Nullius in verba, to the president, council and fellows. The motto comes from Horace's Epistles, where the poet compares himself to a retired gladiator, free from control, and signifies the fellows' determination to establish facts by experiment.

In the 18th century the zeal of the early years faded, and few scientific figures of the first rank emerged. In the second half of the century it became customary for the government to refer important scientific questions to the society's council. In 1777 a dispute over lightning conductors spilled into politics: Benjamin Franklin had invented the pointed conductor in 1749 and Benjamin Wilson the blunted one, and opponents of Franklin's design accused its supporters of being American allies. The debate led to the resignation of the president, Sir John Pringle.

The early 19th century has been seen as a time of decline: of 662 fellows in 1830, only 104 had contributed to the Philosophical Transactions. That year Charles Babbage published Reflections on the Decline of Science in England, deeply critical of the society. A Charters Committee set up by James South recommended limiting the number of Fellows elected each year, and the membership became almost entirely scientific. The first women Fellows, Marjory Stephenson and Kathleen Lonsdale, were elected on 22 March 1945, after a postal ballot of Fellows approved the change by 336 votes to 37.

The society is governed by a council chaired by its president, elected from and by the Fellows. Fellows are scientists and engineers from the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth chosen for a substantial contribution to the improvement of natural knowledge, including mathematics, engineering science and medical science. They are elected for life, may use the postnominal FRS, and are chosen by ten sectional committees of existing Fellows. Each Fellow signs the Charter Book, which has been signed continuously since 1663 and which every British monarch has signed except William and Mary, and Queen Anne.
royal-yugoslav-army: At the end of 1918 a Serbian Army mission arrived in Zagreb to merge the Serbian Army with the National Army of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which the National Council had formed from the Austro-Hungarian units on its territory. An agreement that Croatian and Slovene officers would command regiments in their own lands was ignored. The new army was led by Serbian generals, used Serbian as its official language and kept the Serbian Army's uniforms, ranks, medals and regulations, while former Austro-Hungarian and Croatian Home Guard officers had to apply for admission. Its early fighting was in Carinthia until September 1919, where it briefly occupied Klagenfurt.

By 1921 the army had 16 infantry divisions and two cavalry divisions in four army areas, with headquarters at Novi Sad, Sarajevo, Skoplje and Zagreb, and a conscript peacetime strength of 140,000, cut to 100,000 in 1922. A clique of politically active officers, the White Hand, was present from the start; its founder Petar Živković commanded the Guards division formed in 1925 and became prime minister under King Alexander's dictatorship in 1929. Arms came largely from Czechoslovakia. British attachés reported tough infantry but old tactics, weak training and shortages of machine guns, radios, transport and tanks. Of 165 generals in 1938, two were Croats and two Slovenes.

The Anschluss and the Munich Agreement in 1938 gave Yugoslavia a frontier with Germany and threatened its chief arms supplier. When the Axis invaded in April 1941 the army was still mobilising, with about 600,000 men under arms by 20 March and only some eleven divisions in position. Its 1st Army Group, with the 4th and 7th Armies, was mainly Croatian, and on 10 April some of its units mutinied as a new Croatian government welcomed the Germans into Zagreb.

After the surrender, units that escaped to Egypt formed the Yugoslav Army Outside the Homeland, including the 1st Battalion, Royal Yugoslav Guards, which fought in North Africa with the 4th Indian Division and was disbanded in Italy in 1944 amid feuding between royalists and supporters of Josip Broz Tito. At home, the Chetniks of Draža Mihailović called themselves the Royal Yugoslav Army in the Fatherland. The army was formally disbanded on 7 March 1945, when the government-in-exile of Peter II was abolished.
rozafa-castle: Rozafa Castle, also called Shkodër Castle, rises on a rocky hill 130 metres above sea level, surrounded by the Buna and Drin rivers, in the city of Shkodër. The hill has been settled since the Early Bronze Age. Its earliest fortification walls date from the 4th–3rd century BCE and formed the citadel of the Illyrian city of Skodra, capital of the Labeatae, especially under King Gentius. The visible walls are mostly Venetian. Scholars link the name Rozafa with Resafa, the place where Saint Sergius died, as Shkodër has a long tradition of venerating him.

In the Third Illyrian War the Illyrian king Gentius gathered his forces in Skodra. Attacked by a Roman army under L. Anicius Gallus, he was trapped in the city waiting for a relief army from his brother Caravantius that never came. On the third day of a truce Gentius surrendered, and the Illyrian kingdom fell in 168 BCE.

Inside the castle stand the ruins of a 13th-century Venetian Catholic church, considered by scholars to be St Stephen's Cathedral, which the Ottoman Empire turned into the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Mosque after taking the city in the 15th century. The castle was the site of the sieges of Shkodër of 1478–79 and 1912–13.

A widespread Albanian legend, attested as early as 1505 in Marin Barleti's De obsidione Scodrensi, says that three brothers could not make the castle's foundations stand until they walled up the wife who brought their food. The youngest brother's wife Rozafa accepted, asking that holes be left for her right eye, hand, foot and breast so that she could still care for her infant son. A Serbian epic version, The Building of Skadar, was published by Vuk Karadžić in 1815. Local people believe Rozafa's milk still flows in the walls, seen in milkweed sap and in limestone deposits that women scrape off to make a medicine to increase their milk.
