rozvi-empire: The name Rozvi is taken from the Shona word kurozva, to plunder, and recalls the state's reputation as a warrior nation. Early in the 17th century Mutapa became a Portuguese vassal, and Portuguese prazo-holders, outside the reach of the Mwenemutapa's courts, raided and enslaved Shona villages. From the late 1660s locusts, smallpox, measles and plague emptied fields and villages. In these years Changamire Dombo, probably a Mutapa governor who used royal cattle to win followers, defeated the Portuguese and Mutapa, conquered Butua around 1683 and drove the Portuguese off the plateau in the 1690s.

Dombo also conquered Manyika before his death around 1696. A succession dispute among his sons followed, and offshoots of the dynasty moved away to found the Venda Kingdom at Dzata and the Nambya state at Hwange. Through the 18th century newcomers conquered Rozvi subjects and sometimes stopped paying tribute. Tradition says that Changamire Rupandamananga let his people starve during the drought of 1795 to 1800; the historian Stan Mudenge saw this as the start of civil wars lasting to at least 1808, while David Beach placed the cause of the collapse in the 1830s.

In that decade Nguni groups of the Mfecane invaded in quick succession. After the death of Changamire Chirisamhuru at the hands of Nyamazana's Ngoni, leadership split among the royal houses, and Mzilikazi's Ndebele subdued the state around 1838. His son Tohwechipi rebelled against Ndebele rule and surrendered only after a long siege in 1866.

The mambo ruled from Danamombe, advised by a council of hereditary lineages: four chief councillors, among them Tumbare's father and the Chief Diviner, and two sekuru lineages who served as priests and rainmakers. Below him stood provincial chiefs, lesser chiefs, village heads and householders. Subjects paid yearly tribute in goods and labour and received land, rain ceremonies, famine relief and protection; each year all fires were put out and relit from the mambo's fire as a sign of submission.

Farming of sorghum and millet sustained most people, and herds were lent to clients under the kuronzera system, which turned cattle wealth into political loyalty. The army was organised in regiments under generals answering to Tumbare. Because the Portuguese were barred from the state and oral traditions were disrupted by later conquests, its history is known only in part.
ruaidri-ua-conchobair: Ruaidrí was one of more than twenty sons of King Tairrdelbach Ua Conchobair, and with his sister Mór the only child of his father's third wife, Cailech Dé Ní Eidin of Aidhne. His brother Conchobar was the designated heir. In 1136 Ruaidrí and his brother Aedh rebelled; Aedh was blinded on their father's orders, but Ruaidrí was protected by Muireadhach Ua Dubhthaigh, Archbishop of Connacht. After a second rebellion in 1143 he was imprisoned for about a year, and freed only after Conchobar was killed in Mide in 1144.

Raids on Tighearnán Ua Ruairc in 1146 and the killing of his father's nephew Domnall Ua Conchobar in 1150 raised his standing, and the arrest of the new heir, Donnell Mór Mideach, in 1151 left him his father's heir. In 1153 Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn's northern army surprised and defeated him at Fordruim.

On his father's death in 1156 Ruaidrí became king of Connacht without opposition, arresting three brothers as a precaution; one, Brian Breifneach, was blinded. Mac Lochlainn claimed the high kingship, and Ruaidrí answered his campaigns by burning the country around Strabane and Derry and undoing his settlement of Munster. When Mac Lochlainn died in 1166 Ruaidrí was inaugurated as high king at Dublin, held the Óenach Tailten, expelled Dermot MacMurrough from Leinster and took hostages from the major kings.

The Normans who came to restore MacMurrough took much of Leinster and the cities of Waterford and Wexford. Ruaidrí raised a large army, said to number sixty thousand, burned Norman castles at Trim and Kells and besieged Dublin in 1171, but was routed when the defenders attacked his resting camp. He kept the Midlands, and his forces destroyed a Norman expedition into Munster at the Battle of Thurles. After the Treaty of Windsor, Henry II did not restrain his barons nor Ruaidrí the lesser Irish kings, and the fighting went on.

Ruaidrí abdicated in 1183 but twice returned to rule briefly, and died on 2 December 1198. His sons' lines lost the kingship: the last of them to rule Connacht, Aedh mac Ruaidri, died in 1233, and the Annals of Connacht explain the loss as punishment for Ruaidrí's refusal to give up adultery when the pope offered Ireland to his descendants. Later kings of Connacht descended from his younger brother, Cathal Crobhdearg Ua Conchobair.
rubber: The first use of rubber was by the indigenous cultures of Mesoamerica. The earliest archaeological evidence of the use of natural latex from the Hevea tree comes from the Olmec culture, in which rubber was first used to make balls for the Mesoamerican ballgame. The Maya and Aztec cultures later used it as well, and the Aztecs also made containers and made textiles waterproof with latex sap.

Industrial demand for rubber-like materials began to outstrip natural supplies by the end of the 19th century, which led to the chemical synthesis of synthetic rubber in 1909. Congo rubber, formerly a major source, came from vines of the genus Landolphia and motivated the atrocities in the Congo Free State.

Rubber consists of polymers of the organic compound isoprene. It is harvested mainly as latex from the Pará rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis), once native to Brazil and now grown throughout the tropics. The milky latex is drawn off by making incisions in the bark in a process called tapping. Tapping demands accuracy, since cuts that are too many or too deep can stunt a tree or kill it. Natural rubber has a large stretch ratio and high resilience and is buoyant and waterproof.

Natural rubber is vulnerable to oxidation, but vulcanisation, heating it with sulfur or other agents, improves its resistance and elasticity. Ammoniation, invented around 1920 by Ernest Hopkinson, vice-president of the United States Rubber Company, preserves latex for longer.

Before World War II, rubber went into hoses, belts, gaskets, flooring and antivibration mounts for the automotive industry. Car tires, at first solid rather than pneumatic, consumed a large amount of it, and gloves, balloons, adhesives, rubber bands and pencil erasers were also large uses. From 1939 to 1941 Malaya was the world's largest supplier, producing enough to supply the British Empire and its allies, including the still neutral United States.

Japan's entry into the war in December 1941 and its rapid seizure of Malaya in early 1942 cut the Allied Powers off from most of the global supply. The United States entered a temporary rubber famine and sought to reduce its dependence by developing substantial synthetic rubber production. Ceylon became the Allies' primary source of natural rubber.
ruben-dario: He was born on 18 January 1867 as Félix Rubén García Sarmiento in Metapa, in Matagalpa (now Ciudad Darío), where his mother Rosa Sarmiento had gone after leaving her husband Manuel García, who was said to drink heavily. His baptism gave the surname García, but his paternal family had long been known as the Daríos, after a great-grandfather nicknamed Don Darío. In El Salvador he met the poet Francisco Gavidia, a connoisseur of French poetry, and with his help first tried to adapt the French Alexandrine to Castilian verse. After a return to Nicaragua and work at the National Library in Managua, he sailed for Chile on 5 June 1886.

In Chile he worked for the newspaper La Época in Santiago and published Abrojos in 1887. His book Azul..., which appeared in Valparaíso in July 1888, was the key work of the modernist revolution that had just begun. Its success brought him a post as correspondent of La Nación of Buenos Aires, then the most widely circulated periodical in Hispanic America. He travelled to Spain in 1892 with a Nicaraguan delegation, lived for a time in Buenos Aires as an honorary Colombian consul, and later sent chronicles from Spain on its mood after defeat by the United States, collected in 1901 as España contemporánea.

He covered the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1900 for La Nación, and those chronicles became Peregrinaciones. He later served as Nicaraguan resident minister in Madrid under José Santos Zelaya, resigning on 25 February 1909 after Zelaya was overthrown. He died in León on 6 February 1916, aged 49.

French poetry shaped him: first the romantics, above all Victor Hugo, then the Parnassians Théophile Gautier, Catulle Mendès and José María de Heredia, José Martí, and the symbolists, especially Paul Verlaine. In the opening poem of Cantos de vida y esperanza (1905) he described himself as strong towards Hugo and ambiguous towards Verlaine. He wrote in thirty-seven different metrical lines and 136 stanza forms. His main works are Azul... (1888), Prosas profanas (1896) and Cantos de vida y esperanza.

The critic Roberto González Echevarría holds that Spanish-language poetry divides into the periods before and after Darío, and Octavio Paz described his as one of the most profound poetic revolutions in Spanish. The National Library of Nicaragua was renamed in his honour, and Madrid has a metro station and a plaza named after him.
ruben-um-nyobe: Um Nyobè was born in 1913 in Song Mpeck, in the German colony of Kamerun, which was divided between France and the United Kingdom after the First World War. His family came from an agricultural region of Bassa, and his father was a traditional priest; Um Nyobè was baptised and took the name Ruben. Educated in Presbyterian schools in the French part of the country, he spoke French, Bassa, Bulu and Do, became a civil servant and, at the end of the 1930s, joined the Jeunesse camerounaise Française, set up by the French administration to counter Nazi propaganda.

After the Second World War he joined the Cercle d'études Marxistes, launched in Yaoundé by the French teacher and trade unionist Gaston Donnat. He became general secretary of the trade union USCC in 1947, after the repression that followed the shooting of strikers in Douala in September 1945. He attended the first congress of the African Democratic Rally at Bamako in September 1946, and trade unionists of the USCC founded the Union des populations du Cameroun in a café-bar in Douala on 10 April 1948; he was not present but was placed at its head in November 1948.

Um Nyobè opposed tribalism as a colonial tool of division and urged boycotts, strikes and demonstrations rather than violence. The UPC created the Democratic Union of Cameroonian Women in 1952 and the Jeunesse démocratique du Cameroun in 1954, set up party schools, and published three newspapers calling for independence, the reunification of the former German Kamerun and social justice. He spoke for the people of Cameroon at the United Nations in 1952 and 1954. In Bassa he was named Mpodol Ion, spokesman of the nation.

The French government banned the UPC on 13 June 1955, and its militants went into hiding. Um Nyobè was killed by the French army on 13 September 1958 near his home village of Boumnyebel, in the department of Nyong-et-Kellé, and Félix-Roland Moumié replaced him at the head of the movement. Until the 1990s any mention of him was prohibited in Cameroon. His idea of a revolution of the mind, by which oppressed Cameroonians would overcome their fear of Europeans, is known as Umism.
rudaki: Little information is available about Rudaki's life, and much of it has been reconstructed from his poems. He lived under the Samanid Empire, in which New Persian literature began to develop and flourish. According to the Tajik writer Sadriddin Ayni, he was born in the village of Panjrud in the former Panjakent District of Tajikistan.

By the age of eight he had reportedly memorised the Qur'an and was skilled in poetry, and a musician named Abu'l-Abak Bakhtiar taught him to play the chang. In his early years he became popular for his fine voice, his poetry and his playing. Early poets such as Daqiqi and Ferdowsi imply that he was blind, and the historian Awfi says he was born blind, which some modern scholars question because of the expressive picture of nature in his writing.

The most important part of Rudaki's career was spent at the Samanid court in Bukhara. He is connected with the amir Nasr II, who reigned from 914 to 943, though the literary scholar Sassan Tabatabai argues from a poem comforting Ahmad Samani after the death of Ismail Samani in 907 that he had already joined the court under Ahmad Samani.

His success was largely due to his main patron, the vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami, who regarded him as the best among Persian and Arab poets. He was a close friend of his student Shahid Balkhi and wrote an elegy for him after his death in 936. After Bal'ami's downfall in 937, his career declined, he fell out of favour with the amir and was dismissed from the court. He lived his last years in poverty and died blind and alone in his hometown.

According to Asadi Tusi, Rudaki's divan consisted of more than 180,000 verses, but most is lost. What remains is mostly single verses preserved in Persian dictionaries, especially Asadi Tusi's Lughat-i Furs. A qasida of almost 100 verses survives in the Tarikh-i Sistan, dedicated to Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad, the Samanid governor of Sistan, who rewarded him with 10,000 dinars.

His best-known work is his versification of the Kalila wa-Dimna, a collection of Indian fables, which Nasr II had Bal'ami translate from Arabic into Persian; interpreters read it aloud so that the blind poet could versify it. Though he showed pro-Isma'ili sympathies, his poetry is secular, and he evoked ancient Iranian and Zoroastrian notions more than Muslim ones. In Iran he is acknowledged as the founder of New Persian poetry and in Tajikistan as the father of Tajik literature.
rudamun: Rudamun was the younger son of Osorkon III and the brother of Takelot III. His titulary reads Usermaatre Setepenamun, Rudamun Meryamun, and leaves out the epithets Si-Ese and Netjer-Heqawaset that his father and brother used. He is poorly attested, and Kenneth Kitchen credits him with a brief reign of about two to three years because so few contemporary documents are known for him.

The evidence consists of a small amount of decorative work at the Temple of Osiris Heqadjet, several stone blocks from Medinet Habu and a vase. Two fragments of a faience statuette bearing his name were found more recently at Hermopolis, which suggests that he preserved the unity of his father's large kingdom in Upper Egypt, from at least Herakleopolis Magna to Thebes.

David Aston argued that Rudamun was the anonymous king of Year 19 at Wadi Gasus, but Claus Jurman's work of 2006 redated that graffito wholly to the Nubian period of the 25th Dynasty. G. Broekman proposed instead a Shoshenq VII, but scholars doubt that the Nile Level Text No. 3 on which this rests names Shoshenq rather than Takelot.

Soon after Rudamun's death his kingdom broke into minor city states under local kings such as Peftjaubast of Herakleopolis Magna, Nimlot at Hermopolis and Ini at Thebes. Peftjaubast had married Rudamun's daughter Irbastudjanefu and was therefore his son-in-law. Nothing is known of Rudamun's burial place.
ruder-boskovic: Ruđer Bošković was born on 18 May 1711 in Dubrovnik, in the Republic of Ragusa, the seventh child of the merchant Nikola Bošković and Paola Bettera, whose family had settled from Bergamo in the early 17th century. His father died when he was 10. At 8 or 9 he was sent to the local Jesuit Collegium Ragusinum, where he gained a reputation for a quick mind and an easy memory.

On 16 September 1725 he left Dubrovnik for Rome in the care of two Jesuit priests. He entered the novitiate in 1731, studied mathematics and physics, and in 1740 was appointed professor of mathematics at the Roman college. He was ordained a priest in 1744 and visited his home town only once more, in 1747.

Bošković published a very large number of dissertations on subjects from the transit of Mercury and the aurora to the figure of the Earth and the theory of comets. In 1742 Pope Benedict XIV consulted him, with other men of science, about a crack in the dome of St Peter's, and his suggestion of five concentric iron bands was adopted. Persuaded by the Pope to stay in Italy rather than join a Portuguese expedition to Brazil, he measured with the English Jesuit Christopher Maire an arc of two degrees of the meridian between Rome and Rimini, begun at the end of 1750 and completed in about two years, with a map of the States of the Church.

He served Lucca as an agent in Vienna in 1757, and in 1760 went to London as ambassador of Ragusa to prove the republic's neutrality, a mission he completed with success; there he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society. From 1764 he held the chair of mathematics at Pavia and directed the Brera observatory in Milan. After the suppression of his order he accepted an invitation from the King of France and became director of optics for the navy in Paris, where he stayed ten years. He returned to Italy in 1783 and died in Milan on 13 February 1787.

In De Viribus Vivis (1745) he sought a middle way between Newton's gravitational theory and Leibniz's monad-points. His best-known work, Philosophiæ naturalis theoria redacta ad unicam legem virium in natura existentium, first published in Vienna in 1758, set out his atomic theory and his theory of forces. In 1753 he discovered the absence of an atmosphere on the Moon, and he devised geometric procedures for finding a planet's equator and orbit from three observations. Nietzsche's ideas of force were influenced by him, and a lunar crater and the Ruđer Bošković Institute in Zagreb bear his name. His nationality is claimed in Croatia, Italy and Serbia alike.
rudesheim-am-rhein: Rüdesheim lies at the foot of the Niederwald on the right bank of the Rhine, in the Rheingau wine region and the Rheingau-Taunus-Kreis district. It belongs to the Frankfurt Rhine Main Region and to the Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site, and its full name distinguishes it from Rüdesheim an der Nahe. The municipality has five quarters: Rüdesheim itself, Eibingen, Assmannshausen, Aulhausen and Presberg. Two ferries, one for pedestrians and one for cars, connect it with the left bank, where the town of Bingen faces it.

The area was settled first by Celts, then by the Ubii and later the Mattiaci. In the first century the Romans pushed forward to the Taunus and kept a bridgehead near what is now Rüdesheim, on the way to the Limes. Alamanni and then Franks followed. Glass finds from the Migration Period suggest that winegrowing was already practised. Rüdesheim was first mentioned in a document in 1074, and its livelihood came mainly from winegrowing and shipping, particularly timber rafting.

The town received town rights on 1 January 1818. After Prussia annexed the Duchy of Nassau in 1867, Rüdesheim became the seat of the new Rheingaukreis and kept that status for 110 years, until a municipal reform in 1977 merged the district into the Rheingau-Taunus-Kreis and moved the seat to Bad Schwalbach. In 1939 the National Socialists forcibly merged the self-governing community of Eibingen with the town, against the wishes of its inhabitants. Assmannshausen, Aulhausen and Presberg were incorporated in 1977.

The Brömserburg, built in the 10th century on the site of a Roman fortification, is the oldest castle in the Rhine Gorge. The Archbishop of Mainz owned it from the 10th to the 13th century, and French troops under Henri II d'Orléans, duc de Longueville, destroyed the top of its tower in 1640. The town bought it in 1941, and it now holds a wine museum. Eibingen Abbey, founded by Hildegard of Bingen, stands above Eibingen. Riesling is the main grape grown, and tourism has increasingly replaced shipping as a source of income.
rudolf-diesel: Rudolf Christian Karl Diesel was born on 18 March 1858 in Paris, the second of three children of Bavarian immigrants. His father Theodor, a bookbinder from Augsburg, became a leather goods manufacturer in Paris, and the family had financial difficulties, so the boy worked in his father's workshop. When the Franco-Prussian War broke out in 1870 the family was deported to England, and his mother sent him to relatives in Augsburg, where he finished his basic education at the top of his class in 1873.

At fourteen he wrote to his parents that he meant to become an engineer. He took a merit scholarship at the Royal Bavarian Polytechnic of Munich against his parents' wishes, studied under Carl von Linde, and graduated in January 1880 with the highest honours.

Diesel returned to Paris and helped Linde build a refrigeration and ice plant, becoming its director a year later. In early 1890 he moved to Berlin to manage Linde's research department. Barred from using his patents there for his own ends, he turned to other fields and built a steam engine using ammonia vapour, which exploded and nearly killed him; he spent many months in hospital with health and eyesight problems.

He worked on an internal combustion engine that could approach the maximum theoretical thermal efficiency of the Carnot cycle, knowing that as much as 90 percent of a steam engine's fuel energy was wasted. In 1892 he received the German patent DRP 67207, and in 1893 he published a treatise on a heat engine to replace the steam engine. By summer 1893 he had realised his first theory was wrong and filed another application. In his engine the heat of compressed air ignited the injected fuel, with no spark plug.

From 1893 to 1897 Heinrich von Buz, director of Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, let Diesel test and develop his ideas, with support from the Krupp firm. The first successful engine, Motor 250/400, a 25-horsepower single-cylinder four-stroke, was officially tested in 1897, and royalties made Diesel wealthy.

On the evening of 29 September 1913 Diesel boarded the steamer SS Dresden at Antwerp, bound for a meeting in London. His cabin was empty the next morning, and his hat and folded overcoat were found under the afterdeck railing. Ten days later a Dutch pilot boat's crew found a body in the Eastern Scheldt and took items from its clothing, which his son Eugen identified. Biographers have argued that he died by suicide, others that he was murdered; his death remains unsolved. His engine became an important replacement for the steam piston engine and spread to ships, submarines, locomotives, trucks and automobiles.
rudolf-i-duke-of-saxe-wittenberg: Rudolf, a member of the House of Ascania, was the eldest son of Duke Albert II of Saxony and Agnes of Habsburg, a daughter of King Rudolf I of Germany. In 1290 the king enfeoffed the young Rudolf with the fiefs of the extinct counts of Brehna, and in 1296 the Ascanian lands were divided into the duchies of Saxe-Wittenberg and Saxe-Lauenburg. Still a minor when his father died on 25 August 1298, he succeeded under his mother's regency and took up the rule himself in 1302.

Rudolf first had to make his Saxe-Lauenburg cousins agree that he, and not the eldest of them, John II, had inherited the electoral rank. In 1308 he voted for Henry of Luxembourg and helped him with money and troops. In the double election of 1314 he voted for his Habsburg cousin Frederick the Fair, while John II, claiming the same vote, chose Louis the Bavarian, who won at the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322. Louis then refused Rudolf the Margraviate of Brandenburg, which he had administered as regent since 1319, and gave it with its electoral vote to his son Louis V.

Rudolf turned to mediation, organising the meeting of six electors behind the Declaration of Rhense in 1338. Under his mother's influence he began the expulsion of Jews from Wittenberg, and he outlawed the Slavic languages of his territory. He founded the All Saints' Monastery and around 1340 built Wittenberg Castle. He was the only elector present at the coronation of Charles IV in Bonn on 26 November 1346, and received the Altmark in 1347, which made the Elbe the boundary between Saxony and Brandenburg.

The Golden Bull made the electorates indivisible and inherited by primogeniture, and the Saxe-Lauenburg branch lost all claim to the electoral vote and the office of Imperial Archmarshal. Rudolf died in Wittenberg on 12 March 1356 and was succeeded by his eldest surviving son, Rudolf II. First buried in the Wittenberg Franciscan Church, his remains were moved to the All Saints' Church in 1883. The Saxe-Wittenberg line died out with his grandson Albert III in 1412, and its lands and electoral dignity passed to the Wettin margraves of Meissen.
rudolf-i-of-germany: Rudolf was born on 1 May 1218 at Limburgh Castle near Sasbach am Kaiserstuhl in the Breisgau, the son of Count Albert IV of Habsburg and Hedwig, daughter of Count Ulrich of Kyburg. He was not educated at the royal court and probably knew neither writing nor Latin. When his father died on the Barons' Crusade, Rudolf assumed sole rule of the main Habsburg line, with estates around Habsburg Castle in Aargau and in Alsace.

He built Neuhabsburg Castle on Lake Lucerne around 1244 and married Gertrude of Hohenberg, which strengthened his position in Swabia. In 1254 he joined the Prussian Crusade. During the Great Interregnum that followed the death of Frederick II in 1250 he took advantage of the disorder, seizing the estates of his maternal uncle Count Hartmann IV of Kyburg in 1264 and fighting successful feuds with the bishops of Strasbourg and Basel.

In August 1273 Pope Gregory X told the electors to choose a king. They elected Rudolf unanimously at Frankfurt on 1 October 1273, and Archbishop Engelbert II of Cologne crowned him at Aachen on 24 October. The pope acknowledged the election on 20 September 1274. The Imperial Diet at Nuremberg ordered the return of crown estates, and when Ottokar II of Bohemia refused to give up Austria, Styria and Carinthia, Rudolf had him placed under the imperial ban. War began in June 1276, and on 26 August 1278 Ottokar was defeated and killed at the Battle on the Marchfeld.

In December 1282, at Augsburg, Rudolf invested his sons Albert and Rudolf II with Austria and Styria, laying the foundation of the House of Habsburg. In 1286 he gave Carinthia to Count Meinhard. He was less successful in restoring internal peace: territorial peaces were ordered and the Synod of Würzburg of March 1287 extended one to the whole Empire, but he lacked the power to enforce them. In 1286 he also declared the Jews servi camerae, serfs of the treasury, which negated their political freedoms.

Rudolf died at Speyer on 15 July 1291 and was buried in Speyer Cathedral. In 1291 he had tried to secure the election of his son Albert as German king, but the electors refused, and after Rudolf's death they chose Count Adolf of Nassau. His reign is most remembered for establishing the Habsburgs as a powerful dynasty in the southeast of the realm, while elsewhere the long decline of imperial authority continued. In the Divine Comedy Dante finds him outside the gates of purgatory and calls him the one who neglected what he ought to have done.
rudolf-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Rudolf was born in Vienna on 18 July 1552, the eldest son of Maximilian II, and his mother was the Spanish princess Maria, a daughter of Charles V. From the age of 11 to 19 he lived in Spain at the court of his uncle Philip II. His father worried about his aloof and stiff manner, while his mother saw courtliness and refinement in him.

He remained reserved, secretive and largely a recluse who disliked travelling or taking part in the daily affairs of state. He was drawn to astrology and alchemy, which were mainstream in the Renaissance, and to horses, clocks and collecting rarities. He suffered periodic bouts of melancholy, which grew worse with age. He never married but had several children with his mistress Catherina Strada.

Rudolf succeeded his father on 12 October 1576, and in 1583 he moved the court to Prague. Although raised at a Catholic court, he was tolerant of Protestantism and of Judaism, and Jewish cultural life flourished under his rule. He backed conciliarists, irenicists and humanists, and when the papacy pressed the Counter-Reformation through agents at his court he supported those he thought most neutral, which led to political chaos. Determined to unify Christendom, he began a long and indecisive war against the Ottoman Empire in 1593, the Long Turkish War, which lasted until 1606.

By 1604 his Hungarian subjects were exhausted by the war and revolted under Stephen Bocskai. In 1605 his family forced him to cede control of Hungarian affairs to his brother Matthias, who made peace with the Hungarians and the Ottomans in 1606. Matthias then forced him to cede the crowns of Hungary, Austria and Moravia. In 1609 Rudolf granted the Bohemian Protestants the Letter of Majesty. When he tried to suppress the Protestant estates with troops of his cousin Leopold V, Bishop of Passau, Matthias's army held him prisoner in Prague Castle until he ceded the crown of Bohemia in 1611.

Rudolf died on 20 January 1612, stripped of all effective power. In May 1618 the Defenestration of Prague, in defence of the Letter of Majesty, began the Thirty Years' War. Historians have traditionally blamed his interest in art and the occult for the disasters of his reign, while more recent ones see his patronage as a key part of the Renaissance.

His Kunstkammer at Prague Castle, with Dürer and Bruegel among its paintings, was the most impressive collection in Europe, and artists such as Giuseppe Arcimboldo worked for him. He patronised the astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler, and Kepler's laws of planetary motion rested on this patronage, as Kepler recognised in the Rudolphine Tables.
rudolf-ii-of-burgundy: A member of the Elder House of Welf, Rudolph was the son of the Upper Burgundian king Rudolph I and his wife Guilla of Provence. After he came to the throne in 912, he entered a border conflict with the neighbouring dukes of Swabia and campaigned in the Thurgau and Zürich estates. Duke Burchard II of Swabia defeated him at the Battle of Winterthur in 919. The two rulers then made peace, and in 922 Rudolph married Burchard's daughter Bertha.

At the same time several Italian nobles, led by Margrave Adalbert I of Ivrea, asked Rudolph to intervene in Italy against Emperor Berengar. Having entered Italy, he was crowned king at Pavia in the Basilica of San Michele Maggiore. On 17 July 923 he defeated Berengar at the Battle of Fiorenzuola. Berengar was murdered the following year, possibly at Rudolph's instigation. The king then ruled Upper Burgundy and Italy together, residing alternately in both kingdoms.

In 926 the Italian nobility turned against him and asked Hugh of Arles, the regent in Lower Burgundy, to rule them instead. Rudolph's father-in-law, Burchard II, came to support him but was attacked and killed near Novara by followers of Lambert, Archbishop of Milan. The king returned to Upper Burgundy to protect himself, which assured Hugh's coronation as King of Italy. Rudolph gave the Holy Lance to the East Frankish king Henry the Fowler in exchange for estates at Basel in Swabia, in either 926 or 935.

When King Louis the Blind of Lower Burgundy died in 928, Hugh of Italy, Rudolph's rival, inherited that realm. To secure his position in Italy, Hugh agreed to cede his claims to Lower Burgundy in exchange for Rudolph's renunciation of any Italian claims. The two Burgundian realms were unified from 933 under Rudolph, and the united polity was later known as the Kingdom of Arles. He died in July 937 and was succeeded by his son Conrad.

After his death his daughter Adelaide was married to Hugh's son Lothair, while Hugh married Rudolph's widow Bertha. Adelaide later became the second wife of Otto the Great, crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962, and the mother of Emperor Otto II.
rudolf-iii-of-burgundy: Rudolf III, called the Idle or the Pious, was the son and heir of King Conrad I of Burgundy and of Matilda, a daughter of King Louis IV of France and so a member of the Carolingian dynasty. He was the last legitimate male member of the Burgundian line of the Elder House of Welf. His sisters made notable marriages: his elder half-sister Gisela married Duke Henry II of Bavaria and became the mother of the Emperor Henry II, while Bertha married first Count Odo I of Blois and then King Robert II of France.

Rudolf succeeded his father on 19 October 993 and was crowned at Lausanne. His reign was turbulent: he tried to confiscate several Burgundian estates, could not placate the increasingly powerful nobility, and had to deal with encroachments by Count Otto-William of Burgundy. Like his father he turned to the German Ottonian dynasty for support. His aunt Adelaide, widow of the Emperor Otto I, and her grandson Otto III intervened in Burgundian affairs to secure his accession, and in 1006 Rudolf ceded the city of Basel to his nephew Henry II, elected king of Germany in 1002.

His first marriage, to Agiltrud, who died in 1011, was childless. On 28 June 1011 he married Ermengarde, widow of Count Rotbold II of Provence, and gave her the county of Vienne and Sermorens and large estates as far as Lake Geneva, but this marriage also produced no children. In 1016 a new conflict with Otto-William, over the investiture of the archbishop of Besançon, led Rudolf to meet Henry II at Strasbourg and name him his successor, and a diet at Mainz confirmed Henry's right in 1018.

After Henry's death in 1024 the succession was again unsettled. Henry's successor, King Conrad II, occupied Basel and negotiated to become Rudolf's heir; Rudolf attended Conrad's imperial coronation at Easter 1027, and an inheritance contract was concluded that August, though Counts Odo II of Blois and Reginald I of Burgundy contested it. Rudolf died on 6 September 1032 and was buried in Lausanne Cathedral. Conrad then claimed the kingdom and incorporated it into the Holy Roman Empire. Contemporaries saw him as weak: the chronicler Wipo called him effete, Hermann of Reichenau spoke of idleness and chaos, and Thietmar of Merseburg said the Burgundian counts were the real rulers.
rudolf-iv-duke-of-austria: Rudolf was born in Vienna on 1 November 1339, the eldest son of Duke Albert II of Austria and Joanna of Pfirt. He was the first Habsburg duke of Austria to be born within the duchy, so he considered Austria his home, a sentiment that contributed to his popularity. In 1357 he married Catherine of Bohemia, daughter of Emperor Charles IV. He wished to compete with his father-in-law, who had made Prague a centre of imperial culture, and to raise Vienna to a comparable height.

Rudolf ruled Austria, Styria and Carinthia from 1358. His father had not been among the seven imperial prince-electors named in the Golden Bull of 1356, and Rudolf commissioned the Privilegium Maius, a forged document accompanied by other forgeries, to raise the Austrian dukes to higher titles, rights and privileges. Charles IV refused to recognise the claims, but Rudolf used the title of archduke from the middle of 1359 and asserted it until his death. It became an honorific title of all male Habsburgs from the 16th century.

In Vienna he created a 'metropolitan cathedral chapter' at the church of St Stephen, whose members wore red garments like cardinals, and he began the Gothic nave of St Stephen's Cathedral, which can be seen as rivalry with St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. By founding the University of Vienna in 1365 he sought to match Charles IV's foundation of the Charles University of Prague in 1348. It is the oldest continuously operating university in the German-speaking world, though its faculty of theology was founded only in 1385. He also established a relatively stable currency, the Wiener Pfennig.

In 1363 Rudolf made a contract of inheritance with Countess Margaret of Gorizia-Tyrol, and in 1364 he declared the March of Carniola a duchy. The next year he founded the town of Novo Mesto, whose German name Rudolfswert honours him. He also agreed with Charles IV on mutual inheritance between the Habsburg and Luxembourg dynasties.

Rudolf died suddenly at Milan on 27 July 1365, aged 25, without issue, and he and his wife are buried in the Ducal Crypt beneath the Stephansdom in Vienna. His younger brothers Albert III and Leopold III quarrelled and divided the Habsburg lands in the Treaty of Neuberg of 1379.
rudolf-slansky: Rudolf Slánský was born on 31 July 1901 at Nezvěstice into a conservative Jewish family and attended the Commercial Academy in Plzeň. After the end of World War I he went to Prague, where he found a leftist intellectual scene, and in 1921 he joined the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia when it broke away from the Social Democratic Party. He became a senior lieutenant of its leader Klement Gottwald and in 1929 a member of the Presidium and the Politburo. He lived in hiding from 1929 to 1935 because the party was illegal, and was elected to the National Assembly in 1935.

After Nazi Germany occupied the Sudetenland in October 1938 he fled to the Soviet Union with much of the party leadership. In Moscow he worked on broadcasts to Czechoslovakia and organised Czechoslovak army units, with which he returned in 1944 to take part in the Slovak National Uprising. His time in Moscow brought him into contact with the often brutal methods Soviet communists used to maintain party discipline.

After the war Slánský helped organise the new National Front government under Edvard Beneš, and he became General Secretary of the party, second only to Gottwald. After the communist seizure of power in February 1948 he was the second most powerful man in the country. He was blamed for economic and industrial troubles, which cost him popular support, but he received the Order of Socialism on 30 July 1951.

After Tito broke with Stalin, Stalin decided to purge the communist parties of the satellite states. Most historians think that Gottwald sacrificed his friend to save himself; others point to a rivalry that grew after 1948, in which Stalin backed Gottwald. Slánský was arrested at 1 a.m. on 24 November 1951, one of 14 leaders arrested, and was tortured into confessing and attempted suicide. The party said he was spying for an international Western capitalist conspiracy.

The trial began on 20 November 1952 before the Senate of the State Court, with Josef Urválek as prosecutor, and lasted eight days. As in the Moscow show trials of the late 1930s, the defendants admitted guilt and requested a death sentence. Slánský was found guilty of Trotskyite-Titoist-Zionist activities in the service of American imperialism, and was hanged at Pankrác Prison on 3 December 1952 with ten others. His ashes were scattered on an icy road outside Prague. He and the other victims were cleared in April 1963 and fully rehabilitated in May 1968. He was the most powerful politician executed under communist rule in Czechoslovakia, and afterwards fallen leaders were stripped of power and told to retire.
rudolph-of-france: Rudolph was born around 890, the son of Richard the Justiciar and Adelaide of Auxerre. In Latin documents his name is usually Rodulfus, and he always used that form himself, as on his seal, although he is often called Raoul in modern French and Ralph in English. He inherited the Duchy of Burgundy from his father in 921 and married Emma, daughter of King Robert I of France.

Robert was killed at the Battle of Soissons fighting the deposed King Charles the Simple, and Rudolph was elected to succeed him. He was crowned by Walter, archbishop of Sens, at Saint-Médard de Soissons on 13 July 923 and passed the duchy to his younger brother, Hugh the Black.

Rudolph first led an army against Henry the Fowler, king of East Francia, who had made a pact with Robert and tried to annex Lotharingia. Peace was made, but in 925 Henry took Lotharingia for good, and Rudolph could not resist. In 924 Vikings raided West Francia from the Loire Valley, attacked Burgundy and moved to Melun. Rudolph raised troops with Hugh the Great, and then with Herbert and Arnulf I of Flanders he fought the Normans near Fauquembergues, where the king was wounded.

Magyars invaded the region around Rheims in 930 and Burgundy in 935, and Rudolph's large army made them retreat without a battle. West Francia was temporarily safe from both Vikings and Magyars at his death.

Herbert II of Vermandois held Charles the Simple prisoner and used him to win the archbishopric of Rheims for his son Hugh and the county of Laon for his son Odo. Charles died at Péronne, and Rudolph was not fully recognised in the south until Charles died in captivity on 7 October 929. He received the homage of William Longsword and in 933 granted him the Channel Islands. In 931 he replaced Hugh at Rheims with Artald, and joined by Hugh the Great he burned Herbert's fortresses and cornered him in Château-Thierry.

In the south he also gave the title of prince of Gothia to Raymond Pons, count of Toulouse, and campaigned against the last Viking strongholds. The two men made peace in 935. Rudolph fell ill and died on 14 or 15 January 936, leaving no sons.
rudolstadt: Rudolstadt lies in the Thuringian Forest in Thuringia, to the south-west of Jena and Weimar. It is built along the river Saale inside a wide valley surrounded by woods. The town was the capital of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, and its landmark is the castle Heidecksburg, which stands on a hill above the old town. The former municipality of Remda-Teichel was merged into Rudolstadt in January 2019.

Archaeological evidence points to a hill fort on the Weinberg in Oberpreilipp from the late Urnfield culture and the early Iron Age. A Celtic settlement followed a Germanic one, and from the 6th century onwards the records suggest Slavic settlement in the area. The place-name is first documented in 776 as Rudolfestat, Rudolf's settlement, in a gift from Charlemagne to Hersfeld Abbey. The town has had municipal law since 1326.

A porcelain manufacture was established at Volkstedt in 1762, and Rudolstadt later became well known for its porcelain factories and for the Anchor Stone Blocks of the toy company Richter. The Thüringer Landestheater traces its origins to a court theatre built in 1792/93. Composers who worked there as composer in residence included Niccolò Paganini, Franz Liszt and Richard Wagner, and the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer wrote his dissertation in the town.

The writer Hans Fallada went to school in Rudolstadt, and Charlotte von Lengefeld (1766-1826) was the wife of Schiller. Princess Anna Sophie of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt was the grandmother of King Leopold I of Belgium. The Rudolstadt Festival, formerly the Tanz&FolkFest, takes place annually on the first full July weekend, and the town is twinned with Letterkenny in County Donegal, Ireland.
rudradaman-i: Rudradaman I was a Saka ruler of the Western Kshatrapa dynasty who took the title Mahakshatrapa, Great Satrap, after he became king, and then strengthened his kingdom. Through his victories he regained all the lands once held by Nahapana except the southern territory of Poona and Nasik. His Junagadh inscription names him lord of eastern and western Akaravanti, Anupa, Anarta, Surashtra, Svabhra, Maru, Kachchha, Sindhu-Sauvira, Kukura, Aparanta and Nishada, lands it says were never troubled by robbers, snakes, wild beasts or disease. He played a large part in the decline of the Satavahana Empire, whose lands were reduced to the Deccan and the country around Amaravati.

The inscription says he destroyed by force the Yaudheyas of present-day Haryana, a militant republic proud of its standing among the kshatriyas, who refused to submit. They soon became independent again and grew stronger in the following century, until the Kushan Empire and later the Gupta Empire conquered them.

With the Satavahanas he made a marriage alliance: his daughter married Vashishtiputra Satakarni, as an inscription in a cave at Kanheri records, and he gave Aparanta as her dowry. Even so, at least two wars followed. The Junagadh text says he twice defeated Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight but spared him because of their close connection. Who began either war is not known.

The inscription credits Rudradaman with supporting the arts and Sanskrit literature and with repairing the embankments of the lake Sudarśana, built by the Mauryas to check floods. He was ruling when Yavanesvara translated the Yavanajataka from Greek into Sanskrit, a work that influenced astrology in India. Most scholars, following Rapson, hold that he ruled from Ujjain, but some argue against it, pointing out that Ptolemy named Caṣṭana as king of Avanti and that the inscription itself does not name Avanti.
rufinus-of-aquileia: Rufinus was born in the Roman city of Julia Concordia, now Concordia Sagittaria, near Aquileia, and it appears that both his parents were Christians. Around 370 he lived in a monastic community at Aquileia, where he met Jerome. About 372 he followed Jerome to the eastern Mediterranean and studied in Alexandria under Didymus the Blind. He became close to Melania the Elder, a wealthy Roman widow, and when she moved to Palestine he followed her, moving to Jerusalem in 380.

At Jerusalem, at Melania's expense, Rufinus gathered monks into a new monastery on the Mount of Olives. John II, Bishop of Jerusalem, ordained him a priest in 390. In 394 Epiphanius of Salamis attacked the doctrines of Origen, and a fierce quarrel followed in which Rufinus and Jerome stood on different sides. In the autumn of 397 Rufinus went to Rome and published a Latin version of the Apology of Pamphilus for Origen. His somewhat free translation of Origen's De Principiis played down controversial passages, and its preface described Jerome as an admirer of Origen. The allusion annoyed Jerome and led to a bitter pamphlet war.

Pope Anastasius I summoned Rufinus to Rome to vindicate his orthodoxy. He excused himself in a written Apologia pro fide sua, and the pope condemned Origen but left Rufinus's orthodoxy to his conscience. At the request of Bishop Chromatius of Aquileia he translated Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History, as an antidote to the terror caused by Gothic incursions into Italy, and added two books of his own taking the account to the death of Theodosius the Great in 395.

His original works include a commentary on the Apostles' Creed and the Historia Eremitica, with the lives of thirty-three monks of the Nitrian desert. Origen's Commentary on Romans and the full text of De Principiis survive only in his versions. Jerome condemned his translations as flawed. In 408 Alaric's arrival in northern Italy drove Rufinus to a monastery at Pinetum, and when Alaric pillaged Rome in 410 he fled to Sicily, where he died. By putting the great Greek fathers into Latin he exerted considerable influence on Western theologians.
rufisque: Rufisque lies in the Dakar region of western Senegal, at the base of the Cap-Vert peninsula, 25 kilometres east of Dakar. It was originally a Lebou fishing village called Tenguedj. In the 16th century it became the principal port of the kingdom of Cayor, frequented by Portuguese, Dutch, French and English traders. The Portuguese called it Rio Fresco, meaning freshwater river, which gave the modern name.

A Euro-African Creole, or Métis, community of merchants grew up in Rufisque, in close contact with similar communities at Saint Louis, Gorée and along the Petite Côte south to the Gambia River. By the 1650s the Dutch West India Company had consolidated control of the coastal trade and built a fortified factory there. In 1840 merchants from Saint Louis built warehouses on the waterfront to store peanuts, merchants from Gorée followed, and a period of commercial expansion came as peanut production in Cayor boomed.

The French built a fort in 1859 and annexed Rufisque to the Colony of Senegal. The commercial and administrative quarter along the waterfront, the Escale, was laid out in 1862, and the African inhabitants were pushed out in the process. Rufisque became a commune in 1880, and its port was linked to the Dakar–Saint Louis railway in 1885. In 1909 Galandou Diouf was elected to represent Rufisque on the colony's General Council, the first African to hold that position. Early in the 20th century the growth of neighbouring Dakar, with better port facilities, began Rufisque's decline as a port.
Rufisque is now a suburb of Dakar and the capital of the department of the same name. Its population was 295,459 at the 2023 census. It has a cement works, and it is no longer an active port.
rugila: Rugila, also written Ruga or Ruas, was a ruler who counted as a major factor in the early victories of the Huns over the Roman Empire. He ruled at first in a dual kingship with his brother Octar, possibly a geographical division in which Rugila ruled the Eastern Huns and Octar the Western Huns. Octar died in 430 during a campaign against the Burgundians, and in 432 Rugila is mentioned as sole ruler. The Greek sources give his name as Rougas, Rouas and Roilas. Otto Maenchen-Helfen counted it among names of Germanic or Germanized origin, while Omeljan Pritsak derived it from Old Turkic.

According to Prosper of Aquitaine, Aetius lost office, fled to Rome and then Dalmatia, and reached the Huns by way of Pannonia; through their friendship and help he obtained peace with his rulers and was restored to his old office, and Prosper calls Ruga ruler of the gens Chunorum. The historian Priscus mentions land on the river Sava that, by Aetius's treaty, belonged to the barbarians, and some scholars read this as a cession of part of Pannonia Prima, dated by them to 425, 431 or 433. A major Hunnic incursion into Thracia in 422 had ended with a treaty under which the Romans paid 350 pounds of gold a year.

In 432 or 433 some tribes of the Hunnic confederation on the Danube fled into Roman territory and the service of Theodosius II. Rugila sent his diplomat Esla to demand their return, threatening to end the peace otherwise, but he died soon afterwards. He was succeeded by Bleda and Attila, the sons of his brother Mundzuk, who ruled jointly over the united Hunnic tribes. In the negotiations at Margus, according to Priscus, the annual tribute was raised to 700 pounds of gold and the fugitives were surrendered, among them two of royal descent, who were crucified at Carso.

Socrates of Constantinople wrote that Theodosius II prayed to God and Ruga was struck dead by a thunderbolt, after which plague and fire destroyed his followers; the account is a panegyric of Theodosius. Theodoret ties his death to the harvest that followed an edict against pagan temples, issued on 14 November 435. Both writers present the death as the work of God on behalf of Theodosius.
ruhnama: The Ruhnama was written by Saparmurat Niyazov, president of Turkmenistan from 1990 to 2006. Epics had long played important roles in the social life of Central Asia, and Joseph Stalin had considered them politically suspicious: almost all significant Turkmen epics were condemned and banned under Joseph Stalin, and were rehabilitated only with glasnost. Niyazov claimed to have received a prophetic vision in which eminent Turkmen ancestors urged him to lead the Turkmen to the golden path of life. A first version released in the 1990s was soon withdrawn. The first volume was published in December 2001, and a second followed in September 2004. Victoria Clement and Riccardo Nicolosi suspect that the work was ghost-written.

Scholars describe the book as a mosaic of genres: spiritual and political advice, legends, autobiography, short stories, poems and Turkmen history. The first volume borrows stories and proverbs from the Oğuzname, the Book of Dede Korkut and the Epic of Koroghlu to preach virtues such as generosity, unity and hospitality. It presents the Turkmen as descended from Noah through Oghuz Khagan and credits them with some seventy states, among them the Parthian, Achaemenid and Seljuk empires. It cites no source material in an academic sense. Soviet Turkmenistan is described in a single page, and Niyazov's own life is told in detail.

The second volume was drafted with explicit parallels to the Quran and asked that the Ruhnama be recited as a regular prayer after purification. Its 21 chapters deal with manners and conduct for different situations.

The book was placed first in schools and libraries and then made mandatory reading in schools, universities and government organisations. New government employees were tested on it at interviews, and an examination on it became part of the driving test. In 2002 the months and days of the week were renamed in Turkmen after parts of the Ruhnama, September taking the name of the book itself. Mosques and churches were made to display it as prominently as the Quran and the Bible. In August 2005 the first volume was launched into orbit. In 2004 schools were assigned two to four hours a week to it, and 26 of the 57 examination cards for the 2006 university entrance examination drew on it.

After Niyazov's death in December 2006 official references to the Ruhnama were trimmed, and from about 2009 television broadcasts of it stopped. The requirement to pass a secondary-school examination on it was rescinded in 2011, and in 2014 universities stopped testing applicants on it. It has been translated into over 50 languages.
ruhollah-khomeini: Ruhollah Mostafavi Khomeini came from a family of small landowners, clerics and merchants and was born in the town of Khomeyn, in what is now Markazi province. His father was murdered when he was a small child, and his mother and aunt raised him. In 1920 he began studies at the seminary in Arak under Ayatollah Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi and the following year followed his teacher to Qom, where he studied Islamic law and also philosophy and mysticism. His first political book, Kashf al-Asrar, was published in 1942. He became a marja', a source of emulation, in 1963, after the death of Grand Ayatollah Seyyed Husayn Borujerdi.

In January 1963 Mohammad Reza Shah announced the White Revolution, a programme that included land reform and the enfranchisement of women. Khomeini viewed it as an attack on Islam and on 22 January 1963 issued a declaration denouncing the Shah. On 26 October 1964 he denounced the immunity granted to American military personnel. He was exiled on 4 November 1964, first to Bursa in Turkey and from October 1965 to Najaf in Iraq, where his lectures on the Guardianship of the Jurist were compiled as Islamic Government. In 1978 Saddam Hussein expelled him, and he went to Neauphle-le-Château near Paris.

The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, and Khomeini returned on 1 February to a crowd reported to be as many as five million. On 11 February he appointed Mehdi Bazargan as his own prime minister, in competition with the provisional government of Shapour Bakhtiar. He was de facto head of state until his appointment as supreme leader in December 1979. Iraq invaded in September 1980, and the Iran–Iraq War lasted until August 1988. Khomeini also issued a fatwa calling for the killing of Salman Rushdie, author of The Satanic Verses.

Khomeini died on 3 June 1989 after five heart attacks in ten days. His funeral drew up to 10 million people, and at least ten mourners were trampled to death. In March 1989 he had removed Grand Ayatollah Hussein-Ali Montazeri as his chosen successor after Montazeri criticised the execution of political prisoners. His legacy remains disputed: admirers see a champion of Islamic revival and independence, while critics point to the repression and executions of his rule.
ruhr: The Ruhr area, or Ruhrgebiet, is a polycentric urban area bordered by the river Ruhr to the south, the Rhine to the west and the Lippe to the north. Its cities lie, from west to east, along a line running through Duisburg, Essen, Bochum and Dortmund, and the area has no administrative centre: each city has its own administration. Geologically the region is defined by coal-bearing layers of the upper Carboniferous period. The coal seams reach the surface in a strip along the river Ruhr and dip downward towards the north, lying 600 to 800 metres deep beneath the Lippe, which played a decisive role in the development of coal mining.

In the Middle Ages much of the region lay in the County of Mark, the Duchy of Cleves, the State of Berg and the territories of the bishop of Münster and the archbishop of Cologne, within the Holy Roman Empire. It was mainly agrarian. The free imperial city of Dortmund was its trading and cultural centre on the Hellweg, an important east–west trade route that also brought prosperity to Duisburg.

Industrialisation began in the late 18th century in the nearby Wupper Valley in the Bergisches Land. From 1807 to 1813 the area was part of the kingdom of Westphalia, a client state of France ruled by Napoleon's brother Jérôme, and by about 1820 hundreds of water-powered mills produced textiles and iron. As machines moved from water to steam, the Bergische industry ordered more and more coal from the new mining area along the Ruhr, and railways brought coal and later steel from the Ruhr into the hills.

After the Kapp Putsch of March 1920, which a general strike defeated, an armed revolt in the Ruhr aimed to replace the Weimar Republic with a soviet-style council republic. The Ruhr Red Army took control of the industrial area, but the Reichswehr with Freikorps units put the rising down in early April 1920; an estimated 1,000 insurgents and 200 soldiers were killed. In 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the district and seized its main industrial assets in lieu of unpaid reparations. After the Second World War the Ruhr Authority was created to regulate its coal and steel industries.

The Ruhr is the largest urban area in Germany and part of the larger Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Since the 1980s it has been the target of financial support from the state, the federal government and the European Union. A supracommunal Ruhr Regional Association has its seat in Essen.
rukn-al-dawla: Hasan was the son of Buya, a Dailamite fisherman from Lahijan who left his Zoroastrian faith and converted to Islam. His older brother was 'Ali and his younger brother Ahmad, and he also had a sister named Kama. In around 928 'Ali entered the service of Makan, the Samanid governor of Ray, and found military posts for his brothers; Hasan was then about thirty years old. When Makan was defeated by the Ziyarid prince Mardavij, the brothers transferred their allegiance to him.

Hasan fought in the battles over Fars, where 'Ali built a realm of his own, and was sent to the court of Mardavij as a hostage in around 934. The death of Mardavij in 935 let him escape and opened central Iran to the Buyids. He took Isfahan, lost it to the Ziyarids under Vushmgir three years later, and in 940 appointed Abu 'l-Fadl ibn al-'Amid as his vizier.

Hasan recaptured Isfahan in 940 and occupied Ray in 943. Driven from central Iran by Ibn Muhtaj, the governor of Samanid Khurasan, he returned to Ray only in 946 or 947, then took Gurgan and Tabaristan from Vushmgir. Control of those provinces changed hands several times until 955, and a treaty with the Samanids bound him to respect Ziyarid independence. A less humiliating treaty followed in 971 or 972, though he continued to pay tribute.

When 'Ali, known as 'Imad al-Dawla, died in September 949, Rukn al-Dawla claimed the title of senior amir, and the centre of Buyid power shifted from Shiraz to Ray. His armies twice took Azerbaijan, in 949 and again in 967, when the Sallarid Ibrahim I ibn Marzuban I, his son-in-law, was restored there. In 974 he made his son 'Adud al-Dawla reinstate his cousin 'Izz al-Dawla in Iraq, holding that the line of Mu'izz al-Dawla could not be removed.

At a meeting in Isfahan in January 976 he agreed that 'Adud al-Dawla would succeed him as senior amir, while Ray went to Fakhr al-Dawla and Hamadan to Mu'ayyad al-Dawla. He died a few months later. Because he had won central Iran almost without his elder brother's help, his descendants and those of 'Imad al-Dawla each claimed the senior emirate, which later divided the state. Like the other Buyids he was a Shi'ite, but he protected his Sunni subjects to prevent internal discord.
rukn-al-din-khurshah: Rukn al-Din al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, surnamed Khurshah or Khwarshah and also known as Kahirshah, was born in 627 AH, 1230 CE. He was the eldest son of the imam 'Ala' al-Din Muhammad III, who declared him his successor while he was still a child and saw to his education at home. He counts as the 27th Isma'ili imam and the fifth and last Nizari imam to rule at Alamut.

As he grew up his father made him his deputy to look into disorders in some castles, with orders that he be obeyed as the imam himself. Before his father's death he is reported to have visited Syria with a letter from him, and he spent more than a year in the castles of Rudbar and Kohistan reorganising their administration. Armed guards went with him wherever he travelled. Three days after taking up the imamate he sent an army, as his father had ordered, against Shal-Rud in the district of Khalkhal, and the castle there was taken after a little fighting.

In 1256 he made a series of gestures of submission to the invading Mongols and, at the demand of Hulegu Khan, began to remove towers and battlements at Alamut Castle, Maymundiz and Lambsar Castle. Hulegu took this as a way of delaying, and on 8 November 1256 Mongol troops surrounded Maymundiz, where the imam lived. After days of bombardment with heavy losses on both sides he offered to surrender in return for safe passage for himself and his family, and he came down from the fortress on 19 November.

Hulegu made him send orders of surrender to the castles of the Alamut valley. At Alamut the commander, Muqaddam al-Din, doubted that the message was freely given, but obeyed his oath to the imam and came down; the Mongols entered and began to demolish the fortress.

Hulegu at times treated him with deference and gave him rich gifts. Rukn al-Din asked to visit the Great Khan in person and travelled to Karakorum, where Möngke Khan rebuked him and demanded the surrender of the remaining castles, among them Gerdkuh and Lambsar. He was put to death on the journey home, near a place the sources call Toungat, perhaps the Tannu-Ola mountains. His son Shams al-Din Muhammad succeeded him as imam.
rule-britannia: 'Rule, Britannia!' began as the final musical number of Alfred, a masque about Alfred the Great with music by Thomas Arne and words by James Thomson and David Mallet. It was first performed on 1 August 1740 at Cliveden, the country home of Frederick, Prince of Wales, and was devised to commemorate the accession of Frederick's grandfather George I and the birthday of Princess Augusta. The song is most strongly associated with the Royal Navy but is also used by the British Army.

The text printed in Thomson's Works of 1763 has six stanzas, each ending with the refrain 'Rule, Britannia! rule the waves: Britons never will be slaves.' It tells of Britain rising from the azure main at Heaven's command, as a charter sung by guardian angels, and declares that other nations must in their turn fall to tyrants while Britain shall flourish great and free, that haughty tyrants will never tame her, and that the sea and every shore it circles shall be hers.

In 1751 Mallet reused the text, omitting three of the six stanzas and adding three by Lord Bolingbroke, as the repeated chorus of the comic song Married to a Mermaid. It became extremely popular when Mallet produced his masque Britannia at Drury Lane Theatre in 1755.

First heard in London in 1745, the song achieved instant popularity, and Handel quoted it in his Occasional Oratorio the next year. The Jacobites altered Thomson's words into a pro-Jacobite version. According to Armitage, it was the most lasting expression of a conception of Britain that emerged in the 1730s, which equated naval power with civil liberty, since an island nation with a strong navy could do without a standing army. When it appeared it was an exhortation rather than a celebration, for Britain did not yet rule the waves.

In the Victorian era 'Britannia, rule the waves' came to be sung as 'Britannia rules the waves', and 'will' became 'shall'. In 1945 the song was played at the ceremonial surrender of the Japanese imperial army in Singapore. Malcolm Sargent made his modern arrangement in 1940, and it is traditionally performed at the BBC's Last Night of the Proms, as the closing part of Sir Henry Wood's 1905 Fantasia on British Sea Songs.
rule-of-law: The phrase dates to 16th-century Britain. In the next century the Scottish theologian Samuel Rutherford used it to argue against the divine right of kings, and John Locke wrote that freedom in society means being subject only to laws written by a legislature that apply to everyone. The jurist A. V. Dicey popularised it in the 19th century. The principle, if not the phrase, was recognised by ancient thinkers: Aristotle wrote that it is more proper that law should govern than any one of the citizens. Its development can be traced to ancient Greece, Mesopotamia, India and Rome.

The Mahabharata, whose earliest versions date to the 8th or 9th century BCE, deals with dharma and the duty of the king, and says that a king who does not protect his people should be executed. In 1481 the General Court of Catalonia approved the Constitució de l'Observança, which subjected royal power to the laws of Catalonia.

In general the rule of law entails that law is clear, consistent and open, that people have access to justice, and that government institutions are subject to the law. It is sometimes put as no one is above the law. Its opposite is the rule of man, where one person or group rules arbitrarily. It is closely related to constitutionalism and to the German Rechtsstaat; in France the equivalent is Etat de droit.

Legal scholars divide into two groups. Formalists, among them Dicey, F. A. Hayek and Joseph Raz, hold that it requires general, public, prospective, consistent, equal and certain laws, but sets no requirement on their content. Substantivists, among them Ronald Dworkin, Lon Fuller and Tom Bingham, hold that it necessarily protects individual rights, and some include democracy.

In 1607 the English Chief Justice Sir Edward Coke told James I that the law was the measure by which the causes of the subjects are tried. The king was greatly offended and said that to place him under the law was treason. Coke answered by quoting Bracton, that the king ought to be under no man but under God and the law.

Hayek argued that under the rule of law individuals can plan and invest with some confidence, since government is prevented from frustrating their efforts by ad hoc action. In 1959 the International Commission of Jurists met in New Delhi, with over 185 judges, lawyers and professors from 53 countries, and issued the Declaration of Delhi, which held that the rule of law implied certain rights and freedoms and an independent judiciary. The Statute of the Council of Europe names it among the principles of genuine democracy, and Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union lists it among the common values of the member states.
rumbula-massacre: The Holocaust in Latvia began when the German army invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941. By 15 October 1941 the occupiers had murdered up to 30,000 of the approximately 66,000 Jews who had not been able to flee. By the end of October Hinrich Lohse, the Reichskommissar for the Ostland, had confined the Jews of Riga in a ghetto, the Riga Ghetto, which had not existed before the war. The Nazis wanted to kill its inmates to make room for Jews deported from Germany and Austria.

Heinrich Himmler brought Friedrich Jeckeln from Ukraine, where he had organised the Babi Yar massacre, and told him to kill the entire ghetto. Jeckeln chose Rumbula, a small railway station 12 kilometres south of Riga, for its elevated ground and sandy soil, within walking distance of the ghetto. The operation needed about 1,700 personnel.

On 28 November the able-bodied men were ordered into a cordoned small ghetto. From 4:00 a.m. on 30 November squads of the SD, the Protective Police and the Arajs Kommando drove the rest from their homes, and the first column left at 06:00 for the 10-kilometre march, on which guards murdered anyone who fell out. At the forest the victims were made to undress and were shot in the pits by Jeckeln's sardine packing method, with Jeckeln himself directing the shooters. About 13,000 people were shot that day. The killing resumed on 8 December, and on 9 December about 500 people found hiding in the small ghetto were murdered in the Biķernieki forest.

German Jews deported in December 1941 were housed in the emptied homes. Rudolf Lange, who had helped organise the massacre, was invited to the Wannsee Conference. In 1943 Himmler ordered the bodies dug up and burned by Jewish slave labourers. Jeckeln was hanged in Riga on 3 February 1946 after a Soviet trial, and Viktors Arajs was sentenced to life imprisonment in West Germany in 1979. Herberts Cukurs, connected with the clearing of the ghetto, was assassinated by Mossad agents in South America in 1965. A memorial was unveiled at the site on 29 November 2002.
rumi: Rumi's father, Baha ud-Din Walad, was a theologian, jurist and mystic from Wakhsh, where he lived until 1212, when the family moved to Samarkand. The advance of the Mongol armies later forced the family west. After time in various cities of Iran, in Baghdad and in Damascus, Rumi settled in Konya at the age of 19. His name means the Roman, because Anatolia had belonged to the Byzantine empire and was still known as Rum. When his father died, Rumi, aged twenty-five, inherited his position at a madrassa, and he was trained in the Shariah and the Tariqa by Burhan ud-Din Muhaqqiq Termazi until 1240 or 1241. He then began a public life as a jurist, issuing fatwas and preaching in the mosques of Konya.

His meeting with the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi on 15 November 1244 changed his life, turning an accomplished teacher into an ascetic. When Shams disappeared, Rumi grieved deeply, and the verses he composed were collected in the Divan. His scribe and favourite student, Hussam-e Chalabi, suggested that he write a book like those of Sanai and Attar, and Rumi then dictated the six volumes of the Masnavi to him over twelve years.

The Masnavi, or Spiritual Couplets, has about 27,000 lines of rhyming couplets and is often called the Quran in Persian. Many commentators have ranked it first among the mystical poems of world literature. The Divan-i Kabir, named in honour of Shams, holds about 35,000 Persian couplets and 2,000 quatrains, with 90 ghazals and 19 quatrains in Arabic and a few Turkish and Greek couplets.

Rumi's poetry speaks of a love that infuses the world, and he held that the oneness of God is lived most fully through love. He was a Muslim who praised the Quran and held Muhammad to be the most perfect of the prophets, yet traces of religious pluralism run through his work: the lamps are different, he wrote, but the Light is the same.

Rumi fell ill in December 1273 and predicted his own death. His followers founded the Mevlevi order, also known as the whirling dervishes, in 1273. Hussam Chalabi led it until his death in 1284, when Rumi's younger surviving son, Sultan Walad, became grand master, and leadership has stayed in Rumi's family at Konya since. His poetry shaped the Ottoman Turkish, Chagatai, Pashto, Kurdish, Urdu and Bengali literary traditions, and it has been translated into many languages. In 2007 UNESCO took part in celebrating the eight hundredth anniversary of his birth.
rundale-palace: Rundāle Palace (Latvian Rundāles pils, German Schloss Ruhental) is one of the two major baroque palaces built for the Dukes of Courland, the other being Jelgava Palace. It stands at Pilsrundāle, in Rundāle Parish in the Semigallia region, 12 kilometres west of Bauska. The palace was built in two periods, from 1736 until 1740 and again until 1768. In 1735 Ernst Johann von Biron bought land at Rundāle that held an old medieval castle, which was demolished to make way for the new building to Bartolomeo Rastrelli's design. Work proceeded slowly because part of the materials and resources went to Jelgava Palace, the project that mattered more to the duke.

After Biron's fall in 1740 the palace stood unfinished and empty until his return from exile in 1762. Rastrelli supervised the completion, and Johann Michael Graff made the lavish stucco decorations. Biron moved in almost at once in 1768 and spent summers there until his death in 1772.

After Russia absorbed the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia in 1795, Catherine the Great gave the palace to Count Valerian Zubov, and it later passed to the Shuvalov family. In 1812 it served as a hospital for Napoleon's army, and soldiers who died there were buried in the park. During the German occupation in World War I the army set up a hospital and a commandant's office in it.

The Bermontians partly burned it in 1919, during the Latvian War of Independence. It was listed as a state-protected monument in 1924 but was used as a school and, after World War II, partly as a grain store; the duke's dining room became a school gymnasium. A school remained until 1978.

In 1963 the palace became a branch of the Bauska local history museum, and the Rundāle Palace Museum was established in 1972 with the painter and art historian Imants Lancmanis as director; restoration became his life's work. The state paid for the work until 1992, and afterwards private donations and the Structural Funds and Cohesion Fund of the EU added to it.

In spring 2015 the restoration was announced complete, at an estimated total cost of 8,420,495 euros from 1972 to 2014. The palace and gardens are now a museum, one of Latvia's major tourist destinations, and the palace is also used to accommodate notable guests such as the leaders of foreign nations.
runnymede: Runnymede lies on the Thames flood plain between Old Windsor and Egham, just over 20 miles west of central London. With Long Mede to the north and the wooded Coopers Hill Slopes it is managed by the National Trust: 188 acres of meadow were given in 1929 and 110 acres of woodland in 1963. Langham Pond, formed when the meandering Thames left an oxbow lake, is a wetland Site of Special Scientific Interest. Across the river, now in Berkshire, lie Magna Carta Island and the Ankerwycke Yew, both also linked in popular memory with the charter.

The name is believed to come from the Middle English runinge, taking counsel, and mede, meadow, a place in the meadows used for regular meetings, and the Witan, the council of the Anglo-Saxon kings, met there from time to time in the reign of Alfred the Great. Magna Carta itself names the place as Ronimed between Windsor and Staines. Runnymede proper is the likely site of the sealing, though the river has changed its course here over time.

In 1929 Cara Rogers Broughton, Lady Fairhaven, and her two sons gave the meadows to the nation in memory of her husband, Urban Hanlon Broughton. Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the twin memorials of kiosks, lodges and piers at either end, opened in 1932 by Edward VIII. The last fatal duel in England was fought nearby in 1852, on Priest Hill.

The hillside holds the Air Forces Memorial, designed by Edward Maufe, which records 20,456 airmen of the Second World War with no known grave, and the Magna Carta Memorial of the American Bar Association, unveiled on 18 July 1957. The John F. Kennedy Memorial, dedicated by Queen Elizabeth II and Jacqueline Kennedy on 14 May 1965, stands on ground given to the United States that remains under British sovereignty; Geoffrey Jellicoe designed its garden. Hew Locke's twelve bronze chairs, The Jurors, mark the 800th anniversary of the charter.
rupa-goswami: Rupa Goswami was born at Fateyabad in Bengal into a family of Karnataka origin. He was the younger brother of Sanatana Goswami and the elder brother of Anupama; the three were born Santosha, Amara and Vallabha. The brothers moved to Ramakeli, where Sanatana and Rupa served in the government of the sultan Ḥusayn Šāh under the titles Sakar Mallik and Dabir Khas. While still at court they began to write to Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, and when he passed through Ramakeli on his way to Vrindavan they hurried to meet him.

The brothers gave up their high positions, and Chaitanya initiated them into the ascetic life under the names by which they are known. On his way back from Vraja he told Sanatana and Rupa to go to Vrindavan, study the devotional scriptures, recover lost sacred sites and make their greatness known. They found Vrindavan wooded and empty of people, and set about locating the holy places of Braj by studying the Puranic geography of Krishna's life, while also developing stories of their own. Chaitanya later sent more devotees, and so formed the Six Goswamis, a group led by the two brothers that wrote a large Sanskrit literature on theology, ritual, grammar and literary theory.

Rupa is linked with a site east of Nandīśvara and with Sevakunj in Vrindavan, and he discovered the image of Govindadeva. His possessions passed after his death to his nephew and disciple Jiva Goswami, the son of Anupama.

The Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu traces devotion from faith, its lowest stage, to the highest ecstasy of love. Its sequel, the Ujjvala-nilamani, treats divine conjugal love. Rupa began the dramas Vidagdhamadhava and Lalitamadhava as one work in 1516 and finished them as two, in 1524 and 1529, after a vision in which Satyabhama is said to have told him to divide them. He also wrote the one-act play Danakelikaumudi in 1549, a manual for the worship of Krishna at Janmastami, rules for drama, and the Upadesamrta, eleven verses of instruction.
rupert-of-germany: Rupert of the Palatinate was born at Amberg in the Upper Palatinate on 5 May 1352, the son of Elector Palatine Rupert II and Beatrice of Aragon, daughter of King Peter II of Sicily. He belonged to the House of Wittelsbach, and his great-granduncle was the Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV. He was raised at the Dominican Liebenau monastery near Worms, where his widowed grandmother Irmengard of Oettingen lived as a nun. He took part in governing the Electoral Palatinate from his early years and succeeded his father in 1398. In 1374 he married Elisabeth, daughter of Burgrave Frederick V of Nuremberg.

On 20 August 1400 Rupert and the three ecclesiastical electors of Mainz, Cologne and Trier met at Lahneck Castle and declared King Wenceslaus deposed. The next day the same four met at Rhens and chose Rupert as King of the Romans. Aachen refused to let him in, so Archbishop Frederick III of Saarwerden crowned him at Cologne on 6 January 1401.

Lacking a solid power base, he was contested by the House of Luxembourg, Wenceslaus's family. In the Western Schism he backed the Roman pope Boniface IX, who was reluctant to acknowledge him. He crossed the Alps in autumn 1401 to break the rule of Gian Galeazzo Visconti in Milan and to be crowned emperor, but was defeated at Brescia and returned to Germany in April 1402.

He won the support of England when his son Louis married Blanche of Lancaster, daughter of Henry IV, in July 1402, and in his Palatinate lands he proved a capable ruler.
