In 1405 Archbishop Johan II of Mainz formed an alliance with Count Eberhard III of Württemberg, Margrave Bernard I of Baden and several Swabian cities, and Rupert had to make concessions. It was only the indolence of Wenceslaus that prevented his overthrow.

Rupert died on 18 May 1410 at his castle of Landskrone near Oppenheim and was buried in the Church of the Holy Spirit in Heidelberg. He had divided his lands among his four surviving sons. Louis III became Elector Palatine, John received the County Palatine of Neumarkt, Stephen that of Simmern-Zweibrücken and Otto that of Mosbach. His efforts earned him the surname Clemens, the Gentle, and he commissioned the Ruprecht building in Heidelberg Castle.
rupert-of-salzburg: Rupert was Bishop of Worms as well as the first Bishop of Salzburg and abbot of St Peter's Abbey there, and a contemporary of the Frankish king Childebert III. Holy tradition holds that he came from the Frankish royal Merovingian dynasty. He was possibly related to the Robertians and is likely a descendant of Count Palatine Chrodbert II.

As bishop at Worms he was at first accepted as a wise and devout dignitary, but the mostly pagan community came to reject him and forced him out of the city by the end of the 7th century. Saints Chuniald and Gislar accompanied him in his missionary work, though no records of their acts survive. The Agilolfing duke Theodo of Bavaria then asked him to come to his residence at Regensburg to help spread the Christian faith among the Bavarian tribes.

Rupert moved to Altötting and began by preaching to the locals. He sailed down the Danube, visiting many towns, villages and forts, and converted a large population as far southeast as the Bavarian border with the Pannonian lands, then under the Avar Khaganate. He stayed at Lorch, the former Roman city of Lauriacum, where an early Christian church already existed. Warlike conditions in the borderlands made him give up plans for a mission among the Pannonian Avars.

He instead went by the Roman road to the ruined city of Juvavum, which he made his base and renamed Salzburg. He re-established the monastic community at St Peter's Abbey and laid the foundations of Salzburg Cathedral, finished by his successor Vergilius. He also founded the Benedictine nunnery of Nonnberg, where his niece Erentrude became the first abbess. From Theodo his bishopric received estates around Piding and Reichenhall, where he promoted the saltworks, and he introduced higher education and other reforms.

Rupert reportedly died on Easter Sunday around 710, though other sources say he returned to Worms and died there. Vergilius moved his remains to Salzburg Cathedral on 24 September 774. The Eastern Orthodox Church keeps his feast on 27 March, and Austria on 24 September, the day his relics arrived. Rupertitag is a public holiday in the state of Salzburg. He is patron saint of the state and of the Archdiocese of Salzburg together with Vergilius, is known as the Apostle of the Bavarians, and is patron of settlements such as Sankt Ruprecht in Styria and Šentrupert in Slovenia.
rupprecht-crown-prince-of-bavaria: Rupprecht was born in Munich on 18 May 1869, the eldest of thirteen children of Prince Ludwig and Archduchess Maria Theresa of Austria-Este. As a descendant of Henrietta of England, daughter of Charles I, he was also the Jacobite claimant to the thrones of England, Scotland and Ireland, which he never pressed. He was the first member of the Bavarian royal house to attend a public school, the Maximilian-Gymnasium in Munich, and he later entered the army and studied at the universities of Munich and Berlin.

He travelled widely in the Middle East, India, Japan and China, and in 1910 arranged a large exhibition of Islamic art in Munich. In 1900 he married Duchess Marie Gabrielle in Bavaria, who died in 1912. He became Crown Prince when his father was made king as Ludwig III on 5 November 1913.

Rupprecht took command of the German Sixth Army in Lorraine on 2 August 1914 and fought the Battle of Lorraine. He became a field marshal in July 1916 and on 28 August took command of Army Group Rupprecht, made up of the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th armies. Towards the end of 1917, much earlier than most German generals, he concluded that the war could not be won, and he opposed the scorched-earth policy during withdrawals. He resigned his command on 11 November 1918.

After his father's Anif declaration of 12 November 1918, which the Bavarian government took as an abdication, he fled to Tyrol and returned in September 1919. In 1921 he married Princess Antonia of Luxembourg. He declared his claim to the throne on his father's death that October, became head of the House of Wittelsbach and in 1923 helped form the Wittelsbacher Ausgleichfond. He refused Hitler's attempts to win him over, helped persuade Gustav von Kahr not to support the Beer Hall Putsch, and told George V in 1934 that he thought Hitler insane.

Rupprecht went into exile in Italy in December 1939, after the Nazis confiscated Schloss Leutstetten, and lived mostly in Florence. In October 1944, after Germany occupied Hungary, his wife and children were captured; they were held at Sachsenhausen and then Dachau, where the United States Army freed them in 1945. Antonia died in 1954. Rupprecht returned to Munich in September 1945 and kept advocating a Bavarian monarchy. He died at Schloss Leutstetten on 2 August 1955 and was given a state funeral.
rurik: The earliest mention of Rurik is in the Primary Chronicle, traditionally ascribed to Nestor and compiled in about 1113. It states that East Slavic and Finnic tribes in 860-862, including the Chuds, Slovenes, Krivichs, Meryans and Ves, drove the Varangians back beyond the sea, refused to pay them tribute and set out to govern themselves.

The tribes then began fighting each other and decided to invite the Varangians, led by Rurik, to restore order. He came with his younger brothers Sineus and Truvor and a large retinue. The chronicle says he was one of the Rus', a Varangian tribe, whom most historians regard as Scandinavian in origin, from the coast of what is now eastern Sweden.

Sineus established himself at Beloozero and Truvor at Izborsk. They died shortly afterwards, and Rurik consolidated these lands into his own territory and extended his rule in northern Russia. The oldest surviving version of the Primary Chronicle, the Laurentian Codex of 1377, states that he first settled in Novgorod, while the Hypatian Codex of the 1420s says he first settled in Ladoga and then moved to the newly founded Novgorod, a fort near the source of the Volkhov River, where he stayed until his death. His followers Askold and Dir, sent to Constantinople, seized Kiev before an attack recorded in Byzantine sources for the year 860.

Rurik is said to have remained in power until some time in the 870s, and the Primary Chronicle places his death in 879. On his deathbed he left his realm to his kinsman Oleg and entrusted to him his infant son Igor. Oleg moved the capital to Kiev by murdering its rulers and founded the state of Kievan Rus', which Rurik's successors ruled until the Mongol invasion in 1240.

The Rurikids were its ruling dynasty and ultimately that of the Tsardom of Russia, until the death of Feodor I in 1598, so Rurik is considered the traditional founder of the Russian monarchy. The historicity of Rurik remains a subject of debate. Some have identified him with Rorik of Dorestad, who appears in Frankish chronicles, an idea revived by Boris Rybakov and Anatoly Kirpichnikov in the mid-20th century and objected to by Alexander Nazarenko and others.
rurik-dynasty: Modern scholars consider Rurik a legendary and perhaps entirely fictional figure. The Primary Chronicle, of the early twelfth century, tells of the Calling of the Varangians: tribes at war with one another invited three brothers from overseas to rule them, of whom Rurik settled in Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor in Izborsk. No earlier Kievan source knew of Rurik, and genealogies of the princes usually stopped with Igor of Kiev. Even if Rurik existed, scholars have long doubted or rejected that he was Igor's father.

Before the mid-15th century no source claims that Rurik founded a dynasty. The tradition was set out by churchmen in the 16th century, in the Book of Royal Degrees of 1560 by Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, which traced the ruling house of Moscow to Rurik and to a supposed kinsman of Augustus Caesar named Prus. For this reason some scholars prefer the name Volodimerovichi, descendants of Volodimer I of Kiev.

The house underwent a major schism after the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, dividing into branches descended from his sons Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each under a different branch. Vsevolod's line, the Monomakhovichi, named after Vladimir II Monomakh, became predominant. The Olgovichi, descended from Sviatoslav, ruled in Chernigov until the early 14th century. The Romanovichi, the line of Roman the Great, were crowned kings of Galicia and Volhynia and ruled until 1323.

In the north-east the Yurievichi descended from Yuri Dolgorukiy, the founder of Moscow. His great-grandson was Alexander Nevsky, whose son Daniel of Moscow founded the ruling house of Moscow, the Daniilovichi. In all, the house ruled for 21 generations in the male line, a period of more than 700 years. It was briefly revived in Vasili IV of Russia, of the Shuyskiy line, who died without issue. The Time of Troubles lasted until 1613, when Mikhail I founded the Romanov dynasty; his father was descended from the Rurikids through the female line.

Russian and Ukrainian historians have long debated the inheritance of Kievan Rus'. The Russian view treats the Principality of Moscow as its sole heir, resting largely on religious and historical claims. The Ukrainian view of succession, summarised most clearly by Mykhailo Hrushevsky in his History of Ukraine-Rus', is based on continuity through the Kingdom of Ruthenia, Lithuania-Ruthenia and the Cossack Hetmanate. Several branches of the family survive, among them the houses of Shakhovskoy, Gagarin and Lobanov-Rostovsky.
rurik-rostislavich: Rurik, whose baptismal name was Basil, was a son of Rostislav I of Kiev. In the 1160s he ruled the land of the Drevlians, and in 1168 he became prince of Ovruch. He held Novgorod the Great in 1170 and 1171 and was prince of Belgorod from 1173 to 1194, while the succession conflicts of the princely house brought him briefly to Kiev in 1173 and again in 1180 and 1181. He was married to Anna, and among their children was Rostislav II of Kiev.

The sources disagree about the years after 1181. The Kievan Chronicle describes Rurik as co-ruler with Sviatoslav Vsevolodovich, prince of Kiev since 1177, in a partnership that lasted until Sviatoslav's death in 1194. The Novgorod Fourth Chronicle and the Sofia First Chronicle, in their entries for 1180 and 1185, have Sviatoslav reigning alone and do not name Rurik as co-prince. After 1194 Rurik ruled Kiev in his own right until a conflict with the Olgovichi and with Prince Roman Mstislavich of Galicia cost him the throne.

Having lost Kiev, Rurik sought an alliance with the Cumans. After a short stay in Chernigov, where he built the Church of St. Paraskebas, he attacked Kiev with his kinsmen and a Cuman army and sacked the city in 1203. He was confined to a monastery in 1204, but after Roman's death in 1205 he abandoned his vows and took the throne again.

His cousin Vsevolod Chermny held that Rurik's monastic vows made his rule invalid and seized Kiev from him more than once. In 1210 Rurik was forced to give up the Kievan throne to Vsevolod, and he governed Chernigov for the rest of his life, until his death on 19 April 1212.
rusa-i: Rusa I succeeded his father, King Sarduri II, as King of Urartu. The Assyrians knew him as Ursa, and his birth name may have been Uedipri. Before his reign Sarduri II had expanded the kingdom into southeastern Anatolia and retaken Anatolian territories from Assyria during a brief period of Assyrian weakness. The succession is not entirely clear, since another king, Sarduri III, is also attested and may have been Rusa's father instead. Rusa built the fortress of Rusahinili, the city of Rusa, at modern Toprakkale near Van in eastern Turkey.

The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III, who reigned from 745 to 727 BCE, was a formidable foe, and repeated invasions forced Rusa to spend the early years of his reign fighting Assyria. One Assyrian source reports that he inflicted a heavy defeat in which the Assyrian army was annihilated, probably between 734 and 727 BCE. The same source reports a war with the ruler of the land of Etini in which the Urartians suffered defeats. These conflicts took a heavy toll on the Urartian economy. After reverses Urartu lost the territory annexed under Sarduri II to Tiglath-Pileser and had to pay tribute to Assyria.

Sargon II, who came to the Assyrian throne in 722 BCE, declared war on Urartu in 715 BCE. After defeating Urartu's ally, the Kingdom of Mannea, the Assyrians attacked Urartu, and Rusa was decisively defeated and made to pay large annual tributes. He also lost battles to the Cimmerians in Gamir, and fled into the mountains of Guriania, unknown to many of his generals and governors. His son Melartua was either crowned in his place or led a rebellion. Rusa returned to Tushpa, and officials loyal to him killed Melartua.

In 714 BCE Rusa I committed suicide as a result of the defeats by the Assyrians and the Cimmerians. His reign had begun with Urartu at its widest extent under his father and ended with the kingdom subject to Assyrian tribute. Rusahinili, the fortress he built, survives as the site at Toprakkale.
russelsheim: Rüsselsheim am Main is the largest city in the Groß-Gerau district of the Rhein-Main region. It is one of seven special status cities in Hesse, which carry out several functions that counties normally provide. It lies on the Main between Frankfurt and Mainz, a few kilometres from the river's mouth at Mainz, and Frankfurt Airport is 17 km to the east. The suburbs of Bauschheim and Königstädten belong to it; Haßloch was added in 1951, Königstädten in 1956 and Bauschheim in 1970.

The town's foundation goes back to a Frankish colony in the first half of the 5th century. Its name first appears as Rucilesheim, the house of Rucile, in an inventory of royal hunting rights around 840, and it later grew from a settlement of the Count of Katzenelnbogen. In 1435 Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen was the first to cultivate Riesling there. In the 18th and 19th centuries Rheingau wine estates replanted their vineyards with vines from the Rüsselsheim area, but viticulture disappeared after the First World War.

Adam Opel began as a trainee mechanic and founded a sewing machine factory. The first cars were built in 1899, after his death, when the company was run by his widow and their five sons. The population rose from 1,422 in 1829 to 8,000 in 1914, fell from 16,000 to 9,500 during the Second World War, and reached a record 63,000 in 1978, fed first by refugees from former German territories and then by immigrants drawn to the Opel factories.

The town was bombed several times by the British RAF in the Second World War. On 26 August 1944 residents attacked nine captured American airmen who were walking through the town, after a raid the previous night, and six of them were killed. After the war eleven citizens were tried for war crimes and murder, and six were executed.

Opel remains the best-known name in the town, and the Korean manufacturer Hyundai opened its European centre there in 2003. The Rüsselsheim Museum, which concentrates on labour procedures and conditions from prehistory to the present, received the Council of Europe's museum award in 1980. The town also has a theatre with 865 seats and a branch of the Hochschule RheinMain. It is twinned with Évreux in France, Rugby in England, Varkaus in Finland and Kecskemét in Hungary.
russia: Russia is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries. It stretches over the easternmost part of Europe and the northernmost part of Asia, some 9,000 kilometres from east to west, and is one of only three countries bordering three oceans. The Ural Mountains, running north to south through the west, form the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, at 5,642 metres, is the highest peak in Russia and Europe, and Klyuchevskaya Sopka on the Kamchatka Peninsula is the highest active volcano in Eurasia.

Human settlement on Russian territory dates back to the Lower Paleolithic. The East Slavs became prominent in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries, and Kievan Rus' was established in the 9th century, adopting Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. After it disintegrated in the 12th century the Grand Principality of Moscow became the dominant Russian principality and led the unification of Russian lands, culminating in the Tsardom of Russia in 1547. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721, which became the third-largest empire in history.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 abolished the monarchy and created the Russian SFSR, the first socialist state. After the Russian Civil War it became the principal constituent of the Soviet Union, established in 1922. Amid rapid industrialisation in the 1930s, millions died under Joseph Stalin. The Soviet Union played a decisive role for the Allies on the Eastern Front in World War II, then competed with the United States as a superpower during the Cold War. In 1991 the Russian SFSR emerged from the dissolution of the Soviet Union as the Russian Federation.

Russia had an estimated population of 146 million in 2025, and three-fourths of its people live in urban areas. Moscow is the capital and Saint Petersburg the second-largest city. A constitution adopted after a constitutional crisis in 1993 established a semi-presidential republic. Russian is the official language, and about 81% of the population were ethnic Russians in the 2010 census.
russian-american-company: Emperor Paul I chartered the Russian-American Company in the Ukase of 1799. It was formed largely on the basis of the United American Company and was Russia's first joint-stock company, with the mission of founding settlements in Russian America, trading with the native peoples and carrying out a wider colonisation. A government Correspondent, the first being Nikolai Rezanov, oversaw its affairs, and a board of three directors reported to the tsar and appointed a Chief Manager in North America. Alexander Andreyevich Baranov was the first Chief Manager and founded Pavlovskaya and then New Archangel, now Sitka, which became operating bases. From 1818 the post went only to officers of the Imperial Russian Navy.

The Ukase of 1799 gave the company a monopoly over trade in Russian America south to 55° N. Alexander I's Ukase of 1821 claimed 45°50′ N, later revised to 51° N, and Britain and the United States challenged this, which led to the Russo-American Treaty of 1824 and the Russo-British Treaty of 1825. Alutiiq and Aleut men from Kodiak and the Aleutian Islands were forcibly conscripted for three-year terms as sea otter hunters, and Baranov supplied Aleut labourers to ten American ships sent to California between 1805 and 1812, which gathered over 22,000 pelts. Russian merchants were shut out of Guangzhou, so the furs went to Kyakhta through Okhotsk, and the company struggled to find skilled crews.

In 1812 the company built Fort Ross in what is now Sonoma County, California, its southernmost outpost, on Spanish and later Mexican territory. A proposal of 1824 to colonise California was rejected, and the company sold the settlement in 1841. In 1817 its agent Georg Anton Schäffer built Fort Elizabeth in Hawaii and tried to overthrow the Kingdom of Hawaii, an episode called the Schäffer affair. The Russian government took control from the merchants in 1818, and from the 1820s profits fell as fur-bearing animals declined. In 1838 the company leased part of the Alaska Panhandle to the Hudson's Bay Company.

From 1797 to 1821 the company and its forerunner collected furs worth 16 million rubles, including 72,894 sea otters. The Alaska Purchase of 1867 transferred Alaska to the United States, and the company's commercial interests were sold to Hutchinson, Kohl & Company of San Francisco, which became the Alaska Commercial Company. The Russian-American Company ceased its commercial activities in 1881. Fort Ross is partly reconstructed as an open-air museum, and many names of its chief managers appear as place names in Southeast Alaska.
russian-civil-war: The war began with the overthrow of the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution. The monarchy had ended with the abdication of Emperor Nicholas II in the February Revolution of 1917, after which a coalition of centrist parties governed beside soviets of workers, soldiers and peasants. The Bolsheviks directed the Red Guard to seize Petrograd and began taking cities across the former empire. In January 1918 they dissolved the Constituent Assembly, in which the anti-Bolshevik Right Socialist-Revolutionaries had won the most seats. The conflict became a full-scale civil war in May and June 1918.

The two largest combatants were the Red Army, fighting for a Bolshevik-led socialist state under Vladimir Lenin, and the White movement, led mainly by right-leaning officers of the Russian Empire. Ukrainian anarchists and Left Socialist-Revolutionaries also fought the Bolsheviks. Thirteen foreign states intervened against the Red Army, chiefly the Allies, who aimed first to restore the Eastern Front of the First World War. In May 1918 the Czechoslovak Legion revolted in Siberia, and the former tsar and his family were murdered on 17 July. After an uprising of the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries in Moscow that July, executions grew more frequent and the Red Terror began.

In 1919 the Whites attacked from the east in March, the south in July and the west in October, and each advance was checked by a Red counteroffensive. Admiral Alexander Kolchak's army disintegrated in Siberia. The Red Army forced evacuations from Novorossiysk in March and from the Crimea in November 1920, and fighting was then sporadic until Vladivostok was captured in October 1922.

Estimates put the casualties at 7 to 12 million, mostly civilians. A famine caused between 3 and 10 million deaths, and by 1921 heavy industry produced only 20 percent of its 1913 output. One to two million people fled Russia, many with General Wrangel, among them a large share of the educated and skilled population.

Many non-Russian peoples used the disorder to press for independence. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania repelled Soviet invasions, while Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia were occupied by the Red Army. The Basmachi resistance in Central Asia was not dismantled until 1934. With the failure of revolutions elsewhere, the Bolsheviks moved from world revolution to socialism in one country, the Soviet Union.
russian-conquest-of-central-asia: When the Russians arrived, the organised states of the region were the Khanates of Khiva, Bukhara and Kokand, each surrounded by nomads they tried to control and tax. By the late 18th century Russia held a line of forts, from Guryev and Orenburg to Omsk and Ust-Kamenogorsk, roughly along the boundary of forest and steppe. After the Kazakh Khanate weakened on the death of Tauke Khan in 1715, its three jüzes sought Russian protection: Abū'l-Khair Khan of the Junior jüz in 1730, then the Middle jüz, and the Senior jüz in 1738. The regulations of 1822 and 1824 tightened Russian rule, and Kenesary Qasymuly's revolt from 1837 showed its limits.

A campaign against Khiva in 1839 failed, and Russia turned instead to building forts. Fort Raim rose at the mouth of the Syr Darya, and Ak-Mechet, Kokand's main northern stronghold, was taken and the Syr Darya line built from 1853. Between 1847 and 1864 forts were also built across the eastern steppe. Mikhail Chernayev stormed Tashkent on 27 June 1865, and the elders surrendered on the 29th. In 1866 Romanovsky routed Bukhara on the plain of Irjar, then took Khujand, Ura-Tepe and Jizzakh. In July 1867 the Province of Turkestan was created under General von Kaufmann, who took Samarkand in May 1868.

Superior weapons, breech-loading rifles and explosive artillery, let small Russian forces defeat much larger armies. In 1873 columns converged on Khiva from five directions, and on 4 June the Khan sued for peace. Kokand rebelled in 1875 and was abolished in 1876, becoming Fergana Oblast. In Transcaspia a first attack on Geok Tepe failed; Mikhail Skobelev took it after a month's siege, and at least 14,000 Tekes were killed. The Transcaspian Oblast was annexed in May 1881, Merv followed in 1884, and the capture of the Afghan fort of Panjdeh in 1885 brought Britain close to threatening war.

Most of the conquered land became Russian Turkestan, named for its mostly Turkic population. Russia occupied Kulja in China from 1871 and evacuated it in the spring of 1883 under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881. In the Pamirs a Russian battalion camped near Murghab in 1892, and the Durand Line of 1893 left the Wakhan Corridor between Russian and British territory. Britain, alarmed for India, reacted strongly only when Russia neared Afghanistan, which both sides came to treat as a buffer.
russian-empire: The foundations of a unified Russian state were laid in the 15th century under Ivan III. Moscow became the leading Russian principality, and by the early 16th century the remaining Russian states were united with it. As the only independent Orthodox power after the fall of the Byzantine Empire in 1453, its rulers took symbolic steps towards empire: they married into the Byzantine imperial dynasty, adopted the double-headed eagle and took the title of tsar. Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547. Peter the Great (r. 1682 to 1725) transformed the tsardom into an empire, fought wars that made Russia a major European power, and moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg.

Catherine the Great came to power in a coup against her husband Peter III and presided over further expansion. Poland was partitioned between 1772 and 1815 and most of its land and population came under Russian rule, and by 1795 Russia was the most populous state in Europe, ahead of France. Alexander I helped defeat Napoleon and established the Holy Alliance. By 1812 Russia had also gained Finland from Sweden, Bessarabia from the Ottoman Empire and some territory in the Caucasus, and it administered Alaska between 1799 and 1867. Most of the empire's growth in the 19th century came from gains in central and eastern Asia.

In 1853 to 1856 Russia fought Britain, France, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire in the Crimean War; the defeat, formalised in the Treaty of Paris of 1856, forced it to demilitarise the Black Sea. After the 1905 Revolution Nicholas II authorised the State Duma, though ultimate authority remained with him. Russia entered the First World War in 1914 on the side of the Allies; high casualties and shortages of food and fuel led to unrest, and the February Revolution of 1917 brought the abdication of Nicholas II and a Provisional Government, which proclaimed a republic in September.

At its height in the late 19th century the empire covered about 22,800,000 square kilometres, roughly one-sixth of the world's landmass and the third-largest empire in history after the British and Mongol empires. By the 1897 census the population was 126 million, with more than 100 ethnic groups, ethnic Russians making up about 45 per cent. The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in the October Revolution, and after winning the Civil War against the Whites established the Soviet Union across most of the former Russian territory.
russian-far-east: The Russian Far East is the easternmost part of Russia and of the Asian continent. It is coextensive with the Far Eastern Federal District, which Russia created in 2000 and which stretches between Lake Baikal and the Pacific Ocean, covering 6.95 million square kilometres, over one third of Russia. Its largest city is Khabarovsk, followed by Vladivostok. It borders Mongolia, China and North Korea, and faces Japan and, across the Bering Strait, the United States. Its geography includes the Amur and Lena rivers, Lake Baikal, the Klyuchevskaya Sopka volcano and the Sikhote-Alin range. Foreign writers often treat it as part of Siberia, but Russian regional schemes have long classed it separately.

Russians reached the Pacific coast in 1647 with the founding of Okhotsk, and the empire consolidated its control in the 19th century after annexing part of Chinese Manchuria in 1858-1860. Primorskaya Oblast was set up in 1856, with its centre first at Nikolayevsk-on-Amur and from 1880 at Khabarovsk. Vladivostok, founded in 1860, was operational only in summer, so Russia leased Port Arthur from China from 1896 as a port open all year. Japan attacked the Russian Pacific Squadron there on 8 February 1904, beginning the Russo-Japanese War, which ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth of 5 September 1905; Japan received the southern half of Sakhalin.

Under Stalin, between 1937 and 1939, the Soviet Union deported over 200,000 Koreans from the region to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, fearing they might spy for Japan; many died on the way. Gulag labour camps developed many remote places, especially in the northern half, until forced labour waned after 1953. Soviet and Japanese forces clashed on the Manchurian border between 1938 and 1945, beginning with the Battle of Lake Khasan in July and August 1938. In August 1945 the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria from Primorsky Krai and Transbaikal, and afterwards annexed the Kuril Islands and southern Sakhalin. In 1952 Vladivostok became a closed city, and it hosted the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks in 1974.

The Far Eastern Federal District has a population of about eight million, most of it in the south and about three quarters urban, which makes it one of the most sparsely populated areas in the world. Ethnic Russians form the vast majority. Its original peoples include the Buryats, Sakha, Chukchi, Koryaks, Evenks, Nanais and Nivkhs. The Trans-Siberian Railway and, since 1984, the Baikal-Amur Mainline link it with the rest of Russia. Its fauna includes the Siberian tiger and the Amur leopard.
russian-orthodox-church: The history of the church begins with the Christianization of Kievan Rus', which commenced in 988 with the baptism of Vladimir the Great and his subjects by clergy of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. Christianity had already begun to take root in the 10th century: Christians are mentioned among the Varangians towards the end of the reign of Igor, and his wife Olga was baptized in the mid-10th century, though scholars dispute the year, between 946 and 960, and the place. Her son Sviatoslav opposed conversion. A later tradition, found in the 12th-century Primary Chronicle, holds that the Apostle Andrew visited the site of Kiev, although there is no historical evidence for it.

After the Mongol invasions Kiev lost its significance, and Metropolitan Maximus moved his seat to Vladimir in 1299. His successor Peter moved to Moscow in 1325, allied himself with the prince of Moscow and was buried in the Dormition Cathedral, so designating Moscow as the future centre of the church. The church declared autocephaly in 1448 by electing its own metropolitan without Constantinople's blessing, and in 1589 the metropolitan see became a patriarchate with Constantinople's consent. After the fall of Constantinople the monk Philotheus of Pskov formulated the idea of Moscow as the third Rome.

In the mid-17th century liturgical reforms led to the Schism of the Russian Church, and its opponents formed the Old Believers. After Patriarch Adrian died in 1700, Peter the Great chose not to have a successor elected. In 1721 he replaced the patriarch with the Most Holy Synod, made up of appointed bishops, monks and priests and overseen by an ober-procurator who reported to the emperor. The Synodal period lasted until 1917.

In 1914 Russia had 55,173 Orthodox churches, 550 monasteries and 475 convents. A Local Council opened in Moscow in August 1917 and restored the patriarchate, and on 5 November Metropolitan Tikhon of Moscow was chosen as the first patriarch in about 200 years. The Soviet Union treated the clergy and active believers as anti-revolutionary elements, who were prosecuted, arrested, exiled and imprisoned, and the church was heavily persecuted. Religious belief nevertheless persisted. Under Patriarch Aleksey II, who took office in 1990, some 15,000 churches were reopened or built.

The church is hierarchical. A parish, usually a single church building and its attendees, is headed by a priest; the parishes of a region belong to an eparchy, equivalent to a Western diocese, governed by a bishop. Its autonomous branches include the Japanese Orthodox Church and the Chinese Orthodox Church. The Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, established by émigrés in the 1920s, reconciled with Moscow in 2007 as a self-governing body.
russian-provisional-government: The authority of the tsar's government began to disintegrate on 1 November 1916, when Pavel Milyukov attacked the government of Boris Stürmer in the Duma. During the February Revolution two rival institutions, the State Duma and the Petrograd Soviet, both met in the Tauride Palace and competed for power. Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March (Old Style) and the regency was offered to his brother, Grand Duke Michael, who deferred accepting imperial power until the Constituent Assembly had decided.

The Provisional Government was formed on 15 March 1917 (New Style) by the Provisional Committee of the State Duma in cooperation with the Petrograd Soviet. Its task was to organise elections to the Constituent Assembly while keeping essential services running. Its first declaration promised a full amnesty, freedom of speech, press, unions, assemblies and strikes, the abolition of hereditary, religious and national restrictions, and the replacement of the police by a public militia.

The government could not take decisive decisions amid factionalism and the breakdown of state structures, and real power lay largely with the Petrograd Soviet, which controlled the army and the railways. On 18 April (Old Style) Milyukov told the Allied governments that Russia would continue the war to its glorious conclusion; demonstrations followed, Milyukov and the war minister Guchkov resigned, and six socialist ministers joined a coalition. The June Offensive, begun on 16 June, fell apart within three days amid desertion and mutiny, with thousands of Russian soldiers dead, and was followed by the armed uprising of the July Days. Kerensky became prime minister on 21 July.

In September General Lavr Kornilov attempted a military coup. Kerensky branded his advancing troops counter-revolutionaries and armed the Red Guard, which left the army distrustful of him and strengthened the Bolsheviks. The Russian Republic was proclaimed on 1 September (Old Style) by a decree signed by Kerensky and the justice minister Zarudny. On 24–26 October (Old Style) Red Guard forces occupied most government offices and captured the Winter Palace, where the ministers had held out. Kerensky escaped to Pskov, where his attempt to retake the capital was beaten at Pulkovo, and later went into exile in France and then the United States.

Despite its brief life the government passed liberal legislation: it abolished capital punishment, separated church from state and affirmed civil rights, while Poland was granted independence and Lithuania and Ukraine gained autonomy. Guchkov said it had only the appearance of authority, the real power lying with the Soviet. Pavel Osinsky described the October Revolution as socialism by default, a result both of the government's failures and of Bolshevik strength, and Nicholas Riasanovsky held that its worst mistake was not holding elections to the Constituent Assembly soon enough.
russian-revolution: The Russian Revolution of 1905 laid the groundwork for 1917. Bloody Sunday triggered nationwide protests and soldier mutinies, and a council of workers, the St. Petersburg Soviet, was created. The revolution was crushed, but it led to the creation of a Duma, which later formed the Provisional Government. Nicholas II was a deeply conservative ruler who believed that his power was granted by Divine Right and, even after 1905 moved him to decree limited civil rights and democratic representation, worked to limit them.

The 1914 Battle of Tannenberg was a disaster for Russia, with over 30,000 troops killed or wounded and 90,000 captured. In autumn 1915 Nicholas took direct command of the army and left his wife Alexandra in charge of the government. Reports of corruption and incompetence spread, and the influence of Grigori Rasputin was widely resented.

On 7 March [O.S. 22 February] 1917 a strike closed the Putilov plant, Petrograd's largest. On International Women's Day women marched to nearby factories and brought out over 50,000 workers, and by 10 March virtually every industrial enterprise in the city was shut. Nicholas abdicated on 15 March [O.S. 2 March], and a provisional government led by the Duma took over. The Petrograd Soviet claimed to represent workers and soldiers, so that Russia had two rival centres of power: the Provisional Government held authority in military and international affairs, the Soviets in domestic matters.

The Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin won support with a programme of peace, land and bread, while the Provisional Government continued the war. The October Revolution began on 7 November [O.S. 25 October], an armed insurrection in Petrograd organised by the Revolutionary Military Committee under Leon Trotsky; its initial assault occurred largely without casualties. The Bolsheviks proclaimed the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918.

Many groups did not recognise the Bolshevik government, and Russia fell into a civil war between the Reds and an array of enemies including nationalists, other socialists, anarchists, monarchists and liberals. The Bolsheviks murdered Nicholas II and his family at Yekaterinburg on 16 July 1918. Historians consider the revolutionary period to have ended in 1922 with the defeat of the White Army, and the Soviet Union was formed from the Soviet republics. Historians divide into Soviet-Marxist, Western totalitarian and revisionist schools; the totalitarian school describes a coup by a minority, the revisionists stress the revolution's popular character.
russian-revolution-of-1905: Russian peasants had been freed by the emancipation reform of 1861, but their lives remained limited, and by the time of the revolution the nobility had sold off one third of its land and mortgaged another third. A deep industrial crisis followed the contraction of Western money markets in 1899-1900, and workers faced poor conditions and urban unemployment.

The empire was multi-ethnic, and Jews, who were about 4 percent of the population, were forbidden to settle or acquire land outside the cities and towns and were legally limited in schooling. Mounting losses in the Russo-Japanese War added to the discontent. In December 1904 a strike at the Putilov plant in Saint Petersburg grew, with sympathy strikes, to 150,000 workers in 382 factories.

On 22 January 1905, a Sunday, the priest Georgy Gapon led a procession of workers to the Winter Palace to present a petition to the tsar. Troops opened fire, causing between 200 (according to Sergei Witte) and 1,000 deaths. The event became known as Bloody Sunday and is considered by many scholars the start of the active phase of the revolution.

On 2 March 1905 Nicholas II published the Bulygin Rescript, promising a consultative assembly. In June and July peasants seized land and tools in many uprisings, and the Łódź insurrection took place in Congress Poland. Unrest redoubled when the limits of the proposed Duma were revealed, and the Saint Petersburg Soviet called a general strike in October.

The movement was national as well as social. In Estonia the army fired on a meeting in Tallinn on 29 October, killing 94. In Finland the Social Democrats organised a general strike from 30 October to 6 November, and the revolution led to the creation of the modern Parliament of Finland. In Latvia armed conflict between the Baltic German nobility and Latvian peasants began in autumn, and punitive expeditions executed 1,170 people without trial.

Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto on 17 October 1905, promising civil liberties and a Duma without whose approval no law would pass, and extending the suffrage, though the electoral law of 11 December still excluded women. The Fundamental Laws of 1906 confirmed the tsar's control of the executive, foreign policy, the church and the armed forces, and he kept the power of veto.

In July 1906 he dissolved the first Duma and appointed Pyotr Stolypin as prime minister, and in June 1907 the second Duma was dissolved and an electoral reform favouring the propertied class was decreed. Many historians hold that 1905 set the stage for 1917; Lenin called it the dress rehearsal without which the October Revolution's victory would have been impossible.
russification: Russification is a form of cultural assimilation in which non-Russians adopt Russian culture and the Russian language, either voluntarily or as a result of deliberate state policy. The governments of the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union pursued it, either as a goal in itself or as a consequence of centralization and modernization. In politics it can mean assigning Russians to lead administrative posts in national institutions; in culture it consists chiefly of the dominance of Russian in official business. Some researchers distinguish Russification, a change of one's ethnic identity to Russian, from Russianization, the spread of Russian language, culture and people, and from Sovietization.

The assimilation of Volga-Finnic peoples such as the Merya and Muroma began early in the 2nd millennium CE, with the eastward expansion of the East Slavs. After the defeat in the Crimean War in 1856 and the January Uprising of 1863, Tsar Alexander II increased Russification to reduce the threat of rebellion. In Congress Poland the Polish and Belarusian languages were banned in public places in 1864 and Polish in schools in the 1880s, and a secret Polish education network, including the Flying University, arose in response. The Ems Ukaz of 1876 banned printing in Ukrainian.

Under Alexander III an ukaz of 14 September 1885 made Russian mandatory for officials in the Baltic governorates, and by the early 1890s it was the language of instruction in their schools. In Estonia, Tartu University shifted from German to Russian in 1893. In Finland, Russification between 1899 and 1905 and from 1908 to 1917 aimed at ending the country's autonomy, and Finnish opposition was one of the main factors behind its declaration of independence in 1917.

After the 1917 revolution the Soviet authorities abolished the Arabic alphabet for native languages in Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Volga region, replacing it with one based on the Latin alphabet until the late 1930s. In 1939 and 1940 a number of these languages, including Tatar, Kazakh, Uzbek and Azerbaijani, were moved to the Cyrillic script, with spelling that had to follow Russian. After the Second World War the northern part of East Prussia became the Kaliningrad Oblast, whose German population was expelled and replaced by Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians. Some historians who regard the Soviet Union as a colonial empire have applied to it the phrase prison of nations.
russkaya-pravda: The Russkaya Pravda was the legal code of Kievan Rus' and its principalities, written at the beginning of the 12th century and remade over many centuries. Its basis, the Pravda of Yaroslav, dates from the beginning of the 11th century. According to the Novgorod chronicle, Yaroslav, prince of Novgorod, stopped sending tribute to Kiev in 1013 or 1014 with the support of Novgorod. After his father's death he defeated his half-brother Sviatopolk and gave the Novgorodian troops a law code. Most scholars accept this narrative. The likely source was customary law, and treaties with Byzantium in 911 and 941 already mention a zakon russkii.

The Pravda Yaroslavichey, the Pravda of Yaroslav's sons, is most likely of 1072. The second part of the Expanded Edition, the code of Vladimir Monomakh, was enacted shortly after the Kiev uprising of 1113.

The Pravda tried to abolish blood feud by limiting the number of avengers to the closest relatives. If a male victim had none, the killer paid a fine called vyra to the knyaz with partial compensation to the relatives, and the killer's community helped him pay. For a woman the fine was half. The code protected the health and honour of free people and set compensation for mutilation or insult, with penalties for theft and trespass. It regulated debts and contained rules on liability and inheritance, and it made use of witnesses, oaths and trial by water or iron.

It also stabilised feudal relations and social inequality, with rules for smerds, zakups and kholops, the last of whom could be killed or sold like slaves. After the Kiev riot of 1113 a law limited interest charged by moneylenders. The absence of capital and corporal punishment resembles Norse jurisprudence, not Byzantine law.

Three versions are known: the Short, Extensive and Abridged editions. The shortest is around 850 words and the longest about four times as long. Around 100 copies of the Extensive Edition survive, but only 13 of the Short Edition. Vasily Tatischev rediscovered the code in 1738 in a manuscript of the Novgorod chronicles, though it was not published until 1786. In the Russian state centred on Moscow it was replaced by the Sudebnik of 1497 under Ivan III.
russo-circassian-war: Circassians and Russians had once been allies: in 1557 Temruqo Idar of Eastern Circassia allied with Tsar Ivan the Terrible, who married his daughter Goshenay in 1561. The alliance broke as Circassians converted to Islam, above all after 1717, and turned towards the Ottomans. Russia raided Circassia from 1711, when Araksin, Governor of Astrakhan, led 30,000 troops along the Kuban River, pillaging its ports and villages. The Black Sea coast and fertile valleys of Circassia made it a target as Russia expanded along the Black Sea.

Most scholars date organised war from 17 July 1763, when Russian forces turned Mozdok into a fortress, though a smaller number place its start in 1817. Kabardian nobles demanded the fort's demolition in 1764, and envoys to Catherine II were sent back. In June 1767 Misost Bematuqo Hatokhshoqo began operations against Russia, while other Kabardian princes swore allegiance.

After General Aleksey Yermolov arrived in 1817, Russian forces turned to terror. In May 1818 the village of Tram was surrounded and burned and its inhabitants killed. The army destroyed villages, crops and livestock, cleared forests along roads and settled Russian and other Orthodox farmers. Circassian nobles long divided by blood feuds united against it, and a congress at Abin in 1857 resolved to fight on; Polish volunteers under Teofil Lapinski joined them.

In 1857 Dmitry Milyutin argued for the extermination of the Circassians. The Bjedugh submitted in 1859 and the Abadzekhs on 20 November 1859, and a Circassian Parliament formed at Sochi on 25 June 1861 under Gerandiqo Berzeg appealed to Europe for help. The last Circassian fighters were defeated at the Battle of Qbaada in June 1864.

Russia then drove out most of the surviving population. Ottoman archives record nearly 1 million migrants from the Caucasus by 1879, nearly half of whom died of disease on the shores, and the Russian census of 1897 found only 150,000 Circassians in the conquered region. The killings and expulsions are known as the Circassian genocide. They created a diaspora concentrated in Turkey, Jordan and Syria, and in modern Russia state media and officials have claimed that the invasion never happened.
russo-crimean-wars: The raids began soon after Moscow set up the Qasim Khanate as a buffer state and gained the upper hand in the Russo-Kazan Wars of the late 15th century. The first Crimean invasion came in 1507, after the death of Grand Duke Ivan III, with attacks on Belev and Kozelsk. Through the 16th century the edge of the Wild Steppes lay near Ryazan beyond the Oka River. The main road for the raiders was the Muravsky Trail, which ran from the Isthmus of Perekop between the Dnieper and Seversky Donets basins up to Tula.

The raiders usually reached 100–200 kilometres into Russian land and turned back only after looting and taking captives, who were sold in the slave markets of Caffa. Each spring Russia sent several thousand soldiers to guard a line of forts and towns on the frontier. Among the heaviest invasions were those of 1517, of 1521, made with the Khanate of Kazan, of 1537 and of 1552 and 1555.

In May 1571 Khan Devlet I Giray led some 60,000 Crimean and Ottoman troops, with Nogai and Circassian contingents, round the Russian defences on the Oka. The Russian army fell back to Moscow, and the Crimeans fired its suburbs; driven by the wind, the fire burned the city within three hours, and refugees were crushed at the northern gate. Contemporaries counted up to 80,000 dead and 150,000 taken captive. When the khan returned in 1572 the Russians had prepared fortifications beyond the Oka, and at the Battle of Molodi the Tatars were driven back; only 20,000 horsemen are said to have returned to Crimea.

Raids went on after Molodi. In 1591 Crimean troops reached Moscow for the last time, and a raid of 1633 was the last deep one into Russia. Russia pushed its defensive lines south: the Abatis line about 100 km south of the Oka around 1533, the Belgorod Line around 1650 and the Izium line around 1680. Raiding continued until the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774; Crimea became a Russian vassal in 1774 and was annexed in 1783.
russo-japanese-war: The Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 ceded the Liaodong Peninsula and Port Arthur to Japan, but Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to give them up in the Triple Intervention. In 1898 Russia obtained a lease of Port Arthur and the surrounding territory from China and began building the South Manchurian Railroad. Russian troops stayed in Manchuria after the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, and by 1903 Russia had set no timetable for withdrawal.

Japan signed the Anglo-Japanese Alliance in 1902 and offered to recognise Russian dominance in Manchuria in exchange for recognition of Korea as part of its own sphere. Russia rejected this. Within the Japanese leadership, Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru opposed war on financial grounds, while Katsura Tarō, Komura Jutarō and Yamagata Aritomo favoured it.

On the night of 8 February 1904 a Japanese fleet under Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō attacked the Russian ships at Port Arthur with torpedo boat destroyers, three hours before Japan's declaration of war reached the Russian government. Japanese troops landed in Korea and won the Battle of the Yalu River on 1 May. The siege of Port Arthur began in April; after costly frontal assaults, Japanese howitzers on a captured hilltop shelled the fleet in the harbour, and the fortress fell in January 1905.

In the Battle of Mukden, which began on 20 February 1905 and involved about half a million men, Japanese forces pressed both flanks of the Russian line and took the city. The Russian Baltic Fleet under Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky had left in October 1904 on a seven-month voyage round the Cape of Good Hope. It reached the Sea of Japan in May 1905 and was destroyed at the Battle of Tsushima.

The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed on 5 September 1905 and mediated by United States president Theodore Roosevelt, recognised Japanese interests in Korea. It gave Japan Russia's lease on the Liaodong Peninsula, the South Manchuria Railway and the southern half of Sakhalin. Estimates of the dead on both sides run from about 130,000 to 170,000, and Chinese civilians in Manchuria suffered looting and killing by Russian troops.

Observers noted that entrenched infantry with machine guns and artillery had become decisive, a lesson largely disregarded before the First World War. Russia lost two of its three fleets, and its defeat contributed to the 1905 Russian Revolution. Japan's victory was read abroad as a challenge to European dominance in Asia, and in the West it fed fears of a Yellow Peril.
russo-persian-war-1804-1813: In 1783 the Georgian king Heraclius II signed the Treaty of Georgievsk with Russia, placing his kingdom under Russian protection. Russia failed to defend Georgia against the assault of Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795, but reasserted its protectorate in September 1799, and in December 1800 Tsar Paul I annexed eastern Georgia. From the Iranian view Georgia and all the South Caucasus remained integral Iranian territory, and the new shah, Fath Ali Qajar, could not accept the loss.

After Paul's assassination Tsar Alexander I sought to incorporate the khanates of the eastern Caucasus. The governor Pavel Tsitsianov took the citadel of Ganja on 15 January 1804, killing its governor, Javad Khan Qajar, and slaughtering many inhabitants. In Iran the capture of Shia Muslim territory was seen as an invasion and provoked a strong reaction among the clergy and educated elite.

Russia could commit only a small part of its troops, since Alexander was also at war with France, the Ottoman Empire, Sweden and Great Britain, and some estimates give the Persians a five-to-one advantage in numbers. Crown Prince Abbas Mirza sought French and then British experts to modernise his army. In 1804 Tsitsianov fought him at Echmiadzin, where each side claimed victory, and after a failed siege of Yerevan retreated to Tiflis having lost half his men.

Karabakh and Shaki submitted to Russia in May 1805, and Tsitsianov was murdered on 8 February 1806 while accepting the surrender of Baku. Fighting paused when the Ottoman Empire declared war on Russia, and resumed in 1808; Ivan Gudovich's assault on Yerevan failed and 1,000 men froze to death in the retreat. Abbas Mirza was defeated at Meghri in 1810. In October 1812 Pyotr Kotlyarevsky routed him at Aslanduz and then stormed the fort of Lankaran, where the 4,000-man garrison was killed. A victory at Karabezouk completed the Persian defeat on 3 April 1813.

European diplomacy shaped the war. Britain, allied with Russia in 1805, avoided Persian requests for help. France promised support in the Treaty of Finckenstein on 4 May 1807, but Napoleon's Treaty of Tilsit with Alexander two months later made that untenable, and Britain then offered training and a subsidy through John Malcolm, Harford Jones and Gore Ouseley. Ouseley acted as intermediary once Napoleon's invasion of Russia made Britain and Russia allies again, and he pressed the shah to settle.

In the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813 Persia recognised Russian possession of the khanates it held and gave up all claims to Dagestan and Georgia. Firuz Kazemzadeh judged that the difference between well-drilled, disciplined armies and Abbas Mirza's tribal levies was decisive. Persia tried to regain its lands in a second war in 1826–1828, was defeated and lost the khanates of Yerevan and Nakhichevan.
russo-persian-war-1826-1828: The war was the last major military conflict between the Russian Empire and Qajar Iran, fought over territorial disputes in the South Caucasus. Iran had controlled the Caucasus since 1502 and saw it as a natural extension of its land. The earlier war of 1804-1813 ended with the Treaty of Gulistan, by which Iran conceded the khanates of Baku, Derbent, Ganja, Shakki, Quba, Shirvan and Karabakh and part of Talish, and abandoned its claims over Georgia. The frontier was unclear, and the region between Lake Gokcha and Erivan remained the most disputed. In 1825 Russians under Aleksey Yermolov seized the northern bank of Lake Gokcha, and Crown Prince Abbas Mirza protested.

At Fath-Ali Shah's court a peace party and a war party lobbied the shah. The war party, led by Agha Sayyed Mohammad Esfahani and including Abbas Mirza's adviser Abol-Qasem Qa'em-Maqam II, argued that Russia was weak, citing Yermolov's recent defeats and the Decembrist revolt. The Council of Soltaniyeh gathered to advise, and the decision was for full-scale war.

Iran's entry in the summer of 1826 began well, for Yermolov's men were unprepared and the Muslim population rose against the Russians; garrisons were driven out or withdrew in Shirvan, Ganja, Talish, Shakki and Karabakh, apart from Shusha. Abbas Mirza besieged Shusha from 6 August, but his artillery could not break through, and Colonel Iosif Reutt held out with the help of local Armenians. On 16 September Valerian Madatov defeated Amir Khan Devellu-Qajar at Shamkor, and Ganja surrendered to him the next day. Ivan Paskevich arrived on 22 September and took command from Yermolov on 29 September.

At the Battle of Ganja, on 13-17 October, Abbas Mirza's army of about 30,000 broke up after he ordered two of his young sons evacuated, which split its centre. By 1827 he was defending. In July Paskevich defeated him and the fortresses of Abbasabad and Ordubad surrendered, and in September Erivan fell after a siege and bombardment. On 24 October Tabriz surrendered without a fight, though Asef al-Dowleh had 20,000 men. Ardabil was captured and plundered on 25 January 1828.

On 2 February 1828 Abbas Mirza signed the Treaty of Turkmenchay, ceding Erivan and Nakhichevan and agreeing to heavy reparations. It stripped Iran of its last territories north of the Aras, comprising all of modern Armenia, the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and Iğdır Province, and the shah now needed Russia's acknowledgment of the heir he named. After the war the Qajar state never again faced Russia on equal footing or was treated as an equal by European countries.
russo-swedish-war-1590-1595: Boris Godunov began the war in the hope of winning the lands of the Duchy of Estonia along the Gulf of Finland, which had belonged to Sweden since the Livonian War. The Truce of Plussa of 1583 had left Sweden in possession of Jama, Koporye and Ivangorod as well as Narva. As soon as the truce expired early in 1590, a large Russian army led by Godunov and his sickly brother-in-law, Feodor I of Russia, marched from Moscow towards Novgorod.

On 18 January 1590 the Russians crossed the river Narva, defeated a Swedish detachment and laid siege to the castle of Narva, commanded by Arvid Stålarm. The fortress of Jama, or Jamburg, fell within two weeks, while Russian troops ravaged Estonia as far as Reval (Tallinn) and Finland as far as Helsinki. On 25 February the Swedish governor Karl Henriksson (Horn) was forced to sign an armistice surrendering Jama, Koporye and Ivangorod.

King John III of Sweden rejected the settlement and sent a fleet against Ivangorod, but the attack was checked by the Russian castellan. In summer 1591 the Swedes struck at Gdov and captured its governor, Prince Vladimir Dolgorukov. In the north, in East Karelia, Swedish raiders sacked Kola and other settlements near the White Sea. A party said to have been led by the Finnish peasant chief Pekka Vesainen destroyed the Pechenga Monastery on 25 December 1589, killing 50 monks and 65 lay brothers, and later burned Kandalaksha and a settlement at Kem, though it lacked the men to take the Kola Fortress or the Solovetsky Monastery.

Godunov's government sent Prince Volkonsky to pacify Karelia, and the generals Bogdan Belsky, Fedor Mstislavsky and Prince Trubetskoy devastated Finland. After that the war settled into indecisive skirmishing until Sweden agreed to peace in May 1595.

In the Treaty of Teusina, also written Tyavzino or Täyssinä, Russia renounced every claim on Estonia, including Narva, and Sweden's sovereignty over Estonia since 1561 was confirmed. Historians judge the outcome differently. Many scholarly works count it a Swedish victory or a result favourable to Sweden, and some call it a commercial victory for Sweden. Russian sources often claim a Russian victory and a peace on Moscow's terms; the Cambridge History of Russia also speaks of a Russian victory while noting that not all Russian aims were met, and other writers see a military victory for Russia and a political draw.
russo-turkish-war-1735-1739: The war arose from the Ottoman Empire's war with Persia and from continuing raids by the Crimean Tatars, and it formed part of Russia's long struggle for access to the Black Sea. Russia had secured a favourable position beforehand. It signed treaties with Iran between 1732 and 1735, and by the Treaty of Ganja in 1735 returned its remaining Persian conquests and allied with Persia against the Ottomans. It also supported the accession of Augustus III to the Polish throne against Stanislaw Leszczynski, the candidate of pro-Ottoman France, and had been allied with Austria since 1726. The immediate cause was Tatar raids on the Cossack Hetmanate at the end of 1735.

In 1736 Field Marshal Burkhard Christoph von Münnich led the Dnieper Army of 62,000 men against the Crimean fortifications at Perekop, then occupied Bakhchysarai on 17 June, where the khan's palace was burned, accidentally or deliberately. General Peter Lacy's Don Army took the fortress of Azov. Disease, hunger and famine, not battle, caused almost all of the roughly 30,000 Russian deaths of that campaign, and Münnich withdrew to Ukraine. In July 1737 he stormed Ochakov, after fire reached its powder magazine. Austria joined the war in 1737, but its armies were defeated at Banja Luka and later at Grocka.

Plague struck all sides in 1737 to 1739. Russian forces had to leave Ochakov and Kinburn in 1738, and Lacy's repeated invasions of Crimea each turned back for want of supplies and water. In 1739 Münnich crossed the Dniester, defeated the Ottomans at Stavuchany on 28 August, took Khotin on 30 August and entered Iasi on 14 September.

Austria made a preliminary peace on 1 September and signed the Treaty of Belgrade on 18 September 1739, losing Belgrade, central Serbia, Oltenia and the Bosnian section of Posavina. French mediation also produced a separate Russo-Ottoman preliminary treaty, and the Treaty of Niš followed on 3 October. Azov was demolished and its lands made neutral territory. Russia abandoned its claims to Crimea and Moldavia and consolidated its control over Zaporozhia, and it was not allowed to keep a fleet on the Azov or Black Sea. All three powers wanted out because the war was costing more than they could gain, and Russia feared a Swedish invasion.
russo-turkish-war-1768-1774: The war grew out of troubles in Poland. The Russian ambassador Nicholas Repnin and the Imperial Russian Army stood behind King Stanisław August Poniatowski, and Repnin imposed the Perpetual Treaty of 1768, which disadvantaged Poland and allowed Russian troops to occupy Warsaw. The Bar Confederation, an alliance of noble, Roman Catholic and peasant rebels, was formed on 29 February 1768. When a band of confederates fled towards the Ottoman border, Russian pursuers, among them Zaporozhian Cossacks, clashed with Ottoman garrison troops. In the summer of 1768 Sultan Mustafa III heard that Cossacks had razed the town of Balta, and on 6 October he imprisoned the Russian ambassador Aleksei Mikhailovich Obreskov and his staff, which marked the Ottoman declaration of war.

The Ottoman army was three times the size of the Russian one, but Grand Vizier Mehmed Emin Pasha proved militarily incompetent. In January 1769 a large Turkish and Tatar army under the Crimean Khan Qırım Giray ravaged central Ukraine. In September 1769 the Russians crossed the Dniester into Moldavia, took Khotyn, entered Jassy on 7 October and occupied Bucharest on 17 November. At Kagul on 1 August 1770 they routed the grand vizier's forces, and a third of the Ottoman troops are said to have drowned in the Danube.

At sea, a Russian fleet under Count Alexei Grigoryevich Orlov entered the Mediterranean for the first time, and on 24 June 1770 twelve Russian ships destroyed twenty-two Ottoman vessels off Chesma with fire ships. Russian forces also crossed the Caucasus into Georgia, and the fleet intervened in Syria, where it took part in the Battle of Sidon and bombarded and occupied Beirut. A ceasefire began on 30 May 1772, but talks stalled over Crimea. On 20 June 1774 Alexander Suvorov routed the Ottoman army near Kozludzha.

The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca was signed on 21 July 1774. The Crimean Khanate formally became independent of both powers, though in practice it came to depend on Russia and was annexed in 1783. The Ottomans ceded the seaports of Azov and Kerch, giving Russia direct access to the Black Sea, along with the land between the Dnieper and the Southern Bug, and paid war reparations of 4.5 million rubles. Russia gained the status of protector of the Orthodox Christians of the Ottoman Empire. Northwestern Moldavia, later known as Bukovina, passed to the Habsburg Empire.
russo-turkish-war-1806-1812: The war broke out during the Napoleonic Wars. In 1806 Sultan Selim III, encouraged by the Russian defeat at Austerlitz and advised by France, deposed the pro-Russian Constantine Ypsilantis as Hospodar of Wallachia and Alexander Mourousis as Hospodar of Moldavia. France had occupied Dalmatia and threatened to enter the Danubian Principalities, so a Russian contingent of 40,000 advanced into Moldavia and Wallachia to protect the border. The Sultan blocked the Dardanelles to Russian ships and declared war on Russia.

Emperor Alexander I was reluctant to concentrate large forces against the Ottomans while his army was fighting Napoleon in Prussia. A large Ottoman offensive towards Bucharest was checked at Obilesti on 2 June 1807 by about 4,500 men under Mikhail Miloradovich, and Ivan Gudovich beat a force of 20,000 at Arpachai in Armenia. Dmitry Senyavin's navy blockaded the Dardanelles and defeated the Ottoman fleet, after which Selim III was deposed, and the fleet was destroyed the next month at the Battle of Athos. The Peace of Tilsit then brought an armistice, which Russia used to bring more soldiers south, raising its army to 80,000.
Under Pyotr Bagration and then the brothers Nikolay and Sergei Kamensky the Russians took Silistra and Rousse in 1810, but they had won no victory decisive enough to end the war.

With relations with France worsening, Alexander appointed Mikhail Kutuzov, whom he disliked but needed, to command. Kutuzov beat a larger army under Grand Vizier Ahmed Pasha at Rusçuk on 22 June 1811, then withdrew across the Danube. When 36,000 Turkish troops crossed and set up a fortified bridgehead near Slobozia, the Russians surrounded them. On the night of 1 October a Russian detachment of 7,500 crossed the river and routed the camp on the other bank. The besieged Turks suffered from bombardment, malnutrition and disease, and Ahmed Pasha surrendered on 14 November 1811.

The Treaty of Bucharest was signed on 28 May 1812, and Alexander I approved it on 11 June, 13 days before Napoleon's invasion began. The Ottoman Empire ceded the eastern half of Moldavia, the territory east of the Prut, which Russia named Bessarabia, and Russia became a new power on the lower Danube. In Transcaucasia Turkey regained Poti, Anapa and Akhalkalaki, while Russia kept Sukhum-Kale and the Sultan accepted its annexation of Imereti in 1810. Some sources describe the war as a Russian victory, and others call it indecisive because Russia returned all occupied land except Bessarabia. The commanders brought many soldiers back to the west before Napoleon's attack.
russo-turkish-war-1828-1829: The war grew out of the Greek War of Independence. In October 1827 Great Britain, France and Russia jointly destroyed the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Navarino, and in November 1827 Sultan Mahmud II retaliated by closing the Dardanelles to Russian ships and revoking the Akkerman Convention of 1826. The Ottoman Empire had bloodily abolished its centuries-old Janissary Corps in 1826, so when war began in 1828 it had neither a regular army nor a navy.

On the Balkan front a Russian army of 100,000, nominally under Emperor Nicholas I, moved into the Danubian Principalities in April and May 1828 under Prince Peter Wittgenstein and crossed the Danube in June. With the Black Sea Fleet the Russians took Varna on 29 September, but they failed at Shumen, where the 40,000-strong Ottoman garrison outnumbered them, and many soldiers died of disease or exhaustion.

In February 1829 Hans Karl von Diebitsch replaced Wittgenstein, took Silistra on 19 June and, after defeating a relief force at the Battle of Kulevicha on 30 May, launched a Trans-Balkan offensive on 2 July, the first in Russian history since Svyatoslav I's campaigns. The Russians took Burgas, routed a Turkish force near Sliven on 31 July, and by 22 August had taken Adrianople.

In the Caucasus, Ivan Paskevich, with only about 15,000 men for the Turkish front, took Kars on 23 June 1828, in what was almost an accident, then Akhalkalaki and Akhaltsikhe. The Russians lost about 600 men at Akhaltsikhe against 6,000 Turkish losses, and in one mosque 400 people burned to death. In 1829 Paskevich defeated the Turkish armies near Saganlug and Erzurum surrendered on 27 June, which had not seen Christian soldiers within its walls for five centuries.

Faced with these defeats, the Sultan sued for peace, and the Treaty of Adrianople gave Russia most of the eastern shore of the Black Sea and the mouth of the Danube. Turkey recognised Russian sovereignty over parts of present-day north-west Armenia, and Serbia gained autonomy. Russia was allowed to occupy Moldavia and Wallachia until a large indemnity was paid, and they remained Russian protectorates until the Crimean War. The Sultan recognised the independence of the Kingdom of Greece. Russia kept Anapa, Poti, Atskhur, Akhalkalaki and Akhaltsikhe but returned Ardahan and the pashaliks of Kars and Bayazid. About 90,000 Armenians migrated from Turkish to Russian territory.
russo-turkish-war-1877-1878: Russia sought to recover the territory lost in the Crimean War of 1853–1856, to re-establish itself in the Black Sea and to support the movements freeing Balkan nations from Ottoman rule. The Ottoman Empire, though on the winning side in the Crimean War, kept declining. Foreign loans at steep interest left it with unpayable debts, and it had to settle more than 600,000 Muslim Circassians expelled by Russia from the Caucasus. In 1875 events in the Balkans brought Europe to the brink of war.

On 30 June 1876 Serbia, followed by Montenegro, declared war on the Ottomans. At Reichstadt Alexander II of Russia and Franz Joseph I of Austria-Hungary agreed without a written text that Russia would support Austrian occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Austria-Hungary would support the return of Southern Bessarabia and Russian annexation of Batum.

On 12 April 1877 Romania allowed Russian troops to cross its territory. Russia declared war on the Ottomans on 24 April, and on 10 May the Principality of Romania, under nominal Turkish suzerainty, declared its independence. Romanians call the conflict the Romanian War of Independence.

In the Caucasus the Russian 1st Caucasus Army Corps, about 50,000 men under Grand Duke Michael Nikolaevich, faced an Ottoman army of 100,000 under Ahmed Muhtar Pasha. The Russians were outgunned by the Krupp artillery Germany had supplied to the Ottomans. Greece, held back by British neutrality, did not declare war, though its army under Skarlatos Soutsos entered Thessaly in January 1878 and won the Battle of Mouzaki. A Kurdish uprising broke out in the Bohtan region as the war ended.

Under British pressure Russia accepted an Ottoman truce on 31 January 1878 but kept advancing towards Constantinople. The British sent a fleet, and the Russians stopped at San Stefano. By the Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March, the Ottomans were to recognise the independence of Romania, Serbia and Montenegro and the autonomy of Bulgaria. Russia gained Kars and Batum and annexed the Budjak. A provisional Russian administration governed liberated Bulgarian territory from April 1877, and the Treaty of Berlin ended it in May 1879, when the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia were established.

Russia, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Ottoman Empire and Albanians all carried out massacres and ethnic cleansing during the war. The conflict also split the emblems of the Red Cross movement: the cross reminded the Ottomans of the Crusades, so they adopted the Red Crescent.
russo-turkish-wars: The first war, in 1568–1570, followed the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan by Tsar Ivan the Terrible. Sultan Selim II sent an expedition to Astrakhan in 1569, which failed, and the Ottoman fleet was wrecked by a storm in the Sea of Azov. The peace confirmed Russian rule on the Volga. The Crimean Khanate, an Ottoman vassal, burned Moscow in 1571 but was defeated at the Battle of Molodi in 1572. A century later the two powers clashed over Ukraine, and the Treaty of Bakhchisarai of 1681 set the border on the Dnieper.

Under Peter the Great, Russia annexed Azov by the Treaty of Constantinople of 1700, but the Prut campaign, after the sultan declared war in November 1710, ended with the Russian army surrounded and Azov returned to the Ottomans. The war of 1736–1739 ended with the Treaty of Niš, after Austria made a separate peace.

Under Catherine II the balance turned. The war that began in 1768 saw Russian victories at Larga and Kagul and the destruction of the Ottoman navy at the Battle of Chesma. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 21 July 1774 gave the Crimean Khanate formal independence, though it became dependent on Russia, and gave Russia two Black Sea ports and a protector's role over Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire. Russia annexed Crimea in 1783. The war of 1787 ended with the Treaty of Jassy on 9 January 1792, which left Crimea and Ochakov to Russia and made the Dniester the frontier in Europe.

In the 19th century Russia gained Bessarabia after the decisive campaign of 1811, and the war of 1828–1829 led to Greek independence and Russian control of the Black Sea coast of the Caucasus. The Crimean War of 1853–1856 went against Russia. The war of 1877–1878 followed uprisings in Herzegovina, Bosnia and Bulgaria; the Treaty of San Stefano gave Romania and Montenegro independence, and the Congress of Berlin in 1878 then reduced Bulgarian territory.

In the First World War the Ottomans were defeated at Sarikamish in January 1915 and at Erzurum in 1916. Both empires dissolved soon afterwards, the Russian in 1917 and the Ottoman between 1918 and 1922.
rustaq: Rustaq is a town and district in the Al Batinah South Governorate of northern Oman, in the western Hajar Mountains. The mountains surround it on every side but the north, where it opens onto the Batinah coastal plain towards Al-Musannah and Al-Suwayq. That northern side is a vital passage, and it links the town to Muscat, about 160 km away. To the north-east the surroundings are rocky and sandy desert. The name comes from a Middle Iranian word, rōstāg, meaning a district, and a related New Iranian word, rusta, means a large village.

In the days of the Sasanian Empire, Rustaq had a Persian marzban, or military governor, to whom the Sasanians in the area reported. Dibba and Tuwwam, places that Oman today shares with the U.A.E., were taxed by the Al-Julanda, who were clients of the Sasanians.

The town was once the capital of Oman in the time of Imam Nasir bin Murshid al-Ya'arubi. Its great fort, Rustaq Castle, stands on the slopes of the Green Mountain at the edge of the Batinah plain. The present structure was rebuilt by the first imams of the Ya'aruba dynasty between 1624 and 1649. It has two main floors above the ground floor, with residences, storerooms for weapons, reception rooms, a mosque, prisons and wells, four gates and four towers.

One tower, the Wind Tower, was built by Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Ya'arubi, whose tomb is in the western corner of the castle, and another, the Modern Tower, was added in the reign of Imam Ahmed bin Said. Nearby Al-Hazm Fort was built in 1711 by Imam Sultan bin Saif bin Sultan al-Ya'arubi and is noted for its thick walls and its roof built without wooden supports.

Rustaq is known for its hot springs, such as Ain al-Kasfah, whose sulphurous water runs at about 45 degrees Celsius and is regarded as a cure for rheumatism and skin diseases. Falaj Al-Meisar, one of the traditional irrigation channels at Al-Khubayb in the district, was added to the World Heritage List in 2006 with four other aflaj. Date palms, citrus, beekeeping, Omani halwa and the making of the khanjar dagger are among the local products.
rusyns: The name Rusyn comes from the archaic ethnonym Rus', and the people have also been called Carpatho-Rusyns, Ruthenians and Rusnaks. They speak Rusyn, an East Slavic language variety treated either as a distinct language or as a dialect of Ukrainian. Their homeland, Carpathian Ruthenia, is a cross-border region that takes in Subcarpathian Rus', the Prešov Region in eastern Slovakia, the Lemko Region in south-eastern Poland and Maramureş in Romania.

There are different theories of their origin. Paul Robert Magocsi holds that it is complex and not exclusively related to Kievan Rus'. Their ancestors included early Slavs whose movement to the Danubian Basin was influenced by the Huns and Pannonian Avars between the 5th and 6th centuries, the White Croats who lived on both slopes of the Carpathians, the Rusyns of Galicia and Podolia, and Vlach shepherds of Transylvania. Ukrainian encyclopedias generally consider them descendants of the White Croats.

The Austro-Hungarian monarchy controlled the Carpathians from 1772 to 1918. In the 19th century increasing Magyarization led some educated Rusyns to move to Budapest, while other intellectuals favoured the Russian Empire. A Rusyn national movement formed that stressed a distinct ethnic identity and literary language. On 2 May 1848, during the Spring of Nations, the Main Ruthenian Council was established in Lemberg as the first political representation of the Galician Rusyns, and Greek-Catholic clergy were the most active stratum among them.

In the Kingdom of Hungary the term Ruthene was the official name for the Rusyns of Transcarpathia until 1945. According to Magocsi, after 1945 Communist authorities treated Carpatho-Rusyns as a branch of the Ukrainian nationality and Rusyn as a dialect of Ukrainian, and banned Rusyn nationality and language. Since the revolutions of 1989 there has been a revival of Rusyn culture and identity.

Many Rusyns are Eastern Catholics of the Byzantine Rite who have been in communion with Rome since the Union of Uzhhorod in 1646. Their church, the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church, keeps the Byzantine liturgy, sometimes in Church Slavonic, and married priests. Orthodoxy also has a place: in the 1890s a movement began to return to it, and Alexis Toth, a former Greek Catholic priest, led as many as 20,000 Rusyn Americans to Orthodoxy.
