Rusyn communities also settled outside the Carpathians. The oldest diaspora community lies in the Pannonian Plain, in parts of present-day Serbia and Croatia. At the end of the 19th and the start of the 20th century about 225,000 Rusyns emigrated to the United States, mostly to the industrial centres of the Northeast and Midwest.
rutger-jan-schimmelpenninck: Schimmelpenninck was born in Deventer, Overijssel, on 31 October 1761, into an illegitimate branch of the noble family Schimmelpenninck van der Oye. His father, Gerrit Schimmelpenninck, was a wine trader whose Mennonite faith barred him from rights in the Dutch Republic. He studied law at Leiden University from 1781 and took his doctorate in 1784 with a thesis defending Rousseau's doctrine of popular sovereignty, limited to the wealthy bourgeoisie, and praising the Constitution of the United States.

One of the first Patriots at Leiden, he helped write the Patriot manifesto known as the Leiden Draft in 1785. He then practised as a lawyer in Amsterdam and married Catharina Nahuys, of a wealthy family. After the Prussian intervention of 1787 restored the stadtholder William V, he and fellow Patriots such as Alexander Gogel founded the society Doctrina et Amicitia. In 1792 he joined the Holland Land Company, which invested in northern New York.

After the Batavian Revolution of 19 January 1795 he sat in Amsterdam's temporary government, and in 1796 he was elected to the 1st National Assembly, where he sat with the Moderates between the conservative Federalists and the radical Unitarians. He presided over the assembly twice. On 14 June 1798 he became ambassador in Paris, where he was taken with Napoleon after the coup of 1799, and he took part in the talks before the Treaty of Amiens. He served briefly in London from 8 December 1802 and was back in Paris by 15 September 1803.

As Grand Pensionary from 29 April 1805, ruling under a constitution he had written at Napoleon's request, he was in practice dependent on Napoleon. Gogel, his secretary of state for finance, brought in excises on salt, soap, peat, grain and meat, a land tax and a cadastre, and Hendrik van Stralen introduced subsidised public education. Louis Bonaparte replaced him on 4 June 1806.

Napoleon made him a count of the Empire on 10 April 1811, and from 30 December 1811 he sat in the French Sénat conservateur, the Netherlands having been annexed by France. After 1815 he took a seat in the First Chamber of the States General of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, until an eye disease forced him to retire in 1820. He died in Amsterdam on 15 February 1825. The historian Niek Sas called him the first Dutch liberal politician.
rutgers-university: Rutgers was founded two decades after the College of New Jersey, now Princeton University, was established in 1746 by New Light Presbyterians. Ministers of the Dutch Reformed Church, who sought autonomy in ecclesiastical affairs in the Thirteen Colonies, wanted a college of their own to train men for the ministry in the colony. Their religious body later developed into the Reformed Church in America. Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh, a Dutch Reformed minister who had worked to establish the college, became its first president in 1785.

In its early years, for lack of funds, Queen's College was closed for two extended periods. Early trustees considered merging it with the College of New Jersey at Princeton, but the measure failed by one vote; they later considered moving it to New York City. In 1808, after raising $12,000, the college reopened and broke ground on a building of its own, Old Queens, designed by the architect John McComb Jr. Its third president, Ira Condict, laid the cornerstone on 27 April 1809. The New Brunswick Theological Seminary, founded in 1784, moved to New Brunswick and shared the building, together with the Queen's College Grammar School.

In 1825 the college was renamed Rutgers College in honour of Colonel Henry Rutgers, whose substantial gift had stabilised its finances. The collection of schools became Rutgers University in 1924, as graduate education developed, with Rutgers College continuing as its liberal arts college. University College followed in 1945 and Livingston College in 1969. The state legislature designated Rutgers the state university of New Jersey by acts of 1945 and 1956; as successor to the private college chartered in 1766, it keeps some private rights and protections regarding its character and mission. Before 1930 most of its presidents were clergy of the Reformed tradition.

The university has three campuses, at New Brunswick with the adjacent Piscataway, at Newark and at Camden. The historic core lies along College Avenue in New Brunswick and includes Old Queens, the seat of the university. The Newark campus, originally the University of Newark, took its present name in 1945; the Camden campus began in the 1920s as the College of South Jersey and South Jersey Law School and joined Rutgers in 1950. In 2013 Rutgers merged with the University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey.

Its motto, Sol iustitiae et occidentem illustra, modifies that of Utrecht University and recalls the historic connection of the two. Rutgers is a land-grant, sea-grant and space-grant university. At Rutgers the microbiologist Selman Waksman discovered several antibiotics and, with the graduate student Albert Schatz, streptomycin, the first applied to cure tuberculosis; Waksman received the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1952.
ruthenian-uniate-church: By the late 16th century the East Slavic-speaking Ruthenians of the Commonwealth mostly followed the Byzantine Rite, while the Poles were Roman Catholic. The Ruthenian Church was, in historians' description, the church of a people without statehood, regarded by the Poles as conquered. Bishoprics went as royal rewards to men of the poorer gentry and the burghers, who went on raiding, trading and lending money; there were no cathedral chapters, and the education of the peasantry was falling. Much of the Ruthenian nobility became Catholic and Polish through intermarriage, leaving the church without leaders or benefactors.

The Patriarch in Constantinople could send neither aid nor teachers, and Protestant help was unacceptable to many. The Ruthenian elite therefore turned to the Pope, hoping that Catholic communion would curb Polish Catholic excesses and bring them into the political life of the Commonwealth.

The church had a single metropolis, that of Kiev, Galicia and all Ruthenia. At the time of the negotiations there were eight Ruthenian bishoprics, among them Polotsk, Volodymyr and Brest, Lutsk and Ostroh, Turov and Pinsk, Lviv, Chełm, and Przemyśl and Sambir; an Archeparchy of Smolensk existed from 1625 to 1778. Pope Clement VIII's bull Decet Romanum Pontificem of 1596 gave the metropolitans the rights they had held under Constantinople. Candidates were elected by the bishops and the Proto-Archimandrite of the Basilian order, nominated by the Polish king and confirmed by the pope. Michael Rohoza was the first metropolitan, from 1596 to 1599.

The union brought sharp confrontation among Ruthenians, including the murder of Archeparch Josaphat Kuntsevych in 1623, and its opponents called members Uniates, a term Catholic documents no longer use. During the Great Northern War, Russian troops occupying Volhynia turned the Lutsk eparchy to Orthodoxy until they withdrew. After the partitions the Russian Empire effectively dissolved the church, and in Prussia the Eparchy of Supraśl, which existed from 1798 to 1809, was forcibly converted after the Treaties of Tilsit. In Austria the church continued as a Greek Catholic Church. Suppressed in the Soviet Union from 1946, it became the core of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church from 1989.
ruthenians: Ruthenian is an exonym of Latin origin. Medieval Latin writers used Rutheni for the East Slavs in general, which spared them the need to be specific about the many endonyms. The name Ruteni, also borne by an unrelated Celtic tribe of ancient Gaul, was applied to Rus in the Annales Augustani of 1089. From the 9th century Kievan Rus' was known in Western Europe by names derived from Rus', and Ruthenia and Ruthenorum were applied to it and its rulers from the 11th century.

The Latin term was not used for the Russians of Moscow, who were known as Moscovitae in Western Europe. The Portuguese poet Luís Vaz de Camões distinguished Ruthenians from Muscovites in Os Lusíadas, though documents from Vilnius in 1655 show that Muscovites were also sometimes called Rutheni in Lithuania. A memorial plate of dubious authority of 1521 in Salzburg, which calls Odoacer king of the Rhutenes, gave rise to speculative theories linking Gallic Ruthenes to East Slavs; Paul R. Magocsi called such theories inventive tales.

In the early modern period the term was applied most often to the East Slavic population of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, in the lands of modern Belarus and Ukraine, from the 15th to the 18th centuries. Their varieties of speech, called the Ruthenian language, diverged by the end of the 18th century into Belarusian, Ukrainian and Rusyn. Religion divided them: the Union of Krewo in 1385 made Catholicism the religion of the ruling class, and the Union of Brest in 1595–1596 created the Ruthenian Uniate Church under the Holy See. The confrontation it caused included the murder of the hierarch Josaphat Kuntsevych in 1623.

After the partition of Poland the term referred to the Rusyn- and Ukrainian-speaking people of Austria-Hungary, especially in Galicia, Bukovina and Transcarpathia. In 1843, at the request of Mykhailo Levytsky, it became the official name for them in the Austrian Empire, and Ivan Franko and Stepan Bandera were registered as Ruthenians. By 1900 more and more Ruthenians called themselves Ukrainians. In interwar Poland the government in Galicia replaced the word Ukrainians with rusini, and the census of 1931 counted Belarusian, Rusyn and Ukrainian as separate languages.

After the Second World War the Soviet Union banned the names Rusyn and Carpatho-Rusyn in June 1945 and treated Ruthenians as part of the Ukrainian group; the Greek Catholic church was banned and replaced by Orthodoxy. A Rusyn revival followed the end of communist rule in 1989. Slovakia proclaimed the Rusyns a distinct national minority in 1991 and recognised their language in 1995. Paul R. Magocsi notes that modern Ruthenians have the sense of a nationality distinct from Ukrainians. Konstanty Ostrogski, Bohdan Khmelnytsky and Ivan Mazepa are among those described as Ruthenians in the Commonwealth period.
ruthwell-cross: The cross stands 18 feet (5.5 m) high and was made when Ruthwell lay in the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Northumbria. It belongs to the Insular art tradition, with close links to the Irish high crosses, and carries the largest figurative reliefs on any surviving Anglo-Saxon cross. Nikolaus Pevsner set the crosses of Bewcastle and Ruthwell above any work of their date in Europe. Most scholars hold that its images and texts form one learned programme, though they propose different schemes for it.

The largest panel, on the north side, shows Christ either treading on the beasts or recognised as judge by the beasts in the desert, as its inscription suggests; the nearby Bewcastle Cross has a very similar relief. Below are Saints Paul and Antony breaking bread in the desert and a Flight into Egypt. The south side shows Mary Magdalene drying the feet of Christ, the Healing of the man born blind and the Annunciation, while the Crucifixion is thought on stylistic grounds to be a later addition.

The cross survived the Reformation, but in 1640 the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland ordered idolatrous monuments destroyed, and in 1642 it was taken down and broken; one piece appears to have served as a bench. By 1823 Henry Duncan had collected the pieces, commissioned a new crossbeam and set it up in the manse garden; the side arms and centre roundel are speculative replacements, and the two sections may have been restored the wrong way round. In 1887 it was moved into an apse built for it inside Ruthwell church.

Reginald Bainbrigg of Appleby recorded the runes around 1600 for William Camden's Britannia. Around 1832 Thorleif Repp recognised them as Anglo-Saxon rather than Scandinavian, and John Mitchell Kemble proposed the reading linked to The Dream of the Rood in 1842, filling gaps from the Vercelli Book; his reading is disputed. Many scholars think the runes were added later, perhaps as late as the 10th century. Fred Orton and Patrick W. Conner have argued that the monument may first have been a column rather than a cross. The Visionary Cross project made 3D scans of it in 2012.
ruud-lubbers: Rudolphus Franciscus Marie Lubbers was born on 7 May 1939 in Rotterdam. He studied economics at Erasmus University Rotterdam, where he was a student of Jan Tinbergen, the first laureate of the Nobel Prize in Economics. His 1962 thesis dealt with the influence of differing productivity trends in various countries on the current account of the balance of payments, and his main interest was monetary affairs. He had planned an academic career but family circumstances obliged him to join the management of Hollandia, the construction and machinery firm that bore his family's name. From 1965 he also worked for the Christian Employers' Association.

Lubbers was Minister of Economic Affairs in the Den Uyl cabinet from 11 May 1973 to 19 December 1977, as a member of the Catholic People's Party. He then returned to the House of Representatives and, after the Christian Democratic Appeal was formed as an alliance of the Christian parties, rose unexpectedly in 1978 when its parliamentary leader Willem Aantjes resigned over accusations that he had served in the Germanic-SS. Lubbers succeeded him. In 1982 Prime Minister Dries van Agt announced that he would not serve a third term and Lubbers took over on 4 November 1982, at the age of 43.

He led three cabinets and left office on 22 August 1994, after announcing in October 1993 that he would not stand again. His years in office were marked by extensive cuts in public spending and far-reaching deregulation and privatisation. One of his campaign slogans was Meer markt, minder overheid, 'more market, less government', and many observers saw him as an ideological heir to Margaret Thatcher. In 1983 a very large demonstration in The Hague opposed the planned installation of nuclear-armed American cruise missiles in the Netherlands; the plan was cancelled after arms reduction talks between the United States and the Soviet Union.

From 1995 to 2000 Lubbers taught globalisation studies at Tilburg University and at Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government, and he worked with the Earth Charter Initiative, launched in The Hague in June 2000. Kofi Annan appointed him United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in succession to Sadako Ogata, and he held the post from 1 January 2001. He resigned on 20 February 2005 after a complaint of sexual harassment made in 2004, which he denied and which the Secretary-General had concluded could not be substantiated.

Lubbers was granted the title Minister of State on 31 January 1995 and continued to comment on politics as a statesman. He was married to Ria Hoogeweegen and had two sons and a daughter. He died in Rotterdam on 14 February 2018, aged 78.
ruvo-di-puglia: Ruvo di Puglia has an area of 222.04 km2 and borders Bisceglie, Terlizzi, Bitonto, Altamura, Gravina in Puglia, Spinazzola, Andria and Corato. Its countryside of vineyards, olive groves and arable land has the typical features of an Apulian karst landscape, with sinkholes, karst valleys and caves, among them the Grave della Ferratella, the deepest in the region. Part of the territory lies within the Alta Murgia national park. Two large tectonic valleys hold surface water that has been tapped by wells since ancient times, which favoured the ancient settlements nearby.

The name is first attested on coins of the 3rd century BCE bearing the Greek legends Rhyps, Rhyba and Rhybasteinon. Horace called the inhabitants the Rubi, and Pliny the Elder lists them as the Rubustini. The Iapygians settled the land of Bari and gave rise to the Peucetians, and Ruvo began as a hilltop village. Between the 8th and 5th centuries BCE the Greeks colonised it peacefully. About the 4th century BCE it was at its height, trading with most of the Italic peoples including the Etruscans, minting its own coins and living on olive oil, wine and pottery. After the defeat of Taranto by Rome it became Rubi, a municipium and a station on the Via Traiana.

The Goths reduced the city to rubble in the fifth century, and it was later conquered by Lombards and raided by Saracens. Under Frederick II of Swabia it grew again, and the Romanesque-Gothic cathedral belongs to this age. It became a fief of the Angevins from 1266, and in 1350 Ruggiero Sanseverino razed and sacked it. The Battle of Ruvo, won by Consalvo of Cordova over the French under Jacques de La Palice, destroyed it a third time. Oliviero Carafa bought the fief in 1510, and the Carafa ruled until feudalism was abolished under Napoleonic rule in 1806.

Ruvo di Puglia is a town in the Metropolitan City of Bari. The Jatta National Archaeological Museum, founded on the finds made by the nineteenth-century lawyer Giovanni Jatta, is known for its Hellenistic pieces, among them the Vase of Talos. The cathedral is one of the best-known examples of Apulian Romanesque and was built in the first half of the 12th century. Its coat of arms, recognised by decree in 1950, shows a terracotta amphora on a blue ground. The town produces olive oil and wine.
ruvuma-river: The Ruvuma, formerly also called the Rovuma, lies in the African Great Lakes region. Its drainage basin covers about 155,000 square kilometres. The lower river is formed at 11° 25′ S, 38° 31′ E by the junction of two branches of nearly equal importance: the Lujenda, which comes from the south-west, and a western branch that still bears the name Ruvuma.

The Ruvuma's source lies on an undulating plateau about 1,000 m high immediately east of Lake Nyasa. The head-stream flows first due west before turning south and east. In its eastward course the river runs near the base of the escarpment of an arid sandstone plateau to the north. The streams from that direction have cut deep channels in the plateau edge and almost all have short courses.

On its southern bank the Ruvuma receives the Lujenda, the Msinje River and the Luchulingo River. The Lujenda rises in the small Lake Chiuta, whose swamps are separated from Lake Chilwa only by a narrow wooded ridge. Its stream passes through a swampy valley into the narrow Lake Amaramba, from which the Lujenda issues about 73 m wide.

Lower down, the Lujenda varies greatly in breadth and holds long wooded islands that rise above the flood level and are often inhabited. In many places it can be forded in the dry season, and at its mouth it is about 1.6 km wide. The lower Ruvuma is often 0.8 km wide but generally shallow, and runs through a swampy valley between plateau escarpments. The mouth is near 10° 28′ S, 40° 30′ E.

For the greater part of its course the river forms the border between Tanzania and Mozambique. A bridge across it, called Unity Bridge, was proposed as early as 1975 and begun, but abandoned for lack of funds. After a formal agreement in 2002 a new bridge of 600 metres was opened on 25 May 2010 at Negomano, at a cost of US$28 million.

Presidents Machel and Nyerere chose the site because Frelimo forces first entered Mozambique there on 25 September 1964, in the Mozambican War of Independence. German forces had also crossed the river at Negomano on 25 November 1917. A smaller bridge, Unity Two, was completed in 2007 on the upper river near Matchedge in Niassa Province.
ruy-gonzalez-de-clavijo: Clavijo came from a prominent noble family, but little is known of his life and his date of birth is unknown. He was a native of Madrid and a noted orator who served as chamberlain to Henry III of Castile and later to Henry's successor, John II. He built a grand estate in the parish of San Andrés in Madrid and witnessed the king's will in 1406. After Henry's death in December 1406 he built an ornate sepulchre for himself and his descendants in the convent of San Francisco in Madrid and rebuilt its chapel at great cost.

Timur was seeking alliances with European rulers against the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I. Henry III had sent an embassy to him in 1402, and Timur sent his own ambassador to Castile with gifts that included two women captured from Bayezid's harem. Henry's second embassy, led by Clavijo, also included the theologian Friar Alonso Páez de Santa María and the royal guard Gómez de Salazar. It sailed from Cádiz on 22 May 1403, called at the Balearic Islands, Gaeta and Rhodes, and was received at Constantinople by the Byzantine emperor Manuel II. After the winter the party crossed the Black Sea and arrived at Trebizond on 11 April 1404.

Timur had already left for Samarkand, so the ambassadors followed him through Erzincan, Erzurum, Khoy, Tabriz, Tehran, Nishapur, Mashhad, Balkh and Termez, guided and provided for by Timurid officials. They reached the outskirts of Samarkand on 4 September 1404. Clavijo's first audience with Timur took place in a great orchard with a palace, and he described the painted elephants and the tent-pavilions of jewelled silk. He found the city in constant construction, and noted that Timur, after finishing a mosque for the mother of his wife, found fault with its gateway and ordered it pulled down.

The embassy left Samarkand on 21 November, six days before Timur began his campaign against China. In Karabakh it paid respects to Omar Mirza, Timur's grandson, and while there Timur died. The envoys were sent on to Tabriz, where their possessions were impounded for a time. They reached Constantinople on 22 October 1405 and Henry's court on 24 March 1406. Clavijo died on 2 April 1412 and was buried in the convent of San Francisco. His diary was published in Spanish in 1582 as Embajada a Tamorlán and in English in 1859, and gives the most detailed contemporary description of Timur's court by a westerner.
rwandan-patriotic-front: Rwanda was ruled by Germans from 1899 to 1916 and by Belgians from 1916 to 1962, and the colonial rulers chose its leaders and increased divisions among Tutsi, Hutu and Batwa. The ethnic violence of the Rwandan Hutu Revolution of 1959–1962 sent many Tutsi into exile. In December 1979 young Tutsi refugee intellectuals, most of them raised in Uganda, founded the Rwandese Alliance for National Unity in Nairobi to discuss a return home. After Milton Obote's election in 1980 it became militant, and many refugees joined Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army in the Ugandan Bush War.

After Museveni's government took power in 1986, Fred Rwigema became Uganda's deputy minister of defence and Paul Kagame acting chief of military intelligence. In December 1987 the alliance held its seventh congress in Kampala and renamed itself the Rwandan Patriotic Front.

On 1 October 1990 the Rwanda Patriotic Army, the front's military wing under Major-General Rwigema, invaded Rwanda, then governed by Juvénal Habyarimana and his MRND party, and began the Rwandan Civil War. Rwigema died the next day, and Kagame, who had been on military studies in the United States, returned to command. The army turned to guerrilla attacks around Byumba and Ruhengeri and held much of the north by 1992. The Arusha Accords of 1993 allowed RPF personnel and other refugees to return.

On 6 April 1994 Habyarimana's plane was shot down near Kigali, killing him and Cyprien Ntaryamira, president of Burundi; Hutu extremists and the RPF have each been named as the likely perpetrators. The genocide began within hours, and over about 100 days more than 500,000 Tutsi were killed. The RPF fought the government forces and gradually took the country, and the genocide ended when its army captured Kigali on 4 July.

The RPF then formed a government under President Pasteur Bizimungu, with Kagame as vice-president and minister of defence. Kagame became RPF president in February 1998 and national president in March 2000, and was elected in 2003 with 95 per cent of the vote, then re-elected in 2010, 2017 and July 2024.
rwandan-revolution: Rwanda had been ruled by a Tutsi monarchy since at least the 18th century. King Kigeli Rwabugiri, who reigned between 1853 and 1895, introduced ubuhake, under which Tutsi patrons gave cattle to clients in exchange for service, and uburetwa, forced labour for Tutsi chiefs, reforms that opened a rift between Hutu and Tutsi. German and then Belgian rule worked through the kings and supported Tutsi chiefs.

After 1945 a cash economy, a younger and more often Flemish clergy and seminary education allowed a Hutu counter-elite to form; its best-known figure was Grégoire Kayibanda, editor of Kinyamateka and founder of the Mouvement Social Muhutu. Relations worsened from 1956, when sub-chief elections returned 66% Hutu while higher posts stayed overwhelmingly Tutsi. King Rudahigwa died in July 1959, and his brother Kigeli V Ndahindurwa was installed against Belgian wishes.

On 1 November 1959 nine members of the youth wing of UNAR, the Tutsi party, attacked Dominique Mbonyumutwa, a Hutu sub-chief and PARMEHUTU activist, at Byimana. He survived, but rumours spread that he had been killed, and on 3 November Hutu vigilantes in Ndiza killed two Tutsi officials. Riots and arson against Tutsi homes spread across the country. Colonel Guy Logiest, a friend of the governor Jean-Paul Harroy, arrived on 4 November, restored order and appointed interim leaders chiefly from PARMEHUTU.

Communal elections in mid-1960 gave Hutu parties nearly all communes. After a National Reconciliation Conference in Belgium failed in January 1961, Logiest and Kayibanda convened local leaders, who proclaimed a sovereign democratic Republic of Rwanda with Mbonyumutwa as interim president. A United Nations report said an oppressive system had been replaced by another. PARMEHUTU won the legislature in September 1961, Kayibanda became president, and Rwanda became independent on 1 July 1962.

By late 1964 an official total of 336,000 Tutsi had settled as refugees, chiefly in Burundi, Uganda, Tanganyika and Congo-Léopoldville. Some formed armed groups, called inyenzi, or cockroaches, by the government; after a surprise attack approached Kigali in late 1963, the government defeated the rebels and killed thousands of the Tutsi still in Rwanda. PARMEHUTU ruled unchecked until Juvénal Habyarimana's coup of 1973. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed largely of Tutsi refugees, invaded, and the civil war that followed led to the genocide of 1994.
rwenzori-mountains: The Rwenzori, also written Ruwenzori and known as the Rwenzururu or Rwenjura, are a range in eastern equatorial Africa, about 120 kilometres long and 65 kilometres wide. They consist of six massifs separated by deep gorges: Mount Stanley, Mount Speke, Mount Baker, Mount Emin, Mount Gessi and Mount Luigi di Savoia. The upper regions are permanently snow-capped and glaciated, and rivers fed by mountain streams form one of the sources of the Nile.

The mountains formed about three million years ago, in the late Pliocene, as an uplifted block of crystalline rocks including gneiss, amphibolite, granite and quartzite, and are the highest non-volcanic, non-orogenic mountains in the world. The uplift divided the paleolake Obweruka and created three of the present African Great Lakes: Lake Albert, Lake Edward and Lake George.

The range is occasionally identified with the Mountains of the Moon, described in antiquity as the source of the Nile, and European explorers linked the two for that reason. Samuel Baker reported what he called the Blue Mountains in the distance in 1864, and Henry M. Stanley visited the range in 1875 and 1888, when he recorded the name as Ruwenzori.

In 1906 the Duke of Abruzzi led an expedition whose account was published by Filippo De Filippi. It climbed the highest peaks, several of which the duke named, and Mount Luigi di Savoia was named in his honour. The photographer Vittorio Sella, who accompanied it, recorded glaciers and moraines that already showed the ice in retreat. The first traverse of all six massifs was made between 27 January and 13 February 1975 by the Polish climbers Janusz Chalecki, Stanisław Cholewa and Leszek S. Czarnecki, with Mirosław Kuraś joining the last half. After Uganda's independence the secessionist Rwenzururu movement fought an insurgency in the mountains in the 1960s.

The vegetation runs through five overlapping zones, from evergreen forest up to 2,800 metres through bamboo, heather and alpine zones to the nival zone at 4,400 to 5,000 metres. Giant groundsels and giant lobelias and a heather 6 metres tall grow there, and the vegetation is unique to equatorial alpine Africa. Most of the range is a World Heritage Site, covered by Rwenzori Mountains National Park in southwestern Uganda and Virunga National Park in eastern Congo. In 1906 forty-three named glaciers covered 7.5 square kilometres on six mountains, about half the glacier area of Africa; by 2005 less than half remained, on three mountains, covering about 1.5 square kilometres.
ryazan: Ryazan stands on the Oka River in Central Russia, 196 km south-east of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Ryazan Oblast. An older city, now called Old Ryazan, lay about 50 km east of the modern one and was the capital of the Principality of Ryazan until the Mongol invasion of 1237. The modern city was known as Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky until 1778, when it was renamed Ryazan by order of Catherine the Great.

The first written mention of the city, under the name Pereslavl, dates to 1095. It became part of the Principality of Ryazan, which had existed since 1129 and was centred on the old city. Lying between woodland and steppe, the principality suffered invasions from the Cumans in the south, and Vladimir-Suzdal had burnt its capital several times by the end of the twelfth century.

Ryazan was the first Russian city to face the Mongol army of Batu Khan. On 21 December 1237, after a short siege, it was completely destroyed and never recovered, and the seat of the principality moved to Pereslavl-Ryazansky, which took its name. In 1380 Grand Prince Oleg of Ryazan and his men were caught between Mamai's coalition and Dmitry Donskoy's army at the Battle of Kulikovo.

The principality was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1521. Its last ruler, Ivan V of Ryazan, was suspected of seeking a treaty with the Crimean Khanate and fled to Lithuania, where he died no later than 1534. As the southernmost border of the Rus' lands, Ryazan kept suffering raids by the Crimean Tatars. A railway connected it to Moscow from 1864, and after World War II it grew rapidly into an industrial, scientific and military centre.

Ryazan is the seat of the Diocese of Ryazan and Kasimov of the Russian Orthodox Church, with the Assumption Cathedral in the Ryazan Kremlin, which is a historic museum. The Pozhalostin Museum, one of the oldest art museums in Russia, and the memorial museum-estate of the physiologist Ivan Pavlov are also in the city.
rye: Rye (Secale cereale) belongs to the wheat tribe, Triticeae, which also includes wheat and barley, and is one of several cereals that grow wild in the Levant and central and eastern Turkey. Evidence from the Epipalaeolithic site of Tell Abu Hureyra in northern Syria suggests that rye was among the first cereal crops to be systematically cultivated, around 13,000 years ago, but critics point to inconsistencies in the radiocarbon dates. Domesticated rye occurs in small quantities at a number of Neolithic sites in Anatolia but is otherwise absent from the archaeological record until the Bronze Age of central Europe, around 1800-1500 BCE.

It probably reached Europe as a minor admixture in wheat and was only later cultivated in its own right. Remains have been found in Roman contexts along the Rhine and the Danube and in Britain and Ireland. Pliny the Elder, writing of a grain that may have been rye, called it a very poor food that only served to avert starvation.

Rye is a tall grass, annual or biennial, reaching 1 to 3 metres, with seeds carried in a curved spike. It is much more tolerant of cold and poor soil than other cereals, grows better than any other in heavy clay and light sandy soil, and survives snow cover that would kill winter wheat. It has therefore been especially valuable where the soil is sandy or peaty. Winter rye, sown in autumn, grows again in spring early enough to provide grazing.

Rye is highly susceptible to the ergot fungus. Eating infected rye causes ergotism, with convulsions, miscarriage, necrosis of the digits, hallucinations and death, and damp northern countries that depended on rye were historically subject to periodic epidemics. Modern grain cleaning has practically eliminated it.

Since the Middle Ages rye has been widely cultivated in Central and Eastern Europe, where it is the main bread cereal in most areas east of the France-Germany border and north of Hungary; in Southern Europe it was grown on marginal lands. In Scandinavia it was a staple food in the Middle Ages, and rye crispbread remains popular there. Rye bread, including pumpernickel, is widely eaten in Northern and Eastern Europe. The grain also makes rye beer and rye whiskey, and the drink kvass is fermented from rye bread or flour and malt.

Rye straw is used as livestock bedding, and in Sweden rye flour is boiled with red iron oxide to make the traditional Falun red house paint. In European folklore the Roggenwolf, or rye wolf, is a wolf-shaped field spirit that steals children, and the last heads of grain were often left as a sacrifice to such spirits. The classical scholar Carl A. P. Ruck links these figures with ergot, whose reddish infected grains were known as wolf teeth.
ryotwari: Ryotwari was one of the three main systems by which British India collected revenue from the cultivators of agricultural land, the revenue and rents being taken together. Where the demand fell on the ryots themselves the assessment was called ryotwari; where it was made through agreements with zamindars it was called zamindari. In the Bombay and Madras presidencies, Assam Province and British Burma the zamindar usually had no place as a middleman between the government and the farmer. The system kept many features of the revenue system of the Mughals.

In John Stuart Mill's account, a ryot could each year enlarge or reduce his holding or give it up entirely, and remissions were granted when crops were wholly or partly lost in bad seasons. The money assessment did not change from year to year, though an extra rent was charged for water drawn from a government source of irrigation, and nothing was added for improvements made at the ryot's own expense. The annual settlements only fixed how much of the assessment a ryot would pay after changing his cultivation; they did not reassess the land, and a ryot whose holding was unchanged received no fresh patta or lease.

Payment in cash rather than in kind was introduced in the late 18th century, when the East India Company sought a monopoly as buyer of Indian goods. In Bengal and northern India, by contrast, zamindars bid for the right to collect, the highest bidder became owner of the land, and the cultivators became tenants who paid him in cash. In northern India Edward Colebrooke and successive Governors-General urged the Company's Court of Directors, in vain, to settle the land tax permanently.

Critics have held that the demand, even at a third of the produce, was excessive, and that a ryot who could not pay could lose his land to the government, which made him a lessee of the administration rather than an owner. Cash payment, in this view, forced sales of land, turned it into a commodity and led to fragmentation of holdings, while revenue pressure pushed more land into cultivation and taxation. The system was in operation for nearly 50 years.
ryukyu-islands: The chain is also called the Nansei Islands, literally the southwest islands, and Japan has used that name on nautical charts since 1907. Administratively it divides between Kagoshima Prefecture, whose Satsunan Islands include the Ōsumi, Tokara and Amami groups, and Okinawa Prefecture, which holds the Okinawa, Miyako, Yaeyama and Daitō Islands. The larger islands are mostly volcanic and the smaller mostly coral. The climate runs from humid subtropical in the north to tropical rainforest in the south. The Watase Line marks a major biogeographic boundary, with the Ōsumi Islands in the Palearctic realm and the Amami Islands at the northern limit of the Indomalayan realm.

Chinese sources mention eastern islands of immortals, and in 601 and 607 Chinese expeditions visited the Country of Liuqiu. Japanese records list the Southern Islands from 616, and in 997 pirates identified as Amami islanders raided Kyushu. Tanegashima passed into the Shimazu Estate in the 12th century, and around 1543 a Chinese junk carrying Portuguese merchants was driven there; Tanegashima Tokitaka reproduced their matchlock rifles, which spread across Sengoku Japan as tanegashima.

Polities of the Okinawa Islands were unified as the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1429, a tributary state of Ming China, which conquered the Miyako and Yaeyama Islands and at its peak ruled Amami. The Amami Islands were disputed between the kingdom and the southward-expanding Satsuma Domain until Satsuma conquered them in the 1609 invasion of the kingdom, with a fleet of 13 junks and 2,500 samurai. King Shō Nei ordered surrender to spare lives. The kingdom then paid tribute to both the shogun and the Chinese emperor, and the Tokugawa shogunate granted Satsuma the Amami islands in 1624. The Meiji government annexed the kingdom in 1879 and suppressed Ryukyuan identity, tradition and language.

The Amami, Okinawa, Miyako and Yaeyama Islands have a native population called the Ryukyuan people, who traditionally speak several Ryukyuan languages, though Japanese is now the primary language. Their religion centres on ancestor respect and the relations among the living, the dead and the spirits of nature. The islands were held by the United States after the Treaty of San Francisco of 1951 and returned to Japan under the 1971 Okinawa reversion agreement. Yakushima, with its ancient cedars, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
ryukyuans: The Ryukyu Islands were inhabited from at least 32,000 to 18,000 years ago, though how those inhabitants relate to present Ryukyuans is uncertain. During the Jōmon period the northern islands had a hunter-gatherer society, and from its latter half the islands developed their own culture. Yayoi and Kofun culture did not spread into the Ryukyus, and rice was not widely grown before the 12th century CE. Genetic studies describe the Ryukyuans as a distinct cluster within the Japanese people, with about 28 per cent Jōmon ancestry in one estimate. Linguists such as Thomas Pellard classify the Ryukyuan languages as a subfamily of Japonic that diverged before the 8th century CE.

Between 1416 and 1429 the Chūzan chieftain Shō Hashi united the three polities of Okinawa into the Ryukyu Kingdom, with its capital at Shuri. It prospered through maritime trade, above all tributary relations with Ming China begun in 1372. Under Shō Shin, from 1477 to 1526, overseas trade peaked and the kingdom extended its control over Miyako-jima and the Yaeyama Islands.

In 1609 the Satsuma Domain invaded, and the kingdom kept a fictive independence under dual subordination to China and Japan. In 1879 Japan abolished the Ryukyu Domain it had created and formed Okinawa Prefecture, and the last king, Shō Tai, was exiled to Tokyo. The government sought to assimilate the Ryukyuans, suppressing their culture and language, and in 1899 banned the indigo hand tattoos called hajichi. In the Battle of Okinawa in 1945 about 150,000 civilians, a third of the population, were killed, and the United States occupied the islands until 15 May 1972.

Japan's authorities treat Ryukyuans as a subgroup of the Japanese people, and Japan has not accepted a 2008 recommendation of the United Nations Human Rights Committee to recognise them as an indigenous people. Several Okinawan municipal assemblies have rejected that label. More than 1.4 million Ryukyuans live in Okinawa Prefecture alone. Indigenous Ryukyuan religion gives women a strong role as shamans and guardians of the home, and village priestesses called noro kept the communal hearth fire until the 20th century. Karate grew from local fighting techniques, probably combined with methods from China.
